definitions.definition: A person is 'abducted' when they have been subjected to abduction as understood under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, whereby any person is compelled by force or induced by deceitful means to go from any place. Section 142 uses 'abducted' to describe the condition of a person who has already been subjected to such an act, forming the basis of liability for any person who knowingly conceals or confines such a person.
definitions.plain_english: An 'abducted' person is someone who has been forcibly taken away or lured away through deception from where they were. Section 142 deals with what happens when someone else hides or locks up this already-abducted person. If you knowingly shelter or confine someone who has been abducted, the law treats you as if you yourself had carried out the abduction.
real_world_examples: A woman is abducted from her village in Uttar Pradesh by a group of men; a local shopkeeper, knowing she is being held against her will, allows the group to confine her in his storage room — he is treated as an abductor under Section 142.

A child is abducted in Chennai and hidden in a relative's house; the relative, aware that the child was taken without lawful authority, continues to keep the child confined and is liable under Section 142 as though they had abducted the child.

A businessman in Mumbai is abducted for ransom; an acquaintance who did not participate in the kidnapping but knowingly provides a locked flat where the victim is held is punishable under Section 142 with the same punishment as the actual abductors.

A young girl is abducted from a school in Delhi by traffickers; a person who learns of her condition and willingly conceals her whereabouts from police while she remains confined is deemed to have abducted her under this section.

In a family dispute in Rajasthan, a woman is abducted by her estranged husband's family; a neighbour who is fully aware of the situation actively prevents her escape by locking the gate — that neighbour is liable under Section 142 as if they had committed the abduction.
what_it_covers: A person who has been compelled by force to move from any place and is subsequently hidden or confined by a third party who knows of their abducted status.
A person induced by deceitful means to leave a place and is thereafter concealed by someone aware of the abduction.
A victim of abduction who is kept in confinement by an associate or facilitator of the original abductors, even if that person did not participate in the initial act.
Any individual, regardless of age or gender, who has been abducted and is being wrongfully confined with the knowledge of the confiner.
what_it_excludes: A person who has voluntarily left a place and consented to accompanying someone — consent negates the 'abducted' status.
A person confined for a lawful purpose under legal authority, such as lawful custody by police or a court order, even if the person was initially wrongfully taken.
Someone who unknowingly shelters or houses an abducted person without any knowledge that the person has been abducted — lack of knowledge removes liability under Section 142.
A person removed under a lawful guardian's authority where no force or deception was involved and the removal is legally sanctioned.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as 'abducted' under Section 142 determines whether anyone who subsequently conceals or confines that person bears full criminal liability equivalent to the original abductor, including the same intention or purpose attributed to the confiner. This definition triggers liability for third parties who may not have committed the initial act but who knowingly participate in continuing the unlawful deprivation of liberty.

definitions.definition: Abducting, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the act of abducting a person as defined under the companion term 'abduction', i.e., compelling by force or inducing by deceit any person to go from any place. It denotes the active, ongoing conduct of carrying away or causing a person to be moved through coercion, intimidation, or deception against their will.
definitions.plain_english: Abducting means forcibly taking away or tricking a person into moving from one place to another against their will. It involves using either physical force or deception to make someone go somewhere they would not go voluntarily. Unlike kidnapping, abducting focuses on the means used — force or fraud — rather than the age or guardianship of the victim.
real_world_examples: A gang in Uttar Pradesh physically drags a businessman into a van at gunpoint and drives him to a farmhouse to demand ransom from his family — this constitutes abducting under the BNS.

A woman in Mumbai is lured by false promises of a job interview and then transported to another city where she is held against her will for forced marriage — the deception used to move her amounts to abducting.

In a case of child trafficking in West Bengal, a trafficker convinces a minor's parents under false pretences and then moves the child across state borders for exploitation — the act of moving the child through deceit is abducting.

A political rival in Bihar is forcibly bundled into a vehicle by hired goons during election season and taken to a remote location to prevent him from filing his nomination — this forcible removal constitutes abducting.

A woman in Delhi is grabbed off the street by two men with the intent to sexually assault her and is transported by force to an isolated location — the physical coercion used to move her is abducting under Section 38 of the BNS.

A domestic worker in Chennai is locked in a car and driven to another district by her employer to prevent her from reporting abuse to authorities — the compelled movement against her will constitutes abducting.
semantic_tags: wrongful movement by force or fraud
what_it_covers: Physically forcing a person by violence or threat of violence to leave a place against their will.
Inducing a person through deception, false pretences, or fraudulent means to move from one location to another.
Using criminal intimidation or abuse of authority to compel a person to accompany the offender to another place.
Carrying away a person for the purpose of committing a further offence such as murder, ransom, rape, or wrongful confinement.
The act of transporting a child under ten years of age by force or deceit with intent to steal from the child.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary movement of a person who consents freely and without any deception or coercion — consent negates abducting.
Lawful custody or detention of a person by a police officer or public servant acting under legal authority — such movement is justified by law.
Kidnapping from lawful guardianship of a minor, which is a distinct and separate offence governed by its own provisions and does not require proof of force or fraud.
Mere surveillance or stalking of a person without any physical compulsion or deceptive inducement to move.
Restraining a person in the same place without moving them, which may constitute wrongful confinement but not abducting.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'abducting' directly determines whether the right of private defence under Section 38 extends to causing death of the assailant, and triggers serious penal consequences under Sections 87, 97, and 140 of the BNS including imprisonment for life or even the death penalty where ransom or murder is involved. Establishing 'abducting' as the operative act is essential to framing charges and determining the quantum of punishment for aggravated offences involving kidnapping or compelled movement.

definitions.definition: Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person.
definitions.plain_english: Abduction means making someone leave a place either by using physical force or by tricking them with lies or deception. Unlike kidnapping, abduction can be done against a person of any age and focuses on the act of moving someone from one place to another. The key elements are that the movement must result from either force or deceit, not the person's free and informed will.
real_world_examples: A gang in Mumbai forcibly drags a businessman into a van and drives him to an undisclosed location to demand ransom from his family — the act of forcibly compelling him to leave his office constitutes abduction.

A man in Delhi falsely tells a woman that her husband has been in a serious accident and is in a hospital across town; relying on this lie, she accompanies him, only to be confined at a different location — the deceitful inducement to leave her home constitutes abduction.

In a child custody dispute in Chennai, a non-custodial parent tells the child they are going for an ice cream treat but instead takes the child to another state intending to permanently keep them — the deceitful inducement to go from the lawful guardian's premises amounts to abduction.

A labour contractor in rural Bihar promises village workers high-paying jobs in a city, obtains their consent through false representations about wages and conditions, and transports them to a brick kiln where they are forced to work — the deceitful inducement to leave their village constitutes abduction, which may further constitute trafficking.

A group of men in Hyderabad surrounds a rival and physically forces him into a car at gunpoint to take him to an isolated farmhouse — the use of force to compel him to go from the street constitutes abduction.

A woman in Kolkata is told by an acquaintance that her parents urgently need her at a different address; upon arriving, she realises she has been lured under false pretences for the purpose of sexual exploitation — the deceitful inducement to leave her residence constitutes abduction.
what_it_covers: Physically dragging, pushing, or otherwise forcibly compelling a person against their will to move from any location, including their home, workplace, or public place.
Luring a person away from their location through false representations, fraudulent promises, or any other deceitful means such that their apparent consent to move is vitiated by deception.
Compelling a person to move using threats of immediate violence or by applying criminal force short of full physical dragging, provided it overcomes the person's free will.
Inducing a child, an elderly person, or a person of unsound mind to leave a place through deceit, regardless of whether they appear to comply willingly.
Movement procured through a combination of partial force and partial deception, where either element alone or together results in the person departing from their location.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary movement of a person from a place based on their own free, informed, and uncoerced decision — the absence of force or deceit means no abduction occurs.

Kidnapping as defined separately under the BNS, which involves taking a minor under eighteen (for females) or under sixteen (for males) out of lawful guardianship or taking a person of unsound mind — abduction is a distinct offence with different ingredients.
Merely persuading, advising, or requesting a person to go somewhere through honest and truthful communication, even if the person ultimately leaves against others' wishes.
Lawful arrest, detention, or removal of a person by a public servant or police officer acting under lawful authority and due process of law.
A parent or lawful guardian directing their minor child to move from one place to another in the exercise of legitimate parental or guardianship authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes abduction under Section 138 directly determines liability under a chain of aggravated offences — including kidnapping or abducting to murder or for ransom (Section 140), abduction for wrongful confinement, grievous hurt, slavery or unnatural lust, and trafficking of persons (Section 143) — because abduction is a foundational predicate element for all these compound offences. Without establishing abduction, the prosecution cannot make out the more serious offences that carry penalties ranging from seven years imprisonment to death.

definitions.definition: A person 'abducts' another when they, by force, compulsion, deceitful means, or criminal intimidation, cause that person to be taken or carried away from one place to another, or induces any person to go from any place, with the intent to subject that person to harm, forced marriage, illicit intercourse, murder, ransom, or any other unlawful purpose as specified under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: To 'abduct' someone means to forcibly or deceitfully take them away or cause them to move from one place to another against their will or without their free consent. Unlike kidnapping, abduction can apply to a person of any age and focuses on the method used — force, intimidation, or deception. The act becomes a crime when the purpose is unlawful, such as forcing marriage, committing murder, demanding ransom, or engaging in terrorism.
real_world_examples: A group of men in Uttar Pradesh forcibly bundle a woman into a vehicle and take her to a remote location intending to coerce her into marrying someone against her will — this constitutes abduction under Section 87 of the BNS.

Armed criminals in Mumbai kidnap a wealthy businessman's family member, moving them across state lines and threatening to kill them unless a ransom of ₹5 crore is paid — this constitutes abduction under Section 140 of the BNS.

Militants in a conflict-affected region of Manipur detain a government official and forcibly move him from his home to an undisclosed location, threatening to kill him unless the Government of India meets their demands — this constitutes abduction under Section 113 (terrorist act).

A man in Delhi, using false pretences that a woman's relative is critically ill in a hospital, induces her to leave her residence and then takes her to a location where she is subjected to illegal confinement with intent to force illicit intercourse — this constitutes abduction under Section 87 of the BNS.

A gang in Rajasthan forces a local trader into their vehicle at gunpoint and transports him to an isolated farmhouse intending to eliminate him to prevent him from testifying in a criminal case — this constitutes abduction with intent to murder under Section 140 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Forcibly taking a woman from her residence to compel her into marriage against her will under Section 87 BNS.
Inducing a person to move from a place through criminal intimidation, abuse of authority, or deceitful means for an unlawful purpose.
Detaining and transporting any person by terrorist actors to coerce the Government of India or a foreign government into acting or refraining from acting, under Section 113 BNS.
Kidnapping or abducting any person with intent to murder them or hold them for ransom under Section 140 BNS.
Using deceptive means to cause a woman to leave a place knowing she is likely to be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse.
what_it_excludes: Consensual movement or travel undertaken freely by the person, even if later regretted, where no force, deceit, or compulsion was employed.
Lawful custody or detention of a person by a police officer, court, or other authority acting under due process of law.
Kidnapping from lawful guardianship of a minor, which is governed separately and does not require proof of force or deceit to constitute the offence.
Mere restraint or wrongful confinement of a person in a single location without any movement or transportation from one place to another.
Actions by a parent or lawful guardian acting within the scope of their legal authority over a child, where no criminal intent is present.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'abduction' under the BNS determines liability for serious offences under Sections 87, 140, and 113, carrying punishments ranging from seven years to life imprisonment or death, depending on the intent and outcome. Establishing abduction is a prerequisite element that triggers these aggravated offences and distinguishes mere wrongful restraint or confinement from the more serious crime of abduction with a specified unlawful purpose.

definitions.definition: A person abets the doing of a thing who instigates any person to do that thing; or engages with one or more other persons in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing, if an act or illegal omission takes place in pursuance of that conspiracy and in order to the doing of that thing; or intentionally aids, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing. Abetment also includes wilful misrepresentation or wilful concealment of a material fact which a person is bound to disclose, voluntarily causing or procuring a thing to be done, as well as any act done prior to or at the time of commission of an act to facilitate its commission.
definitions.plain_english: Abetment means helping, encouraging, or assisting someone else to commit a crime or illegal act. It covers three main ways: pushing or convincing someone to do something wrong (instigation), secretly planning with others to do something illegal (conspiracy), and actively helping someone carry out an illegal act (aiding). Importantly, the crime does not need to actually be completed — the act of helping or encouraging is itself an offence.
real_world_examples: A moneylender in a village repeatedly harasses a farmer about unpaid debt and explicitly tells the farmer's family that the farmer should 'just end it all', after which the farmer dies by suicide — the moneylender may be liable for abetment of suicide under Section 108.
A corrupt police officer in Delhi tips off a criminal gang about an upcoming raid, allowing them to escape — the officer abets the gang's evasion of lawful apprehension through intentional aid.

A pharmacist in Mumbai knowingly provides a specific poison to a customer after being told by the customer that he intends to poison a business rival — the pharmacist abets the attempted murder through intentional aid.

A group of persons in Chennai conspire together to commit robbery, agree on the plan, and one of them acts as a lookout during the execution — all members are guilty of abetment even if only one physically committed the robbery.

A senior corporate executive in Bengaluru instructs a subordinate employee to forge invoices to defraud investors, with the executive not personally forging any document — the executive is guilty of abetment of forgery by instigation.

A social media influencer in Hyderabad knowingly shares false incendiary content calling for violence against a particular community, inciting followers who subsequently commit rioting — the influencer may be liable for abetment of rioting.
what_it_covers: Instigating another person to commit an offence, including through wilful misrepresentation or concealment of a material fact the person was bound to disclose.
Joining a criminal conspiracy where any act or illegal omission is carried out in furtherance of that conspiracy, even if the abettor did not personally commit the final criminal act.
Intentionally aiding the commission of an offence by any act or illegal omission, whether done prior to or at the time of the commission of the offence.
Abetting an abettor — since the abetment of an offence is itself an offence, assisting or instigating the abettor is also covered.
Cases where the person being abetted lacks the legal capacity to commit an offence or lacks the same guilty intention or knowledge as the abettor.
Illegal omissions that facilitate an offence, such as a watchman deliberately neglecting his duty to allow trespassers entry.
what_it_excludes: Mere knowledge or passive awareness that an offence is being committed, without any active instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid.
Acts done in good faith for the benefit of a child or person of unsound mind by a guardian, where such acts do not independently attract the exceptions listed under Sections 27 and 30 of the Act.
Unintentional or accidental assistance that facilitates a crime without any deliberate intent to aid the commission of the offence.
Cases where a person is deceived or coerced into facilitating an offence and acts without any guilty intention or knowledge.

definitions.definition: A person abets an offence who abets either the commission of an offence, or the commission of an act which would be an offence, if committed by a person capable by law of committing an offence with the same intention or knowledge as that of the abettor. The abetment of the illegal omission of an act may amount to an offence although the abettor may not himself be bound to do that act.
definitions.plain_english: An abettor is a person who helps, encourages, instigates, or conspires with another to commit a crime, even if the actual crime never takes place or is carried out by someone who cannot legally be held responsible. The abettor shares the same intention or knowledge as the person committing the act. Importantly, even if the main offender does not have criminal intent or capacity, the abettor can still be held fully guilty.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai businessman bribes a local politician by promising land deals, encouraging him to award contracts fraudulently; though the politician accepts, the businessman qualifies as an abettor for instigating the corrupt act.

A Delhi woman instigates her domestic worker, who is of unsound mind, to poison a rival's food; the worker is incapable of criminal responsibility, but the woman is guilty as an abettor and liable for the resulting offence.
In Chennai, a gang leader who never physically participates in a bank robbery but plans the entire operation and assigns roles to each participant is an abettor by conspiracy under Section 46.

A Kolkata resident knowingly provides a fake identity card to a person who then uses it to fraudulently open a bank account; the resident is an abettor even though the account holder alone performs the final act.

In a domestic violence case in Hyderabad, a mother-in-law repeatedly instigates her son to torture his wife for dowry; even if the son does not carry out the act every time, the mother-in-law is an abettor by instigation.

A Pune software engineer provides technical tools and access credentials to a hacker knowing they will be used to breach a company's systems; even if the engineer is not present during the actual breach, they qualify as an abettor.
what_it_covers: A person who instigates another to commit an offence, even if the offence is never actually carried out.
A person who conspires with others for the commission of an offence, regardless of whether they personally concert with the final perpetrator.
A person who aids or abets someone incapable of committing an offence by law (such as a minor or a person of unsound mind), sharing the requisite criminal intention.
A person who abets an illegal omission by encouraging another to fail to perform a legally required act.
A person who abets the abetment of another, forming a chain of secondary liability.
what_it_excludes: A bystander who is merely present at the scene of a crime but has no intention to assist, encourage, or conspire in its commission.
A person who provides innocent assistance without knowledge of the criminal purpose, such as a courier unknowingly delivering stolen goods.
A person who withdraws from a conspiracy before the offence is committed and takes reasonable steps to prevent it.
A person who commits the offence directly as the principal offender — such a person is the perpetrator, not an abettor.
A person who has no guilty intention or knowledge and whose act is legally justified or authorised.

This definition triggers criminal liability for instigation, conspiracy, and aiding, and without it applying, a person cannot be held secondarily responsible for another's criminal act.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 124, 'acid' includes any substance which has acidic or corrosive character or burning nature, that is capable of causing bodily injury leading to scars or disfigurement or temporary or permanent disability.
definitions.plain_english: Acid, under this law, means any substance that is acidic, corrosive, or capable of burning the body and can leave scars, cause disfigurement, or lead to temporary or permanent disability. It is not limited to what we commonly call 'acid' in chemistry — it covers any substance with similar harmful properties. This broad definition ensures that attackers cannot escape punishment by using a different but equally destructive corrosive substance.
real_world_examples: A person throws sulphuric acid (commonly called 'tezaab') on a woman who rejected his marriage proposal in Uttar Pradesh, causing severe burns and facial disfigurement — this is a direct use of acid under Section 124.

An individual pours concentrated hydrochloric acid on a neighbour's face during a land dispute in rural Maharashtra, resulting in permanent partial blindness — the substance qualifies as acid under this definition.

A perpetrator in Delhi uses a strong alkali solution such as concentrated sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) to burn and disfigure a victim's arm — because it has corrosive character and burning nature causing disfigurement, it falls within the definition of acid under Section 124.

In a domestic violence incident in Tamil Nadu, a husband administers a corrosive industrial cleaning chemical orally to his wife, causing internal burns and permanent disability — the substance is covered under the definition of acid.

A factory worker in Gujarat intentionally splashes a highly acidic industrial solvent capable of causing scarring onto a coworker during an altercation — despite being an industrial chemical and not commonly labelled 'acid', it qualifies under the broad statutory definition.

A person in Rajasthan attempts to throw battery acid (dilute sulphuric acid from a vehicle battery) at a woman, intending to disfigure her face — battery acid falls squarely within the definition as it has acidic and burning nature capable of causing scars.
what_it_covers: Commonly known strong acids such as sulphuric acid (tezaab), hydrochloric acid, and nitric acid that cause burns and scarring.
Strong alkalis and bases with corrosive character, such as concentrated sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide, capable of causing burns and disfigurement.

Industrial and household corrosive chemicals — including concentrated cleaning agents, drain cleaners, or battery acid — that have a burning nature capable of causing bodily injury, scars, or disability.

Any substance, regardless of its commercial label or intended use, that is acidic or corrosive in nature and capable of causing temporary or permanent disability or disfigurement when applied to the human body.
what_it_excludes: Mildly acidic household substances such as lemon juice, vinegar, or dilute fruit acids that are incapable of causing bodily injury, scars, disfigurement, or disability.

Hot liquids such as boiling water or hot oil that cause burns through heat rather than through acidic, corrosive, or chemical burning properties — these may be covered under other provisions but do not fall within this specific definition.

Non-corrosive and non-acidic substances that may cause harm through other mechanisms (e.g., blunt trauma, poison ingestion) but do not possess acidic character, corrosive nature, or burning properties.
Substances used in lawful medical or surgical procedures administered by registered medical practitioners with proper consent, where the intent is therapeutic rather than harmful.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'acid' under Section 124 determines whether the offence attracts the severe mandatory minimum sentence of ten years (extendable to life imprisonment) for causing grievous hurt, or five to seven years for an attempt, along with mandatory fine payable to the victim for medical expenses. A substance falling outside this definition would prevent prosecution under Section 124 and the victim would lose access to the specific compensatory fine remedy provided therein.

definitions.definition: "act" denotes as well a series of acts as a single act.
definitions.plain_english: The word 'act' in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita does not just mean one isolated action — it also covers a chain or sequence of related actions treated together as one. So if someone does several things that together make up a crime, all those steps collectively count as 'the act'. This broad meaning ensures that criminals cannot escape liability by breaking their conduct into many small steps.
real_world_examples: A fraudster in Mumbai sends multiple fake emails over several weeks to deceive a victim into transferring money — each email is a separate step, but together they form a single 'act' of cheating under the Sanhita.

A person in Delhi systematically administers small doses of poison to a family member over several days, causing death — the repeated administrations across multiple days collectively constitute a single 'act' of culpable homicide.

A gang in Chennai carries out a series of coordinated robberies across three nights as part of one criminal plan — the series of robberies is treated as a single 'act' for purposes of organised crime liability.

A stalker in Bengaluru repeatedly follows, messages, and physically approaches a woman over several weeks — each instance individually and the series as a whole constitute the prohibited 'act' of stalking under the Sanhita.

A public servant in Kolkata accepts bribes through multiple instalments spread over months in exchange for a single official favour — the entire sequence of receipts is treated as one 'act' of bribery.
what_it_covers: A single, one-time physical action such as striking a person once constituting hurt.
A series of related actions forming a continuous course of conduct, such as multiple acts of cheating spread over time directed at the same victim.
Collective steps undertaken as part of a single criminal plan, where each step advances the same unlawful purpose, treated together as one act.
Repeated administrations of a harmful substance over a period that together cause injury or death.
Multiple communications or electronic transmissions that together constitute a single offence such as criminal intimidation or stalking.
what_it_excludes: Pure omissions — the definition of 'act' does not extend to failures to act, which are separately covered by the term 'omission' under the Sanhita.
Entirely unrelated independent actions that share no common intention or plan, which cannot be aggregated into a single 'act' merely because the same person committed them.
Mental states or intentions alone, such as merely planning or thinking about a crime without any external physical action or series of actions.
Involuntary bodily movements or reflexes not directed by the will of the person, which do not constitute an 'act' for purposes of criminal liability.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether multiple steps amount to a single 'act' determines whether the accused can be charged with one consolidated offence or whether liability is established even when the criminality is spread across many steps; it directly affects the applicability of offences such as cheating, culpable homicide, criminal conspiracy, stalking, and organised crime under the Sanhita, and prevents an accused from fragmenting criminal conduct to avoid prosecution.

definitions.definition: An 'admission' under Section 242 refers to any statement, acknowledgment, or concession made by a person who has falsely assumed the identity of another individual within the context of a suit or criminal prosecution, whereby such person makes a declaration or acknowledgment of facts that may affect the rights or liabilities of the person being impersonated.
definitions.plain_english: An admission, in this context, is when someone pretending to be another person makes a statement or acknowledges something as true during a legal case or court proceeding. This could be saying something that admits guilt, accepts a claim, or concedes a legal point on behalf of the person being impersonated. The danger is that such a false admission can seriously harm the rights and legal standing of the real person whose identity was stolen.
real_world_examples: A fraudster impersonates a defendant in a civil property dispute before a civil court in Mumbai and makes an admission that the defendant owes a debt to the plaintiff, thereby prejudicing the real defendant's case.

A person falsely claims to be an accused in a criminal trial in Delhi and admits guilt on behalf of that accused, causing a wrongful conviction of the real person to proceed on the basis of that false confession.
An individual impersonates a party in a cheque-bouncing case before a Magistrate in Chennai and admits to the dishonour of the cheque, leading to a decree against the real account holder.

A hired impersonator poses as a borrower in a debt recovery tribunal proceeding in Kolkata and makes an admission that the full loan amount is outstanding, waiving legitimate defences available to the real borrower.

Someone pretending to be a complainant in a domestic violence proceeding before a family court in Hyderabad makes admissions withdrawing certain claims, thereby undermining the genuine complainant's legal position.

definitions.definition: A drug or medical preparation is 'adulterated' when it has been tampered with or debased in such a manner as to lessen its efficacy, change its operation, or render it noxious, such that it no longer conforms to its represented composition, strength, or purity.
definitions.plain_english: A drug or medicine is 'adulterated' when something has been done to it — like mixing in inferior or harmful ingredients, reducing its active components, or substituting its contents — that makes it weaker, changes how it works in the body, or makes it dangerous. This applies to medicines sold in pharmacies, dispensed at clinics, or distributed for any medical treatment. The key idea is that the drug no longer is what it claims or is supposed to be.
real_world_examples: A chemist in Patna mixes chalk powder with paracetamol tablets to increase quantity and sells the diluted tablets to unsuspecting customers, reducing the medicine's effectiveness against fever.

A dispensary in Mumbai issues antibiotic capsules where the active ingredient has been partially replaced with starch, causing patients to receive insufficient doses and potentially develop antibiotic resistance.
A drug manufacturer in Hyderabad adds a harmful chemical solvent to a cough syrup formulation that alters how the medicine acts in the body and causes adverse reactions in children consuming it.
A pharmacist in Delhi knowingly sells expired insulin that has degraded and lost its potency, dispensing it as fully effective insulin to a diabetic patient who relies on it for daily treatment.

A fake ayurvedic medicine shop in Kolkata sells herbal tonics adulterated with undisclosed synthetic compounds that change the preparation's pharmacological action and cause unintended side effects in patients.
what_it_covers: A drug whose active ingredient has been diluted or partially replaced with an inert or inferior substance, thereby lessening its therapeutic efficacy.
A medical preparation that has been mixed with a harmful or toxic substance that changes how it acts in the human body or renders it dangerous to health.
A medicine where the original composition has been altered through substitution, contamination, or degradation such that its pharmacological operation is fundamentally changed.
An expired or improperly stored drug that has chemically degraded to the point where it no longer functions as intended and may cause harm.
A preparation issued from a dispensary that contains undisclosed foreign substances making it noxious, even if it superficially resembles the genuine medicine.
what_it_excludes: A drug that fails quality standards due to innocent manufacturing error without any knowing tampering or deliberate adulteration by the seller.
Naturally degraded medicines where the seller is unaware of the degradation and sells them in good faith believing them to be unadulterated.
Food or drink items that may be adulterated, as Section 277 specifically applies only to drugs and medical preparations and not to general food products.
A drug that is mislabelled or incorrectly packaged but whose actual chemical composition and efficacy remain unchanged and unaltered.
Counterfeit drugs where the seller genuinely does not know of the adulteration, as Section 277 requires knowledge of adulteration as an essential element of the offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'adulterated' under Section 277 determines whether the seller, dispenser, or issuer of the drug is criminally liable for imprisonment up to six months and/or a fine up to five thousand rupees; if the substance does not meet the threshold of lessened efficacy, changed operation, or noxiousness, no offence under this section is made out. The definition also requires knowledge of adulteration as a precondition, meaning the legal consequence turns both on the physical state of the drug and the mental state of the person selling or issuing it.

definitions.definition: "Affirmation" is included within the meaning of "oath" in this Sanhita, as oath includes a solemn affirmation substituted by law for an oath, and any declaration required or authorised by law to be made before a public servant or to be used for the purpose of proof, whether in a Court or not.
definitions.plain_english: An affirmation is a solemn, formal promise to tell the truth that a person makes instead of taking a religious oath, typically when the person has no religious belief or objects to swearing on a religious text. It carries the same legal weight as an oath. If a person makes a false statement after taking an affirmation, they can be held legally accountable just as if they had sworn an oath.
real_world_examples: A witness in a Delhi Sessions Court who declares themselves an atheist chooses to make a solemn affirmation instead of swearing on the Bhagavad Gita or Quran before giving testimony; this affirmation is treated as equivalent to an oath under the Sanhita.

A government employee summoned before a Magistrate in Mumbai to provide a statutory declaration under an inquiry affirms solemnly before the Magistrate rather than taking a religious oath, and any false declaration made thereafter can attract liability under Section 213 of the BNS.

A Parsi witness in a Pune civil court, whose community practice does not align with conventional oath-taking on religious scriptures used in court, makes a solemn affirmation before the Judge prior to deposing; false testimony given after this affirmation constitutes an offence under Section 216 of the BNS.

A deponent in an affidavit submitted to the Registrar of Companies in Chennai makes a solemn affirmation instead of an oath before a Notary Public; fabricating facts in that affidavit after such affirmation attracts punishment under the relevant provisions of the BNS.

An accused person in a Kolkata criminal trial who chooses to give a statement on affirmation under the relevant procedural law is bound by the same truthfulness obligations as one who swears an oath, and a false statement exposes them to prosecution under Section 213 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: A solemn affirmation made by a witness in a court of law who conscientiously objects to taking a religious oath, substituted by law for the oath.
A declaration made by a person before a public servant (such as a Magistrate or Notary Public) that is required or authorised by law to be used for the purpose of proof.
An affirmation made outside a court setting — for example, before an administrative authority or in an affidavit — that is authorised by law and intended to serve as evidence of a stated fact.
what_it_excludes: Informal personal promises or assurances made in everyday life that carry no legal authority or statutory backing.
A religious oath taken on a holy text (such as swearing on the Bhagavad Gita or Bible), which is treated as an "oath" in the strict sense rather than an "affirmation" as a substitute.

Statements made voluntarily to police during investigation under Section 161 CrPC/BNSS that are explicitly not on oath or affirmation and therefore do not attract perjury-related liability under Sections 213 or 216 of the BNS.
Contractual declarations or representations made between private parties without any legal requirement or authorisation by a public servant or court.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a statement is made on affirmation (or oath) is a threshold condition for offences under Sections 213 and 216 of the BNS relating to false evidence and giving or fabricating false evidence; only statements made under oath or affirmation can ground a prosecution for perjury-type offences, making the legal validity of the affirmation central to criminal liability. If an affirmation is not properly administered or legally authorised, a false statement made thereunder may not attract punishment under these sections.

definitions.definition: When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray. The offence is punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
definitions.plain_english: An affray happens when two or more people get into a physical fight in a public place and, by doing so, disturb the peace of the surrounding public. It is different from a private fight because the key element is that the fighting must happen in public and must disturb public peace. It is a relatively minor public order offence under Indian criminal law.
real_world_examples: Two men get into a fistfight outside a busy market in Delhi, causing shoppers to panic and flee, thereby disturbing the normal peace of the marketplace.
A group of cricket fans brawl on a public street in Mumbai after a match, shouting and throwing punches in front of pedestrians, alarming passersby and disrupting traffic.
Two neighbours engage in a violent physical altercation on a public road in Chennai, drawing a crowd and causing fear and unrest among residents in the locality.
Rivals from two political groups come to blows near a public bus stand in Lucknow during an election campaign, disturbing the peace of commuters and bystanders waiting at the stand.
Two auto-rickshaw drivers fight physically at a busy chowk in Pune over a fare dispute, causing other drivers and pedestrians to scatter in fear, thus disturbing public tranquillity.
what_it_covers: A fistfight between two individuals on a public road that causes surrounding people to feel threatened or unsafe.
A brawl involving multiple persons in a public market, bus stand, or street that visibly disturbs the peace of onlookers or passersby.
Any physical fighting in a public place — regardless of whether weapons are used — that results in a disturbance to public peace.
Situations where a public servant attempts to suppress the fight and is obstructed or assaulted in the process (triggering additional liability under Section 195).
Disobedience of a public servant's lawful order that causes or tends to cause an affray (as referenced in Section 223).
what_it_excludes: A private fight inside a person's home or on private property that does not disturb public peace, even if violent.
A single person acting alone, since an affray requires two or more persons fighting together.
Mere verbal altercations, threats, or heated arguments in public that do not escalate to actual physical fighting.
Organised sports or martial arts bouts held in public with lawful permission, as these do not constitute unauthorised fighting disturbing public peace.
Riots or unlawful assemblies, which are distinct and more serious offences under the BNS even though they share the element of public disorder.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes an affray determines whether a person is liable to punishment under Section 194 of the BNS and also triggers enhanced penalties under Sections 195 and 223 when a public servant is obstructed while suppressing it or when disobedience of a lawful order causes or tends to cause an affray. It also imposes a legal duty on persons bound by law to assist public servants in suppressing an affray under Section 222, failure of which attracts independent punishment.

definitions.definition: Agricultural produce, as used in Section 326 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any produce or output derived from agricultural activity, including crops, harvested grain, fruits, vegetables, fodder, and other farm outputs that constitute property. The term encompasses both standing crops and harvested produce that are subject to damage by fire or explosive substance.
definitions.plain_english: Agricultural produce means anything that is grown or harvested from farming or agricultural activity, such as crops, vegetables, fruits, grains, or fodder. It includes both crops still standing in the field and produce that has already been harvested and stored. Essentially, it covers the output of a farmer's land and labour that holds economic value as property.
real_world_examples: A person deliberately sets fire to a wheat crop standing in a field in Punjab just before harvest season, destroying the entire yield — the damaged wheat crop qualifies as agricultural produce under Section 326.

Miscreants use a crude explosive device to destroy a stored stockpile of paddy rice in a warehouse in Andhra Pradesh belonging to a farmer's cooperative — the paddy is agricultural produce covered under this section.

A landowner in Maharashtra burns sugarcane fields belonging to a neighbouring farmer during a land dispute, causing extensive damage to the harvested and unharvested cane — sugarcane constitutes agricultural produce for purposes of this offence.

In a communal dispute in Uttar Pradesh, individuals use fire to destroy a mango orchard and the stacked crates of harvested mangoes in an adjoining packhouse — both the orchard produce and stored fruits are agricultural produce.

A tractor owner in Rajasthan intentionally sets fire to bales of harvested cotton stored on a rival farmer's land — the cotton bales represent agricultural produce and damage to them attracts punishment under Section 326.

During a protest in Haryana, agitators torch trucks carrying harvested onions and potatoes destined for the mandi — the vegetables in transit are agricultural produce and their destruction invokes Section 326.
what_it_covers: Standing crops such as wheat, rice, sugarcane, cotton, or vegetables still growing in the field at the time of the act.
Harvested produce stored in fields, warehouses, godowns, or in transit, including grain, fruits, and vegetables.
Fodder crops and plantation produce such as tea leaves, rubber, or jute that form the output of agricultural activity.
Horticultural produce including fruits from orchards and vegetables from kitchen gardens cultivated for commercial or subsistence purposes.
Processed but minimally transformed farm outputs that retain their character as agricultural produce, such as dried grain or bundled hay.
what_it_excludes: Industrial or manufactured goods derived from processing agricultural raw materials, such as flour, refined sugar, or edible oil, which have lost their primary agricultural character.
Livestock, cattle, or poultry raised on agricultural land, which are treated separately as animals or property under other provisions of the Act.
Agricultural machinery, tools, irrigation equipment, or farm infrastructure such as barns or storehouses, which are distinct from the produce itself.
Timber from forests or commercially grown trees where the primary purpose is not food or immediate agricultural output but rather industrial wood supply.
Fishery or aquaculture produce, which does not arise from land-based agricultural activity in the conventional sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether property damaged by fire or explosive substance qualifies as agricultural produce determines the applicability of the specific aggravated mischief limb under Section 326, which prescribes imprisonment up to seven years plus mandatory fine — a significantly more severe punishment than other mischief offences under the section. Establishing that the damaged property is agricultural produce is therefore essential to frame the correct charge and attract the enhanced sentencing provision.

definitions.definition: The term 'aircraft' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in the context of a vehicle capable of flight, including any machine used for aerial navigation, which may be registered in India or otherwise, and is treated alongside rail and vessel as a major mode of transport subject to protection against mischief and destruction under this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: An aircraft refers to any flying machine — such as a commercial airplane, military jet, helicopter, or similar aerial vehicle — used for transporting people or goods through the air. Under this law, it is treated as a critical piece of infrastructure that must be protected from deliberate damage or destruction. Causing mischief to an aircraft, especially by fire or explosives, is treated as a serious criminal offence.
real_world_examples: A person intentionally damages the fuel lines of an Air India passenger aircraft parked at Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi, rendering it unsafe for flight — this constitutes mischief under Section 327 of the BNS.

definitions.definition: An 'airman' refers to a member of the Air Force of the Government of India, including officers and other ranks serving in that force, as used in the context of offences relating to mutiny, abetment of assault on superior officers, and seduction from duty or allegiance under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The term is employed alongside 'officer', 'soldier', and 'sailor' to collectively denote members of India's armed forces.
definitions.plain_english: An airman is a person who serves in the Indian Air Force. This includes anyone who is an enrolled or commissioned member of that military branch, whether a regular officer or a lower-ranked serviceperson. The law uses this term to apply specific rules about loyalty, duty, and discipline to Air Force personnel.
real_world_examples: A civilian politician attempts to convince an Indian Air Force flight sergeant stationed at Hindon Air Base to refuse orders from his commanding officer — this would constitute seducing an airman from his duty under Section 159 of the BNS.

A social media influencer in India publishes posts urging IAF ground crew airmen to disobey commands during a national security operation, amounting to an attempt to abetting mutiny by airmen under Section 159.
A private individual physically incites an IAF airman to assault his Wing Commander during an official inspection parade at Bengaluru Air Station, attracting liability under Section 161 of the BNS.

An anti-establishment group distributes pamphlets at an IAF residential colony in Pune, encouraging airmen to collectively refuse to perform their duties in protest — if mutiny results, the group faces punishment under Section 160 of the BNS.
A foreign intelligence operative contacts an IAF technician airman and persuades him to abandon his allegiance to the Government of India, constituting an offence under Section 159 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Commissioned officers of the Indian Air Force serving in any rank or capacity.
Non-commissioned IAF personnel such as sergeants, corporals, and aircraftsmen enrolled under the Air Force Act, 1950.
Any member of the Air Force of the Government of India who owes a duty of allegiance and is subject to military discipline under applicable service laws.
what_it_excludes: Civilian employees or contractors working on IAF bases who are not enrolled members of the Air Force.
Members of the Indian Army (soldiers) or Indian Navy (sailors), who are treated as separate categories under the same provisions.
Paramilitary personnel such as CISF, BSF, or CRPF members who are not part of the Air Force of the Government of India.
Retired or discharged IAF personnel who no longer owe an active duty of allegiance under service law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an 'airman' under the BNS determines whether Sections 159, 160, and 161 apply to offences involving that individual — including charges of abetting mutiny, seducing from allegiance, or abetting assault on a superior officer, which carry penalties ranging from fines up to death. The definition also determines whether a civilian accused can be prosecuted under these provisions based on their interactions with the targeted individual.

definitions.definition: The term 'ancient monument' is not formally defined within the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, nor does Section 294 define or use it. Based on its appearance in the Act's defined terms list and its contextual usage in Indian law, an 'ancient monument' refers to any structure, edifice, monument, or object of historical, archaeological, artistic, or cultural significance that is of ancient origin and is protected or recognized under applicable law, including the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.
definitions.plain_english: An ancient monument is a historically or culturally significant structure, building, or object that has survived from the past and is considered important to India's heritage. Think of things like old temples, forts, tombs, pillars, or ruins that have been around for a very long time. These are typically protected by law because of their importance to history and culture.
real_world_examples: The Qutub Minar in Delhi, a medieval Islamic monument, is an ancient monument protected under Indian heritage laws, and any act of defacement or damage to it would engage provisions protecting such monuments.

A centuries-old temple in Tamil Nadu with inscriptions and carvings recognized by the Archaeological Survey of India as an ancient monument, where vandalism or obscene graffiti would attract legal liability.
The rock-cut caves at Ajanta and Ellora in Maharashtra, recognized as UNESCO World Heritage Sites and ancient monuments, where desecration or damage constitutes a serious offence.
An ancient stepwell (vav) in Gujarat dating back over 800 years, declared a protected monument, where any unauthorized construction or defacement in its vicinity could trigger criminal liability.
A prehistoric megalithic burial site in Karnataka notified as an ancient monument, where illegal excavation or removal of objects would attract prosecution under relevant laws.
what_it_covers: Structures, buildings, or edifices of historical or archaeological importance such as forts, palaces, tombs, and temples recognized under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958.
Movable or immovable objects of artistic, historical, or cultural significance that are of ancient origin and declared protected by competent authority.
Archaeological sites, ruins, inscriptions, sculptures, and cave formations recognized and notified by the Archaeological Survey of India or State archaeological departments.
what_it_excludes: Modern buildings or recently constructed structures that have no historical, archaeological, or cultural significance, even if they appear old or dilapidated.
Private property or buildings that have not been notified or declared as protected monuments by a competent authority under applicable heritage laws.
Replicas, reproductions, or reconstructions of historical structures built for commercial, tourism, or entertainment purposes without heritage recognition.
Religious structures in active use that have not been specifically designated or notified as ancient monuments under applicable law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a structure or object qualifies as an 'ancient monument' determines the applicability of special legal protections under heritage legislation, and any act of defacement, destruction, obscene display, or damage involving such a monument may attract aggravated criminal liability beyond ordinary offences of mischief or trespass. Its recognition as an ancient monument can also trigger obligations under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, in addition to provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

definitions.definition: "animal" means any living creature, other than a human being.
definitions.plain_english: An animal, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, is any living creature that is not a human being. This includes all creatures in the animal kingdom — whether domesticated, wild, aquatic, or otherwise — as long as they are alive and not human. The definition is deliberately broad to cover the widest possible range of non-human living creatures.
real_world_examples: A person in Rajasthan deliberately poisons a neighbour's cattle herd — the cattle, being living creatures other than human beings, qualify as 'animals' and mischief causing injury or death to them is punishable under Section 325 of the BNS.

A farmer's goats in Uttar Pradesh are beaten and killed during a land dispute — the goats are 'animals' within the meaning of Section 2, making the perpetrator liable for committing mischief against another's animal.

A pet dog in Mumbai is deliberately run over by a vehicle driven with the intent to cause harm — the dog qualifies as an 'animal' and the act can attract liability under the relevant mischief provisions of the BNS.

Fish reared in a commercial aquaculture pond in Andhra Pradesh are poisoned by a rival businessman — the fish, being living creatures other than human beings, fall within the definition of 'animal' and the destruction of such property may constitute mischief under Section 325.
A racing horse in Pune is intentionally injured before a competition by a rival stables owner — the horse is an 'animal' under BNS and the intentional harm to it triggers mischief liability.

A circus elephant in Kerala is subjected to cruelty resulting in serious injury — the elephant qualifies as an 'animal' and the act may be examined under the mischief provisions of BNS in addition to special laws like the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act.
semantic_tags: animal as subject of mischief offence
what_it_covers: Domesticated livestock such as cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, horses, and camels kept by farmers or herders in India.
Pet animals such as dogs, cats, birds, and fish kept in private households.
Wild animals such as deer, elephants, tigers, or monkeys whether in captivity, sanctuaries, or the wild.
Aquatic creatures such as fish, prawns, and other marine life reared in aquaculture or found in natural water bodies.
Working animals such as draught bullocks, police dogs, army horses, or guide dogs for the visually impaired.
Insects, reptiles, and other creatures that are alive and non-human, such as snakes, lizards, or bees kept in apiaries.
what_it_excludes: Human beings, as they are explicitly carved out of the definition regardless of their physical or mental condition.
Dead animals or animal carcasses, since the definition requires the creature to be a 'living' creature at the time of the act.
Artificial representations of animals such as stuffed taxidermy animals, robotic animal models, or animal-shaped objects, as these lack the quality of being living creatures.
Plant life, fungi, or microorganisms, which, though living, are not creatures in the zoological sense contemplated by this definition.
Human foetuses or embryos, which, while non-autonomous living tissue, are considered within the human being category and are governed by separate provisions of the BNS.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'animal' directly determines the scope of Section 325 of the BNS, which punishes mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless any animal — the punishment varying in severity based on the value or type of animal harmed. Correctly identifying a subject as an 'animal' (and not a human being or an inanimate object) is essential to establish the elements of mischief and to determine the applicable punishment.

definitions.definition: Annoyance, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is not formally defined but is consistently employed to denote a state of irritation, disturbance, or displeasure caused to a person through another's intentional act, use of force, false information, or disobedience of a lawful order. It signifies a lesser degree of harm than injury but constitutes a cognisable interference with a person's comfort, peace, or convenience that the law recognises as sufficient to attract criminal liability when caused intentionally or knowingly.
definitions.plain_english: Annoyance means deliberately causing irritation, disturbance, or discomfort to another person without their consent. It is less serious than physical injury but still counts as a form of harm under this law. For example, if someone uses force, gives false information to an official, or disobeys a lawful order in a way that bothers or troubles another person, that counts as causing annoyance. The law treats intentionally annoying someone as a wrong that can lead to criminal punishment.
real_world_examples: A person intentionally splashes dirty water on a pedestrian in a busy Mumbai market by recklessly driving through a puddle, causing disturbance and discomfort to the pedestrian — this constitutes annoyance through use of criminal force under Section 129.

A resident of a Delhi colony gives false information to a police officer that his neighbour is running an illegal business, knowing the police will conduct searches and disturb the neighbour's household, thereby causing annoyance through misuse of lawful power under Section 217.

A factory owner in Pune, despite being ordered by a public servant to stop discharging effluents into a local waterway, continues to do so, causing obstruction and annoyance to farmers who depend on the water — attracting liability under Section 223.
A man in Chennai intentionally pulls off a woman's dupatta in a public bus, intending to frighten or annoy her — a classic use of criminal force causing annoyance as illustrated under Section 129(f).

A neighbour in a Kolkata apartment complex falsely reports to the housing society's designated public functionary that another resident is keeping illegal goods, knowing it will cause unnecessary searches and annoyance to that resident under Section 217.

A shopkeeper in Jaipur disobeys a municipal order directing him to keep his footpath clear, resulting in obstruction and annoyance to pedestrians and lawfully employed municipal workers, attracting punishment under Section 223.
what_it_covers: Intentional physical acts such as pushing, splashing, or inciting an animal against a person that cause irritation or discomfort without consent, as described in Section 129.

Disturbance caused to a person as a result of false information given to a public servant, leading to unwarranted searches, inquiries, or exercise of official power against that person under Section 217.
Obstruction and discomfort suffered by persons lawfully employed or by the public due to a person's deliberate disobedience of a duly promulgated order under Section 223.
Situations where a person knowingly takes an action aware that annoyance to another is a likely consequence, even if it is not the primary intent.
Collective annoyance caused to a group of persons, such as villagers subjected to unnecessary police enquiries due to a false complaint.
what_it_excludes: Unintentional or accidental acts that happen to cause discomfort to another person, where there is no intent or knowledge that annoyance would result.
Grievous hurt, bodily injury, or serious physical harm, which are governed by separate and more serious provisions and exceed the threshold of mere annoyance.
Annoyance arising purely from lawful acts carried out in good faith and in compliance with legal authority, such as a police officer conducting a legitimate search pursuant to a valid warrant.
Abstract mental displeasure or personal dislike that does not result from a specific act of force, false information, or disobedience of a lawful order as contemplated by the relevant sections.
Annoyance caused by an act of omission where no legal duty to act existed, and where no order, force, or false information was involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act causes 'annoyance' determines whether criminal force has been used under Section 129, whether an offence is made out under Section 217 for giving false information to a public servant, and whether disobedience of a lawful order attracts punishment under Section 223. Establishing annoyance can be the threshold element that converts an otherwise neutral act into a criminal offence, triggering imprisonment and fines under these provisions.

definitions.definition: The term 'apprehension' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used therein to mean the act of seizing, taking into custody, or arresting a person by lawful authority. As evidenced by Section 2's definition of 'harbour' — which includes assisting a person 'to evade apprehension' — and its contextual use in Sections 32 and 262, apprehension denotes the lawful capture or arrest of a person accused or suspected of an offence.
definitions.plain_english: Apprehension means the act of catching, seizing, or arresting someone who is suspected of committing a crime. It refers to bringing a person into legal custody, typically by a police officer or other authorised authority. When someone helps another person escape being caught by hiding or assisting them, they are helping that person 'evade apprehension.'
real_world_examples: A Delhi Police officer arrests a suspect wanted in connection with a robbery case — this act of physically taking the accused into custody constitutes apprehension under the BNS.

A person in Mumbai provides shelter and food to a fugitive who has escaped from jail, thereby helping him avoid being caught by police — this assistance to evade apprehension makes the helper liable for harbouring under the BNS.

In a Bihar village, a landlord hides a proclaimed offender in his farmhouse and supplies him with provisions so he can flee before police arrive — the landlord is assisting the offender to evade apprehension.

A wanted accused in a terrorist case in Jammu & Kashmir disguises himself and is provided a vehicle by an associate to escape to another state before police can arrest him — the associate facilitates evasion of apprehension.

A constable in Chennai acting under a magistrate's warrant physically detains and takes to the station a person accused of cheating — this formal arrest constitutes apprehension in accordance with the law.

Under Section 262 of the BNS, a public servant who negligently allows a prisoner to escape prevents the lawful apprehension or re-apprehension of that person, directly engaging the concept of apprehension.
what_it_covers: The physical arrest or seizure of a person by a police officer or other authority empowered by law to make arrests.
Re-arrest or recapture of a person who has escaped from lawful custody, as contemplated in Section 262 of the BNS.
Any lawful act of detaining or taking charge of a person suspected or accused of an offence for the purpose of bringing them before the appropriate authority.
Situations where a person assists another in fleeing before or during an attempted arrest, thereby enabling evasion of apprehension and attracting liability under the 'harbour' provisions.
what_it_excludes: Informal restraint or private detention of a person by a non-authorised individual, which would instead constitute wrongful confinement or wrongful restraint.
The mere suspicion or fear of being caught, which is a subjective mental state and does not constitute apprehension in the legal sense used in the BNS.
Civil detention or custody under non-criminal proceedings, such as detention for recovery of debt or contempt of court orders that are purely civil in nature.
Voluntary surrender by an accused to a court or police station, which is distinct from apprehension as it lacks the element of seizure by an external authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes assistance in evading apprehension is decisive for establishing criminal liability for 'harbouring' under the BNS, which renders the helper criminally culpable for sheltering or aiding a fugitive. Additionally, under Sections 32 and 262, the lawfulness or failure of apprehension directly determines whether a public servant or private person is guilty of an offence such as negligently allowing escape or resisting lawful arrest.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 5, 'appropriate Government' means the Central Government in cases where the sentence is a sentence of death or is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends; and the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced, in cases where the sentence (whether of death or not) is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
definitions.plain_english: The 'appropriate Government' refers to either the Central Government (Government of India) or a State Government, depending on the nature of the offence for which a person has been sentenced. If the crime falls under a subject that the Central Government controls, then the Central Government is the appropriate authority. If the crime falls under a subject controlled by a State Government, then whichever State sentenced the offender becomes the appropriate Government. This determines who has the power to commute (reduce or change) a person's punishment.
real_world_examples: A person is convicted under a Central law such as the Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and sentenced to death — here the Central Government is the 'appropriate Government' with the power to commute the sentence.

A person is convicted of murder (an offence under the BNS, 2023 which relates to law and order, a State subject under the Constitution) and sentenced by a Sessions Court in Maharashtra — the Government of Maharashtra is the 'appropriate Government' empowered to commute the sentence.

An offender convicted of sedition or waging war against the Government of India is sentenced by a court in Tamil Nadu — since the offence relates to the executive power of the Union, the Central Government acts as the appropriate Government for commutation purposes.

A person sentenced to life imprisonment for dacoity in Uttar Pradesh — since dacoity relates to public order which falls under State executive power, the Government of Uttar Pradesh is the appropriate Government that may commute the sentence under Section 5.

A soldier convicted under a military-related offence that falls within Union List subjects is sentenced in a civil court in Rajasthan — the Central Government, not the Rajasthan State Government, is the appropriate Government for any commutation of that sentence.
what_it_covers: The Central Government, when the sentence involves a death sentence or an offence falling under a matter within the executive power of the Union (Union List subjects).

The State Government of the State where the offender was sentenced, when the offence relates to a matter within the executive power of that State (State List subjects), regardless of whether the sentence is death or otherwise.
All scenarios of commutation under Section 5 of the BNS, 2023, where the identity of the commuting authority must be determined before exercising the power to commute any punishment.
what_it_excludes: Courts or judicial bodies — the 'appropriate Government' is exclusively an executive authority and does not include any court or tribunal that may have imposed the sentence.
Local authorities, municipal bodies, or statutory boards — these are not considered 'appropriate Government' for the purpose of commuting sentences under Section 5.

The Government of a State other than the one within which the offender was sentenced — a State has no commutation authority over an offender sentenced in a different State, even if the offender is from or imprisoned in that other State.

The President or Governor acting in their personal discretionary capacity under Articles 72 and 161 of the Constitution — those are separate constitutional powers distinct from the executive government's commutation power under Section 5 of BNS.
definitions.why_it_matters: Identifying the correct 'appropriate Government' is essential because only that authority has the legal power to commute a punishment under Section 5 of the BNS, 2023; any commutation order issued by the wrong government would be without jurisdiction and legally void. This definition directly determines whether the Central Government or a State Government has the executive authority to alter the nature or extent of a convicted offender's punishment, thereby affecting the offender's liberty and the enforcement of the sentence.

definitions.definition: 'Armed forces' means the naval, army and air forces and includes any member of the Armed Forces constituted under any law for the time being in force, including the paramilitary forces and any auxiliary forces that are under the control of the Central Government or the State Government.
definitions.plain_english: Armed forces refers to India's three main military services — the Navy, Army, and Air Force — as well as paramilitary organisations like the CRPF, BSF, and CISF, and any other auxiliary forces controlled by the Central or State Government. Essentially, it covers all uniformed defence and security personnel who are deployed and governed under specific laws enacted by Parliament or State legislatures. This definition is used to identify a special category of accused persons who can attract enhanced punishment when they commit rape in areas where they are deployed.
real_world_examples: A soldier from the Indian Army deployed in a counter-insurgency operation in Manipur commits rape on a local woman within the operational area — he falls squarely within this definition, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 64(2).

A CRPF (Central Reserve Police Force) jawan posted in a Naxal-affected district of Chhattisgarh commits rape on a woman in that district — since CRPF is a paramilitary force under Central Government control, he qualifies as a member of the armed forces for the purpose of this section.

A Border Security Force (BSF) personnel deployed along the Indo-Pakistan border in Rajasthan commits rape on a woman within the border area — BSF being a paramilitary force under the Ministry of Home Affairs qualifies under this definition.

An Indian Air Force officer stationed at an airbase in Pune commits rape on a civilian woman within the airbase or surrounding deployment area — as a member of one of the three primary armed forces, he is directly covered by this definition.

A member of the Assam Rifles, an auxiliary paramilitary force deployed in Northeast India under the control of the Central Government, commits rape on a woman in his area of deployment — he would be covered under the 'auxiliary forces' limb of this definition.

A State Armed Police Battalion personnel deployed by the State Government in a riot-affected area commits rape in that area — being an auxiliary force under State Government control, he may fall within this definition depending on the applicable State legislation constituting such force.
what_it_covers: Members of the Indian Army, Indian Navy, and Indian Air Force constituted under the Army Act 1950, Navy Act 1957, and Air Force Act 1950 respectively.

Paramilitary forces under Central Government control such as the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force (BSF), Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB).
Auxiliary forces under the control of the Central Government or any State Government, including State Armed Police Battalions or special forces raised under State legislation.
Members of the Assam Rifles constituted under the Assam Rifles Act 2006, being an armed force of the Union under Central Government control.
Coast Guard personnel constituted under the Coast Guard Act 1978, being an armed force constituted under a law in force and under Central Government control.
what_it_excludes: Regular state police officers appointed under the Police Act 1861 or State Police Acts, who are separately covered under the 'police officer' category in Section 64 and are not part of the armed forces as defined.

Private security guards or personnel employed by private security agencies under the Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Act 2005, as they are not constituted under any law as armed forces nor under Government control in that capacity.
Intelligence agency officers such as RAW or IB personnel who are not constituted as armed or paramilitary forces under any specific armed forces law, even if they work under the Central Government.
Retired or discharged military personnel who are no longer in active service or deployment, as the definition implies current membership and deployment by the Government.
Civil defence volunteers or home guards who may not be constituted as armed forces or auxiliary forces under the specific legal framework contemplated by this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether the accused qualifies as a member of the 'armed forces' under Section 64 directly determines whether the aggravated form of rape under Section 64(2) applies, which mandates a minimum sentence of ten years rigorous imprisonment extendable to life imprisonment for the remainder of the convict's natural life — a significantly harsher outcome than the ten-year minimum under Section 64(1). This classification also reflects the State's recognition of the special position of trust, authority, and power that armed forces personnel exercise over civilians in deployment areas, and the corresponding heightened criminal accountability.
