definitions.definition: An 'assailant' is a person who commits or attempts to commit an assault upon another, thereby occasioning the exercise of the right of private defence of the body under sections 38 and 39 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The term refers specifically to the aggressor whose unlawful act or threatened act triggers the defender's right to cause harm or death in self-defence.
definitions.plain_english: An assailant is the person who is attacking or threatening to attack someone else. In the context of self-defence law, this is the aggressor — the one who starts or threatens violence — against whom the person being attacked has a legal right to defend themselves. The law uses this word to identify who can lawfully be harmed when someone exercises their right of self-defence.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi forcibly enters a woman's house at night and attempts to rape her; he is the assailant against whom she may exercise her right of private defence, including causing death under Section 38.

A gang of robbers in Mumbai attacks a shopkeeper with knives during a robbery; each gang member is an assailant against whom the shopkeeper or bystanders may cause harm in private defence under Section 39.
A person in Chennai throws acid at a woman's face; that person is the assailant, and the victim or any bystander may lawfully cause harm, including death, to prevent the act under Section 38.

During a street altercation in Kolkata, a man assaults another with a wooden plank in a manner that may cause grievous hurt; the attacker is the assailant, and the victim may cause harm short of death under Section 39 if the threat does not rise to the level described in Section 38.
A kidnapper in Hyderabad attempts to forcibly drag a child into a vehicle; the kidnapper is the assailant and a parent or bystander may cause harm to stop the act under the right of private defence.

An intruder in Bengaluru attempts to wrongfully confine a family in circumstances where they cannot reach public authorities; the intruder is the assailant against whom the family may exercise their right of private defence.
what_it_covers: A person who physically assaults another in a manner likely to cause death or grievous hurt, triggering the right of private defence under Section 38.
A person who attempts rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping, abduction, or wrongful confinement, all of which make the perpetrator an assailant against whom death may be caused.
A person who throws or attempts to throw acid at another, qualifying as an assailant under Section 38's enumerated offences.
A person committing any assault not listed in Section 38 but still constituting an unlawful attack, making them an assailant against whom harm short of death may be caused under Section 39.
Multiple persons acting in concert during an attack, each of whom qualifies individually as an assailant for the purposes of private defence.
what_it_excludes: A public servant lawfully exercising authority, such as a police officer making a lawful arrest — such a person is not an assailant for purposes of private defence.
A person who has already completed the attack and poses no continuing threat, as the right of private defence does not extend to retaliation after the assault has ended.
A person who makes only a verbal threat without any physical act or gesture that could reasonably cause apprehension of imminent harm.
An innocent bystander or third party who has not participated in any assault, even if present at the scene of an attack.
A person acting in legitimate self-defence themselves — a defender does not become an assailant merely by resisting an attack against them.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of a person as an 'assailant' is the legal prerequisite that activates the right of private defence under Sections 38 and 39; if the person causing harm cannot establish that the victim was an assailant, the act of causing harm or death may constitute culpable homicide or grievous hurt punishable under the BNS. The classification of the assailant's act — whether it falls under Section 38's enumerated offences or only Section 39 — determines whether causing the assailant's death is legally justified or constitutes an excess of the right of private defence.

definitions.definition: A person is said to commit 'assault' when he makes any gesture or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person. Explanation: Mere words do not amount to an assault; but the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparations such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault.
definitions.plain_english: Assault means making a threatening gesture or action that causes another person to reasonably fear that they are about to be physically harmed. The threat must be communicated through a gesture or physical preparation — words alone are not enough. However, words spoken alongside a threatening gesture can make that gesture count as an assault.
real_world_examples: A man raises his fist and lunges toward a shopkeeper in a market in Delhi, causing the shopkeeper to fear an imminent beating — this constitutes assault even if no blow is actually struck.

During a road rage incident in Mumbai, a driver steps out of his car and picks up a cricket bat while moving aggressively toward another driver, causing that driver to apprehend immediate physical harm — this is assault.

A person in a village in Uttar Pradesh draws out a knife and moves toward a neighbour during a land dispute, making the neighbour reasonably fear being stabbed — this amounts to assault under the Act.

A group of men in Chennai surround a woman and make threatening gestures and advance toward her with outstretched hands intending to intimidate and touch her without consent — this constitutes assault with intent to outrage modesty under Section 74.

During a protest in Kolkata, an individual picks up a stone and draws back his arm in a throwing motion aimed at a police officer, causing the officer to reasonably apprehend imminent criminal force — this is assault even if the stone is not thrown.
what_it_covers: Any gesture or physical preparation made in the presence of another person that causes that person to reasonably apprehend imminent criminal force.
Threatening movements accompanied by words that give the gesture an assaultive meaning, such as raising a weapon while making a verbal threat.
Acts such as raising a hand to strike, drawing a weapon, or charging toward a person in a menacing manner without actual physical contact.
Gestures made with intent to outrage a woman's modesty or to disrobe her, even where physical contact has not yet occurred.
An advance or preparation toward a person that would reasonably cause apprehension of rape, kidnapping, wrongful confinement, or grievous hurt.
what_it_excludes: Mere words or verbal threats unaccompanied by any gesture or physical preparation, as explicitly stated in the explanation to the definition of assault.
Actual physical contact or application of force, which falls under the separate and distinct offence of use of criminal force rather than assault alone.
Gestures or preparations made in the absence of the person against whom they are directed, as the person must be present and apprehend the threat in real time.
Accidental movements or gestures not intended or known to be likely to cause apprehension of criminal force in another person.
Lawful acts performed by public servants or persons acting in justified circumstances, such as a police officer making a lawful apprehension.

assault: Assault means making a threatening gesture or action that causes another person to reasonably fear that they are about to be physically harmed. The threat must be communicated through a gesture or physical preparation — words alone are not enough. However, words spoken alongside a threatening gesture can make that gesture count as an assault.

Explanation: Mere words do not amount to an assault; but the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparations such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault.

definitions.definition: An 'assessor' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to a person appointed to assist a court in the trial of a case by offering their opinion or lay expertise, particularly in matters requiring specialised local or technical knowledge, as used in the context of Section 268 concerning offences punishable with death where the court may summon assessors to aid in adjudication.
definitions.plain_english: An assessor is a person called upon by a court to sit alongside a judge and provide their opinion during a criminal trial, especially in serious cases. They are not professional judges but serve as advisers to assist the judge in understanding complex or local matters. Their role is advisory — the judge is not bound to follow their opinion but must consider it.
real_world_examples: In a murder trial in a remote tribal district of Odisha, a Sessions Court summons two assessors with knowledge of local tribal customs to help the judge understand the context of a killing alleged under Section 103 BNS, which carries the death penalty.

During a capital punishment trial in Nagaland involving customary practices, the court appoints respected community elders as assessors to provide their opinion on the accused's intent and circumstances, assisting the judge in determining culpability.

A Sessions Judge in Manipur, presiding over a case of organised dacoity with murder, appoints assessors familiar with the terrain and local gang structures to offer their lay assessment of evidence and accused conduct.

In a high-profile honour killing case in Haryana under Section 100 BNS (murder), the presiding judge appoints two assessors from the local community to offer their perspective on the social dynamics and motive, which the judge considers before pronouncing judgment.

A court in Andaman and Nicobar Islands, dealing with a death penalty offence, appoints assessors from the indigenous community as mandated under the applicable procedural law to assist in evaluating evidence presented by both sides.
what_it_covers: A person formally appointed by a Sessions Court to assist in the trial of an offence punishable with death under Section 268 BNS
Community elders or persons with specialised local knowledge called to render opinion on facts or circumstances in a capital case
Lay persons empowered to sit with the judge and offer their assessment of evidence and circumstances in prescribed serious criminal proceedings
Any individual summoned under procedural law to aid the court as an adviser in cases where the gravity of the offence warrants additional opinion
what_it_excludes: Professional judges or magistrates who exercise independent judicial authority and deliver binding verdicts
Expert witnesses who testify on technical matters from the witness box and are subject to cross-examination as ordinary witnesses
Jurors or members of a jury system, which does not exist in the Indian criminal justice system under BNS
Public prosecutors or defence counsel who are legal representatives of parties rather than court-appointed advisory aids
Court clerks, stenographers, or administrative staff who perform ministerial functions without offering judicial opinions
definitions.why_it_matters: The participation of assessors in a trial under Section 268 BNS can influence the judge's reasoning and the ultimate decision in cases involving the death penalty, making their proper appointment and consideration critical to procedural fairness. Failure to comply with the requirement to summon or consider assessors' opinions in prescribed capital cases may constitute a procedural irregularity that affects the validity of the trial or sentence.

definitions.definition: Bail, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the provisional release of an accused person from custody upon furnishing security or surety to ensure appearance before the court as required. It operates as a conditional liberty granted pending investigation, inquiry, or trial of an offence.
definitions.plain_english: Bail is when a person who has been arrested or detained by the police or court is temporarily released from jail, usually after promising to appear in court when required and sometimes after paying money or having someone vouch for them. It is not a permanent release — the person must still face trial. Think of it as a conditional freedom granted while the legal process continues.
real_world_examples: A person arrested in Mumbai for allegedly committing theft under BNS is produced before a Magistrate who grants bail, allowing the accused to return home on the condition that he appears at every court hearing during the trial.

A student in Delhi accused of involvement in an affray is granted bail by the Sessions Court after furnishing a surety bond through a family member, enabling him to continue his studies while the case proceeds.

A businessperson in Bengaluru charged with cheating under BNS is initially denied bail due to flight risk concerns, but later obtains bail from the High Court after depositing a cash security and surrendering his passport.

A farmer in rural Uttar Pradesh arrested for alleged mischief is granted bail by the Magistrate the same day, since the offence is bailable, and he is released upon executing a personal bond without requiring a surety.

An accused in a dowry-related case in Hyderabad applies for anticipatory bail before arrest, fearing imminent detention, and the Sessions Court grants pre-arrest bail subject to conditions of cooperation with the investigation.
what_it_covers: Release of an arrested accused from police custody upon execution of a bail bond with or without surety before or during trial.
Provisional liberty granted by a Magistrate or Sessions Court to an accused charged with a bailable offence as a matter of right.
Discretionary release by a court in non-bailable offence cases where the court is satisfied that bail conditions can be imposed to ensure appearance and non-tampering of evidence.
Anticipatory bail granted in anticipation of arrest where the court permits release should the person be arrested for a specified offence.
Release of an accused on bail during the pendency of an appeal or revision against conviction.
what_it_excludes: Permanent or unconditional acquittal or discharge of an accused, which extinguishes the criminal liability rather than temporarily suspending custody.
Release of a convict after serving the full sentence, as that constitutes completion of punishment and not a bail arrangement.
Release of a person held in lawful custody under a civil contempt order or for non-payment of a court decree, which falls outside the scope of criminal bail.
Remission or commutation of sentence by the Government, which modifies the punishment itself rather than providing conditional pre-trial or pre-conviction release.
Release of a state prisoner or prisoner of war detained on executive orders under special statutes, which is governed by separate statutory provisions outside standard bail jurisdiction.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether bail is granted or denied determines whether an accused person remains in custody or is free during the pendency of investigation and trial, directly affecting personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution. The grant or refusal of bail also governs the applicability of Section 242 of the BNS, which prescribes the offence of non-appearance in response to a proclamation, and triggers obligations tied to bail bonds and sureties whose breach can result in forfeiture and fresh detention.

definitions.definition: A bail bond, as used in Section 269 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is a formal written undertaking or surety instrument executed by an accused person (and/or their surety) upon release from custody, binding them to appear before a Court at specified times and dates in accordance with the terms stipulated therein, subject to forfeiture upon default.
definitions.plain_english: A bail bond is a written promise made by an accused person, sometimes backed by a surety or guarantee, that they will show up in court on the required dates after being released from custody. It acts as a security or commitment that ensures the accused does not flee and participates in the trial process. If the accused fails to appear without a valid reason, they can be punished and the bond can be forfeited by the court.
real_world_examples: A person arrested in Mumbai for alleged cheating under BNS is granted bail by the Sessions Court; they sign a bail bond for Rs. 50,000 with a surety, committing to appear before the court on every hearing date. When they miss a hearing without cause, they face imprisonment up to one year under Section 269.

An accused charged with theft in a Delhi magistrate court is released on a personal bail bond of Rs. 10,000 and subsequently fails to appear on the next hearing date, resulting in the magistrate ordering forfeiture of the bond and issuance of a warrant.

In a Bengaluru case involving assault, the accused is released on a bail bond with two sureties and later travels abroad without informing the court, failing to appear at the next date — leading to prosecution under Section 269 in addition to proceedings for the original offence.

A woman accused of criminal trespass in Kolkata executes a bail bond before the local magistrate, promising to appear on scheduled dates. She repeatedly fails to appear, and the court, in addition to ordering forfeiture of the bond, initiates punishment proceedings under Section 269.

An accused in a road accident case in Chennai signs a bail bond after being charged with a negligent act causing grievous hurt. He defaults on the court appearance date, and the court imposes a fine and records conviction under Section 269, separate from the original charge.
what_it_covers: A written undertaking executed by an accused person and/or their surety promising appearance before a court on specified dates as a condition of release from custody.
Bonds executed with one or more sureties who guarantee the accused's presence in court, where the surety's property or money is at risk upon default.
Personal recognizance bonds (without surety) where the accused themselves undertakes in writing to appear before the court as per bail conditions.
Any formal instrument of release directed by a court requiring the accused to remain available for judicial proceedings and comply with attendance requirements.
what_it_excludes: A simple verbal or informal assurance by the accused to appear in court, which does not constitute a formal bond recognised by the court.
Civil court bonds or undertakings related to civil litigation, such as court bonds in suit proceedings, which are not bail bonds in the criminal law context.
Police custody or remand orders that retain the accused in custody rather than releasing them — no bail bond arises where release has not been granted.
Anticipatory bail orders in themselves, prior to actual execution of the formal bond and release of the accused, do not constitute a bail bond until the bond is formally signed and accepted.
Bonds relating to maintenance or civil security proceedings under laws other than the criminal code, which serve different legal purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a release instrument as a 'bail bond' under Section 269 directly determines whether criminal liability for failure to appear arises — an accused released on a bail bond who fails to appear without sufficient cause is punishable with imprisonment up to one year and/or fine, in addition to punishment for the original offence, and the court is empowered to order forfeiture of the bond. Without this classification, neither the punishment under Section 269 nor the forfeiture power of the court is triggered.

definitions.definition: The expression 'bank-note' means a promissory note or engagement for the payment of money to bearer on demand issued by any person carrying on the business of banking in any part of the world, or issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power, and intended to be used as equivalent to, or as a substitute for money.
definitions.plain_english: A bank-note is any paper document—like a currency note—that promises to pay the person holding it a certain amount of money on demand. It can be issued by a bank or by a government/sovereign authority anywhere in the world. Its purpose is to function as money or as a replacement for money in everyday transactions.
real_world_examples: A counterfeit Indian rupee note of denomination ₹500 printed by a gang in West Bengal and circulated in local markets qualifies as a forged bank-note under this definition, attracting liability under Section 178.
A person in Mumbai who knowingly accepts and re-circulates fake ₹2000 Reserve Bank of India notes to shopkeepers is dealing in counterfeit bank-notes as defined under the BNS.

A criminal syndicate in Delhi that prints fake US Dollar bills—issued under the authority of the US Federal Reserve (a Sovereign Power)—and attempts to use them in India falls within the scope of this definition, since US Dollars are bank-notes intended as substitutes for money.

A hawala operator in Hyderabad who accepts counterfeit Bangladeshi Taka notes (issued by Bangladesh Bank, a state-authorised banking institution) and uses them as payment instruments is handling forged bank-notes under this provision.

An accused in Chennai who possesses printing plates used to manufacture fake Reserve Bank of India promissory engagements payable to bearer is involved in the process of counterfeiting bank-notes under Section 178.
A person in Kolkata who alters the denomination of a genuine ₹100 RBI note to make it appear as a ₹1000 note is committing an offence involving bank-notes as defined under this section.
what_it_covers: Reserve Bank of India currency notes (e.g., ₹100, ₹200, ₹500 notes) issued under the authority of the Government of India and the RBI, payable to bearer on demand.

Foreign currency notes issued by a foreign sovereign power or central bank (e.g., US Dollar bills, British Pound notes, Euro notes) when used or counterfeited in India, as they are issued by or under the authority of a State or Sovereign Power.

Promissory notes or engagements for payment issued by any person carrying on the business of banking anywhere in the world, so long as they are intended to be used as equivalent to or as a substitute for money.
Counterfeit reproductions of any of the above instruments, as the definition underpins offences of counterfeiting, using, or trafficking in such notes under Sections 178–182 of the BNS.
what_it_excludes: Coins (metal currency), which are separately defined and governed under the definition of 'coin' in Section 178 with reference to the Coinage Act, 2011—coins are not promissory notes or bearer engagements.
Cheques, drafts, or bills of exchange drawn on a bank by an account holder, as these are not promissory notes payable to bearer on demand issued by a banking institution or sovereign authority.

Gift vouchers, prepaid cards, wallet credits, or other commercial instruments issued by private companies that are not carrying on the business of banking and are not intended as general substitutes for money.
Government securities, treasury bonds, or fixed deposit receipts, which are not payable to bearer on demand and are not intended to function as a direct substitute for money in everyday transactions.

Tokens or scrips issued by private employers or cooperative societies for internal use among members, as these lack the character of sovereign or banking-authority-backed instruments intended as money equivalents.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an instrument qualifies as a 'bank-note' determines whether the severe penalties under Sections 178–182 of the BNS—including imprisonment for life—are triggered for offences such as counterfeiting, using forged notes, or being in possession of counterfeiting tools; it also determines whether the conduct constitutes an 'economic offence' under Section 111, potentially attracting organised crime liability.

definitions.definition: "Begging" means: (i) soliciting or receiving alms in a public place, whether under the pretence of singing, dancing, fortune telling, performing tricks or selling articles or otherwise; (ii) entering on any private premises for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms; (iii) exposing or exhibiting, with the object of obtaining or extorting alms, any sore, wound, injury, deformity or disease, whether of himself or of any other person or of an animal; (iv) using such child as an exhibit for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms.
definitions.plain_english: Begging means asking for or collecting charity or alms from people, whether on streets, in public spaces, or by entering private homes, and includes using disguised activities like singing, dancing, or selling goods as a cover for soliciting alms. It also includes deliberately showing injuries, wounds, or physical disabilities to attract sympathy and collect money. Under this law, using a child as a prop or display to collect alms is also treated as begging.
real_world_examples: A man on a Mumbai local train platform performs magic tricks but his actual purpose is to collect money from passersby — this constitutes begging under the Act as it falls within the pretence of performing tricks to solicit alms.

An individual in Chennai deliberately exposes a bandaged but old wound or a visibly deformed limb in a busy market area to attract sympathy donations from shoppers — this constitutes begging by exhibiting a deformity or injury to obtain alms.

An organised gang in Kolkata uses a disabled or injured child, holding them up near temple entrances during festivals to elicit donations from pilgrims — this is explicitly covered as begging by using a child as an exhibit to solicit alms.

A person in Hyderabad stands at traffic signals appearing to sell balloons or small toys but primarily collects money without completing transactions, using the sales pretence as cover — this falls within begging under the pretence of selling articles.

what_it_excludes: Genuine commercial street performances or busking where money is earned as legitimate artistic compensation rather than as alms, with no element of solicitation as charity.

definitions.definition: Benefit, for the purposes of Sections 26, 27, and 30, means genuine welfare or wellbeing of a person — including physical, medical, or life-preserving good — done in good faith; mere pecuniary benefit is not benefit within the meaning of these sections.
definitions.plain_english: In this law, 'benefit' means something that is truly good for a person's health, safety, or wellbeing — not just something that gives them money or financial gain. For example, a doctor performing an emergency surgery to save someone's life is acting for their benefit. If the only advantage is financial, it does not count as 'benefit' under these provisions.
real_world_examples: A government hospital doctor in Mumbai performs emergency trepanation on an unconscious road accident victim who cannot consent, intending to prevent brain death — this is acting for the patient's benefit under Section 30.
A parent in Chennai, without their minor child's consent, authorises a surgeon to perform a life-saving appendectomy on the child — the surgery is done for the child's benefit under Section 27.

A bystander in Delhi drops an unconscious child from a burning building onto a safety net held by firefighters below, risking injury from the fall but intending to save the child's life — this constitutes acting for the child's benefit.

A wildlife ranger in Ranthambore fires at a tiger carrying away an injured villager, knowing the shot may also injure the villager, but intending in good faith to save the villager's life — this is acting for the victim's benefit.

A surgeon in Kolkata informs a terminally ill patient of a fatal diagnosis, causing severe distress, intending in good faith that the patient may make informed end-of-life decisions — this communication is made for the patient's benefit under Section 31.

A doctor offering to perform an operation solely in exchange for a large fee, without genuine therapeutic intent, cannot claim the act was done for the patient's 'benefit' in the legal sense, as mere pecuniary gain is excluded.
what_it_covers: Medical or surgical procedures performed in good faith to preserve a person's life or prevent grievous hurt, even without consent when consent is impossible to obtain.
Actions taken by a guardian or parent in good faith for the physical or medical welfare of a child under twelve years of age or a person of unsound mind.
Emergency interventions by bystanders or rescuers who act to prevent death or serious injury to a person who is incapable of consenting at the time.
A surgeon's honest communication of a fatal prognosis to a patient, made with the intention of serving the patient's genuine interests and wellbeing.
what_it_excludes: Mere pecuniary benefit — any act done solely or primarily for financial gain to the person does not qualify as 'benefit' under Sections 26, 27, and 30.
Intentional causing of death, even if the actor claims it was done for the person's benefit — such acts fall outside the protection of the exception.
Acts involving voluntary causing of grievous hurt for purposes other than preventing death, grievous hurt, or curing a grievous disease or infirmity, even if framed as being for the person's good.
Abetment of any offence that would itself not be covered by the good faith exception — such abetment cannot be shielded under the claim of acting for another's benefit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as being done for a person's 'benefit' determines whether the actor can claim the general exceptions under Sections 26, 27, and 30, thereby blocking criminal liability for harm caused — including hurt or grievous hurt — that would otherwise constitute an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. If the act does not meet the threshold of genuine benefit (e.g., it is merely pecuniary), the exception does not apply and the offence stands.

definitions.definition: The term 'bodily injury' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 80, 100, 101, and 105, it means any physical harm, wound, or impairment caused to the body of a person by an external act or force, including injuries that may accelerate death, are sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or are likely to cause death. It encompasses physical trauma ranging from minor wounds to severe injuries that result in or contribute to the death of a person.
definitions.plain_english: Bodily injury means any physical harm done to a person's body — such as a wound, bruise, burn, or internal damage — caused by someone else's action. It is broader than just pain and includes any physical damage to the body. In serious criminal cases, it is particularly important when the injury is so severe that it leads to or is likely to cause the person's death.
real_world_examples: A husband repeatedly beats his wife with a belt during a dowry dispute, causing deep lacerations and broken ribs; she dies within a year of marriage — the burns and bodily injuries constitute the basis for a dowry death charge under Section 80.

A person stabs another with a knife in a brawl in Delhi, intending to cause a deep wound; the victim dies from blood loss — the stab wound constitutes bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, making the act murder under Section 101.

During a road rage incident in Mumbai, a driver strikes a pedestrian with an iron rod, causing severe head trauma; the victim, who had an underlying brain condition, dies faster than a healthy person would — the assailant is deemed to have caused death through bodily injury under Section 100.

In a village dispute in Uttar Pradesh, one person throws acid on another, causing severe burns to the face and chest — the burns constitute bodily injury, and if the victim dies, the perpetrator is liable for culpable homicide or murder depending on intent.

A factory worker in Pune is intentionally pushed into heavy machinery by a co-worker, resulting in the loss of a limb and internal bleeding that leads to death — the injuries caused by the push amount to bodily injury causing death under Section 100.

A woman in Chennai is subjected to repeated physical beatings by her in-laws in connection with dowry demands; the cumulative bodily injuries she sustains ultimately cause her death within three years of marriage, forming the basis of dowry death under Section 80.
what_it_covers: Stab wounds, gunshot wounds, or blunt force trauma inflicted on a person's body by another individual.
Burns caused by fire, acid, or other corrosive substances that damage body tissue.
Physical injuries that accelerate the death of a person already suffering from a pre-existing disease, disorder, or bodily infirmity.
Injuries inflicted with a weapon such as a sword, club, or firearm that are sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
Any physical harm that, while not immediately fatal, contributes to or culminates in the death of the victim.
what_it_excludes: Mental or psychological harm, such as emotional distress or psychiatric injury, which does not manifest as physical damage to the body.
The causing of death of a child in the mother's womb, which the Act expressly states is not homicide and is treated separately.
Harm to property or reputation, which falls under different categories such as mischief or defamation, not bodily injury.
Death caused purely by negligent omission without any physical act inflicting injury on the body of the victim.
Grievous hurt as a standalone offence not resulting in death, which is governed separately and does not automatically constitute bodily injury in the context of homicide provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'bodily injury' is decisive in determining if a person is liable for culpable homicide or murder under Sections 100 and 101, and for dowry death under Section 80; it also determines whether a person who causes injury to someone with a pre-existing condition is deemed to have caused that person's death, thereby attracting the most serious criminal penalties including life imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Bodily pain refers to physical pain caused to any person as one of the three components of 'hurt' under Section 114 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It encompasses any sensation of physical suffering or discomfort inflicted upon the body of another person. Where such bodily pain is severe and persists for fifteen days or more, it may constitute 'grievous hurt' under Section 116.
definitions.plain_english: Bodily pain means any physical pain or suffering caused to a person's body. It is the most common form of 'hurt' — for example, the ache or soreness you feel after being punched, slapped, or kicked. If the pain is severe and lasts fifteen days or more, it is treated as a more serious category of injury under the law.
real_world_examples: A person in a street brawl in Delhi punches another person in the stomach, causing immediate pain and bruising — the pain caused constitutes bodily pain and amounts to hurt under Section 114.

A landlord in Mumbai physically pushes and slaps a tenant during a rent dispute, causing the tenant to experience pain in the face and chest — this physical pain qualifies as bodily pain under the provision.

During a communal scuffle in Uttar Pradesh, a group member strikes a person with an open hand, causing temporary pain without leaving a visible mark — even this transient physical suffering amounts to bodily pain and thus hurt.

A factory supervisor in Chennai physically grabs and twists an employee's arm during a dispute, causing the employee to suffer pain in the arm for several days — this constitutes bodily pain amounting to hurt, and if the pain is severe and lasts fifteen days, it could escalate to grievous hurt.

A domestic violence incident in Kolkata where a husband repeatedly beats his wife causing her pain in her ribs and back — the pain inflicted constitutes bodily pain under Section 114, forming the basis of the hurt offence.

A school teacher in Rajasthan canes a student so hard that the student suffers significant pain for several days — the bodily pain caused constitutes hurt and could be the basis for criminal liability.
what_it_covers: Any physical pain experienced by a person as a direct result of another person's act, including pain from slapping, punching, kicking, or striking.
Pain that is temporary or transient in nature but is nonetheless real and perceptible to the victim, even if it leaves no visible injury or mark.
Severe bodily pain that endures for a period of fifteen days or more, which elevates the offence from simple hurt to grievous hurt under Section 116.
Pain caused by the use of criminal force such as pushing, restraining, or striking a person, even if the act does not cause lasting physical damage.
Physical pain resulting from an act done with criminal intention or knowledge, irrespective of whether a weapon or instrument was used.
what_it_excludes: Mental or emotional distress, psychological suffering, or psychiatric harm, which do not constitute bodily pain under the statutory definition.
Disease or infirmity caused to a person, which are treated as separate and distinct components of 'hurt' alongside bodily pain under Section 114.
Bodily pain that is self-inflicted or voluntarily consented to in a lawful context, such as pain during a consented medical procedure by a registered practitioner.
Mere apprehension or threat of pain without any actual physical contact or causation of pain, which may instead fall under criminal intimidation.
Grievous bodily injuries such as permanent privation of sight, hearing, or fractures of bones, which are governed separately as grievous hurt under Section 116 and are not merely 'bodily pain'.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act causes bodily pain determines whether the offence of 'hurt' under Section 114 is established, which is a foundational element for further offences such as voluntarily causing hurt and voluntarily causing grievous hurt; the severity and duration of bodily pain also determines whether the charge escalates to grievous hurt under Section 116, significantly increasing the potential punishment from a lesser term to up to seven years or more of imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Bodily weakness refers to a physical condition of the body that renders a person helpless or incapable of providing for their own safety or supplying their own wants, such that they require the attendance or assistance of another person bound by lawful contract to care for them. It is used in Section 357 alongside youth, unsoundness of mind, and disease as a qualifying condition that creates vulnerability and legal dependency.
definitions.plain_english: Bodily weakness means a physical frailty or debilitating condition of the body that makes a person unable to take care of themselves or meet their own basic needs. This could include conditions like extreme old age, paralysis, severe disability, or any chronic or acute physical ailment that leaves a person dependent on a caregiver. The key point is that the weakness must make the person helpless — not merely inconvenienced.
real_world_examples: An elderly bedridden person in a nursing home in Pune who is paralysed and fully dependent on a contractually hired attendant for bathing, feeding, and medication, but the attendant deliberately stops reporting to duty, leaving the person unattended for days.

A person with advanced muscular dystrophy living in Chennai who has hired a live-in care assistant under a written agreement, and the assistant voluntarily abandons the job without notice, leaving the patient unable to move or call for help.

A severely malnourished child in a government-run children's home in Delhi, physically too weak to feed herself, whose assigned caretaker staff member wilfully neglects to provide meals as required under the employment contract.

A post-operative patient in a Kolkata hospital recovering from spinal surgery, rendered immobile and helpless, whose contractually engaged private nurse voluntarily fails to administer prescribed care and supply food and water during night shifts.

An aged widow suffering from severe osteoporosis in a rural village in Rajasthan, hired a domestic helper under a formal agreement to assist her daily; the helper deliberately stops attending and the woman is left unable to move or procure food for herself.
what_it_covers: Paralysis or loss of limb function rendering a person completely immobile and unable to perform daily activities without assistance.
Severe chronic illness such as advanced cancer, end-stage organ failure, or muscular dystrophy that leaves a person physically incapable of procuring their own food, medicine, or safety.
Extreme physical debilitation caused by malnutrition, injury, or post-surgical recovery that renders a person temporarily or permanently helpless and dependent on a contracted caregiver.
Conditions such as severe spinal cord injuries, total blindness combined with immobility, or advanced degenerative diseases that prevent self-care.
Acute physical prostration caused by disease or injury where the person cannot call for help or move to obtain necessities on their own.
what_it_excludes: Minor physical ailments or temporary injuries such as a sprained ankle or mild fever that do not render a person helpless or incapable of providing for their own safety and wants.
Mental or psychological conditions, which are separately covered under the term 'unsoundness of mind' in Section 357 and are not classified as bodily weakness.
Youth or minority status of a person, which is a distinct qualifying condition listed separately alongside bodily weakness in Section 357.
Persons who are physically weak but retain the capacity to provide for their own safety and meet their own basic needs without external assistance.
Voluntary self-neglect by a person who is otherwise physically capable, as the weakness must be an objective physical condition and not a chosen lifestyle.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as suffering from 'bodily weakness' is decisive in establishing liability under Section 357 of the BNS, 2023 — if this condition is established, a person contractually bound to care for such a helpless individual who voluntarily omits to do so becomes criminally liable for imprisonment up to three months and/or a fine up to five thousand rupees. Without this qualifying condition being proven, the neglect of duty by a caregiver would not attract criminal punishment under this provision.

Legal text: Bodily weakness refers to a physical condition of the body that renders a person helpless or incapable of providing for their own safety or supplying their own wants, such that they require the attendance or assistance of another person bound by lawful contract to care for them. It is used in Section 357 alongside youth, unsoundness of mind, and disease as a qualifying condition that creates vulnerability and legal dependency.

definitions.definition: A bond, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a formal written obligation or undertaking executed by an accused or any person, binding them to appear before a Court or to fulfil specified conditions under penalty of forfeiture or other legal consequences. It includes a bail bond or personal bond given as a condition of release from custody, as well as any document signed or sealed that creates a legally enforceable obligation, including instruments that may be converted into a valuable security.
definitions.plain_english: A bond is a written promise or guarantee that a person signs, usually when they are released from custody, pledging to appear in court on a specified date or to comply with certain conditions. If the person fails to keep this promise without a valid reason, they can be punished. In everyday terms, it is like a signed legal commitment that holds a person accountable to the court.
real_world_examples: An accused person charged with theft in Mumbai is released from police custody after signing a personal bond of ₹10,000, promising to appear before the Sessions Court on the next hearing date. If he fails to appear without sufficient cause, he is liable for punishment under Section 269.

A resident of Delhi accused of a bailable offence signs a surety bond along with a local guarantor, undertaking to attend all court proceedings. His failure to appear on the scheduled date without explanation exposes him to imprisonment up to one year and forfeiture of the bond amount.

In a Kolkata extortion case under Section 308, the accused threatens a shopkeeper to sign and deliver a bond binding the shopkeeper to pay a sum of money under penalty—this signed bond constitutes extortion as it is a valuable security obtained through fear.

A trader in Chennai accused of cheating is released on a personal bond after arrest. He travels outside the city during the trial period and misses a court date without notifying the court; the court orders forfeiture of his bond and initiates proceedings under Section 269.

In a Hyderabad criminal case, the accused is released on bail bond co-signed by two sureties. One surety withdraws, but the accused still fails to appear in court. The court invokes Section 269, ordering punishment and forfeiture of the remaining bond amount.
what_it_covers: A bail bond executed by an accused upon release from custody, binding them to appear before the court on specified dates.
A personal bond or surety bond signed by an accused or guarantor as a condition of bail or temporary release.
A written instrument signed or sealed under coercion (as in extortion scenarios) that creates a pecuniary or legal obligation, capable of being converted into a valuable security.
A bond executed in the context of criminal proceedings that imposes conditions on the accused's conduct or attendance before the court.
Any formal written undertaking delivered to a court or party that binds the signatory to perform or refrain from specified acts under penalty.
what_it_excludes: Informal verbal promises or oral assurances given by an accused to appear in court, which do not constitute a bond in the legal sense.
Civil contractual agreements between private parties that are unrelated to criminal proceedings or court appearance obligations.
Government securities, promissory notes, or negotiable instruments that are purely commercial in nature and not connected to criminal court proceedings.
A mere undertaking given by an accused to the police during investigation that is not formally executed as a bond before a magistrate or court.
Documents signed under free will for commercial purposes, even if they create financial liability, where no court or criminal proceeding is involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an instrument qualifies as a bond determines whether an accused's failure to appear in court attracts punishment under Section 269 of the BNS, including imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both, in addition to liability for the original offence. It also determines whether the court has power to order forfeiture of the bond amount, and whether a document signed under threat constitutes extortion under Section 308.

definitions.definition: A person is 'bound by law' when they are under a legal obligation or duty, imposed by statute, court order, or lawful authority, to perform a specific act; and nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it.
definitions.plain_english: Being 'bound by law' means a person has a legal duty or obligation to do something — not just a moral or personal choice, but a requirement imposed by the law itself, a court, or a lawful authority. If someone does an act because the law requires them to do it, they cannot be punished for that act even if it would otherwise be considered an offence. This protection also extends to someone who genuinely and reasonably believes they are legally required to act, as long as that belief is based on a mistake of fact and not a mistake of law.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Delhi who arrests a suspect without a warrant because the person has committed a cognizable offence in the officer's presence — the officer is bound by law under the CrPC/BNSS to make such an arrest and commits no offence of wrongful confinement.

A bailiff (court officer) in Mumbai who is ordered by a civil court to attach and seize the property of a judgment debtor under a court decree — the bailiff is bound by law to execute the court's order and commits no offence of theft or trespass.

An Army soldier posted in a disturbed area under the Armed Forces Special Powers Act who fires on a rioting crowd upon receiving a lawful order from a superior officer in conformity with the law — the soldier commits no offence as he is bound by law to obey that command.

A jailor at Tihar Jail who physically restrains a prisoner attempting to escape — the jailor is bound by law to prevent the escape and commits no offence of assault or wrongful confinement by using reasonable force to do so.

A revenue officer in a state who demolishes an illegally constructed structure on government land pursuant to a lawful demolition order issued by the competent authority — the officer is bound by law to execute the order and commits no offence of mischief or trespass.

A doctor at a government hospital who, under a statutory obligation, detains a person suffering from a notified infectious disease under public health law to prevent the spread of the disease — the doctor is bound by law and commits no offence of wrongful confinement.
semantic_tags: non-culpable act under compulsion of law
what_it_covers: A police officer who arrests a person without a warrant for a cognizable offence as mandated by law, even though the arrest involves physical restraint.
A court officer who executes a lawful arrest, attachment, or search warrant issued by a competent court, even if the act would otherwise constitute trespass or confinement.
A soldier who fires on a mob on the lawful order of a superior officer in conformity with the commands of the law.
A person who, by reason of a genuine mistake of fact (not of law), in good faith believes they are legally required to perform an act and acts accordingly.
A citizen who is legally required to assist a public servant under Section 222 of the BNS and renders that assistance, even if the act involves physical intervention.
what_it_excludes: Acts done based on a mistake of law — a person who incorrectly believes a law permits or requires an act, when it does not, cannot claim this protection.
Acts done under moral, social, or religious obligation that are not legally mandated — a person who acts out of personal duty or community pressure without any legal compulsion is not 'bound by law'.

Acts done in excess of or beyond the scope of the legal duty — a police officer who uses grossly disproportionate force far beyond what the law authorises while making an arrest cannot claim this defence for the excessive portion of conduct.
Acts driven by personal motive, malice, or self-interest that merely coincide with a legal duty — bad faith negates the protection even if some legal obligation existed.
Obligations arising purely from private contracts or agreements between parties, which are not imposed by any statute, court order, or lawful authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person is 'bound by law' is decisive in determining criminal liability under Section 14 of the BNS: if the defence applies, an act that would otherwise constitute an offence — such as wrongful confinement, assault, trespass, or mischief — is rendered non-culpable and no offence is made out. Conversely, if the act goes beyond what the law mandates, or is based on a mistake of law rather than fact, the general exception does not apply and the person remains criminally liable.

definitions.definition: A person commits the offence of bribery who gives a gratification to any person with the object of inducing him or any other person to exercise any electoral right or of rewarding any person for having exercised any such right, or who accepts either for himself or for any other person any gratification as a reward for exercising any such right or for inducing or attempting to induce any other person to exercise any such right; provided that a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action shall not be an offence under this section.
definitions.plain_english: Bribery, in this law, means offering or accepting money, gifts, food, drink, or any other benefit to influence how someone votes or to reward them for how they voted in an election. It covers both the person giving the bribe and the person receiving it. Simply making a public promise about government policy or public welfare actions does not count as bribery under this law.
real_world_examples: A candidate in a Lok Sabha election distributes cash envelopes to voters in a constituency in Uttar Pradesh the night before polling day, asking them to vote for him — this constitutes bribery by giving a gratification to induce exercise of an electoral right.

A political party worker in Tamil Nadu organises a free biryani feast for residents of a housing colony shortly before municipal elections to reward and encourage them to vote for a particular candidate — this constitutes bribery by treating, punishable with fine only.

A voter in Maharashtra accepts ₹2,000 from a party agent in exchange for a promise to vote for a specific Assembly candidate — this constitutes bribery by accepting a gratification as a reward for exercising an electoral right.

An intermediary in West Bengal approaches factory workers and offers them free liquor if they collectively vote for a certain candidate in the state election — the intermediary commits bribery by attempting to procure a gratification and by inducing voters to exercise their electoral right in a particular way.

A candidate's representative in Karnataka promises free LPG cylinders to women voters post-election as a reward for having voted for their candidate — this constitutes bribery as accepting or offering gratification as a reward for having exercised an electoral right.

A booth-level agent in Rajasthan offers to pay off the outstanding micro-finance loan of a voter if she votes for a particular party candidate — this is bribery as the loan waiver constitutes a gratification given to induce exercise of an electoral right.
what_it_covers: Offering or giving money, gifts, or any benefit to a voter to induce them to vote for a particular candidate or party.
Accepting money, gifts, food, drink, or any other benefit in exchange for voting in a particular manner or for inducing others to do so.
Providing free food, drink, or entertainment (treating) to voters as a form of inducement or reward related to the exercise of electoral rights.
An intermediary who offers or attempts to procure a gratification on behalf of a candidate for electoral influence, as they are deemed to have given or accepted the gratification.
Rewarding a voter after the election with a benefit as recognition for having voted in a particular way.
what_it_excludes: A candidate or party making a declaration of public policy, such as announcing a manifesto promise to build roads or hospitals, which is explicitly excluded by the proviso to Section 170.
A promise of public action by a candidate, such as pledging to introduce a welfare scheme if elected, which does not constitute bribery under this section.
Bribery by treating (food, drink, entertainment, or provision), which is excluded from imprisonment and is punishable with fine only under the proviso to Section 173.
General political campaigning, canvassing, or persuasion that does not involve conferring any material gratification on the voter.
Corruption or gratification involving public servants in discharge of official duties, which is governed by separate provisions and not by this electoral bribery section.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as bribery under Section 170 determines whether an accused is liable for punishment under Section 173 — imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both (or fine only in the case of treating). A finding of bribery can also affect the validity of an election and expose candidates, agents, and voters to prosecution, thereby directly triggering electoral offence liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

definitions.definition: A brothel, as used in Section 98 and Section 99 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a premises kept or managed for the purpose of prostitution, where one or more persons are employed or used for sexual intercourse or illicit intercourse with others. It is a place over which a person exercises control or management for facilitating prostitution.
definitions.plain_english: A brothel is a place that is run or managed for the purpose of prostitution, where people — often women or children — are made available for sexual activity in exchange for money or other consideration. The person in charge of such a place is referred to as one who 'keeps or manages' a brothel. Under Indian law, running or managing such a place is treated as a serious criminal activity, especially when it involves minors.
real_world_examples: A house in a red-light area in Mumbai where a woman is employed as a manager who arranges clients for multiple women living on the premises — this constitutes a brothel under the Act.

A lodge in Delhi where the owner knowingly rents out rooms exclusively for prostitution and collects a share of the earnings from the women engaging in such activity — the lodge functions as a brothel.

A massage parlour in Bengaluru operating as a front business, where the actual purpose is to provide sexual services to clients and the operator manages the activities and payments — this qualifies as a brothel.

A rented flat in Kolkata controlled by a trafficker who houses multiple trafficked women and directs clients to visit for sexual services, collecting payments and managing the operations — this flat is a brothel for purposes of the Act.

A person in Chennai who purchases a girl under eighteen years and keeps her in a premises for sexual exploitation of clients is presumed under Section 99 to be keeping a brothel for purposes of prostitution.
semantic_tags: criminal liability for sex trade premises
what_it_covers: A house, flat, lodge, or any premises kept and managed specifically for carrying out prostitution or illicit intercourse with clients.
Any establishment where the owner, manager, or controller organises, directs, or facilitates sexual services in exchange for money or other consideration.
A premises to which a female under eighteen years has been disposed of, sold, or hired — triggering the statutory presumption that it is used for prostitution.
A place managed by a person who exercises supervisory or operational control over individuals engaged in prostitution on those premises.
Any location, whether disguised as a legitimate business or not, where the primary or substantial purpose is enabling prostitution or illicit intercourse.
what_it_excludes: A private residence where consensual sexual activity between adults occurs without any element of management, commercial exchange, or third-party control.
A legitimate hotel, lodge, or guest house that may incidentally be misused by guests for sexual activity without the knowledge or facilitation of the owner or manager.
A shelter home, rehabilitation centre, or government-recognised welfare institution housing women, even if those women have previously been engaged in prostitution.
A medical or counselling facility providing support to survivors of sexual exploitation, which does not facilitate ongoing prostitution.
A marriage bureau or social platform that arranges lawful marriages or relationships recognised under personal law or community custom.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a premises qualifies as a brothel directly determines criminal liability under Sections 98 and 99 of the BNS, 2023 — a person who sells or disposes of a female under eighteen to one who 'keeps or manages a brothel' is statutorily presumed to have done so with intent for prostitution, shifting the burden of proof to the accused. This definition also triggers offences and presumptions under complementary legislation such as the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and governs the scope of investigation, prosecution, and punishment for child trafficking and sexual exploitation.

This definition also triggers offences and presumptions under complementary legislation such as the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and governs the scope of investigation, prosecution, and punishment for child trafficking and sexual exploitation.

definitions.definition: "Candidate" means a person who has been nominated as a candidate at any election.
definitions.plain_english: A candidate is any person who has formally been put forward (nominated) to contest an election. This could be for Parliament, a State Legislature, a local body, or any other recognised election. The person must have gone through the official nomination process to qualify as a candidate under this law.
real_world_examples: A person who files their nomination papers before the Returning Officer for a Lok Sabha constituency election in Maharashtra and whose nomination is accepted becomes a 'candidate' under this provision.

A member of a recognised political party who is officially nominated to contest a Rajya Sabha election by their party and whose nomination is filed becomes a candidate protected under these electoral offence provisions.

An independent contestant who submits their nomination form with the required proposers and deposit for a Municipal Corporation election in Delhi qualifies as a candidate for the purpose of these sections.

A person nominated by a political party to contest a Vidhan Sabha bye-election in Bihar, even if they later withdraw before polling day, was a candidate at the time of nomination and any undue influence exerted against them during that period would attract liability.

A person standing for election to a Gram Panchayat in Tamil Nadu who has been formally nominated through the prescribed procedure is a candidate, making any threats, bribery, or false statements made against them actionable under this Chapter.
what_it_covers: A person who has filed a valid nomination paper for a general or bye-election to Parliament or a State Legislature and whose candidacy has been accepted by the Returning Officer.

A person formally nominated to contest local body elections such as Municipal Corporation, Panchayat, or District Council elections, once the nomination process under the relevant election law is completed.
A person nominated for any election recognised by law in India, including elections to statutory bodies, even if they subsequently withdraw from the contest after the nomination was filed.
A person whose nomination is pending scrutiny but has been formally submitted, as the act of nomination itself triggers candidate status under this definition.
what_it_excludes: A person who merely expresses an intention to contest an election or is informally selected by a party but has not yet filed or completed the formal nomination process.
A voter or ordinary elector who participates in the election only by casting a vote and has not been nominated as a contestant.
A political party office-bearer or election agent who assists a candidate but is not themselves nominated to stand for election.
A prospective candidate whose nomination paper has been rejected by the Returning Officer, as post-rejection they no longer hold the status of a validly nominated candidate.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'candidate' directly determines who is protected by and subject to the electoral offence provisions in Sections 171–176 of the BNS, 2023; offences such as undue influence, bribery, making false statements about personal character, and illegal payments are only triggered when the person targeted or promoted is a formally nominated candidate. Without this status, the same conduct may not attract liability under this Chapter.

definitions.definition: A 'capital offence' is an offence which is capital by the law for the time being in force in India, meaning an offence for which the sentence of death is a prescribed punishment under the applicable Indian law. As used in Section 230 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, it refers to any offence punishable by death under the laws in force in India at the relevant time.
definitions.plain_english: A capital offence is a crime so serious that the law allows the court to sentence the convicted person to death. In India, examples include certain cases of murder, gang rape resulting in death, and terrorism causing death. The term is used in the law to identify situations where giving false evidence is especially dangerous because an innocent person could be executed.
real_world_examples: A witness fabricates evidence against an innocent person in a murder trial under Section 103 of the BNS, knowing that murder can attract the death penalty — this would make the false evidence relate to a capital offence.

Someone plants false forensic evidence to frame a person for a gang rape case in which the victim subsequently died, an offence punishable by death under Indian law, thereby implicating a capital offence.
A co-accused gives false testimony to frame an innocent bystander in a terrorist attack case prosecuted under laws where death is a prescribed punishment, making the offence a capital one.

A police officer fabricates a confession document to implicate a suspect in a case of kidnapping followed by murder, where death penalty is a potential sentence, triggering the provisions of Section 230 relating to capital offences.

A person deliberately gives false witness testimony in a case involving dacoity with murder, for which the death sentence may be awarded under Indian law, thereby exposing themselves to life imprisonment or death if the innocent accused is executed.
what_it_covers: Any offence under Indian law for which the sentence of death is a lawfully prescribed punishment, such as murder under aggravated circumstances under the BNS.
Offences where death is one of the alternative punishments available to the court, such as gang rape resulting in death of the victim.
Terrorist acts or waging war against the State where the prescribed punishment includes the death penalty under applicable Indian legislation.
Cases of dacoity accompanied by murder where the death penalty is a legally available punishment under the relevant provisions of the BNS.
what_it_excludes: Offences for which the maximum punishment is imprisonment for life but not death, as these are not 'capital' in the strict legal sense.
Offences punishable only by fine, simple imprisonment, or rigorous imprisonment without the possibility of the death sentence.
Civil wrongs, torts, or administrative violations that carry no criminal punishment, let alone the death penalty.
Offences under foreign laws or international law where death is prescribed but not under the law for the time being in force in India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an offence qualifies as a capital offence is decisive in determining the punishment for giving or fabricating false evidence under Section 230 of the BNS — if the false evidence relates to a capital offence, the punishment escalates to imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years with fine, and if an innocent person is actually executed as a result, the false witness can themselves be sentenced to death. This classification thus directly triggers the most severe penal consequences for perjury and evidence fabrication.

definitions.definition: The term 'caste' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used throughout the Act to denote a hereditary social group or division within Indian society to which a person belongs by birth, constituting a distinct class or community recognised by social custom, tradition, or law, and forming a basis upon which discrimination, enmity, or denial of rights may be perpetrated.
definitions.plain_english: A caste is a social group that a person is born into, passed down through generations, and recognised in Indian society — such as Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes, or upper-caste groups. The law uses this term to identify situations where someone is targeted, harmed, or denied rights specifically because of the caste they belong to. It is not something a person chooses; it is an inherited identity tied to community and social standing in India.
real_world_examples: A mob of five or more persons from a dominant caste attacks and kills a Dalit man in a village in Uttar Pradesh specifically because of his caste identity — each member of the mob can be charged under Section 103 for murder on the ground of caste.

A political leader in Tamil Nadu publishes a speech on social media asserting that members of a particular caste cannot be loyal to the Indian Constitution, thereby attracting prosecution under Section 197 for making imputations prejudicial to national integration on the ground of caste.

A group of upper-caste men in Rajasthan beat a lower-caste youth with rods, causing permanent disability, specifically because he tried to ride a horse in a public procession — this constitutes grievous hurt on the ground of caste under Section 117.

An online content creator in Maharashtra regularly uploads videos promoting hatred and enmity between two caste communities by spreading false narratives about their practices, attracting liability under Section 196 for promoting enmity on the ground of caste.

A leader distributes pamphlets in Bihar claiming that members of a specific caste should be stripped of their voting rights as Indian citizens, making them liable under Section 197 for asserting that a class of persons shall be denied rights as citizens by reason of their caste.
what_it_covers: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes recognised under the Constitution of India who are targeted by reason of their caste identity.
Other Backward Classes and upper-caste groups when their caste identity is the specific ground for commission of an offence such as murder, grievous hurt, or promotion of enmity.

Any hereditary social division recognised by Indian social custom or community practice that is used as a basis to make imputations, assert denial of rights, or cause disharmony under Sections 196 and 197.
Caste-based identity used as the motivating ground for group violence, where five or more persons act in concert to commit murder or grievous hurt under Sections 103 and 117.
what_it_excludes: Religious denominations or sects that are not co-extensive with caste identity, which would fall under the category of 'religious group' or 'community' rather than caste.
Voluntary social or professional associations, clubs, or organisations formed by choice, which are not hereditary or birth-based groups.
Regional or linguistic groups identified solely by language or place of birth, which are separately enumerated in the Act as distinct grounds alongside caste.
Economic or class-based groupings defined purely by income or occupation without a hereditary or socially ascribed caste character.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is committed 'on the ground of caste' is a legally determinative fact under Sections 103 and 117, as it converts an ordinary offence into a group offence attracting mandatory enhanced punishment including death or imprisonment for life for every member of the group. Under Sections 196 and 197, caste-targeted speech or imputations constitute distinct criminal offences punishable with imprisonment, making the caste identity of the targeted class a threshold element that must be established to sustain prosecution.

definitions.definition: A certificate, within the meaning of Sections 234 and 235, is any document required by law to be given or signed, or which relates to any fact that is by law admissible in evidence, and which is issued or signed by a person in an official or authorised capacity. A false certificate is one that is incorrect or untrue in any material point.
definitions.plain_english: A certificate is an official document that a person is legally required to issue or sign, or one that records a fact which courts or authorities are allowed to treat as proof of something. Examples include medical certificates, birth certificates, or fitness certificates issued by authorised persons. If someone signs or uses such a document knowing it contains false information, it is treated as seriously as giving false testimony in court.
real_world_examples: A government doctor issues a medical fitness certificate for a job application knowing the applicant has a disqualifying condition, making the certificate false in a material point under Section 234.
A school principal signs a caste or community certificate for a student, knowing the student does not belong to that category, in order to help them claim a reserved seat in a college admission.
A registered medical practitioner issues a death certificate stating the cause of death as natural causes when they know or suspect it was a homicide, thereby creating a false certificate.
A municipal officer issues a birth certificate with a fabricated date of birth to help a candidate appear eligible for a government job that has an age bar.
A company's authorised signatory issues a false solvency certificate to a bank, knowing the company is insolvent, in order to obtain a loan.
A person corruptly uses a forged domicile certificate — knowing it is false — to claim state-quota admission in a professional college in Maharashtra.
what_it_covers: A medical certificate issued by a registered medical practitioner certifying fitness, illness, cause of death, or disability, where such certificate is required by law or admissible as evidence.
A birth, death, or marriage certificate issued by a competent authority under any statutory requirement.
A caste, domicile, income, or eligibility certificate issued by a government officer in an official capacity and admissible before any authority or court.
A fitness or inspection certificate issued under regulatory law, such as a vehicle fitness certificate or food safety certificate, that is legally required.
Any certificate that a law specifically mandates must be given or signed by a particular person or class of persons.
what_it_excludes: Private letters of recommendation or character references that are not required by law and are not admissible in evidence as certificates.
Informal attestations or self-declarations made by a private individual with no statutory authority to certify, which do not qualify as legally required certificates.
General contractual documents, agreements, or deeds that record transactions rather than certifying facts admissible as evidence under law.
An affidavit or sworn statement, which falls under the separate category of evidence given under oath rather than a certificate issued in an official capacity.
Documents that are forged in their entirety (i.e., where the signatory's identity itself is fabricated), which are more properly governed by forgery provisions under Sections 335 onwards.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'certificate' under Sections 234 and 235 determines whether issuing or using a false version of it attracts punishment equivalent to giving false evidence — one of the most serious evidentiary offences under the BNS — as opposed to lesser offences like forgery or cheating. The classification triggers strict liability-adjacent culpability for authorised signatories and corrupt users alike.
