definitions.definition: Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to cheat. A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section.
definitions.plain_english: Cheating occurs when a person tricks or deceives someone else into handing over property, agreeing to let someone keep property, or doing or not doing something they otherwise would not have done, and this deception causes or is likely to cause some harm to the deceived person. The harm can be to their finances, body, mind, or reputation. Even hiding important facts deliberately counts as deception under this definition. Simply put, it is a deliberate con or fraud that causes real or potential damage to the victim.
real_world_examples: A person poses as a government official online and convinces a Delhi resident to transfer money into a fraudulent account, claiming it is required to unfreeze a bank account, thereby dishonestly inducing delivery of property through deception.

A builder in Mumbai collects booking amounts from multiple flat buyers by showing them forged RERA registration certificates and approved floor plans for a project that does not legally exist, causing wrongful loss to the buyers.

A job placement agency in Hyderabad charges candidates lakhs of rupees as placement fees by falsely claiming to have confirmed job offers from reputed IT companies, when no such offers exist, inducing victims to pay under a misconception of fact.

A seller on an e-commerce platform based in Bengaluru dispatches cheap, counterfeit gold jewellery in place of the hallmarked gold jewellery ordered and paid for by a customer, deceiving the buyer as to the nature and quality of goods delivered.

A moneylender in a rural district of Rajasthan conceals the true rate of interest and penalty clauses in a loan agreement from an illiterate borrower, causing the borrower to sign documents they would not have signed had they known the actual terms, amounting to dishonest concealment of material facts.

A person in Chennai impersonates a civil services topper on a matrimonial platform, induces a family to agree to a marriage alliance and accept gifts, and disappears before the wedding — constituting cheating by false personation causing harm to reputation and property.
semantic_tags: harm to body mind reputation or property
what_it_covers: Deceiving someone by false representation — such as impersonating a civil servant or professional — to dishonestly obtain money, goods, or property from them.
Dishonest concealment of material facts that induces another person to act in a way they would not have acted had the facts been disclosed, causing or likely causing harm.
Inducing a person through deception to do or omit any act — not necessarily involving property transfer — that causes or is likely to cause damage to them in body, mind, reputation, or property.
Using a counterfeit mark, false sample, or forged document to deceive a buyer or lender into parting with money or valuables.
Cheating committed by a member of a group or gang as part of petty organised crime under Section 112.
what_it_excludes: A breach of contract where the person genuinely intended to perform at the time of entering the agreement but later fails to do so — this gives rise only to civil liability and not criminal cheating.
Mere negligent or innocent misstatement not accompanied by fraudulent or dishonest intent, as cheating requires deliberate deception with intent to defraud or cause wrongful loss.
Disputes over quality or quantity of goods arising from differing honest opinions or non-material misunderstandings where no deliberate deception was intended and no wrongful gain or loss results.
Acts of theft, robbery, or extortion where property is taken by force or stealth rather than obtained through deception inducing voluntary delivery by the victim.
Civil fraud or misrepresentation that causes no damage or harm — actual or likely — to the deceived person's body, mind, reputation, or property, as harm is an essential ingredient.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes cheating determines the applicability of Section 318 of the BNS, 2023, which attracts imprisonment ranging from three to seven years depending on the aggravated form of the offence, and also triggers classification of property obtained through cheating as 'stolen property' under Section 317, exposing anyone who receives or retains such property to further criminal liability. The definition also forms the predicate offence for petty organised crime under Section 112, carrying a mandatory minimum sentence of one year.

Examples: A person poses as a government official online and convinces a Delhi resident to transfer money into a fraudulent account, claiming it is required to unfreeze a bank account, thereby dishonestly inducing delivery of property through deception. | A builder in Mumbai collects booking amounts from multiple flat buyers by showing them forged RERA registration certificates and approved floor plans for a project that does not legally exist, causing wrongful loss to the buyers. | A job placement agency in Hyderabad charges candidates lakhs of rupees as placement fees by falsely claiming to have confirmed job offers from reputed IT companies, when no such offers exist, inducing victims to pay under a misconception of fact. | A seller on an e-commerce platform based in Bengaluru dispatches cheap, counterfeit gold jewellery in place of the hallmarked gold jewellery ordered and paid for by a customer, deceiving the buyer as to the nature and quality of goods delivered. | A moneylender in a rural district of Rajasthan conceals the true rate of interest and penalty clauses in a loan agreement from an illiterate borrower, causing the borrower to sign documents they would not have signed had they known the actual terms, amounting to dishonest concealment of material facts. | A person in Chennai impersonates a civil services topper on a matrimonial platform, induces a family to agree to a marriage alliance and accept gifts, and disappears before the wedding — constituting cheating by false personation causing harm to reputation and property.

Tags: fraudulent inducement by deception, dishonest concealment of facts, delivery of property by fraud, wrongful loss through misrepresentation, criminal deception causing harm, false pretence to obtain property, intentional misleading of victim, property fraud offence, consent obtained under deception, harm to body mind reputation or property

Covers: Deceiving someone by false representation — such as impersonating a civil servant or professional — to dishonestly obtain money, goods, or property from them.; Dishonest concealment of material facts that induces another person to act in a way they would not have acted had the facts been disclosed, causing or likely causing harm.; Inducing a person through deception to do or omit any act — not necessarily involving property transfer — that causes or is likely to cause damage to them in body, mind, reputation, or property.; Using a counterfeit mark, false sample, or forged document to deceive a buyer or lender into parting with money or valuables.; Cheating committed by a member of a group or gang as part of petty organised crime under Section 112.

Excludes: A breach of contract where the person genuinely intended to perform at the time of entering the agreement but later fails to do so — this gives rise only to civil liability and not criminal cheating.; Mere negligent or innocent misstatement not accompanied by fraudulent or dishonest intent, as cheating requires deliberate deception with intent to defraud or cause wrongful loss.; Disputes over quality or quantity of goods arising from differing honest opinions or non-material misunderstandings where no deliberate deception was intended and no wrongful gain or loss results.; Acts of theft, robbery, or extortion where property is taken by force or stealth rather than obtained through deception inducing voluntary delivery by the victim.; Civil fraud or misrepresentation that causes no damage or harm — actual or likely — to the deceived person's body, mind, reputation, or property, as harm is an essential ingredient.

Why it matters: Whether an act constitutes cheating determines the applicability of Section 318 of the BNS, 2023, which attracts imprisonment ranging from three to seven years depending on the aggravated form of the offence, and also triggers classification of property obtained through cheating as 'stolen property' under Section 317, exposing anyone who receives or retains such property to further criminal liability. The definition also forms the predicate offence for petty organised crime under Section 112, carrying a mandatory minimum sentence of one year.

definitions.definition: 'Child' means any person below the age of eighteen years.
definitions.plain_english: A child is any human being who has not yet completed eighteen years of age. This applies regardless of gender, nationality, or any other characteristic. The law treats children differently from adults in terms of criminal liability, consent, and protection from exploitation.
real_world_examples: A 15-year-old boy in Mumbai who is lured by a stranger and taken away from his lawful guardian constitutes kidnapping of a child under Section 137 of the BNS.
A 17-year-old girl in Delhi who is trafficked for sexual exploitation is protected under the child-specific provisions of Sections 94–99 of the BNS.
A 10-year-old child in Chennai forced to beg by an adult falls within the protective scope of Section 95 of the BNS, which specifically addresses offences against children.
A 16-year-old in Kolkata exposed to obscene material by an adult invokes child-specific penal protections under Section 295 of the BNS.
A newborn infant abandoned by parents in a public place in Bengaluru is considered a 'child' under Section 93 of the BNS, attracting liability for exposure and abandonment.
A 14-year-old in Hyderabad used by an organised crime syndicate to carry drugs is treated as a child victim under the relevant BNS provisions.
what_it_covers: Any person aged 0 to 17 years, including infants and toddlers, regardless of gender or social status.
A 17-year-and-11-month-old individual who has not yet crossed the eighteen-year threshold on the date of the offence.
A child of foreign nationality present in India who is subjected to an offence covered under the BNS.
An unborn child who is 'quick' (as referenced in related provisions), to the extent the Act's child-protective provisions are engaged.
A child in institutional care, orphanages, or under State guardianship who is below eighteen years of age.
what_it_excludes: Any person who has attained exactly eighteen years of age or is older, even by one day, on the date of the alleged offence.
A person of eighteen years or above who may be mentally or physically immature, as the definition is strictly age-based and not capacity-based.
Legal persons such as companies, associations, or bodies of persons, even if formed or managed by minors.
Animals or non-human living creatures, which are separately defined under Section 2 as 'animal'.
A person whose age cannot be determined but is presumed to be eighteen or above based on available evidence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a victim qualifies as a 'child' directly determines the applicability of aggravated offence provisions under Sections 72, 93–99, 107, 137, 139, 143, 144, and 295 of the BNS, often attracting enhanced punishments and stricter liability. It also determines whether consent of the victim can be a valid legal defence, as a child below eighteen years is deemed legally incapable of providing valid consent for several acts under the Sanhita.

definitions.definition: A 'class of citizens' refers to any identifiable group of citizens of India distinguished by a common religion or religious beliefs, whose collective religious sentiments may be outraged by deliberate and malicious acts of insult directed at their religion or religious beliefs, as contemplated under Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: A 'class of citizens' means any group of people who are citizens of India and share a common religion or set of religious beliefs. This could be Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, or any other religious community within India. The term is used to identify who is protected when someone deliberately insults a religion or its followers.
real_world_examples: A person publishes a social media post in India deliberately mocking the Quran and its teachings with the intention of hurting the sentiments of Indian Muslims — Muslim citizens of India constitute the 'class of citizens' whose religious feelings are outraged.

A public speaker at a rally in Mumbai delivers a speech using derogatory language about Hindu deities and rituals, intending to insult Hindu religious beliefs — Hindu citizens of India form the 'class of citizens' protected under Section 299.

A YouTube channel operated from within India uploads videos systematically ridiculing Sikh religious practices and the Guru Granth Sahib — Sikh citizens of India are the 'class of citizens' whose religious feelings are being targeted.

A pamphlet distributed in Chennai contains deliberate misrepresentations of Christian scriptures with malicious intent to insult Christianity — Christian citizens of India constitute the 'class of citizens' covered under this provision.

An individual in Delhi posts written content online mocking Jain religious rituals and beliefs with the intention of outraging Jain sentiments — Jain citizens of India form the relevant 'class of citizens' for the purpose of Section 299.
what_it_covers: Any recognised religious community of Indian citizens such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, or Parsis whose collective religious sentiments can be targeted.
A sub-group within a religion that is identifiable by distinct religious beliefs or practices, such as a particular sect or denomination, as long as its members are citizens of India.
A geographically dispersed group of citizens united by shared religious beliefs who collectively experience the insult to their religion, regardless of whether they are concentrated in one region.
Minority religious communities in India whose religious beliefs, scriptures, or places of worship are subjected to deliberate and malicious insult by any person.
what_it_excludes: Groups of persons who are not citizens of India, such as foreign nationals or stateless persons residing in India, as Section 299 specifically uses the phrase 'citizens of India.'

Groups defined solely by non-religious characteristics such as caste, ethnicity, language, or political affiliation, which may be protected under other provisions but do not constitute a 'class of citizens' for the purpose of Section 299.
A single individual whose personal religious sentiments are hurt, as the term requires a collective class or group of citizens sharing common religious beliefs rather than an individual complainant.
Groups defined by their secular beliefs or ideologies, such as atheists or agnostics, whose sentiments are not grounded in a religion or religious belief system as contemplated by Section 299.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of the term 'class of citizens' is a threshold requirement for an offence under Section 299; unless the alleged insult is directed at an identifiable group of Indian citizens defined by shared religious beliefs, the offence is not made out and no criminal liability for outraging religious feelings arises. It determines both who can be the victim of this offence and whether the prosecution can establish the requisite element of targeting a protected religious community.

definitions.definition: A 'class of persons' refers to a group of individuals collectively identified by a shared characteristic such as religious affiliation, racial identity, language, regional origin, caste, or community membership. The term is used in the Act to denote any identifiable collective whose members share a common defining attribute that distinguishes them from other persons, and against whom offences of communal disharmony, religious insult, or denial of rights may be directed.
definitions.plain_english: A 'class of persons' means any group of people who share a common identity — such as their religion, caste, language, or region — and are treated as a collective for the purposes of the law. For example, Sikhs as a religious group, Tamils as a linguistic group, or Dalits as a caste group would each be a 'class of persons.' The law uses this term to protect such groups from targeted hate speech, insults to their religion, or statements that deny them their rights as citizens.
real_world_examples: A social media influencer in Maharashtra posts a video claiming that Muslims cannot be loyal to the Indian Constitution because of their religion — this targets a 'class of persons' identified by religious group and attracts liability under Section 197 of the BNS.

A pamphlet distributed in Tamil Nadu asserts that Dalits, by virtue of their caste, should be denied voting rights — the Dalit community constitutes a 'class of persons' identified by caste, and the pamphlet falls within the ambit of Section 197.

A group of agitators in Uttar Pradesh vandalises a church and defiles its altar with the deliberate intention of insulting Christians — Christians as a religious community are a 'class of persons' whose place of worship is protected under Section 298.

A politician in Punjab delivers a speech asserting that Kashmiri Pandits, being a regional and religious group, owe no allegiance to India — Kashmiri Pandits constitute a 'class of persons' and such a statement triggers Section 197.

A WhatsApp forward in Karnataka spreading false claims designed to incite hatred against the Lingayat community, a religious and caste-based group, directly implicates the term 'class of persons' under Section 197 of the BNS.

An individual in West Bengal sprays graffiti on a mosque's walls with slurs intended to insult Islam — the Muslim community as a religious class is a 'class of persons' under Section 298, and the act constitutes deliberate desecration targeting that class.
what_it_covers: A religious community such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, or Buddhists identified collectively by their faith.
A caste-based group such as Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, or other caste communities recognised under Indian social and legal frameworks.
A linguistic or regional group such as Tamil speakers, Bengali speakers, or persons from a particular state or region who share a common linguistic or geographic identity.
A racial group sharing ethnically or ancestrally distinct characteristics recognised in the Indian context, such as tribal peoples of the North-East.
Any community — defined by shared social, cultural, or sectarian identity — whose members can be collectively identified as distinct from other persons.
what_it_excludes: A single named individual, as the term requires a collective group rather than a specific identifiable person.

Groups defined purely by political affiliation, profession, or economic class (e.g., farmers, lawyers, or members of a political party), which are not covered by the religious, racial, linguistic, regional, caste, or community criteria specified in the relevant sections.
Anonymous or unidentifiable aggregates of people with no common defining group characteristic, such as a random crowd at a public event with no shared identity.
Foreign nationals as a group where the context of the provision is specifically tied to rights and allegiance as citizens of India, limiting the class to identifiable citizen communities.
Legally constituted corporate entities or institutions, which are not 'persons' in the human collective sense intended by these provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a targeted group qualifies as a 'class of persons' determines whether offences under Sections 197 and 298 of the BNS are attracted — including imprisonment up to three or five years for communally prejudicial imputations and up to two years for defiling sacred places — making it the threshold criterion for prosecuting hate speech, religious insult, and denial of citizenship rights directed at identifiable communities.

definitions.definition: A person employed in the capacity of a clerk, including those employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in such capacity, in whose possession property may be held on account of another person. A person employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in the capacity of a clerk is a clerk within the meaning of this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: A 'clerk' is someone who works in an office or clerical capacity for another person or employer, whether hired permanently, temporarily, or just for a specific job or occasion. If such a person holds or handles property belonging to their employer as part of their duties, that property is legally considered to be in the employer's possession. Even a short-term or one-time clerical hire counts as a 'clerk' under this law.
real_world_examples: A full-time office clerk at a Delhi trading company who maintains the cash register and account books and steals money from the petty cash box commits theft under Section 306.

A temporary data-entry operator hired by a Mumbai firm for a two-week project who dishonestly takes confidential files or office equipment is treated as a 'clerk' and can be prosecuted under Section 306.
A freelance billing clerk engaged by a Bengaluru medical clinic specifically to prepare patient invoices who misappropriates collected fees is considered a clerk for the purposes of this Sanhita.

A peon-cum-clerk employed at a Kolkata law office who handles filed documents and stamps on behalf of the senior advocate, and who steals client files entrusted to the office, falls within the definition of 'clerk'.

A deceased Hyderabad businessman's personal accounts clerk who, knowing that his employer has died, dishonestly takes cash from the office before any legal heir takes charge, can face enhanced imprisonment under Section 315 because of his clerk status.
what_it_covers: A permanent full-time office clerk employed in a company or firm who handles the employer's property or funds in the course of duty.
A person hired temporarily or on a single specific occasion to perform clerical work, such as a contractual data-entry operator or billing assistant.
A person employed in the capacity of a clerk even if their formal job title is different, provided their actual duties are clerical in nature and they handle property on behalf of the employer.
A deceased employer's clerk who had custody or possession of the employer's property at the time of the employer's death, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 315.
what_it_excludes: An independent contractor who performs clerical-type tasks but does not work under the direction and control of an employer, and holds no property on the employer's account.
A business partner or co-owner of an enterprise, who is not in a subordinate employment relationship and cannot be classified as a 'clerk' even if they perform clerical functions.
A government or public servant who may perform clerical duties but whose liability for property offences is governed by separate provisions applicable to public servants.
A person who merely visits or assists in an office on a voluntary or gratuitous basis without any employment arrangement, whether formal or informal.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'clerk' directly determines liability under Section 306, which prescribes an aggravated punishment of up to seven years' imprisonment for theft by a clerk of property in the master's possession, as compared to ordinary theft; it also triggers enhanced imprisonment under Section 315 when a clerk dishonestly misappropriates a deceased employer's property. The definition ensures that both permanent and temporary clerical workers are equally subject to these elevated penal consequences when they breach the trust placed in them by their employer.

definitions.definition: A 'cognizable offence' means an activity prohibited by law which is punishable with imprisonment of three years or more, as used in the context of 'continuing unlawful activity' under Section 111, and in Section 199 refers to a cognizable offence as understood under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, in relation to which information is required to be recorded by a public servant under Section 173 of that Code.
definitions.plain_english: A cognizable offence is a serious crime for which the police have the power to arrest a person without needing prior permission from a court. In the context of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, it generally refers to offences that carry a punishment of three years or more in prison. These are crimes considered grave enough that immediate police action is permitted and required.
real_world_examples: A gang of criminals in Mumbai repeatedly extorts money from shopkeepers using threats of violence — each act of extortion being a cognizable offence punishable with more than three years, contributing to 'continuing unlawful activity' under organised crime provisions.

A police officer in Delhi who receives a complaint of rape under Section 64 of the BNS but refuses to register the FIR commits the offence under Section 199, because rape is a cognizable offence and recording such information is mandatory.

A drug trafficking syndicate operating across Rajasthan and Gujarat commits multiple cognizable offences of trafficking illicit substances, each carrying imprisonment of more than three years, making their collective activity an organised crime under Section 111.

A cyber fraud ring in Hyderabad conducts hawala transactions and mass-marketing fraud schemes — these economic offences qualify as cognizable offences punishable with three or more years, enabling authorities to treat the group as an organised crime syndicate.

A sub-inspector at a police station in Chennai fails to register an FIR when a woman reports being stalked and assaulted — since the offence is cognizable under the BNS, the officer's failure to record information amounts to a punishable omission under Section 199.
what_it_covers: Any offence prohibited by law and punishable with imprisonment of three years or more, as used to define 'continuing unlawful activity' under Section 111.

Specific offences listed under Section 199 such as rape (Section 64), acid attack (Section 124), and trafficking-related offences (Sections 143, 144) in relation to which a public servant must mandatorily record information.
Economic offences such as criminal breach of trust, forgery, counterfeit currency, and hawala transactions when punishable with three or more years of imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Cohabitation, as used in Section 81 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a woman living with or engaging in sexual intercourse with a man under the belief that she is lawfully married to him, where such belief has been induced by the man's deceit. It denotes the act of living together and/or having sexual relations premised on what the woman genuinely believes to be a valid and subsisting lawful marriage.
definitions.plain_english: Cohabitation here means a woman living with a man and having a sexual relationship with him, believing in good faith that they are legally married. The woman's participation is entirely based on a false belief created by the man's deliberate deception. In simple terms, the woman thinks she is a lawfully wedded wife, but she has actually been tricked into that belief by the man.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi performs a fake Hindu marriage ceremony with a woman, including all customary rituals, but does not register the marriage and is already legally married to another woman. The deceived woman lives with him as his wife and has sexual relations with him, believing the marriage to be valid under the Hindu Marriage Act.

A man in Mumbai presents forged marriage documents and convinces a woman that they are legally married. She moves in with him and cohabits as a spouse, unaware that the documents are fraudulent and no valid marriage exists in law.

A man in Chennai undergoes a religious nikah ceremony with a woman but conceals that a necessary legal condition (such as a previous marriage not being dissolved) renders the marriage void. The woman cohabits with him believing the nikah to be a lawful marriage.

A man in Kolkata persuades a woman from a rural background to live with him by staging an informal 'court marriage' with a fake stamp and fake registrar. She cohabits with him for years under the bona fide belief of being his legally wedded wife, while the entire ceremony was fabricated.

A man in Hyderabad convinces a woman that his previous marriage was dissolved by a valid divorce decree, which was actually forged, and then performs a second marriage ceremony. The woman cohabits with him in the sincere belief of being his lawful wife, not knowing the first marriage subsists and the second is therefore void.
what_it_covers: A woman who lives with and has sexual intercourse with a man sincerely believing herself to be his lawfully wedded wife, where that belief was created by the man's deliberate deceit.
Situations where a man stages or fabricates a marriage ceremony, creates false documentation, or misrepresents legal facts to induce a woman into residing with him as a wife.
Cases where a woman's ongoing sexual relations with a man are entirely premised on her mistaken but genuine belief in the existence of a valid, subsisting, lawful marriage.
what_it_excludes: Consensual live-in relationships where both parties are aware that no formal legal marriage has taken place and neither party claims otherwise.
Cases where the woman is herself aware that the marriage is not legally valid but continues to cohabit voluntarily without any deception by the man.
Cohabitation arising from a marriage that is merely voidable (but not void) and entered into without any deliberate deceit by the man regarding its lawfulness.
Sexual intercourse between parties who are in fact lawfully married to each other, regardless of any domestic dispute or irregularity in the marriage registration.
Situations where a third party (not the man himself) creates a false belief of marriage in the woman's mind without the man's knowledge or participation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether cohabitation falls within Section 81 determines if a man is criminally liable for up to ten years of imprisonment and a fine; the offence is triggered only when the woman's participation in cohabitation or sexual intercourse is shown to rest entirely on a deceit-induced false belief of lawful marriage, making the man's act of deception the operative criminal element rather than the physical act of cohabitation itself.

definitions.definition: 'Coin' shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 2 of the Coinage Act, 2011 and includes metal used for the time being as money and is stamped and issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power intended to be so used. A person commits the offence of counterfeiting coin who, intending to practise deception, or knowing it to be likely that deception will thereby be practised, causes a genuine coin to appear like a different coin.
definitions.plain_english: A 'coin' is any piece of metal that is officially stamped and issued by a government or sovereign authority to be used as money. This includes all current Indian currency coins issued by the Reserve Bank of India or the Government of India, as well as coins issued by any foreign government intended to function as money. The term also covers the act of making a real coin look like a different coin in order to deceive someone.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai melts down zinc and copper to produce fake ₹10 coins resembling genuine RBI-issued coins and attempts to circulate them in local markets — this falls squarely within the 'coin' definition for the offence of counterfeiting under Section 178.

A shopkeeper in Delhi files down the edges of genuine ₹5 coins and recoats them to make them appear as ₹10 coins, intending to pass them off as higher denomination currency — this constitutes counterfeiting a coin by causing one genuine coin to appear like a different coin.

A syndicate in Chennai operates a setup that stamps brass discs with the impression of Indian government coins and distributes them as genuine currency in rural areas — the brass discs being intended to be used as money and stamped to resemble sovereign-issued coins bring them within the definition.

A person in Kolkata uses acid treatment on genuine old colonial-era British Indian coins to make them appear as rare collector's coins of higher denomination, thereby deceiving buyers into paying more — this manipulation of a genuine coin to appear like a different coin constitutes counterfeiting within the meaning of Section 178.

An individual arrested at a border crossing into Nepal is found carrying machine-pressed metal discs stamped with Indian government insignia intended for circulation as ₹2 coins — these discs, being metal stamped to imitate sovereign-issued currency intended as money, fall within the definition of 'coin' for purposes of counterfeiting offences.
what_it_covers: All metal coins currently issued by or under the authority of the Government of India or the Reserve Bank of India (e.g., ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20 coins) intended to be used as money.
Coins issued by any foreign State or Sovereign Power and stamped for use as money, such as US quarters, British pounds sterling in coin form, or UAE dirhams in coin form.
Metal that is stamped and issued by a sovereign authority and used as money at any given time, even if not part of a formal coinage series, including commemorative coins with legal tender status.
A genuine coin that has been manipulated or altered to appear like a different coin, where such manipulation is done with intent to deceive or with knowledge that deception is likely.
Counterfeit metal discs or tokens designed and stamped to resemble and pass off as genuine sovereign-issued coins.
what_it_excludes: Paper currency notes, bank-notes, or promissory notes issued by banking institutions, which are separately defined and governed as 'currency-note' or 'bank-note' under the same section.

Medallions, tokens, or commemorative metal pieces that are not issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power and are not intended to be used as money (e.g., gaming tokens, metro tokens used as transport passes, temple prasad coins).

Digital currency, cryptocurrency, or virtual coins such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, which are not metal, not stamped by a sovereign authority, and not issued as legal tender by a State or Sovereign Power.
Unstamped metal ingots or bullion, even if made of gold or silver, as they are not stamped and issued as money by a sovereign authority.
Foreign coins that are no longer in circulation or have been demonetised and are not currently intended to be used as money, unless retained within the definition by specific notification.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an object qualifies as a 'coin' under Section 178 determines whether a person can be charged with the serious offence of counterfeiting — punishable with imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine — as opposed to a lesser offence involving non-monetary property; it also directly triggers liability under Sections 179, 181, and 187 of the BNS, 2023, which deal with possession and use of counterfeit coins and coining tools.

definitions.definition: A coining tool is any instrument or device used within a lawfully established mint for the purpose of manufacturing, stamping, or producing coins, which if removed without lawful authority from such mint constitutes a punishable offence under Section 188 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: A coining tool is any piece of equipment or machinery specifically used inside a government-authorised mint to make coins. This includes dies, presses, stamps, or any other device that is part of the coin-making process. Taking such a tool out of the mint without permission is a serious crime because it could be used to make fake coins.
real_world_examples: A worker at the India Government Mint in Mumbai secretly removes a die (a metal stamp used to press coin designs) in his bag, intending to use it to produce counterfeit currency at home — this constitutes removal of a coining tool under Section 188.

An employee at the Kolkata Mint takes out a hydraulic coin press component without authorisation, planning to sell it to a criminal syndicate that manufactures fake coins — the component qualifies as a coining tool and its removal is an offence.

A maintenance technician at the Hyderabad Mint removes a hardened steel blanking die, used to cut coin blanks from metal strips, during a night shift without any official sanction — this is an unlawful removal of a coining instrument.

A security guard at the Noida Mint facility smuggles out a collar die (used to give coins their edge markings) intending to sell it to a counterfeiting gang operating in Delhi — the collar die is a coining tool under the meaning of Section 188.

A contractor engaged for renovation at the Mumbai Mint pockets a proof coin polishing instrument used to finish commemorative coins, without authorisation — this instrument, being used in the coin-making process within the mint, qualifies as a coining tool.
what_it_covers: Metal dies used to stamp the design, value, and inscription onto coin blanks inside a government mint.
Hydraulic or mechanical coin presses and their components used to strike metal blanks into finished coins within the mint premises.
Collar dies, blanking dies, proof polishing machines, and any other specialised instrument integral to the coin production process at a lawfully established mint.
Hardened steel or alloy tools used for engraving, reducing, or transferring coin designs as part of the minting process.
Any instrument or device that forms part of the operational machinery of a lawfully established mint and is used at any stage of coin fabrication.
what_it_excludes: General tools such as screwdrivers, hammers, or wrenches used merely for maintenance or repair of mint infrastructure, which are not specific to the coin-making process.
Finished coins or coin blanks themselves, which are products of the minting process rather than instruments used to produce coins.
Documents, records, or administrative equipment (such as computers or weighing scales used for inventory) found within the mint that do not directly participate in the physical production of coins.
Coining tools or instruments that are removed from the mint with proper lawful authority or official sanction, as Section 188 exclusively covers unauthorised removal.

Equipment used in private or unauthorised coin-like token manufacturing operations outside a lawfully established mint, as the provision specifically applies to instruments within government-authorised mints.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'coining tool' determines whether its unauthorised removal from a mint triggers the offence under Section 188, which carries imprisonment of up to seven years and a fine. The definition is also critical because possession of such tools outside the mint could be linked to offences of counterfeiting coin under related provisions, making correct identification of the term essential for prosecution and defence.

definitions.definition: Acting under 'colour of office' means performing or purporting to perform an act in the assumed capacity or apparent authority of a public office, whether or not such act is strictly justifiable by law, so long as it is done in good faith in the exercise of what that officer believes to be the duties or powers of that office. The term also covers acts done by a person who falsely personates a public servant and, in that assumed character, attempts to exercise the functions or authority of such office.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'under colour of office' means doing something while using your official position — or pretending to have one — as the basis or justification for that action, even if the action is not perfectly legal. It refers to situations where a government official (or someone impersonating one) uses the appearance or claim of official authority to carry out an act. The key idea is that the act is dressed up as an exercise of official power, whether or not the person truly has that power.
real_world_examples: A police constable in Mumbai enters a private premises and conducts an informal search without a proper warrant, claiming it is part of an ongoing investigation — this is an act done under colour of his office as a public servant, even if not strictly legally justified.

A revenue official in a district in Uttar Pradesh seizes agricultural produce from a farmer claiming it is contraband, acting on a mistaken belief that his office empowers him to do so — such seizure, done in good faith, is an act under colour of office.

A person in Delhi dresses up in a police uniform and pretends to be a sub-inspector, then 'inspects' a shopkeeper's goods and demands documentation — this is an act done under colour of office by someone falsely personating a public servant, attracting punishment under Section 204.

A forest officer in Jharkhand detains a group of villagers cutting wood, believing (even if incorrectly) that his forest department authority permits such detention — this detention, undertaken as part of his official duties, is carried out under colour of his office.

An excise inspector in Karnataka seizes a vehicle carrying what he believes to be smuggled liquor, acting under departmental instructions that are later found to be procedurally defective — the seizure is still considered done under colour of office since it was done in good faith in his official capacity.
what_it_covers: An act done by a genuine public servant in good faith, purportedly within the scope of their official duties, even if that act exceeds or is not strictly permitted by law.

A direction given by a public servant to another person to carry out an act, where that direction is issued in the apparent exercise of the servant's official authority, even if the direction is not wholly lawful.
An act done by a person who falsely personates a public servant and, while maintaining that false identity, attempts to exercise the powers or functions of that assumed office (Section 204).

Conduct of a public servant that creates a reasonable appearance of being an exercise of official power, including issuing orders, making arrests, conducting searches, or seizing property under claimed departmental authority.
what_it_excludes: Acts done by a public servant in a purely private or personal capacity, with no connection whatsoever to the duties or powers of their office, do not fall under colour of office.

Acts motivated by purely personal malice, corruption, or private gain where the officer makes no claim to be acting in any official function — such acts are not shielded by the colour of office doctrine.
Acts that cause or reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt — even if done under colour of office, these do not extinguish the right of private defence under Section 37.

Actions where the person acting under an assumed official role has no plausible or apparent connection to the office claimed, and no reasonable person would believe them to be exercising genuine official authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'under colour of office' directly determines whether a citizen retains the right of private defence against that act — under Section 37, such acts by public servants acting in good faith suspend that right even if the act is not strictly legal. Under Section 204, doing any act 'under colour of' a falsely assumed public office constitutes a cognizable criminal offence punishable with imprisonment of not less than six months and up to three years.

Examples: A police constable in Mumbai enters a private premises and conducts an informal search without a proper warrant, claiming it is part of an ongoing investigation — this is an act done under colour of his office as a public servant, even if not strictly legally justified. | A revenue official in a district in Uttar Pradesh seizes agricultural produce from a farmer claiming it is contraband, acting on a mistaken belief that his office empowers him to do so — such seizure, done in good faith, is an act under colour of office. | A person in Delhi dresses up in a police uniform and pretends to be a sub-inspector, then 'inspects' a shopkeeper's goods and demands documentation — this is an act done under colour of office by someone falsely personating a public servant, attracting punishment under Section 204. | A forest officer in Jharkhand detains a group of villagers cutting wood, believing (even if incorrectly) that his forest department authority permits such detention — this detention, undertaken as part of his official duties, is carried out under colour of his office. | An excise inspector in Karnataka seizes a vehicle carrying what he believes to be smuggled liquor, acting under departmental instructions that are later found to be procedurally defective — the seizure is still considered done under colour of office since it was done in good faith in his official capacity.

Tags: apparent official authority, public servant good faith act, official capacity defence, right of private defence limitation, personation of public servant, colour of authority doctrine, non-strictly-justified official act, assumed government office powers, public office impersonation offence, good faith exercise of duty

Covers: An act done by a genuine public servant in good faith, purportedly within the scope of their official duties, even if that act exceeds or is not strictly permitted by law.; A direction given by a public servant to another person to carry out an act, where that direction is issued in the apparent exercise of the servant's official authority, even if the direction is not wholly lawful.; An act done by a person who falsely personates a public servant and, while maintaining that false identity, attempts to exercise the powers or functions of that assumed office (Section 204).; Conduct of a public servant that creates a reasonable appearance of being an exercise of official power, including issuing orders, making arrests, conducting searches, or seizing property under claimed departmental authority.

Excludes: Acts done by a public servant in a purely private or personal capacity, with no connection whatsoever to the duties or powers of their office, do not fall under colour of office.; Acts motivated by purely personal malice, corruption, or private gain where the officer makes no claim to be acting in any official function — such acts are not shielded by the colour of office doctrine.; Acts that cause or reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt — even if done under colour of office, these do not extinguish the right of private defence under Section 37.; Actions where the person acting under an assumed official role has no plausible or apparent connection to the office claimed, and no reasonable person would believe them to be exercising genuine official authority.

Why it matters: Whether an act is done 'under colour of office' directly determines whether a citizen retains the right of private defence against that act — under Section 37, such acts by public servants acting in good faith suspend that right even if the act is not strictly legal. Under Section 204, doing any act 'under colour of' a falsely assumed public office constitutes a cognizable criminal offence punishable with imprisonment of not less than six months and up to three years.

(Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)

definitions.definition: Combustible matter refers to any substance or material, other than fire itself, that is capable of catching fire and burning, and which when handled rashly or negligently may endanger human life or cause hurt or injury to any person. The term is used in Section 287 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 in conjunction with fire to describe materials whose careless possession or use may attract criminal liability.
definitions.plain_english: Combustible matter means any material that can easily catch fire and burn. This includes things like petrol, kerosene, LPG gas cylinders, firecrackers, dry hay, and similar substances that pose a fire hazard. If a person handles such material carelessly and puts others' lives at risk, they can be punished under the law. It is different from fire itself — it refers to the fuel or substance that can ignite.
real_world_examples: A shop owner in a Delhi market negligently stores large quantities of loose firecrackers without proper safety measures during Diwali season, causing a fire that injures several customers — this constitutes rash handling of combustible matter under Section 287.

A truck driver in Gujarat carelessly parks a petrol tanker near a residential colony without engaging safety protocols, allowing fuel vapours to accumulate and risking explosion and injury to residents nearby.

A factory worker in Maharashtra leaves industrial solvent-soaked rags in an open area next to electrical equipment without disposing of them safely, creating a fire hazard that endangers co-workers' lives.
A street vendor in Mumbai uses a makeshift kerosene stove in a congested market lane without a safety guard, rashly causing the kerosene container to tip over and catch fire, injuring bystanders.

A construction contractor in Chennai stores large drums of tar and flammable paint thinners in an open, unventilated space adjacent to a school building, negligently endangering the lives of children inside.

A gas agency worker in Kolkata negligently mishandles LPG cylinders during delivery, allowing gas to leak in a residential apartment building, thereby creating a life-threatening fire hazard for all occupants.
what_it_covers: Petroleum products such as petrol, diesel, and kerosene that are easily ignitable and commonly stored or transported in India.
Industrial chemicals and solvents like paint thinner, acetone, and turpentine that have low flash points and can combust rapidly.
Fireworks, crackers, and pyrotechnic materials that are combustible and widely used in Indian festivals and celebrations.
Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) in cylinders used in households and commercial kitchens across India, which is highly combustible if mishandled.
Dry biomass materials such as straw, hay, sugarcane waste (bagasse), and dry leaves that are commonly found in rural India and can catch fire easily.
Gunpowder, explosives, and propellants stored or transported in manufacturing or mining contexts that qualify as combustible matter.
what_it_excludes: Fire itself, which is separately mentioned alongside combustible matter in Section 287 and is treated as a distinct hazard from the material that burns.
Poisonous or toxic substances that do not combust but endanger life through chemical harm, which are governed separately under Section 286 of the BNS.
Non-flammable corrosive substances such as concentrated acids or alkalis that cause harm through chemical reaction rather than combustion, covered under the term 'corrosive substance'.
Explosive substances as a distinct legal category, which may attract separate and more specific provisions under special laws such as the Explosives Act, 1884.
Electrical equipment or machinery that may cause fire as a secondary consequence but is not itself a combustible matter in the primary sense.
Water or inert non-flammable materials that present no risk of combustion and therefore cannot trigger liability under Section 287.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'combustible matter' determines whether Section 287 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is attracted, exposing the accused to imprisonment of up to six months and/or a fine of up to two thousand rupees for rash or negligent conduct. The definition is critical in distinguishing liability under Section 287 (fire and combustibles) from Section 286 (poisonous substances) and in establishing the actus reus of negligent endangerment offences.

definitions.definition: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. Common intention denotes a pre-arranged plan or shared purpose among multiple persons to commit a specific criminal act together.
definitions.plain_english: Common intention means that two or more people share the same goal or plan to commit a crime, and each person actively participates in carrying it out. When people act together with this shared purpose, the law treats each of them as if they personally committed the entire crime themselves. This means every member of the group can be held equally responsible even if only one of them directly performed the harmful act.
real_world_examples: A group of five men in Delhi plan together to assault and rob a shopkeeper; even if only two of them physically beat the shopkeeper while the others stood watch, all five are equally liable for the assault and robbery under common intention.

In a gang rape case in Mumbai, where three men acting together rape a woman, each of the three is deemed to have committed rape individually and faces the same punishment under Section 70 of the BNS, even if not all physically participated in every act.

Members of a mob in Uttar Pradesh who collectively plan to destroy a rival's property and then proceed to burn down his shop — each member shares the common intention and is equally liable for mischief by fire, regardless of who struck the match.

In a contract killing case in Chennai, where one person hires two others to murder a business rival and all three plan the murder together, each of the three — including the one who did not physically deliver the fatal blow — is held liable for murder under common intention.

A group of thieves in Kolkata plan and execute a house burglary together: one breaks the lock, one keeps watch outside, and one collects the valuables. All are equally guilty of house-breaking and theft because they acted in furtherance of their common intention.

During a communal riot in Ahmedabad, where members of a group collectively attack individuals from another community with the shared intent to cause grievous hurt, every participating member is liable for the grievous hurt caused by any member of the group.
what_it_covers: A situation where multiple persons pre-plan and jointly execute a criminal act, each being held fully liable as if they committed the act alone.
Cases where only one member of a group physically commits the harmful act but all members shared the same intention beforehand, such as one person stabbing a victim while others restrained him.
Gang rape scenarios under Section 70 where one or more persons act together in furtherance of a common intention, resulting in each being deemed to have committed rape independently.
Situations where members play different supportive roles (lookout, driver, attacker) in executing a criminal plan, all being equally culpable for the final criminal act.
Acts done by a group where the common intention was formed on the spot before the criminal act but sufficiently in advance of execution, indicating a shared plan even if briefly pre-arranged.
what_it_excludes: Situations where persons independently and coincidentally commit similar acts without any prior meeting of minds or shared plan — mere presence at the scene of a crime without shared intent is not sufficient.

Cases where one accused had a different or separate intention from the others; common intention requires unity of purpose, so if one person intended only to cause hurt while others intended murder, the divergent member does not share common intention for murder.
Acts committed by a person under criminal knowledge alone without sharing intention — the provision on criminal knowledge (also in Section 3) is a separate and distinct concept from common intention.

Offences where the criminal act was an independent, spontaneous reaction by one group member that went beyond the shared plan — liability for such excess acts does not automatically flow from common intention.
Situations involving a child under seven years of age, who by the general exceptions in the BNS cannot be party to a common intention as they are incapable of forming criminal intent.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of common intention determines whether all accused in a group crime are equally punishable for the entire offence regardless of their individual physical role, which is critical for convictions in cases of murder, robbery, dacoity, and gang rape. Without establishing common intention, each accused can only be held liable for their own specific act, drastically reducing criminal liability and potential sentencing.

definitions.definition: The 'common object' of an unlawful assembly is the shared unlawful purpose that unites five or more persons, as enumerated in Section 189 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, including overawing governmental authority by criminal force, resisting execution of law, committing mischief or criminal trespass, taking possession of property by criminal force, or compelling any person to do or omit an act by criminal force. Every member of such assembly is guilty of any offence committed by any member in prosecution of that common object, or which the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution thereof.
definitions.plain_english: The 'common object' is the shared goal or purpose that brings a group of five or more people together to do something unlawful. Unlike a secret agreement, this shared purpose can be inferred from the group's conduct and need not be formally agreed upon. If any member of the group commits a crime while pursuing this shared goal, every other member of the group is also legally responsible for that crime.
real_world_examples: A mob of more than five people gathers outside a government office in Lucknow with the common object of preventing revenue officers from carrying out a lawful eviction, blocking them by showing force and threatening them — every member of that mob is guilty of the offence of rioting and obstructing public servants.

A group of villagers in Haryana assemble with the common object of forcibly taking back agricultural land from a neighbouring farmer they believe has encroached, using lathis and threatening violence — each member is liable for criminal trespass and any hurt caused, even those who did not personally strike anyone.

During a communal tension episode in Ahmedabad, a crowd of over five persons assembles with the shared purpose of looting and burning shops belonging to a particular community — each member of that assembly is guilty of mischief and rioting regardless of their individual acts.

A group of workers in Mumbai, numbering more than five, assemble outside a factory gate with the common object of physically preventing the management from entering and conducting business, using threats and criminal force — every member is liable for unlawful assembly and any offence committed in furtherance of this object.

A gang of over five persons in Delhi gathers with the shared goal of intimidating a witness scheduled to testify in a court case, surrounding and threatening him on the street — each member bears criminal liability for criminal intimidation committed in prosecution of that common object.
what_it_covers: A shared goal to overawe the Central or State Government, Parliament, State Legislature, or any public servant in the exercise of lawful power by criminal force or show of criminal force.
A collective purpose to resist execution of any law or legal process, such as a group jointly preventing police from executing a lawful arrest warrant.
A joint intention to commit mischief, criminal trespass, or any other offence as the unifying aim of five or more assembled persons.
A shared objective of taking or obtaining possession of property, or depriving any person of enjoyment of a right of way or incorporeal right, through criminal force or show thereof.
A common aim to compel any person to do something they are not legally bound to do, or to omit doing something they are legally entitled to do, by means of criminal force.
what_it_excludes: A lawful assembly that subsequently disperses before committing any act in furtherance of an unlawful purpose — the common object must exist at the time of the offence being committed.

A purely private or individual intention of a single member of the assembly that is not shared by the others and is not known to them — isolated personal motives do not constitute the common object of the whole assembly.

A mere agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act without any assembly of five or more persons — that would be criminal conspiracy under Section 61, not an unlawful assembly with a common object.

A gathering of five or more persons assembled for a lawful purpose, such as a licensed public meeting or religious procession, even if some individual members harbour unlawful intentions unknown to the rest.
An accidental or spontaneous congregating of people at an incident scene without any shared unlawful purpose uniting them, such as bystanders gathering at an accident.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of a 'common object' is the cornerstone that triggers collective criminal liability under Sections 189, 190, and 191 of the BNS — if established, every member of the unlawful assembly becomes equally guilty of any offence committed by any member in prosecution of that object, regardless of their individual acts, and is liable for punishment including imprisonment. Conversely, if no common object is proved, individual members can only be held liable for their own specific acts, significantly limiting the scope of prosecution.

definitions.definition: The term 'community' is not independently defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; however, it is subsumed within the definition of 'public', which states: 'public' includes any class of the public or any community. As used in Sections 196, 197, and 353, 'community' refers to a group of persons sharing a common identity such as religion, race, caste, language, region, or similar social characteristic, whose harmony, peace, or collective interests may be affected by acts of provocation, hatred, or incitement.
definitions.plain_english: A 'community' is a group of people who share something in common — such as their religion, caste, race, language, or where they come from. The law uses this word to refer to such groups when someone's actions could cause hatred, violence, or unrest among or between these groups. It is a broad term and is treated as part of the wider 'public' under the Act.
real_world_examples: A person in Uttar Pradesh publishes and distributes pamphlets making false and inflammatory claims about the Muslim community, claiming they are engaged in anti-national activities, thereby promoting enmity between Hindu and Muslim communities — this triggers Section 196 of the BNS.

A politician in Maharashtra gives a public speech targeting the Scheduled Caste community, using derogatory language intended to incite hatred and violence against them from dominant caste groups — an offence under Section 196 read with Section 197.

A WhatsApp message circulated in Tamil Nadu falsely claims that people from a particular linguistic community (e.g., Hindi-speakers) attacked local residents, leading to communal tension — the originator of the message may be prosecuted under Section 353 for statements conducing to public mischief against that community.

A YouTube channel repeatedly broadcasts videos vilifying the Sikh community by spreading false narratives about their religious practices to provoke public disorder — this constitutes an act prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between religious communities under Section 196.

During elections in West Bengal, a candidate circulates fake news targeting the Bengali Hindu community claiming another community is responsible for local crimes, thereby inciting inter-community violence — an offence under Section 197 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Religious communities such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, and Parsis when targeted collectively by acts of incitement or hatred.
Communities defined by caste, race, or tribe, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, when subjected to group-directed hostility or prejudice.
Linguistic or regional communities (e.g., speakers of a particular language or residents of a particular region) when acts are designed to promote enmity or disharmony against them as a group.
Any identifiable group of persons sharing a common social, ethnic, or cultural identity whose collective peace or dignity is harmed by provocative statements or acts.
what_it_excludes: A single individual or a private dispute between two persons, which does not involve group identity or collective harm — personal offences do not invoke the 'community' dimension of Sections 196, 197, or 353.

A purely professional or occupational grouping (e.g., all doctors or all lawyers) that does not share a social, religious, caste, racial, or linguistic identity recognised as a community under social and legal norms.

The general undifferentiated public at large where no specific community identity is targeted — mere public disturbance without a community-directed element does not satisfy the 'community' threshold in the relevant sections.

Corporations, companies, or incorporated associations, which are covered separately as 'persons' under Section 2 but do not constitute a 'community' in the social or ethnic sense used in Sections 196, 197, and 353.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a group qualifies as a 'community' determines the applicability of Sections 196, 197, and 353 of the BNS, which create criminal liability for promoting enmity, hatred, or ill-will between groups and for making statements prejudicial to public peace; if the targeted group constitutes a 'community', acts directed against it can attract imprisonment of up to three to five years, whereas acts against non-community groupings may not attract these specific provisions.

Examples: A person in Uttar Pradesh publishes and distributes pamphlets making false and inflammatory claims about the Muslim community, claiming they are engaged in anti-national activities, thereby promoting enmity between Hindu and Muslim communities — this triggers Section 196 of the BNS. | A politician in Maharashtra gives a public speech targeting the Scheduled Caste community, using derogatory language intended to incite hatred and violence against them from dominant caste groups — an offence under Section 196 read with Section 197. | A WhatsApp message circulated in Tamil Nadu falsely claims that people from a particular linguistic community (e.g., Hindi-speakers) attacked local residents, leading to communal tension — the originator of the message may be prosecuted under Section 353 for statements conducing to public mischief against that community. | A YouTube channel repeatedly broadcasts videos vilifying the Sikh community by spreading false narratives about their religious practices to provoke public disorder — this constitutes an act prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between religious communities under Section 196. | During elections in West Bengal, a candidate circulates fake news targeting the Bengali Hindu community claiming another community is responsible for local crimes, thereby inciting inter-community violence — an offence under Section 197 of the BNS.

Covers: Religious communities such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, and Parsis when targeted collectively by acts of incitement or hatred.; Communities defined by caste, race, or tribe, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, when subjected to group-directed hostility or prejudice.; Linguistic or regional communities (e.g., speakers of a particular language or residents of a particular region) when acts are designed to promote enmity or disharmony against them as a group.; Any identifiable group of persons sharing a common social, ethnic, or cultural identity whose collective peace or dignity is harmed by provocative statements or acts.

Excludes: A single individual or a private dispute between two persons, which does not involve group identity or collective harm — personal offences do not invoke the 'community' dimension of Sections 196, 197, or 353.; A purely professional or occupational grouping (e.g., all doctors or all lawyers) that does not share a social, religious, caste, racial, or linguistic identity recognised as a community under social and legal norms.; The general undifferentiated public at large where no specific community identity is targeted — mere public disturbance without a community-directed element does not satisfy the 'community' threshold in the relevant sections.; Corporations, companies, or incorporated associations, which are covered separately as 'persons' under Section 2 but do not constitute a 'community' in the social or ethnic sense used in Sections 196, 197, and 353.

Why it matters: Whether a group qualifies as a 'community' determines the applicability of Sections 196, 197, and 353 of the BNS, which create criminal liability for promoting enmity, hatred, or ill-will between groups and for making statements prejudicial to public peace; if the targeted group constitutes a 'community', acts directed against it can attract imprisonment of up to three to five years, whereas acts against non-community groupings may not attract these specific provisions.

definitions.definition: Community Service is a form of punishment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, enumerated alongside death, imprisonment, forfeiture of property, and fine as one of the punishments to which offenders are liable. It constitutes unpaid work performed by an offender for the benefit of the community as directed by a Court, and in default of community service, the Court may impose simple imprisonment not exceeding two months where the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees, four months where it does not exceed ten thousand rupees, and one year in any other case.
definitions.plain_english: Community service is a punishment where instead of going to jail or paying a fine, a convicted person is ordered by the court to do unpaid work for the benefit of the public or community. It is one of the official punishments listed under Indian criminal law. If the person refuses to do the community service ordered by the court, they can be sent to simple imprisonment for a limited period.
real_world_examples: A government clerk in Delhi, convicted of engaging in trade while being a public servant under Section 202 of BNS, is ordered by the magistrate to perform community service at a local government hospital for three months instead of imprisonment.

A first-time offender in Mumbai who fails to appear before the court in response to a proclamation under Section 209 of BNS is sentenced to community service such as cleaning public parks or assisting at municipal shelters as an alternative to fine or imprisonment.

A young person convicted of a minor offence in a Bengaluru court is sentenced to community service at an old-age home or an orphanage for 60 days, reflecting the reformative purpose of the new criminal code.

A public servant in Chennai found illegally engaging in private trade is ordered to perform community service at a government dispensary, assisting staff on weekends, as part of a rehabilitative sentence under Section 202 BNS.

A proclaimed offender in Hyderabad whose case falls under the lesser limb of Section 209 (without the seven-year enhanced punishment) is directed by the sessions court to undertake community service at a local school, teaching basic literacy skills.
what_it_covers: Unpaid work directed by a court for the benefit of the public or community as a standalone or alternative punishment for a convicted offender.
Situations where a court sentences an offender to community service in lieu of or alongside fine or imprisonment for offences such as those under Sections 202 and 209 of BNS.

Default imprisonment triggered when an offender fails to comply with a court-ordered community service, which shall be simple imprisonment and shall not exceed two months, four months, or one year depending on the corresponding fine amount.
Community service as a punishment available for offences declared punishable with fine or community service, where the court exercises discretion in choosing the appropriate penal consequence.
what_it_excludes: Rigorous imprisonment with hard labour, which is a separate and distinct form of punishment and cannot be imposed in default of community service — default imprisonment must be simple in nature.
Payment of monetary compensation or fine to the victim or the State, which constitutes a separate punishment category ('Fine') distinct from community service.
Forfeiture of property, death, or imprisonment for life, which are independent punishments under Section 4 and are not substitutable with or convertible into community service.
Voluntary social work or charitable activities undertaken by an individual outside of a court order, which carry no penal authority or legal obligation.
Enhanced punishment for proclaimed offenders under the second limb of Section 209 (imprisonment up to seven years with fine), where community service is not available as an alternative.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether community service applies determines whether a court may impose a rehabilitative non-custodial sentence rather than imprisonment or fine, directly affecting the liberty and record of the offender; non-compliance with a community service order triggers default simple imprisonment, making its imposition a legally enforceable judicial directive with penal consequences.

definitions.definition: Commutation, as governed by Section 5 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the substitution of one form of punishment awarded by a Court with another lesser or different form of punishment, effected by the appropriate Government without requiring the consent of the offender, in accordance with Section 474 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. It also denotes the altered punitive status of an offender whose original sentence has been so substituted, as referenced in Sections 8, 260, and 263 of the Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: Commutation means that the government officially changes a person's punishment to a different, usually less severe one — for example, changing a death sentence to life imprisonment. This change is made by the Central or State Government depending on the nature of the offence, and the offender's agreement is not needed. Once commuted, the offender serves the new, substituted punishment instead of the original one.
real_world_examples: A convict on death row in a case involving a Union subject (e.g., a terrorism offence) has their sentence commuted by the Central Government to life imprisonment following a mercy petition review.
A State Government commutes the life imprisonment sentence of an elderly convict to rigorous imprisonment for ten years on grounds of medical condition and good conduct in prison.

A public servant who intentionally allows a person subject to a commuted sentence of life imprisonment to escape is punished under Section 260, because the offender's commuted status is treated as equivalent to the original sentence for purposes of that offence.

A convict sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for fourteen years has their sentence commuted to simple imprisonment for seven years by the State Government following a constitutional review under Article 161.

In default of payment of a fine, a court calculates additional imprisonment ensuring it does not exceed the term that would apply under a commutation of the original sentence, as required under Section 8 of the Sanhita.

The Maharashtra Government commutes the death sentence of a murder convict to life imprisonment after the President's rejection of a mercy petition, and the commuted sentence is then used to determine the public servant's liability under Section 260 if confinement is breached.
what_it_covers: Substitution of a death sentence with imprisonment for life by the appropriate Government under Section 5.
Substitution of a sentence of life imprisonment or any other imprisonment with a lesser term or different description of punishment by the Central or State Government.
The commuted status of an offender for determining a public servant's culpability under Section 260 when the offender escapes or is allowed to escape.
The commuted sentence as a reference point for calculating default imprisonment in lieu of fine under Section 8.
Commutation effected without the offender's consent, making it a unilateral executive act.
what_it_excludes: Remission of sentence, which reduces the duration of a punishment without changing its character, as opposed to commutation which substitutes one type of punishment for another.
Pardons or acquittals granted by the judiciary, which extinguish punishment altogether rather than substituting it.
Voluntary agreements or plea bargains between the offender and the prosecution, which are not commutations and require the offender's participation and consent.
Suspension of sentence or bail, which temporarily delays execution of punishment rather than permanently altering it.
Changes to punishment effected by a court through appeal or revision, which are judicial modifications distinct from the executive act of commutation.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal status of an offender as subject to a commuted sentence directly determines the severity of punishment imposed on a public servant who intentionally allows that offender to escape under Section 260, and affects the calculation of default imprisonment in lieu of fine under Section 8. Whether a sentence has been commuted also determines which level of government — Central or State — has the authority to act, and triggers or blocks liability under offences related to confinement and lawful apprehension.
