definitions.definition: Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal force means deliberately applying physical force on another person without their permission, either to commit a crime, or to cause that person pain, fear, or discomfort. The force can be direct (like pushing someone) or indirect (like setting an object in motion that affects them). The key elements are that it must be intentional, without consent, and aimed at causing some harm, fear, or annoyance, or done to facilitate another offence.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi deliberately shoves a woman in a crowded metro to outrage her modesty — the intentional push without her consent, intended to cause fear and annoyance, constitutes criminal force under Section 74 read with Section 129.

A mob leader in Mumbai directs his followers to physically restrain a shopkeeper and drag him out of his shop to prevent him from calling police during a robbery — the intentional application of bodily force without consent to facilitate the commission of a dacoity amounts to criminal force.

A landlord in Chennai sets a large aggressive dog on a tenant who has refused to vacate, causing the tenant to flee in fear — using the animal as an instrument to cause motion resulting in fear and annoyance to the tenant qualifies as criminal force.

During a political rally in Uttar Pradesh, a local strongman grabs a candidate's microphone out of his hand with a forceful yank, intending to silence him and cause him annoyance — this intentional physical act without consent to cause annoyance constitutes criminal force.

A factory supervisor in Surat forcibly pushes a worker against a wall to intimidate him into withdrawing a wage complaint — the deliberate physical contact intended to cause fear and injury falls squarely within the definition of criminal force.

In Kolkata, a group of individuals deliberately unfasten a vendor's cart on a slope, causing it to roll into him, knowing it would injure him — this indirect but intentional causation of motion resulting in injury constitutes criminal force.
what_it_covers: Directly striking, pushing, grabbing, or restraining a person without their consent with the intent to cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
Indirectly causing force by setting objects or animals in motion that act upon a person's body, such as releasing a vehicle, untying a boat, or directing an animal to attack.
Using force on a person without consent in order to facilitate the commission of another offence, such as robbing, outrage of modesty, or disrobing.
Causing motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in another person's body by any means, including through a third substance or mechanism, where such act is intentional and without consent.

Force applied to a person who is in a particular position or state — such as drugged or restrained — where the accused intentionally manipulates circumstances to produce a physical effect on that person.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or unintentional application of force — for example, accidentally bumping into someone in a crowd without any intent to cause injury, fear, or annoyance does not constitute criminal force.
Force applied with the free and voluntary consent of the person on whom it is used, such as physical contact in a consensual sporting contest or medical procedure performed with patient consent.

Mere threats or gestures that do not involve any actual application of force to the body of another person — these may constitute assault or criminal intimidation but not criminal force by themselves.
Lawful exercise of force by a public servant or private individual acting within the right of private defence or under lawful authority, provided such force does not exceed what is legally justified.
Force used in the exercise of a legal right, such as a police officer lawfully arresting a person under a valid warrant using only proportionate and authorised physical restraint.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as criminal force is the threshold determination for offences under Sections 74, 76, 130–136, 148, 189, 195–196, and 330 of the BNS, 2023 — conviction under all these provisions requires proof that criminal force was used. It also determines whether an act escalates from a mere threat (assault) to an executed physical offence, directly affecting the severity of punishment and the applicable charge.

definitions.definition: Criminal intention, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, denotes a conscious and purposeful mental resolve to commit an act that is prohibited by law or to cause a harm that the law seeks to prevent, as distinguished from accidental, negligent, or knowledge-based conduct. Its absence is a decisive factor in granting exemption from criminal liability under Sections 18 and 19, where an act done without criminal intention — though it may cause harm — does not constitute an offence if performed lawfully and in good faith.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal intention means that a person deliberately planned or purposefully meant to do something wrong or cause harm that is against the law. It is the deliberate mental aim to commit a wrongful act, not merely knowing that harm could result. If someone causes harm by accident or while trying to prevent greater harm, and they never intended to do wrong, they are generally not treated as a criminal under this law.
real_world_examples: A carpenter in Mumbai accidentally drops a heavy beam from scaffolding that strikes a pedestrian below. Because he was working lawfully, took proper precautions, and had no intention to harm anyone, he lacks criminal intention and commits no offence under Section 18.

A driver in Delhi, faced with a sudden brake failure on a crowded road, steers into a divider to avoid hitting a group of schoolchildren, knowing his vehicle may be damaged. Acting in good faith without criminal intention to harm, he is protected under Section 19.

A forest officer in Assam sets a controlled fire to create a firebreak and prevent a larger jungle fire from spreading to a village. He does so without any intention to cause damage and in good faith, meaning criminal intention is absent and no offence is committed.

A doctor in a Chennai government hospital performs an emergency amputation knowing it will cause permanent injury, but does so to save the patient's life from gangrene. Without any criminal intention to maim, the act is not an offence even though grievous hurt results.

A construction worker in Hyderabad unknowingly uses a defective tool that breaks apart and injures a co-worker. Provided he exercised proper care and had no criminal intention, his act falls within the accidental exemption of Section 18.
semantic_tags: mens rea in Indian criminal law
what_it_covers: A person who deliberately plans and executes an act knowing it is prohibited by law with the purpose of causing harm or an illegal outcome.
An accused who consciously resolves to bring about a specific prohibited consequence, such as intentionally striking someone to injure them.
A person who acts with a purposeful design to violate the law even while outwardly appearing to engage in a lawful activity, thereby rendering the act an offence.
what_it_excludes: Acts done by accident or misfortune in the course of a lawful activity performed with proper care and caution, where no wrongful purpose exists (Section 18).

Acts done with the knowledge that harm is likely but performed in good faith to prevent or avoid greater harm to persons or property, as long as no criminal intention to cause harm is present (Section 19).

Negligent or rash conduct where the person did not consciously intend the harmful outcome but failed to take adequate care — such conduct may attract negligence-based liability but does not satisfy the definition of criminal intention.
Acts performed under a genuine mistake of fact or in exercise of a right of private defence where the mental element of purposeful wrongdoing is absent.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of criminal intention is determinative of whether an accused is guilty of an offence: its absence entitles a person to exemptions under Sections 18 and 19 of the BNS, 2023, shielding them from prosecution even where harm results. Conversely, proof of criminal intention is an essential ingredient for establishing culpability in offences requiring mens rea, and without it, a court cannot convict the accused for those offences.

definitions.definition: Whoever threatens another by any means, with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal intimidation means deliberately threatening someone — through any means — with harm to their body, reputation, or property (or that of someone they care about), with the aim of frightening them or forcing them to do something they are not required to do, or to stop them from doing something they have a legal right to do. It is not just about making someone afraid; the threat must be aimed at controlling their actions. Even anonymous threats or threats made while hiding one's identity qualify as criminal intimidation.
real_world_examples: A landlord in Mumbai threatens a tenant that he will get the tenant's daughter harassed by local goons unless the tenant vacates the flat before the lease ends — this constitutes criminal intimidation as it aims to compel an act the tenant is not legally bound to do.

A factory owner in Surat threatens a labour union leader that he will falsely implicate him in a criminal case if the leader does not call off a legally organised workers' strike — this is criminal intimidation intended to stop a legally entitled act.

A man in Delhi sends anonymous letters to a witness in a court case threatening to burn down his house if he testifies — this is criminal intimidation by anonymous communication attracting enhanced punishment under Section 351.

A moneylender in a rural district of Uttar Pradesh threatens a borrower that he will spread false rumours about the borrower's wife's character in the village unless the borrower repays immediately — this amounts to criminal intimidation as it threatens injury to reputation.

A real estate developer in Hyderabad threatens a journalist that he will destroy the journalist's car and assault him if the journalist publishes an investigative article exposing the developer's illegal constructions — this is criminal intimidation aimed at suppressing a legally entitled act.

A politician's aide in Chennai calls a government contractor and threatens to get him arrested on false charges unless the contractor withdraws his complaint before the Vigilance Commission — criminal intimidation to cause omission of a legally entitled act.

what_it_covers: A threat made verbally, in writing, electronically, or through gestures to cause injury to a person's body, property, or reputation.
A threat directed not only at the person themselves but also at someone in whom the threatened person is interested, such as a family member or close associate.
Threats made anonymously or where the sender has taken precautions to conceal their identity, which attract additional punishment.
Threats intended to make a person do an act they are not legally bound to do, or to stop them from doing an act they are legally entitled to do.
Threats to impute unchastity to a woman, or to cause death, grievous hurt, or destruction of property by fire, which attract enhanced imprisonment up to seven years.
Threats to injure the reputation of a deceased person in whom the threatened individual has an interest.
what_it_excludes: A general expression of anger or frustration without a specific threat aimed at causing alarm or controlling conduct, such as casual heated remarks in a dispute.
A lawful warning of legal consequences, such as a lawyer informing an opposing party of intent to file a civil suit if dues are not paid, which does not constitute a threat of unlawful injury.
Threats that are entirely vague or impossible to carry out and lack any reasonable ability to cause alarm to a person of ordinary firmness.
Acts of actual physical force or violence already executed, which fall under assault, hurt, or other offences rather than intimidation.
Mere persuasion or moral pressure without any accompanying threat of injury to person, property, or reputation.

definitions.definition: Criminal knowledge, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the state of mind in which a person, at the time of doing an act, is aware that such act is likely to cause a prohibited consequence or constitutes an offence, even if there is no specific intent to bring about that consequence. It is distinguished from criminal intention in that knowledge connotes awareness of probable consequences rather than a desire to produce them. An act done without any criminal knowledge, as in the case of a genuine accident while performing a lawful act with proper care and caution, does not constitute an offence.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal knowledge means that a person knew, at the time they acted, that what they were doing could likely cause harm or result in an offence — even if they did not want that outcome. It is different from intention: you do not have to want something to happen, you just have to know it probably would. If someone acts carefully and genuinely has no such awareness, they cannot be held criminally responsible on the basis of knowledge.
real_world_examples: A pharmacist in Mumbai knowingly supplies a scheduled poison to a customer without a valid prescription, aware that such supply is likely to cause harm or death, even though he does not personally wish to harm anyone — he possesses criminal knowledge.

A truck driver in Delhi continues driving a vehicle with severely worn-out brakes, knowing the brakes are likely to fail and cause a fatal accident; when a pedestrian is killed, the driver's awareness of the risk establishes criminal knowledge even without intent to kill.

A factory supervisor in Surat knowingly allows workers to operate machinery without safety guards, aware that injury is a probable consequence; when a worker loses a hand, the supervisor cannot claim absence of criminal knowledge as he was fully aware of the danger.

A person in Kolkata mixes a substance known to him to be adulterated into food sold at his stall, knowing it is likely to cause food poisoning among customers, even though his sole motive is profit rather than harm — criminal knowledge is established.

A landlord in Chennai knowingly stores large quantities of explosive materials in a densely populated residential building, aware that an accidental ignition could kill or injure occupants; his awareness of the probable consequences constitutes criminal knowledge.

A doctor in Hyderabad administers a drug to a patient while knowing that the patient is severely allergic to it (as recorded in the medical file) and that administration is likely to cause anaphylactic shock; proceeding despite that awareness establishes criminal knowledge.
what_it_covers: Situations where a person is aware that their act is likely to cause a harmful or unlawful consequence, even without desiring that consequence.
Cases where multiple persons join in an act, each knowing the criminal nature of the act, making each individually liable as if they had acted alone with that knowledge.
Circumstances where a person knowingly omits to perform a legal duty, being aware that the omission will likely result in harm or an offence.
Acts performed in a reckless disregard of known risks, where the actor is subjectively aware of the likelihood of a prohibited outcome.
Situations where a person possesses specialised or professional knowledge that makes them aware of consequences that a layperson might not foresee.
what_it_excludes: Acts done entirely by accident or misfortune where the person genuinely had no awareness of any criminal consequence — such acts are explicitly protected under Section 18.
Acts done with proper care and caution while pursuing a lawful objective, where the harmful outcome was neither intended nor foreseen by the actor.
Mistakes of fact, where a person acts under a sincere and reasonable but mistaken belief that negates awareness of the criminal nature of the act.
Acts by a child under seven years of age, who is legally incapable of possessing criminal knowledge regardless of apparent awareness.
Acts performed by a person of unsound mind who, due to their mental condition, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is likely to cause harm.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether criminal knowledge is present directly determines criminal liability: its absence in the context of an accident under Section 18 completely negates the offence, while its presence can render each participant in a jointly committed act individually and fully liable as though they acted alone. It is a foundational element for numerous offences under the BNS, 2023, including culpable homicide, grievous hurt, mischief, and others where knowledge — rather than intent — suffices to establish guilt.

definitions.definition: Criminal misappropriation of property occurs when a person dishonestly misappropriates or converts to their own use any movable property. Unlike theft, the property is not taken from another's possession; rather, it comes into the accused's possession innocently or by chance, and is subsequently dealt with dishonestly for personal use or gain.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal misappropriation happens when someone finds or comes across property that belongs to another person and then keeps it or uses it for themselves dishonestly, instead of returning it to the rightful owner. The key difference from theft is that the person did not steal the item — they came to have it lawfully or by accident — but then decided to wrongfully keep or use it. For example, finding a lost wallet on the road and keeping the cash inside instead of trying to return it would be criminal misappropriation.
real_world_examples: A labourer in Mumbai finds a gold chain lying on a footpath with no one around. Instead of handing it over to the police or attempting to find the owner, he sells it to a local jeweller and keeps the money — this constitutes criminal misappropriation.

An auto-rickshaw driver in Chennai finds a passenger's mobile phone left behind in his vehicle. Rather than trying to contact the owner or depositing it at a police station, he uses the phone as his own — he has committed criminal misappropriation.

A bank employee in Delhi is accidentally credited with an extra sum of money due to a clerical error. Knowing the money does not belong to him, he nevertheless withdraws and spends it dishonestly — this amounts to criminal misappropriation.

A contractor in Hyderabad receives building materials delivered to his site by mistake that were meant for a neighbouring plot. Instead of informing the supplier or the rightful recipient, he uses the materials in his own construction — he commits criminal misappropriation.

A student in Kolkata borrows a friend's textbook with permission but later, when the friend forgets about it, dishonestly sells the book and pockets the proceeds — this can amount to criminal misappropriation once the intent to permanently deprive the owner is formed.
what_it_covers: Property found by a person (e.g., on a road or public place) that is subsequently retained or converted to personal use without attempting to trace the owner.
Property that comes into a person's possession by mistake, accident, or delivery error, which the person then dishonestly uses or appropriates for themselves.
Property jointly owned or held temporarily where one person dishonestly converts the shared or entrusted property to their own exclusive use without authority.
Situations where a person initially comes into possession of property innocently but later forms a dishonest intention to misappropriate it and acts on that intention.
what_it_excludes: Theft, where the property is taken directly and dishonestly out of another person's possession without their consent — the element of prior lawful or accidental possession is absent in theft.
Criminal breach of trust, where the property is entrusted to the accused in a fiduciary or contractual capacity — misappropriation of entrusted property falls under a distinct offence.
Situations where the person genuinely believes the property belongs to them or acts under a honest mistake of fact, as dishonest intent is absent.
Property that is immovable in nature, as criminal misappropriation under the BNS applies only to movable property.
Cases where the owner has expressly or impliedly consented to the other person's use or retention of the property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether this definition applies determines whether a person is charged under Section 314 of the BNS (criminal misappropriation, punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both) as opposed to theft, criminal breach of trust, or other property offences. The definition is critical in Section 317's context of stolen property, as property subject to criminal misappropriation may affect the chain of possession and culpability of subsequent receivers of such property.

definitions.definition: A criminal proceeding, as used in Section 248 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any formal legal process instituted before a competent court or authority charging a person with the commission of a criminal offence, including the filing of a complaint, First Information Report, or any step taken to set the criminal justice machinery in motion against a specific individual.
definitions.plain_english: A criminal proceeding is any official legal action taken against a person that accuses them of committing a crime before a court or law enforcement authority. This includes filing a police complaint, an FIR, or approaching a magistrate with a criminal complaint. It is the formal process through which a person is brought before the criminal justice system to face charges.
real_world_examples: A business rival in Mumbai files a false FIR at the local police station accusing a competitor of cheating under Section 316 of BNS, knowing fully well that no such fraud took place, with the intent to damage the competitor's business reputation and get them arrested.

A landlord in Delhi, wanting to evict a tenant, files a fabricated criminal complaint before a Metropolitan Magistrate alleging that the tenant committed criminal trespass, despite knowing there is no legal basis for such a charge.

In a matrimonial dispute in Chennai, a spouse lodges a false dowry harassment complaint against the other spouse and in-laws with the police, instituting criminal proceedings without any genuine grounds, solely to harass and pressurize the family for settlement.

A person in Kolkata, out of personal vendetta, approaches the police and falsely accuses a neighbour of having committed theft, leading to the registration of a criminal case and arrest of the innocent neighbour, when in fact no theft occurred.

A corporate employee in Bengaluru, colluding with management, engineers a false criminal proceeding against a whistleblower colleague by filing a fabricated complaint of extortion before the magistrate to silence and intimidate them.
what_it_covers: Filing of a First Information Report (FIR) with a police officer alleging commission of a cognizable offence by a specific person.
Filing of a private complaint before a Judicial Magistrate under Chapter XIV of BNSS, 2023, accusing a person of having committed a criminal offence.
Any formal accusation or charge sheet submitted before a court or competent authority that sets the machinery of criminal law in motion against an identifiable individual.
A complaint made to a police officer or magistrate that results in the arrest, detention, or summoning of the accused person to face criminal charges.
what_it_excludes: Civil proceedings such as suits for recovery of money, injunctions, or declaration of rights filed before a civil court, which do not involve criminal charges.
Departmental or disciplinary proceedings initiated by an employer or government authority against an employee, which are administrative in nature and not criminal.
Informal or private accusations, verbal allegations, or complaints made outside a formal legal forum that do not set the criminal justice machinery in motion.
Proceedings before consumer forums, arbitration tribunals, or revenue authorities that do not involve the determination of criminal liability or criminal punishment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an action qualifies as a 'criminal proceeding' under Section 248 directly determines if a person who falsely institutes it can be prosecuted and punished with imprisonment up to five years and a fine of up to two lakh rupees, or up to ten years if the false charge relates to an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or ten years or more. The definition thus triggers criminal liability for malicious prosecution and protects individuals from abuse of the criminal justice system.

definitions.definition: A 'criminal prosecution' refers to a formal legal proceeding initiated before a competent court or authority for the purpose of determining the guilt or innocence of a person accused of committing a criminal offence, including all acts, processes, admissions, statements, confessions of judgment, bail, security, and other steps taken in the course of such proceeding. As used in Section 242, it encompasses the entire process of pursuing criminal charges against an accused person through judicial machinery.
definitions.plain_english: A criminal prosecution is the official legal process where the government or a complainant takes a person accused of a crime to court to prove that the person committed the crime. It includes all the steps from filing a complaint or charge sheet to the final judgment of the court. definitions.definition: Criminal trespass is the act of entering into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy any person in possession of such property, or having lawfully entered into or upon such property, unlawfully remaining there with intent thereby to intimidate, insult, or annoy any person, or with intent to commit an offence. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 uses this term as a foundational category of property offence triggering rights of private defence, forming a basis for unlawful assembly, and governing the commencement and duration of defence of property rights.
definitions.plain_english: Criminal trespass means going onto someone else's property either to commit a crime, or to frighten, insult, or annoy the person who owns or lives there. It also includes staying on someone's property without permission after lawfully entering, if your purpose is to cause trouble or commit an offence. It is more serious than ordinary trespass because it requires a wrongful intention behind the entry or stay.
real_world_examples: A person climbs over the boundary wall of a neighbour's house in a Delhi residential colony with the intention of stealing valuables kept inside, thereby committing criminal trespass by entering with intent to commit theft.

A group of individuals forcibly enters a farmer's agricultural land in Punjab during a land dispute and refuses to leave, with the intent to intimidate the farmer and prevent him from cultivating his field, constituting criminal trespass by unlawful remaining with intent to annoy.

A former business partner enters the locked office premises of a company in Mumbai after business hours using a duplicate key, with the intent to access and destroy confidential documents, amounting to criminal trespass with intent to commit mischief.

A landlord, engaged in a rent dispute, enters the rented premises of a tenant in Chennai without consent and begins removing the tenant's belongings, constituting criminal trespass with intent to intimidate and annoy the person in possession.

A group of people enters a place of worship in Varanasi during a religious ceremony with the intent to disrupt proceedings and insult the congregation, amounting to criminal trespass on property in the possession of religious authorities.

A dismissed employee re-enters the factory premises in Pune after being officially barred from entry, with the intent to tamper with machinery, constituting criminal trespass by unlawful remaining with intent to commit an offence.

entry with intent to commit offence
what_it_covers: Entry onto another person's property with the intent to commit theft, mischief, or any other offence on those premises.
Lawful entry onto property followed by deliberate unlawful remaining with the specific intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person in possession.
Entry onto property with the purpose of intimidating or insulting the owner or occupant, even if no physical harm is caused.
Entry by a person onto land or immovable property in possession of another without consent and with a wrongful intent, regardless of whether the intended offence is ultimately completed.
Acts of criminal trespass committed as part of a common object of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons.
what_it_excludes: Innocent or accidental entry onto another's property without any intent to commit an offence or cause intimidation, insult, or annoyance, which amounts to mere civil trespass and not criminal trespass.
Entry onto property with lawful authority or legal right, such as entry by a police officer acting under a valid search warrant or a court-appointed receiver taking possession of disputed property.
Remaining on property with the consent of the person in possession, even if the entrant later becomes unwelcome, unless accompanied by a specific criminal or intimidatory intent.
Entry onto property that does not belong to or is not in the possession of any identifiable person, such as open public land with no possessor, which cannot sustain a charge of criminal trespass.
House-trespass and lurking house-trespass, which are aggravated and distinct forms of trespass separately defined and penalised under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes criminal trespass determines whether the victim can lawfully exercise the right of private defence of property under Sections 35, 42, and 43, including the extent of force permissible against the trespasser. It also establishes criminal liability for the trespasser, forms the predicate for more serious aggravated offences such as house-trespass and house-breaking, and can render an assembly unlawful under Section 189 if commission of criminal trespass is its common object.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of section 85, 'cruelty' means any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.
definitions.plain_english: Cruelty, in this law, means two things: first, any deliberate harmful behaviour by a husband or his relative that is serious enough that it could push the woman to attempt suicide or cause severe physical or mental harm to her; second, repeatedly pressuring or harassing the woman or her family to fulfil an illegal demand for money, property, or other valuables. Both emotional abuse and financial coercion are covered. The law recognises that cruelty is not only physical beating but also psychological torment and economic exploitation.
real_world_examples: A husband in Lucknow repeatedly beats his wife and threatens to abandon her, causing her such severe depression that she attempts suicide — his conduct constitutes cruelty under the first limb of Section 86.

A woman's in-laws in Hyderabad constantly taunt her, call her worthless, and threaten to throw her out of the house unless her parents bring an additional Rs. 5 lakh as dowry — this harassment to coerce an unlawful property demand is cruelty under the second limb.

A husband in Mumbai refuses to allow his wife to eat, withholds medication, and isolates her from all family contact, causing serious deterioration of her mental health — this wilful conduct endangering health constitutes cruelty.

A woman's mother-in-law in Delhi repeatedly humiliates her in front of guests, threatens her with black magic, and tells her she will be 'sent back' unless her brother transfers a plot of land to the husband — this coercive harassment for property is cruelty under Section 86.

A husband in Chennai threatens to file false cases against his wife's elderly father unless she surrenders her stridhan jewellery to him, causing the wife extreme anxiety and suicidal ideation — this amounts to cruelty combining both mental harm and unlawful demand.

A husband in Kolkata systematically denies his wife food, forces her to work without rest, and verbally abuses her daily, leading to documented chronic mental illness — the wilful nature and health impact make this cruelty under Section 86.
what_it_covers: Wilful conduct by a husband or his relative that is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide, such as severe verbal abuse, threats, or emotional torture sustained over time.
Physical violence or endangerment inflicted deliberately on a woman that causes or is likely to cause grave injury or danger to her life, limbs, or physical health.
Harassment of the woman or her relatives to coerce them into meeting an unlawful demand for property, money, or valuable security — including demands made after marriage as additional dowry.
Psychological abuse that causes grave danger to the mental health of the woman, such as systematic humiliation, gaslighting, isolation, or threats.
Harassment by the husband's relatives (not just the husband) directed at the woman or her family members to extract unlawful property demands.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary marital disputes, disagreements, or arguments that do not rise to the level of wilful conduct likely to cause grave injury or drive the woman to suicide.
Conduct by persons who are not the husband or relative of the husband — cruelty by strangers or the woman's own family members does not attract Section 85 liability.
Demands that are lawful in nature — the second limb specifically requires the demand to be unlawful; a legitimate contractual or legal financial claim does not constitute cruelty under Section 86.
Accidental or negligent harm caused to the woman, since the first limb expressly requires 'wilful conduct', excluding acts done without deliberate intent.

Conduct occurring outside the marital relationship context — cruelty in Section 86 is defined exclusively for the purposes of Section 85 and does not extend to cruelty between other categories of persons.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'cruelty' under Section 86 directly determines criminal liability under Section 85, which carries imprisonment up to three years and a fine; it also forms an essential element in establishing whether a death qualifies as 'dowry death' under Section 80, which carries a minimum sentence of seven years up to life imprisonment. Without satisfaction of this definition, neither offence can be established against the husband or his relatives.

definitions.definition: Culpable homicide is the act of causing death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. It is the genus of which murder is the species, and is either 'culpable homicide amounting to murder' or 'culpable homicide not amounting to murder' depending on the presence of aggravating circumstances defined in the Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: Culpable homicide means causing a person's death in a blameworthy or legally punishable way — either on purpose, or by doing something you knew was very likely to kill someone. It is broader than murder: all murders are culpable homicide, but not all culpable homicide rises to the level of murder. Think of it as the umbrella category for any criminal killing, with murder being the most serious form within it.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi gets into a heated brawl and strikes the victim repeatedly on the head with a wooden plank knowing such blows are likely to cause death; the victim dies — this is culpable homicide, and depending on the intention, may amount to murder.

A driver in Mumbai, in a sudden fit of road rage and under grave provocation after being abused, runs over another driver intentionally, causing death. Because of the provocation, the act may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder under the relevant exception.

A factory supervisor in Surat knowingly instructs workers to operate defective heavy machinery without safety guards; a worker is crushed to death. The supervisor's knowledge that death was a likely outcome makes this culpable homicide.

In a domestic dispute in Chennai, a husband administers a substance to his wife knowing it is likely to cause her death, but without premeditation or any of the special aggravating factors for murder; the wife dies — this constitutes culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

A person in Kolkata, aware that a quick unborn child may die, attacks a pregnant woman under circumstances that would amount to culpable homicide; the woman survives but the unborn child dies — Section 92 of the BNS specifically extends culpable homicide liability to this scenario.

A group engaged in a sudden fight in Hyderabad, without any prior planning, inflicts injuries on a rival that result in death. Because there was no premeditation and only knowledge (not intent) of likely death, courts may classify this as culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
semantic_tags: bodily injury likely to cause death
culpable homicide not amounting to murder
what_it_covers: Intentionally causing the death of a person by a direct act such as stabbing, poisoning, or striking with a weapon.
Causing death by an act done with knowledge that it is likely to cause death, even if death was not the primary intention — such as knowingly administering a dangerous dose of a substance.
Causing death by an act done with the intention of causing bodily injury that is likely to result in death, such as delivering severe blows to a vital organ.
Causing the death of a quick unborn child by an act that, had it caused the mother's death, would have amounted to culpable homicide (Section 92).
Causing death through an illegal omission where one is legally bound to act, such as a jailor intentionally starving a prisoner to death.
what_it_excludes: Death caused purely by accident or misfortune without any criminal intention or knowledge — such as an unforeseeable traffic accident with no negligence — which falls under general exceptions.
Acts of private defence where death is caused within the lawful limits of the right of private defence as provided in the general exceptions, which do not constitute culpable homicide.
Death caused by a child under seven years of age, which is excluded from criminal liability under the general exceptions incorporated by Section 3 of the Sanhita.
Acts done in good faith for a person's benefit by consent, where death results despite lawful medical or surgical intervention, which may be excluded under general exceptions.
Suicide, which is addressed separately under the Sanhita and is not classified as culpable homicide of another person.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes culpable homicide determines the entire range of criminal liability for causing death: it triggers prosecution under the homicide provisions of the BNS (Sections 100–106) and fixes whether the accused faces the punishment for murder (potentially death or imprisonment for life) or the lesser punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It also governs liability in derivative offences such as causing the death of a quick unborn child (Section 92) and acts done in furtherance of common intention (Section 3).

definitions.definition: A currency-note, for the purposes of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a note issued by or under the authority of a State or Sovereign Power that is intended to be used as legal tender or as a medium of exchange in monetary transactions, and is distinct from a bank-note issued by a banking entity. It is primarily governed in the context of counterfeiting offences under Chapter XII of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A currency-note is a paper note issued by a government or its authorised central authority — in India's case, notes issued by the Reserve Bank of India or the Government of India — that people use as money in everyday transactions. It is the standard paper money that citizens carry and use to buy and sell goods and services. The law specifically protects currency-notes by making it a serious crime to fake, copy, or reproduce them.
real_world_examples: A person in Kolkata uses a printing press to reproduce high-quality fake ₹500 notes issued by the Reserve Bank of India and circulates them in local markets — this constitutes counterfeiting of a currency-note under Section 178.

A syndicate in Delhi imports chemically washed genuine lower-denomination Indian currency notes and reprints them to appear as higher-denomination notes, then uses them at petrol pumps and shops — these altered notes are counterfeit currency-notes under the Act.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai knowingly accepts a stack of fake ₹2000 notes from a customer and passes them on to other customers as change — this involves trafficking in counterfeit currency-notes under Section 179.

A person found in possession of a machine and currency-note printing plates designed to produce fake Indian Rupee notes during a police raid in Hyderabad is held liable for possessing instruments for counterfeiting currency-notes under the relevant provisions.

An online fraudster in Chennai digitally transfers designs of Indian currency-notes to a buyer abroad for the purpose of counterfeiting — this act of abetting counterfeiting of currency-notes falls within the scope of the Act.

Notes issued directly by the Government of India, such as ₹1 notes bearing the signature of the Finance Secretary, which constitute legal tender.

Any note issued by or under the authority of a Sovereign State intended to function as a medium of monetary exchange, including foreign currency notes within the scope of the counterfeiting provisions.

what_it_excludes: Bank-notes issued by private banking entities carrying on the business of banking, which are separately defined and governed as 'bank-note' under Section 178 of the Act.
Coins, whether metallic legal tender or commemorative, which are separately defined under the term 'coin' as having the same meaning as in Section 2 of the Coinage Act, 2011.
Government stamps issued for revenue purposes, which are separately categorised and protected as 'stamp issued by Government for purpose of revenue' under the same Chapter.
Cheques, demand drafts, promissory notes, or other negotiable instruments, which are classified as 'valuable security' and governed by separate provisions of the Act.

definitions.definition: Custody, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the state of being under the lawful or official control, charge, or detention of a person in authority, including a police officer, public servant, jail superintendent, or any person managing a place of confinement established by law, such that the person in custody is subject to the supervision and power of the custodian. It encompasses both physical detention in a formal institution and constructive control exercised by a person in a position of authority over another.
definitions.plain_english: Custody means being under the control or care of someone in authority, like a police officer, a jail warden, or a government official. When a person is in custody, they are not free to leave and are subject to the supervision of whoever is holding them. This can happen in a police station, jail, remand home, hospital, or any other official place of detention. The person in custody is dependent on and vulnerable to the authority of their custodian.
real_world_examples: A woman arrested by the Delhi Police and held in a police station lock-up overnight pending production before a magistrate is in the custody of the police officer in charge of that station.
A juvenile offender placed in a government-run observation home in Mumbai pending trial is in the custody of the superintendent of that institution.

A patient admitted to a government hospital in Chennai who is under the care and supervision of the hospital staff and cannot discharge herself without official clearance is considered to be in the custody of the hospital management.
A convicted prisoner serving a sentence in Tihar Jail, Delhi, is in the custody of the jail superintendent and is subject to the rules and authority of the prison administration.

A child obtained by a person — not the lawful guardian — from a family in rural Bihar under the pretext of employment, and thereafter kept under that person's control for begging, is considered in that person's unlawful custody.
A woman working as a domestic helper who is confined to the employer's home in Hyderabad and not permitted to leave is effectively in the custodial control of that employer.
what_it_covers: A woman detained in a police station lock-up who is under the charge of the police officer appointed to that station.
An inmate of a jail, remand home, or any place of custody established under any law in force, under the supervision of the jail superintendent or managing staff.
A woman present in a hospital under the management or staff of that hospital, where she is under their care and control.
A child obtained unlawfully by a person who is not the lawful guardian, for the purpose of begging, and kept under that person's physical control.
A person under the charge of a public servant, including any person subordinate to that public servant, who exercises supervisory authority over them.
what_it_excludes: A person who is voluntarily accompanying a police officer or public servant without being detained or formally placed under arrest.
A guardian who has lawful parental or court-sanctioned custody of a child in a purely domestic, non-institutional context not involving confinement.
An employee or worker who is under the supervision of an employer in a workplace but retains freedom of movement and is not subject to detention.
A patient who voluntarily checks into a private clinic and can discharge themselves at will, without any formal or coercive hold by the institution.
A person in the company of another individual based on a consensual personal relationship, where no formal authority or power of detention is exercised.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person is in 'custody' is a decisive factor in determining the applicability of aggravated offences under the BNS, 2023: for instance, rape committed on a woman in a police officer's or public servant's custody attracts mandatory minimum imprisonment for life under Section 64(2), rather than the standard ten-year minimum. It also determines liability under Section 68 for sexual intercourse by a person in authority and under Section 139 for unlawful obtaining of a child's custody for begging, directly elevating both the gravity of the offence and the severity of the punishment.

definitions.definition: Dacoits are members of a gang of persons who commit or are associated with the commission of dacoity (robbery by five or more persons). A person who voluntarily joins or belongs to such a gang, knowing their character, is treated as a dacoit regardless of subsequent compulsion by associates. The term is used in the Act to distinguish organised armed robbery gangs from other criminal associations.
definitions.plain_english: A dacoit is a member of an organised criminal gang that carries out violent robberies, typically involving five or more people. These are not ordinary thieves — they operate in groups and use force or fear to commit crimes. Someone who knowingly joins such a gang is considered a dacoit, even if they later claim they were forced to participate by their fellow gang members.
real_world_examples: A group of six armed men from a village in Chambal ravine systematically loot highway trucks and terrorise travellers — all six are dacoits and members of a dacoit gang.

A local blacksmith in rural Madhya Pradesh is kidnapped by a dacoit gang and forced at gunpoint to break open doors of a house for the gang to plunder — he is not considered a dacoit because he was coerced under threat of instant death.

A young man in Uttar Pradesh knowingly joins a notorious gang of dacoits operating in the district because he fears being beaten if he refuses — he is treated as a dacoit since he joined from fear of harm short of instant death, not instant death itself.
A woman who regularly provides food and shelter to a dacoit gang operating in Rajasthan, knowing their identity and criminal activities, is harbouring dacoits and can be prosecuted under Section 254.

A fence in Bihar who regularly buys looted goods from a known dacoit gang, aware that the property was seized during dacoity, is punishable with imprisonment for life under Section 317 for receiving stolen property transferred by dacoity.
what_it_covers: A person who voluntarily joins a gang of dacoits with knowledge of their criminal character, even if later compelled by gang members to commit specific offences.
A person who joins a dacoit gang out of fear of being beaten (i.e., harm short of instant death), as such fear does not entitle them to the compulsion defence.
Any member of an organised gang habitually committing robbery as part of a group engaged in dacoity, distinguishable from gangs involved only in theft.
what_it_excludes: A person forcibly seized by a dacoit gang and compelled under threat of instant death to assist in a criminal act — such a person is entitled to the compulsion defence under Section 32 and is not treated as a dacoit.

A gang of persons associated in habitually committing theft or robbery who do not constitute a gang of dacoits — such persons fall under Section 313 as a distinct category explicitly contrasted with dacoits.
A person who unknowingly assists or associates with members of a dacoit gang without knowledge of their criminal character, as knowledge of the gang's nature is a required element for dacoit status.
The spouse of an offender who harbours a dacoit, who is explicitly exempted from liability under Section 254's harboring provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a dacoit or a member of a dacoit gang determines which penal provisions apply — ranging from denial of the compulsion defence under Section 32, to enhanced punishment for harbouring (Section 254), to life imprisonment for receiving property stolen in dacoity (Section 317). It also distinguishes the offence from lesser gang-based offences under Section 313, which carry a maximum of seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Dacoity is the commission of robbery by five or more persons conjointly, as defined under Section 310 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Where the whole number of persons conjointly committing robbery, and persons present and aiding such commission, amount to five or more, every person so committing, aiding, or being present is said to commit dacoity.
definitions.plain_english: Dacoity is a serious gang robbery committed by five or more people acting together. All members of the group — whether actively robbing or just present and helping — are equally guilty of dacoity. It is considered far more dangerous than ordinary robbery because of the organised, collective use of force or threat by a large group.
real_world_examples: A gang of six armed men storms a rural bank branch in Madhya Pradesh, threatens staff and customers at gunpoint, and flees with cash — all six are guilty of dacoity.

Five individuals in Uttar Pradesh enter a wealthy farmer's home at night, tie up the family, and loot gold jewellery and cash; even the two members who only stood guard outside are liable for dacoity.

A highway robbery in Rajasthan where eight persons stop a truck convoy, assault the drivers and loaders, and steal goods — all participants, including the driver of their getaway vehicle present at the scene, commit dacoity.

In Bihar, a group of five persons raid a money-lender's house, threaten to kill the residents unless valuables are handed over, and escape with cash — this constitutes dacoity regardless of whether any weapon was actually used.

Five persons in Maharashtra conspire and conjointly snatch gold chains from multiple victims on a busy street using force — their collective action and number elevate the offence from robbery to dacoity.
A gang of seven people in Jharkhand loot a post office van carrying pension disbursements by overpowering the guards — all seven are charged with dacoity under Section 310.
what_it_covers: Any robbery committed conjointly by five or more persons, including those who are present and aiding even if not directly executing the theft or assault.
Situations where some members of the group threaten or cause hurt while others physically carry away property, provided the total number present and participating is five or more.
Preparatory acts and conspiracies to commit dacoity that are caught at the planning stage, which attract distinct liability under Sections 311 and 312.
A person who is part of an assembly of five or more that commits robbery, even if that individual's specific role was limited to keeping watch or blocking escape routes.
Acts committed outside India that would constitute dacoity if committed in India, for purposes of related offences such as harbouring and furnishing false information.
what_it_excludes: Robbery committed by fewer than five persons, even if it involves extreme violence — such an act constitutes robbery under Section 309 but not dacoity.
Theft or extortion carried out by a large group where the element of force, threat, or putting in fear required to constitute robbery is absent — mere numbers do not transform theft into dacoity.
A person who had no knowledge of the gang's criminal purpose and was coincidentally present at the scene, and who did not aid or abet the commission of the robbery.
Acts of mere conspiracy to commit dacoity that have not yet progressed to an attempt, which are governed separately under Section 311 and Section 312 rather than Section 310 itself.
Offences of criminal breach of trust or cheating involving large groups, which do not involve force or threat against the person and therefore fall outside the definition of dacoity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes dacoity (rather than robbery or theft) determines the severity of punishment — dacoity is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for life or up to ten years with fine, and dacoity with murder attracts mandatory imprisonment for life or death. The classification also triggers enhanced ancillary liability for harbouring offenders (Section 249), concealing designs (Section 58), making false statements (Section 212), and fabricating evidence (Section 231), all of which carry heavier penalties when the underlying offence is dacoity.

definitions.definition: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not formally define 'deadly weapon' in a definitions section; however, as used across Sections 189, 191, 311, and 312, a 'deadly weapon' means any weapon or instrument that is inherently capable of causing death or is used or carried in a manner likely to cause death, and is distinguished from anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is merely likely to cause death, the latter being treated as an equivalent but separate category throughout the Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'deadly weapon' is any object that is designed or commonly used to kill or cause fatal injury — such as a gun, sword, or knife. The law treats carrying or using such a weapon during a crime as making that crime much more serious. It is different from an ordinary object (like a stone or stick) that someone might use as a weapon, though both can be treated similarly in some situations.
real_world_examples: A mob in Delhi during a riot is found to have members carrying licensed revolvers and country-made pistols (katta) — these firearms qualify as deadly weapons under Section 191, increasing the punishment from two years to five years imprisonment.

During a dacoity in rural Uttar Pradesh, the accused carry machetes (gandasa) and threaten the victims with them — the use of such bladed weapons as deadly weapons attracts a mandatory minimum sentence of seven years under Section 311.

A group of hired goons in Mumbai, engaged to intimidate a rival business, go armed with swords and axes — their carrying of these deadly weapons while being part of an unlawful assembly attracts enhanced punishment under Section 189.

A person in Chennai, while attempting to commit robbery, is found carrying a licensed double-barrel shotgun — the presence of this firearm as a deadly weapon during the attempt attracts aggravated punishment under Section 312.

During communal tension in Hyderabad, a member of an unlawful assembly is found carrying a kirpan (ceremonial dagger used offensively) — this is treated as a deadly weapon under Section 189, attracting two years' imprisonment.

A professional criminal in Kolkata uses a sharpened iron rod during a dacoity, causing grievous hurt to a victim — the iron rod, wielded in a manner capable of causing death, is treated as a deadly weapon under Section 311.
what_it_covers: Firearms such as pistols, revolvers, rifles, shotguns, and country-made guns (katta) that are inherently designed to cause death.
Sharp-edged or bladed weapons such as swords, daggers, kirpans, machetes (gandasa), and cleavers that are capable of inflicting fatal wounds.
Heavy blunt instruments specifically designed as weapons, such as axes, spears, and lances, that are ordinarily used to cause death.
Explosives and incendiary devices carried as offensive weapons during assembly or robbery that are capable of causing mass fatalities.
Any instrument declared by its design and common use to be lethal, even if not discharged or used at the time of the offence, when carried during commission of the relevant act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary household objects such as stones, bricks, or iron rods that are not inherently deadly but may be separately covered under the Act as 'anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death' — a distinct statutory category.
Agricultural tools like sickles or spades carried for legitimate agricultural purposes, unless deployed or intended as offensive weapons in the specific criminal context.
Non-lethal weapons such as tear gas canisters, rubber batons, or tasers that are designed to incapacitate rather than kill, unless used in a manner actually likely to cause death.
Objects carried by lawful authority, such as weapons held by police officers or armed forces personnel acting in the discharge of their official duty.
Verbal threats or simulated weapons (e.g., a toy gun) that cannot physically cause death, even if intended to terrorise.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'deadly weapon' directly determines the severity of punishment: under Section 191 rioting is punishable by up to five years (instead of two) when a deadly weapon is involved; under Section 311 the minimum sentence for robbery or dacoity rises to seven years; and under Section 312 an attempt to commit robbery or dacoity while armed with a deadly weapon attracts enhanced mandatory imprisonment. It also independently aggravates liability for members of an unlawful assembly under Section 189.

It is different from an ordinary object (like a stone or stick) that someone might use as a weapon, though both can be treated similarly in some situations.

Legal text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not formally define 'deadly weapon' in a definitions section; however, as used across Sections 189, 191, 311, and 312, a 'deadly weapon' means any weapon or instrument that is inherently capable of causing death or is used or carried in a manner likely to cause death, and is distinguished from anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is merely likely to cause death, the latter being treated as an equivalent but separate category throughout the Act.

Examples: A mob in Delhi during a riot is found to have members carrying licensed revolvers and country-made pistols (katta) — these firearms qualify as deadly weapons under Section 191, increasing the punishment from two years to five years imprisonment. | During a dacoity in rural Uttar Pradesh, the accused carry machetes (gandasa) and threaten the victims with them — the use of such bladed weapons as deadly weapons attracts a mandatory minimum sentence of seven years under Section 311. | A group of hired goons in Mumbai, engaged to intimidate a rival business, go armed with swords and axes — their carrying of these deadly weapons while being part of an unlawful assembly attracts enhanced punishment under Section 189. | A person in Chennai, while attempting to commit robbery, is found carrying a licensed double-barrel shotgun — the presence of this firearm as a deadly weapon during the attempt attracts aggravated punishment under Section 312. | During communal tension in Hyderabad, a member of an unlawful assembly is found carrying a kirpan (ceremonial dagger used offensively) — this is treated as a deadly weapon under Section 189, attracting two years' imprisonment. | A professional criminal in Kolkata uses a sharpened iron rod during a dacoity, causing grievous hurt to a victim — the iron rod, wielded in a manner capable of causing death, is treated as a deadly weapon under Section 311.

Tags: weapon capable of causing death, aggravated punishment trigger, armed unlawful assembly, robbery and dacoity aggravation, inherently lethal instrument, firearm or bladed weapon, criminal force with weapon, enhanced sentencing provision, weapon of offence distinction, rioting with arms

Covers: Firearms such as pistols, revolvers, rifles, shotguns, and country-made guns (katta) that are inherently designed to cause death.; Sharp-edged or bladed weapons such as swords, daggers, kirpans, machetes (gandasa), and cleavers that are capable of inflicting fatal wounds.; Heavy blunt instruments specifically designed as weapons, such as axes, spears, and lances, that are ordinarily used to cause death.; Explosives and incendiary devices carried as offensive weapons during assembly or robbery that are capable of causing mass fatalities.; Any instrument declared by its design and common use to be lethal, even if not discharged or used at the time of the offence, when carried during commission of the relevant act.

Excludes: Ordinary household objects such as stones, bricks, or iron rods that are not inherently deadly but may be separately covered under the Act as 'anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death' — a distinct statutory category.; Agricultural tools like sickles or spades carried for legitimate agricultural purposes, unless deployed or intended as offensive weapons in the specific criminal context.; Non-lethal weapons such as tear gas canisters, rubber batons, or tasers that are designed to incapacitate rather than kill, unless used in a manner actually likely to cause death.; Objects carried by lawful authority, such as weapons held by police officers or armed forces personnel acting in the discharge of their official duty.; Verbal threats or simulated weapons (e.g., a toy gun) that cannot physically cause death, even if intended to terrorise.

Why it matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'deadly weapon' directly determines the severity of punishment: under Section 191 rioting is punishable by up to five years (instead of two) when a deadly weapon is involved; under Section 311 the minimum sentence for robbery or dacoity rises to seven years; and under Section 312 an attempt to commit robbery or dacoity while armed with a deadly weapon attracts enhanced mandatory imprisonment. It also independently aggravates liability for members of an unlawful assembly under Section 189.

definitions.definition: "Death" means the death of a human being unless the contrary appears from the context.
definitions.plain_english: In the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 'death' refers specifically to the death of a human being. This means whenever the law talks about causing death or death occurring as a consequence of an act, it is referring to the end of life of a person. The definition can be read differently only if the surrounding text of a specific section clearly implies otherwise.
real_world_examples: A driver in Mumbai recklessly runs a red light and fatally strikes a pedestrian — the pedestrian's death is the 'death' referred to in offences like causing death by negligence under the Sanhita.
In a dowry death case in Delhi, a young woman dies due to burns caused by her in-laws — her death as a human being triggers the application of sections dealing with culpable homicide and dowry death.

A factory owner in Surat fails to maintain safety standards and a worker dies due to toxic gas exposure — the worker's death is the legally relevant 'death' that may attract criminal liability for the employer.

During a communal riot in Uttar Pradesh, a person is killed by a mob — the victim's death as a human being is the central fact that determines whether charges of murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder are invoked.

A physician in Chennai administers a wrong drug dosage and the patient dies — the patient's death is the 'death' under the Sanhita that could result in prosecution for causing death by a rash or negligent act.
what_it_covers: The death of any human being, regardless of age, gender, or identity, caused by another person's act or omission.
Death resulting from direct physical violence, such as murder or culpable homicide, where a human life is extinguished.
Death caused indirectly through rash, negligent, or unlawful acts, such as a fatal accident due to reckless driving or unsafe working conditions.
Death of a victim as a consequence of grievous hurt or bodily injury that escalates to a fatal outcome.
what_it_excludes: The death of any animal — the Sanhita separately defines 'animal' as any living creature other than a human being, and harm to animals is governed by different provisions.
The destruction or termination of a legal entity such as a company or association, which is covered under 'person' but does not constitute 'death' in this sense.
Situations where context clearly indicates a non-human meaning, such as metaphorical or figurative uses of the word 'death' in legal documents or arguments.
The concept of civil death or legal death of a person's rights or status, which is a distinct legal notion not captured by this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a death has occurred within the meaning of this definition is the threshold fact for invoking the most serious criminal offences under the Sanhita, including murder (Section 100) and culpable homicide (Section 100 read with Section 102), as well as offences like causing death by negligence and dowry death — without a 'death' of a human being as defined, these provisions cannot be triggered and the associated punishments, including the death penalty or life imprisonment, cannot be imposed.

definitions.definition: The term 'debt' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 8, it refers to any legally enforceable monetary obligation or financial liability owed by a person, including unpaid fines imposed by a Court, which may survive the death of the debtor and attach to property legally liable for such obligations after his death.
definitions.plain_english: A 'debt' here means any money that a person is legally required to pay, such as a court-imposed fine that remains unpaid. Even after a person dies, this obligation does not simply disappear — it can be recovered from the property or assets that person left behind. In simple terms, if you owe money to the court and you die, your estate can still be made to pay it.
real_world_examples: A convicted person in Mumbai is sentenced to pay a fine of ₹50,000 under the BNS. He dies before paying it. The court can still recover the unpaid fine from his inherited property, such as a flat in his name, as it constitutes a debt binding on his estate.

A trader in Delhi is convicted of adulteration and fined ₹1,00,000. He refuses to pay and dies two years later. His legal heirs inherit his shop. The outstanding fine, being a debt, can be levied against the shop within the six-year period specified under Section 8.

In a theft case in Chennai, the offender is fined ₹20,000. The offender passes away after paying only ₹5,000. The remaining ₹15,000 qualifies as a debt that can be recovered from any immovable property legally liable for his debts, such as ancestral land.

A person in Kolkata convicted of mischief is sentenced to pay a fine of ₹75,000. He dies intestate within months. His bank savings account, being property legally liable for his debts, can be attached to recover the unpaid fine as a statutory debt.

An offender in Hyderabad is convicted under BNS Section 303 for theft and fined ₹10,000. He flees and dies in another state. His provident fund or fixed deposits, to the extent legally attachable, can be used to discharge the debt arising from the unpaid court fine.
what_it_covers: Unpaid court-imposed fines under BNS that remain outstanding at the time of the offender's death.
Any monetary liability of the offender that attaches to property legally inheritable or transferable after death.
Financial obligations arising from a criminal sentence that survive the offender and can be levied against his estate within six years of the sentence being passed.
Residual fine amounts not discharged by imprisonment in default, which continue to constitute a recoverable debt against the offender's property.
what_it_excludes: Private civil debts owed by the offender to other individuals or creditors, which are governed by separate civil law and not by BNS Section 8.
Moral or social obligations that are not legally enforceable, such as informal promises to pay money, which do not constitute 'debt' in this statutory context.
Fines that have already been fully paid or levied by process of law, as they extinguish the debt and no further liability survives.
Community service obligations imposed in lieu of fine, which are personal in nature and cannot attach to property or survive the death of the offender.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of an unpaid fine as a 'debt' under Section 8 of the BNS is critical because it determines whether the State can recover outstanding criminal fines from a deceased offender's estate — if the obligation qualifies as a debt, property legally liable for debts after death can be attached and proceeds used to satisfy the fine, extending State recovery rights beyond the offender's lifetime. Without this classification, death would otherwise extinguish all criminal financial liabilities.

definitions.definition: Deceit, as used in Section 81 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a deliberate act by which a man causes a woman to form a false belief that she is lawfully married to him, thereby inducing her to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him on the basis of that false belief. It encompasses any fraudulent misrepresentation, concealment of identity, or false conduct designed to mislead a woman into believing a legal marital union exists when it does not.
definitions.plain_english: Deceit here means deliberately tricking a woman into believing she is legally married to a man when she is not. The man uses lies, false ceremonies, or other dishonest methods to make her think their relationship is a lawful marriage so she agrees to live with him or have a physical relationship. It is essentially a planned deception about marital status that the woman would never have agreed to if she knew the truth.
real_world_examples: A man performs a fake marriage ceremony (sham nikah or fraudulent saptapadi) with a woman, using a hired 'priest' and fake registration documents, convincing her they are legally wed, and thereafter cohabits with her for months before she discovers the marriage was never valid.

A man who is already lawfully married conceals his existing marriage, presents himself as a bachelor, goes through a second marriage ceremony with a second woman, and lives with her as husband and wife while she genuinely believes she is his lawfully wedded wife.

A man uses a completely false name and fabricated identity documents during a marriage registration process, causing the woman to believe she has married a specific person of reputed status; after cohabitation begins, the deception about his true identity is uncovered.

A man convinces a woman that their live-in arrangement constitutes a valid customary marriage recognised by law in their community, knowing fully that no such legal recognition exists, and she cohabits with him believing herself to be lawfully married.

A man whose previous marriage was never legally dissolved tells a woman that he is divorced, produces a forged divorce decree, performs a marriage ceremony, and induces her to cohabit with him in the sincere belief that she is his lawful wife.
what_it_covers: A man staging a fake or legally invalid marriage ceremony to induce a woman to believe she is his lawful wife and thereafter cohabiting with her.
A man suppressing or misrepresenting his true identity, existing marital status, or legal incapacity to marry in order to cause a woman to believe a lawful marriage subsists between them.

Any deliberate fraudulent act, misrepresentation, or concealment of a material fact about the legal validity of a marriage that causes the woman to genuinely and erroneously believe she is lawfully married.
Use of forged or false documents (such as a fabricated marriage certificate or divorce deed) to maintain a woman's false belief in the existence of a lawful marriage while cohabiting with her.
what_it_excludes: Conduct that amounts to rape under the BNS, 2023 — Section 81 expressly operates only where the sexual intercourse does not itself constitute rape.
Genuine mutual mistake or misunderstanding about the legal validity of a marriage where neither party intended to deceive the other, as there is no deliberate fraudulent intent.
A situation where the woman was aware or had reasonable means to know that the marriage was not legally valid, negating the element of induced false belief.
Consensual cohabitation between parties who both know no lawful marriage exists, as the element of deceit causing the belief of lawful marriage is absent.
Civil matrimonial disputes about the validity of a marriage arising from procedural defects or voidable conditions where no fraudulent intent to deceive the woman about marital status is present.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether the element of deceit causing a woman to believe she is lawfully married is established determines criminal liability under Section 81 BNS, 2023, which carries imprisonment up to ten years and a fine; without proof of this deceit, the conduct may fall outside Section 81's ambit entirely, affecting both prosecution and the protection afforded to the victim.
