definitions.definition: A disease dangerous to life refers to any infectious or communicable disease whose spread poses a serious risk of death or severe harm to human life, as contemplated under Sections 271 and 272 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in the context of acts — whether negligent or malignant — that are likely to propagate such infection among persons.
definitions.plain_english: A 'disease dangerous to life' is any illness that can spread from person to person and is serious enough that it could kill or gravely harm those who catch it. Think of diseases like cholera, tuberculosis, plague, or COVID-19 — illnesses where infection can be life-threatening. The law uses this term to punish people who carelessly or deliberately do things that could cause such diseases to spread to others.
real_world_examples: A person who is confirmed COVID-19 positive defies quarantine orders and attends a crowded wedding in Mumbai, knowingly risking the spread of the virus to hundreds of guests — this constitutes a negligent or malignant act likely to spread a disease dangerous to life.

A tuberculosis patient in Delhi, knowing their diagnosis, deliberately spits in a public water supply tank used by a residential colony, potentially infecting many people with a life-threatening disease.

A street food vendor in Kolkata, diagnosed with cholera by a government doctor, continues to sell food and handle water without any sanitation precautions, negligently risking a cholera outbreak in the locality.

During a plague outbreak in a village in Rajasthan, a person who knows they are infected smuggles themselves past a quarantine checkpoint established under health regulations and boards a crowded train to another city, deliberately risking spreading the disease.

A healthcare worker in Chennai, aware they are a carrier of a highly infectious and lethal strain of meningitis, reports to duty without informing authorities or taking protective measures, negligently exposing patients and colleagues to a life-threatening infection.

A person infected with Ebola-like hemorrhagic fever, having returned from an affected region, knowingly refuses to report to health authorities and continues to live communally in a densely populated Mumbai chawl, malignantly risking transmission to residents.
what_it_covers: Diseases such as cholera, plague, tuberculosis, smallpox, Ebola, and COVID-19 that are both communicable and carry a significant risk of causing death if contracted.
Any infectious or contagious illness formally notified by the government as dangerous under public health legislation, including diseases under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 or similar frameworks.
Diseases spread through airborne, waterborne, or direct contact routes that have a documented potential to cause fatality, even if not every infected person dies.
Emerging or novel infectious diseases whose transmission is known or reasonably believed to pose a mortal threat, even before formal legislative notification.
Vector-borne diseases like plague (transmitted by fleas) or diseases like rabies that, once transmitted to humans, are dangerous to life.
what_it_excludes: Non-communicable diseases such as cancer, diabetes, or heart disease, which cannot spread from one person to another through infection.
Communicable diseases that are mild, self-limiting, or not ordinarily life-threatening, such as the common cold or minor seasonal flu with no serious fatality risk.
Diseases that may cause discomfort or illness but where the risk to life is negligible under normal circumstances, such as a minor skin infection or conjunctivitis.
Conditions or ailments caused by genetic disorders, environmental toxins, or lifestyle factors that are not infectious in nature and cannot be transmitted between individuals.
Injuries or physical trauma caused by external agents (e.g., acid burns or weapon wounds) which, though dangerous to life, are not diseases in the epidemiological sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act involves a 'disease dangerous to life' is the central threshold that determines criminal liability under Sections 271 and 272 of the BNS, 2023 — without this element, no offence is made out under either provision. The distinction between negligent conduct (Section 271, up to six months imprisonment) and malignant conduct (Section 272, up to two years imprisonment) further determines the severity of punishment, making the characterisation of the disease as 'dangerous to life' the foundational trigger for both charges.

definitions.definition: "Dishonestly" means doing anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'dishonestly' means you do something with the deliberate intention of either gaining something you are not entitled to, or making someone else lose something they are entitled to. It is not about secrecy or deception alone — the key is the specific intent to create an unfair financial or property advantage or disadvantage. Even if no actual gain or loss occurs, the intention alone is sufficient to satisfy this definition.
real_world_examples: A bank employee in Mumbai transfers funds from a customer's dormant account to a relative's account, intending to give the relative money they have no right to — this is acting dishonestly under theft and criminal breach of trust provisions.

A property dealer in Delhi removes boundary markers on a plot and registers a sale deed covering a neighbour's land, intending to cause wrongful loss to the neighbour and wrongful gain to the buyer — constituting dishonest misappropriation.

A shopkeeper in Chennai sells adulterated goods by substituting cheaper materials while charging full price, intending to gain more profit at the wrongful loss of the consumer — satisfying the dishonesty element in cheating offences.

A company accountant in Bengaluru manipulates stock inventory records to conceal missing assets, intending to prevent the employer from discovering a wrongful loss already caused — acting dishonestly under criminal breach of trust provisions.

A person in Kolkata who finds a wallet containing cash and, instead of returning it, keeps the money intending to gain what is not rightfully theirs, acts dishonestly under criminal misappropriation of property provisions.
what_it_covers: Any act done with the intention of securing wrongful gain for oneself or a third party, even if no actual gain results.
Any act done with the intention of causing wrongful loss to another person, even if no actual loss ultimately occurs.
Situations where a person holds property on behalf of another and intentionally retains or disposes of it to benefit themselves at the owner's expense, such as in criminal breach of trust.
Transfer or manipulation of documents, records, or property with the intent to shift value from a rightful owner to an unentitled person.
Acts by intermediaries, agents, or fiduciaries who divert assets intending to deprive the principal of what they are legally entitled to.
what_it_excludes: Acts done carelessly or negligently that cause loss, but without any intention of creating wrongful gain or wrongful loss.
Acts done with the intention to defraud through deception alone, where there is no element of wrongful gain or loss — such intent falls under 'fraudulently' rather than 'dishonestly'.
Acts done in good faith under a genuine but mistaken belief of legal entitlement, where the person honestly believes they have a right to the property or benefit.
Accidental or inadvertent conduct that results in another person's loss, since the definition requires a deliberate intention and not mere consequence.
Acts intended only to harm reputation or cause emotional harm, as 'dishonestly' is specifically directed at wrongful gain or wrongful loss in a property or financial sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'dishonestly' is a foundational element for numerous serious offences under the BNS, including theft (Section 303), cheating (Section 318), criminal breach of trust (Section 316), criminal misappropriation (Section 314), and forgery (Section 334) — without proof of this mental state, the offence is not made out and the accused cannot be convicted under those provisions. It distinguishes criminal liability from mere civil wrong or negligence, making it a critical determinant of whether a prosecution succeeds or fails.

definitions.definition: In the context of Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'dishonour' refers to the act of degrading, humiliating, or stripping a person of their dignity, reputation, or self-respect through the use of assault or criminal force. It connotes an intentional affront to a person's honour, social standing, or personal dignity, as opposed to mere physical injury.
definitions.plain_english: Dishonour means deliberately humiliating or degrading someone in a way that damages their dignity or social reputation. It is when a person physically attacks or uses force against another person not just to cause bodily harm, but specifically to shame or disgrace them. For example, slapping someone in public to insult them in front of others would count as an act intended to dishonour that person.
real_world_examples: A man slaps a woman in front of her family members during a dispute, intending not merely to hurt her physically but to publicly shame and humiliate her — this constitutes assault with intent to dishonour under Section 133.

A landlord physically pushes a Dalit tenant out of a common area in front of neighbours to assert caste-based dominance and publicly degrade the tenant's dignity, amounting to criminal force with intent to dishonour.

A senior colleague in an office forcibly removes a junior employee's identity badge and shoves him in front of other staff during a dispute, intending to strip him of his professional standing and dignity.

During a village panchayat gathering, a man forcibly garlands another person with footwear (juta-mala) — a known act of public humiliation in parts of India — to disgrace him in front of the community, constituting criminal force with intent to dishonour.

A person throws ink or slaps a politician during a public rally specifically to humiliate and disgrace them before a crowd, going beyond mere physical assault to target the victim's reputation and social honour.
what_it_covers: Physically striking a person in a public setting with the deliberate intent to shame or disgrace them rather than merely to cause bodily harm.
Using criminal force such as pushing, shoving, or forcibly undressing someone to publicly humiliate them and damage their social standing.

Intentional acts of degradation carried out through physical contact, such as forcing someone to bow, removing their turban or headwear, or throwing objects at them to disgrace them in the eyes of others.
Any assault directed at a person belonging to a particular caste, community, or gender, where the primary purpose is to strip them of dignity rather than cause physical injury.
what_it_excludes: Physical assaults driven purely by anger or self-interest where there is no specific intent to degrade the victim's reputation or dignity — such as a brawl over property.
Acts of assault carried out in response to grave and sudden provocation given by the victim, which are explicitly excepted by the language of Section 133 itself.
Verbal insults, defamatory statements, or social ostracism that do not involve any element of assault or criminal force, as dishonour under Section 133 is tied specifically to physical acts.
Accidental physical contact that results in embarrassment or loss of face for the victim, as the offence requires deliberate intent to dishonour.
Dishonour in the commercial or financial sense, such as dishonour of a cheque or bill of exchange, which falls under separate legal provisions entirely.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an assault or use of criminal force is accompanied by intent to 'dishonour' the victim determines whether the offence falls under Section 133 of the BNS, triggering a punishment of up to two years' imprisonment, fine, or both — distinct from a plain assault charge. The presence of this specific intent elevates the gravity of the offence by recognising harm to dignity as a legally cognisable injury, and its absence (or the presence of grave and sudden provocation) may reduce or negate criminal liability under this section.

definitions.definition: A dispensary, as used in Sections 277 and 278 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is a place or establishment from which drugs or medical preparations are issued or dispensed for medicinal purposes. It includes any facility, whether public or private, that functions as a point of distribution of medicines or medical preparations to patients or the public.
definitions.plain_english: A dispensary is any place where medicines are given out or distributed to patients for treatment or health purposes. This could be a government health centre, a clinic attached to a hospital, a charitable medical outlet, or any shop-like facility that hands out medicines. The term is used to capture situations where someone running such a facility gives out fake, adulterated, or mislabelled medicines to unsuspecting patients.
real_world_examples: A government Primary Health Centre (PHC) dispensary in rural Maharashtra issues anti-malarial tablets that have been adulterated, reducing their potency, without informing patients — this falls under Section 277.
A private clinic dispensary in Delhi hands out a cheaper generic substitute labelled as a branded antibiotic to a patient without disclosure, constituting an offence under Section 278.

An Ayurvedic dispensary in Kerala issues a herbal preparation mixed with a prohibited chemical compound to patients who believe they are receiving a pure herbal remedy, attracting liability under Section 277.
A charitable hospital dispensary in Chennai gives out an expired cough syrup as a valid medical preparation to patients attending a free health camp, which is an offence under Section 278.

A municipal corporation dispensary in Kolkata stocks and issues adulterated iron supplements to pregnant women under a government scheme without informing health authorities or patients, triggering criminal liability under Section 277.
what_it_covers: Government-run health centre or PHC dispensaries that issue medicines to patients under public health schemes.
Private clinic or hospital dispensaries that distribute prescribed medicines directly to patients on the premises.
Charitable or NGO-run medical dispensaries that supply drugs to underprivileged patients for medicinal purposes.
Municipal or local authority dispensaries attached to urban health posts that dispense medicines to walk-in patients.
Ayurvedic, Unani, or Homeopathic dispensaries registered under applicable laws that issue traditional medical preparations for treatment.
what_it_excludes: Retail pharmacies or chemist shops operating purely as commercial establishments under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act — they are sellers, not dispensaries in this functional context.
Warehouses or storage facilities for medicines that do not directly issue drugs to patients for medicinal purposes.
Manufacturing units or pharmaceutical factories that produce drugs but do not dispense them directly to end patients.
Online pharmacies or e-commerce platforms that facilitate drug sales remotely without a physical point of medicinal dispensation.
Diagnostic laboratories or pathology centres that handle medical substances for testing purposes but do not issue drugs for treatment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a place qualifies as a dispensary is critical to establishing criminal liability under Sections 277 and 278, as the offences specifically penalise the act of issuing adulterated or misrepresented drugs 'from a dispensary for medicinal purposes.' If the location does not qualify as a dispensary, the accused may not be prosecuted under these provisions, and the case may need to be pursued under other laws such as the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

definitions.definition: Dissemination, as used in Section 77 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the act of spreading, sharing, distributing, publishing, or transmitting to third persons any image captured of a woman engaging in a private act, including where the victim may have consented to the capture of such image or act but has not consented to its dissemination to third parties.
definitions.plain_english: Dissemination means sharing or spreading a private or intimate image of a woman with other people without her permission. This includes sending it over WhatsApp, posting it on social media, uploading it to websites, or showing it to others. Even if the woman originally agreed to the image being taken, sharing it without her consent is still a crime under this law.
real_world_examples: A man secretly records a woman in a hotel bathroom using a hidden camera and then sends the video to his friends via WhatsApp — the act of sending the video to others constitutes dissemination under Section 77.

An ex-partner uploads intimate photographs of a woman (originally taken with her consent during their relationship) to a public pornography website in India after their breakup without her permission — this dissemination is an offence even though she had consented to the original capture.

A person who received a voyeuristically captured video of a woman changing clothes then forwards it to a Telegram group of hundreds of members — the act of forwarding to third parties constitutes dissemination.

A stalker who filmed a woman through her window without her knowledge emails the footage to her colleagues and family members to harass and humiliate her — this sharing with third persons amounts to dissemination under this section.

A college student who obtained a private video of a female classmate through deception posts it on Instagram and college group chats — each act of posting or sharing to persons beyond the original victim constitutes dissemination.
semantic_tags: consent to capture vs. consent to share
what_it_covers: Sharing or forwarding a captured private image of a woman to any third person via digital means such as WhatsApp, Telegram, email, or social media platforms.
Uploading voyeuristically captured images or videos of a woman to websites, online forums, or pornographic platforms without her consent.
Distributing intimate images originally captured with the woman's consent but shared with third parties without her consent — expressly covered under the third paragraph of Section 77.
Physically showing a captured private image of a woman to other individuals, such as displaying it on a phone or printing and circulating it.
Broadcasting or publishing a private image of a woman on any electronic or non-electronic medium that makes it accessible to persons beyond the victim.
what_it_excludes: The original act of capturing or recording the private image itself — that is separately penalised as 'watching or capturing' under Section 77 and is distinct from dissemination.
Consensual sharing by the woman herself of her own intimate images — dissemination is only an offence when done by the perpetrator or a third party without the woman's consent to that sharing.

Retention or possession of a privately captured image without sharing it with any third party — mere possession, while potentially part of the broader voyeurism offence, does not constitute dissemination unless the image is actually transmitted or spread.
Sharing images that are not of a private or intimate nature and were captured in a public setting with no reasonable expectation of privacy.
Dissemination of images of persons other than women, as Section 77 is specifically confined to protecting women from voyeurism and related acts.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as dissemination directly determines criminal liability under Section 77 of the BNS, triggering punishment of one to three years imprisonment on first conviction and three to seven years on subsequent conviction, along with fine. It also activates the special protection clause for victims who consented to image capture but not to sharing, ensuring such non-consensual distribution is independently punishable as a complete offence.

definitions.definition: A state of supernatural or religious disfavour that a person is induced or threatened to believe will befall them or someone they care about, as a consequence of their action or inaction, where such belief is deliberately engineered by another person to coerce conduct. Under Section 354, it refers specifically to the belief that some act of the offender will render the victim or a person in whom the victim is interested an object of Divine displeasure, used as a means to cause that person to do or omit to do something they are not legally bound or entitled to do.
definitions.plain_english: Divine displeasure means making someone believe that God or a supernatural power will be angry or punish them (or someone they love) if they do not comply with a demand. A person exploits religious fear or superstition to pressure someone into doing something or stopping them from doing something. It is essentially using the threat of God's wrath as a tool of coercion or manipulation.
real_world_examples: A village tantric tells a widow that unless she hands over her land to him, her deceased husband's soul will remain cursed and she will face divine punishment — inducing her to transfer property she is not legally obligated to give up.

A temple priest warns a devotee that if he does not withdraw his complaint against a powerful local politician, God will strike his family with disease and misfortune, causing the devotee to omit a legal act he is entitled to perform.

A self-styled godman sits dharna at a farmer's doorstep declaring that his presence will cause divine wrath to fall upon the farmer unless the farmer pays a disputed sum of money, which the farmer is not legally bound to pay.

A religious leader tells voters in a village that if they vote for a particular candidate, they will become objects of divine displeasure and their crops will fail — using religious fear to interfere with their free electoral right under Section 171.

A moneylender employs a local jyotishi (astrologer) to warn a borrower that a curse has been placed and only by repaying double the agreed amount immediately will the divine wrath be lifted, coercing the borrower beyond his legal obligation.

A person threatens a neighbour that unless she abandons her legal claim to a disputed piece of land, he will perform a ritual that will make her an object of divine anger, causing her to withdraw a legally entitled action out of religious fear.
what_it_covers: A threat by a religious figure, godman, or tantric that a person will face God's wrath or a deity's curse unless they comply with a demand.
Sitting dharna at a person's door with the deliberate intent to create the belief that such an act invokes divine punishment on that person.
Threatening a voter or candidate during elections that their failure to vote in a particular way will render them an object of divine displeasure or spiritual censure.
Inducing a person to believe that a third party they care about — such as a child or spouse — will face divine displeasure if the person does not comply with the offender's demands.
Any staged or artificial act (ritual, curse, or proclamation) deliberately performed or claimed to be performed by the offender to manufacture the belief of divine disfavour as a coercive tool.
what_it_excludes: Genuine religious instruction or preaching that describes divine consequences of sin generally, without targeting a specific person to compel a specific act or omission.
A sincere personal expression of religious belief where no coercive intent or demand is attached — such as a priest advising a devotee on moral conduct without any underlying demand.
Legal acts accompanied by a declaration of public policy or promises of public action, even if framed in moral or religious language, as expressly excluded by Section 171(3).
Threats of purely secular injury — such as physical harm, financial loss, or reputational damage — which fall under criminal intimidation rather than this specific provision.
Situations where a person voluntarily and independently believes an act will displease God without any inducement or attempt by another person to create or exploit that belief.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as inducing belief in Divine displeasure determines criminal liability under Section 354 (punishable with up to one year imprisonment, fine, or both) and also constitutes undue influence at elections under Section 171, which is itself a criminal offence. Establishing this element distinguishes coercive exploitation of religious fear — which is punishable — from lawful religious expression or mere persuasion, directly affecting whether an accused is guilty of a cognisable offence.

definitions.definition: "document" means any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, and includes electronic and digital record, intended to be used, or which may be used, as evidence of that matter. Whatever is expressed by means of letters, figures or marks as explained by mercantile or other usage, shall be deemed to be expressed by such letters, figures or marks within the meaning of this section, although the same may not be actually expressed.
definitions.plain_english: A document is anything written, drawn, or marked on any surface — including paper, stone, or digital media — that is meant to record or prove some fact or agreement. It covers physical writings like contracts and cheques, as well as digital files and electronic records. The key requirement is that it must be capable of being used as evidence of whatever it expresses.
real_world_examples: A written sale deed for a flat in Mumbai, signed by the buyer and seller and registered at the Sub-Registrar's office, is a document because it records the terms of property transfer and can be used as evidence in court.

A WhatsApp message or email sent by an accused in a fraud case in Delhi, stored on a mobile phone, qualifies as a document under BNS because it is an electronic record intended to communicate and capable of being used as evidence.

A cheque drawn on an SBI branch in Chennai bearing the account holder's signature and a specific amount is a document, as expressly illustrated in the definition, and can be produced as evidence of a financial transaction or dishonour.

A Google Maps screenshot or a hand-drawn map of a village boundary used as evidence in a land dispute before a civil court in Uttar Pradesh constitutes a document because it is a mark-based expression of spatial information intended for evidentiary use.

A digital prescription generated by a doctor on a hospital management system in Bengaluru, electronically signed and stored in the hospital's server, is a document as it is an electronic record describing a medical direction capable of being used as evidence.

An endorsement made by a payee on the back of a hundī (bill of exchange) in a merchant transaction in Gujarat, even without spelling out the full instruction, is a document because mercantile usage gives it a definite meaning.
what_it_covers: A written contract of employment or lease executed on stamp paper and signed by parties, which can be produced as evidence of the terms agreed upon.
An electronic record such as a PDF, email, spreadsheet, or digitally signed certificate stored on a computer or cloud server that is capable of being used as evidence.
A cheque, demand draft, or promissory note bearing signatures, amounts, and dates — expressly listed as illustrations in the definition.
A power-of-attorney authorising another person to act on behalf of the executant, whether registered or unregistered.
A map, architectural plan, or satellite image printout intended to be used or capable of being used as evidence of location, boundaries, or structure.
An endorsement on a bill of exchange whose meaning is determined by mercantile usage, even if the full words are not written out.
what_it_excludes: A purely oral statement or verbal communication that has not been reduced to writing, marks, figures, or any electronic record, as it lacks expression upon a substance.
A blank piece of paper or an unmarked surface that carries no letters, figures, or marks conveying any matter, since there is nothing expressed or described upon it.

Physical objects or real evidence (such as a weapon, bloodstained cloth, or fingerprint on glass) that are not themselves expressions of matter by letters, figures, or marks — these may be evidence but are not 'documents'.
A transient display on a screen that is never stored, recorded, or capable of retrieval, as it does not qualify as an electronic or digital record intended to be used as evidence.
Mental impressions, thoughts, or intentions that have not been externalised into any written, marked, or electronic form.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'document' under BNS directly determines the applicability of offences such as forgery (Sections 336–338), making a false document (Section 337), using a forged document (Section 339), and destroying evidence embodied in a document (Section 228); if the item is not a document, these offences cannot be charged. It also governs liability under provisions dealing with fabrication of evidence, false property marks, and cheating by document, making the definition a foundational gating element for multiple categories of criminal liability.

Examples: A written sale deed for a flat in Mumbai, signed by the buyer and seller and registered at the Sub-Registrar's office, is a document because it records the terms of property transfer and can be used as evidence in court. | A WhatsApp message or email sent by an accused in a fraud case in Delhi, stored on a mobile phone, qualifies as a document under BNS because it is an electronic record intended to communicate and capable of being used as evidence. | A cheque drawn on an SBI branch in Chennai bearing the account holder's signature and a specific amount is a document, as expressly illustrated in the definition, and can be produced as evidence of a financial transaction or dishonour. | A Google Maps screenshot or a hand-drawn map of a village boundary used as evidence in a land dispute before a civil court in Uttar Pradesh constitutes a document because it is a mark-based expression of spatial information intended for evidentiary use. | A digital prescription generated by a doctor on a hospital management system in Bengaluru, electronically signed and stored in the hospital's server, is a document as it is an electronic record describing a medical direction capable of being used as evidence. | An endorsement made by a payee on the back of a hundī (bill of exchange) in a merchant transaction in Gujarat, even without spelling out the full instruction, is a document because mercantile usage gives it a definite meaning.

Excludes: A purely oral statement or verbal communication that has not been reduced to writing, marks, figures, or any electronic record, as it lacks expression upon a substance.; A blank piece of paper or an unmarked surface that carries no letters, figures, or marks conveying any matter, since there is nothing expressed or described upon it.; Physical objects or real evidence (such as a weapon, bloodstained cloth, or fingerprint on glass) that are not themselves expressions of matter by letters, figures, or marks — these may be evidence but are not 'documents'.; A transient display on a screen that is never stored, recorded, or capable of retrieval, as it does not qualify as an electronic or digital record intended to be used as evidence.; Mental impressions, thoughts, or intentions that have not been externalised into any written, marked, or electronic form.

It also governs liability under provisions dealing with fabrication of evidence, false property marks, and cheating by document, making the definition a foundational gating element for multiple categories of criminal liability.

definitions.definition: Dominion over property, as used in Section 316 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the authority, control, or power entrusted to a person to deal with, manage, or exercise rights over property belonging to another, in a fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary capacity. Such dominion may be conferred by law, contract, or the nature of the relationship between the parties, imposing an obligation to exercise that control only in the prescribed or agreed manner.
definitions.plain_english: Dominion means the power or control a person has over someone else's property because they have been trusted to look after it. It is broader than just physically holding the property — it includes having the authority to manage, deal with, or make decisions about it on behalf of the true owner. For example, a bank manager, an attorney, or a company executive who controls funds on behalf of others has 'dominion' over that property. If they misuse that control dishonestly, they can be guilty of criminal breach of trust.
real_world_examples: A company's Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in Mumbai who is authorised to manage and disburse corporate funds on behalf of the company exercises dominion over those funds; if the CFO fraudulently transfers money to a personal account, this amounts to criminal breach of trust through misuse of dominion.

A stockbroker in Delhi who is given authority by clients to buy and sell shares in their portfolios holds dominion over the clients' securities; if the broker sells the shares and siphons off the proceeds, the dominion over property has been dishonestly misused.

An estate manager in Chennai entrusted by an NRI landlord with full authority to collect rents, pay maintenance expenses, and manage tenants has dominion over the rental income; diverting those funds for personal use constitutes criminal breach of trust.

An attorney (vakil) in Kolkata given a Power of Attorney by an elderly client to manage property and bank accounts holds dominion over those assets; unauthorised sale of the client's property for personal gain is a criminal breach of trust arising from misuse of that dominion.

A factory owner in Pune who deducts employees' Provident Fund contributions from salaries holds dominion over those deducted amounts until they are deposited with the PF authority; failure to deposit them and instead using the money for business operations constitutes criminal breach of trust.

A warehouse-keeper in Ahmedabad who accepts goods for storage under a contract holds dominion over those goods; selling them without the owner's consent is a misuse of dominion and constitutes criminal breach of trust.
what_it_covers: Authority granted to a bank manager or financial officer to manage, invest, or disburse funds belonging to clients or an institution.
Power of attorney granted to an individual giving them control to sell, lease, or manage immovable or movable property on behalf of the owner.
Control exercised by a public servant over government funds or property in the course of their official duties.
Authority of an employer over employee contributions deducted from wages and held pending deposit to statutory funds like EPF or ESI.
Control exercised by a broker, agent, factor, or merchant over goods or money belonging to their principal in the ordinary course of business.
Authority of an executor or administrator over the estate of a deceased person pending distribution to beneficiaries.
what_it_excludes: Mere physical possession of property without any accompanying authority to deal with or manage it, such as a delivery person temporarily holding a parcel.
Ownership of one's own property, where there is no trust, entrustment, or delegated authority — a person cannot have 'dominion' in this legal sense over their own property.
Situations where control over property is obtained unlawfully or through theft or robbery, as dominion requires a lawful entrustment or delegation of authority.
Incidental or transient access to property that does not carry any obligation or authority to manage or deal with it on another's behalf.
Control exercised pursuant to a court order or statutory lien that does not create a relationship of trust or fiduciary obligation between the parties.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person holds 'dominion' over property is a foundational element for establishing criminal breach of trust under Section 316 of the BNS — without entrustment of property or dominion over it, the offence cannot be constituted. The degree of dominion, and the capacity in which it is held (e.g., as a public servant, banker, clerk, or employer), also determines the severity of punishment, ranging from five years to life imprisonment.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'dowry' shall have the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, which defines it as any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given either directly or indirectly by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by the parents of either party, or by any other person, as consideration for the marriage.
definitions.plain_english: Dowry refers to money, property, jewellery, or any other valuables that one family demands or gives to the other family as a condition of or in connection with a marriage. It is not a gift given out of love or affection, but rather something demanded or expected as part of the marriage deal. The law treats dowry as an illegal demand, and deaths linked to such demands are treated as serious criminal offences.
real_world_examples: A bride's parents are pressured by the groom's family to give a car, gold jewellery worth several lakhs, and household appliances as a precondition for finalising the marriage — all such items collectively constitute dowry.

After marriage, the husband and his relatives repeatedly harass the wife demanding an additional amount of ₹5 lakh in cash that was promised by her parents before the wedding; this demand is a demand for dowry under the law.

A groom's family demands that the bride's family give them a plot of land as consideration for the marriage, and when the demand is not met, the bride is subjected to cruelty — the land demanded constitutes dowry.

A young woman in Uttar Pradesh dies under suspicious burn injuries within three years of marriage after her in-laws harassed her for not bringing a refrigerator and a television that were allegedly promised at the time of the wedding; the promised items are treated as dowry.

A bride's family voluntarily transfers valuable securities and fixed deposits in the groom's name as part of marriage negotiations — even though framed as a 'gift,' if given in connection with the marriage consideration, it qualifies as dowry.
what_it_covers: Cash, jewellery, land, or any movable or immovable property given or agreed to be given by the bride's family to the groom's family as consideration for the marriage.
Valuable securities such as shares, bonds, fixed deposits, or property deeds transferred directly or indirectly in connection with the marriage agreement.
Any property demanded by the groom or his relatives after marriage that was part of an original or subsequent promise tied to the marriage, including additional post-marriage demands.
Property given by a third party — such as the bride's relatives or friends — to either party as a condition of or in consideration of the marriage.
what_it_excludes: Dower or mehr given under Muslim personal law, which is a right of the wife rather than a demand made upon her family.

Gifts given voluntarily at the time of marriage out of love or affection, without any demand or consideration tied to the marriage contract, provided they are not in the nature of consideration for the marriage.
Stridhan — personal property such as gifts received by the bride from her own family that are not given as consideration to the groom's side, and which legally belong exclusively to the bride.
Maintenance or alimony payments ordered by a court after marriage dissolution, which arise from legal proceedings and not from pre-marital negotiation or demand.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a demand or transfer of property qualifies as 'dowry' under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 is the foundational element of Section 80 of the BNS; if a woman's death occurs within seven years of marriage following harassment linked to such a demand, it constitutes 'dowry death,' attracting mandatory minimum imprisonment of seven years and up to life imprisonment for the husband or his relatives.

definitions.definition: The term 'drink' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 274 and in the definition of 'harbour', it refers to any liquid intended or used for human consumption, including water, beverages, and intoxicating liquids, that may be adulterated, poisoned, or rendered noxious so as to be dangerous to health or life.
definitions.plain_english: A 'drink' refers to any liquid that a person consumes by mouth, such as water, juice, tea, milk, or alcohol. In the context of this law, it becomes legally significant when such a liquid is tampered with, poisoned, or made harmful in a way that could injure or endanger anyone who consumes it. The law is concerned with protecting people from being given contaminated or adulterated drinks.
real_world_examples: A food stall vendor in Mumbai mixes a toxic substance into a cold drink being sold to customers, rendering it dangerous to health — this constitutes adulteration of a drink under Section 274.
A person in Delhi adds a sedative drug to a guest's water glass intending to incapacitate them — the water as a drink is made noxious and falls within the ambit of Section 274.
A dairy supplier in Punjab adulterates packaged milk (a drink) with a harmful chemical to increase volume, endangering consumers — this is an offence involving an adulterated drink.
A domestic worker in Chennai is accused of mixing rat poison into the tea (a drink) served to the household employer — the tea becomes a poisoned drink triggering liability under Section 274.

During a communal event in Rajasthan, someone deliberately contaminates the common water supply or sherbet distributed to attendees with a noxious substance, endangering mass consumption of the drink.

A bartender at a nightclub in Bengaluru intentionally adulterates an alcoholic beverage served to a patron with a harmful chemical — the adulterated alcohol qualifies as a noxious drink under this provision.
what_it_covers: Water, whether packaged or supplied through a common source, that has been mixed with a poisonous or harmful substance.
Alcoholic beverages such as liquor, wine, or beer that have been adulterated with toxic or noxious chemicals.
Non-alcoholic beverages such as milk, juice, tea, coffee, or sherbet that have been rendered dangerous to health by the addition of a harmful substance.
Any liquid provided as refreshment or sustenance in a domestic, public, or commercial setting that has been deliberately contaminated.
Liquids supplied as part of 'harbour' assistance (as defined under Section 2) including food and drink given to a person to help them evade apprehension.
what_it_excludes: Solid food items or edibles that are not in liquid form, even if similarly adulterated — these fall under 'food' rather than 'drink'.
Medicines or medical preparations in liquid form intended for therapeutic use rather than general consumption, which are governed by separate provisions.
Liquids used for external purposes such as cleaning, bathing, or industrial use, which are not intended for human consumption.
Naturally occurring contamination of water or beverages not caused by a deliberate human act, as the offence requires intentional adulteration or rendering noxious.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a liquid qualifies as a 'drink' under Section 274 determines whether adulterating or poisoning it constitutes a punishable offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which prescribes imprisonment and fine for making any drink noxious or dangerous to health. It also bears on the definition of 'harbour' under Section 2, where supplying drink to a person aids their evasion of law enforcement, thereby establishing abetment liability.

definitions.definition: The term 'drug' as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to any drug or medical preparation intended or used for medicinal purposes, which may be subject to adulteration that lessens its efficacy, changes its operation, or renders it noxious. It encompasses substances administered or dispensed in a medicinal or pharmacological context, including those sold, offered for sale, or issued from a dispensary for therapeutic use.
definitions.plain_english: A 'drug' in this law means any medicine or medical substance that is meant to be used for treating or managing health conditions. This includes tablets, syrups, injections, or any other form of medicine that a person might buy from a pharmacy or receive from a dispensary. The law is concerned with ensuring that such substances are genuine, effective, and not tampered with in ways that could harm the person using them.
real_world_examples: A pharmaceutical manufacturer in Mumbai dilutes antibiotic capsules with an inert filler powder, reducing their therapeutic potency, and sells them to hospitals under the label of full-strength medication — this constitutes adulteration of a drug under Section 276.

A chemist in Delhi knowingly sells paracetamol tablets that have been adulterated with a harmful chemical by his supplier, without disclosing this fact to customers purchasing them for fever treatment — attracting liability under Section 277.

A dispensary in Chennai issues adulterated insulin injections to diabetic patients as if they were of standard medicinal grade, causing the patients' blood sugar levels to remain uncontrolled due to reduced efficacy — a direct application of Section 277.

A drug wholesaler in Kolkata purchases cough syrup that has been adulterated to change its chemical composition, makes no disclosure, and distributes it to retail pharmacies across West Bengal for sale to unsuspecting consumers — triggering offences under both Sections 276 and 277.

A counterfeit drug ring in Hyderabad produces fake antimalarial drugs with minimal active ingredients and supplies them to rural health clinics, where they are issued to patients who believe they are receiving genuine medicine — illustrating the harm that the drug adulteration provisions are designed to prevent.
what_it_covers: Tablets, capsules, syrups, injections, or any pharmaceutical formulation sold or intended for medicinal/therapeutic use.
Medical preparations issued from a dispensary or pharmacy for the purpose of treating illness or managing a health condition.
Any drug whose efficacy has been lessened, operation changed, or which has been rendered noxious through adulteration, when sold or offered as unadulterated medicine.
Substances administered to a person with intent to cause hurt or facilitate commission of an offence, as referenced in Section 123 under the broader category of drugs.
what_it_excludes: Narcotic or psychoactive drugs used for trafficking or abuse purposes, which fall under the category of 'drugs' in organised crime provisions (Section 111) and are governed by the NDPS Act, 1985, not these sections.
Poisonous or stupefying substances administered with criminal intent under Section 123, which are addressed under a separate offence framework and are not limited to medicinal preparations.
Food, drink, or non-medicinal consumable substances, even if they may have pharmacological effects, as these are treated as distinct categories under the Act.
Cosmetic or non-therapeutic topical preparations not intended for internal medicinal use or disease treatment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'drug' or 'medical preparation' under this definition determines whether Sections 276 and 277 are triggered — establishing criminal liability for adulteration or knowing sale of adulterated drugs, with penalties including imprisonment up to one year and fines. Establishing this classification is essential to prosecuting pharmaceutical fraud and protecting public health by ensuring accountability in the medicinal supply chain.

definitions.definition: A 'dwelling' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to any building, tent, or vessel used as a human residence or habitation. It encompasses any place where a person resides, sleeps, or maintains a home, as evidenced by its usage in provisions relating to house-breaking, theft, mischief by fire, and private defence of property.
definitions.plain_english: A 'dwelling' is any place where a person lives or stays as their home — this could be a house, flat, hut, tent, or even a boat used as a residence. It is essentially any structure or space that serves as a human living space. The law treats crimes committed in or against dwellings more seriously because people have a heightened expectation of safety in their homes.
real_world_examples: A pucca house or apartment flat in a city like Mumbai or Delhi where a family permanently resides qualifies as a dwelling, and theft from it attracts enhanced liability under petty organised crime provisions.
A tent set up by a tribal family in Jharkhand used as their living quarters constitutes a dwelling, and setting fire to it would trigger the right of private defence extending to causing death.
A houseboat on Dal Lake in Srinagar used as a permanent or seasonal residence by a family qualifies as a dwelling vessel under the Act.

A jhuggi or slum shelter in a Delhi basti used as a home by a migrant worker is a dwelling, and house-breaking into it after sunset and before sunrise is an offence that justifies private defence causing death.
A servant's quarter attached to a bungalow in Chennai where a domestic worker resides is treated as a dwelling for purposes of house-trespass and related offences.
A dharamshala room in Varanasi occupied by a pilgrim as a temporary residence may qualify as a dwelling for the duration of their stay.
what_it_covers: A permanent residential house, flat, or apartment used as a family home.
A tent used as a human dwelling, such as those used by nomadic communities or military personnel on the move.
A vessel or boat used as a place of human residence, such as a houseboat.
A temporary shelter or hut used as a living space by a person or family.
A room in a shared residence or chawl occupied by a person as their home.
Business premises that double as a place of residence for the owner or occupant.
what_it_excludes: A building used purely for commercial purposes, such as a shop, office, or warehouse, with no residential use.
A vehicle such as a car or truck not adapted or used as a place of human habitation.
An unoccupied or abandoned structure not currently serving as anyone's home.
A place of worship, hospital, or public institution not functioning as a personal residence.
Land or open spaces without any structure serving as a shelter for habitation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a place qualifies as a 'dwelling' directly determines the applicability of enhanced offences and defences: it triggers the right of private defence extending to causing death (Section 41), elevates theft to an aggravated category under petty organised crime (Section 112), and governs the scope of house-breaking and house-trespass offences (Sections 305 and 329), thereby significantly affecting both criminal liability and available legal justifications.

definitions.definition: "Economic offence" includes criminal breach of trust, forgery, counterfeiting of currency-notes, bank-notes and Government stamps, hawala transaction, mass-marketing fraud or running any scheme to defraud several persons or doing any act in any manner with a view to defraud any bank or financial institution or any other institution or organisation for obtaining monetary benefits in any form.
definitions.plain_english: An economic offence is a financially motivated crime that involves cheating, defrauding, or manipulating financial systems, institutions, or people to gain money or other monetary benefits. This includes acts like forging documents, counterfeiting currency, illegal money transfers (hawala), large-scale fraud schemes targeting many victims, or deceiving banks and other financial bodies. It is not a standalone offence but rather a category of unlawful financial activity that, when carried out by an organised crime syndicate, elevates the crime to 'organised crime' under this law.
real_world_examples: A group of individuals operates a Ponzi scheme promising high returns to thousands of investors across multiple states in India, collecting crores of rupees before absconding — this constitutes mass-marketing fraud under the economic offence definition.

A bank manager in collusion with external members of a crime syndicate dishonestly transfers funds from customer accounts over several years for personal gain — this amounts to criminal breach of trust against a financial institution.

A counterfeit currency printing ring operating out of a city produces fake Rs. 500 and Rs. 2000 notes and circulates them through hawala networks — this falls squarely within economic offence as it involves counterfeiting of currency-notes and hawala transactions.

A real estate developer forges government land records and sale deeds to illegally obtain bank loans worth hundreds of crores from multiple public sector banks, with no intention of repayment — this constitutes forgery combined with an act to defraud a financial institution.

A syndicate runs a fake investment app targeting rural populations across India, collecting small amounts from lakhs of users under false pretences of stock market returns, amounting to a scheme to defraud several persons.

An organised group uses forged government revenue stamps on fraudulent property documents to illegally transfer ownership of properties and extract loans from housing finance companies — involving both counterfeiting of Government stamps and defrauding a financial organisation.
what_it_covers: Criminal breach of trust committed by individuals managing property or funds belonging to banks, financial institutions, or other organisations.
Forgery of documents such as sale deeds, loan agreements, government stamps, or identity records for the purpose of financial gain.
Counterfeiting of currency-notes, bank-notes, and Government stamps and circulating them through illegal channels including hawala networks.
Mass-marketing fraud schemes or Ponzi schemes designed to defraud a large number of persons by promising false returns or benefits.
Any deliberate act — whether direct or indirect — aimed at defrauding a bank, non-banking financial company, cooperative society, or any other financial institution to obtain monetary benefits.
Hawala transactions used as a mechanism to facilitate or conceal the proceeds of organised criminal activity.
what_it_excludes: Simple theft or robbery not involving any element of financial fraud or deception of an institution — these are separately listed unlawful activities under Section 111 and do not fall within the economic offence sub-definition.

Cyber-crimes that are purely technical in nature (e.g., hacking for non-financial purposes or data theft without monetary motive) — cyber-crimes are listed separately in Section 111 and are not subsumed under economic offence.

Trafficking of persons, drugs, or weapons, which are independently listed as continuing unlawful activities under Section 111 and are not classified as economic offences even if they yield financial benefit.

Individual or isolated acts of petty fraud or cheating involving small sums between private individuals that do not target a bank, financial institution, or multiple victims through a scheme, and which are not carried out as part of an organised crime syndicate.

Land grabbing through purely physical force or intimidation without any document forgery or financial institution fraud — land grabbing is separately enumerated in Section 111 and is not categorised as an economic offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a financially motivated act qualifies as an 'economic offence' is legally significant because it determines whether the act constitutes a 'continuing unlawful activity' under Section 111, thereby triggering the organised crime provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — which carry a minimum sentence of five years and up to life imprisonment, with fines of not less than five lakh rupees. Classification as an economic offence also broadens the scope of what counts as organised crime, allowing prosecution of syndicate members, abettors, and those harbouring offenders under the enhanced penalty framework.

definitions.definition: The term 'election' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 172–176, it denotes any election held under any law for the time being in force for the purpose of choosing members of Parliament, of any Legislature, of any local authority, panchayat, municipality, or any other public body, by means of voting by electors entitled to participate therein.
definitions.plain_english: An 'election' refers to any formal process through which citizens cast votes to choose their representatives for Parliament, State Legislatures, local bodies like municipal corporations, panchayats, or any other public authority. It covers the entire process from nomination of candidates to declaration of results. The term is broadly used to protect the fairness and integrity of any such voting process under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A candidate contesting elections to the Lok Sabha (House of the People) in India — any interference with voters or bribery during this process falls under the election-related offences in Sections 172–176 of the BNS.

Elections to the Maharashtra State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) where a political party agent threatens voters at a polling booth to vote for a specific candidate — such conduct is covered under offences relating to 'election' in the BNS.

Elections to the Delhi Municipal Corporation where a person impersonates a registered voter and casts a fraudulent vote — the 'election' referred to in BNS Sections 172–176 covers such local body elections.

Gram Panchayat elections held in rural Rajasthan under State Panchayati Raj law, where a candidate bribes villagers with liquor to secure votes — these elections are protected under BNS election-related offence provisions.

Rajya Sabha elections conducted by Members of State Legislative Assemblies, where cross-voting is induced through unlawful gratification — such conduct in the context of this 'election' triggers offences under Sections 172–176 BNS.

By-elections to fill a vacant seat in a State Legislative Council, where false statements about a candidate's character are spread to harm electoral prospects — the BNS election offence provisions apply equally to such elections.
what_it_covers: Elections to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (Parliament of India) conducted under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Elections to State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabhas) and State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishads) across all Indian states.
Elections to local authorities including municipal corporations, municipal councils, panchayats, district boards, and other public bodies constituted under Central or State law.
By-elections and mid-term elections held to fill vacancies in any of the above bodies.
Elections conducted under any law in force in India for choosing members of any public body by means of votes cast by eligible electors.
what_it_excludes: Internal elections within political parties for choosing office-bearers or party candidates, as these are not elections held under a law for public representation.
Elections conducted by private organisations, trade unions, cooperative societies, or clubs that are not public bodies constituted by law.
Appointment processes or nominations to public offices where no voting by electors takes place, such as presidential nominations to the Rajya Sabha.
Referendums or public opinion polls that are not formal elections for choosing representatives to a public body.
Elections to statutory bodies or professional councils (such as bar councils or medical councils) that are not 'public bodies' in the sense of representative governance under electoral law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as occurring in relation to an 'election' determines the applicability of Sections 172–176 of the BNS, which criminalise bribery at elections, undue influence at elections, personation at elections, and false statements in connection with elections — offences that carry imprisonment and fines. If the relevant process does not constitute an 'election' under this context, these penal provisions cannot be invoked, and the conduct may remain unpunishable under this Sanhita.

definitions.definition: The term 'elector' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Section 172, 'elector' means any person who is enrolled or entitled to vote in any election conducted under any law for the time being in force, whether for Parliament, State Legislature, local body, or any other statutory body, and whose vote may be sought, influenced, or affected in connection with such election.
definitions.plain_english: An 'elector' is any person who has the legal right to vote in an election — whether it is for the national Parliament, a State Assembly, a local municipal body, or any other elected body. This includes any registered voter whose choice at the ballot box could be influenced or harmed. The term is relevant in the context of offences that try to improperly influence how people vote.
real_world_examples: A registered voter in Patna who is enrolled in the electoral roll for the Bihar Legislative Assembly election and is approached with cash to vote for a particular candidate — that voter is an 'elector' under this provision.

A citizen in Mumbai whose name appears on the municipal corporation election voter list, and who receives a threat not to vote for a rival candidate, qualifies as an 'elector' whose electoral right is being interfered with.
A voter in Chennai enrolled on the Lok Sabha electoral roll who is given free liquor on the eve of polling day to influence their vote is an 'elector' for purposes of the offence under Section 172.

A person registered to vote in a Panchayat election in a village in Rajasthan, who is told their family's land papers will be withheld unless they vote for the incumbent sarpanch, is an 'elector' whose free exercise of electoral right is being obstructed.

A tribal voter in Jharkhand whose name is on the voter list for a State Assembly constituency and who is impersonated at the polling booth by another person — that registered individual is the 'elector' whose vote has been misappropriated.
what_it_covers: Any person whose name is enrolled on an electoral roll for a Parliamentary constituency election in India.
A person entitled to vote in a State Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council election under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
A registered voter in local body elections such as Municipal Corporation, Panchayat, or Town Council elections conducted under State laws.
A person entitled to vote in elections to any statutory or quasi-governmental body where voting rights are governed by law.
A person whose vote is solicited, threatened, purchased, or otherwise interfered with in connection with any election covered under applicable law.
what_it_excludes: A candidate contesting the election, who is a distinct participant in the electoral process and not merely an 'elector' for purposes of these offences.
A person who has been disenfranchised or whose name has been struck off the electoral roll and therefore has no subsisting entitlement to vote.
Election officials, polling agents, or returning officers who administer the election rather than exercise a vote.
A non-citizen residing in India, who has no legal entitlement to be enrolled as a voter under Indian electoral laws.
A person below the age of eighteen years who is not yet eligible for enrollment on any electoral roll under Indian law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'elector' is central to the operation of Section 172 of the BNS, 2023, which criminalises bribery and undue influence in elections — the offence is only triggered when the person whose vote is being improperly solicited or coerced qualifies as an 'elector'. If an individual does not fall within this category, the specific electoral offences under Section 172 cannot be invoked, and the conduct may need to be prosecuted under different provisions.

definitions.definition: "Electoral right" means the right of a person to stand, or not to stand as, or to withdraw from being, a candidate or to vote or refrain from voting at an election.
definitions.plain_english: An electoral right is any right a person has in relation to participating in an election — whether that means choosing to run as a candidate, deciding not to run, pulling out of a race after entering it, casting a vote, or deliberately choosing not to vote. It covers both the active and passive dimensions of democratic participation. Essentially, it is the legal protection of a person's free choice in any electoral matter.
real_world_examples: A political party worker in Uttar Pradesh offers cash to a voter in exchange for voting for a particular candidate in a Lok Sabha election — this directly implicates the voter's electoral right to vote or refrain from voting, attracting the offence of bribery under Section 170.

A local strongman in Bihar threatens an independent candidate's family with physical harm unless the candidate withdraws their nomination — this is an interference with the candidate's electoral right to stand or withdraw on their own free will, constituting undue influence under Section 171.

A religious leader in Maharashtra issues a public statement warning voters that they will face 'divine displeasure' if they vote for a particular party — this is deemed interference with the electoral right of voters to cast their vote freely, punishable under Section 171.

A candidate in a Panchayat election in Rajasthan is offered a government contract as an inducement to withdraw their candidacy — this amounts to bribery affecting the electoral right to stand or withdraw as a candidate, triggering liability under Section 170.

A returning officer in Tamil Nadu is bribed to falsely certify that a legitimate candidate has voluntarily withdrawn — this fraudulently affects the electoral right of that candidate to stand in the election.

A booth-level worker in West Bengal intimidates a voter by threatening job loss if the voter does not refrain from voting — this constitutes undue influence over the voter's electoral right to vote or refrain from voting.
what_it_covers: The right of a person to stand as a candidate at any election, including contesting Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assembly, Panchayat, or Municipal elections.
The right of a person to choose NOT to stand as a candidate, i.e., the freedom to decline nomination or not file a nomination at all.
The right of a nominated candidate to voluntarily withdraw their candidacy from an election without coercion.
The right of a registered voter to cast their vote for a candidate or party of their choice at an election.
The right of a voter to refrain from voting entirely, i.e., the freedom to abstain from casting a ballot without being penalised or coerced.
what_it_excludes: The right to campaign or canvass on behalf of a candidate — this is an activity ancillary to the election process and is not part of the definition of electoral right.

Administrative or procedural rights related to elections, such as the right to inspect electoral rolls, file election petitions, or seek recounts — these are statutory rights distinct from electoral rights as defined.
A mere declaration of public policy or a promise of public action, which is explicitly excluded from constituting interference with or bribery of an electoral right under Sections 170 and 171.
Rights of election officials, returning officers, or poll workers in conducting the election — their duties are official functions, not electoral rights as defined under Section 169.
Rights arising under electoral law that do not pertain to standing, withdrawing, or voting, such as the right of a political party to be recognised or to receive election symbols.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's 'electoral right' as defined under Section 169 is engaged determines whether acts of inducement or coercion constitute the cognisable offences of bribery (Section 170) or undue influence at elections (Section 171) under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; without the existence of an electoral right being exercised or capable of being exercised, neither offence can be made out. definitions.retrieval_text:
electoral right: An electoral right is any right a person has in relation to participating in an election — whether that means choosing to run as a candidate, deciding not to run, pulling out of a race after entering it, casting a vote, or deliberately choosing not to vote. It covers both the active and passive dimensions of democratic participation. Essentially, it is the legal protection of a person's free choice in any electoral matter.

Legal text: "Electoral right" means the right of a person to stand, or not to stand as, or to withdraw from being, a candidate or to vote or refrain from voting at an election.

definitions.definition: The term 'electronic communication' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 78, 152, 196, and 197, it denotes any transmission of information, messages, signals, images, sounds, or data by means of electronic devices or digital networks, including the internet, e-mail, social media platforms, messaging applications, and any other digitally mediated channel. It encompasses every mode of communication effected through electronic or digital means where content is created, sent, received, or monitored using electronic systems.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic communication means any kind of message, post, or content that is sent or received using electronic devices and the internet — such as emails, WhatsApp messages, social media posts, or online comments. It covers both direct person-to-person digital messages and broadcasts to large online audiences. Essentially, if information travels through a phone, computer, or any digital network, it qualifies as electronic communication under this law.
real_world_examples: A man repeatedly sending WhatsApp messages and Instagram DMs to a woman who has clearly told him to stop constitutes monitoring and contacting through electronic communication, attracting the offence of stalking under Section 78.

A person posting inflammatory content on Twitter or Facebook deliberately inflaming religious tensions between Hindu and Muslim communities in India would be committing an offence through electronic communication under Section 196.

An individual sending a series of emails containing secessionist propaganda calling for the separation of a north-eastern state from India would be using electronic communication to commit an offence endangering the sovereignty and integrity of India under Section 152.

Someone running a YouTube channel that repeatedly asserts that members of a particular caste community cannot be loyal to the Indian Constitution and disseminates this content across digital platforms would be using electronic communication to commit the offence under Section 197.

A person sending mass SMS messages containing false and misleading information designed to incite communal violence between two religious groups in Maharashtra would be using electronic communication in violation of Sections 196 and 197.

An activist group using a Telegram channel to coordinate and spread content that encourages armed rebellion against the Indian State would be using electronic communication to endanger national integrity under Section 152.
what_it_covers: Emails sent through platforms like Gmail or Yahoo to contact, threaten, or spread harmful content
Social media posts, stories, or direct messages on platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, and LinkedIn
Instant messaging through applications like WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, or iMessage
Online broadcasts, video uploads, or live streams on platforms like YouTube or ShareChat containing seditious or communally divisive content
Monitoring a woman's internet usage, tracking her e-mail activity, or surveilling her digital footprint as part of stalking behaviour
Bulk SMS or automated digital message campaigns used to spread anti-national or communally harmful content
what_it_excludes: Purely verbal or face-to-face spoken communication not transmitted through any electronic medium
Physical written communications such as handwritten letters, printed pamphlets, or posters distributed manually without digital transmission

Traditional broadcast media such as analogue radio or terrestrial television transmissions where the content is not specifically channelled through digital electronic communication networks as understood in the context of these sections
Non-communicative electronic activity such as purely internal data processing or storage on a device that is not transmitted to any other party
Communication conducted under lawful interception or authorised surveillance by State agencies acting under the Information Technology Act, 2000 or other enabling legislation
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'electronic communication' determines whether the offences under Sections 152, 196, and 197 — which carry imprisonment of up to three years to life — are triggered when harmful content is disseminated digitally, and under Section 78, whether a man's digital monitoring of a woman constitutes the criminal offence of stalking punishable with imprisonment of up to three to five years. It expands the reach of these offences beyond physical or oral acts to cover the full spectrum of modern digital behaviour.
