definitions.definition: Electronic form, as used in Section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the display or representation of any content — including books, pamphlets, papers, writings, drawings, paintings, representations, figures, or other objects — in a digital or electronic medium, and as further clarified in Section 337, it carries the meaning assigned to it under clause (r) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, encompassing any information generated, sent, received or stored in media, magnetic, optical, computer memory, micro film, computer generated micro fiche or similar device.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic form means any content that exists or is shown in a digital format — such as on a website, mobile app, social media platform, email, or any other digital device or storage medium — rather than in a physical printed form. It covers everything from images and videos posted online to documents stored on a computer or shared over the internet. If obscene material is displayed or circulated digitally, it is treated the same as if it were a physical obscene object under the law.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai uploads sexually explicit images to a public WhatsApp group or Telegram channel, making them accessible to numerous users — this display of obscene content in electronic form on a digital platform falls squarely under Section 294.

An e-commerce website based in Delhi lists and sells access to obscene digital books or e-publications that are lascivious in nature — the sale of such material in electronic form triggers liability under Section 294.

A content creator in Bengaluru posts an obscene video on Instagram or YouTube that appeals to prurient interests and is accessible to the general public — the circulation of such content in electronic form constitutes an offence.

An individual in Chennai sends obscene digital drawings or AI-generated pornographic images via email or SMS to multiple recipients for commercial gain — distributing such material in electronic form is punishable under Section 294.

A company operating an adult website from Hyderabad allows Indian users to stream or download obscene material — hosting and distributing such content in electronic form amounts to putting obscene material into circulation under the section.

A person in Kolkata shares a link to an obscene PDF document through social media, enabling others to download and read it — the act of distributing an obscene document in electronic form is covered under Section 294.
what_it_covers: Obscene images, videos, or written content displayed or shared on social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, or Telegram.
Obscene e-books, PDFs, digital pamphlets, or other documents distributed via email, file-sharing apps, or websites.
Digital drawings, computer-generated paintings, or AI-generated obscene representations stored on or transmitted through electronic devices.
Content streamed or hosted on websites, cloud storage, or OTT platforms that is accessible to users in India in a digital format.
Obscene data or records stored on magnetic media, optical discs, computer memory, or similar electronic storage devices.
Display of lascivious content through mobile applications, messaging services (such as WhatsApp or Signal), or internet-based communication channels.
what_it_excludes: Physical printed books, pamphlets, magazines, photographs, or painted representations that exist solely in tangible paper or material form and have no electronic component.
Content that is not obscene — i.e., material that does not appeal to prurient interest and does not tend to deprave and corrupt its audience, even if it exists in electronic form.
Private, consensual electronic communication between adults that is not put into public circulation, distributed, sold, or exhibited to others, and does not constitute commercial exploitation.
Electronic records or documents that are official, governmental, or judicial in nature and are not obscene, even if they fall within the definition of electronic form under the IT Act.
Legitimate educational, scientific, medical, or artistic content in digital form that does not meet the legal threshold of obscenity under Section 294.
Content transmitted or stored electronically for bona fide law enforcement, evidentiary, or archival purposes by authorised public servants.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether content qualifies as being in 'electronic form' determines whether the offence of selling, distributing, or publicly exhibiting obscene material under Section 294 can be extended beyond physical objects to digital platforms and media — thereby enabling prosecution of online obscenity, digital pornography distribution, and internet-based circulation of obscene content. If this definition applies, a first conviction can attract up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to five thousand rupees, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenders.

definitions.definition: The term 'electronic means' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in Sections 299 and 353 to denote any mode of communication, transmission, publication, or circulation carried out through digital or electronic technology, including the internet, social media platforms, messaging applications, email, websites, and any other digital medium capable of conveying words, signs, visible representations, statements, or information electronically.
definitions.plain_english: Electronic means refers to any digital or internet-based method used to send, share, or publish content — such as posting on social media, sending messages via WhatsApp, uploading videos online, or sending emails. It covers any technology that transmits information in electronic form rather than through physical speech or printed material. In simple terms, if something is communicated through a phone, computer, or the internet, it is done through 'electronic means'.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai posts a video on YouTube deliberately mocking the religious practices of a particular community with the intent to outrage their religious feelings — this constitutes using electronic means under Section 299 of the BNS.

A WhatsApp group admin in Delhi forwards a fabricated rumour claiming that a particular religious group is poisoning water supplies, likely to incite communal violence — this amounts to publishing false information through electronic means under Section 353.

A Twitter/X user in Chennai tweets inflammatory statements insulting the beliefs of a minority religion, aiming to provoke religious hatred — this is an offence committed through electronic means under Section 299.

A Telegram channel operator in Hyderabad circulates fake news reports falsely alleging that soldiers of the Indian Army have committed atrocities, intending to cause public fear and alarm — this is dissemination through electronic means punishable under Section 353.

A Facebook page administrator in Kolkata publishes a series of posts containing false information designed to create enmity between two religious communities ahead of a festival — this constitutes an offence through electronic means under Section 353(2).

A person sends mass SMS messages across Punjab containing statements insulting the sacred texts of a religious community with deliberate malicious intent — this use of digital telecommunication infrastructure qualifies as electronic means under Section 299.
what_it_covers: Posts, comments, or videos published on social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X (Twitter), or YouTube that insult religious beliefs or circulate false information.
Messages, forwards, or content shared via instant messaging applications such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, or similar platforms.
Emails, bulk SMS, or electronic newsletters used to disseminate statements, rumours, or content intended to outrage religious feelings or cause public mischief.
Content uploaded to websites, blogs, online forums, or news portals that contains religiously inflammatory or false alarm-inducing material.
Live-streaming sessions or podcast recordings distributed digitally that insult a religion or spread false alarming information to the public.
what_it_excludes: Spoken words communicated in person or through a physical public gathering, which are covered separately by the phrase 'words, either spoken' in Section 299.
Printed pamphlets, newspapers, books, or physical placards — these fall under 'written' words or 'visible representations' in physical form, not electronic means.
Private conversations conducted face-to-face or through non-electronic means such as handwritten letters delivered physically, which lack the electronic transmission element.

Content stored on an electronic device but never transmitted, published, or circulated through any network or digital channel, as mere possession without dissemination does not constitute use of electronic means in this context.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is carried out through 'electronic means' determines whether offences under Section 299 (outraging religious feelings) and Section 353 (statements conducing to public mischief) are attracted in the context of digital communication, significantly expanding the territorial and temporal reach of the offence beyond physical or oral acts. It enables prosecution for online hate speech, viral misinformation, and digital communal incitement that would otherwise be difficult to prosecute solely under traditional modes of expression recognised in earlier law.

definitions.definition: "Electronic record" is not expressly defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; however, as used throughout the Act, it means any data, record, or information generated, sent, received, or stored in electronic form, and includes any document or communication created, maintained, or transmitted by means of a computer resource or electronic device, as understood in accordance with the Information Technology Act, 2000.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic record is any document, file, message, or piece of information that exists in digital or electronic form — for example, a WhatsApp message, an email, a PDF file, a computer-generated report, or data stored on a server. It is the digital equivalent of a paper document. Just like a physical document can be produced in court or before a government officer, an electronic record can also be demanded, submitted, or used as evidence.
real_world_examples: A government officer in Delhi is asked to produce CCTV footage stored on a DVR as evidence before a magistrate — this digital footage constitutes an electronic record under the Act.

A chartered accountant emails a falsified balance sheet to a company's board in Mumbai — the email and the attached PDF file together form an electronic record that could be subject to offences under the Act.

A police officer in Chennai issues a summons requiring a telecom company to produce call detail records (CDRs) stored on its servers — those CDRs are electronic records, and failure to produce them triggers liability under Section 210.

A public servant in Bengaluru deliberately alters an officially digitised land record in a government database to cause wrongful gain — the modified entry in the database is an electronic record, and the act attracts punishment under Section 201.

A person in Hyderabad absconds to avoid complying with a court order directing him to produce WhatsApp chat logs saved on his phone — those chat logs are electronic records, and absconding to avoid producing them attracts Section 206.

A hospital in Kolkata maintains patient records in a digital health management system; when a court directs the hospital to submit a specific patient's digital file, that file is an electronic record whose non-production attracts Section 210.
what_it_covers: Emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS messages, and other digital communications stored on a device or server.
Scanned copies of official documents, digitised government registers, and database entries maintained by public servants.
CCTV footage, audio-video recordings, call detail records (CDRs), and log files stored in electronic or binary form.
Digital financial records such as bank statements in electronic format, e-invoices, and electronically filed returns.
Electronic court filings, e-summons, and digital notices issued or received through government portals.
what_it_excludes: Physical paper documents, handwritten manuscripts, or printed records that have never been digitised or stored electronically.
Oral statements, verbal testimonies, or declarations made in person that are not reduced to any electronic form.
Physical property marks, stamps, or seals impressed on tangible objects that carry no accompanying electronic data.
Real-time analogue audio or video transmissions that are not captured or stored in any electronic medium.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a particular record qualifies as an 'electronic record' directly determines the applicability of Sections 201, 206, 207, and 210 of the BNS, 2023 — attracting enhanced punishments (up to six months' imprisonment) for absconding to avoid producing it, preventing its service, or omitting to produce it before a court, and also exposing public servants to prosecution for falsifying it under Section 201. Without this classification, such digital material would fall outside the specific penal provisions that parallel protections traditionally afforded to physical documents.

Covers: Emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS messages, and other digital communications stored on a device or server.; Scanned copies of official documents, digitised government registers, and database entries maintained by public servants.; CCTV footage, audio-video recordings, call detail records (CDRs), and log files stored in electronic or binary form.; Digital financial records such as bank statements in electronic format, e-invoices, and electronically filed returns.; Electronic court filings, e-summons, and digital notices issued or received through government portals.

Excludes: Physical paper documents, handwritten manuscripts, or printed records that have never been digitised or stored electronically.; Oral statements, verbal testimonies, or declarations made in person that are not reduced to any electronic form.; Physical property marks, stamps, or seals impressed on tangible objects that carry no accompanying electronic data.; Real-time analogue audio or video transmissions that are not captured or stored in any electronic medium.

definitions.definition: An electronic signature, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any authentication affixed to an electronic record by a person to signify their identity and intent, equivalent in legal effect to a handwritten signature on a document. It encompasses any mark, process, or symbol affixed to or associated with an electronic record for the purpose of authenticating or executing that record. Its forgery or unauthorised affixation constitutes a criminal offence under Section 335.
definitions.plain_english: An electronic signature is a digital way of signing a document or record online — similar to signing your name on paper, but done electronically. It could be a scanned signature, a PIN, a one-time password, or a cryptographic key that confirms who approved or created a digital document. Just like forging someone's physical signature is a crime, forging or misusing someone's electronic signature is also a criminal offence in India.
real_world_examples: A fraudster uses a stolen Aadhaar-based eSign credential to digitally sign a property transfer deed on a government portal, falsely making it appear that the original owner authorised the transfer.

An employee at a fintech company affixes a client's Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) on a loan agreement without the client's knowledge or consent, creating a false electronic record binding the client to a debt.
A person intercepts a company director's digital signature token and uses it to sign and submit falsified financial statements to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs on the MCA21 portal.
An individual forges a doctor's electronic signature on a digitally generated medical fitness certificate to submit to an employer or court as genuine evidence of health clearance.
A software developer maliciously alters a digitally signed government tender document after it has been electronically executed, changing the bid amount to favour a particular contractor.
what_it_covers: A Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000, affixed to any electronic record or form.
An Aadhaar-based eSign or OTP-based electronic authentication used to execute contracts, agreements, or government submissions online.
Any cryptographic mark, symbol, or process associated with an electronic record that identifies the signatory and indicates their approval or execution of the record.
A scanned or digitised version of a handwritten signature embedded in an electronic document for the purpose of authentication.
Electronic signatures used on e-stamped documents, court filings, or regulatory submissions on platforms like MCA21, GSTN, or Income Tax e-filing portals.
what_it_excludes: A physical handwritten signature on a paper document, even if that document is later scanned and stored digitally — this would constitute a conventional signature, not an electronic signature.
A mere typed name at the end of an email without any cryptographic, OTP-based, or certified authentication mechanism, which does not meet the threshold of a legally recognised electronic signature.
A seal or stamp affixed physically on a paper document, as this constitutes a conventional seal rather than an electronic signature on an electronic record.
Verbal or oral consent given over a phone call, even if recorded digitally, as this does not constitute an electronic signature on an electronic record.
Unsigned electronic records or documents that are transmitted without any authentication mechanism attached — absence of a signature cannot itself constitute an electronic signature.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as an electronic signature determines whether its forgery, unauthorised affixation, or fraudulent use constitutes the offence of making a false electronic record under Section 335, which is the predicate act for forgery offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Proof that a genuine electronic signature was forged or affixed without authority is essential to establishing criminal liability for forgery, fraud, and related offences involving electronic records.

definitions.definition: Encryption, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any technique or method of converting information into a coded or concealed form that renders it inaccessible, unreadable, or unintelligible to unauthorised persons, employed as an information-hiding tool. It is referenced in Sections 58 and 59 as a specific means by which a person may voluntarily conceal the existence of a design to commit an offence, alongside other information-hiding tools.
definitions.plain_english: Encryption means using a technical method to scramble or lock information so that only authorised people can read or access it. In the context of this law, it refers to using such a technique to hide plans or designs to commit serious crimes from authorities. Think of it like putting a secret code on a message so no one else can understand what it says.
real_world_examples: A suspect in a planned dacoity uses an end-to-end encrypted messaging app like WhatsApp or Signal to communicate the time, location, and method of attack with co-conspirators, deliberately choosing encrypted communication to prevent police interception and conceal the design of the offence.

A corrupt police officer, who is legally bound to report intelligence about an imminent terrorist attack, uses an encrypted folder or application on his personal device to store and hide all information about the planned attack he has received, thereby facilitating the offence under Section 59.

A gang planning a kidnapping for ransom uses encrypted emails and PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) encryption to exchange target details, ransom demands, and escape routes, ensuring that even if the communications are intercepted by law enforcement, the content of the design remains hidden.

A person aware of a planned organised crime hit uses encrypted voice-over-IP calls routed through anonymising networks (such as Tor) to relay information about the victim's movements to the perpetrators, actively concealing the design of the offence from investigators.

A public servant in a municipal corporation uses an encrypted USB drive to store details about a planned large-scale fraud scheme, deliberately preventing any audit or investigation from accessing the design of the criminal enterprise, thereby attracting liability under Section 59.
what_it_covers: Use of end-to-end encrypted messaging applications (e.g., Signal, WhatsApp) to conceal plans for commission of a serious offence from authorities.
Encryption of digital files, folders, or drives containing evidence of a criminal design, rendering them inaccessible to investigators or concerned authorities.
Use of encrypted email protocols or encrypted voice communication tools (VoIP with encryption) to transmit details of an ongoing criminal conspiracy.

Deployment of cryptographic tools such as PGP, AES encryption, or similar technologies deliberately chosen for the purpose of hiding the existence of a design to commit an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment.
A public servant using encrypted communication channels to conceal information about an offence they are legally bound to prevent or report.
what_it_excludes: Routine use of encryption for legitimate personal or commercial data security purposes where there is no intent to conceal a criminal design (e.g., a business encrypting customer data for compliance with IT regulations).
Encryption used by law enforcement, intelligence agencies, or authorised government bodies in the lawful performance of their duties to protect sensitive operational information.
Mere possession or use of encryption tools without any accompanying intent to facilitate or conceal the design of a specific offence punishable under the BNS.
Use of passwords or basic access controls on personal devices that do not specifically function to hide a design to commit an offence, absent the requisite criminal knowledge or intent.
Encryption employed by journalists, lawyers, or activists to protect privileged or sensitive communications in a lawful professional context.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether encryption is used to voluntarily conceal a design to commit an offence directly determines criminal liability under Sections 58 and 59 of the BNS — a non-public servant may face up to seven years of imprisonment if the offence is committed, while a public servant may face up to ten years for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment. The use of encryption as an information-hiding tool transforms what might otherwise be mere passive awareness into active culpable concealment, attracting serious penal consequences.

definitions.definition: A State prisoner or prisoner of war is said to escape from lawful custody if such prisoner goes beyond the limits within which he is allowed to be at large, including where a prisoner permitted to be at large on parole within certain limits in India goes beyond those limits. More broadly, 'escape' encompasses any act by which a State prisoner or prisoner of war leaves or is removed from lawful custody without authorisation.
definitions.plain_english: Escape means when a State prisoner or prisoner of war leaves the place or limits where they are legally held or permitted to stay, without permission. This includes not just physically breaking out of a prison, but also when a prisoner on parole goes beyond the geographical boundaries set for them. Essentially, any unauthorised departure from the place or limits of lawful custody counts as an escape.
real_world_examples: A Pakistani prisoner of war held in a detention facility in Jodhpur during a period of armed conflict breaks through a perimeter fence and flees into the city — this constitutes an escape from lawful custody.

A State prisoner in India who has been granted parole and is permitted to remain within the city limits of Pune travels to Mumbai without authorisation — by crossing beyond the permitted limits, he is deemed to have escaped from lawful custody under Section 158.

A political detainee classified as a State prisoner, while being transported from Tihar Jail to a court hearing in Delhi, overpowers his guards and flees — this is a classic case of escape from lawful custody.

A prisoner of war held in a camp in Rajasthan is granted restricted movement within the camp premises but is found outside the camp boundary in a nearby village — this constitutes an escape even though no physical barrier was breached.

A person knowing that a State prisoner has escaped from Nagpur Central Jail hides him in their home in a different district, thereby harbouring an escaped prisoner — the prior escape triggers liability under Section 158.
A civilian who bribes a guard at a State prisoner facility in Chennai, enabling the prisoner to walk out undetected, is guilty of aiding an escape under Section 158.
what_it_covers: A State prisoner physically breaking out of a confined facility and fleeing beyond its walls without authorisation.
A prisoner of war who is on parole within specified geographical limits in India and travels beyond those limits, even without physical coercion or force.
A State prisoner who is aided, assisted, or rescued by a third party in leaving lawful custody, where the departure itself constitutes the escape.

Any attempt by a State prisoner or prisoner of war to leave or evade the place or limits of confinement, whether or not the attempt is ultimately successful in the context of associated liability for third parties.
A prisoner permitted limited movement within a defined area who exceeds those boundaries, regardless of intent or duration.
what_it_excludes: An ordinary undertrial or convicted criminal prisoner who escapes from a regular jail — such a person is not a 'State prisoner' or 'prisoner of war' and their escape is governed by separate provisions, not Section 158.
A prisoner who is formally and lawfully released or discharged from custody by a competent authority — a lawful release does not constitute an escape.
A State prisoner who moves within the explicitly permitted limits of a parole order — remaining within authorised boundaries is not an escape even if the prisoner is unsupervised.
A civilian who unknowingly assists a State prisoner without knowledge of the prisoner's status or escape — Section 158 requires knowing assistance, so unknowing help is excluded.

Transfer of a prisoner between facilities by authorised public servants — an authorised movement under official orders does not qualify as an escape even if the prisoner is temporarily outside a fixed facility.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'escape' directly determines criminal liability under Section 158 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: anyone who knowingly aids, rescues, harbours, or resists the recapture of a State prisoner or prisoner of war who has 'escaped' faces imprisonment for life or up to ten years plus fine. Whether a parole-boundary breach qualifies as an escape is legally significant because it activates all downstream offences related to aiding, harbouring, or obstructing recapture.

definitions.definition: Supplies or services essential to the life of the community in India or in any foreign country, the disruption of which by means of bombs, explosives, firearms, hazardous substances or any other means constitutes an element of a terrorist act under Section 113 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The term encompasses those supplies and services whose interruption would critically undermine the basic functioning, survival, or welfare of the general population or any section thereof.
definitions.plain_english: Essential supplies refers to goods, utilities, and services that people depend on for their day-to-day survival and wellbeing, such as water, electricity, fuel, food distribution networks, and medical supplies. If a terrorist deliberately disrupts or destroys these supplies, it falls within the scope of a terrorist act under Indian law. The idea is that cutting off such supplies can cause widespread harm to ordinary people across a community or nation.
real_world_examples: A terrorist group plants explosives on a major water pipeline supplying drinking water to Mumbai, causing large-scale water shortages across the city.
Militants sabotage a high-voltage electricity transmission tower in Punjab, causing a cascading blackout affecting hospitals, homes, and industries across multiple districts.
Armed insurgents attack and destroy a government food grain storage facility (FCI warehouse) in a conflict-affected region of Manipur, cutting off ration supply to thousands of beneficiaries.
A terrorist cell contaminates a natural gas pipeline network in Gujarat, disrupting cooking gas supply to hundreds of thousands of households and commercial establishments.
Extremists blow up a fuel depot on a national highway in Jammu & Kashmir, halting petrol and diesel distribution across the region and crippling transportation and emergency services.
what_it_covers: Drinking water supply systems and pipelines that serve entire cities or regions
Electricity generation and transmission networks upon which hospitals, homes, and industries depend
Food grain distribution networks, ration supply chains, and government-managed food storage facilities
Fuel and petroleum distribution infrastructure including pipelines, depots, and refineries
Medical supply chains delivering critical medicines and equipment to hospitals and dispensaries
Public transportation networks such as railways and metro systems that are vital to community movement
what_it_excludes: Disruption of purely commercial or private supply chains that do not affect the general life of the community (e.g., a private luxury goods warehouse)
Temporary or accidental supply interruptions caused by natural disasters or technical failures without any terrorist intent
Disruption of services that affect only a single private individual or a very limited group not constituting a recognisable 'community'
Trade disputes, strikes, or industrial actions that lawfully interrupt supplies without the use of explosive or hazardous means and without terrorist intent
Mere possession of hazardous material without any act causing or likely to cause disruption to essential supplies
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a disrupted supply qualifies as an 'essential supply' under Section 113 determines whether the act of disruption constitutes a terrorist act, attracting the severe penalties of the section including imprisonment for life or even the death penalty if deaths result. If the disruption does not involve essential supplies or services, the accused may instead face lesser charges under other provisions of the BNS relating to mischief, sabotage, or damage to property.

definitions.definition: The term 'evidence' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in sections 233, 238, and 241, it denotes any matter, whether oral, documentary, electronic, or material, presented or capable of being presented before a court or legal proceeding to establish or disprove a fact in issue. It encompasses testimony, documents, electronic records, and physical objects tendered to influence judicial determination of guilt, innocence, or liability.
definitions.plain_english: Evidence is anything — spoken words, written documents, electronic records, or physical objects — that is used in a court case to prove or disprove whether something happened. Think of it as the information a judge looks at to decide a case. In India, this could be a witness's statement, a WhatsApp message, a signed contract, or a weapon found at a crime scene. Without evidence, claims in court cannot be established.
real_world_examples: A CCTV footage recording from a Delhi market showing an accused snatching a mobile phone is produced before a Metropolitan Magistrate as evidence during trial under BNS section 304.
A doctor's medical report documenting grievous hurt injuries on a victim's body is submitted as documentary evidence in a Sessions Court trial in Mumbai for an offence under BNS section 117.

WhatsApp chat messages between conspirators planning a dacoity, extracted from a mobile phone seized by the Uttar Pradesh Police, are tendered as electronic evidence in proceedings under BNS section 310.
An eyewitness who personally saw the accused commit murder in a Chennai street testifies before a High Court — their oral testimony constitutes evidence in the criminal trial under BNS section 101.
A forged property deed submitted by an accused to fraudulently transfer land in Bengaluru is placed before the court as fabricated evidence in proceedings under BNS section 238.
A forensic ballistics report confirming a firearm recovered from an accused matches the bullet used in a Hyderabad shooting is presented as expert evidence during a murder trial.
what_it_covers: Oral statements made by witnesses before a court or judicial proceeding to establish facts in issue.
Documentary evidence including written agreements, contracts, official records, maps, and digital or electronic records such as emails, SMS, and CCTV recordings.
Physical or material objects such as weapons, forged currency, or seized contraband produced before the court to prove the commission of an offence.
Expert reports, forensic analyses, and medical certificates tendered by qualified professionals to assist the court in determining technical or scientific facts.
Confessions, admissions, and prior statements of the accused or witnesses that are admissible under applicable procedural law.
what_it_excludes: Arguments, legal submissions, or pleadings made by lawyers before a court, which are advocacy and not evidence.

definitions.definition: The phrase 'execution of office' refers to the active and lawful discharge of the duties, functions, and responsibilities attached to a superior officer's official position within the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India, such that the officer is actively engaged in performing their official role at the time the relevant act or offence occurs.
definitions.plain_english: This term means that a military officer is actually carrying out their official duties or responsibilities at the moment something happens to them. It is not enough that the person holds an official rank or position — they must be actively performing that role at the relevant time. For example, a commanding officer giving lawful orders on parade or supervising a military operation would be 'in execution of his office'.
real_world_examples: A superior Indian Army Colonel is conducting a formal inspection of troops at a cantonment in Pune; a soldier, instigated by a third party, assaults him during this inspection — the Colonel is in execution of his office at that moment.

A Naval Commander is overseeing a training exercise aboard an INS vessel near Mumbai when an airman, abetted by a civilian, strikes him — the Commander is actively executing his official naval duties.

An Air Force Squadron Leader is issuing operational orders to ground crew at an airbase in Bengaluru; a subordinate airman, encouraged by an external person, commits an assault — the Squadron Leader is in execution of his office as he performs command functions.

A Subedar Major in the Indian Army is presiding over a disciplinary hearing at a military base in Ambala when he is attacked by a soldier acting on instigation — the Subedar Major is discharging his official adjudicatory duty and is thus in execution of his office.

A Naval officer is boarding a merchant vessel as part of a lawful security check off the coast of Chennai when assaulted after being abetted by a third party — the officer is actively executing his official patrol and inspection functions.
semantic_tags: official role at time of offence
what_it_covers: A superior officer actively commanding troops, conducting parade, or issuing operational orders during service hours at a military installation.
A naval officer performing a lawful boarding, inspection, or patrol duty in the course of their assigned naval responsibilities.
An Air Force officer supervising maintenance, training, or operational briefings in their official supervisory capacity at an airbase.
A superior military officer presiding over or conducting a disciplinary or administrative proceeding within the armed forces.
A military officer engaged in enforcement of discipline, security duties, or active deployment operations as part of their assigned role.
what_it_excludes: A superior officer who is off-duty, on leave, or engaged in purely personal activities unconnected to their official military responsibilities at the time of the assault.
An officer who holds a rank but has been temporarily suspended from duty or relieved of their official responsibilities at the material time.
Retired or discharged military personnel who no longer hold an active commission or appointment in the Army, Navy, or Air Force.
Actions taken by the officer that exceed their lawful authority or are entirely outside the scope of their official functions, such as purely personal disputes.
A situation where the officer is present at a military location but not actively engaged in any official duty, function, or responsibility at the time of the incident.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a superior officer is 'in the execution of his office' at the time of the assault is a critical element under Section 162 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; if this condition is satisfied, anyone who abets such an assault faces imprisonment of up to seven years and liability to fine. Without proof that the officer was actively executing their office, the aggravated offence under Section 162 may not be established, reducing the applicable charge and punishment.

definitions.definition: The expression 'exploitation' shall include any act of physical exploitation or any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary or forced removal of organs.
definitions.plain_english: Exploitation means using a person for someone else's benefit in a harmful and abusive way, without the person's genuine free choice. This includes forcing or tricking someone into physical labour, sexual acts, slavery-like conditions, begging, or even taking their organs against their will. It is the core purpose that makes human trafficking a crime under the law.
real_world_examples: A trafficking network in Mumbai lures young women from rural Bihar with promises of jobs, then forces them into commercial sexual services in brothels — this constitutes sexual exploitation under Section 143.

A contractor in Telangana recruits tribal children by paying small sums to their parents, then keeps the children in bondage working on brick kilns without wages or freedom to leave — this qualifies as servitude and practices similar to slavery.

An organised gang in Delhi kidnaps homeless individuals and forces them to beg on streets, retaining all money collected and threatening violence if they refuse — this is exploitation in the form of beggary.

A criminal syndicate in Chennai traffics a person from Nepal and surgically removes their kidney for sale on the black market without consent — this constitutes forced removal of organs, a recognised form of exploitation.

A domestic worker from Jharkhand is brought to Gurugram under false pretences and then confined, denied salary, and made to work 18-hour days under constant threat — this amounts to physical exploitation and servitude.

A network in Kolkata recruits young men promising factory work abroad but then confiscates their passports and forces them to work in a foreign country without pay — this is exploitation through debt bondage and practices similar to slavery.
what_it_covers: Any form of sexual exploitation, including forcing a trafficked person into prostitution or pornography.
Slavery or practices similar to slavery, such as debt bondage, serfdom, or selling a person as property.
Servitude, including compelled domestic or industrial labour with no freedom of movement or exit.
Beggary, where a person is forced or compelled to beg for the financial benefit of another.
Forced removal of organs, such as non-consensual kidney or other organ extraction for commercial sale.
Any act of physical exploitation where the body of the trafficked person is used as an instrument for another's gain.
what_it_excludes: Consensual adult employment, even in hazardous occupations, where genuine free consent exists and no trafficking is involved.
Court-ordered community service or imprisonment with labour, which is legally sanctioned and not trafficking-related.
Voluntary religious or personal acts of renunciation or self-denial, which are not imposed by another person for their benefit.
Lawful medical procedures including organ donation performed with the free and informed consent of the donor.
Economic hardship or poverty alone, without an act of recruitment, transport, or control by another person for exploitative purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'exploitation' is the operative purpose-element of the offence of trafficking under Section 143 — if the acts of recruitment, transport, harbouring, or transfer are not carried out 'for the purpose of exploitation', no offence of trafficking is made out. The breadth of the definition directly determines the scope of punishment, which ranges from seven years' rigorous imprisonment to life imprisonment, and also activates related liability under Section 144 for those who knowingly engage trafficked persons.

definitions.definition: The term 'explosive substance' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used throughout the Act it denotes any substance capable of producing an explosive effect, including gunpowder, dynamite, bombs, grenades, and any chemical compound or mixture that, by reason of its properties, is capable of a sudden release of energy through detonation, deflagration, or rapid combustion, causing destruction, injury, or death. It encompasses both the explosive material itself and any device or article manufactured or adapted to cause an explosion.
definitions.plain_english: An explosive substance is any material or device that can suddenly explode or blow up, releasing a large amount of energy in a very short time, causing damage, injury, or death. Examples include bombs, dynamite, grenades, and similar materials. It does not matter whether the substance is commercially manufactured or homemade — if it can cause an explosion, it counts. This term is used in Indian law to identify especially dangerous weapons or means of causing harm.
real_world_examples: A person plants an improvised explosive device (IED) made from ammonium nitrate and fuel oil near a railway track in Pune with the intent to derail a train — the IED constitutes an explosive substance under the Act.
A militant group in Jammu uses military-grade grenades to attack a police patrol — the grenades are explosive substances, attracting enhanced punishment under Sections 326 and 327 of the BNS.

An individual sets off a country-made bomb (desi bomb) during a political rally in Kolkata, causing grievous hurt to several attendees — the country-made bomb qualifies as an explosive substance for purposes of Section 118.

A criminal syndicate in Mumbai uses dynamite sticks to blow open the door of a bank vault during a robbery — the dynamite constitutes an explosive substance, escalating the offence under the relevant provisions.

A person deliberately throws a pipe bomb into a residential building in Delhi, setting it on fire and destroying property — the pipe bomb is an explosive substance, engaging the right of private defence extending to causing death under Section 41 of the Act.

A terror cell in Hyderabad stores RDX explosive material in a warehouse for use in a planned attack — possession of RDX, being an explosive substance, attracts liability under the terrorist act provisions of Section 113.
what_it_covers: Commercially manufactured explosives such as dynamite, TNT, RDX, and C-4 used for criminal or terrorist purposes.
Improvised explosive devices (IEDs) or country-made bombs assembled from readily available chemicals such as ammonium nitrate, potassium nitrate, or other reactive compounds.
Military-grade ordnance such as grenades, shells, and landmines when used outside lawful military application.
Pipe bombs, pressure-cooker bombs, or any device specifically constructed or adapted to cause an explosion.
Chemical mixtures or compounds designed to detonate upon ignition, impact, or remote triggering, regardless of their form or container.
what_it_excludes: Flammable or combustible substances that burn progressively rather than detonate explosively, such as petrol, kerosene, or ordinary fire accelerants, which are treated separately as 'fire' or 'inflammable substance' in the Act.
Poisonous, corrosive, or noxious substances that cause harm through chemical reaction with the body rather than by explosion, which are covered under separate limbs of Section 118.
Fireworks or pyrotechnic articles used for celebratory purposes that do not have the destructive capacity associated with explosive substances in a criminal context.
Radioactive, biological, or nuclear materials, which are separately enumerated in Section 113 as distinct categories of hazardous substances used in terrorist acts.
Substances that are merely pressurised (such as LPG cylinders in normal use) unless specifically weaponised or adapted to cause an explosion in the commission of an offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as an 'explosive substance' directly determines the severity of punishment — its use in voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt under Section 118 attracts enhanced penalties compared to ordinary hurt offences, and its deployment in committing dacoity or robbery under Sections 326 and 327 or in a terrorist act under Section 113 triggers the most serious punishments including life imprisonment or death. Additionally, its use in mischief against a dwelling activates the right of private defence extending to causing death under Section 41.

definitions.definition: Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to any person any property, or valuable security or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security, commits extortion.
definitions.plain_english: Extortion occurs when someone deliberately threatens another person with harm — to themselves or someone they care about — and uses that fear to force them to hand over money, property, or important documents. The key elements are: an intentional threat, the creation of fear of injury, and the dishonest taking of something of value as a result. Unlike simple theft, extortion involves the victim being coerced into 'giving' rather than having something taken without their knowledge.
real_world_examples: A local strongman in a Mumbai market threatens a shopkeeper that his shop will be vandalized and his family harassed unless he pays a monthly 'protection fee' (hafta) of ₹20,000 — the shopkeeper pays out of fear, constituting extortion.

A person sends a WhatsApp message to a Delhi businessman threatening to release private compromising photographs unless the businessman transfers ₹5 lakh to a specified bank account — this digital threat followed by payment constitutes extortion.

A gang in Bengaluru kidnaps a child and sends a ransom note to the parents demanding ₹10 lakh, threatening to harm the child if the money is not paid — inducing the parents to pay constitutes extortion.

A corrupt government officer tells a contractor in Chennai that his pending project payment will be blocked and false complaints filed against him unless he signs over a blank cheque — inducing the contractor to sign the cheque constitutes extortion.

A land grabber in Hyderabad threatens a farmer with false criminal cases and physical violence unless the farmer signs a sale deed transferring his agricultural land at a grossly undervalued price — the signing under such threat constitutes extortion.

An individual threatens to send club-men to destroy crops in a Punjab village unless the village head signs a bond agreeing to supply produce exclusively at below-market prices — constituting extortion as illustrated in the Act's own example.
what_it_covers: Threatening to publish defamatory content unless the victim pays money, thereby inducing payment through fear of reputational injury.
Sending threats via electronic devices (phone, WhatsApp, email) demanding money or property in exchange for releasing a kidnapped person or refraining from harm.
Inducing a person to sign or seal a blank paper or promissory note by putting them in fear of grievous hurt, where the document may be converted into a valuable security.
Threatening wrongful confinement of a third party (such as a child or relative) to compel the victim to deliver property or sign legal documents.
Demanding a 'protection fee' or 'hafta' under threat of violence or property damage, where payment is made out of fear of the threatened injury.
Extortion committed as part of organised crime syndicate activity, which separately attracts enhanced punishment under Section 111 of the BNS, 2023.
what_it_excludes: Simple theft or robbery where property is taken without the victim's induced participation — robbery involves force or threat at the moment of taking without requiring the victim to voluntarily deliver property through sustained coercive inducement.

Legitimate legal demands for payment or performance of a lawful contractual obligation, even if accompanied by a warning of legal consequences (such as filing a civil suit), as these do not constitute unlawful injury threats.

Mere attempts to put a person in fear of injury without any actual delivery of property, valuable security, or signed document — these are punished separately as a lesser offence under Section 308 itself (up to two years) and do not constitute the completed offence of extortion.
Situations where a person voluntarily and freely delivers property without any threat or fear being intentionally induced — absence of coercive fear negates the essential element of extortion.
Criminal intimidation that does not result in the delivery of property or a valuable security — such standalone threats fall under criminal intimidation provisions, not extortion.
Cheating or fraud achieved through deception rather than through inducing fear of injury — these are governed by separate provisions on cheating under BNS, 2023.
definitions.why_it_matters: A finding that extortion has been committed triggers imprisonment of up to seven years, fine, or both under Section 308, and where it forms part of organised crime activity under Section 111, punishment escalates to a minimum of five years up to life imprisonment with a fine of not less than five lakh rupees. The definition also determines whether related charges of attempt, abetment, or conspiracy to extort apply, and whether enhanced liability under the organised crime syndicate framework is attracted.

definitions.definition: Evidence that has been manufactured, invented, or altered so as to be false, and which did not genuinely arise from or correspond to actual facts or events; evidence is 'fabricated' within the meaning of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 when it is created or tampered with to produce a false belief in a court or authority as to a matter of fact, as contemplated by Sections 227–233 governing false and fabricated evidence.
definitions.plain_english: Fabricated evidence means any proof or material — such as documents, witness statements, or physical objects — that has been made up, forged, or dishonestly altered to mislead a court or official proceeding. It is evidence that the person using or creating it knows is not genuine or truthful. In simple terms, it is 'planted' or 'manufactured' proof intended to deceive a judge or investigating authority.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Delhi plants a forged FIR extract or doctored CCTV footage in a criminal trial to falsely implicate an accused person, knowing the footage has been edited to misrepresent events.

A litigant in a property dispute before a civil court in Mumbai submits a fabricated sale deed bearing a forged signature of the original landowner, presenting it as genuine documentary evidence of title.

An accused in a corruption case before a CBI special court in Hyderabad produces a counterfeit bank statement showing a zero balance, manufactured to create a false impression of innocence regarding disproportionate assets.

A witness in a matrimonial case before a family court in Chennai brings a forged medical certificate purporting to show the spouse's mental illness, which was never actually issued by any registered medical practitioner.

An employee in a labour tribunal proceeding in Kolkata submits a fabricated attendance register showing continuous service, which was actually created after the dispute arose by altering original records.
what_it_covers: A document, record, or electronic record that has been created from scratch or altered to misrepresent facts and is then used or produced in a judicial or official proceeding.
Physical objects such as weapons, fingerprints, or samples that have been planted, tampered with, or manipulated to create a false evidentiary impression before a court or authority.
Statements, affidavits, or confessions that are forged or fabricated to attribute words or admissions to a person who never made them, and are submitted in a judicial proceeding.
Digital or electronic evidence such as doctored emails, edited audio recordings, or manipulated metadata, produced before a court knowing it has been altered to misrepresent the truth.
what_it_excludes: Evidence that is merely weak, insufficient, or unconvincing but was gathered and presented in good faith without any intent to deceive — such evidence is not fabricated even if ultimately disbelieved.
Honest mistakes in the preparation or presentation of evidence, where the person producing it genuinely believed it to be true and accurate at the time of production.

Evidence that is disputed or contradicted by the opposing party but was not manufactured or altered — a contested document or witness account does not become fabricated merely because it is challenged.
Evidence collected through procedurally defective but otherwise genuine investigation methods, where the underlying material itself is real and unaltered.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether evidence qualifies as 'fabricated' determines liability under Sections 227–233 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; a person who corruptly uses fabricated evidence as true or genuine is punishable in the same manner as one who fabricates false evidence, attracting imprisonment and fine. This definition is critical to prosecutions for perjury-related offences and for determining whether an accused has attempted to obstruct or pervert the course of justice.

definitions.definition: A person 'fabricates' false evidence when they cause any circumstance to exist, make any false entry in a book or record, or make any document containing a false statement, intending that such circumstance, false entry, or false statement may appear in evidence in a judicial proceeding and cause any person to form an erroneous opinion touching any point material to the result of such proceeding. As used in Section 229, fabricating false evidence refers to the deliberate creation or manufacture of false evidence intended to be used at any stage of a judicial proceeding.
definitions.plain_english: Fabricating evidence means deliberately creating, planting, or manufacturing false evidence so that it can be used in a court case or legal proceeding to mislead a judge or authority into making a wrong decision. It is different from simply lying under oath — instead, it involves actually constructing or arranging false material, documents, records, or circumstances. For example, forging a document and presenting it in court, or planting an object at a crime scene to implicate an innocent person, would both count as fabricating false evidence.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Mumbai plants narcotics in the bag of an innocent suspect and then produces those narcotics as 'recovered evidence' before a Sessions Court to secure a conviction under the NDPS Act.
A litigant in a property dispute in Delhi creates a forged sale deed dated several decades ago and submits it before a civil court as genuine evidence of ownership to defeat a rightful claim.

An accused in a criminal trial in Bengaluru bribes a lab technician to alter forensic test results so that blood samples show a different DNA profile, intending to use the manipulated report during trial.
A corporate fraudster in Hyderabad manufactures fake bank statements and balance sheets and submits them as evidence before the National Company Law Tribunal to support a false claim of insolvency.

A landlord in Chennai stages a break-in at his own property and plants stolen goods belonging to a tenant in the tenant's room, then files a police complaint to initiate proceedings against the tenant.

A party to a matrimonial dispute in Kolkata creates fabricated WhatsApp screenshots purporting to show threats by the spouse and presents them before the Family Court to obtain an ex-parte injunction.
what_it_covers: Forging or creating a false document — such as a forged contract, deed, or certificate — and submitting it as genuine evidence in a court proceeding.
Physically planting or arranging false circumstances at a scene — such as planting a weapon or contraband — so that those circumstances appear as evidence in a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding.
Making a false entry in an official book, account, register, or electronic record with the intention that the entry will be relied upon as evidence in a legal proceeding.
Altering, tampering with, or manipulating an existing document or forensic report so that it conveys a false fact intended to mislead a court or investigating authority.
Fabrication carried out at any stage of a judicial proceeding, including preliminary investigations directed by law before the matter reaches a court.
what_it_excludes: Merely giving false oral testimony (false statement under oath) without creating or planting any physical evidence or document — that conduct falls under 'giving false evidence' rather than 'fabricating' it.
Honest mistakes or inadvertent errors in preparing documents or records that are later used as evidence, since fabrication requires deliberate intent to deceive.
Legitimate advocacy activities by a lawyer who presents evidence given by a client in good faith, without knowledge of its falsity.
Suppression or concealment of existing true evidence, which is a distinct act and does not amount to fabrication unless coupled with the creation of false substitutes.
Acts of perjury committed in proceedings that are entirely private and not judicial in nature, where no intent to influence any stage of a judicial proceeding exists.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'fabricating false evidence' under Section 229 directly determines whether the accused is liable for imprisonment up to seven years (for judicial proceedings) or three years (for other proceedings), in addition to a fine; where fabrication is intended to cause conviction for a capital offence, it escalates liability under Sections 230 and 231 to imprisonment for life or even death, making the precise characterisation of the act critical to sentencing.

As used in Section 231, fabricating false evidence specifically encompasses creating or manufacturing such false evidence with the intent or knowledge that it will cause a person to be convicted of a serious offence punishable with imprisonment for life or for a term of seven years or more.
definitions.plain_english: Fabricating evidence means deliberately creating fake or false proof — such as planting a physical object at a crime scene, making false entries in records, or producing a false document — so that it appears to be real evidence in a legal case. The purpose is to mislead a court or investigating authority into reaching a wrong conclusion about someone's guilt or innocence. Under Section 231, the specific concern is when this fake evidence is made with the goal of getting an innocent person convicted of a serious crime carrying a heavy prison sentence.
real_world_examples: A police officer plants a stolen mobile phone in the bag of an innocent suspect and then presents it as recovered evidence before a Sessions Court, intending to get the suspect convicted of a dacoity offence punishable with imprisonment for life.

A witness in a murder trial creates and submits a forged CCTV footage timestamp or a doctored photograph to falsely show the accused at the scene of the crime, knowing this will likely lead to the accused being sentenced to life imprisonment.

A business rival pays a corrupt forensic technician to tamper with a drug sample and falsify a chemical analysis report, so that an innocent person is framed under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act for an offence carrying rigorous imprisonment of ten years or more.

A land dispute litigant fabricates a false registered sale deed and enters false records in the revenue register, intending that this manufactured documentary evidence will be presented in a civil-turned-criminal proceeding to cause wrongful conviction of the rightful owner for an offence of forgery punishable with seven years or more.

A co-accused in a terrorism case plants incriminating material such as explosives manuals and fake communication logs on an innocent person's computer and presents them to the investigation agency, intending to shift criminal liability and cause the innocent person to be convicted of a terrorist act punishable with imprisonment for life.
what_it_covers: Physically planting an object (such as a weapon, contraband, or stolen property) at a crime scene or on an accused's person so that it appears as incriminating evidence in a judicial proceeding.

Making false entries in books, official records, or registers — such as forged revenue records, tampered forensic reports, or altered financial ledgers — intended to be used as evidence in a serious criminal trial.

Creating or causing a false document, such as a fabricated confession, a forged witness statement, or a doctored electronic record, with the intent that it will deceive a court into convicting an innocent person of a grave offence.

Digitally manipulating electronic evidence such as CCTV footage, call records, or email communications to falsely implicate a person in an offence carrying imprisonment for life or seven years or more.

Causing a false circumstance to exist — such as staging a crime scene — with the knowledge that the manufactured circumstance will appear before a court or inquiry and produce an erroneous finding of guilt.
what_it_excludes: Merely giving false oral testimony (i.e., lying on the witness stand) without creating any physical, documentary, or circumstantial fabrication — that conduct falls under 'giving false evidence' rather than 'fabricating evidence'.

Suppression or concealment of true evidence, which may constitute a separate offence but does not amount to fabrication since it does not involve the affirmative act of creating or causing false evidence to exist.

Fabrication of evidence intended to be used in civil proceedings only, where the intended outcome is not the criminal conviction of a person for an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or seven years or more, as Section 231 specifically requires that grave penal consequence.
Good-faith errors or mistakes in preparing records or documents without any intent to deceive a court or cause an erroneous opinion in a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding.
Acts of an accused person who destroys their own incriminating evidence to avoid self-incrimination, as destruction differs from the affirmative creation of false evidence against another.

Excludes: Merely giving false oral testimony or a false statement on oath in a proceeding, which constitutes 'giving false evidence' under Section 227 rather than fabricating false evidence, as fabrication requires the active creation or planting of material.; Submitting a genuine document that happens to contain an honest mistake or an inadvertent error, since fabricating false evidence requires deliberate intent to cause an erroneous opinion on a material point.; Acts of concealment or destruction of existing evidence, which may constitute a separate offence but do not amount to fabrication as they do not involve creating or causing a false circumstance to exist.; False statements made outside of any judicial proceeding, proceeding before a public servant, or arbitration — such as lies told in private negotiations or in non-legal contexts — as the definition requires the false matter to be intended to appear as evidence in a qualifying proceeding.; Fabrication done after a proceeding has concluded with no intent that the material will be used in any current or future qualifying proceeding, since the requisite intent to influence a live or anticipated proceeding is absent.

definitions.definition: A statement, representation, or assertion is 'false' when the person making it either knows it to be untrue or does not believe it to be true at the time of making it. Within the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'false' denotes a deliberate departure from truth — whether in spoken words, written documents, or conduct — made with knowledge of its untruth or without genuine belief in its truth.
definitions.plain_english: Something is 'false' when the person saying or doing it knows it is not true, or at least does not actually believe it is true. It is not just being mistaken — a false statement requires an element of knowing deceit. For example, signing a form that says facts you know are wrong makes those statements false.
real_world_examples: A witness in a Delhi court testifies under oath that he saw the accused at a particular location, knowing fully well that the accused was nowhere near that place — this constitutes false evidence under the BNS.

A person applies for a government welfare scheme in Maharashtra and submits an income certificate bearing fabricated figures, knowing the figures do not reflect actual income — the certificate contains false statements.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai stamps his goods with a mark falsely indicating they were manufactured by a reputed brand, knowing the goods have no connection with that brand — the mark is false within the meaning of the Act.

An accused person provides a false name and address to a police officer during arrest proceedings in Chennai, knowing the details given do not correspond to his actual identity — the representation is false.

A public servant in a UP district office submits a report to his superior falsely stating that an inspection was carried out and all records were found in order, when no such inspection took place — the report constitutes a false representation.

A person informs a magistrate in Kolkata that a dacoity is about to occur at Location A, knowing the actual plan is to commit it at Location B, in order to mislead law enforcement — the information given is false.
what_it_covers: A sworn statement made in judicial proceedings where the deponent knows the content is untrue at the time of making it.
A written document or certificate submitted to a court or authority that the maker knows contains incorrect facts.
A verbal representation made to a police officer or public servant that the speaker knows to be contrary to the actual state of affairs.
A property mark or label affixed to goods that the person affixing it knows does not accurately describe the origin, nature, or manufacturer of those goods.
Any act of concealment paired with a representation that the person making it knows does not reflect the truth, as in concealing a design to commit an offence while falsely denying its existence.
what_it_excludes: A statement that is factually incorrect but made in genuine good faith based on the honest belief of the person making it — an honest mistake is not 'false' under this law.
An opinion or prediction about a future event that turns out to be wrong, where no present fact was misrepresented and no knowledge of untruth existed at the time.
A statement made under duress or coercion where the person had no real choice and did not voluntarily intend to assert an untruth.
Exaggerated trade puffery or vague assertions that both parties understand are not precise factual claims.
A statement made by a person of unsound mind who lacks the capacity to understand the nature of truth or falsity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a statement or representation is 'false' is a foundational element in establishing offences such as giving false evidence (Sections 227 and 216 BNS), fabricating evidence, forgery, cheating, and concealing a design to commit an offence under Sections 58 and 59 — without proof of falsity, these charges cannot be sustained. The presence of knowingly false conduct can elevate a mere irregularity into a cognisable criminal offence attracting imprisonment and fine.

definitions.definition: A person is said to make a false document or false electronic record who dishonestly or fraudulently makes, signs, seals, executes, transmits, or affixes any electronic signature on a document or electronic record with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document or electronic record was made, signed, sealed, executed, transmitted, or affixed by or by the authority of a person by whom he knows it was not; or who without lawful authority alters a document or electronic record in any material part after it has been made or executed; or who dishonestly or fraudulently causes any person to sign, seal, execute or alter a document or electronic record knowing that such person, by reason of unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or deception practised upon him, does not know the contents or nature of the alteration.
definitions.plain_english: A 'false document' is any document or electronic record that has been created, signed, or altered in a dishonest or fraudulent way — for example, by forging someone else's signature, backdating it, adding or erasing information without authority, or tricking a person who doesn't understand what they are signing. The key idea is that the document is made to look genuine or authoritative when it is actually not. This can include both physical paper documents and digital records.
real_world_examples: A property dealer in Delhi backdates a sale deed to show that a plot of land was transferred before a court attachment order was served, in order to defeat a creditor's claim — making it a false document.
A bank employee in Mumbai alters the amount on a customer's signed cheque from ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 without the customer's knowledge or authority, thereby creating a false document.

A job applicant in Bengaluru obtains an experience certificate by submitting a forged letter purportedly signed by a former employer who never issued any such certificate — constituting a false document.

A person in Chennai signs a power of attorney in the name of his deceased father, presenting it to a registrar as if the father had executed it, intending to transfer property fraudulently — making it a false document.

A contractor in Hyderabad submits a government tender with a fabricated completion certificate, forging the signature of a public works officer to show experience he does not have — creating a false document.

A moneylender in Kolkata causes an illiterate borrower, under the influence of alcohol, to sign a document that he represents as a simple receipt but which is actually a mortgage deed transferring the borrower's land — constituting a false document.
what_it_covers: A document made, signed, or sealed by one person in the name of another without that person's authority and with dishonest or fraudulent intent.
Any electronic record or electronic signature that is transmitted or affixed dishonestly to make it appear as though it was authorised by someone who did not authorise it.
A document or electronic record that has been materially altered — such as changing dates, amounts, names, or parties — after it was originally executed, without lawful authority.
A document signed or executed by a person who was tricked, intoxicated, or of unsound mind such that they did not know the contents or the nature of what they were signing.
A document signed by a person using their own name but with the intent to impersonate another person of the same name, such as endorsing a cheque payable to a different person of identical name.
what_it_excludes: A document containing a factual error or incorrect information that was made without any dishonest or fraudulent intent — innocent mistakes do not constitute a false document.
A document that is merely inadmissible in evidence or procedurally defective (e.g., unregistered when registration is required) but has not been fabricated or altered with dishonest intent.
A document lawfully altered by the authorised party before it is fully executed, such as a party correcting a typographical error in a draft contract before signing it.
A document that a person signs in their own name for their own account under a validly granted authority, even if the underlying transaction is later disputed.
A blank instrument that has been filled in strictly within the limits of the authority given by the authorising person, such as an agent filling a cheque up to the authorised limit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'false document' is the foundational element that determines liability for forgery under Section 336 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; without establishing that a false document was made, no charge of forgery can be sustained. It also directly triggers associated offences such as using a forged document as genuine and possession of a forged document, making it the critical threshold concept for an entire category of document-fraud crimes.

definitions.definition: Whoever, being legally bound by an oath or by an express provision of law to state the truth, or being bound by law to make a declaration upon any subject, makes any statement which is false, and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, is said to give false evidence. A statement is within the meaning of this section whether it is made verbally or otherwise. A false statement as to the belief of the person attesting is within the meaning of this section, and a person may be guilty of giving false evidence by stating that he believes a thing which he does not believe, as well as by stating that he knows a thing which he does not know.
definitions.plain_english: False evidence means making a false statement when you are legally required to tell the truth — such as when you are under oath in a court or bound by law to make a declaration. It does not matter whether you say it out loud or write it down. Even saying you 'believe' something you actually do not believe counts as false evidence, not just outright lying about facts.
real_world_examples: A witness in a Delhi Sessions Court swears under oath that he saw the accused at the scene of a murder, knowing fully well the accused was elsewhere at the time — this constitutes giving false evidence.

A government employee, legally bound to make a sworn declaration about his assets, states in the declaration that he owns no property abroad when he knows he holds a flat in Dubai — this amounts to false evidence.

An interpreter appointed by a Mumbai court certifies under oath that the translated version of a Hindi document into English is accurate, when he knows the translation omits key incriminating phrases — this is false evidence.

A witness in a property dispute before a civil court in Chennai states under oath that he believes a certain signature on a sale deed belongs to the plaintiff, when in truth he has no such belief and is merely supporting a fabricated claim — this constitutes false evidence.

During an arbitration proceeding in Bengaluru, a party's representative, legally bound to make truthful declarations, states facts about delivery of goods that he knows never occurred, in order to influence the arbitrator's decision — this amounts to giving false evidence.

A doctor, summoned as an expert witness in a Kolkata court and placed under oath, testifies that a patient's injuries are consistent with a fall when he genuinely believes they are consistent with assault — deliberately mis-stating his professional belief constitutes false evidence.

An interpreter or translator who, being bound by oath, certifies a false or inaccurate translation of a document or statement.
A person legally required to make a declaration (such as an affidavit or statutory declaration) who states something he does not believe to be true.
A statement made in writing or electronically (not only orally) that is false and made under a legal obligation to tell the truth.
A statement about one's own belief that is false — i.e., asserting belief in something one actually does not believe.
what_it_excludes: A false statement made by a person who is not legally bound by oath or law to state the truth — such as an ordinary conversation or an informal written statement.
A statement that is objectively incorrect but which the person genuinely and honestly believes to be true at the time of making it, as illustrated by example (c) in Section 227.
Fabricating or planting physical or documentary evidence without making a false statement, which falls under fabricating false evidence under Section 228 rather than giving false evidence.
A statement made in a non-legal or non-official context where no legal duty to declare the truth exists.
Mistaken or erroneous testimony arising from poor memory, misperception, or honest misunderstanding, where there is no intention to deceive and no knowledge of falsity.

This definition is the foundational threshold that triggers prosecution for perjury, and also governs abetment liability under Sections 49 and 56 for those who instigate others to give false evidence.
