definitions.definition: A 'false mark' is any mark made upon a case, package, or other receptacle containing goods that is reasonably calculated to cause a public servant or any other person to believe that such receptacle contains goods which it does not contain, or that it does not contain goods which it does contain, or that the goods contained therein are of a nature or quality different from their real nature or quality.
definitions.plain_english: A false mark is a misleading label, stamp, or marking placed on a container or packaging that tricks people — including government officials — into thinking the container holds different goods than it actually does, or that the goods are of a different quality than they really are. For example, putting a mark on a box to make it look like it contains premium goods when it actually contains inferior or different goods. The law punishes anyone who creates or uses such a false mark, unless they can prove they had no intention to cheat.
real_world_examples: A trader in Mumbai marks crates of substandard rice with labels indicating they contain premium Basmati rice, causing customs officials and buyers to believe the goods are of higher quality than they actually are.

A pharmaceutical distributor in Delhi labels boxes of generic medicines with markings suggesting they contain a branded drug, misleading government health inspectors and hospital procurement officers about the actual contents.

An exporter in Chennai marks packages of mixed-grade cotton as 'Grade A' cotton on all outer packaging, causing port authorities and foreign buyers to believe the consignment is of uniform superior quality.

A grocery wholesaler in Kolkata marks empty or partially filled sacks of pulses with weight and content indicators suggesting they are fully loaded with a specific variety, deceiving food safety inspectors conducting warehouse checks.

A manufacturer in Surat places markings on textile bales indicating they are made of pure silk when they actually contain synthetic fibres blended with silk, misleading both government excise officers and retail purchasers.
what_it_covers: A mark on a package that falsely indicates the type or variety of goods contained within, such as labelling a container of adulterated oil as pure mustard oil.
A marking on a receptacle that misrepresents the quality or grade of the enclosed goods, such as stamping 'ISI certified' or 'Grade 1' on substandard products.
A mark on a case suggesting it contains a specific quantity or nature of goods when it is actually empty or contains entirely different goods.
Use of any existing false mark on a receptacle by a person other than the one who created it, in a manner designed to deceive public servants or other persons.
Markings on crates or boxes that cause customs or tax authorities to believe the goods are exempt from duty or belong to a different tariff category than they actually do.
what_it_excludes: Marks that are accidentally incorrect due to a genuine clerical or printing error, where no intent to defraud can be established by the prosecution.

Marks on documents, seals, or instruments that do not relate to the nature, quality, or identity of goods inside a physical receptacle, which would fall under forgery or false document provisions instead.
Marks on goods themselves rather than on the receptacle or packaging containing those goods, which may be governed by property mark or trade mark provisions rather than this section.
Accurate and truthful marks that correctly represent the nature, quality, and contents of the goods in the receptacle, even if the goods themselves are of poor commercial value.
Marks placed on receptacles with the full knowledge and consent of all relevant parties where no deception of any public servant or third party is intended or likely.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as a 'false mark' under Section 350 determines whether the person who made or used it is liable for imprisonment up to three years, a fine, or both; crucially, the section places the burden on the accused to prove absence of intent to defraud, making this definition a trigger for a reverse-burden criminal offence with significant penal consequences for fraudulent trade and commerce.

definitions.definition: Whoever marks any movable property or goods or any case, package or other receptacle containing movable property or goods, or uses any case, package or other receptacle having any mark thereon, in a manner reasonably calculated to cause it to be believed that the property or goods so marked, or any property or goods contained in any such receptacle so marked, belong to a person to whom they do not belong, is said to use a false property mark.
definitions.plain_english: A false property mark is when someone puts a mark on goods, products, or their containers in a way that tricks people into thinking those goods belong to someone they actually do not belong to. For example, stamping a competitor's brand or owner's symbol on your own goods to pass them off as theirs. The key is that the marking is designed to deceive about ownership or origin.
real_world_examples: A Delhi trader stamps a well-known Mumbai textile manufacturer's ownership mark on his own fabric bales before sending them to retailers, making buyers believe the goods came from that manufacturer.

A Pune warehouse operator reuses crates bearing the property mark of a reputed FMCG company like Amul or Britannia to pack and sell inferior products, causing buyers to believe they are purchasing original goods belonging to that company.

A roadside vendor in Chennai affixes counterfeit ownership stamps of a government-approved khadi cooperative on locally made cloth bundles, misleading wholesale buyers into thinking the cloth belongs to the cooperative.

A Kolkata exporter relabels and remarkes second-hand machinery with the ownership insignia of a reputed original equipment manufacturer, shipping them to overseas buyers who believe the machines are the OEM's property.

A Ludhiana hosiery dealer marks garment packages with the trade ownership symbol of a branded sportswear company to deceive stockists into accepting the consignment as part of that company's official inventory.
what_it_covers: Placing another person's or entity's ownership mark on movable goods or products to suggest they belong to that person when they do not.
Using a crate, box, package, or other receptacle that already bears a genuine ownership mark to pack and sell different goods, thereby misrepresenting the ownership of the contents.
Marking raw materials or agricultural produce with an ownership symbol of a certified producer or cooperative to which they do not belong.
Applying any symbol, stamp, or sign on goods in a manner reasonably calculated to create a false impression of ownership in the mind of the buyer or recipient.
what_it_excludes: A genuine property mark placed on goods by the actual owner or with the owner's authorisation, which correctly identifies ownership.

Marks placed on goods for purposes other than denoting ownership, such as quality grade marks, regulatory compliance marks (e.g., BIS hallmark, FSSAI label), or descriptive trade labels that do not purport to identify a particular owner.
Accidental or mistaken use of an incorrect mark where the person can prove they acted without any intent to defraud.
Trade marks or brand names used in a manner governed separately under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, where the dispute relates to brand identity rather than ownership of specific movable property.
Marks on immovable property such as land boundary markers or building plaques, as the provision applies only to movable property and goods.

This definition directly triggers the penal consequence under Section 345 and distinguishes a mere labelling irregularity from a criminal act of fraudulent misrepresentation of ownership.

definitions.definition: In section 186, 'fictitious stamp' means any stamp falsely purporting to be issued by Government for the purpose of denoting a rate of postage, or any facsimile or imitation or representation, whether on paper or otherwise, of any stamp issued by Government for that purpose.
definitions.plain_english: A fictitious stamp is any fake or counterfeit postage stamp that falsely appears to have been issued by the Government to show a postal rate. This includes exact copies, imitations, or any kind of reproduction of a genuine government postage stamp, regardless of the material it is made on. Essentially, it is any fraudulent postage stamp designed to look like a real one issued by the postal authorities.
real_world_examples: A small printing shop in Mumbai produces high-quality color photocopies of India Post stamps and sells them in bulk to local businesses so they can affix them to envelopes without paying actual postage charges.
A trader in Delhi purchases a machine that can emboss imitation postage stamps on paper and uses it to create stamps that visually resemble genuine India Post stamps for use on parcels.

A person in Chennai downloads a high-resolution image of an official Indian postage stamp from the internet, prints multiple copies on adhesive paper, and uses them to send letters without paying postal fees.

A market vendor in Kolkata is found selling sheets of stamps that appear identical to genuine government-issued stamps but are not official India Post products, at a discounted price to unsuspecting customers.
An e-commerce seller in Bengaluru affixes self-made stamp facsimiles — cut-outs of scanned postage stamps — on packages sent through courier services claiming postal prepayment.

A philately enthusiast in Hyderabad creates detailed replica stamps of vintage Indian postal stamps on paper for display purposes, but the replicas so closely resemble current government stamps that they could be mistaken for genuine postage stamps.
what_it_covers: A stamp printed or manufactured to falsely appear as if issued by the Government of India or a foreign government for denoting a rate of postage.
A photocopy, digital print, or any facsimile of a genuine government-issued postage stamp, regardless of whether it is made on paper or any other material.
Any imitation, replica, or artistic representation of an official postage stamp that could be used or mistaken for a genuine stamp for postal purposes.

Stamps purporting to be issued by a foreign government for postal rates, since the definition of 'Government' under this section is extended to include persons administering executive government in any foreign country.
Any die, plate, instrument, or material specifically made for producing such imitation or counterfeit postage stamps.
what_it_excludes: Genuine postage stamps actually issued by the Government of India or any authorized postal authority, which are legal tender for postal purposes.
Revenue stamps issued by the Government for tax or duty purposes (governed separately as 'stamp issued by Government for purpose of revenue'), as fictitious stamp relates only to postage rate stamps.
Educational or illustrative representations of stamps that are clearly marked as specimens or samples and cannot be mistaken for genuine postage stamps.
Commemorative or souvenir stamp-like items issued officially by India Post or authorized agencies, which bear government authorization and are not falsely purporting to be postage stamps.
Cancelled or used genuine stamps that have already been validly used for postal purposes and are no longer in circulation as valid postage.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'fictitious stamp' under Section 186 determines criminal liability for making, uttering, dealing in, selling, using, or possessing such stamps — all of which are punishable offences attracting a fine of up to two hundred rupees. Additionally, the classification triggers mandatory seizure and forfeiture of the stamps and any machinery used to produce them.

definitions.definition: A fiduciary relationship, as used in Section 68 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a relationship in which one person places trust, confidence, and reliance in another who is obligated to act in that person's best interest, and where the latter holds a position of power or influence over the former. Such a relationship arises where one party has a duty of care, loyalty, or guardianship toward the other, creating a power imbalance that can be exploited.
definitions.plain_english: A fiduciary relationship is a special relationship of trust where one person depends on another to act honestly and in their best interest. Examples include a doctor and patient, a teacher and student, or a therapist and client. The person in the position of trust has power or influence over the other and must not misuse it. This term is used in the law to protect vulnerable individuals from being taken advantage of sexually by those they trust.
real_world_examples: A psychiatrist in a government hospital in Mumbai who uses the emotional dependency of a female patient undergoing treatment to persuade her to engage in sexual intercourse — the doctor-patient relationship constitutes a fiduciary relationship under Section 68.

A university professor in Delhi who is also the thesis supervisor of a postgraduate student uses his academic authority and the trust the student places in him to induce her into a sexual relationship — this academic mentorship is a fiduciary relationship.

A lawyer in Chennai who is handling a distressed woman's divorce case exploits her vulnerability and trust in him as her legal representative to seduce her into sexual intercourse — the advocate-client relationship is a fiduciary relationship.

A social welfare officer in Kolkata assigned as a guardian to rehabilitate a woman rescued from trafficking uses his custodial and protective role to induce sexual intercourse, abusing the fiduciary trust placed in him by the State and the woman.

A religious head or priest in a temple trust in Varanasi who provides spiritual counseling to a woman and exploits her faith and emotional dependence on him to engage in sexual intercourse — such a spiritual authority relationship constitutes a fiduciary relationship.

A corporate HR manager who controls appraisals and promotions of a female employee uses that power imbalance, combined with the trust the employee places in the HR function, to seduce her — this may constitute a fiduciary relationship in the employment context.
what_it_covers: A doctor or therapist who holds a position of professional trust and care over a patient and exploits that dependency for sexual purposes.
A teacher, professor, or educational guardian who exercises academic authority and mentorship over a student and uses that trust to induce sexual intercourse.
A lawyer, financial advisor, or counselor who manages sensitive personal affairs of a client and abuses the confidence reposed in them to seduce the client.
A social worker, probation officer, or welfare official assigned to protect or rehabilitate a woman who misuses the trust and custodial responsibility of that role.
A religious leader, spiritual guide, or priest who exploits the emotional and spiritual trust of a follower to engage in sexual intercourse.
what_it_excludes: Relationships based purely on commercial transactions or contractual exchange where no special trust, dependency, or duty of care is established — such as a shopkeeper and a customer.
Relationships between equals where no power differential or duty of loyalty exists, such as two colleagues of similar rank with no supervisory or custodial connection.

A person who is a public servant acting solely in an administrative capacity without any personal duty of care or trust toward the woman in question — that person is separately covered under the public servant clause of Section 68, not under fiduciary relationship.
Casual acquaintances or strangers who interact without any pre-existing relationship of trust, confidence, or authority over the other person.
Relationships of mere friendship or family ties not accompanied by a formal or recognised duty of care, guardianship, or professional obligation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a fiduciary relationship exists is determinative of criminal liability under Section 68 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — if established, a person who abuses such a relationship to induce or seduce a woman into sexual intercourse (not amounting to rape) faces rigorous imprisonment of five to ten years plus fine. Without proof of such a relationship or another specified status, the same conduct may not attract this specific aggravated offence.

definitions.definition: The term 'fine' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used throughout the Sanhita, 'fine' denotes a monetary penalty imposed by a Court upon a convicted person as punishment for an offence, either as the sole punishment or in addition to imprisonment, and includes the liability to suffer imprisonment in default of payment of such fine as provided under Section 8.
definitions.plain_english: A fine is a sum of money that a court orders a person to pay as punishment after they are found guilty of a criminal offence. It can be the only punishment given, or it can be given alongside imprisonment. If the person does not pay the fine, the court can send them to jail for an additional period as a consequence of non-payment.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of negligently causing hurt to someone in a road accident in Mumbai is sentenced by a magistrate to pay a fine of ₹5,000 instead of being sent to prison.
A shopkeeper in Delhi found guilty of using a false weight and measure under related provisions is ordered to pay a fine of ₹10,000 along with a short term of simple imprisonment.
A person convicted of defamation in a Chennai court is sentenced to pay a fine of ₹50,000 as the sole punishment, with a direction that failure to pay will result in imprisonment for three months.

A youth convicted of mischief causing damage to public property in Kolkata is fined ₹20,000, and upon his failure to pay, the court orders him to undergo simple imprisonment for thirty days in default.

A person convicted of cheating a consumer of a small amount in a Pune market is ordered to pay a fine, a portion of which is directed to be paid as compensation to the victim under the provisions of the Sanhita.
what_it_covers: A monetary sum imposed by a competent court as punishment upon conviction of an offence under the Sanhita.
Fines imposed as the sole punishment where the offence does not warrant imprisonment or the court exercises discretion accordingly.
Fines imposed in addition to a sentence of imprisonment, whether simple or rigorous, as a combined punishment.
Imprisonment suffered by a convicted person in default of payment of the fine, as provided under Section 8.
A portion of the fine that a court may direct to be paid as compensation to the victim of the offence.
what_it_excludes: Civil damages or compensation awarded in a civil suit, which are not criminal penalties imposed under the Sanhita.
Penalties, fees, or monetary levies imposed by regulatory or administrative authorities under special or local laws, which are not fines in the criminal sentencing sense.
Bail bonds or security deposits paid for release pending trial, which are not punishments imposed upon conviction.
Costs awarded against a party in civil or criminal proceedings that do not constitute punishment for a criminal offence.
Community service as a form of punishment, which is a distinct category of sentence separately recognised under the Sanhita.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of a punishment as a 'fine' under Section 8 determines the court's powers regarding default imprisonment, the period and nature of such default sentence, and the portion that may be applied as victim compensation; it also affects whether an offence is bailable, the jurisdiction of courts, and the computation of aggregate sentences when multiple punishments are combined.

definitions.definition: The term 'food' is not separately defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; however, as used in Section 274, it refers to any article or substance intended for human consumption, including solid or liquid matter meant to be eaten or drunk, which may be adulterated, noxious, or otherwise rendered unfit or injurious to health.
definitions.plain_english: Food refers to any substance that people eat or drink to sustain themselves, such as grains, vegetables, cooked meals, packaged products, or beverages. In the context of Indian criminal law, it specifically includes any article meant for human consumption that someone might tamper with, poison, or make harmful. The law focuses on protecting people from being given dangerous or adulterated food.
real_world_examples: A shopkeeper in Mumbai adulterates milk with harmful chemicals and sells it to customers — the milk qualifies as 'food' under Section 274 and the act constitutes an offence.
A street food vendor in Delhi knowingly uses rotten or toxic ingredients in chaat or samosas that are served to the public, rendering the food noxious and injurious to health.
A factory in Gujarat packages expired or contaminated biscuits and relabels them with fresh dates for sale — the biscuits constitute 'food' that has been made unfit for consumption.

A canteen contractor supplying mid-day meals to a government school in Uttar Pradesh mixes harmful substances to cut costs, poisoning children — the meals are 'food' falling within the purview of Section 274.

A restaurateur in Chennai knowingly serves food prepared with adulterated cooking oil known to cause serious illness, exposing consumers to health risk under the food-adulteration provisions of the Sanhita.
what_it_covers: Any solid edible article intended for human consumption, such as grains, cooked meals, packaged snacks, bread, or vegetables.
Liquid food items intended to be consumed, such as milk, fruit juice, soup, or other beverages that provide nutrition.
Adulterated or noxious food articles that have been rendered unfit or injurious to health through deliberate tampering or mixing of harmful substances.
Processed or packaged food products sold commercially that have been contaminated or mislabelled to deceive consumers.
Mid-day meals, canteen food, or institutionally supplied eatables where harmful ingredients have been knowingly introduced.
what_it_excludes: Medicines, drugs, or medical preparations that are ingested for therapeutic purposes rather than general nourishment, which fall under separate provisions.
Animal feed or substances not intended for human consumption, even if they resemble food articles.
Water supplied through public or domestic plumbing systems, which is governed by separate provisions relating to public water supply rather than food adulteration.
Alcoholic beverages regulated exclusively under State Excise laws, to the extent they are not treated as food for the purposes of this section.
Tobacco products and non-nutritive substances not ordinarily considered food even if orally consumed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'food' under Section 274 determines whether a person who adulterates or renders it noxious is criminally liable under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, attracting punishment for selling or offering for sale food that is injurious to health. This classification triggers serious penal consequences for food sellers, manufacturers, and distributors who knowingly compromise the safety of consumable articles meant for the public.

definitions.definition: Any article intended for human consumption by eating or drinking, including all edible substances and potable liquids. In the context of Sections 274 and 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'food or drink' refers to any article sold, offered, or exposed for sale for the purpose of human ingestion, whether in solid or liquid form, which may be rendered noxious or unfit for consumption through adulteration or deterioration.
definitions.plain_english: Food or drink means anything a person eats or drinks, such as cooked meals, packaged snacks, water, milk, juice, or any other item meant to be consumed by humans. The law is concerned with ensuring that such items are safe and have not been tampered with or made harmful before being sold to people. If someone sells food or drink that has been made unsafe or has gone bad, they can be punished under this law.
real_world_examples: A street vendor in Mumbai selling pani puri made with contaminated water that has been knowingly mixed with a harmful substance, rendering the drink unfit for human consumption.
A wholesale grocery trader in Delhi selling adulterated milk powder mixed with chalk or urea, knowing the product is noxious and will be consumed by customers as food.
A restaurant owner in Chennai serving spoiled or rotting food items to customers while knowing the food has become unfit for consumption due to improper storage.
A packaged juice manufacturer in Pune selling fruit juices with artificially added chemicals or adulterants that make the drink harmful, while still labelling and selling it as safe juice.
A tea stall owner in Kolkata knowingly serving tea brewed with water from a polluted source, aware that the drink has become noxious and dangerous for customers to consume.
what_it_covers: All solid edible articles sold or offered for sale to humans, including cooked food, packaged snacks, grains, spices, and dairy products.
All potable liquids intended for human consumption, including water, milk, juice, tea, soft drinks, and alcoholic beverages sold commercially.
Any article that has been adulterated, rendered noxious, or has naturally become unfit, but is still being sold or exposed for sale as food or drink.
Articles of food or drink sold by street vendors, retail shops, restaurants, and wholesale traders intended for direct human consumption.
Food or drink that has deteriorated due to improper storage or contamination but is still being offered to consumers in that unfit state.
what_it_excludes: Medicines, tonics, or medical preparations intended for therapeutic use rather than ordinary consumption as food or drink, even if ingested.
Animal feed or fodder not intended for human consumption, even if the substance is technically edible.
Substances used in manufacturing or industrial processes that may be food-grade in composition but are not sold or intended for direct human consumption.
Water used purely for agricultural irrigation or industrial purposes, not being sold or supplied as drinking water for human consumption.
Cosmetic or topical products that may contain food-grade ingredients but are not intended to be eaten or drunk.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an article qualifies as 'food or drink' determines whether Sections 274 and 275 of the BNS are attracted — specifically, liability for adulteration or sale of noxious articles, carrying imprisonment up to six months and/or a fine up to five thousand rupees. If the article falls outside this definition, these provisions cannot be invoked, and the offender may escape criminal liability under this chapter entirely.

definitions.definition: A person is said to use 'force' to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other person, or if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to any substance, in such a manner as to bring such substance into contact with any part of that other person's body, or with anything which that other person is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other person's sense of feeling; provided that the person causing the motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion causes it by his own bodily power, or by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or by inducing any animal to move, change its motion, or cease to move.
definitions.plain_english: Using 'force' on someone means physically affecting their body in any way — whether by pushing, pulling, striking, or even causing an object or animal to make contact with them. It covers any act that produces movement, stops movement, or changes movement in the other person's body. Force does not require a weapon; even making a substance touch someone or directing an animal at someone counts.
real_world_examples: A rowdy supporter at a political rally in Mumbai shoves a journalist backward by pushing him forcefully against a barricade — this constitutes use of force.
A landlord in Delhi sets his dog on a tenant to drive her out of the premises; the dog lunges at and pushes her — use of an animal to cause motion qualifies as force.
A factory worker in Pune throws a bucket of water at a fellow employee during a dispute, drenching their clothes — causing a substance to contact clothing amounts to force.
An auto-rickshaw driver in Chennai deliberately brakes sharply to throw a passenger forward into the front partition — causing cessation of the passenger's motion constitutes force.
A shopkeeper in Kolkata grabs and pulls the arm of a customer to prevent them from leaving — the act of causing change of motion in the customer's body is force.
A protestor in Bengaluru hurls a stone that strikes a police officer's shield, which is being carried by the officer — contact with something the officer is carrying qualifies as force.
what_it_covers: Directly striking, pushing, or pulling another person's body using one's own physical strength.
Causing an animal (such as a dog or bull) to move against or into contact with another person.
Throwing, releasing, or placing any substance (liquid, solid, or object) so that it contacts the other person's body, clothing, or anything they are carrying.
Inducing sudden stopping or change of direction of a person's movement, such as deliberately braking a vehicle carrying a passenger.
Causing a physical object wielded by or attached to another person (e.g., a bag, shield, or tool they are holding) to be struck or moved.
what_it_excludes: Verbal threats, intimidation, or coercive words without any accompanying physical act — these may constitute criminal intimidation but not force.
Psychological or emotional pressure exerted without any physical contact or movement being caused to the other person's body or belongings.
Accidental or involuntary contact not caused intentionally or knowingly by the person, as force requires a deliberate act causing the motion or contact.
Remote electronic or digital interference with a person's activities, which does not produce physical motion in or on their body.
Merely standing in someone's path or obstructing their movement without physically touching them or causing any substance or animal to contact them.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of 'force' is a foundational element that determines whether an act constitutes 'criminal force' under Section 129 or escalates to 'assault' under Section 130 of the BNS, 2023; without satisfying the definition of force, charges for criminal force, assault, robbery, and related offences that require its application cannot be established.

definitions.definition: A 'foreign State' refers to any sovereign nation or State other than India, recognised as a political entity with its own government and territory, that is at peace with the Government of India. The term is used in the context of offences involving depredation on the territories of such a State or compulsion of such a State through criminal acts.
definitions.plain_english: A 'foreign State' simply means any country other than India — for example, Pakistan, China, the United States, or any other nation with its own government. In this law, it specifically refers to such countries when they are not at war with India, i.e., they are friendly or neutral nations. The law protects these countries from being attacked or plundered by persons operating from Indian soil.
real_world_examples: A group of Indian nationals based in Mumbai plans and launches a raid on property located within Nepal's territory to loot valuables — Nepal being a foreign State at peace with India, this would constitute depredation under Section 154.

An Indian mercenary group operating from Tamil Nadu crosses into Sri Lanka and pillages coastal villages — Sri Lanka qualifies as a foreign State, and the perpetrators can be prosecuted under Section 154 in Indian courts.

A gang kidnaps a Bangladesh government official and threatens to harm him unless the Bangladesh government releases certain prisoners — Bangladesh is a foreign State, making this a Section 140 offence where compelling a foreign State through kidnapping is specifically criminalised.

Indian extremists plan an armed incursion into Bhutan's forests to destroy infrastructure — Bhutan, as a foreign State at peace with India, is protected, and preparatory acts alone are punishable under Section 154.

A group of individuals in Rajasthan organises a raid on villages across the Pakistan border during peacetime — Pakistan, if it is formally at peace with India at that time, would qualify as a foreign State for purposes of this provision.
what_it_covers: Any sovereign nation officially recognised by the Government of India and currently at peace with it, such as France, Japan, or Bangladesh.
Neighbouring countries like Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, or Myanmar when India is not in a state of war or armed conflict with them.
A foreign State whose government may be targeted through ransom demands, kidnapping, or depredation originating from Indian territory.
Any member state of the United Nations that maintains diplomatic or peaceful relations with India and whose territories are subject to acts of depredation by persons in India.
what_it_excludes: India itself — the definition necessarily refers to States other than the Republic of India.
International inter-governmental organisations such as the United Nations or SAARC, which are separately mentioned alongside foreign States in Section 140 and are not subsumed within this term.
A foreign State that is currently in a declared state of war or active armed conflict with India, as the 'at peace' qualifier removes such States from the protective scope of Sections 153 and 154.
Non-State actors, terrorist organisations, or unrecognised entities operating within foreign territories but not constituting a recognised sovereign government.
Indian states or Union Territories — sub-national units within India are not 'foreign States' under any interpretation of this term.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'foreign State' determines whether offences under Sections 153 and 154 of the BNS are attracted — specifically, waging war against or committing depredation on a foreign State at peace with India. It also activates criminal liability under Section 140 where compelling a foreign State through kidnapping or ransom is an aggravated offence punishable with death or life imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Forfeiture of property is a punishment prescribed under Section 4 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, whereby a court compulsorily divests an offender of property used in, intended for use in, or acquired through the commission of a specified offence, transferring such property to the State. It operates as a distinct head of punishment or ancillary penalty imposed upon conviction, and extends to any property or interest therein that the offender seeks to fraudulently remove, conceal, or transfer to defeat such judicial order.
definitions.plain_english: Forfeiture means that when a person is convicted of certain crimes, the court can take away their property as part of the punishment. This could be property the person used to commit the crime, planned to use, or gained as a result of the crime. The ownership of that property then passes to the government. It is not a fine — it is the actual seizure and permanent loss of specific assets.
real_world_examples: A Maharashtra-based smuggler uses a truck to transport contraband goods across state borders; upon conviction, the court orders forfeiture of the truck as property used in committing the offence under the relevant provisions.

A Delhi businessman funds an attack on a foreign embassy operating in India while the foreign state is at peace with India; the court orders forfeiture of the funds and equipment used or intended to be used in the attack under Section 154 of the BNS.

A person in Mumbai receives antique artefacts knowing they were looted from a foreign country during a conflict; upon conviction under Section 155, the court orders forfeiture of the received property.

A Kolkata property dealer, anticipating a court order of forfeiture in a pending fraud case, secretly transfers ownership of three commercial flats to a relative; this fraudulent concealment of property to prevent forfeiture itself constitutes an offence under Section 243, punishable with imprisonment and fine.

A gang conducting depredation raids on the territory of a neighbouring country at peace with India accumulates cash and vehicles from those raids; on conviction, the court orders forfeiture of all such acquired assets in addition to imposing a prison sentence.
what_it_covers: Property actually used in the commission of a specified offence, such as vehicles, tools, or equipment deployed during the criminal act.
Property intended to be used in committing an offence, even if the offence was not ultimately completed, where such intent is established by a court.
Property acquired by or as a result of the commission of an offence, including money, goods, or assets obtained through depredation or fraud.
Property that an offender or third party attempts to fraudulently remove, conceal, transfer, or deliver to prevent its seizure as forfeiture under a pronounced or anticipated court sentence.
Property received by a person knowing it was taken during the commission of offences such as those under Sections 153 and 154 of the BNS.
what_it_excludes: Property that belongs to an innocent third party who had no knowledge of or involvement in the offence and did not receive it knowing it was criminally obtained.
Monetary fines imposed as a separate head of punishment under Section 4 — forfeiture is a distinct punishment and does not overlap with or substitute for a fine.
Community service or imprisonment sentences, which are separate categories of punishment enumerated in Section 4 and are not forms of forfeiture.
Legitimately acquired property of the offender that has no nexus to the offence committed and was neither used in, intended for use in, nor acquired through the offence.

Civil attachment or execution of decrees in civil suits, which are distinct legal processes under civil law and not punishments under the BNS, though Section 243 protects against fraud in those proceedings as well.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether forfeiture applies determines whether a convicted person permanently loses specific assets to the State as part of their criminal punishment, beyond imprisonment or fines. It triggers the offence under Section 243 when an accused fraudulently attempts to conceal or transfer property to defeat such an order, and it forms a mandatory ancillary punishment for offences such as depredation on foreign territories under Sections 154 and 155.

definitions.definition: A document, coin, currency-note, bank-note, or Government stamp is said to be 'forged' when it is made, altered, or counterfeited so as to falsely appear genuine, having been produced through an act constituting forgery under Section 335 of this Sanhita, or when any coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note is counterfeited so as to resemble and be passed off as the authentic instrument it imitates. The term encompasses both outright fabrication of a false instrument and the fraudulent alteration of a genuine instrument in any material part.
definitions.plain_english: Something is 'forged' when it has been dishonestly made, altered, or copied to look like the real thing, with the intent to deceive someone into believing it is genuine. This includes fake currency notes, fake government stamps, fake signatures on documents, or genuine documents that have been tampered with to change their meaning. The key idea is that someone created or altered it to trick others for dishonest gain.
real_world_examples: A person prints counterfeit Rs. 500 currency notes using a high-quality printer and circulates them in a busy Delhi market, passing them off as genuine Reserve Bank of India notes — the notes are 'forged'.

A government contractor in Mumbai alters the figures on a sanctioned work order, changing the approved amount from Rs. 5 lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs by adding a zero, intending to draw excess payment from the Treasury — the altered document is 'forged'.

A person in Bengaluru creates a fake stamp paper bearing a forged Collector's seal and uses it to execute a fraudulent sale deed for a property he does not own — the stamp paper and deed are 'forged'.
An employee in Chennai signs his manager's name on a cheque without authorisation and presents it at the bank to withdraw company funds — the cheque bearing the unauthorised signature is 'forged'.

A student in Kolkata obtains a genuine university mark sheet and uses chemical erasure to change failing grades to passing grades before submitting it for a job application — the tampered mark sheet is 'forged'.

A money lender in Lucknow induces an illiterate borrower to sign a blank stamp paper and then fills in loan terms the borrower never agreed to — the completed document is 'forged' as the borrower did not know its contents.
what_it_covers: A currency note or bank-note that has been printed or produced to resemble a genuine Reserve Bank of India note without authorisation.
A genuine document such as a cheque, will, or conveyance deed that has been materially altered by erasure, addition, or substitution to misrepresent its original contents.
A document bearing a signature, seal, or mark of a person who never authorised or executed it, affixed with the intent to make it appear authentic.
A Government stamp or revenue stamp that has been reproduced or imitated without lawful authority to be passed off as genuine.
An electronic record that has been dishonestly altered in a material part after its original execution or transmission.
what_it_excludes: A document that contains a false statement of fact but has been genuinely signed and executed by the actual author — lying in a document is not forgery unless the instrument itself is falsely made or altered.
A lawful copy or authorised reproduction of a document or currency made by the competent authority (e.g., reprinting of notes by RBI), even if identical in appearance to other originals.

definitions.definition: A false document or electronic record made wholly or in part by forgery is designated a forged document or electronic record. Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document or electronic record which he knows or has reason to believe to be a forged document or electronic record, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had forged such document or electronic record.
definitions.plain_english: A forged document is any written paper or digital record that has been falsely made or tampered with through the act of forgery, either entirely or in some part. It includes documents that someone has fabricated, altered, or signed without authority to deceive others. Even if you did not create the forgery yourself, using such a document knowing it is fake is treated as seriously as committing the forgery in the first place.
real_world_examples: A job applicant submits a degree certificate from a Delhi university that was manufactured by a fake document agency, with the university's seal and registrar's signature fabricated — this certificate is a forged document.

A land dealer in Maharashtra presents a property sale deed to a buyer, where the original owner's signature has been forged and the registration details altered to show false ownership, making it a forged document used as genuine.

A government employee submits a forged caste certificate issued in their name but produced without authority from the issuing office, using it to claim reservation benefits in a public sector job application.

A person in Chennai uses a digitally altered income tax return (an electronic record) with inflated figures to obtain a bank loan, knowing it was manipulated — constituting a forged electronic record used as genuine.

A student in Uttar Pradesh presents a forged marksheet of Class 12 examinations, where marks have been manually altered after printing and the board's stamp replicated, to secure admission in a professional college.
what_it_covers: A document made entirely from scratch without any lawful authority, such as a fictitious court order or fabricated property title deed.
A document that was originally genuine but has been partially altered through forgery, such as a genuine salary slip with the income figure changed.
An electronic record such as a digitally manipulated Aadhaar data file, altered bank statement in PDF form, or tampered e-mail used as evidence, made through forgery.
The act of using a forged document or electronic record as if it were genuine, even when the user did not personally create the forgery but knows or has reason to believe it is forged.
what_it_excludes: A document that contains factual errors or honest mistakes but was not created or altered with fraudulent or dishonest intent — it does not qualify as a forged document.
An authentic document issued lawfully by a competent authority, even if its contents are disputed or incorrect, as it lacks the element of forgery in its creation.
A document prepared under a genuine but mistaken belief about one's authority or the facts, where neither fraudulent intent nor dishonest purpose is present.
Oral misrepresentations or verbal false statements, as the definition applies strictly to documents and electronic records made through the act of forgery.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'forged document' is central to establishing liability under Section 340 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, because it triggers punishment for forgery offences including for those who merely use such documents fraudulently or dishonestly. This definition determines whether a person faces criminal prosecution for fraud, cheating, or forgery-related offences, and equates the culpability of a knowing user with that of the original forger.

definitions.definition: Forgery is the making of a false document or false electronic record with the intent to cause damage or injury to the public or to any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property, or to enter into any express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed. A person makes a false document who dishonestly or fraudulently makes, signs, seals, executes, or alters a document or electronic record, or causes another to do so under deception, in the manner described under Section 335.
definitions.plain_english: Forgery means creating, signing, altering, or using a fake document or electronic record to deceive someone or to gain an unfair advantage. This includes changing the content of a real document to misrepresent what it says, or making a document appear to have been signed or authorized by someone who never did so. The key element is that it is done dishonestly or fraudulently with the intention to cause harm or commit fraud.
real_world_examples: A person alters a property sale deed in Mumbai by changing the sale price and forging the seller's signature to claim a higher stamp duty refund or mislead a buyer.
A job applicant in Delhi submits a forged degree certificate from a recognized university to secure a government position they are not qualified for.
A borrower in Chennai creates a false bank statement showing higher income and submits it to a housing finance company to fraudulently obtain a home loan.
A shopkeeper in Kolkata forges a government licence or permit to continue operating a business after the original licence has been cancelled by authorities.
A person adds an extra zero to a cheque amount — for example, changing ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 — and presents it to a bank for encashment, as illustrated in the Act itself.
An employee in Bengaluru creates a fake power of attorney purportedly signed by an elderly property owner to transfer land without the owner's knowledge or consent.
what_it_covers: Dishonestly making a document appear to be signed or executed by a person who never signed or authorized it.
Materially altering an existing genuine document or electronic record without lawful authority, such as changing monetary figures, dates, or parties named in a contract.
Causing a person who is of unsound mind, intoxicated, or deceived about the nature of the document to sign or execute a false document.
Affixing a forged electronic signature on any electronic record to make it appear authentic.
Creating a fictitious document purporting to convey property rights or authority that was never granted.
what_it_excludes: Honest mistakes or inadvertent errors in drafting or executing a document where there is no dishonest or fraudulent intent.
Lawful corrections or amendments made to a document with the knowledge and consent of all parties concerned and within authorized procedures.
Mere possession of a forged document without knowledge of its falsity, as the offence requires dishonest or fraudulent intent at the time of making or using the document.
Acts of impersonation that do not involve the creation or alteration of any physical or electronic document or record.
Verbal misrepresentations or oral false statements, as forgery specifically pertains to documents and electronic records.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes forgery determines the applicability of Sections 336 to 341 of the BNS, 2023, which prescribe punishments including imprisonment for up to two years (for basic forgery) and up to seven years for forgery of court records, wills, or valuable securities; it also qualifies as an 'economic offence' under Section 111, meaning it can serve as a predicate act for the offence of organised crime, attracting significantly enhanced penalties including minimum five years' imprisonment and heavy fines.

definitions.definition: A person 'forges' when they make, execute, alter, or authenticate a false document or electronic record purporting to be a record or proceeding of or in a Court, an identity document issued by Government (including voter identity card or Aadhaar Card), a register of birth, marriage or burial, a register kept by a public servant, a certificate or document purporting to be made by a public servant in his official capacity, an authority to institute or defend a suit or confess judgment, or a power of attorney, with the intent to cause damage or injury or to support any claim or title or to commit fraud.
definitions.plain_english: To 'forge' means to fraudulently create, alter, or fake an important official document — such as a court record, Aadhaar card, voter ID, birth certificate, or a government-issued certificate — making it look genuine when it is not. The person doing this intends to deceive others and cause harm or gain an unfair advantage. It includes both physical paper documents and digital/electronic records.
real_world_examples: A person creates a fake birth certificate using a forged stamp of a municipal corporation in Maharashtra to falsely claim Indian citizenship during a National Register of Citizens verification process.

An individual alters a court decree from a civil court in Delhi to falsely show that a property dispute was decided in their favour, and presents it to a Sub-Registrar to register a property transfer.
A candidate for government employment fabricates a fake Aadhaar Card with a different date of birth to appear eligible for an age-restricted post in a public sector undertaking.
A land fraudster creates a counterfeit registered power of attorney purportedly executed by an NRI property owner in Bengaluru to illegally sell the owner's land to a third party.
A person forges a marriage register entry in a government office to falsely establish a spousal relationship for the purpose of claiming insurance or inheritance benefits.

An accused tampers with digital court proceeding records stored in an e-court database to delete criminal entries from their record before applying for a government job requiring a clean police verification.
what_it_covers: Creating a fake Aadhaar Card or voter identity card purporting to be issued by the Government of India.
Altering or fabricating a court order, decree, or any proceeding record of a civil or criminal court.
Forging a birth, marriage, or burial register entry maintained by a government or municipal authority.
Making a false power of attorney document purporting to authorise a person to act on behalf of another.
Fabricating a certificate or order purporting to be issued by a public servant in their official capacity.
Tampering with digital or electronic records, including entries in e-court systems or electronically maintained registers as defined under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
what_it_excludes: Forgery of private commercial documents such as cheques or promissory notes that are not issued by or purporting to be from a government authority or court (covered under different provisions like Section 338).
Making an honest clerical or typographical error in an official document without any intent to defraud or deceive.
Legitimate authorised correction or amendment of a public record carried out by the competent authority under due process of law.
Forging a valuable security, will, or authority to adopt, which falls under Section 338 and carries a higher penalty.
Mere possession of a forged document without any act of creation, alteration, or authentication, which would attract separate provisions on using forged documents.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'forges' under Section 337 determines whether the accused is liable for imprisonment of up to seven years and fine for forgery of court records, identity documents, public registers, or official certificates; the definition is foundational to establishing the primary offence of forgery, and also triggers liability under related provisions dealing with using forged documents, possession of forged documents, and fraud.

definitions.definition: The term 'fraud' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in Section 336 in the context of acts done by or representing oneself as a public servant. Based on its usage alongside 'fraudulently' (defined as doing anything with the intention to defraud but not otherwise), 'fraud' denotes any intentional deception or misrepresentation practised upon another person with the purpose of causing wrongful gain to oneself or wrongful loss to another.
definitions.plain_english: Fraud means deliberately tricking or deceiving someone in order to gain something illegally or to cause harm to that person. It involves a conscious intention to cheat — it is not an accident or a mistake. In everyday terms, if someone lies or misrepresents facts to get money, property, or any benefit they are not entitled to, that is fraud.
real_world_examples: A person impersonates a government officer in Delhi and collects 'fines' from shopkeepers, pocketing the money — this constitutes fraud under Section 336 of the BNS.
A property dealer in Mumbai forges ownership documents and sells a plot of land to multiple buyers simultaneously, deceiving each buyer into believing they are the sole purchaser.
An individual in Bengaluru creates a fake job placement agency, collects registration fees from unemployed youth promising government jobs, and disappears without delivering any service.

A person in Kolkata falsely claims to be a licensed medical practitioner and charges patients consultation fees while issuing fake prescriptions, thereby defrauding both patients and the public health system.

A vendor in Chennai adulterates edible oil with cheaper substitutes and sells it at premium prices by fraudulently labelling the containers as pure and certified, deceiving consumers for wrongful gain.
what_it_covers: Any deliberate misrepresentation of facts or identity made with the intention of obtaining a wrongful gain or causing wrongful loss to another person.
Acts of impersonation of a public servant or authority figure carried out with the intent to deceive others and extract money, compliance, or property.
Fabrication or forgery of documents used to deceive another party into parting with money, property, or a valuable security.
Schemes where false promises or false credentials are used to induce another person to act to their financial or legal detriment.
what_it_excludes: Honest mistakes or negligent misstatements made without any intention to deceive, as fraud requires a specific intent to defraud.
Acts of deception carried out without any element of wrongful gain or wrongful loss, such as harmless pranks or innocent misrepresentations.
Civil disputes involving breach of contract where there is no fraudulent intent — mere non-performance of a contract does not constitute fraud under the BNS.
Acts done in good faith with due care and attention, even if they result in unintended harm to another party, as good faith negates fraudulent intent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'fraud' under the BNS directly determines criminal liability under Section 336, which punishes persons who fraudulently represent themselves as public servants; establishing fraud triggers penal consequences including imprisonment, whereas absence of fraudulent intent may reduce the act to a civil wrong or a lesser offence.

definitions.definition: A fraudulent intention, as used in Section 83 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the deliberate purpose of deceiving another person by going through the outward form or ceremony of marriage while knowingly being aware that no lawful marriage is thereby constituted, intending to cause the other party to believe a valid marital union has been formed when it has not.
definitions.plain_english: Fraudulent intention in this context means that a person deliberately tricks someone else into believing they are legally married, even though the person knows that the ceremony being performed does not create a real, legally valid marriage. It is not a mistake or misunderstanding — the person consciously intends to deceive. The focus is on the deliberate plan to mislead the other party about the legal status of the marriage.
real_world_examples: A man already legally married to a woman performs a second marriage ceremony with another woman in a temple, knowing full well that Hindu law prohibits bigamy and the second marriage is void — he goes through the ceremony with the intent to make the second woman believe she is his lawful wife.

A person who has not obtained a valid divorce from their previous spouse participates in a full wedding ceremony with a new partner in Rajasthan, knowing that the divorce was never legally finalised, thereby deceiving the new partner into believing the marriage is lawful.

A man misrepresents himself as unmarried and performs a nikah ceremony under Muslim personal law in Lucknow, despite knowing that his existing marriage was never dissolved and the second nikah would not be legally recognised under applicable law.

A woman and her family stage a complete marriage ceremony with a wealthy groom in Mumbai, fully aware that certain mandatory registration or legal requirements under the Special Marriage Act have been deliberately omitted to keep the union legally invalid, intending to defraud the groom of his property.

A person performs a court marriage ceremony in Delhi using forged documents, knowing the procedural fraud renders the marriage legally void, but allowing the other party to believe they are lawfully married in order to gain financial benefits from the relationship.

definitions.definition: "Fraudulently" means doing anything with the intention to defraud but not otherwise.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'fraudulently' means doing something with the deliberate purpose of cheating or deceiving someone to gain an unfair advantage or cause them a loss. The key requirement is that there must be an actual intention to defraud — accidental or careless acts do not qualify. If someone does something dishonest but without a conscious plan to defraud, it does not meet this definition.
real_world_examples: A property dealer in Mumbai forges a seller's signature on a sale deed and registers it with the sub-registrar to transfer property to himself — he acts fraudulently because he deliberately intends to deprive the true owner of their property.

A Kolkata-based businessman presents fabricated financial statements to a bank to obtain a loan he has no intention of repaying, knowing the bank would not sanction the loan on true figures — this is a fraudulent act under sections dealing with cheating and forgery.
A Delhi jeweller sells ornaments coated to resemble gold to a customer, deliberately misrepresenting them as pure gold — the intentional deception for financial gain constitutes acting fraudulently.

A company director in Chennai transfers company assets to a shell company he secretly owns, just before insolvency proceedings, intending to keep creditors from recovering their dues — he acts fraudulently within the meaning of sections on dishonest or fraudulent removal of property.

A Bengaluru insurance agent submits a claim with fabricated medical records on behalf of a policyholder in exchange for a commission, knowing the claim is false — both the agent and policyholder act fraudulently by intending to deceive the insurer.

A person in Hyderabad creates a duplicate will falsely attributing it to a deceased relative and presents it in court to obtain inheritance — the deliberate creation and use of a false document with intent to defraud the rightful heirs constitutes fraudulent conduct.
what_it_covers: Deliberately forging a document to mislead a court or government authority into conferring a benefit or causing loss to another party.
Intentionally making a false representation to a lender, buyer, or official knowing the representation is untrue and intending them to act on it to their detriment.
Concealing or transferring property with the conscious purpose of defeating a creditor's lawful claim or depriving another of their legal entitlement.
Creating or using false accounts, records, or instruments with the specific design of obtaining money, property, or advantage by deception.
Personating another person or falsely assuming an identity with the deliberate aim of cheating that person or a third party.
what_it_excludes: Acts done carelessly or negligently without any intention to deceive — a mistake made in good faith, even if it causes loss to another, does not amount to acting fraudulently.

Acts accompanied by dishonest intention but lacking any design to defraud a specific person or class of persons — dishonesty and fraud are distinct mental states under the Sanhita, and mere dishonesty does not automatically constitute acting fraudulently.
Acts done under a genuine belief in one's own legal right or claim, even if that belief turns out to be wrong — absence of deceptive intent removes such conduct from the scope of 'fraudulently'.

Rash or impulsive actions that cause unintended harm without any premeditated plan to defraud — rashness is a separate mental element and does not satisfy the intentionality requirement of this definition.
Acts that are merely irregular or in breach of procedure but carried out without any intention to deceive or cheat anyone of a benefit or right.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'fraudulently' is a critical element of mens rea that determines criminal liability under numerous provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, including offences related to forgery (sections 335–343), cheating (sections 318–323), and fraudulent property transfers (sections 243–247); without proof of fraudulent intent, the prosecution cannot establish the offence and the accused cannot be convicted under those sections. It also distinguishes punishable fraud-based crimes from civil wrongs or negligent conduct, directly affecting the quantum of punishment and the nature of proceedings.

definitions.definition: Funeral rites refer to any place set apart for the performance of rituals, ceremonies, or observances connected with the disposal of the dead, as used in Section 301 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which protects such places and assemblies from trespass and disturbance made with the intention of wounding the feelings or insulting the religion of any person.
definitions.plain_english: Funeral rites are the religious or customary ceremonies and rituals performed when someone dies, such as cremation, burial, or prayer gatherings. These include any practices — Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh, or other — carried out to respectfully dispose of a dead body. The law protects both the places where these rites happen and the people gathered to perform them.
real_world_examples: A Hindu cremation ceremony (antim sanskar) conducted at a cremation ground (shamshan ghat) in Varanasi, where the body is ritually bathed, wrapped, and placed on a funeral pyre with Vedic chants.
A Muslim janaza (funeral prayer) and subsequent burial at a qabristan (graveyard) in Hyderabad, including the washing of the body and recitation of Islamic prayers before interment.
A Christian burial service held at a church cemetery in Goa, where last rites are administered by a priest and the body is interred following Catholic traditions.
A Sikh antam sanskar ceremony at a gurdwara in Amritsar, where the body is cremated after recitation of Gurbani and Ardas, followed by the immersion of ashes in a river.
A Parsi funerary ritual at a Tower of Silence (dokhma) in Mumbai, where the body is ritually cleansed and exposed according to Zoroastrian tradition.
A tribal community's customary death ceremony in Jharkhand, involving traditional songs, rituals, and burial rites conducted over several days according to indigenous custom.
what_it_covers: Hindu cremation ceremonies (antim sanskar) conducted at cremation grounds or ghats, including all associated rituals.
Muslim burial prayers (janaza) and interment rituals conducted at graveyards or mosques.
Christian burial services and last rites conducted at churches, cemeteries, or designated burial grounds.
Sikh antam sanskar ceremonies held at gurdwaras or cremation grounds involving scriptural recitation and ritual cremation.
Parsi dokhmenashini rites at Towers of Silence and associated purification ceremonies.
Any place formally set apart for performance of such rites, whether permanent or temporarily designated for the purpose.
what_it_excludes: Memorials or commemorative events held long after burial or cremation that are not part of the immediate funerary observance, such as annual death anniversaries (barsi).
Medical or scientific procedures involving human remains in hospitals, forensic labs, or mortuaries, which are not conducted as part of any religious or customary funeral ritual.
General religious ceremonies unconnected to the death of a specific individual, such as routine daily prayers at a place of worship.
Private mourning or grief at a personal residence that does not involve formal ritual or ceremony constituting 'rites'.
Commercial or administrative activities at a crematorium or cemetery, such as record-keeping, maintenance, or construction, which do not form part of the funeral rites themselves.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of this definition determines whether a place qualifies as protected under Section 301, triggering criminal liability (imprisonment up to one year and/or fine) for anyone who trespasses or causes disturbance there with intent to wound religious feelings. If an act or location does not fall within the scope of funeral rites, the specific protections and penal consequences of Section 301 cannot be invoked.

definitions.definition: A 'gang' refers to a group of two or more persons who, acting either singly or jointly, as a syndicate or gang, indulge in any continuing unlawful activity; in the context of dacoity and organised crime, it denotes an association of persons united for the purpose of committing criminal acts, including but not limited to robbery, dacoity, or other unlawful activities carried out collectively or in furtherance of a common criminal purpose.
definitions.plain_english: A 'gang' is a group of two or more people who come together to carry out illegal activities, whether they act all at once or one at a time. It can refer to a band of robbers or dacoits, or more broadly to any organised criminal group operating as a unit. The key idea is that these people are working together — formally or informally — toward criminal ends.
real_world_examples: A group of five men from Bihar who systematically rob highway trucks travelling between Patna and Varanasi, coordinating roles such as lookout, driver, and armed attacker, constitutes a gang engaged in organised robbery.

A criminal network in Mumbai operating kidnapping-for-ransom operations across three states, with members playing distinct roles — planners, enforcers, and negotiators — forms a gang within the meaning of an organised crime syndicate under Section 111.

A cluster of persons in Delhi who coerce local shopkeepers into paying weekly 'protection money' through threats of violence, operating under a common leader, qualifies as a gang engaged in extortion.

A band of armed dacoits in Chambal who forcibly enter rural homes together to steal valuables and terrorise villagers constitutes a gang of dacoits as contemplated under Sections 310 and 32 of the BNS.

A group of cybercriminals operating from Jamtara, Jharkhand, collectively running phishing and banking fraud schemes under coordinated leadership, can be classified as a gang for purposes of organised crime under Section 111.
A human trafficking ring operating across West Bengal and Bangladesh, involving recruiters, transporters, and exploiters acting in concert, constitutes a gang engaged in continuing unlawful activity.
what_it_covers: A group of two or more persons who jointly or severally commit robbery, dacoity, or other continuing unlawful activities as part of a coordinated criminal enterprise.
A band of dacoits who act together to commit crimes using force, threat, or intimidation, including persons who voluntarily join such a group knowing its criminal character.
An organised crime syndicate operating as a gang to carry out activities such as kidnapping, extortion, drug trafficking, cyber-crimes, or human trafficking for financial gain.
Persons who, while not physically present at the scene, act as members of a gang by facilitating, planning, or financing criminal operations carried out by the group.
A group of persons acting in furtherance of a common criminal intention across multiple incidents, where more than one charge-sheet has been filed before a competent court.
what_it_excludes: A lone individual acting independently without association or coordination with others, even if committing the same type of offence repeatedly.
A spontaneous, unplanned gathering of persons who coincidentally commit an unlawful act without prior agreement or shared criminal purpose, lacking the organised character of a gang.
A person who is forcibly seized and compelled under threat of instant death to assist dacoits, as such a person is protected under Section 32 and is not treated as a member of the gang.

Legitimate associations, companies, or organisations of individuals, even if two or more members independently commit offences, where no shared criminal syndicate structure or continuing unlawful activity exists.
Groups whose activities are not cognizable offences punishable with imprisonment of three or more years, or where the requisite charge-sheets have not been filed before a competent court.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a group of persons qualifies as a 'gang' is critical because it determines liability under Sections 111 (organised crime) and 310 (dacoity), attracting mandatory minimum sentences of five years to life imprisonment and fines of not less than five lakh rupees; it also governs whether a person who joins such a group voluntarily can claim compulsion as a defence under Section 32, which is expressly denied to voluntary gang members.

definitions.definition: A 'garb' refers to any dress, uniform, clothing, or outward appearance worn by or characteristic of a particular class — specifically the uniform or attire used by soldiers, sailors, airmen, or public servants — such that wearing it by an unauthorised person, with the intention or knowledge that others may believe them to belong to that class, constitutes an offence under this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: A 'garb' is any clothing or uniform that is associated with or looks like the official dress of a soldier, sailor, airman, or government official. If someone wears such clothing while not actually belonging to that group, and does so to make others believe they are part of that group, it is a criminal offence. Essentially, it means impersonating someone through their official outfit or appearance.
real_world_examples: A civilian in Mumbai purchases an Indian Army uniform from a surplus store and wears it at a railway station to gain access to reserved military coaches, intending fellow passengers and railway staff to believe he is a serving army officer.

A fraudster in Delhi dresses in a police uniform (garb of a public servant) and goes door-to-door in a residential colony, collecting 'fines' from residents by pretending to be an on-duty police officer conducting an inspection.

A man in Chennai wears a Navy petty officer's uniform to attend a college function with the intention of impressing attendees and being believed to be a serving Naval personnel, even though he was never enlisted.

A tout near a government office in Lucknow wears clothing closely resembling the khaki uniform of revenue department officials to deceive farmers into paying him unofficial fees, exploiting the belief that he is a legitimate government functionary.
A person in Kochi wears an Indian Air Force flying suit with rank insignia at a public event to fraudulently obtain discounts and privileges reserved for serving airmen at a commercial establishment.
what_it_covers: The full official uniform of a soldier, sailor, or airman of the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force when worn by a civilian with deceptive intent.
Any clothing or dress closely resembling the official attire of a class of public servants, worn by a non-member of that class to deceive others into believing they are a government official.
Partial or near-identical imitation clothing that so closely resembles the official garb of a recognised public or military functionary that it is likely to cause belief of official status.
Theatrical or replica costumes of military or government uniforms when worn in real-world public settings with the intention of being mistaken for genuine officials.
what_it_excludes: Wearing military or official uniforms by persons who are genuinely serving soldiers, sailors, airmen, or public servants of the relevant class, as they are authorised wearers.

Persons subject to the Air Force Act 1950, Army Act 1950, or Navy Act 1957, who are governed by those respective service laws and are explicitly excluded from punishment under this Sanhita for such offences.
Wearing military-style or government-style clothing in clearly theatrical, cinematic, or dramatic contexts where no reasonable person could form the belief that the wearer is an actual official.
Generic or fashion clothing that merely uses military-inspired colours or patterns without bearing specific insignia, rank markings, or identifiers of any particular service or government department.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item of clothing qualifies as a 'garb' under Sections 168 and 205 determines criminal liability for the offences of impersonating a soldier, sailor, airman, or public servant — triggering punishment of up to three months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to two thousand or five thousand rupees respectively. This definition is essential to establishing the actus reus of these impersonation offences and directly connects to the proof of fraudulent or deceptive intent.
