definitions.definition: Nothing is said to be done or believed in 'good faith' which is done or believed without due care and attention.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means acting with proper care and attention, not carelessly or recklessly. It is not enough to simply mean well — a person must actually take reasonable precautions and apply their mind to the situation. If someone acts without exercising the care that a reasonable person would, they cannot claim to have acted in good faith.
real_world_examples: A doctor in a rural government hospital performs emergency surgery on an accident victim without obtaining written consent because the patient is unconscious and there is no time to locate family. If the doctor applies proper medical judgment and follows established protocols, this act is done in good faith and the doctor is protected from criminal liability.

A police officer, acting on a warrant issued by a magistrate, arrests a person later found to be wrongly named. If the officer verified the warrant and took reasonable steps to confirm the identity of the accused before making the arrest, the arrest is made in good faith.

A pharmacist dispenses a common over-the-counter medicine to a customer who later misuses it. If the pharmacist had no reason to suspect misuse and followed standard dispensing practice, the act of dispensing is considered done in good faith.

A bank employee transfers funds based on a seemingly authentic power of attorney that later turns out to be forged. If the employee followed due diligence procedures prescribed by the bank and verified the document through standard checks, the transfer may be considered done in good faith.

A teacher in a school reports a student to the police after genuinely and carefully believing the student possesses a dangerous weapon, based on credible information from other students. If the report is made after applying reasonable care to assess the information, the act is done in good faith.

A citizen hands over a found wallet to the nearest police station after checking the contents carefully to record what was inside. This act of handing over property to authorities, done with attention and care, constitutes good faith action.
what_it_covers: An act performed after the person applied reasonable diligence, thought, and care appropriate to the circumstances, even if the outcome is harmful.
A belief sincerely held after careful inquiry and consideration of available facts, even if the belief later proves to be incorrect.
Professional actions taken by doctors, police officers, or public servants following established procedures and protocols with proper attention to their duties.
Emergency interventions by private individuals who assess the situation carefully before acting, such as preventing imminent harm to another person.
Judicial or quasi-judicial acts performed by persons empowered by law who apply their mind diligently to the facts before them.
what_it_excludes: Acts performed carelessly, hastily, or without applying the mind, even if the person subjectively intended no harm — good intentions alone do not satisfy good faith.
Beliefs formed without any inquiry or verification, based purely on assumption, rumour, or deliberate ignorance of available information.
Actions taken recklessly or with wilful blindness to obvious risks or red flags that a reasonably careful person would have noticed and investigated.
Professional conduct that falls below the standard of care ordinarily expected in that profession, such as a doctor ignoring basic diagnostic steps before administering treatment.
Acts motivated by personal gain, malice, or bias, even if the person claims to have believed they were acting correctly.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done in good faith determines whether a person can avail statutory defences and protections available under sections such as 14 to 37 and others across the Sanhita — for example, a public servant or private person acting in good faith to prevent harm or execute a duty is shielded from criminal liability, whereas the same act done without due care attracts full penal consequences. It is a pivotal threshold that separates protected lawful conduct from punishable offences across a wide range of provisions.

definitions.definition: The term 'goods' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 348 and 350, it refers to any movable tangible items or merchandise that are capable of being delivered, transferred, or made the subject of a commercial or fraudulent transaction, including articles of trade, commodities, and physical products.
definitions.plain_english: Goods means any physical, movable items or products that can be handed over, sold, delivered, or transferred from one person to another. This includes things like food items, manufactured products, raw materials, livestock, electronic devices, or any other tangible merchandise. Essentially, if something is a physical object that can be moved and traded or delivered, it qualifies as 'goods' under this law.
real_world_examples: A shopkeeper in Mumbai promises to deliver a consignment of textiles to a buyer but instead delivers substandard fabric after receiving full payment — the textiles constitute 'goods' under the relevant cheating provisions.
An e-commerce seller listed on Flipkart ships counterfeit mobile phones instead of the genuine branded products ordered by the customer — the mobile phones are 'goods' within the meaning of the Act.

A wholesale trader in Delhi's Chandni Chowk market delivers adulterated ghee in containers labelled as pure desi ghee to retailers — the ghee constitutes 'goods' for purposes of fraudulent delivery offences.

A lottery scheme in Chennai promises participants the delivery of a refrigerator or motorcycle as prizes — these physical prizes are 'goods' as referred to in Section 297 and related provisions of the Act.
Stolen consignments of electronic components intercepted during transport on a truck in Bengaluru represent 'goods' involved in theft from a means of transport under Section 305.
Agricultural produce such as wheat or rice stored in a government warehouse and subsequently misappropriated by a custodian amounts to 'goods' subject to criminal breach of trust provisions.
what_it_covers: Manufactured products such as electronics, garments, or appliances that are bought, sold, or promised for delivery in a commercial transaction.
Agricultural commodities like grain, cotton, or perishable produce that are stored, transported, or traded and can be the subject of misappropriation or fraud.
Raw materials, industrial inputs, and bulk cargo transported via road, rail, or vessel that can be stolen or fraudulently dealt with.
Consumer items such as food products, medicines, or household goods offered as consideration or prize in a lottery or fraudulent scheme.
Livestock and animals classified as movable property that are transferred, delivered, or made subject to criminal transactions.
what_it_excludes: Immovable property such as land, buildings, or permanently fixed structures, which cannot be physically moved or delivered and are governed by separate legal provisions.
Intangible assets such as intellectual property rights, software licences, or contractual rights that have no physical form and cannot be handed over as tangible items.
Services rendered by a person, such as labour, professional advice, or contractual work, which do not constitute physical deliverable objects.
Currency notes, coins, and negotiable instruments such as cheques or demand drafts, which are governed by specific definitions like 'valuable security', 'coin', and 'currency-note' under the Act.
Electronic records or digital data, which fall under separate definitions such as 'electronic record' and 'electronic form' in the Act and are not treated as physical goods.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as 'goods' determines the applicability of offences under Sections 348 and 350 relating to cheating by delivery of lesser or different items than those contracted for, directly affecting whether criminal liability for fraud or cheating is established. Misclassification of an item as outside the scope of 'goods' could prevent prosecution under these cheating provisions and deny a victim their legal remedy.

definitions.definition: "Government" means the Central Government or a State Government.
definitions.plain_english: In the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 'Government' refers to either the Central (Union) Government of India or any of the State Governments. This means that whenever the law mentions 'Government,' it can apply to actions, orders, or authority exercised by either the national government in New Delhi or the government of any individual state like Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, or Uttar Pradesh. It is a broad term that covers both levels of governmental authority in India's federal structure.
real_world_examples: A public servant employed by the Maharashtra State Government who accepts a bribe in connection with a state contract — the 'Government' in this context refers to the State Government of Maharashtra, making the act an offence against the State.

A Central Government official from the Ministry of Railways who uses their position to commit criminal misconduct — the 'Government' here is the Central Government, and offences against their official duties fall under this definition.

When the Uttar Pradesh State Government issues a quarantine order and a person knowingly violates it, causing spread of disease, the 'Government' whose order is being defied is the State Government under Section 273.

A person forges a document purporting to be issued by the Government of India (Central Government) to fraudulently claim a subsidy — the Central Government is the 'Government' whose authority is being misused.
Under Section 305, when a Government official is found abetting a suicide of a person in their custody, 'Government' encompasses both Central and State Government employees holding such custody.

When the Rajasthan State Government declares a public emergency and officers act under that authority, any obstruction or offence against those officers is treated as an offence against the Government.
what_it_covers: The Central Government of India, including all its ministries, departments, and central authorities operating under the Union executive.
Any State Government of India, including the governments of all 28 states and 2 union territories with legislatures (Delhi and Puducherry), acting through their respective state executive.
Government bodies, officials, and entities acting on behalf of or deriving authority from either the Central or State Government in the exercise of their statutory functions.
Orders, directions, notifications, and acts issued in the name of either the Central Government or a State Government within the scope of their respective constitutional powers.
what_it_excludes: Local authorities such as municipal corporations, gram panchayats, or district boards, which are bodies of local self-government and are not synonymous with 'Government' under this definition.
Autonomous statutory bodies, public sector undertakings (PSUs), or government-owned corporations (e.g., ONGC, BHEL) that are distinct legal entities and not themselves the Government.
Union Territories without a legislature (such as Chandigarh or Lakshadweep), which are administered by the Central Government but are not themselves a 'State Government.'
Foreign governments or international organisations, which fall entirely outside the scope of this definition.

The Judiciary (courts and tribunals) and the Legislature (Parliament and State Legislatures), which are separate constitutional organs and are not encompassed by 'Government' in the executive sense used in this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition determines the scope of several critical offences — such as offences against the State (Sections 184 and 186), causing public harm through adulteration (Section 273), and abetment of suicide by a Government official (Section 305) — by establishing whose authority, orders, or servants are protected or implicated. Whether an act constitutes an offence against the 'Government' directly affects the applicable punishment, the nature of the charges, and the jurisdiction of prosecuting authorities.

definitions.definition: The Government of India refers to the Central Government of the Republic of India, constituted under the Constitution of India, encompassing the executive authority of the Union as vested in the President and exercised through the Council of Ministers. As used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, it denotes the sovereign governing authority of the Indian Union, including all its departments, ministries, agencies, and instrumentalities functioning under the Union executive.
definitions.plain_english: The Government of India means the Central Government — the national government that runs the country from New Delhi. It includes the President, the Prime Minister, all Union Ministries and departments, and agencies that act on behalf of the Union of India. When the law refers to the Government of India, it means the top-level national authority, not any state or local government.
real_world_examples: A terrorist group kidnaps a foreign diplomat and demands that the Government of India release imprisoned militants — this constitutes a terrorist act under Section 113 because it is an attempt to compel the Government of India to abstain from lawful action.

A militant organisation destroys a building owned by the Ministry of Defence in Pune — the destruction of property used in connection with the purposes of the Government of India constitutes a terrorist act under Section 113.

Under Section 1 of the BNS, a provision exempts statutes punishing mutiny and desertion of soldiers in the service of the Government of India, such as the Army Act, 1950, which operates under the Union's authority.

A group of insurgents attempts to damage the Indian Space Research Organisation's satellite launch facility in Sriharikota — since ISRO is an agency of the Government of India, such an attack targets property used for the purposes of the Government of India under Section 113.
A person is charged under Section 147 (waging war against the Government of India) for leading an armed rebellion aimed at overthrowing the Union executive, which is the Government of India.

An individual is prosecuted under Section 150 for conspiring with foreign operatives to compel the Government of India to cede territory by threatening mass civilian harm, directly implicating the 'Government of India' as the coerced authority.
what_it_covers: All Union Ministries and departments, such as the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Home Affairs, and Ministry of Finance, acting under the President's executive authority.
Agencies and instrumentalities of the Union, such as ISRO, defence research establishments (DRDO), and intelligence agencies like RAW, when acting on behalf of the Union.
The President of India acting in the exercise of executive power of the Union, including orders and directions issued through the Council of Ministers.
Property owned, used, or intended to be used by the Union Government for defence, public administration, or other official purposes of the Indian state.
Actions or decisions of the Central Government that terrorists or insurgents attempt to influence, compel, or obstruct under Sections 113, 147, 149, and 150.
what_it_excludes: State Governments (such as the Government of Maharashtra or the Government of Tamil Nadu), which are separate constitutional entities with their own executive authority.
Local bodies, municipal corporations, panchayats, or urban local authorities, which are not part of the Union executive structure.
Foreign governments or international organisations, even if they have agreements or treaties with India, as they do not constitute the Government of India.
Private companies or public sector undertakings operating independently under corporate law, unless they are directly functioning as instruments or agents of the Union Government.
Judicial institutions such as the Supreme Court of India or High Courts, which constitute a separate branch of government distinct from the executive Government of India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Offences under Sections 147, 149, and 150 of the BNS — including waging war, collecting arms, and concealing design to wage war — are specifically directed against the Government of India, and the applicability of these grave offences (punishable up to death or life imprisonment) depends entirely on whether the target or object of the criminal act is the Government of India. Similarly, under Section 113, terrorist acts involving compulsion or destruction targeting the Government of India attract the most severe penalties, making this definition pivotal in determining the nature and severity of the charge.

definitions.definition: A 'Government stamp' means a stamp issued by the Government for the purpose of revenue. A person commits the offence of 'counterfeiting Government stamp' who counterfeits by causing a genuine stamp of one denomination to appear like a genuine stamp of a different denomination.
definitions.plain_english: A Government stamp is an official stamp issued by the Indian Government to collect revenue, such as court fee stamps, postal stamps, or excise stamps. Faking or altering such a stamp — for example, making a lower-value stamp look like a higher-value one — is treated as counterfeiting a Government stamp. This is a serious criminal offence under the law.
real_world_examples: A person chemically washes a used 10-rupee court fee stamp and re-presents it as an unused stamp to avoid paying the proper court fee — this constitutes counterfeiting a Government stamp.

A trader in Mumbai alters a lower-denomination revenue stamp affixed on a sale deed to make it appear as a higher-denomination stamp, thereby fraudulently misrepresenting the duty paid — this is an offence under Section 178.
A stamp vendor in Delhi sells forged non-judicial stamps bearing inflated face values, which are then used by buyers to execute property agreements, constituting counterfeiting of Government stamps.

A person in Uttar Pradesh soaks cancelled postal stamps in chemical solution to remove cancellation marks and re-sells them as valid unused stamps, amounting to counterfeiting Government stamps for financial gain.

definitions.definition: Gratification, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any benefit, reward, or inducement — whether in the form of money, food, drink, entertainment, provision, or any other advantage — given or accepted to influence, reward, or procure any action or omission, including the exercise of an electoral right, the concealment of an offence, or the screening of any person from legal punishment. A person who offers, agrees to give, or attempts to procure a gratification shall be deemed to give it, and a person who obtains, agrees to accept, or attempts to obtain a gratification shall be deemed to accept it.
definitions.plain_english: Gratification means anything of value — such as money, food, drinks, gifts, or entertainment — that is given or received as a bribe, reward, or inducement to make someone do something or refrain from doing something. It does not have to actually change hands; merely offering or agreeing to give or accept it is enough. For example, paying someone to vote a certain way or giving gifts to someone to hide a crime both count as gratification.
real_world_examples: A political party worker distributes cash to voters in a constituency in Uttar Pradesh before elections to influence them to vote for a particular candidate — the cash distributed constitutes gratification under Section 170.

A local MLA candidate organises a free biryani feast for villagers in Tamil Nadu the night before polling day to win their votes — the food and drink provided amounts to gratification in the form of 'treating' under Section 173.

A witness to a road accident in Mumbai accepts ₹50,000 from the accused driver in exchange for not reporting the incident to the police — the money accepted constitutes gratification under Section 250.

A person involved in a financial fraud in Delhi offers a government official expensive jewellery and foreign liquor in exchange for the official not filing a complaint or initiating prosecution — the jewellery and liquor constitute gratification under Section 251.

A booth-level election agent in Rajasthan promises free motorcycle repairs and petrol vouchers to voters in exchange for their votes — the promised services and vouchers amount to gratification under Section 170.
A landlord in Kolkata pays a local councillor a sum of money to suppress an FIR registered against him for illegal construction — the payment constitutes gratification under Section 250.
what_it_covers: Cash payments made to voters to influence their voting choice in an Indian election.
Food, drink, or entertainment provided to voters as an inducement or reward for voting a particular way (treating).
Any monetary or non-monetary benefit offered or accepted as consideration for concealing a crime or shielding an offender from prosecution.
Promises or agreements to give a benefit — even where the benefit has not yet been transferred — as these are deemed equivalent to actual giving.
Non-cash advantages such as gifts, jewellery, property, services, or promises of employment given as rewards or inducements in the contexts covered by the relevant sections.
what_it_excludes: Declarations of public policy or promises of public action by political candidates or parties, which are expressly excluded from constituting bribery under the proviso to Section 170.
Lawful compounding of offences — Sections 250 and 251 expressly do not apply where the offence may lawfully be compounded, so restitution or settlement in such cases is excluded.
Voluntary gifts given without any object of inducing or rewarding the exercise of an electoral right, or without any consideration relating to concealment of an offence.
Legitimate restitution of property made through lawful legal processes or court-ordered settlements, not intended to screen any person from legal punishment.
General acts of charity, welfare distribution, or community service not connected to any electoral purpose or any criminal concealment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a benefit constitutes 'gratification' is the pivotal element that determines criminal liability under Sections 170, 173, 250, and 251 of the BNS, 2023 — if the threshold is met, the giver and receiver both commit cognisable offences attracting imprisonment and/or fine. Conversely, if a benefit falls outside this definition (e.g., a public policy promise), no criminal liability for bribery or screening arises.

definitions.definition: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident. Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent the offence from amounting to murder is a question of fact.
definitions.plain_english: Grave and sudden provocation refers to a trigger or act by another person so serious and unexpected that it temporarily causes the accused to lose control of themselves and act in the heat of passion. If someone kills under such extreme, unplanned emotional reaction caused by the victim's own provocation, the law may treat it as the lesser offence of culpable homicide rather than murder. The provocation must be both severe enough ('grave') and immediate ('sudden') — it cannot be something the accused planned, invited, or had time to cool down from.
real_world_examples: A husband returns home unexpectedly and finds his wife in the act of adultery with another man. In a fit of sudden rage and emotional shock, he immediately picks up a nearby object and kills the man. A court may consider whether this constitutes grave and sudden provocation reducing the offence from murder to culpable homicide.

During a heated verbal altercation in a village in Rajasthan, a man publicly accuses another of being a thief and a coward in front of the entire community, following which the accused immediately strikes the man with an agricultural tool causing his death. The court examines whether the public humiliation constituted grave and sudden provocation.

A father in Maharashtra is told by a neighbour, face to face, that his daughter was sexually assaulted by a specific person. The father, overcome with immediate uncontrollable rage, confronts and kills that person moments later. The court considers whether the disclosure constituted grave and sudden provocation.

During a street fight in Delhi, a man repeatedly slaps and spits on another person in front of bystanders. The person who was spat upon instantly retaliates with a knife, killing the aggressor. The court evaluates whether the humiliating physical acts amounted to grave and sudden provocation.

A woman in Tamil Nadu is told abruptly by her husband, in a cruel and degrading manner, that her child is not his and that he plans to abandon the family. In a moment of sudden overwhelming distress and rage, she strikes him fatally. The defence of grave and sudden provocation is raised to reduce the charge from murder to culpable homicide.
what_it_covers: A sudden, severe act or words by the victim that would deprive a reasonable person of self-control, causing immediate retaliatory killing of the provoker.
Accidental or mistaken killing of a third party (not the provoker) caused by an act done in the heat of passion immediately following grave and sudden provocation.
Situations where the provocation is spontaneous and not sought or engineered by the accused as a pretext for violence.
Cases where the accused had no time to cool down between receiving the provocation and committing the fatal act, establishing temporal immediacy.
what_it_excludes: Provocation that is voluntarily sought or deliberately engineered by the accused as a pretext or excuse for causing harm or death.
Provocation arising from a lawful act done by a public servant in the lawful exercise of their official powers, such as a police officer making a lawful arrest.
Provocation given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence by the victim or any other person.
Situations where the accused had sufficient time to cool down after receiving the provocation but still chose to kill, negating the 'sudden' element.
Premeditated acts of violence dressed up as provoked reactions, where the accused had a prior intention or design to cause harm.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of grave and sudden provocation is a statutory exception that reduces the offence from murder (punishable with death or imprisonment for life under Section 101 read with Section 103) to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (punishable under Section 105), significantly altering the nature of the charge and the quantum of punishment. Whether this exception applies is treated as a pure question of fact, making it a critical issue in trial proceedings under Sections 101, 122, 131, 133, and 136 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

definitions.definition: Grave injury, as used in Section 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to serious bodily or mental harm caused or likely to be caused to a woman as a result of wilful conduct by her husband or his relatives, constituting a level of harm that endangers life, limb, or health, whether mental or physical, falling short of immediate danger to life but beyond trivial or minor hurt.
definitions.plain_english: Grave injury means serious physical or mental harm done to a woman that is significant enough to put her body, mind, or overall health at serious risk. It is more than a minor injury but may not necessarily be life-threatening. In the context of cruelty against a married woman, it refers to harm severe enough to seriously affect her wellbeing, whether through physical violence, emotional abuse, or other harmful conduct.
real_world_examples: A husband repeatedly beats his wife causing fractures, internal bleeding, or permanent scarring, resulting in lasting physical damage that qualifies as grave injury to her body.

A woman suffers a severe mental breakdown, requiring hospitalisation for psychiatric treatment, after being subjected to persistent verbal abuse, isolation, and emotional torture by her in-laws, constituting grave injury to her mental health.

A husband deprives his wife of food, medical care, and sleep for extended periods, causing her to develop serious nutritional deficiencies and chronic health conditions, amounting to grave injury to her physical health.

A woman is subjected to sustained harassment and threats by her husband over dowry demands, leading to a documented anxiety disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, constituting grave injury to her mental health under Section 86.

A husband throws a heavy object at his wife during a domestic dispute, causing a serious head injury requiring surgery and leaving her with partial vision loss, which constitutes a grave injury to her limb and health.
what_it_covers: Severe physical injuries such as fractures, burns, internal injuries, or permanent bodily damage inflicted on a woman by her husband or his relatives.
Serious mental health deterioration including clinically diagnosed depression, anxiety disorders, or psychiatric illness caused by sustained emotional or psychological abuse.
Significant harm to a woman's reproductive or general health resulting from wilful denial of medical care, forced starvation, or physical assault.
Permanent or long-term disability or disfigurement resulting from acts of domestic violence committed by the husband or his family members.
Harm to a woman's limb or organ that impairs normal functioning, caused intentionally or through reckless wilful conduct by the accused.
what_it_excludes: Minor or trivial physical injuries such as small bruises, superficial scratches, or temporary discomfort that do not rise to the level of seriousness contemplated by the term.
Emotional displeasure, normal marital disagreements, or general unhappiness in a marriage that do not result in identifiable or clinically significant harm to health.
Harm caused by accident or without any wilful conduct on the part of the husband or his relatives, as the definition in Section 86 requires wilful conduct.
Purely financial or economic harm such as loss of property or deprivation of maintenance, unless such deprivation directly causes serious physical or mental health consequences.
Harm caused to third parties or relatives of the woman, as the grave injury limb of the definition is specifically directed at injury to the woman herself.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes a grave injury is critical in establishing the offence of cruelty under Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which is a cognizable and non-bailable offence attracting imprisonment of up to three years and a fine. If the wilful conduct of a husband or his relative is found to have caused or to be likely to cause grave injury, it satisfies one of the two limbs of the definition of cruelty, making the accused liable for criminal prosecution and punishment.

definitions.definition: The term 'grievous bodily harm' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in Section 64 to describe serious physical injury caused to a woman during the commission of rape, including harm that maims, disfigures, or endangers her life. It denotes an aggravated category of physical injury that goes beyond ordinary hurt and encompasses lasting or life-threatening bodily damage inflicted upon the victim.
definitions.plain_english: Grievous bodily harm refers to very serious physical injury caused to a woman while she is being raped. This includes injuries that permanently damage her body, disfigure her appearance, cause lasting disability, or put her life at risk. It is not minor or temporary harm — it must be severe enough to have a major lasting impact on the victim's body or health.
real_world_examples: A rapist in Mumbai fractures the victim's spine during the assault, leaving her paralysed — this constitutes grievous bodily harm as it permanently disables her.
During a rape in Delhi, the perpetrator strangles the woman so severely that she suffers brain damage due to oxygen deprivation, endangering her life and causing lasting neurological harm.
A victim in Kolkata is beaten with a blunt object during rape, resulting in the loss of sight in one eye — the permanent disfigurement and loss of sensory function qualifies as grievous bodily harm.
In a case in Hyderabad, a rapist slashes the victim's face with a blade during the assault, leaving permanent disfiguring scars — this constitutes grievous bodily harm under Section 64.

A woman in Chennai is subjected to rape during which her arm is broken and her internal organs are injured, requiring emergency surgery — the life-threatening internal injuries amount to grievous bodily harm.
what_it_covers: Permanent disability or loss of limb caused to the victim during the commission of rape.
Disfigurement of the victim's face or body through cutting, burning, or beating during the rape.
Injuries that endanger the victim's life, such as strangulation, severe internal bleeding, or organ damage inflicted during the assault.
Maiming of the victim, including destruction or permanent impairment of a bodily organ or function during the rape.
Brain injury, spinal injury, or any other injury causing permanent or severe neurological damage inflicted during the commission of rape.
what_it_excludes: Minor bruises, scratches, or temporary pain caused incidentally during rape that heal without lasting consequences.
Psychological or emotional trauma suffered by the victim, which does not constitute bodily or physical harm under this provision.
Harm caused after the completion of the act of rape and not directly connected to the commission of the offence.
Pre-existing medical conditions or disabilities of the victim that were not caused or aggravated by the accused during the rape.
Harm caused to a third party rather than to the woman who is the direct victim of the rape under Section 64.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of grievous bodily harm elevates the offence of rape from the basic category under Section 64(1) to an aggravated category under Section 64(2), attracting a mandatory minimum sentence of ten years rigorous imprisonment extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the offender's natural life. This determination is therefore critical in sentencing and in framing the charge against the accused.

definitions.definition: Grievous disease is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 27 and Section 30, it refers to a disease or infirmity of a serious, severe, or dangerous nature affecting a person's health, for the purpose of curing which otherwise harmful or potentially fatal acts may be performed in good faith on behalf of a child or person of unsound mind. It denotes a condition whose severity justifies medical intervention that may cause harm or risk death, distinct from minor or trivial ailments.
definitions.plain_english: A 'grievous disease' is a serious, severe illness or medical condition that is significant enough to justify a doctor or guardian taking risky medical steps to treat it, even if those steps might cause harm or could be life-threatening. It is not a minor or ordinary illness but one that poses a substantial threat to a person's health or life. The term is used to carve out an exception allowing harmful medical acts done in good faith to treat such serious conditions without criminal liability.
real_world_examples: A child in Mumbai is diagnosed with an aggressive brain tumour; a neurosurgeon, with the parents' consent, performs a high-risk craniotomy knowing it may cause serious harm or death, but intending to cure the child — this falls within the 'grievous disease' exception under Section 27.

A person of unsound mind residing in a government psychiatric facility in Delhi develops severe, life-threatening tuberculosis; the facility's guardian consents to a prolonged and painful treatment regimen involving drugs known to have serious side effects, acting in good faith to cure the grievous disease.

A ten-year-old child in Chennai suffers from a grievous cardiac disease requiring open-heart surgery; the parents consent to the operation knowing it carries a risk of death, and the surgeon proceeds in good faith — the act is protected as it aims to cure a grievous disease.

A minor in Kolkata is afflicted with end-stage kidney disease; a doctor, with the lawful guardian's consent, performs a risky kidney transplant procedure that could cause grievous hurt, justified under the exception of curing a grievous disease.

A person of unsound mind in a Pune hospital is found to have a rapidly spreading gangrenous infection in the leg; the treating doctor, with the guardian's consent, amputates the leg in good faith to prevent death, treating the gangrene as a grievous disease or infirmity warranting the drastic intervention.
semantic_tags: benefit of child or unsound mind
what_it_covers: Life-threatening or severely debilitating diseases such as advanced cancer, serious cardiac conditions, or end-stage organ failure in a child or person of unsound mind.
Rapidly spreading or gangrenous infections that, if untreated, would cause death or permanent severe disability.
Serious congenital or acquired disorders requiring dangerous surgical intervention where the risk of harm or death is known but the purpose is cure.
Conditions such as severe tuberculosis, aggressive tumours, or critical organ failure that necessitate risky medical procedures performed with guardian's consent in good faith.
what_it_excludes: Minor, trivial, or self-limiting ailments such as a common cold, minor fever, or superficial wounds that do not pose a serious threat to life or health.
Cosmetic or elective procedures not aimed at curing a serious disease, even if they carry some risk of harm.
Diseases or conditions where the harmful act is performed not to cure but for pecuniary benefit or any purpose unrelated to the patient's medical welfare.
Ordinary discomforts or non-serious chronic conditions that do not rise to the level of severity implied by the word 'grievous', such as mild hypertension managed by routine medication.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done to cure a 'grievous disease' determines whether a doctor or guardian is protected from criminal liability under Sections 27 and 30 of the BNS, 2023; without this exception applying, performing a harmful or potentially fatal medical act on a child or person of unsound mind — even in good faith — could constitute an offence such as causing grievous hurt or culpable homicide. The applicability of this term directly blocks prosecution for acts that would otherwise attract serious criminal penalties.

definitions.definition: Grievous hurt is defined under Section 114 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and includes the following kinds of hurt only: emasculation; permanent privation of the sight of either eye; permanent privation of the hearing of either ear; privation of any member or joint; destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint; permanent disfiguration of the head or face; fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth; any hurt which endangers life or which causes the sufferer to be during the space of twenty days in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits.
definitions.plain_english: Grievous hurt means a serious physical injury that goes well beyond minor pain or bruising. It includes injuries like loss of an eye or ear, breaking a bone, permanently disfiguring the face, cutting off a body part, or any injury so severe that it puts someone's life at risk or leaves them bedridden and unable to work for at least 20 days. Ordinary cuts, bruises, or short-term pain do not qualify as grievous hurt.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi attacks his neighbour with an iron rod, fracturing his leg bone — the fracture constitutes grievous hurt under the category of fracture or dislocation of a bone.
During a communal clash in Uttar Pradesh, a person throws acid on a woman's face, causing permanent disfiguration of her face and destruction of vision in one eye, both amounting to grievous hurt.
A factory worker in Maharashtra has his hand caught in unguarded machinery, resulting in the amputation of two fingers — privation of a member or joint constitutes grievous hurt.

A victim of a road rage incident in Chennai is hit on the head with a cricket bat, causing a severe skull fracture that leaves him hospitalised and bedridden for 25 days, satisfying the 20-day incapacitation threshold for grievous hurt.

A man in Kolkata is deliberately blinded in one eye after being struck with a sharp object during a robbery, amounting to permanent privation of the sight of one eye — a classic instance of grievous hurt.

A woman in Hyderabad is pushed down a staircase during a domestic dispute, dislocating her shoulder joint and causing injuries that endanger her life — qualifying as grievous hurt on two separate counts.
what_it_covers: Permanent loss of vision in one or both eyes caused by deliberate assault or acid attack.
Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth resulting from a physical attack.
Amputation or permanent destruction of a limb, finger, or joint.
Permanent disfiguration of the head or face, including severe acid burn scarring.
Any injury that endangers the life of the victim, such as a deep stab wound to the abdomen.
Any hurt that keeps the victim in severe bodily pain or unable to perform ordinary activities for 20 or more days.
Permanent impairment of the hearing of either ear due to deliberate physical assault.
what_it_excludes: Minor cuts, bruises, or abrasions that heal within a short period without endangering life.
Temporary pain or discomfort lasting fewer than 20 days that does not result in severe bodily pain or incapacitation.
Emotional or psychological harm not accompanied by qualifying physical injury.
Injuries caused purely by accident without any criminal intent or knowledge, where no grievous hurt was intended or known to be likely.
Superficial injuries such as a black eye or minor sprain that do not permanently impair any organ, member, or joint.
Hurt voluntarily consented to by a person over eighteen years of age in a non-grievous context, such as consented medical procedures without grievous risk.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an injury qualifies as 'grievous hurt' determines the severity of the offence charged and the corresponding punishment — voluntarily causing grievous hurt attracts significantly higher penalties under Sections 117–120 compared to ordinary hurt under Sections 115–116, and the distinction also governs the scope of exceptions such as private defence, consent, and good faith under Sections 25, 27, 30, and 37, where the right to cause or risk causing grievous hurt is specifically restricted.

definitions.definition: A 'group' means one or more persons acting together in furtherance of a common intention, including in the context of gang rape (Section 70) where persons constituting such a group are each deemed to have committed the offence, and in the context of organised crime (Section 111) where a group of two or more persons acting singly or jointly as a syndicate or gang indulge in any continuing unlawful activity. In the context of murder under Section 103, a group specifically refers to five or more persons acting in concert.
definitions.plain_english: A 'group' refers to two or more people who come together and act with a shared purpose or plan to commit an unlawful act. When people act as a group, each member is legally responsible for the crime committed by the group, even if not every person directly performed every act. The law treats the collective action as making each participant equally guilty.
real_world_examples: Five men in a village in Uttar Pradesh together assault and rape a woman — each of the five is treated as having committed rape individually under Section 70, and each faces a minimum of 20 years rigorous imprisonment.

A gang of extortionists in Mumbai, with three members collecting money and two providing armed backup, collectively constitute a 'group' for the purpose of organised crime under Section 111, making all five equally liable.

A group of six upper-caste men in Rajasthan acting in concert kill a Dalit man on grounds of caste — all six fall under Section 103's special provision for group murder and may be sentenced to death or life imprisonment.

Four members of a trafficking syndicate in Kolkata who jointly manage the movement and exploitation of trafficked persons form a 'group' under Section 111, each liable for organised crime penalties regardless of their specific individual role.

Three men who gang-rape a 16-year-old girl in Delhi, acting with a common intention, constitute a group under Section 70(2) and each faces imprisonment for life or death, along with a fine payable to the victim.
what_it_covers: Two or more persons who jointly commit rape on a woman, acting in furtherance of a common intention, making each liable as if they individually committed the offence under Section 70.
Five or more persons who act in concert to commit murder on discriminatory grounds such as caste, race, sex, or religion, triggering enhanced punishment under Section 103.
Two or more persons forming an organised crime syndicate who act singly or jointly in continuing unlawful activities such as extortion, kidnapping, trafficking, or cyber-crime under Section 111.
Members of a group where only some physically perpetrate the offence but all share a common intention, resulting in equal criminal liability for each member of the group.
what_it_excludes: A lone individual acting entirely alone without any co-conspirators or shared intention, who cannot constitute a 'group' by definition.
Persons who are merely present at the scene of a crime but have no common intention or concerted action with the perpetrators — mere presence does not make one a member of the group.

A group of fewer than five persons in the context of Section 103's aggravated group murder provision, which explicitly requires five or more persons acting in concert for that enhanced punishment to apply.
Persons who independently commit similar offences at different times and places without any coordination, shared plan, or common intention linking their actions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an accused person is found to be part of a 'group' determines whether each member is individually deemed guilty of the entire offence regardless of their specific act — triggering mandatory minimum sentences of 20 years to life for gang rape under Section 70, death or life imprisonment for group murder under Section 103, and severe organised crime penalties under Section 111. Establishing group membership can thus be the decisive factor between a lesser individual charge and an aggravated, non-compoundable offence carrying the harshest punishments under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

definitions.definition: A group of five or more persons acting in concert means five or more individuals who collectively and jointly participate in committing murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each sharing common purpose and coordinated action in the commission of such offence.
definitions.plain_english: A 'group acting in concert' refers to five or more people who together, with a shared purpose and coordinated effort, commit murder targeting someone because of their caste, religion, gender, birthplace, language, or personal beliefs. Each member of such a group is equally responsible under the law, regardless of their individual role. This is commonly associated with mob lynching or hate-crime killings carried out collectively.
real_world_examples: A mob of seven persons from a dominant caste community in Rajasthan collectively attacks and kills a Dalit man for marrying outside his caste, with each member participating in the assault — all seven are liable under Section 103 as a group acting in concert.

Eight members of a religious vigilante group in Uttar Pradesh intercept and lynch a Muslim man transporting cattle, believing him to be involved in cow slaughter — the entire group is treated as acting in concert and each faces punishment of death or imprisonment for life.

A gang of six persons in Manipur attack and kill a person from a rival tribal community in retaliation for a boundary dispute, motivated by ethnic identity — all six are prosecuted as a group acting in concert under Section 103.

Five individuals in Tamil Nadu collectively kill a man belonging to a different linguistic community during communal tensions, motivated by his place of birth and language — each member faces the same punishment as the principal offender under the group acting in concert provision.

A group of six persons in Haryana kills a young couple from different castes who eloped, in a so-called 'honour killing' — all members who participated in planning and execution are treated as a group acting in concert and face capital punishment or life imprisonment.
what_it_covers: Five or more persons who jointly plan and execute the killing of a person targeted on grounds of caste, religion, sex, language, place of birth, or personal belief.

Members of a mob who are physically present and actively participating in a hate-motivated lynching, including those who assist, restrain the victim, or act as lookouts as part of the coordinated action.

Any individual who is part of a group of five or more that commits murder on discriminatory grounds, regardless of whether they personally delivered the fatal blow, as long as they acted in concert with the others.

what_it_excludes: A group of fewer than five persons committing murder, even if motivated by caste or communal grounds — such cases would be governed by the general murder provision under Section 103 without the enhanced group liability clause.

definitions.definition: A 'guardian' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to any person who has lawful charge of another person — particularly a child under twelve years of age or a person of unsound mind — and who is legally empowered to give consent on that person's behalf for acts done in good faith for their benefit. The term encompasses both formally appointed guardians and any other person standing in a position of lawful custodial responsibility over such a person.
definitions.plain_english: A guardian is a person who is legally responsible for taking care of someone who cannot take care of themselves — such as a young child or someone with a mental illness. This person has the authority to make decisions on behalf of the person in their care, including giving permission for medical or other procedures done for that person's benefit. The term is broad and includes not just court-appointed guardians but also anyone who lawfully has charge of such a vulnerable person.
real_world_examples: A father in Mumbai consents to his 8-year-old child undergoing a complex cardiac surgery knowing there is some risk of death, but acting in good faith for the child's benefit — the father is acting as the child's guardian under Section 27 and no offence is committed by the surgeon.

A mother in Delhi, as the natural guardian of her 10-year-old daughter, gives consent to a doctor to administer a painful but necessary treatment for a grievous bone disease — her consent as guardian shields the doctor from criminal liability.

A court-appointed guardian of a person of unsound mind in Chennai consents to psychiatric treatment involving sedation for the ward's benefit — this guardian's consent is legally valid under Section 27 to protect the treating doctor.

A warden of a government-run children's home in Kolkata who has lawful charge of orphaned children gives consent for a necessary surgical procedure on a child under twelve in their care — the warden functions as the 'other person having lawful charge' and acts as a guardian for the purposes of this section.

In a case of miscarriage under Section 29, the consent of the woman's guardian does not justify the act of causing miscarriage unless done in good faith to save the woman's life, illustrating the limits of guardian consent.

Any other person having lawful charge of a child or person of unsound mind, such as a warden of a government-run children's institution or a hospital superintendent caring for an incapacitated patient.
Persons who give either express or implied consent on behalf of a vulnerable person for acts done in good faith for that person's benefit.
A teacher or institutional authority who has been entrusted with lawful custodial responsibility over a minor in the absence of the natural guardian.
what_it_excludes: A person who assumes informal or unauthorized charge of a child or person of unsound mind without any legal basis or lawful authority.
A guardian whose consent is sought to justify an act that is an offence independently of harm caused, such as causing miscarriage (as explicitly stated in Section 29).
Any person who acts in bad faith or for purposes other than the genuine benefit of the person under their charge — mere pecuniary benefit does not qualify as 'benefit' under this framework.
A stranger or bystander who has no established lawful relationship of charge or custody over the vulnerable person, even if acting with good intentions.

A guardian who consents to the intentional causing of death, voluntary causing of grievous hurt without therapeutic justification, or the abetment of an offence — such consent is expressly excluded from protection under the provisos to Section 27.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'guardian' directly determines whether their consent can legally shield another person — such as a doctor or caregiver — from criminal liability for acts that might otherwise constitute offences under the BNS, 2023. If no guardian exists or no consent can be obtained in time, Section 30 may independently protect a person acting in good faith for the benefit of an incapacitated individual.

definitions.definition: Harassment, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, means the harassment of a woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security, or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand (Section 86). In the context of Section 80, it refers to the subjection of a woman to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry.
definitions.plain_english: Harassment in this law refers to tormenting, pressuring, or mistreating a woman to force her or her family to fulfill an unlawful demand — most commonly a demand for dowry or property. It also covers persistent ill-treatment connected to such demands even after the woman fails to meet them. This is distinct from general harassment and is specifically tied to unlawful coercion or dowry-related pressure in the context of marriage.
real_world_examples: A husband and his parents repeatedly threaten and emotionally torment their daughter-in-law after her family fails to bring the demanded amount of gold jewellery as dowry during the wedding.
A woman's in-laws lock her in a room, deny her food, and verbally abuse her daily to pressure her father into giving them a car that was promised as part of the marriage settlement.

A husband constantly berates, demeans, and physically pushes his wife every time she calls her parents, demanding they hand over the title of agricultural land as a condition for continued marital peace.

Relatives of the husband make threatening phone calls and visit the woman's parental home repeatedly, warning of consequences unless a substantial cash amount is paid, resulting in the woman living in fear.
A woman is subjected to continuous verbal abuse and social isolation by her in-laws because her family could not afford to meet a demand for household appliances placed after the marriage.
The husband withholds money for essential medical care and threatens to send the wife back to her parents unless her family pays an additional sum demanded three years into the marriage.
what_it_covers: Persistent mental or physical torment inflicted on a woman by her husband or his relatives to compel her or her family to meet a demand for property or valuable security.
Continued ill-treatment of a woman on account of her or her family's failure or inability to satisfy an unlawful demand, even after the demand has been refused.
Any course of conduct—including threats, abuse, confinement, or intimidation—directed at a woman in connection with dowry demands that creates coercive pressure on her or persons related to her.
Harassment occurring within seven years of marriage that, if resulting in death under abnormal circumstances, constitutes the basis for a dowry death charge under Section 80.
what_it_excludes: General workplace harassment or sexual harassment unrelated to marital demands, which is separately governed under Section 75 of the BNS.

Wilful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave danger to life, limb, or health that is not connected to any property or unlawful demand — this falls under the first limb of cruelty under Section 86(a), not harassment.
Harassment by persons who are not the husband or relatives of the husband, as Sections 80 and 86 specifically address conduct within the marital relationship context.
Lawful demands made between spouses or family members in the ordinary course, even if they cause distress, as the term requires the demand to be 'unlawful' in nature.
Stalking or sexual harassment by strangers or acquaintances outside the matrimonial context, which are addressed under separate provisions of the BNS.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'harassment' under Section 86 directly determines if it constitutes 'cruelty' for the purposes of Section 85, which carries imprisonment up to three years. Additionally, proof of pre-death harassment in connection with a dowry demand is an essential ingredient for convicting an accused of 'dowry death' under Section 80, which mandates a minimum sentence of seven years and can extend to life imprisonment.

definitions.definition: 'harbour' includes supplying a person with shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition or means of conveyance, or the assisting a person by any means, whether of the same kind as those enumerated in this clause or not, to evade apprehension.
definitions.plain_english: Harbouring means helping someone who has committed an offence to escape from being caught by the police or other authorities. This help can take many forms — giving them a place to stay, food, money, clothing, weapons, a vehicle, or any other kind of assistance. The definition is broad and is not limited only to the specific forms of help listed.
real_world_examples: A person wanted by police for dacoity hides at a relative's house in Uttar Pradesh; the relative provides him food and lets him sleep there for several days to help him avoid arrest — this constitutes harbouring.

A terrorist who has carried out an attack in Mumbai is given a change of clothes, cash, and a motorcycle by an associate so he can flee to another state before police can apprehend him — the associate has harboured him.

A proclaimed offender wanted for murder in Rajasthan is assisted by a shopkeeper who gives him provisions and directs him to a safe route to cross the border — this act of assistance amounts to harbouring.

An individual convicted of a heinous offence who escapes from judicial custody in Delhi is sheltered by a friend in a rented apartment in Noida, who also funds his transport to Nepal — the friend has harboured the escaped convict.

A gangster evading arrest in Punjab is given a new SIM card and a fake identity document by an acquaintance specifically to help him avoid detection by law enforcement — this qualifies as harbouring through means of conveyance and assistance.
what_it_covers: Providing physical shelter (a house, room, or hiding place) to a person wanted by the police or fleeing lawful apprehension.
Supplying food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition, or means of conveyance to enable a fugitive to evade arrest.

Any other form of assistance — including non-material help such as giving directions, providing communication devices, or creating diversions — that facilitates evasion of apprehension, even if not specifically listed in the clause.
Helping a proclaimed offender, escaped prisoner, or person wanted under a warrant to avoid being caught by any law enforcement authority.
Arranging transport (e.g., a car, boat, or bus ticket) for a person to flee from the jurisdiction where they are being sought.
what_it_excludes: Assistance provided without knowledge that the person being helped is wanted for an offence or is attempting to evade apprehension — absence of knowledge negates the act of harbouring.
Providing shelter, food, or other necessities to a person in good faith (e.g., humanitarian relief) where there is no intent or knowledge related to helping them evade lawful apprehension.
Legal and legitimate professional assistance such as a lawyer advising an accused on their rights, which does not amount to actively helping them evade arrest.
Actions taken under duress or coercion, where the person providing assistance had no voluntary choice in the matter.
Ordinary commercial transactions (e.g., a hotel booking) where the service provider has no knowledge of the person's fugitive status.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'harbouring' under Section 2 directly determines criminal liability under Section 253 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which punishes harbouring an offender; establishing harbouring triggers criminal prosecution and punishment, while its absence negates the offence entirely. The broad definition ensures that any form of assistance — material or otherwise — intended to help a person evade lawful apprehension is criminalised.

definitions.definition: A person 'harbours' another when they intentionally shelter, conceal, or provide assistance to a person who has committed an offence, thereby enabling that person to evade detection, arrest, or legal consequences. As used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, harbouring encompasses any act of knowingly giving refuge or concealment to an offender, including those who have committed organised crime or terrorist acts.
definitions.plain_english: To 'harbour' someone means to deliberately hide, shelter, or protect a person who has committed a crime so that they can avoid being caught by the police or brought to justice. It is essentially helping a criminal stay hidden or safe. Even if you do not commit the crime yourself, knowingly providing a safe place or assistance to a criminal makes you legally liable.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai landlord knowingly allows a member of an organised crime syndicate to stay in a rented flat under a false name, providing food and shelter while the syndicate member evades arrest for extortion offences.

In Delhi, a shop owner lets a person suspected of a terrorist attack hide in a storeroom at the back of the shop for several days, providing them with food and clothing to help them escape the police.
A farmer in Punjab allows a gangster involved in vehicle theft and drug trafficking to hide in an outhouse on his agricultural land, fully knowing the person is wanted by the police.

In Chennai, a distant relative provides a safe house to a person who has been part of a human trafficking racket, helping them evade law enforcement by giving them money and arranging transport out of the city.

A hotel manager in Hyderabad checks in a wanted organised crime syndicate member under a fictitious identity, deliberately concealing the person's whereabouts from the police despite being aware of the ongoing investigation.
what_it_covers: Providing physical shelter, such as a house or room, to a person who has committed organised crime or a terrorist act, knowing they are wanted by law enforcement.
Concealing the whereabouts or identity of a criminal offender from police or investigative authorities to help them avoid arrest or prosecution.
Supplying food, money, transport, or other material assistance to an offender to enable them to remain hidden or flee from justice.
Allowing an offender to use one's property, vehicle, or resources as a refuge, even temporarily, with knowledge of the person's criminal status.
Actively misleading law enforcement authorities about the presence or location of an offender in order to protect that person from detection.
what_it_excludes: Harbouring by the spouse of the offender, which is expressly exempted under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 by way of a statutory proviso.
Unknowingly or innocently providing shelter or assistance to a person without knowledge of that person's offence or wanted status, as criminal intent or knowledge is a prerequisite.
Persons who provide purely incidental or casual contact with an offender without any intention to conceal or protect them from legal consequences.
Legitimate legal professionals such as advocates who provide legal representation to an accused person in their professional capacity, as this does not constitute harbouring.
Family members or individuals coerced or threatened into providing shelter against their will, where voluntary intent to harbour is absent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'harbouring' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 determines criminal liability under Sections 111 and 113 — a person found guilty of harbouring an organised crime offender faces rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years extending to life imprisonment and a fine of not less than five lakh rupees, making the distinction between innocent assistance and deliberate concealment critical to prosecution and sentencing.

definitions.definition: The term 'harm' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in its ordinary legal sense to denote any adverse effect, hurt, or detriment caused to a person's body, mind, reputation, or property. It is distinct from 'injury', which is defined as any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property, indicating that 'harm' is the broader underlying concept of which legally actionable 'injury' is a specific subset.
definitions.plain_english: Harm refers to any negative effect or damage suffered by a person — whether physical, mental, to their reputation, or to their belongings. Unlike 'injury' under this law, harm does not require that it be caused illegally; it simply means the adverse result itself. In other words, harm is the bad outcome, and when that bad outcome is caused illegally, it becomes an 'injury' in legal terms.
real_world_examples: A factory in Pune releases toxic fumes that cause respiratory illness to nearby residents — the physical suffering of those residents constitutes harm to their bodies, and if caused through an illegal act or omission, it becomes a legally actionable injury.

A doctor in Delhi negligently administers the wrong medication to a patient, causing permanent damage to the patient's kidneys — the damage to the patient's health is harm, which when proven to be caused illegally, qualifies as injury under Section 2.

An employer in Mumbai spreads false rumours about a former employee to prevent them from getting new employment — the damage to the person's professional reputation and mental distress constitutes harm, and if done illegally, it amounts to injury in reputation.

A landlord in Chennai illegally demolishes a tenant's belongings stored on the premises — the destruction of the tenant's property is harm to property, forming the basis of an injury as defined under the Act.

A person in Kolkata is threatened online repeatedly, causing severe anxiety and psychological distress to the victim — the mental suffering constitutes harm to the mind, and if caused through an illegal act such as criminal intimidation, it amounts to injury.

A municipal contractor in Hyderabad deliberately cuts off water supply to a residential area as an act of spite, causing inconvenience and health issues to residents — the adverse effects suffered by residents constitute harm, triggering potential legal liability.
what_it_covers: Physical damage to a person's body such as wounds, fractures, or illness caused by another's act or omission.
Psychological or mental suffering, including anxiety, trauma, or distress inflicted upon a person.
Damage to a person's reputation, such as spreading false information that lowers their standing in society.
Loss or destruction of a person's property, whether movable or otherwise.
Any detriment suffered by a person as a result of another's conduct, regardless of whether that conduct is illegal.
what_it_excludes: Harm that is lawfully caused in the exercise of a legal right, such as harm resulting from a court-ordered penalty or punishment — such harm is legally justified and does not give rise to injury.
Trivial or negligible effects that do not constitute any real or cognisable detriment to body, mind, reputation, or property.
Harm caused with the free and informed consent of the affected person, where such consent negates unlawfulness, such as harm in the course of a consented medical procedure.
Self-inflicted harm, i.e., harm a person causes to themselves voluntarily, as the Act's use of 'harm' in Sections 25 and 33 concerns harm caused to others.
Abstract or speculative harm that has not actually materialised into any tangible adverse effect on the person.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether harm is established is critical because it is the underlying factual foundation for the defined concept of 'injury' under Section 2, which in turn is a required element for several offences under the BNS including those involving hurt, grievous hurt, and criminal acts causing damage; without proof of harm, the prosecution of many offences under Sections 25 and 33 — and related penal provisions — would fail to meet the essential ingredient of resulting detriment to the victim.

definitions.definition: "Hospital" means the precincts of the hospital and includes the precincts of any institution for the reception and treatment of persons during convalescence or of persons requiring medical attention or rehabilitation. This definition applies uniformly across Sections 64, 68, and 200 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, as expressly cross-referenced in Section 68.
definitions.plain_english: A 'hospital' under this law means not just the main building of a hospital, but the entire campus or premises where patients are treated, including places where people recover after illness or receive rehabilitation care. This broad definition covers any institution that receives and treats sick, recovering, or disabled persons, regardless of what the institution is formally called. The term is used to identify a protected environment where exploitation of vulnerable patients is treated as a more serious offence.
real_world_examples: A government-run AIIMS campus in New Delhi, including its wards, ICU, corridors, and outdoor recovery areas — all fall within 'hospital precincts,' so any staff member committing rape there faces enhanced punishment under Section 64(2).

A private physiotherapy and rehabilitation centre in Mumbai where stroke patients undergo motor recovery therapy qualifies as a 'hospital' because it receives and treats persons requiring medical attention or rehabilitation, triggering Section 68 liability for its management or staff.

A convalescent home in Chennai where post-surgery patients are kept for recovery before being discharged to their families is covered under this definition, meaning any sexual exploitation by staff on those premises constitutes an aggravated offence.

A district government hospital in Patna that fails to provide emergency medical treatment to a rape survivor in violation of Section 397 of the BNSS — the person in charge of that hospital can be prosecuted under Section 200 BNS, which expressly applies to hospitals public or private.

A privately run nursing home in Hyderabad providing post-operative care and wound management is included within 'hospital' under this definition, making its staff liable for aggravated sexual offence charges if they abuse their position over admitted patients.
what_it_covers: The entire physical campus and precincts of a government or private hospital, including wards, corridors, outbuildings, and outdoor grounds forming part of the hospital premises.

Convalescent homes or recovery institutions where patients are housed after medical procedures and before full discharge — these are expressly included as places of reception and treatment during convalescence.
Rehabilitation centres that receive and treat persons requiring physical, occupational, or mental health rehabilitation, even if not formally named a 'hospital.'
Institutions providing ongoing medical attention to chronically ill or disabled persons, such as long-term care facilities associated with medical oversight.
Both publicly funded hospitals run by Central or State Governments and privately owned hospitals or nursing homes, as confirmed by Section 200's explicit reference to both categories.
what_it_excludes: A doctor's standalone private clinic or outpatient consultation room that does not receive or admit patients for treatment, convalescence, or rehabilitation — such premises do not constitute 'hospital precincts' under this definition.
A pharmacy or medical shop, even one attached to a hospital building, when operated as a separate commercial establishment outside the defined precincts of the hospital.
A yoga centre or wellness spa that offers general health or fitness services but does not receive or treat persons requiring medical attention or rehabilitation in a clinical sense.
A first-aid post or temporary medical camp set up at a public event or construction site that is not an institution established for reception and treatment of patients on an ongoing basis.

Residential quarters or staff housing located outside the defined precincts of a hospital, even if exclusively used by hospital employees, as these fall outside the campus/precincts included in the definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a location qualifies as a 'hospital' directly determines whether an accused person faces the aggravated minimum sentence of ten years to life imprisonment under Section 64(2)(vi) instead of the standard ten-year minimum, and whether Section 68 applies to sexual intercourse falling short of rape by hospital management or staff. Additionally, the definition triggers the criminal obligation under Section 200 for persons in charge of a hospital to provide treatment to victims, with imprisonment of up to one year for non-compliance.
