definitions.definition: A person is said to commit house-breaking who commits house-trespass if he effects his entrance into the house or any part of it, or quits the house or any part of it, in any of six specified ways: through a passage made by himself or an abettor; through a passage not intended for human entrance or accessed by scaling or climbing; through a passage opened by himself or an abettor by means not intended by the occupier; by opening any lock; by using criminal force, committing an assault, or threatening assault; or through a passage he knows was fastened against such entrance or departure and was unfastened by himself or an abettor.
definitions.plain_english: House-breaking means illegally entering or exiting someone's house or building in a forceful, sneaky, or unauthorized way — for example, by breaking a lock, climbing over a wall, forcing open a door, or using violence or threats to get in or out. It is a more serious form of house-trespass because of the method used to enter or exit. Even if someone entered lawfully but then used one of these methods to leave after committing a crime inside, it still counts as house-breaking.
real_world_examples: A thief in Mumbai breaks the padlock of a ground-floor flat, enters the home, and steals jewellery — this constitutes house-breaking because he opened a lock to commit house-trespass.

A burglar in Delhi scales the boundary wall of a residential bungalow and enters through a window not meant for human entry to commit robbery — this is house-breaking by climbing over a wall to access a non-human passage.
An accused in Chennai, having entered a shop to commit theft, threatens the watchman with assault to force his way out after the act — this is house-breaking on exit by threatening assault.
A person in Kolkata cuts through a wooden plank in the rear of a house, creating a new passage to enter and steal valuables — this is house-breaking by entering through a passage made by himself.

An offender in Hyderabad unfastens a door he had previously bolted from inside while hiding in the house, and exits through it after committing theft — this is house-breaking by quitting through a passage he knows was fastened and which he himself unfastened.

A group of criminals in Bengaluru force open the sliding gate of a warehouse using a crowbar in a manner the occupier never intended, and enter to steal goods — this is house-breaking through a passage opened by means not intended by the occupier.
what_it_covers: Entering a house by breaking or opening a lock not intended to be opened by the trespasser.
Gaining entry by scaling or climbing over a wall or building to access a passage not meant for human entrance.
Quitting a house after committing an offence by using criminal force, assault, or threats of assault against any person.
Creating a new passage through a wall, floor, or roof of a building in order to enter and commit house-trespass.
Entering or exiting through a door or window that was fastened and was unfastened by the offender or an abettor.
House-breaking committed after sunset and before sunrise, which attracts enhanced punishment under Section 330.
what_it_excludes: Simple house-trespass where entry is made through an open, unlocked, and accessible passage without any of the six specified methods — that remains mere house-trespass, not house-breaking.
Lurking house-trespass, which involves concealment of the trespass from a person with the right to eject the trespasser, but does not require entry or exit by any of the six specified methods.
Entry into a building by the owner, lawful occupier, or a person with express or implied permission of the occupier, even if a lock is opened, as lawful authority negates trespass entirely.
Trespass on open land or an unfenced area not constituting a 'house' or enclosed building, tent, or vessel as contemplated under house-trespass provisions.
Criminal force or assault committed independently of entry into or exit from a house, which would be prosecuted separately and not as house-breaking.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as house-breaking determines the severity of punishment under Section 330 — attracting imprisonment up to three years for basic house-breaking, up to ten or fourteen years if committed with intent to steal or after sunset, and up to life imprisonment if grievous hurt is caused during the act. It also activates the extended right of private defence under Sections 41 and 43, including the right to cause death in defence of property when house-breaking occurs after sunset and before sunrise.

definitions.definition: Whoever commits criminal trespass by entering into or remaining in any building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling or any building used as a place for worship, or as a place for the custody of property, is said to commit house-trespass. The introduction of any part of the criminal trespasser's body is entering sufficient to constitute house-trespass.
definitions.plain_english: House-trespass is when someone illegally enters or stays inside a building where people live, a place of worship, or a building used to store property, with the intention to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person who has the right to be there. Even inserting just a hand or foot into such a building with that intent counts as house-trespass. It is a more serious form of criminal trespass because it involves protected spaces like homes and temples.
real_world_examples: A person breaks open the latch of a neighbour's flat in Mumbai and steps inside with the intent to steal jewellery kept there — this is house-trespass as the flat is used as a human dwelling.

An individual enters a temple in Varanasi without permission late at night intending to steal the donation box — since the temple is a place of worship, unlawful entry with that intent constitutes house-trespass.

A debt collector in Delhi forcibly pushes open the door of a household and enters the premises to intimidate the occupant into repaying a loan — entering a dwelling to intimidate the person inside amounts to house-trespass.

A person in Chennai inserts their arm through a window grille of a locked warehouse (used for custody of property) intending to take goods stored inside — even this partial entry satisfies the definition of house-trespass.

A man in Kolkata who was lawfully invited as a guest refuses to leave a residential house after being asked to go, remaining there with the intent to annoy the owner — unlawfully remaining in a dwelling with such intent is house-trespass.

A group enters a dharamshala in Amritsar, which functions as a residential shelter, against the will of the caretaker with the intent to commit mischief — entry into a building used as a human dwelling with criminal intent constitutes house-trespass.
what_it_covers: Entering a residential house, flat, or hut used as a human dwelling with intent to commit an offence or intimidate/insult the occupant.
Unlawfully remaining inside a temple, mosque, church, gurudwara, or any place of worship after having entered, with criminal intent.
Entry into a warehouse, locker room, or godown used solely for the custody of property, with intent to commit theft or mischief.
Inserting any part of the body — such as an arm, leg, or hand — through a window or door of such a building, which alone is sufficient to constitute house-trespass.
Remaining in a tent or vessel used as a human dwelling after lawful entry but with subsequent unlawful intent to intimidate, insult, or commit an offence.
what_it_excludes: Entry into open land, fields, or agricultural property not used as a dwelling or for custody of property — such conduct may amount to criminal trespass but not house-trespass.
Entering a commercial office building, shop, or factory that is neither used as a human dwelling, place of worship, nor for custody of property in the relevant sense.
Trespass without any accompanying criminal intent, intent to intimidate, or intent to insult — mere accidental or innocent entry into a building does not satisfy the definition.
Entry by a person who has a lawful right or authority to enter the premises, such as a landlord exercising a legal right or a police officer acting under a valid warrant.
Acts that constitute only lurking house-trespass or house-breaking, which are distinct and aggravated forms defined separately under Section 330 of the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Establishing house-trespass triggers imprisonment up to one year and fine under Section 329, and escalates punishment significantly when combined with concealment (lurking house-trespass) or forcible entry (house-breaking) under Section 330. It also determines the scope of the right of private defence under Section 41, potentially extending that right to causing death if the house-trespass occurs under circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

Why it matters: Establishing house-trespass triggers imprisonment up to one year and fine under Section 329, and escalates punishment significantly when combined with concealment (lurking house-trespass) or forcible entry (house-breaking) under Section 330. It also determines the scope of the right of private defence under Section 41, potentially extending that right to causing death if the house-trespass occurs under circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

definitions.definition: 'Hurt' means the causing of bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person. It is distinct from 'grievous hurt', which involves more severe forms of bodily injury as enumerated separately under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Hurt means causing physical pain, illness, or weakness to another person's body. It covers any act that results in bodily discomfort or injury, no matter how minor, as long as it is caused by one person to another. It does not include more serious injuries like broken bones or permanent disfigurement, which fall under the separate and graver category of 'grievous hurt'.
real_world_examples: A person slaps another individual during a street argument in Delhi, causing pain and a reddened cheek — this constitutes hurt.
During a brawl at a local market in Mumbai, one trader pushes another causing bruising on the arm — the bruise and pain amount to hurt.
A man deliberately splashes scalding tea on his colleague's hand during an office dispute in Bengaluru, causing a mild burn and temporary pain — this is hurt.
A neighbour in Chennai throws a small stone at another person, hitting them on the leg and causing pain without breaking any bone — this constitutes hurt.
A school teacher in Kolkata strikes a student with a ruler causing brief bodily pain — this act, if intentional and unjustified, amounts to voluntarily causing hurt.
A person deliberately infects another with a minor communicable disease during close contact in a village in Uttar Pradesh — the resulting disease suffered by the victim constitutes hurt.
what_it_covers: Any act that causes bodily pain to another person, such as a slap, punch, or kick that results in physical discomfort.
Deliberately causing disease to another person, such as intentionally infecting someone with an illness.
Causing infirmity — temporary physical weakness or incapacity — in another person through any act.
Minor burns, bruises, cuts, or physical injuries that cause pain but do not rise to the level of grievous hurt.
Situations where a person uses criminal force that results in bodily pain even if the injury is not visible or lasting.
what_it_excludes: Grievous hurt, which involves more serious injuries such as emasculation, permanent loss of sight or hearing, fractures, or disfigurement — governed separately under the Act.
Psychological or emotional harm that does not manifest as bodily pain, disease, or infirmity.
Harm caused to a person above eighteen years of age who has given free and informed consent, where the act was not intended to cause death or grievous hurt (covered under Section 25 exceptions).
Harm caused in good faith for the benefit of a child or person of unsound mind by a lawful guardian, within the limits prescribed by Section 27.
Death caused to another person, which constitutes a separate and graver category of offence under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'hurt' determines the applicable charge and corresponding punishment — offences like voluntarily causing hurt (Section 115), causing hurt by dangerous weapons (Section 118), and causing hurt to extort property (Section 331) all depend on this definition being satisfied. If the injury crosses into 'grievous hurt', significantly higher punishments apply, making the precise classification of injury critical to the outcome of criminal proceedings.

definitions.definition: A 'husband' means a man who is lawfully married to a woman, and includes a man whose marriage to a woman is subsisting at the relevant time, as used in the context of Section 85 which penalises a husband or relative of a husband who subjects a woman to cruelty.
definitions.plain_english: A husband is a man who is legally married to a woman under any personal law or statute applicable in India. In the context of this law, the word 'husband' identifies the married male spouse as a specific person who can be held criminally responsible for subjecting his wife to cruelty. The term is used to establish a marital relationship that triggers particular criminal liability.
real_world_examples: A man married under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, repeatedly beats his wife and demands she bring more dowry from her parents — he is liable as a 'husband' under Section 85 of the BNS, 2023.

A Muslim man, married through a valid nikah ceremony, mentally torments his wife by threatening to divorce her unless she hands over her gold jewellery — he can be prosecuted as a 'husband' under Section 85.

A Christian man married under the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, persistently humiliates his wife in front of family members and withholds money for basic necessities — he falls within the definition of 'husband' attracting cruelty charges.

A man who married his wife through a court marriage under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, forces her to perform domestic labour under threats of violence — he qualifies as a 'husband' and can be prosecuted for cruelty under Section 85.

A husband in a registered marriage who conspires with his mother and brothers to harass his wife for additional dowry — all are liable, with him specifically identified as the 'husband' and the others as 'relatives of the husband' under Section 85.
what_it_covers: A man married under Hindu personal law (Hindu Marriage Act, 1955) whose marriage is legally subsisting at the time of the alleged cruelty.
A man married under Muslim personal law through a valid nikah whose wife is alive and the marriage has not been validly dissolved.
A man married under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, or the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, who subjects his wife to cruelty or harassment.
A man in a customary marriage recognised under the applicable personal law, where the marriage is acknowledged as valid and subsisting.
what_it_excludes: A former husband whose marriage has been dissolved by a valid decree of divorce — he no longer holds the status of 'husband' for the purposes of Section 85.
A live-in partner or companion who has not contracted a lawful marriage with the woman, regardless of the duration or nature of the relationship.
A man whose marriage is void ab initio (e.g., a bigamous marriage under Section 82 of BNS, 2023) and thus never legally constituted a valid marital relationship.
Relatives of the husband such as brothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, or mothers-in-law — they fall under the separate category of 'relative of the husband' within the same section.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'husband' is decisive in determining criminal liability under Section 85 of the BNS, 2023 — only a man with the legal status of husband (or a relative of such a husband) can be prosecuted for the offence of cruelty to a woman in a marital context, which carries imprisonment up to three years and a fine. Without establishing this marital relationship, the specific offence under Section 85 cannot be made out, though other general offences may still apply.

definitions.definition: An 'identity document' means a document issued by the Government for the purpose of establishing the identity of an individual, and includes a voter identity card or Aadhaar Card, as referenced in Section 337 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: An identity document is any official paper or card that the Government issues to prove who a person is. Examples include your Voter ID card and Aadhaar Card. These documents are considered especially important because forging them is treated as a serious criminal offence.
real_world_examples: A person creates a fake Aadhaar Card with altered biometric details and a different name to open a fraudulent bank account — the forged Aadhaar Card constitutes forgery of an identity document under Section 337.
An individual submits a counterfeit Voter Identity Card (EPIC) to election officials to fraudulently enrol on a voter list in a constituency where they do not reside.
A gang produces duplicate PAN cards issued under the Government of India's income tax system by tampering with an original government-issued document to commit financial fraud.
A person forges a government-issued domicile certificate (which serves as proof of identity and residence) to illegally claim state-specific educational reservation benefits.
A fraudster digitally manipulates the QR code and photograph on an Aadhaar Card and circulates the electronic record to deceive a telecom provider into issuing a SIM card under a false identity.
what_it_covers: Voter Identity Card (EPIC) issued by the Election Commission of India to eligible voters
Aadhaar Card issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) containing biometric and demographic data
Any other document issued by the Government of India or a State Government whose primary purpose is to establish the identity of the holder
Electronic records of identity documents issued by the Government, including digital Aadhaar or e-EPIC in electronic form
what_it_excludes: Private or institutional identity cards such as those issued by universities, private companies, or banks, which are not government-issued
Passports, which though government-issued, are separately governed under the Passports Act, 1967 and are not specifically referenced under this section
Caste certificates, income certificates, or domicile certificates that are government-issued but serve primarily as eligibility or entitlement documents rather than pure identity documents
Court records, public registers of birth or marriage, and certificates made by public servants in official capacity, which are separately enumerated in Section 337 and treated as distinct categories
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a forged document qualifies as an 'identity document' under Section 337 determines whether the offender is liable for the aggravated forgery offence attracting imprisonment of up to seven years plus fine, rather than a lesser forgery offence; it thus directly governs the severity of punishment and the classification of the cognisable offence charged.

definitions.definition: The word 'illegal' is applicable to everything which is an offence or which is prohibited by law, or which furnishes ground for a civil action; and a person is said to be 'legally bound to do' whatever it is illegal in him to omit.
definitions.plain_english: Something is 'illegal' if it is a criminal offence, if a law specifically forbids it, or if doing it (or failing to do it) gives another person the right to sue in a civil court. So the word covers more than just crimes — it also includes things that are civilly wrongful or prohibited by any law. If omitting to do something would be illegal, then a person is legally required to do that thing.
real_world_examples: A factory owner in Maharashtra dumps untreated chemical waste into a river, violating the Environment Protection Act, 1986. The act is 'illegal' because it is prohibited by law and furnishes ground for a civil action by affected parties.

A landlord in Delhi refuses to return a tenant's security deposit without any valid reason, breaching a contractual obligation. The refusal is 'illegal' because it furnishes ground for a civil action for recovery of the deposit.

A police officer in Tamil Nadu detains a person beyond the maximum permissible 24-hour period without producing them before a Magistrate, violating Article 22 of the Constitution and Section 57 of the CrPC/BNSS. The continued detention is 'illegal' as it is prohibited by law.

A public servant in Uttar Pradesh demands a bribe from a contractor, which constitutes an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The demand is 'illegal' because it is an offence punishable by law.
A shopkeeper in Mumbai sells adulterated food items contrary to the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The sale is 'illegal' because it is both a statutory offence and grounds for civil liability.
A driver in Bengaluru drives a vehicle without a valid licence, contravening the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. This is 'illegal' as it is expressly prohibited by law.
what_it_covers: Any act that constitutes an offence punishable under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or any other penal statute, such as theft, assault, or cheating.

Any act or omission expressly prohibited by statute, regulation, or binding legal rule, even if it does not carry criminal punishment — for example, violation of licensing requirements under trade or environmental laws.
Any act or omission that gives rise to a valid civil cause of action, such as breach of contract, tortious harm, or unlawful dispossession of property.
An omission to perform a legal duty — for instance, a public servant's failure to register an FIR as required by law, which is both prohibited and civilly actionable.
Acts prohibited under special or local laws applicable in a specific part of India, such as state-level prohibition laws or local body regulations.
what_it_excludes: Acts that are merely morally or socially disapproved but neither criminalised nor civilly actionable under any law — for example, rudeness or ingratitude between private individuals.
Acts that are contrary to internal organisational rules or private contracts alone, where no statutory prohibition exists and no recognised civil cause of action arises.
Actions that are expressly permitted or justified by law, such as a police officer effecting a lawful arrest under a valid warrant, which cannot be characterised as illegal.
Acts that may have been illegal in the past but have since been decriminalised or legalised, and no residual civil liability survives — they no longer fall within this definition.
Mere procedural irregularities that do not affect substantive rights and do not constitute a statutory offence or found a civil action.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of an act or omission as 'illegal' directly determines criminal liability, civil remedies, and the scope of offences under the BNS — for example, Section 192 BNS uses 'illegal' to define punishable omissions, and terms such as 'injury' (harm illegally caused) and 'wrongful gain/loss' depend on this definition to establish the actus reus of multiple offences. Whether conduct is 'illegal' also determines whether a person is 'legally bound' to act, triggering criminal liability for failure to do so.

definitions.definition: An 'illegal act' means any act which is an offence, or which gives rise to a civil cause of action, or which is prohibited by law. It is the object or means of criminal conspiracy under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and it is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of an agreement or merely incidental to that object.
definitions.plain_english: An illegal act is anything that is either a crime, something that can be sued over in a civil court, or something that is simply forbidden by any law. When two or more people agree to do such an act together, that agreement becomes a criminal conspiracy. It does not matter if the illegal act was the main goal or just a side step in achieving another goal.
real_world_examples: Two business partners in Mumbai agree to bribe a government official to obtain a construction licence — committing an offence under anti-corruption law constitutes an illegal act, making the agreement a criminal conspiracy under Section 61.

A group of individuals in Delhi agree to forge land registry documents to dispossess a farmer of his ancestral land — forgery being an offence under the Sanhita is an illegal act, and their agreement amounts to criminal conspiracy.

A gang in Chennai conspires to kidnap a tech entrepreneur's child and demand ransom — kidnapping being an offence is an illegal act, and the conspiracy itself is punishable even before the act is carried out.

Promoters of a company in Hyderabad secretly agree to create fictitious financial records to defraud investors — fabricating false evidence and cheating investors are illegal acts, and the prior agreement constitutes criminal conspiracy.

A group of smugglers in Gujarat coordinate to import contraband goods in violation of customs law — the prohibited importation is an illegal act, and their coordinated agreement forms a criminal conspiracy punishable under Section 61.
what_it_covers: Any act that constitutes an offence punishable under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or any other penal statute in force in India.
Any act that gives rise to a civil cause of action, such as trespass, fraud, or breach of a statutory duty enforceable by civil suit.
Any act expressly prohibited by a statute or law even if not separately classified as an offence, such as violations of regulatory prohibitions under special acts.
An act that is merely incidental to the ultimate criminal object of a conspiracy, as expressly clarified by Section 61.
Causing hurt or constraining a person to do something illegal, as referenced in Section 119 where compelling someone to commit an illegal act is itself an aggravated offence.
what_it_excludes: An act that is merely immoral or unethical but is not prohibited or penalised by any law, statute, or enforceable regulation.
An act done under a lawful exception or justified by law, such as a public servant acting within the scope of official duty or a person exercising the right of private defence.
A lawful act carried out through legal means, even if its consequences are harmful to another person, as such acts fall entirely outside the definition of 'illegal'.
An agreement to do a lawful act through lawful means, even if the outcome is commercially damaging to a competitor or third party.
Acts that are void under civil law purely due to procedural defects but are not otherwise prohibited or punishable by any substantive law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as an 'illegal act' is the foundational element determining whether an agreement between two or more persons constitutes criminal conspiracy under Section 61 of the BNS, 2023, triggering punishment as severe as that for abetment of the underlying offence including imprisonment for life. It also determines liability under Section 119 where compelling someone to commit an illegal act elevates the offence of voluntarily causing hurt to a more seriously punishable crime.

definitions.definition: An 'illegal omission' is an omission which is an offence by virtue of being illegal under this Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force, where a person is legally bound to act and fails to do so. Words referring to acts done extend also to illegal omissions throughout this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context.
definitions.plain_english: An illegal omission is when someone fails to do something they are legally required to do, and that failure itself is treated as a criminal act. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, simply not doing something — when you had a legal duty to do it — can make you just as guilty as if you had actively done a harmful act. For example, a jailor who deliberately stops feeding a prisoner is committing an illegal omission, not merely being inactive.
real_world_examples: A jailor in a Central Jail in Lucknow, intending to cause a prisoner's death, deliberately stops providing the prisoner with food supplied to him for that purpose; the prisoner dies of starvation. The jailor's failure to supply food is an illegal omission constituting murder.

A government doctor posted at a Primary Health Centre in rural Rajasthan is legally bound to provide emergency medical treatment to a patient brought in with severe injuries; the doctor deliberately refuses to treat the patient, who dies as a result. This deliberate non-treatment constitutes an illegal omission causing death.

A factory supervisor in Pune, legally bound under labour safety laws to report a gas leak immediately, deliberately omits to do so to avoid production downtime; workers are injured as a result. The supervisor's failure to report is an illegal omission.

Two police officers in Mumbai, who have taken a person into lawful custody, conspire to allow the person to escape by deliberately failing to lock the cell — an act each is legally bound to perform. Their deliberate omission constitutes an illegal omission in furtherance of a conspiracy.

A trustee managing a charitable fund in Chennai, who is legally bound to file accounts with the court, deliberately omits to do so to conceal misappropriation of funds, thereby facilitating the commission of criminal breach of trust through an illegal omission.

A person who has agreed to abet a robbery deliberately omits to raise an alarm or inform the police, despite being legally bound and in a position to do so, thereby aiding the commission of the offence through an illegal omission under Section 45.
what_it_covers: A jailor who deliberately fails to provide food to a prisoner in his charge, where he is legally bound to do so, causing the prisoner's death.
A conspirator who, in furtherance of a conspiracy to commit an offence, deliberately refrains from performing a legally required act, thereby enabling the offence to occur.

A person who intentionally aids the commission of an offence by deliberately failing to perform an act he is legally obligated to perform, such as a public officer failing to discharge a duty imposed by law.
A person who partly causes a criminal effect through an illegal omission combined with a positive act, such as causing death partly by withholding food and partly by assault.
Two persons who cooperate in causing a criminal result each through their separate illegal omissions during their respective periods of responsibility.
what_it_excludes: A mere failure to act that is not backed by any legal obligation to act — for example, a bystander who has no legal duty to rescue a drowning person and does not attempt to do so.
An omission arising from incapacity, accident, or genuine ignorance, where there is no criminal knowledge or intention, and no legal duty was imposed on the person to act.
A failure to perform a moral or social duty that is not legally mandated, such as a neighbour failing to help during a domestic dispute when not bound by law to intervene.
Omissions that fall within the General Exceptions of the Sanhita, such as an act or omission done by a child under seven years of age.
Omissions resulting from factors beyond a person's control, where the person was physically or legally incapable of performing the required act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an omission qualifies as an 'illegal omission' determines whether criminal liability — including for offences such as murder, abetment, conspiracy, and culpable homicide — can be fastened on a person for inaction rather than a positive act. It directly triggers or expands liability under Sections 45 and 46 for abetment by omission, and under Section 3 it ensures that all offence definitions in the Sanhita that refer to 'acts' are equally applicable to illegal omissions.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 98, 'illicit intercourse' means sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any union or tie which, though not amounting to a marriage, is recognised by the personal law or custom of the community to which they belong or, where they belong to different communities, of both such communities, as constituting between them a quasi-marital relation. In other sections, the term is used contextually to denote sexual intercourse that is unlawful, unsanctioned, or obtained by force, seduction, or compulsion outside a recognised marital or quasi-marital bond.
definitions.plain_english: Illicit intercourse means sexual relations between two people who are not married to each other and whose relationship is not recognised as marriage-like under their community's personal law or custom. It includes sexual acts obtained by force, seduction, or exploitation where no legitimate union exists. The law uses this term to protect women and children from being lured, trafficked, or coerced into such relationships.
real_world_examples: A man in Mumbai lures a married woman away from her husband under false pretences of employment, intending to engage in sexual relations with her — this falls under illicit intercourse as her marital bond is legally recognised and the intended act is outside it.

A trafficker in Chennai sells a 15-year-old girl to a brothel operator knowing she will be used for sexual purposes with paying clients — this constitutes use for illicit intercourse under Section 98 of the BNS.

A person in Delhi kidnaps a woman and takes her to another state intending to force her into sexual relations with a third party — the intended forced sexual act qualifies as illicit intercourse under Section 87.

A man in Kolkata induces a 16-year-old child with gifts and money to accompany him to a rented flat, knowing the child will likely be seduced into sexual activity by another person present there — this is procuration for illicit intercourse under Section 96.

A live-in couple whose relationship is recognised as a quasi-marital union under their community's custom engages in consensual sexual relations — this would NOT constitute illicit intercourse as their union is community-recognised.

A person in Hyderabad uses criminal intimidation to compel a woman to travel with him to another city, knowing she will be forced into sexual relations with a business associate — this constitutes inducement to illicit intercourse under Section 87.
what_it_covers: Sexual intercourse between two persons who are not married to each other and whose relationship is not recognised as quasi-marital by the personal law or custom of their community.
Sexual acts obtained through force, seduction, kidnapping, or criminal intimidation where the victim has not consented within a lawful union.
Sexual use of a child sold or trafficked to a brothel or any person for purposes outside any recognised marital or quasi-marital relationship.
Sexual intercourse procured through inducement of a child or woman to go from one place to another for the benefit of a third party.
Sexual relations between persons belonging to different communities where neither community's personal law or custom recognises their union as quasi-marital.
what_it_excludes: Sexual intercourse between lawfully married spouses, which is expressly outside the scope of illicit intercourse as defined in the Act.

Sexual relations within a union recognised by the personal law or custom of the community as constituting a quasi-marital relationship, such as certain customary or tribal unions formally acknowledged by community practice.
Consensual live-in relationships that have been recognised as quasi-marital by the applicable personal law or community custom of both parties' communities.
Acts of rape as defined under the BNS, which are separately and specifically penalised and are not merely subsumed under 'illicit intercourse' for offence-triggering purposes.
Sexual intercourse within a void or voidable marriage where both parties genuinely and reasonably believed the marriage to be valid at the time of the act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'illicit intercourse' determines whether offences under Sections 84, 87, 96, 98, and 99 of the BNS are triggered, directly affecting criminal liability for enticing married women, kidnapping, child procuration, and trafficking; if the sexual relationship falls within a recognised marital or quasi-marital union, the essential ingredient of the offence is absent and prosecution under these sections cannot be sustained.

definitions.definition: Imprisonment as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 denotes the deprivation of personal liberty of a convicted person by confinement in a prison or correctional facility, pursuant to a sentence passed by a competent court. It encompasses both 'rigorous imprisonment', which involves hard labour, and 'simple imprisonment', which does not. The term also extends to imprisonment for life as a distinct category of punishment.
definitions.plain_english: Imprisonment means being locked up in a jail or prison as a punishment after being convicted of a crime by a court. There are two kinds: one where the prisoner has to do hard physical work (rigorous), and one where they simply remain confined without forced labour (simple). A court decides which type and for how long, based on the offence committed.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of theft under the BNS is sentenced by a Sessions Court in Mumbai to rigorous imprisonment for three years, meaning they must perform hard labour such as weaving or carpentry inside the prison during their term.

A first-time offender convicted of a minor assault in Delhi is awarded simple imprisonment for six months, where they are confined in Tihar Jail without being compelled to perform any physical labour.
A person convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder by a court in Chennai is sentenced to imprisonment for life, meaning confinement in prison for the remainder of their natural life.

An accused found guilty of cheating under the BNS in Kolkata is sentenced to two years of rigorous imprisonment along with a fine, requiring the individual to carry out prison labour assigned by the jail superintendent.

A government servant convicted of accepting a bribe under relevant provisions is awarded simple imprisonment for one year in Hyderabad, serving the term in a correctional facility without any compulsory work obligation.

A person convicted of house-trespass with intent to commit an offence in Bengaluru is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years, during which they are required to perform physical tasks assigned by prison authorities under the supervision of a superintendent.
what_it_covers: Rigorous imprisonment, where the convicted person is required to perform hard labour inside prison as part of the sentence.
Simple imprisonment, where the convicted person is confined in prison but is not compelled to perform any labour.
Imprisonment for life, which constitutes confinement of the convicted person in prison for the remainder of their natural life.
Short-term imprisonment sentences of days or weeks imposed for minor offences under the Sanhita.
Imprisonment ordered as an alternative to payment of fine when a convicted person defaults on payment.
what_it_excludes: Detention under preventive detention laws (such as the National Security Act) that does not arise from a criminal conviction by a court.
Custody during the pendency of trial (remand or judicial custody), which is not a punishment but a procedural measure.
Community service as an alternative form of punishment, which is a distinct category of punishment under the BNS not involving confinement.
Civil imprisonment ordered in execution of a decree in civil proceedings, which falls outside the criminal punitive framework of the BNS.
House arrest or electronic monitoring orders that restrict liberty without physical confinement in a prison facility.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a sentence constitutes 'imprisonment' and its type — rigorous or simple — directly determines the conditions of a convict's incarceration, their eligibility for remission, and the severity of the punishment imposed by the court. Specific offences under the BNS mandate minimum or maximum terms of imprisonment and prescribe whether it must be rigorous or may be simple, making this distinction critical for both sentencing and appeal outcomes.

definitions.definition: Imprisonment for life is a punishment listed under Section 4 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, whereby an offender is sentenced to confinement in prison for the remainder of their natural life. For the purpose of calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life shall be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years unless otherwise provided.
definitions.plain_english: Imprisonment for life means a person is sent to prison and, in principle, must remain there for the rest of their life. However, when courts or authorities need to calculate partial or fractional terms — for example, for remission or commutation purposes — the law treats this sentence as equal to 20 years. It is one of the most serious punishments available under Indian criminal law, just below the death penalty.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of murder under Section 103 of the BNS, where the court does not impose the death penalty but considers the crime grave enough, may be sentenced to imprisonment for life, meaning they remain in a central prison such as Tihar Jail, Delhi, for the rest of their natural life.

A gang rape convict sentenced to imprisonment for life under Section 70 of the BNS serves the remainder of their life in prison; however, if the State Government considers remission, the 20-year equivalent rule under Section 6 is applied to calculate the remissible portion.

A person convicted of dacoity with murder under Section 310 of the BNS may receive imprisonment for life; prison authorities computing earned remission under prison manuals use the 20-year reckoning provided by Section 6 to determine the maximum remission admissible.

An offender previously convicted of a serious offence under Chapter XVII and again found guilty of a similar offence under Section 13 of the BNS faces imprisonment for life as an enhanced punishment for the subsequent offence.

A terrorist convicted under Section 113 of the BNS for an act causing mass casualties, where the court awards imprisonment for life instead of death, will be held in high-security confinement at a facility like Yerawada Central Prison, Pune, for the remainder of their natural life.
what_it_covers: Confinement of a convicted offender in prison for the entirety of their remaining natural life as imposed by a competent court.
The deemed equivalent of twenty years of imprisonment when calculating fractions of punishment terms for purposes such as remission, commutation, or sentencing arithmetic under Section 6.

Sentences awarded for the most serious offences under the BNS including murder (Section 103), gang rape (Section 70), dacoity (Section 104), kidnapping for ransom (Section 140), and terrorist acts (Section 113).
Enhanced punishment imposed under Section 13 upon repeat offenders previously convicted of specified serious offences under Chapter X or Chapter XVII.
Cases where a court exercises discretion between imposing death and a lesser severe punishment, opting for life imprisonment as the appropriate sentence.
what_it_excludes: Simple imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment for a fixed number of years, which are distinct descriptions of imprisonment under Section 4 and do not constitute imprisonment for life.
The death penalty, which is a separate and superior punishment listed under Section 4 and is not subsumed within or interchangeable with imprisonment for life.
Community service, fine, and forfeiture of property, which are entirely different categories of punishment under Section 4 and have no connection to imprisonment for life.
Imprisonment for a definite term — even if it is the maximum of 10 or 14 years — which remains a fixed-term sentence and is legally distinct from imprisonment for life.
Situations where an offender is acquitted or given a lesser sentence; imprisonment for life only applies upon conviction and judicial imposition of that specific sentence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a sentence constitutes imprisonment for life directly determines the severity of punishment, the applicable provisions for remission and commutation by the appropriate Government, and the arithmetic basis (20 years) used in calculating fractional terms under Section 6. It also activates or defines the punishment threshold for abetment offences under Section 55, enhanced sentencing under Section 13, and numerous grave offences across the BNS where imprisonment for life is the prescribed maximum or mandatory sentence.

definitions.definition: 'Imprisonment of either description' refers to a form of punishment that may be imposed as either rigorous imprisonment (with hard labour) or simple imprisonment (without hard labour), at the discretion of the sentencing court. It encompasses both categories of custodial punishment recognised under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, giving the court flexibility to impose whichever form is appropriate to the gravity of the offence and circumstances of the offender.
definitions.plain_english: When a law says someone can be punished with 'imprisonment of either description', it means the judge can choose between two types of jail sentences: one where the prisoner must do hard labour (rigorous imprisonment), or one where the prisoner simply stays in jail without being required to work (simple imprisonment). The judge decides which type is suitable based on how serious the crime is and the circumstances of the case. Both types still result in the person being locked up in prison.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of abetting a murder that was not ultimately committed (under Section 55 of BNS) may be sentenced to up to seven years of either rigorous imprisonment — requiring daily hard labour such as grinding grain or weaving — or simple imprisonment, where the convict resides in jail without any compulsory work, depending on the judge's assessment of culpability.

Under Section 13 of the BNS, a repeat offender previously convicted of theft (Chapter XVII) who commits another Chapter XVII offence may be sentenced to imprisonment of either description for up to ten years. A Sessions Court in Delhi may impose rigorous imprisonment if the accused used violence, or simple imprisonment if the offence was opportunistic and non-violent.

A person who publicly abets a riot by posting inflammatory messages online targeting a religious community of more than ten persons (Section 57 BNS) could be sentenced to imprisonment of either description for up to seven years. A Magistrate in Mumbai may choose simple imprisonment for a first-time offender but rigorous imprisonment for a repeat communal offender.

An individual who knowingly conceals a design to commit dacoity (Section 58 BNS) and the dacoity is subsequently committed may be sentenced to imprisonment of either description for up to seven years. A court in Uttar Pradesh dealing with a gang-related concealment case may impose rigorous imprisonment to serve as a deterrent.

A person convicted of abetting an offence that causes hurt to a victim (under Section 55 BNS) can be sentenced to imprisonment of either description for up to fourteen years. A Kolkata court may award rigorous imprisonment where the abettor actively planned the attack, versus simple imprisonment where the abettor's role was peripheral.
what_it_covers: Rigorous imprisonment, where the convicted person is required to perform hard labour such as grinding, weaving, or other prescribed work within the prison.
Simple imprisonment, where the convicted person is confined in jail but is not compelled to perform any hard labour.
Any judicially imposed custodial sentence under BNS provisions that do not specify a fixed type of imprisonment, leaving the description to the court's discretion.
Sentences awarded to repeat offenders under Section 13 BNS, where the court may choose either description of imprisonment for a term extending up to ten years.
Sentences for abetment of serious offences under Sections 55, 57, and 58 BNS where the court selects the appropriate description based on the facts.
what_it_excludes: Imprisonment for life, which is a distinct and separate category of punishment and is not encompassed within 'imprisonment of either description' — it is separately specified in the Act.
Death penalty, which is an entirely separate form of punishment and does not fall under any description of imprisonment.
Community service, which is a non-custodial penalty available under the BNS and does not involve confinement of either description.
Solitary confinement, which is a specific additional punishment imposed in conjunction with rigorous imprisonment and is not itself a standalone 'description' of imprisonment.
Fines and forfeitures, which are financial penalties and do not constitute any form of custodial imprisonment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether 'imprisonment of either description' applies directly determines the sentencing latitude available to the court — if a specific description (rigorous or simple) were mandated, the judge would lose discretion, but this formulation allows calibration of punishment to the offender's role and culpability. Under Section 13 BNS, it also governs whether a repeat offender is subject to enhanced punishment of up to ten years' imprisonment or imprisonment for life.

definitions.definition: An imputation, in the context of Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is any statement, assertion, or representation—made by words spoken or intended to be read, by signs, or by visible representations—concerning any person, which is intended to harm, or which the maker knows or has reason to believe will harm, the reputation of such person. An imputation harms a person's reputation if it directly or indirectly, in the estimation of others, lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person, lowers their character in respect of caste or calling, lowers their credit, or causes it to be believed that the body of that person is in a loathsome or disgraceful state.
definitions.plain_english: An 'imputation' is a statement or claim made about a person that damages or is meant to damage how others think of them. It can be spoken, written, shown as a sign, or communicated visually. It covers claims that make people think less of someone's honesty, profession, social standing, or physical condition. Even a statement made sarcastically or as a hypothetical can count as an imputation if it harms someone's reputation.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based journalist publishes an article falsely claiming that a respected doctor deliberately misdiagnosed patients for financial gain, causing other patients to avoid that doctor's clinic.
A person posts a video on social media falsely accusing a well-known Delhi businessman of embezzling funds from his employees, intending to ruin his business reputation.

During a village panchayat meeting in rural Rajasthan, a community elder states sarcastically that a local teacher 'must be very honest' after describing alleged instances of bribery, knowing the statement will be understood as an accusation.
A WhatsApp message circulated in a Chennai neighbourhood claims that a female schoolteacher is engaged in immoral conduct, causing her colleagues and parents to shun her.
A rival political candidate in a Uttar Pradesh state election spreads pamphlets falsely stating that the sitting MLA has a criminal record of fraud, intending to harm his electoral prospects.
An anonymous letter sent to a law firm in Bengaluru accuses one of its senior advocates of fabricating evidence in past cases, damaging the advocate's professional standing among clients and peers.
what_it_covers: A spoken statement at a public gathering accusing a person of financial dishonesty, knowing it will harm their business reputation.
A written social media post falsely claiming that a public figure engaged in immoral conduct, intended to lower their social standing.
An ironically or sarcastically worded statement that, in context, carries an accusatory meaning harmful to the subject's reputation.
A visual representation such as a cartoon or poster depicting a person engaged in criminal or disgraceful behaviour.
Any assertion that a person's body is in a loathsome or generally disgraceful physical state, causing others to avoid or stigmatise them.
An imputation made about a deceased person where it would harm that person's reputation if living and is intended to wound the feelings of their family or close relatives.
An imputation made concerning a company, association, or collection of persons as a group.
what_it_excludes: Statements expressed in good faith as opinions on the conduct of a public servant discharging public functions, to the extent the opinion relates only to that conduct.
Substantially true reports of court proceedings or the results of such proceedings, published in good faith.
Fair criticism expressed in good faith regarding the merits of a publicly submitted literary, artistic, or other performance, or the character of the author as it appears in such performance.
Censure passed in good faith by a person holding lawful authority over another, relating to matters within the scope of that authority.
Statements that do not, directly or indirectly, lower the moral, intellectual, or professional character of the subject, or affect their credit or bodily reputation in the eyes of others.
Accusations or complaints preferred in good faith against a person to a competent authority regarding their conduct.
Warnings issued in good faith to a person about another for the protection of the interests of the person giving or receiving the warning.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as an 'imputation' is the threshold determination for establishing the offence of defamation under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; if an imputation is established and no statutory exception applies, the accused is liable to simple imprisonment extending up to two years, fine, or community service. The definition also determines whether related liabilities for printing, engraving, or selling defamatory matter are attracted under the same section.

definitions.definition: The term 'infectious disease' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Section 273, it refers to any communicable or contagious disease capable of spreading from person to person or through modes of transport, intercourse between places, or other vectors, which the Government has recognised as requiring quarantine regulation to prevent its propagation across localities or regions.
definitions.plain_english: An infectious disease is a disease that can spread from one person to another, or from one place to another, through contact, travel, or other means. In this law, it refers to those diseases serious enough that the Government has made special rules about quarantine and restricting movement to stop the disease from spreading. Examples include diseases like cholera, plague, or COVID-19, where travel restrictions are imposed to protect public health.
real_world_examples: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government issued quarantine rules restricting ships and aircraft arriving at Indian ports and airports; a passenger vessel knowingly bypassing these quarantine protocols would be violating Section 273 involving an infectious disease.

A truck driver travelling from a district affected by a cholera outbreak to another city, knowingly ignoring state government quarantine checkpoints set up under disease control rules, commits an offence under Section 273 as cholera is an infectious disease.

A train operator who knowingly allows passengers from a region under quarantine due to a plague outbreak to board and travel to unaffected cities, in violation of government orders, would attract liability under Section 273 for facilitating intercourse from an infectious disease-affected place.

During a Nipah virus outbreak in Kerala, state authorities impose quarantine on certain zones; a private bus operator who knowingly continues to ferry passengers from quarantined villages to other districts in defiance of official orders commits the offence under Section 273.

A cargo ship arriving at Mumbai harbour from a country with an active Ebola outbreak that knowingly evades the mandatory quarantine anchorage period ordered by the Port Health Authority would be in violation of Section 273, as Ebola qualifies as an infectious disease requiring quarantine control.
what_it_covers: Diseases officially recognised by the Government as contagious and subject to quarantine rules, such as cholera, plague, COVID-19, and Ebola.
Any disease capable of spreading between persons or localities through movement of people, animals, or modes of transport, warranting government-imposed restrictions on intercourse between places.
Diseases notified under allied legislation such as the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, or National Disaster Management Act, 2005, where quarantine rules have been promulgated by competent authorities.
Airborne, waterborne, or contact-transmitted diseases that the Government deems serious enough to regulate travel and quarantine of modes of transport to contain their spread.
what_it_excludes: Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, cancer, or heart disease that do not spread from person to person and hence cannot be the basis for quarantine rules under Section 273.

Diseases that are contagious in nature but have not been the subject of any government quarantine rule or notification, as Section 273 is triggered only when a rule regulating quarantine or intercourse actually exists.
Mental illnesses or psychiatric conditions, which are not capable of spreading through contact or movement and therefore do not fall within the concept of infectious disease as used in this section.
Genetic or hereditary conditions and lifestyle-related disorders, which have no transmission mechanism relevant to quarantine or movement restrictions between places.
definitions.why_it_matters: The application of this term determines whether Section 273 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is attracted; only conduct involving disobedience of quarantine rules relating to an infectious disease can result in punishment of up to six months' imprisonment, fine, or both. If the disease in question is not an infectious disease triggering government quarantine rules, no criminal liability arises under this section.

definitions.definition: Infirmity, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a bodily weakness, disability, or impaired physical condition of a person. Under Section 114, causing infirmity to any person constitutes 'hurt'; under Section 100, causing bodily injury to a person labouring under a disorder, disease, or bodily infirmity that accelerates their death is deemed to have caused their death.
definitions.plain_english: Infirmity means a weakness or impaired condition of the body — for example, a chronic illness, a physical disability, or a debilitating condition that reduces a person's normal bodily function. In everyday terms, if someone causes another person to suffer such a weakened physical state, that act amounts to 'hurt' under the law. The law also recognises that a person who already has an infirmity is in a more vulnerable position, and anyone who injures such a person and thereby speeds up their death is treated as having caused that death.
real_world_examples: A man with a pre-existing heart condition is assaulted by his neighbour during a dispute; the physical assault triggers a cardiac arrest and the victim dies. The neighbour is deemed to have caused the victim's death because the bodily injury accelerated death in a person labouring under a bodily infirmity.

A factory worker in Mumbai develops chronic nerve damage and loss of limb function due to repeated exposure to toxic chemicals deliberately added to her workstation by a jealous coworker. The resulting permanent weakness of her limbs constitutes 'infirmity' and the coworker has caused hurt under Section 114.

A doctor in Chennai, performing surgery on a child in good faith but without the guardian's consent in an emergency, causes temporary weakness in the child's limb. Because the act was done in good faith for the child's benefit and not to cause grievous disease or infirmity, it falls within the statutory exception under Section 30.

An elderly diabetic patient in Delhi, who already suffers from weakened kidney function, is beaten during a robbery. The beating accelerates his renal failure and he dies within days. The attacker is held liable for culpable homicide because the injury accelerated death in a person with a pre-existing bodily infirmity.

A school teacher in Kolkata slaps a student with a known seizure disorder, triggering a prolonged seizure that leaves the child with permanent partial paralysis. The resulting permanent impairment of bodily function amounts to causing 'infirmity' under Section 114 and may additionally constitute grievous hurt.
what_it_covers: Chronic physical conditions such as paralysis, renal failure, or cardiac disease that impair normal bodily function and are caused or worsened by another person's act.
Temporary but medically significant weakening of a person's physical capacity resulting from an assault, poisoning, or other harmful act.
A pre-existing bodily weakness or disability in a victim that, when combined with an injury inflicted by another, accelerates the victim's death, making the perpetrator liable for causing that death.
Permanent or partial loss of use of a bodily organ or limb resulting from another's deliberate or negligent act, giving rise to liability for hurt under Section 114.
Conditions surgically or medically induced without lawful justification that leave a person in a weakened physical state.
what_it_excludes: Purely mental or psychological suffering that does not manifest as a physical bodily weakness or impairment — such suffering may constitute another form of harm but does not fall within 'infirmity' as used in Section 114.

Acts done in good faith by or with the consent of a guardian for the benefit of a child or person of unsound mind, for the purpose of curing a grievous disease or infirmity, are explicitly exempted and do not constitute an offence (Section 27).
Naturally occurring deterioration of health due to age, hereditary illness, or disease progression not caused or accelerated by another person's act.
Financial or economic harm suffered by a person, which does not amount to bodily weakness or physical impairment and is therefore outside the scope of 'infirmity' as defined in the context of hurt.
Emotional distress or reputational damage, which are governed by separate provisions (e.g., defamation) and do not constitute 'infirmity' under Section 114.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act causes 'infirmity' determines whether the offence of 'hurt' under Section 114 is established, which triggers criminal liability for the accused. Additionally, where the victim already labours under a bodily infirmity and an accused's act accelerates their death, the accused is deemed to have caused that death under Section 100, potentially elevating liability from causing hurt to culpable homicide or murder.

definitions.definition: The term 'information' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Sections 217 and 238, 'information' means any communication, report, tip-off, or disclosure of facts provided to a public servant or authority, whether oral or written, concerning the commission of an offence, the whereabouts of an accused, or any matter relevant to a legal or investigative proceeding.
definitions.plain_english: In simple terms, 'information' refers to any facts, details, or knowledge that a person passes on to a police officer, public servant, or official authority about a crime or a person involved in one. This could be a verbal tip-off, a written complaint, or any disclosure that helps or is meant to help in catching an offender or conducting an investigation. The law specifically penalises those who give false or misleading information to frustrate legal proceedings.
real_world_examples: A witness in Mumbai tells a police inspector that the accused in a robbery case is hiding in a specific locality — this communication is 'information' within the meaning of Section 217.

A person in Delhi falsely reports to a police station that a suspect wanted for theft has fled to another city, knowing the information is untrue, in order to help the suspect evade arrest — this constitutes false information under Section 217.

An informant in Chennai provides a written tip to a magistrate disclosing the location of a fugitive accused of dacoity, assisting the authorities in apprehension — this is a classic instance of information provided to a public servant.

A shopkeeper in Kolkata, having seen the accused in a murder case, deliberately gives incorrect information to the investigating officer about the direction in which the accused fled, thereby screening him from legal punishment — this falls squarely within the mischief targeted by Section 238.

A village resident in Uttar Pradesh verbally informs the local police about the presence of counterfeit currency at a neighbour's house, enabling a search — this oral disclosure constitutes actionable information under the Sanhita.

A corporate employee in Bengaluru sends an anonymous written complaint to the Economic Offences Wing about ongoing financial fraud by a colleague, which triggers an investigation — this written disclosure constitutes 'information' for the purposes of the Act.

definitions.definition: "Injury" means any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.
definitions.plain_english: Injury refers to any kind of harm that is unlawfully caused to a person. This harm can be physical (to the body), psychological (to the mind), reputational (to one's standing in society), or financial/material (to one's property). The key requirement is that the harm must have been caused illegally — harm caused lawfully does not count as 'injury' under this law.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi physically assaults his neighbour, causing bruises and a broken arm — this is a bodily injury illegally caused, squarely within the definition.
A factory owner in Surat repeatedly threatens and harasses a worker through abusive messages, causing severe anxiety and depression — the psychological harm constitutes injury to the mind.
A person circulates false and defamatory statements on social media about a shopkeeper in Chennai, destroying his business reputation in the community — this constitutes injury to reputation.
A fraudster in Mumbai deceives an elderly widow into transferring her savings to a fake investment scheme, causing financial loss — this is an injury to property within the meaning of the term.
A contractor in Bengaluru deliberately damages the boundary wall and crops on a farmer's land during a dispute — the destruction of property constitutes illegal injury to the farmer.
A rival businessman in Kolkata bribes a regulatory official to wrongfully cancel a trader's licence, causing loss of livelihood — this constitutes injury to the trader's property and rights.
what_it_covers: Physical harm to the body such as bruises, fractures, internal injuries, or grievous hurt caused by an unlawful act.
Psychological or mental harm such as trauma, depression, or fear caused by criminal intimidation, stalking, or harassment.
Damage to a person's reputation caused by defamatory statements, false imputations, or malicious publications.
Financial or material loss caused to a person's property through theft, criminal mischief, fraud, or extortion.
Any combination of the above forms of harm, provided the causing of that harm is illegal under the law.
what_it_excludes: Harm that is lawfully caused — for example, a surgeon causing bodily pain during a consented medical procedure is not 'injury' because it is not illegal.
Harm resulting from acts expressly justified by law, such as a police officer lawfully restraining a violent accused — the resulting discomfort is not an injury under this definition.
Self-inflicted harm, as the definition requires harm to be 'caused to any person' by another party acting illegally.
Harm caused with the valid consent of the person affected and within the bounds permitted by law, such as sports injuries in a lawful contact sport.
Mere inconvenience or hurt feelings not rising to the level of identifiable harm to body, mind, reputation, or property.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of 'injury' is a constituent element or aggravating factor in numerous offences under the BNS 2023, including those relating to hurt, grievous hurt, criminal intimidation, defamation, mischief, and extortion (Sections 129, 171, 198, 201, 224, 225, 232, 287, 288, 289, 308, 346, 351); establishing that illegal injury was caused determines criminal liability, the gravity of the offence charged, and the quantum of punishment. Where no illegal injury is shown, the threshold for several offences may not be met, shielding an accused from prosecution.

definitions.definition: Instant death refers to the immediate and imminent threat of death to a person at the very moment of the act being compelled, such that a reasonable person in that situation would apprehend that death will occur then and there if compliance is refused. It is not a remote, conditional, or future threat of death, but one that is proximate, present, and credible enough to override the free exercise of will.
definitions.plain_english: Instant death means that a person genuinely believes, with good reason, that they will be killed right then and there if they do not comply with a threat. It is the fear of being killed immediately — not sometime in the future. This immediate fear of being killed on the spot can, in certain situations, excuse a person from criminal responsibility for actions they were forced to take.
real_world_examples: A dacoit gang in rural Uttar Pradesh captures a local locksmith and holds a loaded gun to his head, ordering him to break open the lock of a neighbour's house; the locksmith complies out of fear that he will be shot dead immediately if he refuses.

During a violent robbery in Mumbai, a shopkeeper is threatened at knifepoint by armed robbers who demand he open the safe, telling him they will slit his throat on the spot if he refuses; the shopkeeper opens the safe under this immediate threat of death.

A truck driver in Jharkhand is intercepted by Naxal militants who threaten to shoot him dead instantly unless he transports their weapons to the next village; the driver, believing death is certain and immediate, complies.

A village carpenter in Bihar is dragged from his home by a gang of dacoits at night and threatened with instant shooting unless he uses his tools to break open the main door of a wealthy neighbour's house for the dacoits to loot.
During communal violence in a city, a person is surrounded by a mob holding weapons who demand he participate in an act of arson under threat of being killed on the spot if he refuses.

A petrol pump attendant in Delhi is held at gunpoint during a robbery and forced to hand over cash from the register, with the robber making clear that any hesitation will result in being shot dead immediately.
what_it_covers: A threat to shoot, stab, or kill a person at the exact moment of the act, leaving no time for escape or deliberation.
A situation where an armed person is physically present and capable of immediately executing the threat of death if the compelled person refuses to comply.
The apprehension felt by a person seized by dacoits who hold a weapon to their person and demand immediate participation in an unlawful act under pain of death.
The fear experienced by a robbery victim who is confronted in person by an offender threatening to kill them on the spot unless they surrender property.
The ongoing fear of instant death during a robbery that sustains the right of private defence of property as long as the threat persists.
what_it_excludes: A threat of future or conditional death, such as 'we will kill you next week if you report this to the police', which is not proximate enough to constitute instant death.
A threat of harm short of death, such as a threat of beating or grievous hurt, even if serious, which does not satisfy the threshold of instant death for the Section 32 defence.
A situation where a person voluntarily joins a criminal gang knowing its character and is later directed to commit offences, even under threats from associates.
Threats made remotely or at a distance, such as a telephonic death threat where the threatener is not physically present and cannot immediately execute the threat.

Offences of murder and offences against the State punishable with death, which are explicitly excluded from the defence of compulsion by instant death under Section 32 even if the threat was genuine and immediate.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether instant death applies determines if a person can claim the complete defence of coercion under Section 32, thereby escaping criminal liability for an otherwise unlawful act; it also determines whether a theft escalates into robbery under Section 309 and whether the right of private defence of property continues to subsist under Section 43.

definitions.definition: A person is said to instigate the doing of a thing when they actively urge, encourage, or incite another person to do that thing; a person who, by wilful misrepresentation or by wilful concealment of a material fact which he is bound to disclose, voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done, is also said to instigate the doing of that thing.
definitions.plain_english: Instigation means actively pushing, urging, or encouraging someone else to commit an act, whether through direct persuasion, threats, emotional pressure, or by deliberately lying or hiding important facts to cause them to act. It does not require the other person to actually carry out the act. Even tricking someone into doing something by hiding the truth counts as instigation under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A husband repeatedly taunts and humiliates his wife by telling her she is worthless and should end her life; she dies by suicide. The husband can be charged with abetment by instigation under the BNS.

A factory owner tells a supervisor, falsely representing that a rival worker has stolen company property, causing the supervisor to file a false police complaint against that worker — the owner is guilty of instigation by wilful misrepresentation.

A political leader delivers an inflammatory speech at a rally in Mumbai directly urging the crowd to attack members of a particular community; the crowd proceeds to do so. The leader's speech constitutes instigation of the resulting offences.

A school teacher tells a student, who is below the age of criminal responsibility, that a classmate stole his lunch box and that he should beat him up; the student does so. The teacher is guilty of abetment by instigation even though the child cannot be prosecuted.

A moneylender in rural Rajasthan relentlessly harasses a farmer over debt and explicitly tells him 'the only way out for you is death', leading the farmer to die by suicide. This constitutes instigation to suicide under the BNS.

A corrupt customs officer conceals from a colleague the fact that a shipment has been declared contraband, thereby inducing the colleague to clear it, amounts to instigation by wilful concealment of a material fact the officer was bound to disclose.
what_it_covers: Directly urging or goading a person through words, gestures, or conduct to commit an offence, even if that person refuses or fails to carry it out.
Deliberately lying about a material fact or concealing a fact one is legally obligated to disclose, thereby inducing another person to do something they otherwise would not have done.
Instigating a person legally incapable of committing an offence (such as a child or person of unsound mind) to commit an act that amounts to an offence if committed by a capable person.
Indirect instigation through an intermediary, such as instigating B to instigate C to commit an offence, making the original instigator equally liable.
Causing a public officer to apprehend the wrong person by wilfully misrepresenting that person's identity, as illustrated in the Section 45 example of B falsely identifying C as Z.
what_it_excludes: Mere presence at the scene of an offence without any active encouragement or urging, which does not by itself constitute instigation.
Providing assistance or aid after an act has been decided upon and commenced, which falls under the separate limb of 'aiding' rather than instigation.
Entering into a conspiracy with another person to do a thing, which is a distinct mode of abetment under Section 45 and is not classified as instigation.
Passive silence or failure to prevent an offence where there is no legal duty to disclose or act, as concealment that constitutes instigation requires a duty to disclose the concealed fact.
General advice or abstract discussion about an act without directing or urging a specific person to commit it, which does not meet the threshold of active instigation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as instigation determines whether a person can be held criminally liable as an abettor under Sections 45 and 46 of the BNS, even if the principal offence is never completed or the person directly committing it lacks criminal capacity; it triggers liability for punishment equivalent to the offence abetted under Section 49, including in cases of suicide abetment, murder, and other serious offences.
