definitions.definition: The term 'instrument' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used throughout the Act to mean any tool, device, die, machinery, or implement — whether mechanical or physical — designed or capable of being used for a specific purpose, including shooting, stabbing, cutting, coining, forging, counterfeiting, or making stamps, depending on the context of the provision in which it appears.
definitions.plain_english: An 'instrument' refers to any physical tool or device that is used or intended to be used to carry out a particular action. In criminal law under this Act, it includes weapons like knives or guns, as well as tools used to make fake coins, stamps, or currency notes. The exact meaning of the word depends on the section it appears in — for example, a coining tool taken from a mint, or a die used for forgery.
real_world_examples: A person is caught carrying a sharpened metal screwdriver into a market in Mumbai and uses it to stab a rival — the screwdriver qualifies as an 'instrument for stabbing' under Section 118 of the BNS, making the accused liable for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous instrument.

An accused in Delhi is found in possession of a custom-made metal die and stamping press capable of producing fake ₹500 currency notes — these constitute 'instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting currency-notes' under Section 181 of the BNS.

A government mint worker in Kolkata is apprehended while attempting to smuggle a coining punch and collar set outside the mint premises — this coining tool qualifies as a 'coining instrument' unlawfully taken from the mint under Section 188 of the BNS.

A vendor in Chennai is found selling rubber stamps and dyes that mimic official postal stamps for use without payment of postage fees — the plate and instrument used to produce such fictitious stamps are covered under Section 186 of the BNS.

A gang in Hyderabad manufactures counterfeit revenue stamps using engraved plates and inking rollers — these plates and rollers are 'instruments for forging Government stamps' within the meaning of Section 181 of the BNS.

A person in Pune uses a modified air rifle (instrument for shooting) to injure a neighbour during a dispute — the air rifle constitutes an instrument under Section 118, attracting enhanced punishment for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon.
what_it_covers: A knife, sword, or sharpened implement used to stab or cut a person, constituting an instrument for stabbing or cutting under Section 118.
A mechanical die, mould, roller, or press used for manufacturing counterfeit coins, currency notes, or Government revenue stamps under Section 181.
A coining punch, collar, or any specialised coining tool physically removed from a lawfully established Government mint in India under Section 188.
An engraved plate, rubber stamp block, or any device used to make fictitious postal stamps under Section 186.
A firearm or air gun used as an instrument for shooting a person, causing hurt, under Section 118.
what_it_excludes: Abstract or intangible means of causing harm, such as verbal threats or electronic transmissions, which are not physical instruments in the sense contemplated by the Act.

Ordinary household items or tools not adapted or intended for use in committing the specific offences enumerated (e.g., a kitchen knife not used or intended as a weapon of offence in the relevant context).

Machines or equipment used in lawful and authorised minting operations by Government employees acting within their sanctioned duties — possession or use within the mint under lawful authority is excluded from Section 188.

Documents, electronic records, or written materials — these are governed separately under 'document', 'false document', or 'electronic record' definitions and are not treated as 'instruments' in the physical tool sense.

Corrosive substances, poisons, or explosive materials, which are separately enumerated as distinct means of causing hurt under Section 118 and are not classified as 'instruments' within the same provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as an 'instrument' determines the applicability and severity of punishment — for instance, under Section 118, using an instrument for stabbing or shooting attracts up to three years' imprisonment or life imprisonment for grievous hurt, as opposed to lesser penalties for simple hurt; under Section 188, unauthorised removal of a coining instrument from a mint attracts up to seven years' imprisonment. Establishing the nature of the item as an 'instrument' within the relevant section is therefore central to framing and proving the charge.

Examples: A person is caught carrying a sharpened metal screwdriver into a market in Mumbai and uses it to stab a rival — the screwdriver qualifies as an 'instrument for stabbing' under Section 118 of the BNS, making the accused liable for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous instrument. | An accused in Delhi is found in possession of a custom-made metal die and stamping press capable of producing fake ₹500 currency notes — these constitute 'instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting currency-notes' under Section 181 of the BNS. | A government mint worker in Kolkata is apprehended while attempting to smuggle a coining punch and collar set outside the mint premises — this coining tool qualifies as a 'coining instrument' unlawfully taken from the mint under Section 188 of the BNS. | A vendor in Chennai is found selling rubber stamps and dyes that mimic official postal stamps for use without payment of postage fees — the plate and instrument used to produce such fictitious stamps are covered under Section 186 of the BNS. | A gang in Hyderabad manufactures counterfeit revenue stamps using engraved plates and inking rollers — these plates and rollers are 'instruments for forging Government stamps' within the meaning of Section 181 of the BNS. | A person in Pune uses a modified air rifle (instrument for shooting) to injure a neighbour during a dispute — the air rifle constitutes an instrument under Section 118, attracting enhanced punishment for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon.

Covers: A knife, sword, or sharpened implement used to stab or cut a person, constituting an instrument for stabbing or cutting under Section 118.; A mechanical die, mould, roller, or press used for manufacturing counterfeit coins, currency notes, or Government revenue stamps under Section 181.; A coining punch, collar, or any specialised coining tool physically removed from a lawfully established Government mint in India under Section 188.; An engraved plate, rubber stamp block, or any device used to make fictitious postal stamps under Section 186.; A firearm or air gun used as an instrument for shooting a person, causing hurt, under Section 118.

Excludes: Abstract or intangible means of causing harm, such as verbal threats or electronic transmissions, which are not physical instruments in the sense contemplated by the Act.; Ordinary household items or tools not adapted or intended for use in committing the specific offences enumerated (e.g., a kitchen knife not used or intended as a weapon of offence in the relevant context).; Machines or equipment used in lawful and authorised minting operations by Government employees acting within their sanctioned duties — possession or use within the mint under lawful authority is excluded from Section 188.; Documents, electronic records, or written materials — these are governed separately under 'document', 'false document', or 'electronic record' definitions and are not treated as 'instruments' in the physical tool sense.; Corrosive substances, poisons, or explosive materials, which are separately enumerated as distinct means of causing hurt under Section 118 and are not classified as 'instruments' within the same provision.

Establishing the nature of the item as an 'instrument' within the relevant section is therefore central to framing and proving the charge.

definitions.definition: An act of insubordination refers to a wilful refusal or failure by an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman in the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India to obey lawful orders, commands, or authority of a superior, constituting a breach of military discipline. The term is used in Section 166 in the context of abetting such conduct, where a person who knowingly encourages or facilitates such defiance of military authority is held criminally liable if the act of insubordination is committed as a consequence of that abetment.
definitions.plain_english: Insubordination means when a member of India's armed forces — an army soldier, naval sailor, or air force airman — deliberately refuses to follow or disobeys a lawful order from a superior officer. It is essentially an act of defiance against military authority and discipline. Section 166 deals not with the military person committing this act, but with any civilian or outsider who knowingly encourages or helps them do it.
real_world_examples: A civilian activist in Pune knowingly convinces an Indian Army soldier to refuse orders to deploy to a conflict zone, and the soldier subsequently disobeys his commanding officer's lawful deployment order — the civilian can be punished under Section 166.

A contractor working near a Naval base in Visakhapatnam persuades a sailor to abandon his post during active duty by promising him financial rewards, and the sailor does so — the contractor is liable for abetting an act of insubordination.

A political agitator in Jammu distributes pamphlets among jawans of the Indian Army urging them to refuse orders from their officers during a security operation, and a jawan refuses such an order — the agitator is punishable under this section.

A social media influencer in Delhi posts videos specifically directed at Indian Air Force airmen, encouraging them to disobey orders related to a training exercise, and an airman acting on this content refuses to comply with his superior's instruction — the influencer can be prosecuted under Section 166.

A family member of a soldier stationed in Siachen repeatedly pressures him to disobey transfer orders from his commanding officer, and the soldier ultimately refuses the transfer — the family member who abetted this act may face criminal liability under this section.
what_it_covers: A soldier in the Indian Army who wilfully refuses to obey a lawful command issued by a superior officer after being instigated by an outsider.
A sailor in the Indian Navy who abandons an assigned duty or post as a direct consequence of being abetted or encouraged by another person.
An airman in the Indian Air Force who disobeys a direct operational order from a commanding officer following instigation by a civilian or another person.
Any act of deliberate non-compliance with military authority by a commissioned or non-commissioned officer in any branch of India's armed forces when it is consequent upon abetment.
Collective refusal of orders by a group of soldiers when individually abetted by an external person who knowingly facilitated the insubordination.
what_it_excludes: Acts of disobedience by armed forces personnel that are entirely spontaneous and not causally linked to any external abetment or instigation by another person.
Lawful refusal of an illegal or unconstitutional order by a military officer, which is protected conduct and does not constitute insubordination in the punishable sense.

Disobedience of orders by civilians or non-military government employees, as Section 166 expressly restricts its application to officers, soldiers, sailors, and airmen of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.
Insubordination by paramilitary or Central Armed Police Forces personnel (such as CRPF or BSF) since the section specifies only the Army, Navy, and Air Force of the Government of India.
Mere criticism or expression of dissatisfaction with military orders by a service member that does not amount to an actual refusal or failure to comply with a lawful command.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as insubordination under Section 166 determines whether a third party who encouraged it can be prosecuted and punished with imprisonment up to two years and/or fine; the definition is the threshold condition — without a committed act of insubordination as a consequence of abetment, no criminal liability attaches to the abettor under this section.

definitions.definition: The 'integrity of India' refers to the territorial and constitutional wholeness of the Indian nation, encompassing the inviolability of its borders, the unity of its people, and the indivisibility of its sovereign territory as constituted under the Constitution of India; any act that encourages separatist activities, promotes secession, or undermines the unified constitutional identity of any class of persons in relation to the Indian State is treated as endangering the integrity of India.
definitions.plain_english: The integrity of India means keeping India together as one complete, undivided country. It refers to ensuring that no part of Indian territory is broken away and that all citizens, regardless of religion, caste, language, or region, remain bound together under one Constitution. Any attempt to split the country, encourage groups to seek separation, or deny loyalty of any group to India is seen as a threat to this integrity.
real_world_examples: A social media influencer in Punjab regularly posts videos claiming that a particular religious community owes no allegiance to the Indian Constitution and should seek a separate homeland, thereby endangering the integrity of India under Section 197.

A political pamphlet distributed in Manipur asserts that people belonging to a specific tribal community are not true citizens of India and should secede to form an independent state, directly threatening the integrity of India.

A YouTuber in Tamil Nadu publishes a series of videos propagating that Tamil-speaking people should form a separate nation and are being denied their rights as Indian citizens on linguistic grounds, constituting an act prejudicial to national integration.

A religious leader in Uttar Pradesh delivers a speech at a mosque asserting that members of a particular faith cannot be loyal to the Indian Constitution and encourages them to resist the sovereignty of the Indian State, jeopardising the integrity of India.

A regional newspaper in Jammu & Kashmir publishes a false and misleading report claiming that a particular linguistic group has formally renounced its citizenship obligations, causing disharmony and threatening the integrity and unity of India.

An online platform hosted from abroad circulates fabricated content suggesting that residents of a northeastern state have voted to separate from India, with the intent of fomenting unrest and endangering India's territorial integrity.
semantic_tags: religious or regional identity and loyalty
what_it_covers: Assertions that any religious, racial, linguistic, or regional group cannot bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India, thereby challenging the unity of the Indian nation.

Publication or dissemination of false or misleading information that jeopardises the sovereign and territorial completeness of India, including fabricated claims about secession or separation of any region.

Speeches, writings, or electronic communications that encourage feelings of separatism or portray any community as being outside the constitutional fold of India, thereby undermining national integration.

Acts committed in places of worship or during religious ceremonies that promote enmity between communities on grounds of religion, caste, language, or region in a manner that threatens national unity.
Content that portrays citizens of a particular caste or community as incapable of upholding India's sovereignty, effectively denying the unified territorial and constitutional identity of India.
what_it_excludes: Peaceful academic or scholarly analysis of regional autonomy, federal structure, or constitutional rights of minority communities that does not advocate secession or separatism.

Legitimate political criticism of government policies, administrative decisions, or legislative measures aimed at securing lawful change through democratic processes, as expressly protected under Section 152.
Journalistic reporting that accurately documents regional grievances, social inequalities, or communal tensions without propagating hatred, enmity, or secessionist ideology.

Cultural expressions, literary works, or artistic performances that depict regional identity, linguistic pride, or religious customs without encouraging disaffection toward the Indian State or its Constitution.

Legal advocacy or court proceedings challenging specific laws or government actions on constitutional grounds, which falls within the bounds of lawful dissent and does not threaten the integrity of India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is found to endanger the 'integrity of India' determines liability under Sections 152 and 197 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, with penalties ranging from three years to life imprisonment depending on the nature of the offence; it also governs whether speech, publication, or electronic communication crosses the threshold from protected expression into a punishable criminal act threatening national unity.

definitions.definition: A person 'intends' a consequence when that consequence is the purpose or aim of their act — the desired or consciously chosen outcome they seek to bring about through their conduct. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'intends' is used in contradistinction to 'knows to be likely', denoting a direct, purposive mental state directed at a specific result, as opposed to mere foresight or awareness of probability.
definitions.plain_english: When someone 'intends' something, it means they actually wanted that specific result to happen — it was their goal or purpose. It is different from simply knowing that something might happen as a side effect. For example, if a person aims a gun at someone to kill them, they 'intend' that person's death; if they fire recklessly into a crowd, they may 'know' deaths are likely but may not specifically 'intend' any particular death.
real_world_examples: A person in Delhi poisons their business partner's food specifically to kill them so as to inherit the business — they intend the death of that specific person, making this culpable homicide with the highest level of mens rea.

A man in Mumbai fires a gun at his estranged wife but the bullet accidentally strikes and kills the neighbour standing nearby — under Section 102, he 'intends' his wife's death, and the culpable homicide of the neighbour is treated as if he had intended the neighbour's death as well.

A factory owner in Surat deliberately releases toxic chemicals into a water supply intending to harm a rival village's cattle, but instead causes the deaths of several villagers — the intent was directed at property harm, but the legal doctrine of transferred intent operates under Section 102.

A person in Chennai who intentionally strikes another on the head with a heavy iron rod, aiming to cause grievous hurt, is said to 'intend' grievous hurt — the purposive nature of the blow determines the category of offence under Sections 117 and 122.

During a communal altercation in Hyderabad, an accused deliberately targets a specific individual in the crowd with a knife — the 'intent' to cause grievous hurt to that specific person distinguishes the act from reckless conduct causing similar injuries.
what_it_covers: A person who deliberately aims to cause death or grievous hurt to a specific identified victim as the conscious purpose of their act.
Cases of transferred intent under Section 102 where the accused intends harm to one person but accidentally causes the same harm to another — the intent is legally transferred to the actual victim.
An accused who uses a weapon or poison with the specific design of injuring or killing a particular individual, where the purposive aim is established by circumstantial or direct evidence.
A person who intends to cause grievous hurt of one kind but ends up causing grievous hurt of a different kind — the intent attaches to the category of harm aimed at, not the precise form it takes.
what_it_excludes: Acts where the accused merely knows that death or grievous hurt is a likely consequence but does not desire or aim at that outcome — this falls under 'knowledge' rather than 'intends'.

Rash or negligent acts where the accused neither desires nor consciously aims at the harmful result, such as a driver who accidentally kills a pedestrian due to reckless speed without any desire to cause harm.
Accidental or inadvertent consequences that arise without any purposive mental state directed at the result — pure accidents without foreknowledge or desire are excluded from the scope of 'intends'.

Situations where an accused acts under grave and sudden provocation and does not consciously direct harm toward a specific person, which may negate the element of specific intent required under Section 122.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an accused 'intends' a harmful result directly determines the category and severity of the offence — distinguishing culpable homicide from negligent causing of death, and voluntarily causing grievous hurt from rash acts — and under Section 102, the presence of intent fixes criminal liability at the highest culpability level even when the actual victim is not the intended target. The presence or absence of 'intends' can determine whether a person faces charges under murder, culpable homicide, or lesser offences, and correspondingly triggers or blocks the most severe punishments available under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

definitions.definition: The term 'intent' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used in Section 24 to signify a deliberate and conscious purpose to bring about a specific result or consequence through one's act or omission, as distinguished from mere knowledge or recklessness. It denotes a state of mind wherein the person wills the outcome and acts with a design to achieve that particular end.
definitions.plain_english: Intent means that a person consciously wanted a particular result to happen and acted deliberately to bring that result about. It is more than just knowing something might happen — it means you actually aimed for it. For example, if someone plans and carries out a harmful act specifically to hurt another person, they have 'intent'. It is the purposeful, goal-directed mental state behind an action.
real_world_examples: A person in Delhi mixes poison into a neighbour's food specifically to kill them — the deliberate plan to cause death shows clear intent to commit murder under the BNS.
A shopkeeper in Mumbai systematically overcharges customers by falsifying weights on a weighing scale, intending to cause wrongful financial gain to himself — this demonstrates intent to cheat.

A factory owner in Chennai continues to dump toxic waste into a river knowing it will harm the public but specifically aiming to save disposal costs — the purposeful decision to harm public health shows intent.

A person in Kolkata sends threatening letters to a business rival specifically intending to cause fear and compel the rival to withdraw from a commercial bid — this constitutes criminal intimidation with clear intent.

A driver in Hyderabad, after an argument, deliberately accelerates a vehicle towards a pedestrian intending to cause bodily harm — the deliberate aim to injure establishes intent as opposed to mere rash or negligent driving.
what_it_covers: A premeditated plan to cause harm where the person consciously directs their actions toward achieving a specific unlawful outcome.
Situations where a person selects a particular course of action knowing it will achieve a forbidden end and desires that end, such as intentional poisoning or deliberate arson.
Acts where the purpose behind the act is to defraud, deceive, or injure another, and that purpose is the driving motivation rather than a side-effect.
Cases where a person uses indirect means — such as forging documents or fabricating evidence — specifically to achieve a desired unlawful result.
Circumstances where a person's words or conduct unambiguously reveal a fixed design to bring about a criminal consequence, as inferred from the totality of their behaviour.
what_it_excludes: Rash or negligent acts where a person does not desire the harmful outcome but merely fails to take adequate precautions — negligence does not constitute intent.
Accidental consequences that arise without any deliberate design or purpose on the part of the actor, even if the person had knowledge of a possible risk.
Knowledge alone — a person who knows a harmful consequence is likely but does not specifically aim for it does not satisfy the element of intent, though they may satisfy knowledge-based offences.
Acts committed under sudden and grave provocation where the person's mental state does not reflect a settled, deliberate design but rather an impulsive reaction.
Omissions that are careless or inadvertent rather than deliberate and purposeful, which fall under negligence or rash omission rather than intentional conduct.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of intent is a decisive factor in determining criminal liability and the gravity of an offence under the BNS — offences such as murder, cheating, forgery, and criminal conspiracy expressly require proof of intent, and without it a higher charge may not be established. Intent also determines whether a person is guilty of an attempt or a completed offence, and can be the difference between a more serious charge carrying life imprisonment and a lesser offence carrying minimal punishment.

definitions.definition: A person is said to have 'intent to defraud' whenever they act dishonestly or fraudulently with the purpose of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another, particularly in the context of making, altering, or using a false document or electronic record so as to deceive or injure another party. It encompasses any deliberate design to deceive by means of a false representation, document, or act, resulting in or intended to result in harm to another's legal right or property.
definitions.plain_english: Intent to defraud means a person deliberately plans to cheat or deceive someone in a way that causes that person to lose money, property, or a legal right, or causes the fraudster to gain something unlawfully. It is not an accidental or mistaken act — the person must know what they are doing is wrong and do it on purpose to cause harm or obtain an unfair advantage. For example, forging someone's signature on a cheque or falsely backdating a document to steal property both show intent to defraud.
real_world_examples: A property dealer in Delhi alters the sale deed of a plot by changing the registered buyer's name to his own relative's name, with the purpose of unlawfully transferring ownership and depriving the original buyer of the property.
A borrower in Mumbai adds extra zeros to a promissory note signed by a lender, inflating the amount from ₹50,000 to ₹5,00,000, intending to use it in court to falsely claim a larger debt was owed.

A trader in Chennai, on the verge of insolvency, secretly backdates a lease agreement for his warehouse to a date before attachment of his assets, so that the property appears encumbered and beyond the reach of his creditors.

A government contractor in Hyderabad forges official inspection certificates to make substandard construction materials appear approved, intending to deceive the government authority and secure payment for work not done to specification.

A person in Kolkata picks up a signed blank cheque dropped by another person, fills in an amount of ₹2,00,000 without authorisation, and presents it for encashment at a bank, intending to unlawfully obtain funds from the account holder.
what_it_covers: Altering a document such as a cheque or deed to increase an amount or change a name with the purpose of deceiving the counterparty and gaining unlawfully.
Backdating a lease, conveyance, or agreement to make it appear executed before a legally significant date, so as to defeat another person's lawful rights or claims.
Causing an intoxicated or mentally unsound person to sign or execute a document, knowing they do not understand its contents, in order to extract a benefit from them.
Forging another person's signature or seal on a document with the knowledge that it is unauthorised and with the purpose of inducing a third party to act on the false document to their detriment.
Lodging property or assets in another person's name in anticipation of insolvency proceedings, with the deliberate purpose of putting those assets beyond the reach of legitimate creditors.
what_it_excludes: Honest mistakes or errors in documents made without any awareness of their falsity or any purpose to deceive, such as a clerical error in filling out a form.
Acts done under a genuine but mistaken belief in one's legal entitlement to alter or execute a document, where there is no dishonest or fraudulent design.
Mere negligence or carelessness in the preparation or execution of documents that results in harm, without any deliberate plan to deceive or defraud another party.
Acts authorised by law or carried out under lawful authority, even if they cause loss to another party, as they lack the element of dishonest or fraudulent purpose.
A situation where a person fills in a blank document exactly as authorised and within the limits given, since there is no departure from consent and no intention to harm.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of 'intent to defraud' is a critical mental element that converts an otherwise ordinary act of signing, altering, or executing a document into the criminal offence of forgery under Sections 336–350 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and directly triggers liability under Sections 344, 345, and 350 relating to forging valuable securities, wills, and using forged documents. Without proof of this intent, the essential mens rea for forgery and related offences is absent, and no conviction under these provisions can be sustained.

definitions.definition: The term 'intention' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used throughout the Sanhita to denote a conscious and deliberate purpose or design to bring about a specific consequence or result through one's act or omission, where the person foresees that consequence as substantially certain to follow from their conduct and consciously directs their will towards it.
definitions.plain_english: Intention means that a person does something on purpose — they have made up their mind to cause a particular outcome and they act deliberately to bring that outcome about. It is different from an accident or carelessness; the person actually wants the result or knows it is virtually certain to happen. Courts look at what was going on in a person's mind at the time they acted to decide whether they truly intended something.
real_world_examples: A person in Delhi purchases rat poison, mixes it into his business partner's food, and serves it knowing it will cause death — the act of mixing and serving demonstrates a clear intention to kill, attracting liability for murder under Section 100 of the BNS.

A landlord in Mumbai threatens his tenant in writing saying 'I will burn your shop down if you do not vacate in three days' — the deliberate drafting and delivery of the threat reveals intention to cause alarm, relevant under criminal intimidation provisions.

A pickpocket in Chennai who follows a commuter onto a bus, waits for the right moment, and quietly removes the wallet from their pocket acts with the intention to cause wrongful gain to himself and wrongful loss to the victim, establishing the mental element for theft under the Sanhita.

A factory owner in Surat who knowingly discharges toxic effluent into a river supplying drinking water to a village, aware that it is likely to cause mass illness, acts with intention to cause harm, which becomes relevant in determining culpability under offences affecting public health.

A man in Kolkata forges his deceased father's signature on a property deed to transfer ownership to himself — the deliberate act of creating a false document to deceive demonstrates fraudulent intention, triggering liability for forgery under the BNS.
what_it_covers: A person who premeditated a crime and takes steps to execute it, such as planning and carrying out a poisoning, demonstrating conscious desire to cause death.
A person who, while not desiring a secondary consequence, knows with virtual certainty that it will result from their deliberate act and proceeds anyway, treating that consequence as intentional.

An accused who uses deceptive means with a specific objective — such as forging a document to dishonestly acquire property — where the purpose of gain or deception is the driving motive behind the act.
Abettors or conspirators who consciously direct others towards committing an offence, sharing the common intention that the offence be committed, covered under Sections 109 and 110 of the BNS.
what_it_excludes: Acts done carelessly or negligently without any conscious desire to bring about the harmful result — negligence does not constitute intention under the Sanhita.
Accidental consequences that were neither foreseen nor desired by the person at the time of the act, even if harm results.
Acts done under a genuine mistake of fact, where the person did not know the true nature of circumstances and therefore could not have formed the requisite intention towards the actual outcome.
Rash acts done with indifference to consequences but without a conscious design to cause a specific result — rashness is treated as a separate mental element from intention in the Sanhita.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence or absence of intention is decisive in determining the severity of criminal liability — for example, it distinguishes murder (intentional killing) from culpable homicide not amounting to murder or death by negligence, each attracting vastly different punishments. Intention is also the essential mental element required to establish offences such as abetment, criminal conspiracy, cheating, and forgery under the BNS, and its absence can entirely negate criminal responsibility or reduce the grade of offence.

definitions.definition: A person is said to act 'intentionally' when the act or omission is done with a conscious and deliberate purpose to bring about a specific result, as distinguished from acts done accidentally, negligently, or rashly. Within the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'intentionally' denotes that the person directing the act has a fixed design or purpose to cause the particular consequence that the law treats as criminal.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'intentionally' means doing something on purpose, with a clear goal in mind. It is not an accident or a mistake — the person knows what they are doing and wants that specific outcome to happen. For example, if someone deliberately fires a gun at another person aiming to kill them, that act is intentional. Courts look at the circumstances, conduct, and surrounding facts to decide whether the person truly meant to bring about the result.
real_world_examples: A person in Delhi deliberately poisons a business rival's food with the aim of killing him; the act of administering poison is done intentionally, attracting liability for murder under Section 101 of the BNS.

A factory owner in Mumbai, knowing that toxic waste is being discharged into a river used by villagers for drinking, continues the practice to avoid costs — the continued omission to stop is intentional, establishing criminal liability for causing harm.

Two accused in Chennai agree to beat a victim at different times using separate instruments; each intentionally cooperates in committing grievous hurt as described in Section 3 of the BNS, making both equally liable.

A jailor in Kolkata intentionally withholds food from a prisoner over several days with the design of causing that prisoner's death — each deliberate omission to supply food constitutes an intentional act leading to murder.

Under Section 211 of the BNS, a complainant in Hyderabad knowingly and intentionally files a false criminal charge against an innocent neighbour to harass him, fulfilling the element of 'intentionally' required to constitute the offence of false charge of offence made with intent to injure.
what_it_covers: Acts performed with a premeditated, conscious purpose to bring about a specific harmful or criminal outcome, such as deliberate poisoning or planned assault.

Intentional illegal omissions where a person, fully aware of their duty, deliberately fails to act knowing the harmful consequence that will result — for example, a jailor withholding food to cause a prisoner's death.

Cooperative acts by multiple persons, each of whom deliberately performs their part knowing it contributes to the commission of an offence, such as two persons jointly administering poison in planned doses.
Filing of a false criminal charge or instituting false proceedings against a known innocent person with the deliberate purpose of harming or harassing them, as covered under Section 211 of the BNS.
Situations where a person directs a third party to perform an act knowing and desiring the criminal outcome, thereby intentionally participating in the offence through another.
what_it_excludes: Acts done accidentally or by genuine mistake of fact, where the person had no design or foresight of the harmful consequence — such as a hunter accidentally shooting another person while aiming at an animal.
Rash or negligent acts where the person may have been careless or failed to exercise due caution but did not consciously aim to bring about the specific harmful result.
Acts committed under irresistible impulse caused by sudden and grave provocation, where the deliberate design is negated by the involuntary nature of the reaction.
Acts performed under bonafide belief of legal right or mistake of law where there is no underlying wilful intent to cause the criminal consequence.
Omissions resulting from incapacity, ignorance of duty, or genuine inability to act, as opposed to a deliberate decision not to perform an obligation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'intentionally' is decisive in determining criminal liability and the severity of punishment — for instance, under Section 211 of the BNS, the offence of making a false charge is only constituted when the accusation is made intentionally against a person known to be innocent, and absence of intent can entirely negate the offence. The presence of intentionality can elevate a charge from mere negligence or rashness to a graver offence attracting higher punishment, including imprisonment for life.

definitions.definition: Intoxication, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a state in which a person is under the influence of any intoxicating substance such that their capacity for knowledge, intent, understanding, or consent is materially affected. Where such intoxication was administered without the person's knowledge or against their will, it may excuse the person from criminal liability if they were incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law. Where intoxication was self-induced, the person is presumed to have the same knowledge they would have had in a sober state.
definitions.plain_english: Intoxication means being under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or any other substance that impairs a person's ability to think clearly, understand what they are doing, or form a deliberate intention. If someone was made intoxicated without their knowledge or against their will, they may not be held criminally responsible for what they did while in that state. However, if a person voluntarily got intoxicated, the law generally treats them as if they were sober and fully aware of their actions.
real_world_examples: A man in Maharashtra is drugged by business rivals who secretly spike his drink at a party; he then signs a document transferring property under that influence. The consent given is not valid under Section 28 as he was intoxicated without his knowledge.

A labourer in Delhi is forcibly made to consume liquor by his employer and, in that state, causes hurt to a co-worker without knowing the nature of his act. He may be excused from criminal liability under Section 23 as the intoxication was against his will.

A person in Bengaluru voluntarily consumes large quantities of alcohol at a bar and then commits theft. Under Section 24, he is presumed to have the same knowledge and intent as if he were sober, and remains fully liable for the offence.

A woman in Mumbai is given a sedative in her food without her knowledge by a relative, and in that incapacitated state she is made to sign away her inheritance rights. Her consent is rendered invalid under Section 28 as she was unable to understand the nature and consequence of her act due to intoxication.

A driver in Chennai voluntarily takes cannabis and then drives rashly, causing an accident. His intoxication does not reduce his liability, as it was self-induced and he is presumed to have the knowledge of the risk of driving in such a state.

A victim in Kolkata is forcibly administered alcohol by an attacker before being assaulted. The attacker may face additional culpability, while the victim's incapacitated state is relevant to assessing absence of consent.
what_it_covers: A state of incapacity produced by alcohol, drugs, or any intoxicating substance that renders a person unable to know the nature of their act or that it is wrong or contrary to law.
Intoxication administered to a person without their knowledge or against their will, which may fully excuse criminal liability under Section 23.
Intoxication that renders a person unable to understand the nature and consequence of a consent given, thereby invalidating that consent under Section 28.
Voluntary intoxication where the person is presumed by law to retain the same knowledge they would have had if sober, maintaining criminal liability under Section 24.
The intoxicated state of a person who performs an act that would otherwise be an offence, entitling others to exercise the right of private defence against that act under Section 36.
what_it_excludes: Mild consumption of alcohol or substances that does not materially impair a person's capacity to know the nature of their act or form requisite intent.
Voluntary intoxication as a complete defence to a crime — a self-intoxicated person is not excused from liability and is treated as having full knowledge of their actions under Section 24.
States of mental incapacity arising from unsoundness of mind or mental illness unrelated to any intoxicating substance, which are governed separately under provisions dealing with unsound mind.
Feigned or pretended intoxication used as a strategic excuse, which does not attract the protections afforded to genuinely intoxicated persons.
Consent given while intoxicated that is claimed to be valid where the person was capable of understanding the nature and consequence of the act despite being under some influence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether intoxication applies determines if a person escapes criminal liability entirely (involuntary intoxication under Section 23), retains full liability with presumed knowledge (voluntary intoxication under Section 24), or renders a consent legally void (Section 28); it also determines whether another person may lawfully exercise the right of private defence against the intoxicated person's act under Section 36.

definitions.definition: Investigation, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the process conducted by a police officer or an officer-in-charge of a police station into an alleged offence, including the collection of evidence, examination of persons, and steps taken preliminary to proceedings before a Court. An investigation directed by law preliminary to a proceeding before a Court constitutes a stage of a judicial proceeding, though it may not take place before a Court. It also includes any investigation directed by a Court according to law and conducted under the authority of a Court.
definitions.plain_english: An investigation is the official process by which police or authorised officers look into whether a crime has been committed. This includes gathering evidence, questioning people, visiting crime scenes, and recording information about the alleged offence. It happens before a case goes to court and is a formal step in the criminal justice process. Even though it does not happen inside a courtroom, it is treated as an important legal stage.
real_world_examples: A Delhi Police officer investigating a rape complaint under Section 64 BNS by recording the victim's statement, collecting forensic evidence, and visiting the crime scene — this entire process constitutes an 'investigation' under Section 199.

A Station House Officer (SHO) at a Mumbai police station who, after registering an FIR for kidnapping, directs constables to gather witness statements and CCTV footage — the collective steps taken by the police constitute an investigation.

A Magistrate in Chennai directs a police officer to investigate the boundaries of land in a property dispute before the matter proceeds to trial — this court-directed inquiry conducted under the authority of the Court is a stage of judicial proceeding and thus an investigation.

A public servant in Kolkata, during a departmental inquiry, requires a private citizen to appear at a police station for questioning regarding a cognizable offence under Section 67 BNS — the attendance requirement and questioning process form part of the investigation.

A police officer in Hyderabad fails to register an FIR under Section 173 of BNSS in relation to an acid attack offence under Section 124 BNS — the failure to initiate the investigative process exposes the officer to punishment under Section 199 BNS.

An officer-in-charge of a police station in Lucknow, during investigation of a gang rape case, authorises in writing the publication of the victim's identity for purposes of the investigation under Section 72 BNS — this is a lawful exercise of authority during investigation.
what_it_covers: The process conducted by a police officer or SHO after registration of an FIR, including collection of evidence, examination of witnesses, and arrest of accused persons.

An inquiry or investigation directed by law as a preliminary step before proceedings before a Court, even if it does not take place in a courtroom — treated as a stage of judicial proceeding under Section 229 BNS.
An investigation directed by a Court and conducted under the Court's authority, such as when a Magistrate deputes an officer to ascertain facts on the spot.
Steps taken by an officer-in-charge of a police station in good faith during investigation, such as authorising publication of a victim's identity under Section 72 BNS.
Recording of information under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, in relation to cognizable offences listed under Section 199 BNS.
what_it_excludes: Internal departmental inquiries or administrative proceedings by government bodies that are not connected to a criminal offence or directed by a Court or law.
Civil proceedings, suits, or arbitrations aimed at resolving private disputes, which are not investigations into criminal offences.
Trial proceedings before a Court, which are a subsequent and distinct stage from investigation in the criminal justice process.
Informal or private fact-finding exercises undertaken by individuals, organisations, or media without legal authority or direction of law.
Proceedings before a quasi-judicial body such as a tribunal or commission that are not directed by law as preliminary to criminal proceedings before a Court.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a particular process qualifies as an 'investigation' determines whether a public servant can be punished under Section 199 BNS for disobeying directions of law regulating the manner of investigation or for failing to record cognizable offence information. It also determines whether false statements made during such a process attract liability for giving false evidence under Section 229 BNS, since an investigation directed by law is a stage of a judicial proceeding.

definitions.definition: "Judge" means a person who is officially designated as a Judge and includes a person who is empowered by law to give, in any legal proceeding, civil or criminal, a definitive judgment, or a judgment which, if not appealed against, would be definitive, or a judgment which, if confirmed by some other authority, would be definitive; or who is one of a body of persons which body of persons is empowered by law to give such a judgment. A Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in respect of a charge on which he has power to sentence to fine or imprisonment, with or without appeal, is a Judge.
definitions.plain_english: A Judge is any person who is officially given the title of Judge, or anyone who has the legal authority to make a final decision in a court case — whether civil or criminal. This includes magistrates who have the power to convict and sentence someone to a fine or jail. It also includes members of a group of decision-makers who together have the power to deliver such final rulings.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Judge in a district court in Mumbai presiding over a murder trial and delivering a conviction — this person is a 'Judge' under the BNS.
A Chief Judicial Magistrate in Lucknow hearing a criminal complaint and sentencing the accused to three months imprisonment — the Magistrate qualifies as a 'Judge' for purposes of the Sanhita.

A member of a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court hearing an appeal in a criminal matter — each member of that bench is a 'Judge' since the bench collectively has power to give a definitive judgment.
An Executive Magistrate who has been specifically empowered by law to try certain offences and impose fines would qualify as a Judge under this definition when exercising that judicial power.
A Special Court judge designated under a specific statute (such as a POCSO court in Delhi) hearing a case involving offences under the BNS — that judge falls squarely within this definition.
A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class in Bengaluru trying a cheating case punishable with imprisonment — such a magistrate is a Judge under the Sanhita since he has power to impose imprisonment.
what_it_covers: A person officially designated as a Judge by law, such as a High Court Judge or Sessions Judge.
A Magistrate who has the power to sentence an accused to fine or imprisonment, with or without appeal.
Any member of a bench or body of persons collectively empowered by law to deliver a definitive judgment in a civil or criminal proceeding.
A person empowered to give a judgment that becomes final if not appealed against, even if it is subject to appeal.
A person whose judgment, though not immediately final, becomes definitive upon confirmation by a higher authority.
what_it_excludes: An Executive Magistrate performing purely administrative or executive functions who has no power to sentence to fine or imprisonment.
An arbitrator or tribunal member whose authority derives from contract or private agreement rather than statutory empowerment to give a judicially binding definitive judgment.
A police officer or investigating officer who records statements or makes orders during investigation but has no power to give a judicially definitive judgment.
A public servant acting in a quasi-judicial capacity only for preliminary or procedural matters without power to impose criminal sentence or render a definitive civil judgment.
A witness, assessor, or court official (such as a clerk or reader) who participates in court proceedings but does not have decision-making or sentencing authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'Judge' is critical because several offences under the BNS — including those relating to false evidence, fabricating evidence, contempt-adjacent conduct, and offences against judicial proceedings under Section 15 — can only be committed 'before a Judge' or in relation to a judicial proceeding; whether a person qualifies as a Judge determines whether these penal provisions are triggered. Injuries or corrupt acts directed at a person fitting this definition attract specific aggravated liability, making the precise scope of 'Judge' essential to prosecution and defence alike.

definitions.definition: The term 'judgment' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 242, it refers to a definitive legal pronouncement or decision made by a Judge or Court in any legal proceeding, civil or criminal, which determines the rights or liabilities of parties and is intended to be used as an authoritative record of the Court's conclusion. It includes a judgment which, if not appealed against, would be definitive, or one which, if confirmed by some other authority, would be definitive.
definitions.plain_english: A judgment is the official final decision given by a court or judge at the end of a legal case. It tells the parties what the court has decided about the matter before it — for example, whether someone is guilty or innocent, or who wins a civil dispute. It is a formal, written record of the court's conclusion that carries legal authority.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Court in Mumbai delivers a written judgment convicting an accused person under BNS for culpable homicide and sentencing him to ten years of rigorous imprisonment — this constitutes a judgment as contemplated under Section 242.
The Delhi High Court pronounces a judgment acquitting an accused charged with cheating under BNS after finding that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

A Magistrate in Chennai passes a judgment in a summary trial finding a person guilty of causing hurt under BNS and imposing a fine, which becomes definitive if not appealed within the prescribed period.

The Supreme Court of India delivers a judgment confirming the conviction and death sentence of an accused convicted of gang rape and murder under BNS provisions, making it the final and definitive pronouncement in the matter.
A family court in Kolkata passes a judgment in a matrimonial case determining issues of cruelty under BNS, which is used as evidence of the court's final decision in subsequent proceedings.
what_it_covers: A conviction or acquittal order passed by a Sessions Court or High Court at the conclusion of a criminal trial under BNS.
A Magistrate's final order in a summary or warrant trial that determines guilt and imposes fine or imprisonment, whether or not subject to appeal.
An appellate court's final pronouncement confirming, modifying, or setting aside a lower court's decision in a BNS matter.
A judgment passed by a body of judges acting judicially as a bench, such as a Division Bench of a High Court, determining criminal liability under BNS.
A definitive ruling by a competent court that, if confirmed by a superior authority, attains finality in a proceeding involving an offence under BNS.
what_it_excludes: Interlocutory orders or interim directions passed during the pendency of a case, such as bail orders or orders for adjournment, which do not finally determine the matter.
Administrative or executive decisions made by government authorities or public servants that are not rendered in the exercise of judicial power by a Court.
Opinions, recommendations, or reports of inquiry commissions or fact-finding bodies that lack judicial power to give a definitive determination.
Orders passed by a police officer or investigating agency, such as a closure report or charge sheet, which are not judicial pronouncements.
Consent terms or settlement agreements between parties that have not been incorporated into or confirmed by a formal court order rendered judicially.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 242 of the BNS, giving or fabricating false evidence in a judicial proceeding with intent to procure a conviction or acquittal turns critically on whether the proceeding culminates in a 'judgment'; the severity of punishment prescribed depends on whether the false evidence was intended to influence such a definitive judicial pronouncement. The integrity of the judgment as a legal instrument is what Section 242 seeks to protect, making the correct identification of what constitutes a judgment essential to determining criminal liability for offences against justice.

definitions.definition: A judicial proceeding includes any proceeding taken by law before a public servant as such, or before an arbitrator, and encompasses all stages thereof, including: (i) a trial before a Court-martial; (ii) an investigation directed by law preliminary to a proceeding before a Court, though such investigation may not take place before a Court; and (iii) an investigation directed by a Court according to law and conducted under the authority of a Court, though such investigation may not take place before a Court.
definitions.plain_english: A 'judicial proceeding' refers to any formal legal process conducted before a court, a government official acting in an official capacity, or an arbitrator. It is not limited to what happens inside a courtroom — it also covers police or court-directed investigations that happen before or outside the main trial. Even a preliminary inquiry by a Magistrate to decide whether someone should be sent for trial counts as a stage of a judicial proceeding.
real_world_examples: A witness gives a sworn statement before a Metropolitan Magistrate in Delhi during a committal inquiry to decide whether the accused should be sent to the Sessions Court for trial — this inquiry is a stage of a judicial proceeding under BNS.

A Court Commissioner appointed by the Bombay High Court visits a disputed property in Pune to record the positions of boundary markers on oath; any false statement made during this on-site investigation constitutes giving false evidence in a judicial proceeding.

During a CBI investigation directed by the Supreme Court into a corruption case, a public servant makes a false statement under oath before the investigating officer — this investigation is a stage of a judicial proceeding and the false statement amounts to fabricating false evidence.

A soldier is tried before a Court-martial in Bengaluru Cantonment for an offence under military law; any witness who gives false testimony during this trial is committing an offence in a judicial proceeding as a Court-martial trial is explicitly recognised as a judicial proceeding.

A revenue officer deputed by a District Court to ascertain on the spot the boundaries of agricultural land in a land-dispute suit records false statements from a party on oath — this constitutes giving false evidence in a judicial proceeding.

An arbitration proceeding under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 initiated before a registered arbitrator in Mumbai to resolve a commercial dispute is a judicial proceeding, and any fabricated documentary evidence submitted therein attracts liability under Section 228 read with Section 229 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Trials conducted before any civil or criminal court, including Sessions Courts, Magistrate Courts, and High Courts in India.
A trial before a Court-martial, as expressly stated in Section 229 of the BNS.
Preliminary investigations directed by law before a court proceeding, such as a Magistrate's committal inquiry, even if conducted outside a courtroom.
Investigations directed by a court and conducted under its authority, such as a local commissioner's inquiry or a court-appointed expert investigation.
Proceedings before a public servant acting in an official judicial or quasi-judicial capacity, such as a revenue tribunal or an inquiry officer.
Arbitration proceedings conducted before a legally appointed arbitrator.
what_it_excludes: Purely administrative or executive proceedings that are not directed by or before a court or public servant acting in a judicial capacity, such as departmental disciplinary inquiries not sanctioned by a court.
Legislative proceedings, such as parliamentary committees or state assembly proceedings, which are not judicial in nature.
Private dispute resolution mechanisms such as informal mediation or negotiation sessions that have no legal sanction or authority and are not conducted before a public servant or arbitrator.
Investigations conducted solely on police initiative without any direction from a court or legal mandate to be used in a judicial forum at a specific stage.
Internal corporate or institutional inquiries not recognised or directed by any court or law as preliminary to a judicial proceeding.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a proceeding qualifies as a 'judicial proceeding' is decisive in determining criminal liability under Sections 228, 229, 257, and 267 of the BNS: only false evidence given or fabricated within a judicial proceeding attracts the higher punishment of up to seven years' imprisonment, and only conduct before a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding triggers the offence of intentional insult or interruption under Section 267. If the proceeding does not qualify as a judicial proceeding, the acts may either go unpunished or attract lesser penalties.

definitions.definition: An act is 'justified by law' when it is expressly or impliedly authorised or sanctioned by law, such that the person performing it incurs no criminal liability; and by extension under Section 17, a person who by reason of a mistake of fact (and not a mistake of law) in good faith believes himself to be so justified is equally protected, provided the act done falls within the scope of such believed legal authority.
definitions.plain_english: An action is 'justified by law' when the law itself gives a person the right or authority to do it, making it perfectly legal. Even if the person is factually mistaken about the situation but genuinely and honestly believed the law permitted the action, they are still protected from criminal liability. However, being wrong about what the law says (as opposed to being wrong about the facts) does not provide this protection.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Mumbai arrests a person she reasonably and honestly believes has committed a cognizable offence based on available evidence at the scene; even if the person later turns out to be innocent, the officer's act of arrest is justified by law and she commits no offence.

A private citizen in Delhi witnesses a man stabbing another person in broad daylight and restrains the attacker until police arrive; even if the 'stabbing' was later found to be part of a film shoot, the citizen's bona fide belief that he was exercising his lawful power to apprehend a murderer in the act justifies his conduct.

A jailer in Chennai who continues to detain a prisoner genuinely believing, due to a clerical error in court records, that the prisoner's sentence has not yet expired acts under a mistaken belief of fact rather than law; his detention may be justified by law if the mistake was honest and in good faith.

A forest officer in Assam seizes timber from a vehicle believing in good faith, based on available documents and the area of transit, that it constitutes illegal contraband under applicable rules; even if the timber was validly licensed, the officer's factual mistake made in good faith means the act is justified by law.

A magistrate in Kolkata orders the demolition of a structure genuinely believing, on the basis of survey records placed before him, that it encroaches on government land; the act is justified by law even if the records later prove inaccurate, as the honest factual belief supports the legal authorisation.
what_it_covers: Acts expressly authorised by statute, court order, or other legal instrument, such as a police officer executing a valid arrest warrant.

Acts performed by a private person who honestly and in good faith believes, due to a mistake of fact, that the law authorises them to act — such as a bystander apprehending someone they genuinely believe to have committed a cognizable offence.
Official acts performed by public servants within the scope of their lawful duties, including seizure of property, use of reasonable force during arrest, or enforcement of quarantine orders.
Acts done under a court's direction or order, including a court-appointed receiver taking possession of disputed property based on a decree.
what_it_excludes: Acts done under a mistake of law — if a person incorrectly believes a law permits something when it does not, that mistaken legal interpretation does not constitute justification by law.
Acts performed in bad faith or without honest belief in legal authority, even if the person claims to have believed they were justified — the good faith requirement must be genuinely satisfied.

Excessive or disproportionate acts that go beyond what the law actually authorises or what a person could honestly believe the law authorises, such as a police officer using lethal force where it is wholly unwarranted.

definitions.definition: Kidnapping as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 comprises two forms: kidnapping from India, which means conveying any person beyond the limits of India without consent or against lawful authority; and kidnapping from lawful guardianship, which means taking or enticing any minor under sixteen years (male) or eighteen years (female), or any person of unsound mind, out of the keeping of a lawful guardian without the guardian's consent.
definitions.plain_english: Kidnapping means forcibly or deceitfully taking away a person — especially a child or someone who cannot protect themselves — from the care of their legal guardian or from India itself, without proper consent. It is different from simply holding someone against their will. The law pays special attention to children and mentally vulnerable persons who cannot consent on their own behalf.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi lures a 14-year-old girl away from her parents' home by promising her a modelling job, thereby taking her out of the lawful guardianship of her parents without their consent — this constitutes kidnapping from lawful guardianship.
A trafficker in Mumbai convinces a mentally unsound adult to board a flight to Dubai without the knowledge or consent of the person's court-appointed guardian — this amounts to kidnapping from India.

In a child custody dispute in Chennai, a non-custodial parent takes the 10-year-old child from school during the other parent's custody period and moves to another city without consent — this constitutes kidnapping from lawful guardianship.

A gang in Bihar kidnaps a 7-year-old boy from his village and carries him to another state with the intention of stealing ornaments from his person, attracting the specific offence under Section 97 of the Sanhita.

An organised crime syndicate operating across Rajasthan and Haryana abducts young women from their families and transports them across state borders with intent to force them into marriage — constituting kidnapping as part of organised crime under Section 111.
what_it_covers: Taking or enticing a male under 16 or female under 18 years of age out of the keeping of a lawful guardian without the guardian's consent.
Conveying any person beyond the geographical limits of India without that person's consent or against a lawful authority.
Taking or enticing a person of unsound mind out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without consent.
Kidnapping a child under ten years of age with the intention of dishonestly taking movable property from the child's person (Section 97).
Kidnapping a woman with intent to compel her into marriage or illicit intercourse (Section 87).
Kidnapping as a continuing unlawful activity carried out by an organised crime syndicate (Section 111).
what_it_excludes: Abduction of an adult of sound mind who accompanies the accused voluntarily and with full consent, which falls under a separate offence of abduction rather than kidnapping.
Wrongful confinement of a person within India without any removal from guardianship, which constitutes a distinct offence under the Sanhita.
A lawful guardian themselves moving the child to another location in exercise of their own guardianship rights, as consent of the guardian is present.
Rescue of a person from unlawful detention by a public authority acting under due process of law.
Persuading an adult of sound mind who is not under any guardianship to travel to another country, where no force, deceit, or incapacity is involved.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes kidnapping determines the applicability of serious penal consequences under the Sanhita, including imprisonment up to seven years for kidnapping a child with intent to steal (Section 97), up to ten years for kidnapping a woman for compelled marriage or illicit intercourse (Section 87), and potential life imprisonment or death when kidnapping forms part of organised crime causing death (Section 111). It also triggers the right of private defence extending to causing death under Section 38 when an assault is committed with the intention of kidnapping.

definitions.definition: A person 'kidnaps' within the meaning of Section 87 when they take or carry away any woman with intent that she may be compelled to marry any person against her will, or in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, as defined under Section 137 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which recognises two kinds of kidnapping: kidnapping from India and kidnapping from lawful guardianship.
definitions.plain_english: Kidnapping means unlawfully taking or carrying away a person — in this context specifically a woman — without her consent and against her will, typically to force her into marriage or sexual exploitation. It involves removing someone from the protection of their legal guardian or from India entirely. The key element is that the act is done without the person's free and genuine agreement.
real_world_examples: A man in Uttar Pradesh, with the help of his relatives, forcibly takes a woman from her home in order to conduct a forced marriage ceremony in a village, threatening her family to prevent interference.
A group of persons in Rajasthan abducts a young woman from a mela and transports her to another district with the intent of compelling her to marry a local landlord who had arranged the kidnapping.

In Mumbai, a woman is lured from her college under false pretences and then held captive in a flat, with perpetrators planning to force her into illicit intercourse with a third party for financial gain.
In a rural area of Bihar, a woman is taken by members of a rival family during a land dispute and threatened with forced marriage to weaken her family's legal claim over property.
A trafficking network in West Bengal deceives a woman with a job offer, transports her to another state, and holds her with intent to coerce her into sexual exploitation against her will.
what_it_covers: Taking a woman by force or deceit with intent to compel her into marriage against her will.
Carrying away a woman knowing it is likely she will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse.
Removing a minor woman from the custody of her lawful guardian without the guardian's consent for any unlawful purpose covered under Section 87.
Inducing a woman to go from any place through criminal intimidation or abuse of authority with intent that she will be forced into illicit intercourse with another person.
Transporting a woman across regions or state lines with the knowledge that she is to be subjected to forced sexual exploitation or compelled marriage.
what_it_excludes: A woman who voluntarily and freely accompanies a person without any coercion, deceit, or criminal intent — even if family members disapprove.
Lawful custody or restraint exercised by a parent, legal guardian, or court-appointed authority acting within their legal rights.
Abduction or taking of a male person, which would be governed by separate provisions and not specifically by Section 87.
Cases where a woman is taken with her full and informed consent and without any intention of forced marriage or illicit intercourse.
Mere criminal intimidation or inducement that does not result in the woman actually going from any place, as the act of movement or taking must be established.

It also governs whether ancillary liability arises for those who use criminal intimidation or abuse of authority to induce a woman's movement, expanding the scope of prosecution beyond the primary perpetrator.

definitions.definition: A person acts 'knowingly' when they are aware of a fact or circumstance with certainty or near-certainty, or are conscious that a particular consequence will or is substantially likely to result from their act or omission. It denotes actual subjective awareness of the relevant fact, circumstance, or consequence at the time the act or omission is committed, as distinguished from mere suspicion, negligence, or constructive notice.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'knowingly' means that a person is fully aware of what they are doing and what the likely result will be, yet they still go ahead with the act or fail to act. It is not enough to say 'I did not know' — if the facts show that the person clearly understood the situation, the law treats them as having acted knowingly. This is stronger than being careless (negligent) but may not always require the specific desire to cause harm (intention).
real_world_examples: A jailor in a Delhi prison is aware that food supplied by the government for a prisoner is not being delivered to that prisoner, and continues to withhold it day after day. Even if he does not actively wish the prisoner to die, he is acting knowingly because he is fully aware that starvation is the likely outcome of his continued omission.

A pharmacist in Mumbai sells a drug that he knows has been adulterated or is dangerous to a customer who requests it for medicinal purposes. Even though he does not intend the customer's death, he acts knowingly because he is aware of the drug's harmful nature at the point of sale.

A civil engineer overseeing construction of a bridge in Hyderabad is made aware through written reports that a particular structural component is defective and likely to cause collapse, but proceeds without repair or warning. Any resulting injury occurs as a result of his knowingly continuing a dangerous situation.

A person in Chennai who receives stolen goods from a known thief and resells them, having been explicitly told that the goods were stolen, acts knowingly — the awareness of the stolen character of the property is established by the circumstances of how and from whom he received them.

A factory owner in Surat who is informed by safety inspectors that certain machinery poses a serious risk of injury to workers, but fails to shut it down or warn workers, causes any resulting injury knowingly, even if his primary motivation was merely to avoid financial loss from shutting production.

A bank employee in Kolkata who is clearly aware that a transaction being processed involves proceeds of fraud — because the customer explicitly stated so or the documentation is obviously forged — but nonetheless processes it, participates in the offence knowingly.
what_it_covers: A person who is clearly informed of a dangerous fact or circumstance and nonetheless proceeds with the act or omission that causes harm.
A person who, due to their professional position or prior communications, has received explicit notice of the relevant risk or consequence and fails to act accordingly.
Cooperative or joint acts where each participant is aware of the common unlawful purpose and the likely consequence, even if they do not share a specific intent to cause the ultimate harm.
Deliberate omissions where the person is fully conscious that their failure to act will cause a specific harm, such as withholding food from a person in one's custody.

Acts done in the face of near-certain consequences that a reasonable person in the actor's position would have been fully aware of, especially where the actor has special knowledge due to their role or information received.
what_it_excludes: Acts done out of mere carelessness, inadvertence, or lack of attention, where the person genuinely had no awareness of the risk — these fall under negligence or rashness, not knowingly.
Situations where a person had only a vague suspicion or an unverified rumour about a harmful fact, without sufficient certainty to constitute actual knowledge.
Acts committed under a genuine and reasonable mistake of fact, where the person honestly believed in a state of affairs that, if true, would have made the act innocent.
Persons acting under coercion or compulsion who had no real choice to avoid the act, and whose awareness of the consequence did not translate into voluntary participation.
Cases where the harmful consequence was entirely unforeseen and could not have been anticipated by the person in the circumstances, even with due care.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person acts 'knowingly' is decisive in determining liability under Sections 289 and 290 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, where knowing participation in a negligent or harmful act elevates culpability beyond mere rashness. It also affects the degree of punishment — an act done knowingly attracts greater criminal liability than one done negligently or rashly, as it reflects a higher degree of moral blameworthiness in the eyes of the law.
