definitions.definition: The term 'likely' is not formally defined in the Sanhita, but is used throughout the Act to denote a reasonable probability or reasonable expectation that a particular consequence or event will occur, as distinguished from a mere possibility; it connotes that a result is more probable than not in the ordinary course of events, or that a reasonable person would anticipate such an outcome given the circumstances.
definitions.plain_english: The word 'likely' means something that is reasonably expected or probable to happen, not just a remote or unlikely chance. It is stronger than 'possible' but does not require absolute certainty. In legal terms, if someone does an act knowing it is 'likely' to cause harm, they are treated as having anticipated that harm as a probable outcome.
real_world_examples: A person fires a gun into a crowded market in Mumbai — it is 'likely' that someone will be injured or killed, making the shooter criminally liable under Section 53 even if no specific target was intended.
A driver in Delhi drives at excessive speed through a school zone during dismissal hours — it is 'likely' that a child may be hit, establishing the element of criminal negligence or rashness.

A factory owner in Surat releases toxic chemical waste into a river knowing that downstream villages use it for drinking water — it is 'likely' that residents will suffer injury or death, attracting liability under relevant sections.

A person spreads false rumours of communal violence in a sensitive neighbourhood in Hyderabad — it is 'likely' that riots or public disorder will break out, satisfying the mental element required for offences against public tranquillity.
A contractor uses substandard materials in constructing a building in Chennai knowing the structure is 'likely' to collapse, thereby endangering lives of future occupants.
what_it_covers: A consequence that a reasonable person in the same circumstances would anticipate as probable, even without certainty of its occurrence.
Acts where the accused knew or had reason to know that harm to person, property, or public order was a probable result of their conduct.
Situations where the natural and ordinary course of events following a particular act would, in the experience of a reasonable person, lead to the anticipated harmful outcome.
what_it_excludes: Outcomes that are merely possible or speculative in a remote or far-fetched sense — bare possibility does not meet the 'likely' threshold.
Consequences that require an extraordinary, unprecedented, or wholly unforeseeable chain of events to materialise.
Situations where the accused had no reason, given the facts and circumstances, to anticipate the harmful result — i.e., purely accidental or unforeseen outcomes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a consequence was 'likely' directly determines the accused's culpable mental state under the Sanhita — it can be the difference between criminal liability and innocence, as many offences under Section 53 require that the accused knew or had reason to believe the harmful result was likely to occur. It also affects whether an act constitutes culpable homicide, grievous hurt, mischief, or other serious offences by establishing the required degree of foresight or knowledge.

Why it matters: Whether a consequence was 'likely' directly determines the accused's culpable mental state under the Sanhita — it can be the difference between criminal liability and innocence, as many offences under Section 53 require that the accused knew or had reason to believe the harmful result was likely to occur. It also affects whether an act constitutes culpable homicide, grievous hurt, mischief, or other serious offences by establishing the required degree of foresight or knowledge.

definitions.definition: A 'local authority' refers to a municipal corporation, municipality, panchayat, cantonment board, port trust, or any other body constituted by or under any law for the time being in force for the purpose of local self-government or management of a local area, whose property is subject to enhanced protection under Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: A local authority is any officially constituted body responsible for governing or managing a specific local area, such as a city council, town municipality, village panchayat, or cantonment board. These bodies are set up by law to provide public services and manage public assets within their jurisdiction. Property belonging to such bodies receives special legal protection under the law.
real_world_examples: Theft of streetlights, benches, or signage owned by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) from a public park in Mumbai.
Stealing tools, equipment, or construction materials belonging to a Gram Panchayat in a rural village in Uttar Pradesh that were meant for a public works project.
Theft of water supply pipes or meters installed by the Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board, a body functioning under local authority.
Removal of boundary stones or survey equipment owned by a Cantonment Board in Pune from a cantonment area.
Theft of garbage collection vehicles or waste management equipment belonging to the Delhi Municipal Corporation from a municipal depot.
Stealing solar panels or LED lights installed by a Port Trust authority along a harbour road in Kolkata.
what_it_covers: Municipal corporations and municipalities constituted under State Municipal Acts, such as Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation or Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation.
Gram Panchayats and Panchayati Raj institutions established under State Panchayati Raj Acts governing rural local bodies.
Cantonment Boards established under the Cantonments Act, 2006, managing civil areas within military stations.
Port Trusts constituted under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, managing major ports and their properties.
Urban Development Authorities or Improvement Trusts constituted under specific State laws for local area management.
what_it_excludes: Central Government ministries and departments, which fall under the broader category of 'Government' rather than local authority.
Private companies or corporations, even if they provide public utility services such as private water supply or electricity distribution firms.
State Government bodies and State public sector undertakings that operate at the State level rather than at a local area level.
Autonomous bodies or statutory commissions functioning at the national level, such as the National Human Rights Commission or Election Commission of India.
Cooperatives and registered societies, even those serving community purposes, unless specifically constituted under a local governance statute.
definitions.why_it_matters: If the stolen property belongs to a local authority, the offence of theft is aggravated under Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, attracting a punishment of up to seven years of imprisonment along with a fine, as opposed to the lesser punishment prescribed for ordinary theft under Section 303. This classification determines whether an accused faces enhanced penal consequences, making the identity of the property owner a critical factor in prosecution and sentencing.

definitions.definition: A lottery, as used in Section 297 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any scheme or arrangement in which tickets, lots, numbers, or figures are drawn and prizes or benefits are distributed by chance, not being a State lottery or a lottery authorised by the State Government. It includes any proposal to pay a sum, deliver goods, or do or forbear from doing anything for the benefit of any person upon any event or contingency relative to the drawing of such ticket, lot, number, or figure.
definitions.plain_english: A lottery is a game of chance where people buy tickets or numbers and winners are chosen randomly through a draw. Under this law, running an unofficial lottery — one not approved by a State Government — is a criminal offence. This includes any scheme where someone promises money, goods, or any other benefit to a person based on the result of an unauthorised draw.
real_world_examples: A shopkeeper in Pune sets up a private 'lucky draw' scheme where customers pay to pick numbered chits from a box, with cash prizes for winners — this is an unauthorised lottery under Section 297.

An organiser in a Delhi residential colony runs a weekly raffle where residents buy tickets and prizes are distributed based on a random number draw, without any State Government authorisation, making it an illegal lottery office.
A WhatsApp group admin in Chennai collects money from members, assigns each a number, conducts an online random draw, and pays out winnings — this constitutes operating an illegal lottery.

A trader in Kolkata distributes printed pamphlets promising to pay Rs. 50,000 to anyone whose purchased ticket number matches the draw result of an unrecognised private lottery — this amounts to publishing a proposal related to an unauthorised lottery, punishable with fine.

A fair organiser in a rural Maharashtra mela operates a spinning-wheel game where participants pay money and win prizes based on where the wheel stops, structured as a ticket-based draw — this qualifies as keeping a lottery office under Section 297.
what_it_covers: Any private draw, raffle, or scheme where participants purchase tickets or lots and prizes are distributed by chance without State Government approval.
Online or digital lottery-style schemes where numbers or figures are randomly drawn and prizes or benefits are promised to participants.
Any published proposal, advertisement, or communication offering money, goods, or other benefits contingent on the outcome of an unauthorised lottery draw.
Physical offices, premises, or digital platforms set up specifically for the purpose of operating or managing an unauthorised lottery.
Any scheme involving chits, numbered cards, or figures where winners are determined by a random draw and no State sanction exists.
what_it_excludes: State lotteries organised and operated directly by a State Government under applicable state law, such as the Kerala State Lotteries or Maharashtra State Lottery.
Lotteries expressly authorised by a State Government under a valid statutory framework or licence, which are exempt from criminal liability under Section 297.
Skill-based competitions or contests where the outcome is determined by merit, knowledge, or ability rather than pure chance, as these do not constitute lotteries.
Games of chance that do not involve a ticket, lot, number, or figure draw mechanism, and which are separately governed by other provisions.
Social or religious fundraising draws where no monetary consideration or profit motive exists and no formal ticket or draw system is operated.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an arrangement qualifies as a lottery under Section 297 determines criminal liability: operating an unauthorised lottery office attracts imprisonment up to six months and/or fine, while publishing proposals related to such a lottery attracts a fine up to five thousand rupees. The distinction between an authorised State lottery and an unauthorised lottery is the pivotal factor that either shields or exposes the organiser to prosecution.

definitions.definition: Whoever commits house-trespass having taken precautions to conceal such house-trespass from some person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser from the building, tent or vessel which is the subject of the trespass, is said to commit lurking house-trespass.
definitions.plain_english: Lurking house-trespass is when someone illegally enters a building, tent, or vessel and deliberately takes steps to hide their entry from the owner, occupier, or anyone else who has the right to remove them. The key element is the deliberate concealment — the trespasser is not just sneaking in, but actively trying to avoid being detected by those who have authority over the premises. It is a more serious form of ordinary house-trespass because of this intentional stealth.
real_world_examples: A person enters a locked residential flat in Mumbai by quietly picking the lock late at night while the family is asleep, deliberately avoiding making any noise so that the occupants do not discover his presence — this constitutes lurking house-trespass.

A thief in Delhi crawls through a low window of a shopkeeper's godown after closing hours, wearing dark clothing and avoiding lit areas so that the night watchman patrolling the premises does not spot him entering.

An estranged family member, who has been legally barred from entering an ancestral house in Chennai, enters through the rear servant's entrance during the afternoon when the owners are out, deliberately timing the entry to avoid detection by the caretaker.

A person in Kolkata hides inside a commercial warehouse before it closes, then conceals himself behind stored goods so that the security guard who locks up does not find him — effectively committing lurking house-trespass by concealing his continued presence from persons with the right to eject him.

An individual in Bengaluru climbs over the boundary wall of a gated residential bungalow at dusk, crouches behind bushes in the garden, and waits until lights go off before moving toward the house, taking active precautions to remain unseen by the owner or domestic staff.
what_it_covers: A person who enters a residential home through a back door in complete silence at night to avoid waking the family, thereby concealing his trespass from the occupants who have the right to eject him.
A trespasser who disguises himself as a maintenance worker to gain entry into an apartment building and then hides within the premises to avoid detection by the resident or security staff.

An individual who enters a tent or temporary structure (such as a construction site worker's camp) by crawling under the walls at a time and in a manner specifically calculated to avoid notice by the person responsible for the structure.
A person who enters a vessel (such as a houseboat) by boarding from the water side in darkness, deliberately avoiding the main gangway where the owner or caretaker might observe entry.
A trespasser who cuts off CCTV power supply before entering a property, as a precaution to conceal the house-trespass from the owner who monitors the premises remotely.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary house-trespass where the person enters openly without taking any precautions to conceal his entry from the occupier or owner — absence of concealment disqualifies it from being lurking house-trespass.

House-breaking, which is a distinct offence defined in the same section involving entry or exit through one of six specified means (such as using criminal force, opening a lock, scaling a wall), even if it also involves stealth.
Criminal trespass on open land or in outdoor spaces that do not constitute a building, tent, or vessel, as lurking house-trespass specifically requires the trespass to be upon such enclosed premises.

Entry made under a mistaken belief of having permission or lawful right to enter — where no deliberate precaution to conceal is taken, the concealment element is absent and the offence does not qualify.
Trespass where the concealment is directed only at a third party or a passerby and not at a person who has the right to exclude or eject the trespasser from the specific premises in question.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes lurking house-trespass determines whether higher penalties under Section 331 BNS apply — including imprisonment up to two years for the basic offence, extendable to three years if committed after sunset, up to ten years if done with preparation for causing hurt, and up to life imprisonment if grievous hurt is caused or death is attempted during its commission. The classification also affects whether offences committed in conjunction with it (such as theft or assault) attract the enhanced sentencing scales specifically prescribed for lurking house-trespass under Section 330.

definitions.definition: The term 'machinery' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 289, it refers to any mechanical apparatus, device, equipment, or assemblage of moving parts designed to perform work or transmit force, the rash or negligent use, operation, or custody of which is capable of endangering human life or causing hurt or injury to any person.
definitions.plain_english: Machinery means any mechanical device or equipment — such as factory machines, industrial equipment, construction tools, or heavy mechanised apparatus — that has the potential to cause harm if operated carelessly. The law is concerned with machinery that, if handled rashly or left without adequate safety precautions, could endanger people's lives or cause them physical injury. It covers both actively using machinery dangerously and negligently failing to secure it against foreseeable risks.
real_world_examples: A factory supervisor in Pune operates a power press machine without fitting the mandatory safety guards, resulting in a worker's hand being crushed — the supervisor's negligent omission regarding machinery in his care attracts liability under Section 289.

A construction contractor in Mumbai parks a running concrete mixer near a crowded footpath without any barriers or safety measures, endangering pedestrians passing by — this constitutes rash conduct with machinery likely to cause hurt.

A sugarcane mill operator in Uttar Pradesh knowingly allows a defective and unguarded centrifuge machine to run during a shift, despite knowing it poses danger to workers, resulting in injury to a labourer — this triggers the offence under Section 289.

A textile mill owner in Ahmedabad fails to switch off or fence off a running loom during a maintenance break, and a technician suffers grievous injury — the owner's negligent omission to take sufficient safety precautions with machinery under his care invites criminal liability.

A crane operator at a Kolkata port, while rashly manoeuvring the crane without proper signals, swings the jib dangerously close to dock workers, endangering their lives — this constitutes a rash act with machinery under Section 289.

An agricultural equipment dealer in Haryana demonstrates a running threshing machine to customers without safety covers, and a bystander is injured by the exposed blades — this amounts to negligent conduct with machinery.
what_it_covers: Industrial factory machines such as power presses, lathes, grinders, and centrifuges used in manufacturing units
Heavy construction equipment such as cranes, bulldozers, concrete mixers, and drilling rigs used on building sites
Agricultural machinery such as threshers, harvesters, tractors with power take-off attachments, and chaff cutters
Machinery in the possession or under the care of a person, whether owned or operated by them, that poses danger if left unguarded
Any mechanical device or apparatus being actively operated in a rash or negligent manner that is likely to cause hurt or endanger human life
what_it_excludes: Simple hand tools such as hammers, chisels, or hand-held knives that do not involve mechanical force or moving parts
Explosive substances, which are separately and specifically addressed under Section 288 of the same Act
Forging or counterfeiting instruments referred to in Section 181, which are governed by a distinct penal provision unrelated to negligent conduct
Chemical or poisonous substances that cause harm through their inherent nature rather than through mechanical operation
Electronic devices and software systems that do not involve physical moving parts or mechanical operation capable of direct physical endangerment
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as 'machinery' under the BNS determines if Section 289 is attracted, exposing the operator, owner, or custodian to criminal punishment of up to six months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to five thousand rupees for rash or negligent conduct. The definition also governs the scope of the duty of care — persons 'in possession or under whose care' machinery falls are legally obligated to guard against probable danger, and failure to do so constitutes a punishable omission.

definitions.definition: The term 'maiming' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 139 and 325, it denotes the act of deliberately inflicting severe physical injury upon a person or animal that permanently impairs, disables, or destroys the functional use of a body part or organ. In the context of Section 139, maiming specifically refers to the intentional infliction of such disabling or disfiguring injury upon a child so as to render that child suitable for exploitation in begging.
definitions.plain_english: Maiming means deliberately hurting someone so badly that a part of their body is permanently damaged, disabled, or destroyed. For example, breaking a child's limbs or blinding them on purpose so they look pitiful and can be used to beg for money. It is a severe form of intentional physical harm that goes beyond ordinary injury — the damage is lasting and takes away the normal use of that body part.
real_world_examples: A criminal gang in Mumbai deliberately breaks the legs of a seven-year-old child and then sends that child onto local train platforms to beg, exploiting the child's visible disability to evoke sympathy from commuters and collect more alms.

An organised begging syndicate in Delhi blinds a young child by pouring a corrosive liquid into the child's eyes so that the child appears more pitiable and generates greater income for the gang when stationed at traffic signals.

In a case reported in Kolkata, a trafficker amputates the fingers of a kidnapped child using a blade, permanently disfiguring the child's hand, in order to use the child as a begging prop outside a temple.

A person in Chennai deliberately severs a child's arm using a sharp instrument to make the child appear disabled and employs the child at a busy bus stand to solicit alms from the public, exploiting the permanent disability caused.

A cattle thief in rural Rajasthan intentionally hamstrings a farmer's ox — severing the tendons of its hind legs — rendering the animal permanently lame and useless for agricultural work, constituting maiming under Section 325.
what_it_covers: Deliberately breaking or crushing the limbs of a child so as to cause permanent disability for the purpose of using the child in begging.
Intentionally blinding, deafening, or otherwise destroying a sense organ of a child to exploit the resulting infirmity for begging activities.
Amputating or severing a body part of a child or causing permanent disfigurement to make the child appear pitiable for begging purposes.
Killing, poisoning, or permanently disabling an animal in a manner that constitutes mischief under Section 325, such as rendering a farm animal useless.
Any act using acid, instruments, or brute force that permanently impairs the functional capacity of a body part of a child used in begging.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or unintentional injuries that result in permanent disability, as maiming requires deliberate intent to incapacitate.
Temporary injuries or those that heal without lasting impairment, since maiming involves permanent or lasting destruction of bodily function.
Psychological or emotional harm alone, as maiming is confined to physical bodily injury that destroys or disables a body part.
Lawful medical procedures such as surgical amputations performed by a registered medical practitioner for therapeutic purposes.
Ordinary hurt or grievous hurt not connected to the purpose of employing or using the victim for begging, which would fall under different provisions.

definitions.definition: The term 'malicious' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 299, it denotes a state of mind characterised by a deliberate, wilful, and intentional desire to cause harm, insult, or injury to another — specifically, an intention to outrage the religious feelings of any class of citizens by insulting their religion or religious beliefs, done without just cause or excuse and with full awareness of the wrongful nature of the act.
definitions.plain_english: When the law uses the word 'malicious,' it means the person acted on purpose with a bad or spiteful intention — they wanted to cause harm or hurt feelings, and they knew what they were doing was wrong. In the context of Section 299, it means someone deliberately chose to insult a religion or religious beliefs, not accidentally or out of ignorance, but out of a clear intent to wound or outrage people of that faith. It goes beyond carelessness or recklessness — the person had a calculated, hostile motive.
real_world_examples: A social media influencer in Mumbai posts a video deliberately mocking the rituals of a particular religious community, using offensive language and symbolic desecration, intending to provoke outrage among followers of that religion — this would be considered malicious under Section 299.

A political activist in Uttar Pradesh distributes pamphlets that intentionally misrepresent the sacred texts of a minority religion with the stated goal of inciting contempt among members of another community — the deliberate intent to wound religious feelings constitutes malicious conduct.

A stand-up comedian in Bengaluru knowingly and repeatedly insults the core religious beliefs of a specific caste-based religious group during a public performance, despite prior warnings that the content is offensive — the persistence and deliberateness establishes malicious intent.

A person in Chennai sends a series of WhatsApp messages containing fabricated blasphemous statements falsely attributed to a revered religious figure, with the express purpose of inflaming inter-community tensions — the calculated nature of the act makes it malicious within the meaning of Section 299.

A website administrator in Delhi knowingly hosts and promotes content that systematically ridicules and degrades the religious practices of a tribal religious community, intending to demean their beliefs before a wider audience — this deliberate targeting constitutes malicious intent under the provision.
what_it_covers: A person who intentionally and knowingly uses spoken words, written material, signs, or electronic means to insult a religion or religious belief with the specific purpose of outraging the religious feelings of a class of citizens.

Acts of deliberate desecration, mockery, or misrepresentation of religious symbols, texts, or practices carried out with the conscious goal of causing religious offence, as distinct from inadvertent or uninformed conduct.

Repeated or persistent conduct directed at insulting a religion after the offender has been made aware of the offensive nature of the act, demonstrating a calculated and hostile intention rather than mere negligence.

Publication or dissemination through electronic means — such as social media posts, viral videos, or messaging platforms — of content specifically crafted to wound the religious sensibilities of a particular class of citizens.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or unintentional statements that offend religious sensibilities without any deliberate purpose to insult, such as an academic misquoting a religious text out of ignorance during a lecture.
Good faith scholarly criticism, academic analysis, or artistic commentary on religious practices that, while potentially controversial, is not motivated by a desire to outrage or demean believers.

Satire or expression that may incidentally offend religious groups but lacks a deliberate and calculated intention to insult or outrage religious feelings, particularly where the primary purpose is social or political commentary rather than religious attack.
Statements made under coercion, duress, or without full understanding of their religious implications, which negate the deliberate volitional element required to establish a malicious state of mind.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of 'malicious' intent is a mandatory element of the offence under Section 299 — without proof that the accused acted with deliberate and malicious intention, no conviction can be secured under this provision, making it a critical threshold that distinguishes criminal liability from protected speech or unintentional offence. Establishing malicious intent directly triggers punishment of up to three years of imprisonment, a fine, or both, while its absence defeats the charge entirely.

definitions.definition: The term 'maliciously' as used in Section 258 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, denotes the exercise of legal authority to commit, confine, or detain a person with ill will, spite, or an improper motive, knowing that such exercise of authority is contrary to law. It implies a deliberate, wanton, or wicked intent beyond mere negligence or error, driven by personal animosity or malice rather than bona fide official duty.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'maliciously' means doing something with a bad or spiteful motive, knowing it is wrong and against the law. When a government officer uses their power to arrest or imprison someone not because the law requires it, but out of personal grudge, bias, or ill will, they are acting maliciously. It is not a simple mistake — it is a deliberate misuse of power to harm someone.
real_world_examples: A magistrate in Delhi, harbouring a personal grudge against a local businessman, issues a commitment order sending him to judicial custody despite knowing there is no legal basis for detention, purely to harass and financially damage the businessman.

A jail superintendent in Maharashtra, acting on personal animosity, refuses to release a prisoner whose bail has been lawfully granted by the court, continuing to keep him in confinement knowing that the continued detention is contrary to the court's valid order.

A Sessions Court judge in Tamil Nadu, influenced by political pressure and personal bias against a social activist, pronounces a remand order committing the activist to custody while knowingly overlooking statutory provisions that do not permit such commitment at that stage of proceedings.

A district magistrate in Uttar Pradesh, motivated by caste-based ill will, uses his authority to commit a person from a particular community to trial confinement on charges he knows are legally insufficient, using the process as a tool of oppression rather than justice.

A sub-divisional magistrate in West Bengal, out of personal rivalry with a local opposition leader, issues an executive detention order under a bailable offence knowing that the law does not permit remand in such cases, deliberately targeting the individual for political reasons.
semantic_tags: ill will or spite by public servant
what_it_covers: A public servant who commits a person to confinement with personal ill will or spite, knowing the action is contrary to law.
An officer exercising authority to detain or remand someone driven by an ulterior motive such as political rivalry, caste animosity, or personal grudge.
Any deliberate and knowing misuse of legal authority to commit a person for trial or keep them in confinement when the officer is aware that the law does not permit such action.
Actions by a judicial or quasi-judicial authority that are motivated by wanton disregard for the legal rights of the detained person combined with knowledge of illegality.
what_it_excludes: Honest mistakes or errors of judgment by an authority who genuinely believed the commitment or confinement was lawful — absence of knowledge that the act is contrary to law negates maliciousness.
Acts performed in good faith under a bona fide belief that the law authorises the detention, even if the legal interpretation later proves incorrect.
Negligent or careless exercise of authority where there is no ill will, personal motive, or awareness that the action violates the law.
Actions taken under direct and binding superior orders which the officer follows without personal malicious intent, provided knowledge of illegality is absent.
Lawful confinement or commitment to trial that is procedurally and substantively in accordance with the applicable law, regardless of any personal feelings of the officer.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'maliciously' is a critical element that distinguishes a punishable offence under Section 258 from a lawful or merely erroneous official act — its presence, combined with knowledge of acting contrary to law, exposes the public servant to imprisonment up to seven years and/or fine. Without proof of malicious or corrupt intent, the offence under Section 258 is not made out, shielding officers who act in genuine good faith from criminal liability.

definitions.definition: The term 'malignantly' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used to describe conduct done with deliberate, wicked, or evil intent to cause harm — specifically, an act performed with the conscious and purposeful desire to bring about an injurious or dangerous result, going beyond mere negligence or recklessness. It denotes a state of mind characterised by active ill-will or spite directed toward causing serious harm to others or to society.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'malignantly' means doing something on purpose with a mean or wicked intention to cause harm — not by accident, carelessness, or even recklessness, but with a deliberate desire to hurt others or create a dangerous situation. It is a stronger mental state than being negligent or even reckless; it implies the person actually wanted the harmful outcome to happen. Think of it as doing something bad on purpose because you want to cause damage or suffering.
real_world_examples: A person infected with a dangerous communicable disease like tuberculosis or COVID-19 deliberately coughs or spits on multiple people in a crowded Delhi metro station, intending to infect them — this would constitute a malignant act under Section 272 of the BNS.

A factory worker in Surat, knowing he is a carrier of a life-threatening infectious disease, deliberately contaminates the shared water supply of a residential colony out of a grudge against the residents, thereby malignantly spreading disease dangerous to life.

An individual in Mumbai, angry at a community, deliberately releases infected animals or materials carrying a dangerous pathogen into a public market, intending to cause an outbreak of a fatal illness among the local population.

A person in Chennai who is aware he carries a highly contagious and deadly illness deliberately attends a large public gathering such as a temple festival without taking any precautions and intentionally moves close to vulnerable individuals to spread the infection.

Someone in Kolkata deliberately tampers with a hospital's ventilation system to release air carrying infectious pathogens, knowing and intending that patients and staff will contract a life-threatening disease as a result.
what_it_covers: Deliberately performing an act with full knowledge that it is likely to spread a disease dangerous to life, driven by ill-will or wicked intent toward the victims.
Intentionally provoking a riot by doing an act that is illegal, with the specific desire or knowledge that rioting will result, as contemplated under Section 192 of the BNS.
Consciously and purposefully contaminating food, water, or public spaces with infectious agents, knowing the lethal consequences and wishing them upon others.
Any act done with a pre-formed evil design to cause serious harm to identifiable or general victims, where the harmful consequence is the very goal of the actor's conduct.
what_it_excludes: Acts done negligently or rashly without any intention to cause harm — a person who accidentally spreads disease due to ignorance of their condition does not act malignantly.
Acts done in good faith for a lawful or medical purpose, such as a healthcare worker transporting infectious samples for treatment or research, even if there is a risk of spread.
Reckless conduct where the person is indifferent to the risk but does not actively desire the harmful outcome — recklessness falls short of the deliberate ill-will required for malignancy.
Acts done under a mistake of fact or genuine misunderstanding of the dangerous nature of the conduct, where there is no conscious awareness of the likely harmful result.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is done 'malignantly' is the central mens rea element that triggers liability under Section 272 BNS (malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life) and Section 192 BNS (wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot); without proof of this deliberate, evil intent, the accused cannot be convicted under these sections, and the prosecution must instead rely on provisions covering negligence or recklessness. Establishing malignancy elevates the moral culpability of the accused and justifies the prescribed punishment of imprisonment up to two years, distinguishing the offence from lesser forms of harmful conduct.

definitions.definition: A 'master' in the context of Section 165 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the person in command or overall charge of a merchant vessel, being the individual primarily responsible for the discipline, supervision, and management of all persons on board, and who is legally accountable for ensuring that deserters from the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India are not concealed on the vessel through neglect of duty or want of discipline.
definitions.plain_english: A 'master' is the captain or person in charge of a merchant ship. This person holds ultimate responsibility for everything that happens on the vessel, including ensuring that military deserters are not hiding on board. Even if the master does not personally know about a deserter being hidden, they can still be held responsible if their negligence or poor discipline on the ship allowed it to happen.
real_world_examples: The captain of a cargo ship sailing from Mumbai to Colombo fails to conduct proper crew and passenger checks before departure; a deserter from the Indian Navy is found hidden in the cargo hold — the captain is liable under Section 165 for neglect of duty as master.

The person in charge of a merchant vessel operating along the Kerala coast does not maintain a discipline register or conduct routine inspections; a soldier who has deserted from the Indian Army is discovered stowed away — the officer-in-charge faces penalty as the 'master' responsible for the vessel.

The master of a coastal trading vessel plying between Chennai and Vizag is aware that some crew members are not following boarding protocols, yet takes no corrective action; a deserter from the Indian Air Force is later found on board — the master is held accountable for want of discipline.

A ship owner who is also the person in charge of a merchant vessel operating in the Andaman Sea neglects to verify identity documents of all personnel boarding at Port Blair; an Army deserter is subsequently found concealed — the ship owner acting as master is liable for the penalty under Section 165.

The relief officer temporarily placed in charge of a merchant vessel during the captain's illness fails to enforce boarding checks; a Navy deserter is discovered hidden in a crew cabin — the relief officer, acting as 'person in charge', is treated as the master for purposes of liability under Section 165.
what_it_covers: The appointed captain of a registered merchant vessel who holds formal command authority over the ship and its crew.
Any person temporarily placed in charge of a merchant vessel in the absence of the regular captain, exercising command and disciplinary authority during that period.
A ship owner or operator who personally assumes the role of commander and day-to-day management of the merchant vessel.
An officer designated as the person-in-charge of a merchant vessel under maritime law or employment contract, responsible for maintaining discipline on board.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary crew members, deckhands, or sailors who work on the vessel but do not hold command or supervisory authority over the ship as a whole.
A ship owner or company that does not personally assume command or operational charge of the vessel, but has delegated all authority to a designated captain.
Government or naval vessel commanders, as Section 165 specifically applies to 'merchant vessels' and not warships or State-operated vessels.
A harbour master or port authority official who exercises jurisdiction over ships in port but does not serve as the person in command of any specific merchant vessel.
Passengers or non-crew personnel on board the merchant vessel who have no authority or duty with respect to vessel management or discipline.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as 'master' under Section 165 directly determines criminal liability for harbouring a military deserter on a merchant vessel — even in the absence of actual knowledge — if negligence of duty or want of discipline is established, attracting a penalty of up to three thousand rupees. If a person does not qualify as the 'master or person in charge', they cannot be held liable under this provision, making the identification of the commanding officer of the vessel a decisive legal threshold.

definitions.definition: The term 'material' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used to qualify facts, circumstances, or information that are substantially relevant and consequential to a legal matter, decision, or obligation — as in a 'material fact which he is bound to disclose' (Section 45), indicating information whose presence or absence would influence the outcome of a legal proceeding or act.
definitions.plain_english: Something is 'material' when it is important enough to make a real difference to the outcome of a legal situation. For example, a 'material fact' is a piece of information so significant that if someone hid it or lied about it, it could change what another person decided to do. It is not about minor or irrelevant details — only information that truly matters in the eyes of the law.
real_world_examples: A person applying for bail conceals from the court the fact that they are already out on bail in another criminal case in a different state — this hidden information is a material fact that would have affected the court's decision.

An accused instigates a police officer to arrest the wrong person by wilfully concealing the material fact that the person pointed out is not the named accused, thereby causing wrongful arrest under Section 45.

A seller of a property conceals from the buyer that the land is the subject of an ongoing criminal dispute — this suppressed information constitutes a material fact relevant to the transaction and any resulting criminal fraud charge.
A witness before a magistrate omits to mention that he was present at the scene of the crime, a material fact that, if disclosed, would alter the entire course of the investigation and trial.
In a case under Section 236 (impersonation at an examination), a candidate conceals the material fact that they are not the registered examinee, which directly triggers criminal liability.
Under Section 342, a person executing a document conceals a material fact about the nature of the transaction, leading to a charge of fraud by wilful misrepresentation.
what_it_covers: A fact whose suppression or misrepresentation directly causes another person to act in a legally significant way, such as making an arrest or executing a document.
Information that a person is legally bound to disclose and whose omission would alter the decision of a court, officer, or party involved.
Any circumstance or detail that is so central to a legal proceeding, transaction, or obligation that it would change the nature of the act or its legal consequences if known.
Details about the identity, status, or prior conduct of a person that bear directly on the legality or validity of an official action being taken.
what_it_excludes: Trivial, peripheral, or collateral information that does not affect the legal outcome of a proceeding or transaction.
Facts that are already known to the other party, a court, or the relevant authority, as concealment of known facts cannot constitute wilful concealment of a material fact.
Information that has no causal link to the act being done or the decision being made — i.e., facts whose disclosure or suppression would not have changed anything.
Mere opinions, beliefs, or predictions about future events that do not constitute factual information capable of influencing a legal determination.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a fact qualifies as 'material' determines whether its wilful concealment or misrepresentation amounts to abetment by instigation under Section 45, thereby making a person criminally liable for causing or procuring an unlawful act. In Sections 236 and 342, the materiality of concealed or misrepresented information is the threshold that separates innocent non-disclosure from a punishable criminal offence.

definitions.definition: A material fact, in the context of Section 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is a fact which a person is legally or morally bound to disclose, and whose wilful concealment amounts to instigation if it voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done. It is a fact of such significance and relevance that its non-disclosure would induce or influence the conduct or action of another person, thereby constituting abetment by instigation.
definitions.plain_english: A 'material fact' is an important piece of information that someone is required to share with another person and that, if hidden, could cause that other person to act in a certain way — often to their detriment or contrary to law. It is not just any fact, but one that is crucial and directly relevant to the decision or action being taken. Hiding such a fact deliberately is treated in law as if you had actively pushed or encouraged the other person to do something they might not otherwise have done.
real_world_examples: A police officer holds a valid arrest warrant for accused 'X'. Person B, knowing that the individual present is actually 'Y' and not 'X', deliberately conceals this fact and allows or encourages the officer to arrest 'Y'. The identity of the individual is a material fact B was bound to disclose, and concealing it constitutes instigation of wrongful arrest.

A bank employee processing a loan application is aware that the applicant has a prior default history with another bank, which the applicant has concealed. The employee, despite being bound to verify and disclose this, wilfully conceals it from the loan approval committee, enabling the fraudulent disbursement. The applicant's default history is a material fact.

A real estate broker facilitates the sale of a plot of land while deliberately concealing from the buyer that the land is under a government acquisition notification — a fact the broker is bound to disclose. The acquisition notification is a material fact whose concealment abets the fraudulent transaction.

A medical professional, asked by a court or insurance authority about a patient's pre-existing condition relevant to a compensation claim, wilfully conceals the diagnosis, causing the authority to make a payment it would not otherwise have made. The pre-existing condition is a material fact the doctor was bound to disclose.

A company director conceals from co-signatories of a contract that a key regulatory clearance has been refused, causing them to sign the agreement under a mistaken belief that all approvals are in order. The refusal of regulatory clearance is a material fact whose concealment abets execution of a void or fraudulent contract.
what_it_covers: A fact that a person is legally or professionally bound to disclose to another party, such as an officer of law, court, or contracting party, whose suppression directly influences or causes an action.

Information of such relevance to a transaction, proceeding, or action that its absence would alter the course of conduct of the person to whom it is owed — for example, the true identity of an accused, the status of a title deed, or a prior criminal record.
Facts whose wilful concealment results in a third party being caused or procured to do something, thereby constituting the concealing person an abettor by instigation under Section 45.

Information that a person holds in a fiduciary, official, or statutory capacity and is obligated to communicate, such as a public servant withholding knowledge of an encumbrance or a professional concealing a diagnosis relevant to a legal proceeding.
what_it_excludes: Irrelevant or trivial facts that have no bearing on the decision, action, or conduct of the person to whom disclosure is owed — their concealment does not satisfy the threshold of 'material'.
Facts that a person is not legally, morally, or professionally bound to disclose — mere silence about information one has no duty to share does not constitute wilful concealment of a material fact.
Inadvertent or accidental non-disclosure of a fact, since Section 45 requires the concealment to be wilful; an innocent omission or honest mistake does not meet the standard.

Facts already known to the person whose action is sought to be influenced — concealing something the other party already knows cannot causally produce or procure any action and hence is not a material fact in this context.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a concealed fact qualifies as a 'material fact' determines whether the person who conceals it can be held liable as an abettor by instigation under Section 45 of the BNS, 2023, making them equally culpable for the offence that results. If the withheld fact is not material, no criminal liability for abetment by concealment arises, fundamentally affecting prosecution for offences of abetment.

definitions.definition: A 'material point' refers to any fact, assertion, or detail contained in a certificate or declaration that is significant, consequential, or essential to the legal validity, purpose, or effect of that instrument, such that a falsehood in that respect would affect the rights, liabilities, or legal consequences flowing from the document.
definitions.plain_english: A 'material point' is any important fact or detail in a certificate or formal declaration that actually matters to its legal purpose. If a detail is so significant that lying about it would mislead someone or affect their legal rights, it is a material point. It is not just any minor or irrelevant detail — it must be the kind of fact that the certificate or declaration is meant to establish or record.
real_world_examples: A government doctor issues a fitness certificate for a public servant's reinstatement, falsely stating the person is medically fit when they are not — the health status is a material point as it directly determines the person's eligibility to resume duty.

A revenue officer signs a land holding certificate required for a court proceeding, knowingly stating the acreage as 5 acres when it is 15 acres — the land measurement is a material point because it affects property rights and tax liability adjudicated in the case.

A school principal issues a caste certificate required for reserved category admission to a government college, falsely certifying a student's caste — the caste classification is a material point since the entire entitlement to the reservation depends on it.

A registered medical practitioner issues a death certificate citing natural causes when the death was caused by poisoning — the cause of death is a material point because it determines whether a criminal investigation is initiated and affects insurance claims.

A customs officer signs a certificate of origin for imported goods falsely declaring them as domestically manufactured to avail export incentives — the origin of goods is a material point as it determines the legal duty exemption or subsidy eligibility.

A municipal officer issues a building completion certificate falsely certifying that fire safety norms have been complied with when they have not — the safety compliance status is a material point as occupancy permissions and public safety depend on it.
what_it_covers: Any fact in a certificate that determines a person's legal eligibility, entitlement, or rights — such as age, caste, income, or health status — where a false statement would alter the outcome of a legal or administrative process.

Any assertion in a statutory declaration that is required by law to be accurate and upon which courts or authorities place reliance in evidence, such that falsehood in that assertion would amount to giving false evidence.

The central or operative finding in a certificate, such as the cause of death in a death certificate, the fitness assessment in a medical certificate, or the ownership claim in a property certificate, which defines the entire legal effect of the document.

Details in a certificate that affect criminal, civil, or administrative proceedings — for instance, a forensic certificate incorrectly stating that a weapon tested negative for blood when it tested positive.
what_it_excludes: Trivial, clerical, or administrative errors in a certificate that have no bearing on its legal effect or purpose — such as a misspelling of a street name in an address field that does not affect the identity of the person or property.
Inaccuracies in parts of a certificate that are merely formal, incidental, or procedural, and which do not affect the rights or liabilities of any party relying on the certificate.

False statements in documents that are not legally required certificates or statutory declarations, such as informal letters or unauthenticated personal communications, which fall outside the scope of Sections 234–237.

Errors or omissions that render a declaration inadmissible on purely technical or informality grounds, as Section 237 expressly treats such declarations as still being within its scope — meaning the inadmissibility itself is not the material point.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a false statement constitutes a 'material point' determines if the issuer of a certificate or declaration is criminally liable under Sections 234–237 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and is to be punished as if they gave false evidence. Only falsehoods on material points attract this serious criminal consequence; errors on immaterial points do not trigger the offence.

definitions.definition: Maturity of understanding refers to the sufficient cognitive and moral capacity of a child above seven years and under twelve years of age to judge the nature and consequences of his conduct on a particular occasion. It is not formally defined but is used in Section 21 to denote the developmental threshold at which a child may be held criminally responsible for an act.
definitions.plain_english: Maturity of understanding means that a child is mentally and intellectually developed enough to know what he or she is doing and to understand the likely outcome or harm of that action. For children between 7 and 12 years of age, this is assessed case by case. If the child lacks this level of understanding at the time of the act, no criminal offence is made out against the child.
real_world_examples: A 9-year-old boy in a Delhi neighbourhood picks up a stone and throws it at a passing vehicle, breaking the windscreen, but has no understanding that this could injure the driver or constitute damage to property — he lacks maturity of understanding and commits no offence.

An 11-year-old girl in Mumbai, having watched older children steal from a shop, takes a biscuit packet without paying, unaware that such conduct constitutes theft under the law — a court may find she had not attained sufficient maturity of understanding.

A 10-year-old child in rural Rajasthan sets fire to a pile of dry hay near a neighbour's farm while playing with matches, not appreciating that this could cause widespread property damage — the absence of maturity of understanding may excuse the act.

An 8-year-old boy in Chennai, during a quarrel with a classmate, pushes the classmate off a school bench causing a fracture, but without any comprehension that the act could cause grievous injury — the court must assess whether he had sufficient maturity of understanding to be held liable.

A 11-year-old from Kolkata who participates in a group act of vandalising a public bus during a local protest, having been instigated by adults, may be found to lack the maturity of understanding to judge the consequences of participating in such conduct.
semantic_tags: seven to twelve years age group
what_it_covers: A child aged above 7 and under 12 who demonstrably lacks the cognitive ability to appreciate the harmful or criminal nature of the specific act committed on that occasion.
Situations where a young child performs a physically harmful act — such as causing injury or damage to property — without the mental development to foresee its consequences.

Cases where a child between 7 and 12 participates in a group act that constitutes an offence, but whose personal developmental stage is insufficient to comprehend the nature of the collective conduct.

Acts done by a child in this age group that would otherwise constitute an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, but are excused because the child could not judge the nature and consequences of the act at that specific time.
what_it_excludes: Children above 12 years of age, who are presumed to have sufficient maturity of understanding regardless of their actual cognitive development.
Children under 7 years of age, who are given an absolute exemption from criminal liability under the Act without any inquiry into their maturity of understanding.

An 11-year-old child who clearly demonstrates — through prior knowledge, deliberate planning, or post-act concealment — that he understood both the nature and consequences of his conduct at the time of the act.
Acts committed by adults or persons of unsound mind, whose criminal capacity or incapacity is governed by separate provisions and not by the maturity of understanding standard.
Cases involving civil liability of a child, which are governed by separate civil law principles and are not affected by the criminal threshold of maturity of understanding under this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a child aged between 7 and 12 has attained 'maturity of understanding' is the decisive legal question that determines whether the child can be held criminally liable for an act that would otherwise constitute an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. If the child is found to lack such maturity, the act is not an offence, and no prosecution, conviction, or punishment can follow; conversely, it also affects the right of private defence of others under Section 36.

definitions.definition: "Means of transport" refers to any vehicle, vessel, or conveyance used for the transport of goods or passengers, including but not limited to motor vehicles, trains, buses, aircraft, ships, boats, and any other mode of conveyance employed for carrying persons or property from one place to another.
definitions.plain_english: A 'means of transport' is any vehicle or conveyance that is used to carry people or goods from one place to another. This includes everyday vehicles like trucks, buses, trains, and auto-rickshaws, as well as boats and aircraft. The term is important in theft law because stealing from or stealing an entire transport vehicle used for passengers or goods is treated as a more serious offence.
real_world_examples: A thief steals cargo loaded on a goods truck (lorry) parked at a highway dhaba in Rajasthan — the truck is a means of transport used for goods, making the offence punishable under Section 305.

Pickpockets steal mobile phones and wallets from passengers travelling in a Delhi Metro train coach — the metro train qualifies as a means of transport, attracting the enhanced punishment under Section 305.
A person steals an entire auto-rickshaw plying for hire on the streets of Mumbai, which is used to transport passengers — the auto-rickshaw is a means of transport, triggering Section 305.

Thieves break into a cargo container aboard a goods vessel docked at the Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Mumbai, and steal electronic equipment — the vessel used for transporting goods is a means of transport under Section 305.

A thief steals luggage from the overhead rack of a passenger bus travelling on the Bengaluru–Chennai route — the bus is a means of transport used for passengers, and the theft attracts punishment under Section 305.

A gang steals fuel from a tanker truck transporting petroleum products on a national highway in Gujarat — the tanker truck, being a means of transport used for goods, brings the offence within Section 305.

what_it_excludes: Buildings, tents, or dwelling structures, which are separately covered under the dwelling-house limb of Section 305 and do not qualify as a means of transport.

Stationary storage structures like warehouses, godowns, or shipping containers that are not themselves a conveyance but merely used to store goods.
Places of worship, which are separately addressed under a distinct limb of Section 305 and fall outside the definition of means of transport.

definitions.definition: A 'medical preparation' is any substance or compound prepared or formulated for medicinal purposes, intended to be sold or used for the treatment, prevention, or management of illness or disease, and includes any such preparation that may be subject to adulteration or substitution so as to lessen its efficacy, change its operation, or render it noxious.
definitions.plain_english: A medical preparation is any product that is made or put together specifically to be used as medicine — such as a tablet, syrup, ointment, or injection — and is meant to treat or manage a health condition. It is different from raw drugs in that it has been processed or compounded into a ready-to-use medicinal form. The law protects people from being given adulterated, fake, or mislabelled versions of such preparations.
real_world_examples: A pharmacist in Mumbai compounds a cough syrup using inferior or substitute ingredients and sells it as a branded formulation, reducing its therapeutic effectiveness — this constitutes adulteration of a medical preparation under Section 276.

A dispensary in Chennai issues insulin vials that have been diluted with saline water and labels them as full-strength insulin for diabetic patients who are unaware of the adulteration — an offence under Section 277.
A drug retailer in Delhi knowingly sells paracetamol tablets as ibuprofen to a customer, misrepresenting one medical preparation as another — punishable under Section 278.

A chemist in Kolkata stocks ayurvedic capsules that have been adulterated with non-medicinal fillers and sells them as genuine therapeutic products to patients suffering from joint pain, thereby lessening the preparation's efficacy.

A rural medical store in Uttar Pradesh issues a preparation labelled as an antibiotic when it actually contains only a vitamin supplement, causing a patient to rely on it for treatment of a bacterial infection.
what_it_covers: Compounded or formulated products such as tablets, capsules, syrups, ointments, injections, and tonics prepared for medicinal use and dispensed or sold as such.
Any ready-to-use pharmaceutical or ayurvedic formulation stocked and issued by a dispensary, chemist, or hospital pharmacy for the purpose of treating or managing a disease or condition.
Proprietary or generic drug combinations processed and packaged for sale to the public or for issue to patients for medicinal purposes, whether allopathic, homeopathic, or traditional.
what_it_excludes: Raw or unprocessed drug substances in their natural botanical, mineral, or chemical state that have not yet been formulated or compounded into a preparation intended for direct medicinal use.
Food products, dietary supplements, or nutritional items sold solely for general health or nourishment rather than specifically for medicinal treatment, prevention, or management of a disease.
Cosmetic preparations such as creams, lotions, or ointments intended purely for external beautification and not marketed or used for any therapeutic or medicinal purpose.
Industrial chemicals or laboratory reagents that may incidentally have medicinal properties but are not prepared, packaged, or sold as medicinal preparations for human or animal use.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'medical preparation' determines whether Sections 276, 277, and 278 of the BNS are attracted — covering criminal liability for adulteration, knowing sale of adulterated medicine, and fraudulent substitution of one preparation for another, each carrying imprisonment and fines. If a product does not fall within this definition, these penal provisions cannot be invoked, leaving the conduct outside the scope of these specific drug-adulteration offences.

definitions.definition: A medicinal purpose, as contextually employed in Section 276 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the intended use of a drug or medical preparation for the treatment, cure, prevention, or alleviation of disease, ailment, or bodily condition in human beings or animals. It encompasses any therapeutic, prophylactic, or remedial application for which a drug or medical preparation is sold, dispensed, or administered.
definitions.plain_english: A 'medicinal purpose' means using a medicine or drug to treat, prevent, or cure an illness or health condition. This includes any situation where someone takes or is given a drug because it is meant to help their body fight a disease, manage pain, or restore health. The term covers drugs sold at pharmacies, dispensed at hospitals, or administered by healthcare providers for health-related reasons.
real_world_examples: A patient in Mumbai purchases paracetamol tablets from a chemist shop to treat fever — the tablets are being used for a medicinal purpose, and if the manufacturer had diluted the active ingredient to reduce its efficacy, Section 276 would apply.

A diabetic patient in Chennai is prescribed insulin by a doctor; the insulin is dispensed from a hospital dispensary for controlling blood sugar — this constitutes a medicinal purpose, and adulterating the insulin would attract liability under Section 276.

An Ayurvedic preparation sold in Delhi for treating arthritis is found to have been mixed with inert substances reducing its therapeutic value — since it was sold for a medicinal purpose, the adulterator faces punishment under Section 276.

A rural health centre in Rajasthan dispenses oral rehydration salts (ORS) to children suffering from diarrhea — the ORS is being used for a medicinal purpose, and any adulteration making it noxious or less effective would be punishable.

A homeopathic remedy sold in Kolkata pharmacies for treating respiratory infections is adulterated by the manufacturer — as it is intended for a medicinal purpose, liability under Section 276 is squarely attracted.

A veterinary drug used by farmers in Punjab to treat cattle infections is adulterated to lessen its efficacy — since drugs used for animals for therapeutic ends also fall under medicinal purposes, the adulterator is liable under this provision.
what_it_covers: Drugs sold at licensed pharmacies or chemist shops intended to treat or cure a diagnosed illness or medical condition.
Medical preparations dispensed from hospital or clinic dispensaries for therapeutic administration to patients.
Over-the-counter medicines such as analgesics, antacids, or antiseptics sold to consumers for self-treatment of common ailments.
Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha, or homeopathic preparations sold or administered for treating health conditions under any recognised system of medicine.
Veterinary drugs or preparations administered to animals for the treatment or prevention of disease.
what_it_excludes: Drugs or substances used purely for recreational purposes without any therapeutic intent, such as narcotics consumed for intoxication rather than medical treatment.
Cosmetic preparations such as skin creams, hair dyes, or perfumes that are not intended to treat, cure, or prevent any disease or ailment.
Food or dietary supplements sold only to supplement nutrition rather than to treat or prevent a specific medical condition.
Industrial chemicals or substances that may incidentally have medicinal properties but are not sold or used in a therapeutic context.
Substances used in laboratory research or testing that are not intended for direct administration to humans or animals for treatment.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of 'medicinal purpose' is the foundational trigger for offences under Sections 276, 277, and 278 of the BNS, 2023 — without establishing that a drug or medical preparation was intended for or likely to be used for a medicinal purpose, no criminal liability for adulteration or fraudulent sale of drugs can arise. If this element is satisfied, an adulterator faces imprisonment up to one year and/or a fine up to five thousand rupees, while a knowing seller of adulterated drugs faces imprisonment up to six months and/or a similar fine.

definitions.definition: A merchant vessel, as used in Section 165 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any commercial watercraft engaged in trade, transport, or navigation, which is under the command of a master or person in charge, and on board of which members of the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India may be concealed as deserters.
definitions.plain_english: A merchant vessel is a commercial ship or boat used for carrying goods or passengers, as opposed to a warship or government naval vessel. It is operated by a captain (called a 'master') or another person in charge who is responsible for discipline and order on the ship. In everyday terms, think of cargo ships, tankers, passenger ferries, or trading vessels that sail for business purposes.
real_world_examples: A cargo ship operated by a private Indian shipping company sailing from Mumbai to Colombo, on board which a soldier who has absconded from the Indian Army is hiding in a cargo hold without the captain's knowledge — the captain may be liable if he failed to conduct proper checks.

A passenger ferry operating between Chennai and the Andaman Islands where a deserter from the Indian Navy stows away, and the vessel's master is found to have neglected routine headcount and inspection procedures before departure.

An oil tanker registered under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and operating along India's western coastline, where a deserter from the Indian Air Force is concealed in the engine room due to lax security protocols maintained by the person in charge.

A fishing trawler upgraded to a commercial trading vessel operating out of Kochi where an Army deserter hides among the crew, and the master failed to verify identity documents of all persons on board before sailing.

A coastal merchant vessel travelling between Kolkata and Visakhapatnam where a Navy deserter conceals himself in a cargo container, and the ship's officer in charge did not enforce mandatory muster calls or discipline checks that could have revealed the presence of an unauthorized person.

Government of India armed forces connection
what_it_covers: Commercial cargo ships registered under Indian merchant shipping laws and operating domestically or internationally under the command of a master.

Passenger-carrying vessels engaged in trade or transport on navigable waters, including coastal ferries and inter-island vessels, having a designated person in charge responsible for onboard discipline.

Private or corporate-owned trading vessels, including tankers, bulk carriers, and container ships, where the master owes a duty of care to prevent concealment of deserters from the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force.
Any vessel operating for commercial purposes on which a deserter from the armed forces of the Government of India could foreseeably be harboured due to lack of proper inspection or discipline.
what_it_excludes: Warships and naval vessels of the Indian Navy, which are government military vessels and not classified as merchant vessels.
Private recreational or pleasure craft not engaged in commerce or trade, such as personal yachts or non-commercial fishing boats.
Aircraft and other non-waterborne means of transport, which are governed separately under the BNS and other aviation laws even if used for commercial transport.
Government-owned non-commercial vessels such as coastguard ships, survey vessels, or research ships operated by public authorities for non-trade purposes.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a vessel qualifies as a 'merchant vessel' under Section 165 determines whether its master or person in charge can be held liable for a penalty of up to three thousand rupees for the negligent concealment of a deserter from the Indian armed forces on board. If the vessel does not fall within this category, the provision cannot be invoked and no penalty attaches to the person in command.

definitions.definition: A mint, within the meaning of Sections 187 and 188, refers to any mint lawfully established in India, being an official government-authorised facility for the manufacture and issuance of coins. It encompasses the physical premises, the coining tools and instruments contained therein, and the lawful processes by which coins of fixed weight and composition are produced under authority of law.
definitions.plain_english: A mint is an officially authorised government facility in India where coins are manufactured according to legally prescribed standards of weight and metal composition. It is a regulated establishment — not a private workshop — set up under the authority of law to produce currency coins. Examples in India include the government mints at Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, and Noida, which operate under the Ministry of Finance.
real_world_examples: An employee at the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India (SPMCIL) mint in Hyderabad deliberately adjusts the alloy composition of one-rupee coins so they contain less metal than prescribed by law — this directly invokes Section 187 because the act occurs within a lawfully established mint.

A technician working at the Kolkata Mint secretly removes a coining die (a specialised coining instrument) from the mint premises without any authorisation, intending to use it to produce counterfeit coins outside — this triggers Section 188 as an unlawful removal of a coining tool from a lawfully established mint.

A supervisor at the Mumbai Mint omits to report a malfunctioning press that is systematically producing coins below the legally mandated weight, knowing this will result in underweight coins being issued into circulation — such an omission with criminal intention constitutes an offence under Section 187.

A maintenance contractor at the Noida Mint takes out a coining punch under the pretext of external repair but without proper written authorisation from mint authorities — even if the intention was not to commit counterfeiting, removing it without lawful authority makes it an offence under Section 188.

A senior assayer at the SPMCIL mint in Mumbai alters the prescribed gold-to-copper ratio in commemorative coins during the minting process to divert surplus precious metal for personal gain — this constitutes an act done with the intention of causing coins to be of a different composition, attracting liability under Section 187.
what_it_covers: Any mint established and operating under lawful authority of the Government of India, such as the four government mints operated by SPMCIL at Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, and Noida.
The physical premises of the mint, including all internal departments, workshops, and secure areas where coins are manufactured, assayed, and stored before issuance.
All coining tools and instruments housed within the mint, including dies, punches, presses, and other equipment used in the lawful production of coins.
Acts and omissions of persons employed within the mint that affect the weight, composition, or integrity of coins issued from that mint.
Any person who, regardless of their specific role, is 'employed' in the mint and therefore subject to legal obligations regarding coin integrity under Section 187.
what_it_excludes: Private or unauthorised coin-making establishments that lack government sanction — these do not constitute a 'mint' within the meaning of these sections, and offences arising there would be governed by counterfeiting provisions rather than Sections 187–188.

Facilities that produce medals, tokens, commemorative medallions, or other non-legal-tender metal objects, even if they use similar manufacturing processes, as these are not mints issuing coins in the legal sense.
Foreign mints or coin-producing facilities established outside India — Sections 187 and 188 explicitly apply only to mints 'lawfully established in India'.

Persons who are not employed in the mint but who may be involved in counterfeiting coins through other means outside the mint premises — their liability would arise under separate counterfeiting provisions.
Currency note printing presses (e.g., the note presses at Nasik and Dewas), which produce paper currency rather than coins and are distinct from a 'mint' as used in these sections.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a facility qualifies as a 'mint lawfully established in India' is the foundational jurisdictional threshold for Sections 187 and 188 — only acts or omissions occurring within such a mint, or involving instruments taken from it, attract the specific penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment under those sections. If the facility is not a lawfully established mint, the accused cannot be charged under Sections 187 or 188 and would instead fall under the general counterfeiting or forgery provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
