definitions.definition: To misappropriate means to dishonestly take or convert to one's own use any movable property, particularly property that one has found or that has come into one's possession, without lawful authority and with the intent to deprive the rightful owner of it. As used in Section 328 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the term denotes the dishonest appropriation or use of movable property belonging to another person.
definitions.plain_english: To 'misappropriate' means to dishonestly take something that belongs to someone else and use it as if it were your own, without the owner's permission. This usually applies when you find something that isn't yours, or when property comes into your hands lawfully but you then decide to keep or use it dishonestly. It is different from theft because the property is not necessarily taken by force or stealth — the dishonesty lies in deciding to keep or use it wrongfully.
real_world_examples: A labourer in Mumbai finds a gold chain on the street, knows it belongs to someone else, and instead of handing it over to the police, sells it at a jewellery shop and keeps the money — this is misappropriation.

A bank employee in Delhi is handed cash by a customer to deposit into their account but instead uses the money to pay off his personal debts, intending to replace it later — this constitutes misappropriation.

A domestic worker in Chennai finds an expensive watch left behind by her employer who has gone abroad, and, believing the employer won't return soon, gives the watch to her relative to keep — this is misappropriation.
A college student in Kolkata borrows a classmate's laptop for a day but sells it when he runs short of money, planning to buy a new one later — this amounts to misappropriation of the property.

A warehouse manager in Pune who is entrusted with storing agricultural produce uses part of the stored goods for his own household consumption without the owner's consent — this is misappropriation of movable property.
what_it_covers: Keeping and using movable property found by a person when the owner is identifiable or the property should be handed over to authorities.
Converting property entrusted to one's care — such as goods stored, cash deposited, or items for safekeeping — to one's own personal use dishonestly.
Using another person's movable property temporarily given for a specific purpose in an entirely different, unauthorised manner that amounts to dishonest conversion.
A person who discovers lost property and, instead of taking reasonable steps to find the owner, sells or uses it for personal benefit.
what_it_excludes: Taking property by stealth directly from another person's possession without their consent, which constitutes theft under Section 303 rather than misappropriation.
Acts done in good faith under a genuine and reasonable belief that the property belongs to the person using it — absence of dishonest intent excludes misappropriation.
Lawful retention of property under a legal right such as a lien, court order, or contractual entitlement, even if the owner demands its return.
Property obtained through fraud or coercion, which falls under cheating or robbery provisions rather than misappropriation.
Immovable property — misappropriation under the Act applies only to movable property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'misappropriate' under the BNS determines whether an accused is charged with criminal misappropriation of property under Section 314 (or related provisions such as Section 328), attracting imprisonment and fine, rather than a lesser civil wrong or no offence at all. The presence of dishonest intent to misappropriate is the critical element that elevates a civil dispute over property into a cognisable criminal offence.

definitions.definition: Misappropriation, as used in Sections 314 and 315 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the act of dishonestly taking or converting any movable property to one's own use, including property found or entrusted, without lawful authority or justification. It denotes the wrongful appropriation of another's property for personal benefit, without the owner's consent and with a dishonest intent.
definitions.plain_english: Misappropriation means taking something that belongs to someone else and using it as your own, knowing you are not entitled to do so. This could happen when someone finds a lost item and keeps it instead of returning it, or when someone uses money or property given to them for a specific purpose for their own benefit instead. The key element is dishonest intent — the person knows the property is not theirs but uses or keeps it anyway.
real_world_examples: A person finds a wallet containing cash and a debit card on a Mumbai local train platform. Instead of handing it to the railway authorities or attempting to trace the owner, they pocket the cash and spend it on personal items — this amounts to criminal misappropriation of property.

A construction contractor in Delhi is given Rs. 5 lakh by a housing society to purchase building materials. He instead deposits the funds in his personal bank account and uses a portion to pay off his personal loan, constituting misappropriation of entrusted funds.

A domestic worker in Chennai, while cleaning the house, finds a gold ring that had slipped under the sofa and belongs to the homeowner. Knowing it belongs to the employer, the worker takes and sells the ring at a local jeweller — this is misappropriation of movable property.

An employee of a Kolkata trading firm is given petty cash for office expenses. Over several months, he systematically uses a portion of this cash for personal purchases, recording false entries — this constitutes dishonest misappropriation of movable property.

A person borrows a colleague's bicycle in Bengaluru for a day but instead sells it to a second-hand dealer and keeps the proceeds, knowing the bicycle belongs to the colleague — this is misappropriation by conversion to own use.

A government peon in Hyderabad is handed official stationery and postage stamps for office use. He consistently takes a portion home and sells them to a local shop for personal gain — constituting misappropriation of government movable property.
semantic_tags: wrongful use of another's movable property
what_it_covers: A person who finds lost movable property and, instead of taking steps to locate the rightful owner, keeps it for personal use or sells it dishonestly.
An individual entrusted with money or goods for a specific purpose who diverts those resources to their own use, knowing they are not entitled to do so.
A person who comes into possession of movable property under a mistake or accident and, knowing the property belongs to another, dishonestly converts it to their own use instead of returning it.
Conversion of another's movable property by intermixing it with one's own goods with the intention of later claiming the whole as one's own, thereby depriving the true owner.
Using property belonging to a deceased person, before legal heirs are identified, for personal benefit without authority.
what_it_excludes: Theft, which requires the additional element of moving property out of another person's possession without consent — misappropriation typically involves property already in one's possession or found property, not property taken from another's active possession.

Criminal breach of trust, which involves misappropriation specifically of property that was entrusted or dominion over which was entrusted in a fiduciary or contractual capacity — governed separately under Section 316 of the BNS.
Good-faith use of property by a person who genuinely and reasonably believes the property is their own or that they have lawful authority to use it, as dishonest intent is a required element.
Rightful possession or use of property under a valid legal claim, court order, or owner's express or implied consent.
Robbery or extortion, which involve coercion or force to obtain property and are governed by distinct provisions.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes misappropriation under Section 314 determines if the accused faces imprisonment extendable to two years, or fine, or both; a more aggravated form under Section 315 (misappropriation of property found) attracts the same punishment but with specific conditions relating to found property. The distinction between misappropriation, theft, and criminal breach of trust directly affects which charge is framed, the applicable punishment, and the elements the prosecution must prove.

definitions.definition: Miscarriage, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, refers to the voluntary or involuntary termination of a pregnancy, whether by causing a woman with child to expel the foetus or by any act done with intent to bring about such termination. Causing miscarriage is an offence independently of any harm it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman, unless done in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman.
definitions.plain_english: Miscarriage means ending a pregnancy by causing the expulsion or destruction of the foetus in the womb. Under this law, deliberately causing a woman to miscarry is a crime, unless a doctor does it in genuine good faith to save the woman's life. Even the woman herself can be guilty under this section if she voluntarily causes her own miscarriage outside the legal exceptions.
real_world_examples: A man mixes an abortifacient substance into a pregnant woman's food without her knowledge in order to terminate her pregnancy — this amounts to causing miscarriage without the woman's consent under Section 89.

A traditional practitioner in a rural village performs an unsafe procedure on a pregnant woman to end her pregnancy, outside any medical facility and without lawful justification — this constitutes voluntarily causing miscarriage under Section 88.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester self-administers pills obtained from an unlicensed source to abort her foetus without any medical supervision or legal sanction — she falls within the meaning of Section 88 as a person who causes herself to miscarry.

A person beats a pregnant woman severely with the intent to terminate her pregnancy, and the woman subsequently dies as a result — this constitutes the offence under Section 90 (death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage).

A qualified doctor, facing a medical emergency where continuing the pregnancy would certainly kill the mother, performs a termination procedure in a registered hospital — this is excluded from criminal liability as it is done in good faith to save the life of the woman.
semantic_tags: maternal death due to abortion attempt
what_it_covers: Any voluntary act by a third party that causes a pregnant woman to expel or lose her foetus, whether or not the woman consents.
A woman who voluntarily causes herself to miscarry, as she is expressly brought within the scope of Section 88.
An act intended to cause miscarriage that results in the death of the pregnant woman, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 90.
Causing miscarriage of a woman who is quick with child (i.e., where foetal movement is perceptible), which carries a higher maximum sentence of seven years.
Causing miscarriage without the woman's consent at any stage of pregnancy, whether or not the woman is quick with child, which is punishable with life imprisonment or up to ten years.
what_it_excludes: Termination of pregnancy performed in good faith by a registered medical practitioner for the purpose of saving the life of the woman, which is expressly excepted from criminal liability.
Spontaneous or natural miscarriage not caused by any voluntary human act, as the sections require a voluntarily caused act or a deliberate intent to cause miscarriage.
Medical terminations of pregnancy carried out lawfully under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971, which provides a separate statutory framework overriding the general criminal prohibition.

Accidental harm to a pregnant woman that incidentally results in miscarriage, where there was no intent or knowledge that the act was likely to cause miscarriage, as voluntary causation or specific intent is a required element.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes 'causing miscarriage' under BNS 2023 determines whether the accused faces punishment ranging from three years to life imprisonment, and the presence or absence of the woman's consent and the stage of pregnancy (quick with child or not) further calibrates the severity of the offence. The definition also establishes that consent of the woman or her guardian cannot justify the act, making it an offence independent of harm, which blocks the usual consent-based defences available under Sections 25–27.

definitions.definition: Mischief is not formally defined in the sections provided, but as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, it refers to an act by which a person intentionally causes, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person by destroying or diminishing the value or utility of any property, or by affecting it injuriously. It is an offence against property that may trigger the right of private defence and, in aggravated forms involving fire or explosive substances on dwellings, may justify even lethal defensive force.
definitions.plain_english: Mischief means deliberately damaging or destroying someone else's property, or doing something you know will cause that kind of damage or loss. It is a crime against property — like breaking windows, setting fire to a building, or wrecking a vehicle on purpose. The law treats it seriously enough that if someone commits mischief against your home using fire or explosives, you are legally allowed to use even deadly force to protect yourself and your property.
real_world_examples: A political activist in Uttar Pradesh deliberately smashes the windows and headlights of a rival party worker's car during an election dispute, causing significant financial damage — this constitutes mischief under the BNS.

A disgruntled tenant in Mumbai, before vacating the premises, intentionally breaks all the sanitary fittings, tears out electrical wiring, and damages the walls of the rented flat, knowing this will cause wrongful loss to the landlord — a classic instance of mischief.

A group of persons in a communal dispute in Rajasthan sets fire to a rival community's shop, which is also used as a residence — this amounts to aggravated mischief by fire on a dwelling, enabling the occupants to exercise their right of private defence to the extent of causing death under Section 41.

A factory worker in Pune, angered by his dismissal, deliberately pours acid on the factory's machinery, destroying expensive equipment and halting production — this constitutes mischief with potential aggravated consequences under Section 326 or 327 of the BNS.

Farmers in Haryana in a land dispute breach an irrigation canal or destroy standing crops belonging to a neighbouring farmer, knowing it will cause wrongful loss — this act of destroying agricultural property intentionally amounts to mischief.

An individual in Chennai, to settle a personal grudge, cuts the brake lines of a neighbour's vehicle, knowing it is likely to cause damage or injury — this knowing causation of potential harm to property and person amounts to mischief.
semantic_tags: right of private defence of property
what_it_covers: Intentionally setting fire to a building, tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling or for custody of property.
Deliberately damaging or destroying movable or immovable property of another person, knowing such damage will cause wrongful loss.
Using any explosive substance to destroy or injure property belonging to another person or the public.
Wilfully breaking, defacing, or rendering useless any machinery, infrastructure, or other property of economic or public utility.
Acts committed against property under circumstances that may reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt if the right of private defence is not exercised.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or negligent damage to property that lacks the element of intention or knowledge that damage is the likely consequence — such acts do not constitute mischief.
Theft, robbery, or criminal trespass, which are separately defined offences against property under the BNS and are distinct from mischief even though they may co-occur.
Damage caused in the lawful exercise of a legal right, such as demolition of an encroachment pursuant to a valid court order or government direction.
Acts of civil dispute such as withholding property or breach of contract, which may cause financial loss but do not involve direct physical damage or destruction of property.
Self-inflicted damage to one's own property, as mischief requires that the loss or damage be caused to the property of another person or the public.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as mischief determines whether the right of private defence of property is triggered under Sections 35, 42, and 43, and in its aggravated form (mischief by fire or explosive substance on a dwelling), whether the defender may lawfully cause death under Section 41; it also determines criminal liability and sentencing under Sections 324–327 and 334 of the BNS.

Why it matters: Whether an act qualifies as mischief determines whether the right of private defence of property is triggered under Sections 35, 42, and 43, and in its aggravated form (mischief by fire or explosive substance on a dwelling), whether the defender may lawfully cause death under Section 41; it also determines criminal liability and sentencing under Sections 324–327 and 334 of the BNS.

definitions.definition: A misconception, in the context of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a false belief or erroneous understanding of fact held by a person at the time of performing an act, which causes that person to act in a manner they would not have otherwise acted. Where a person acts under such a misconception, the act may not constitute an offence, but the right of private defence against that act is preserved in the same manner as if the act were a full offence (Section 36).
definitions.plain_english: A 'misconception' means a wrong or mistaken belief about the facts of a situation that leads a person to do something they would not have done had they known the truth. For example, someone might genuinely but wrongly believe they are defending themselves or entering their own property, when in fact they are not. Even if this mistaken belief means the person has committed no crime, others who are harmed by their actions still have the legal right to defend themselves. The concept also appears in consent law, where consent given due to a false belief about facts is treated as no valid consent.
real_world_examples: A security guard at a Delhi housing society, believing in good faith that a resident entering late at night is a burglar, physically restrains the resident. The guard acts under a misconception of fact and commits no offence, but the resident has the full right of private defence against the guard's unlawful restraint.

A farmer in rural Maharashtra finds what he believes to be an abandoned bicycle on his land and takes it home, genuinely thinking it is ownerless property. He acts under a misconception of fact; while he may not be guilty of theft, the true owner retains all legal rights to reclaim the bicycle.

A woman in Mumbai gives her consent to a financial transaction after a fraudster falsely represents that the funds will be used for a government welfare scheme. Her consent is vitiated by misconception of fact under Section 28, making the transaction legally invalid and potentially fraudulent.

A man in Chennai, tricked by a fraudster into believing he is authorised to collect documents on behalf of a company, retrieves papers from an office. Induced by misconception, he commits no dishonest act himself, but the person who created the misconception is liable for abetment under Section 46.

In a property dispute in Kolkata, a person mistakenly believes he has a court order permitting him to enter and occupy a disputed flat, and forcibly enters the premises. Acting under misconception, he may not have criminal intent, but the occupant has the same right of private defence as if the entry were a deliberate criminal trespass.
what_it_covers: A person who genuinely but wrongly believes they are entering their own property and is therefore not guilty of trespass, yet the actual occupant retains the right of private defence against them.
A situation where consent to an act is given by a person who has been misled about a material fact, rendering such consent legally invalid under Section 28.

An act performed by a person who holds a false belief about the identity, ownership, or legal status of a thing or person involved in the act, negating criminal intent for that person while preserving others' defensive rights.

An abettor who creates a false belief in the mind of another, causing that other person to act under misconception, thereby making the abettor criminally liable even though the immediate actor commits no offence.
what_it_excludes: A deliberate or wilful misrepresentation of facts by the person performing the act — this would constitute fraud or deceit, not an innocent misconception.
A mistake purely of law (as opposed to a mistake of fact) — misunderstanding a legal rule or one's legal rights does not constitute a misconception of fact under the Act.
Reckless or negligent disregard for the truth, where a person makes no genuine attempt to verify facts before acting — mere carelessness does not qualify as acting under a misconception.
Consent given by a person who is below twelve years of age or who is of unsound mind or intoxicated — the invalidity of such consent arises from incapacity, not misconception.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person acts under a misconception directly determines criminal liability: if the act is performed under a genuine misconception of fact, the actor may be entirely absolved of the relevant offence (e.g., theft, trespass, or criminal force), while the person who induced the misconception may become liable for abetment. Simultaneously, under Section 36, the victim of the act retains the full right of private defence regardless of the actor's innocent mental state, ensuring that the absence of criminal intent in the actor does not leave affected parties without legal protection.

definitions.definition: A misconception of fact, within the meaning of Section 28, refers to a false belief held by a consenting person regarding a material fact, where such belief is not true, and where the person doing the act knows or has reason to believe that the consent was given in consequence of such misconception. Consent so obtained does not constitute valid consent under this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: A 'misconception of fact' means that a person agreed to something based on a false or incorrect belief about a real-world fact. For example, if someone is tricked into thinking they are doing one thing when they are actually doing something completely different, their agreement does not count as real consent. The law says that if the person who benefits from that agreement knew the other person had the wrong idea, the consent is invalid.
real_world_examples: A man in Mumbai poses as a licensed Ayurvedic doctor and convinces a woman to undergo a physical examination, claiming it is a standard medical procedure. She consents based on the false belief that he is a qualified professional. Her consent is vitiated by misconception of fact as to his credentials.

In a matrimonial fraud case in Delhi, a man falsely represents to a woman that he is unmarried and induces her to enter into a sexual relationship on the promise of marriage. The woman's consent is given under a misconception of fact regarding his marital status.

A pharmaceutical salesperson in Chennai tells a patient that a particular pill is a vitamin supplement, when it is actually a sedative. The patient consumes it based on that false belief. Any act performed on the unconscious patient thereafter cannot rely on that consent, as it was induced by a misconception of fact.

A property dealer in Bengaluru induces a landowner to sign a power of attorney by falsely describing the document as a simple tenancy agreement. The owner's signature (consent) is given under a misconception of fact about the nature of the document.

A fraudster in Kolkata poses as a government official and convinces a shopkeeper to hand over goods, claiming it is for an official survey. The shopkeeper's consent to give away the goods is based on a misconception of fact about the official's identity and authority.

A man in Hyderabad impersonates a woman's husband in darkness and engages in sexual intercourse with her. Her consent is entirely based on a misconception of fact as to the identity of the person, rendering the consent legally void.
what_it_covers: Consent given by a person who falsely believes the other party to be someone else, such as a spouse or a licensed professional.
Consent given based on a false representation about the nature or purpose of an act, such as believing a medical examination is routine when it is not.
Consent given in reliance on a false claim about a material circumstance, such as marital status, official authority, or qualification, where the other party is aware of the false belief.
Any situation where the consenting party would not have agreed had they known the true facts, and the acting party had reason to know this.
what_it_excludes: Consent given under a mistake of law rather than a mistake of fact; an erroneous belief about one's legal rights or obligations does not constitute misconception of fact.
Cases where the acting party had no knowledge of and no reason to believe that the other person's consent was based on a false belief, as knowledge or reasonable belief is a required element.
Consent given freely and with full knowledge of all material facts, even if the consenting party later regrets the decision.
Consent vitiated solely by fear of injury or by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication, which are governed by separate limbs of Section 28 and are distinct from misconception of fact.
definitions.why_it_matters: If consent is shown to have been given under a misconception of fact, it is treated as no consent at all under this Sanhita, which can convert an otherwise lawful act into a criminal offence — for instance, transforming a consensual act into an offence of rape, cheating, or criminal misappropriation. It directly determines criminal liability by negating the defence of consent that an accused might otherwise raise.

definitions.definition: The term 'misconduct' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 120 and cognate provisions, it denotes improper, wrongful, or unprofessional behaviour by a person — particularly a public servant or official — in the discharge or abuse of their duties, which may be subject to detection, inquiry, or departmental action. It encompasses acts or omissions that violate applicable rules, codes of conduct, or legal obligations governing the conduct of an individual in an official or fiduciary capacity.
definitions.plain_english: Misconduct refers to bad or improper behaviour, especially by someone in an official position like a government employee or police officer, that breaks rules or codes of conduct. It is not a crime in the same sense as murder or theft, but it can lead to departmental action, suspension, or dismissal. In the context of Section 120 of the BNS, 'misconduct' is something a person might be tortured into confessing to, showing it is an act of wrongdoing that authorities might investigate.
real_world_examples: A police officer is suspected of taking bribes and a colleague tortures another officer to extract a confession about the bribe-taking misconduct — the torturer commits an offence under Section 120 BNS.

A revenue department employee is alleged to have manipulated land records, and a superior tortures a subordinate to get information leading to detection of this official misconduct — this constitutes an offence under Section 120.

A government school teacher is accused of departmental misconduct for persistently absent from duty; a local official wrongfully confines a witness and coerces them to reveal information about the teacher's conduct, attracting liability under Section 127 BNS.

A senior bureaucrat is under departmental inquiry for financial irregularities; a subordinate is tortured by investigators acting outside lawful authority to extract a statement about the bureaucrat's misconduct, triggering Section 120 of the BNS.

A public servant gives false information to a Magistrate alleging misconduct by a police officer, knowing the information is false and likely to cause the officer's dismissal — attracting liability under Section 217 BNS.
what_it_covers: Improper or unprofessional acts by public servants or officials in the discharge of their duties, such as accepting bribes, neglecting duty, or abusing authority.

Any act or omission by an individual in an official or fiduciary capacity that violates applicable service rules, departmental codes, or legal obligations and is subject to departmental inquiry or disciplinary proceedings.
Situations where a person in authority acts beyond their sanctioned powers or in a manner that causes harm, prejudice, or violation of trust placed in them by the State or employer.
Conduct that, while not necessarily a criminal offence, is sufficiently blameworthy to warrant institutional investigation or punishment, such as dereliction of duty or misuse of official position.
what_it_excludes: Acts that constitute substantive criminal offences under the BNS (such as theft, murder, or fraud) — these are independently categorised as 'offences' rather than mere 'misconduct'.
Personal or private behaviour of individuals that has no nexus to any official, professional, or fiduciary duty — purely private wrongdoing not connected to any position of responsibility.
Lawful exercise of official discretion or authority, even if the outcome is adverse to another person, provided it is within sanctioned limits and not in violation of any rule or duty.
Civil wrongs or tortious acts between private individuals that do not involve any breach of a duty owed in an official or institutional capacity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'misconduct' within the meaning of Section 120 BNS determines whether the purpose of causing hurt or grievous hurt — extracting information leading to its detection — constitutes an aggravated criminal offence punishable with up to seven or ten years of imprisonment; if no misconduct is involved, the specific aggravated purpose element of Section 120 is not satisfied, potentially reducing liability to a lesser hurt offence.

definitions.definition: A mistake of fact, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to an erroneous belief about a factual circumstance (and not an error about the content or existence of a law) held in good faith by a person, which causes that person to believe themselves bound or justified by law in doing an act that would otherwise constitute an offence. Such a belief, when held honestly and not arising from negligence or deliberate ignorance, absolves the person of criminal liability for the act done under that mistaken belief.
definitions.plain_english: A 'mistake of fact' means that a person genuinely and honestly believed a certain factual situation to be true, and because of that wrong belief, they did something that turns out to be an offence. The key is that the mistake was about facts (like who a person is, or what a situation actually was), not about what the law says. If someone acts in good faith based on a wrong factual belief, the law may excuse them from punishment. This protection does not apply if the person was simply wrong about what the law allows.
real_world_examples: A police officer in Mumbai, acting on credible information and after due inquiry, arrests a person he genuinely believes to be a wanted criminal, but the person turns out to be an innocent individual with a similar appearance and name — the officer is not guilty of wrongful confinement because he acted under a genuine mistake of fact.

A forest guard in Madhya Pradesh, having received orders to shoot at poachers entering a protected reserve at night, fires at a figure he honestly and reasonably believes to be an armed poacher, but it turns out to be a villager who had strayed in — the guard may be protected under mistake of fact if the belief was genuine and in good faith.

A shopkeeper in Delhi, believing that certain goods stored by a customer in his shop were unclaimed abandoned property (a factual belief), disposes of them — he may claim mistake of fact as a defence if he genuinely and honestly believed the goods were abandoned, even though they were not.

A private citizen in Chennai witnesses what appears to him to be a murder in progress and, exercising the power available to all persons to apprehend an offender caught in the act, restrains and hands over the person to police — it later emerges the person was acting in self-defence. The citizen is protected because his belief, based on what he observed, was a genuine mistake of fact.

An Army jawan posted for riot control in a sensitive area of Manipur follows the order of a superior officer to use force, genuinely believing the order to be lawful and the situation to legally warrant such action — even if the factual premise of the order was incorrect, he may be protected if his belief in the factual justification was honest and in good faith.
semantic_tags: good faith act under wrong facts
what_it_covers: An honest and good-faith erroneous belief about an existing factual situation (such as the identity of a person, the nature of an object, or the circumstances of an event) that causes someone to act as though they are bound or justified by law.
Acts performed by a public servant or private individual who, after due inquiry, forms a genuine but incorrect factual belief that the act they are performing is required or permitted by law.

Cases where the person's erroneous belief is about a matter of fact external to the law itself — such as who a person is, what a situation involves, or what factual conditions are present — rather than about the interpretation or content of a legal rule.
what_it_excludes: A mistake about the law itself — i.e., a person's wrong belief that a particular law permits a certain act, or ignorance of what the law provides — does not qualify as a mistake of fact and does not provide a defence.

Beliefs that are not held in good faith, are careless, reckless, or result from wilful ignorance of facts that could have been ascertained with reasonable diligence — such negligent mistakes do not attract the protection of this defence.
Acts done with actual criminal knowledge or criminal intention, where the person was aware of the true factual situation but chose to act anyway, cannot be shielded by pleading a mistake of fact.

Situations where the erroneous belief is clearly unreasonable or implausible given the circumstances, and no prudent person in that position would have formed such a belief, are generally excluded from the protection afforded by this principle.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act was performed under a genuine mistake of fact determines whether it falls within the general exceptions to criminal liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — if it does, no offence is constituted and the person cannot be convicted or punished. It is therefore a complete defence that blocks liability for offences that would otherwise arise, including wrongful confinement, assault, use of force, or even culpable homicide, provided the belief was honest and in good faith.

Why it matters: Whether an act was performed under a genuine mistake of fact determines whether it falls within the general exceptions to criminal liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — if it does, no offence is constituted and the person cannot be convicted or punished. It is therefore a complete defence that blocks liability for offences that would otherwise arise, including wrongful confinement, assault, use of force, or even culpable homicide, provided the belief was honest and in good faith.

(Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)

definitions.definition: The term 'modesty' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 74 and 79, it refers to the sense of decency, dignity, and sexual propriety that is attributed to a woman, encompassing her right to be free from unwanted physical contact, lewd gestures, sexually offensive words or sounds, or any act that violates her bodily or personal integrity in a sexual or indecent manner. An act outrages a woman's modesty when it is intended to, or is likely to, humiliate, shame, or violate her dignity as a woman in a sexual or indecent context.
definitions.plain_english: Modesty, in this context, refers to a woman's dignity, decency, and the right to not be subjected to sexual or indecent behaviour without her consent. It includes her right to be free from unwanted physical touching, lewd gestures, offensive words or sounds directed at her, or any intrusion into her privacy in an indecent way. If someone deliberately does something that is likely to make a woman feel sexually humiliated, violated, or disrespected, they are said to have 'outraged her modesty'.
real_world_examples: A man on a crowded Mumbai local train deliberately gropes or touches a woman passenger in a sexual manner — this constitutes use of criminal force to outrage her modesty under Section 74.

A group of men outside a college in Delhi whistle, make lewd gestures, and pass sexually explicit remarks loudly as a woman walks by, intending her to hear and see them — this falls under Section 79 as an act intended to insult modesty.

A male colleague in a Bengaluru office repeatedly makes suggestive sounds or cat-calls directed at a female employee within her earshot, intending to embarrass or demean her — this amounts to insulting modesty under Section 79.
A man in a marketplace in Chennai forcibly pulls a woman's dupatta or saree in a sexually suggestive manner — this is an assault using criminal force to outrage her modesty under Section 74.

A person in a residential colony in Hyderabad repeatedly peeks through windows or intrudes upon a woman's private space while she is in her home, violating her privacy in an indecent manner — this attracts Section 79 for intruding upon her privacy.

A delivery person in Kolkata sends unsolicited obscene photographs or exhibits an obscene object to a woman with the intent that she sees it — this constitutes an act intended to insult modesty under Section 79.
what_it_covers: Unwanted or forcible physical touching of a woman in a sexual or indecent manner, such as groping or molestation.
Uttering sexually explicit or derogatory words, making lewd sounds or gestures directed at a woman with the intent that she hears or sees them.
Exhibiting obscene objects or images to a woman in a manner intended to insult or humiliate her.
Intruding upon a woman's privacy in an indecent or sexually violating manner, such as voyeurism or stalking.
Any assault or use of criminal force against a woman where the perpetrator intends to, or knows it is likely to, outrage her sense of sexual decency and dignity.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or incidental physical contact with a woman in a public place without any sexual intent, such as an unintentional bump in a crowded area.
Medical examinations or procedures performed by a registered medical practitioner with proper consent, even if involving physical contact with intimate parts.
Consensual acts of a sexual or intimate nature between adults where the woman has freely and voluntarily agreed, as there is no violation of modesty against her will.
General verbal altercations, abuses, or insults that are not of a sexual or indecent nature and are not directed at the woman's gender or sexual dignity.
Acts committed without the intention or knowledge of outraging modesty, where there is a genuine mistake of fact or lack of any indecent intent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act outrages or insults a woman's modesty determines whether the offender is liable under Section 74 (punishable with mandatory minimum one year imprisonment up to five years plus fine) or Section 79 (punishable with up to three years simple imprisonment plus fine). The applicability of this concept is the foundational threshold that distinguishes these gender-specific offences from ordinary assault or nuisance offences, directly affecting the nature and severity of punishment.

definitions.definition: A person is said to cause 'motion' to another when he causes physical movement of that other person's body or causes any substance to move so as to come into contact with any part of that other's body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling, as described under the definition of 'force' in Section 128 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: Motion means physically moving a person or causing something to move and touch them or what they are wearing or carrying. It does not require direct physical contact by the person using force — throwing an object, releasing a tied boat, or setting an animal upon someone can all count as causing motion. It is one of the three physical states (motion, change of motion, cessation of motion) that define the use of force under the law.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai intentionally shoves a commuter on a crowded railway platform, physically displacing the commuter's body — this is causing motion to another person by bodily power.
A man in Delhi throws a stone at a woman walking on the street, causing the stone to strike her dupatta — the stone's contact with what she is wearing constitutes causing motion amounting to force.

A vendor in Chennai pours hot water from a vessel toward a customer in a dispute, and the water splashes onto the customer's arm — causing the water to move and contact the person is causing motion under Section 128.

A person in Kolkata releases a tied boat on the Hooghly river while someone is sitting in it, causing the boat and hence the person to drift — this causes motion to the person by disposing a substance without further act, satisfying the definition under Section 128.

A farmer in Punjab deliberately drives his cattle toward a trespasser, causing the animals to push against and move the trespasser — inducing animals to cause motion to another falls squarely within this definition.

A protestor in Bengaluru throws a bag of paint at a police officer, which lands on the officer's uniform — causing that substance to contact what the officer is wearing constitutes causing motion under the section.
what_it_covers: Directly pushing or shoving another person using one's own bodily strength, causing their body to physically move.
Throwing or propelling any object or substance that strikes the other person's body, clothing, or anything they are carrying.
Releasing, displacing, or setting in motion a vehicle, vessel, or object that carries another person, thereby causing that person to move.
Inducing or inciting an animal to physically push, charge at, or move against another person.
Pouring, spraying, or directing any liquid or substance so that it comes into contact with the other person's body or their worn/carried items and affects their sense of feeling.
what_it_excludes: Verbal threats or spoken words alone that cause fear but involve no physical displacement or contact — such conduct may constitute criminal intimidation but does not amount to 'motion' under Section 128.
Mere gestures or movements by the accused that do not result in any actual physical contact with or displacement of the other person or any substance touching them.
Psychological or emotional distress caused without any accompanying physical movement, contact, or displacement of the person or a substance reaching them.
A person's own voluntary movement in response to a request or instruction, where no external physical compulsion or displacement is applied to them by the accused.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether 'motion' has been caused to a person determines whether the accused has used 'force' under Section 128, which is a foundational element for establishing the offences of criminal force under Section 129 and assault under Section 130; without proof of motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion, neither offence can be made out. It also bears on offences involving theft under Section 303, where moving a movable property is the actus reus of the offence.

definitions.definition: "Movable property" includes property of every description, except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth.
definitions.plain_english: Movable property refers to any type of property that can be physically moved or carried, as long as it is not land itself or something fixed permanently to the ground. This includes everyday objects like money, jewellery, vehicles, electronics, and livestock. Essentially, if it can be picked up and taken away, it is likely movable property under this law.
real_world_examples: A thief in Mumbai steals a gold necklace and cash from a household — both the jewellery and cash are movable property under the BNS, making the act theft under Section 303.
A person in Delhi snatches a mobile phone from a pedestrian's hand — the smartphone qualifies as movable property, attracting the offence of snatching under Section 304.
A cattle trader in Rajasthan dishonestly misappropriates buffaloes entrusted to him for transport — livestock being movable property triggers criminal misappropriation under Section 314.

A contractor in Chennai removes electrical wiring and copper pipes from a building under construction without authorisation — these detached items constitute movable property once separated from the structure, potentially constituting theft.

A person in Kolkata commits dacoity by forcibly taking a car, laptops, and cash from a family at gunpoint — all these items being movable property satisfy the property element of dacoity under Section 310.

A shopkeeper in Hyderabad dishonestly retains a customer's pawned motorcycle beyond the agreed period with intent to sell it — the motorcycle as movable property attracts criminal breach of trust under Section 238.

Livestock and animals such as cattle, horses, and poultry
Motor vehicles including cars, motorcycles, and trucks
Goods stored in warehouses or shops, including agricultural produce and merchandise
Documents and valuable securities that have physical form
Building materials or fixtures that have been detached or severed from the earth or a permanent structure
what_it_excludes: Land itself, including agricultural land, residential plots, and any other category of land
Things permanently attached to the earth, such as buildings, walls, and boundary structures that have not been severed
Trees and crops that remain rooted in the ground and are still attached to the earth
Permanently embedded infrastructure such as underground pipelines or railway tracks that are fastened to the earth
Rights over immovable property such as easements or mortgages that pertain to land

If the property involved is immovable, these specific offences cannot be charged, and different or no criminal provisions may apply.

definitions.definition: Murder is culpable homicide committed with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused, or with the intention of causing bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury. Culpable homicide is murder except in the cases reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Murder is the unlawful killing of a person done intentionally or with full knowledge that the act will almost certainly cause death. It is the most serious form of unlawful killing and is distinguished from lesser forms of homicide by the presence of deliberate intent or extreme recklessness equivalent to intent. In simple terms, if someone kills another person on purpose or does something so dangerous that death is virtually certain, it is murder.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi poisons his business partner's food deliberately to inherit the partnership assets; the partner dies — this is murder under Section 103 as the act was done with the intention of causing death.

A woman in Mumbai hires a contract killer to shoot her estranged husband, and the husband is killed — both the woman and the killer are guilty of murder, as the killing was premeditated and intentional.

During a communal riot in Uttar Pradesh, a mob leader instructs members to set fire to a house knowing a family is trapped inside; the family perishes — this constitutes murder as the act was done with knowledge that death would certainly result.

A farmer in Punjab thrashes a labourer repeatedly on the head with an iron rod over a wage dispute until the labourer dies — this is murder since the injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

A gang in Chennai pushes a rival gang member off a high-rise building terrace during a confrontation — this is murder as the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death.

A domestic worker in Kolkata administers repeated small doses of a toxic substance to her employer over several weeks resulting in death — this is murder as it falls within the category of cooperative or gradual administration of poison with intent to kill.
what_it_covers: Intentional killing where the accused directly intended the death of the victim, such as stabbing or shooting with the purpose of killing.
Killing caused by inflicting a bodily injury which the offender subjectively knew was likely to cause the victim's death given the victim's known condition.
Acts so imminently dangerous — such as setting someone on fire, drowning, or pushing from a height — that death is virtually certain and the offender had no excuse for taking such a risk.
Deaths resulting from a series of acts collectively causing death, including joint administration of poison by multiple persons acting in concert with intent to kill.
Murder committed by a citizen of India outside Indian territory, which remains triable in India under the Act's extra-territorial application provisions.
what_it_excludes: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder — where death is caused under grave and sudden provocation, or where the offender exceeded the right of private defence without premeditation, which attracts lesser punishment under Section 104.
Accidental or negligent killing without criminal intention or knowledge, which may constitute a rash or negligent act causing death but does not rise to the level of murder.
Causing death in the exercise of lawful private defence within permissible limits, which is justified by law and does not constitute an offence.
Killing by a person of unsound mind who is incapable of understanding the nature of the act, which is exempt from criminal liability under the general exceptions.
Culpable homicide committed by a child below seven years of age, which is entirely excluded from criminal liability under the general exceptions of the Sanhita.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an unlawful killing qualifies as murder rather than culpable homicide not amounting to murder is determinative of the punishment — murder under Section 103 attracts the death penalty or imprisonment for life, whereas culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 105 carries a lighter maximum sentence. The classification also triggers specific procedural consequences including the nature of trial, bail eligibility as a capital offence, and whether group liability provisions under gang or organised crime sections of the Sanhita apply.

definitions.definition: Mutiny, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a collective or individual act of insubordination, revolt, or refusal of duty by officers, soldiers, sailors, or airmen in the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India, directed against the lawful authority and discipline of the armed forces. The Act does not provide an express statutory definition but treats mutiny as an established military-law concept, addressing civilian abetment of such conduct in Sections 159 and 160.
definitions.plain_english: Mutiny means a rebellion or organized uprising by members of the Indian military — such as soldiers, sailors, or air force personnel — against their commanders or the lawful authority governing them. It involves refusing orders, overthrowing discipline, or collectively acting against the chain of command. The BNS does not punish the mutineers directly (that is handled by military law), but it does punish civilians or others who help, encourage, or incite such acts.
real_world_examples: A civilian political activist distributes pamphlets inside a cantonment area urging Army jawans to disobey orders and refuse to deploy in a conflict zone, thereby attempting to seduce soldiers from their duty — this would attract liability under Section 159.

A social media influencer in India posts videos targeting Indian Navy sailors stationed at a base, encouraging them to collectively refuse orders as a form of protest against government policy — this constitutes abetment of mutiny under Section 159.

A person secretly coordinates with a group of Air Force airmen to collectively abandon their posts and seize control of an air base; if the airmen do carry out the mutiny, the coordinator faces the death penalty or life imprisonment under Section 160.

A foreign agent operating in India contacts Indian Army officers through encrypted messaging apps and persuades them to revolt against their commanding officers during a military operation, which constitutes both abetment of mutiny and an offence against the State.

A retired military officer, nursing grievances, organizes a meeting where serving soldiers are encouraged to collectively disobey orders from their superior officers — even if the mutiny does not ultimately occur, the attempt to seduce them from duty is punishable under Section 159.
what_it_covers: Collective or individual revolt by serving officers, soldiers, sailors, or airmen of the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force against lawful military authority.
Refusal of orders or abandonment of duty amounting to a deliberate act of rebellion within the armed forces against the Government of India's chain of command.
Any organized uprising within the military establishment aimed at overthrowing or undermining the lawful authority of superior officers or the Government.
Acts of sedition within the armed forces where members attempt to seize control, refuse deployment, or collectively disregard their military obligations.
what_it_excludes: Individual acts of indiscipline or disobedience by a single soldier that fall short of a collective revolt or rebellion — these are governed by service regulations and military law, not BNS Sections 159–160.

Mutiny and desertion by armed forces personnel themselves, which are expressly excluded from BNS jurisdiction under Section 1 and governed by special military laws such as the Army Act, 1950, Navy Act, 1957, and Air Force Act, 1950.
Civilian protests, strikes, or acts of civil disobedience that do not involve members of the armed forces and do not constitute abetment of military insubordination.
Lawful representations, petitions, or complaints made by military personnel through proper channels regarding grievances, which do not amount to refusal of duty or revolt.

definitions.definition: A navigable channel, as used in Section 326 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any waterway — whether natural or artificial — that is used or capable of being used for the passage of vessels, boats, or other watercraft for the purpose of travel or conveyance of property, and includes canals, cuts, and artificial watercourses maintained for navigation.
definitions.plain_english: A navigable channel is any waterway — man-made or natural — through which boats, vessels, or other watercraft can travel or transport goods. This includes canals dug by irrigation or transport authorities, as well as natural streams or rivers wide and deep enough to support boat traffic. The law protects such channels from acts that make them impassable or unsafe for use.
real_world_examples: The Buckingham Canal in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, historically used for inland barge navigation, is an artificial navigable channel — any deliberate act of blocking or damaging it to prevent boat movement would fall under Section 326.

The canals of the Kerala backwaters network, used by country boats and houseboats for transporting passengers and goods, constitute navigable channels — dumping debris to obstruct ferry routes would attract liability under this provision.

The Ganga-Brahmaputra river system in West Bengal and Assam, where river ferries and cargo vessels operate, includes navigable channels — an act of sabotaging a canal lock or placing deliberate obstructions in the channel could constitute mischief under Section 326.

The Buckingham Canal and the National Waterway 1 (Allahabad to Haldia along the Ganga) include artificial and natural navigable channels — a contractor who illegally dumps construction waste into such a channel making it unnavigable for cargo vessels would be liable under this section.

In Goa, the Mandovi and Zuari rivers serve as navigable channels for ferry and cargo services — a person who deliberately installs underwater obstructions or sabotages the dredging works to render these channels less safe for navigation commits mischief punishable under Section 326.
what_it_covers: Artificial canals constructed and maintained by government or public authorities for navigation, such as the Buckingham Canal or National Waterways of India.
Natural rivers and streams that are wide, deep, and habitually used for passage of vessels or boats for travel or conveyance of goods.
Irrigation channels or cuts that are also used for the navigation of small boats and country craft for transporting agricultural produce or passengers.
Backwater channels and estuarine waterways used by commercial or public ferry services, such as those in Kerala's backwater network.
Any waterway, whether tidal or non-tidal, natural or artificially improved, that is open to public use for navigation of vessels carrying persons or property.
what_it_excludes: Private drainage ditches or irrigation channels too narrow or shallow to support navigation of any vessel or boat, used solely for agricultural water supply.
Underground sewage channels, storm water drains, or public drainage systems not designed or used for navigation purposes.
Seasonal or intermittent waterways that are dry for most of the year and do not support regular or habitual navigation of any vessel.
Ornamental water bodies such as decorative ponds, fountains, or water features in parks or gardens that are not used for navigation.
Swimming pools, water tanks, or reservoirs maintained solely for drinking water supply or storage, with no navigable function.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a waterway qualifies as a 'navigable channel' determines whether an act of mischief against it attracts punishment under Section 326 of the BNS, 2023, which prescribes imprisonment of up to five years, fine, or both. If the waterway does not meet this definition, the act may still constitute mischief under a lesser or different clause but would not trigger the specific aggravated penalty reserved for obstructing public navigation routes.

definitions.definition: A navigator is any person engaged in navigating or directing the course of a vessel, aircraft, or any watercraft through navigable waters or airways, who may be misled by false lights, marks, or buoys. The term encompasses all persons responsible for or subject to the guidance of navigation signals, marks, and aids to navigation on sea, river, or other navigable channels.
definitions.plain_english: A navigator is a person who steers or guides a ship, boat, or aircraft from one place to another, especially on water. This includes the captain, pilot, or any crew member responsible for determining and following the correct route using navigation aids like lights, buoys, and markers. The term is used in the law to protect such persons from being deliberately misled by fake or false navigation signals.
real_world_examples: A captain of a cargo vessel sailing through the Hooghly River near Kolkata who relies on riverbank buoys and lights to safely navigate the channel — if someone places a false buoy redirecting the vessel toward shallow waters, that captain is the navigator being protected under Section 283.

A fisherman operating a trawler off the coast of Kerala who depends on coastal light markers to avoid rocky outcrops at night — displaying a false light near a hazardous reef to mislead him constitutes an offence against the navigator under Section 283.

The pilot of a small aircraft approaching a private airstrip in Gujarat who is guided by runway approach lights — installation of false lights nearby to confuse the landing approach makes the pilot a potential victim as a navigator.

A ferry operator navigating between islands in the Andaman archipelago who uses channel marker buoys to stay in safe water — a person who moves or falsifies those buoys to mislead the ferry operator targets the operator as a navigator under the provision.

A merchant vessel officer approaching Mumbai Port who follows designated light signals and buoy markers to enter the harbour safely — anyone who exhibits false signals to mislead that officer is committing an offence against the navigator under Section 283.
what_it_covers: A ship captain or officer responsible for steering a merchant or fishing vessel through Indian coastal or inland waters.
A ferry operator or boatman navigating a river, estuary, or lake using lights, buoys, or channel markers as reference points.
An aircraft pilot relying on aeronautical lights and visual signals for navigation during approach, landing, or en-route flight.
Any crew member aboard a vessel who is entrusted with the navigational duties of determining course and avoiding hazards.
A professional river pilot guiding large vessels through narrow or complex waterways such as the Brahmaputra or Hooghly rivers.
what_it_excludes: A passenger aboard a ship or aircraft who has no role in directing or controlling the navigation of the vessel.
A port authority official or harbourmaster based onshore who provides advisory services but does not personally navigate any vessel.
A road vehicle driver or railway engine operator, who is guided by road or rail signals rather than nautical or aeronautical navigation aids.
A cartographer or hydrographic surveyor who charts navigable waters but does not actively navigate a vessel.
Maintenance workers or dock personnel who service vessels in port without being engaged in actual navigation or course-setting.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a navigator determines the applicability of Section 283, which punishes exhibiting false lights, marks, or buoys with up to seven years imprisonment and a minimum fine of ten thousand rupees. The definition is critical because the offence is specifically framed around the intent or knowledge that the false exhibition will mislead a navigator, making the identity and role of the deceived party a necessary element to establish criminal liability.

definitions.definition: An act is 'negligent' when it is done without reasonable care or caution that a prudent person would exercise in the circumstances, falling short of the standard of care required by law, thereby creating an unjustifiable risk of harm to human life or the personal safety of others. Unlike rashness, negligence involves inadvertence rather than conscious risk-taking. The term is used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 to describe conduct that, while not intentionally harmful, breaches the duty of care owed to others.
definitions.plain_english: Being 'negligent' means failing to take the reasonable care and precaution that any sensible, careful person would take in the same situation. It is not about wanting to hurt someone — it is about being careless enough that someone gets harmed as a result. Think of it as a serious lapse in attention or caution that a responsible person would not have made. It is less blameworthy than doing something recklessly on purpose but is still a punishable offence under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A doctor in a government hospital in Patna administers the wrong dosage of anaesthesia during a routine surgery without checking the patient's medical records, resulting in the patient's death — this constitutes a negligent act by a registered medical practitioner under Section 106.

A truck driver in Mumbai, distracted by his mobile phone while driving on the Western Express Highway, runs over a pedestrian crossing at a zebra crossing and causes grievous hurt — the act of driving without due care constitutes negligent driving under Sections 106 and 281.

A construction supervisor in Delhi fails to erect safety barricades around an open excavation pit near a busy footpath, and a child falls in and sustains serious injuries — the supervisor's omission to take necessary precautions amounts to a negligent act endangering personal safety under Section 125.

A pyrotechnics handler at a festival in Rajasthan negligently stores explosive fireworks near a residential area without following safety protocols, causing an accidental explosion that injures bystanders — this constitutes a negligent act endangering human life under Section 286.

A prison warden in Chennai, tasked with guarding an undertrial prisoner, leaves the cell door unlocked while taking an unauthorised nap, allowing the prisoner to escape — this amounts to negligently suffering a prisoner to escape under Section 261.

A pharmacist in Hyderabad dispenses a wrong prescription drug due to failure to read the prescription carefully, causing the customer to suffer a serious adverse reaction — this careless act without intent to harm constitutes negligence under the relevant provisions of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Acts done without reasonable care that result in death, hurt, or grievous hurt to another person, such as a driver failing to observe traffic signals and causing an accident.
Omissions by persons in positions of legal duty, such as a public servant failing to exercise proper vigilance over a prisoner in their custody, thereby allowing escape.

Professional acts performed without the requisite standard of care, such as a registered medical practitioner conducting a surgical procedure without following prescribed protocols, resulting in patient death.
Handling of dangerous substances, machinery, or vehicles without adequate precaution, where the lack of care endangers public safety.
Acts or omissions by any person — whether private individual or public servant — that fall below the objective standard of care expected by law and result in legally cognisable harm.
what_it_excludes: Acts done with deliberate intention to cause harm, which fall under intentional offences such as culpable homicide or murder rather than negligence.

Rash acts involving conscious and deliberate disregard of a known risk — rashness is treated as a distinct and separately enumerated mental state under the BNS, even when it co-exists with negligence in some sections.
Acts that result in harm despite all reasonable care having been taken, i.e., pure accidents where no objective breach of the standard of care can be established.
Acts done in good faith for the benefit of another person with their consent and without criminal intent, which may attract specific defences under the BNS.
Mere errors of professional judgment that do not fall below the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner in the relevant field, as distinguished from gross or actionable negligence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'negligent' determines criminal liability and the quantum of punishment under Sections 106, 125, 157, and 261 of the BNS — for instance, a negligent act causing death attracts up to five years' imprisonment, while negligence by a medical practitioner is capped at two years, reflecting a legislative distinction in culpability. Without establishing negligence, the accused cannot be convicted under these sections, making it the foundational element that triggers or blocks prosecution.

definitions.definition: A negligent act, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is an act done without due care and caution that a reasonable person would exercise, resulting in harm or risk of harm to others, where the doer fails to guard against a probable consequence that they should have foreseen, but without the intent or knowledge characteristic of culpable homicide. It includes acts done unlawfully or negligently that are likely to cause injury, disease, or death, as referenced in Sections 106 and 271.
definitions.plain_english: A negligent act means doing something carelessly or without proper attention, in a way that a reasonable person would have avoided, and which causes harm or danger to someone else. The person doing it does not necessarily mean to cause harm — they simply fail to take the precautions they should have taken. For example, a driver who does not pay attention to the road and accidentally kills a pedestrian has committed a negligent act.
real_world_examples: A construction worker in Mumbai fails to secure scaffolding properly, causing it to collapse and kill a passerby — the worker's failure to take standard safety precautions constitutes a negligent act under Section 106.

A doctor in a government hospital in Delhi administers the wrong dosage of medication to a patient without verifying the prescription, leading to the patient's death — this qualifies as a negligent act by a registered medical practitioner under Section 106.

A truck driver in Bengaluru, fatigued and driving at high speed, loses control and kills a cyclist, then flees the scene without informing the police or a magistrate — this constitutes a negligent act in rash and negligent driving with failure to report under Section 106.

A street food vendor in Kolkata knowingly uses contaminated water while preparing food, knowing it could spread a waterborne disease dangerous to life, and negligently serves it to customers — this is a negligent act under Section 271.

A factory owner in Surat fails to dispose of chemical waste safely, allowing toxic substances to seep into a local water supply, likely spreading disease dangerous to life among residents — constituting a negligent act under Section 271.

A school bus driver in Chennai, distracted by his mobile phone while driving, jumps a red light and fatally injures a schoolchild crossing the road — this is a classic negligent act causing death under Section 106.
what_it_covers: An act done carelessly without the intention to cause death but resulting in the death of a person, not amounting to culpable homicide, such as an untrained person operating heavy machinery that crushes a bystander.
Rash and negligent driving of a vehicle that causes death, especially where the driver flees without reporting to a police officer or magistrate after the incident.

An act by a registered medical practitioner during a medical procedure that, through lack of due care, causes the death of a patient — attracting a lesser maximum sentence under the proviso to Section 106.

Unlawful or negligent acts that the doer knows or has reason to believe are likely to spread infection of a disease dangerous to life, such as knowingly releasing contaminated wastewater into a public reservoir.
Conduct by any person — whether professional or layperson — that falls below the standard of care expected in the circumstances and directly results in death or serious risk of disease to others.
what_it_excludes: Acts done with the intention to cause death or with knowledge that death is likely, which would amount to culpable homicide or murder and are governed by separate provisions of the BNS, 2023.
Accidents caused by unforeseeable circumstances or Acts of God where no reasonable person could have anticipated or prevented the harm — such acts lack the element of negligence.
Deliberate or wilful acts carried out with full knowledge of their harmful consequences, as these cross the threshold into intentional wrongdoing or culpable homicide, not mere negligence.
Acts that cause harm but where there is no duty of care or reasonable expectation of caution on the part of the doer in the given circumstances.
Acts by persons of unsound mind or those acting under a bona fide mistake of fact, where the mental element required for a negligent act is absent.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'negligent act' under Section 106 determines whether the accused faces up to five years of imprisonment (or two years if a registered medical practitioner, or ten years if involving negligent driving with escape) rather than the more severe penalties for culpable homicide or murder. It also triggers liability under Section 271 for acts negligently spreading life-threatening disease, making the distinction between negligent, rash, and intentional conduct critical to the nature of the charge and the quantum of punishment.
