definitions.definition: Permanent or partial damage means any damage or deformity caused to any part or parts of the body of a person, including by burning, maiming, disfiguring, or disabling, whether resulting from acid attack or any other means, and for the purposes of Section 124, such permanent or partial damage or deformity shall not be required to be irreversible.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to any significant harm done to a person's body that causes lasting or partial impairment, disfigurement, or loss of function to any body part — for example, scarring, loss of vision, or disability caused by an acid attack. Importantly, under this law, the damage does not need to be completely irreversible to count as 'permanent or partial.' Even significant but potentially treatable harm can qualify if it causes substantial injury at the time.
real_world_examples: A woman in Delhi has acid thrown on her face by a rejected suitor, resulting in severe scarring, loss of vision in one eye, and disfigurement of her cheek — this constitutes permanent or partial damage even if reconstructive surgery could partially restore appearance.

A man in Mumbai has acid poured on his arm by a business rival, causing deep burns that destroy muscle tissue and permanently reduce the mobility and strength of his arm — qualifying as partial damage and disability.

A teenage girl in Uttar Pradesh has acid administered to her by a family member in a property dispute, resulting in damage to her ear and partial hearing loss — this constitutes permanent or partial damage even if some hearing is retained.

A factory worker in Chennai is attacked with a corrosive chemical by a co-worker, causing severe burns across her neck and shoulders that leave permanent scars and impair her ability to turn her head — satisfying the definition of permanent or partial damage.

A woman in Kolkata survives an acid attack that damages her scalp and causes partial loss of hair follicles along with skin disfigurement — even if medically manageable, this qualifies as permanent or partial damage under Section 124.
what_it_covers: Complete or partial loss of vision in one or both eyes resulting from acid thrown at a person's face.
Severe scarring or disfigurement of skin, tissue, or facial features caused by acid or corrosive substances, even if partially treatable through surgery.
Loss or reduction of mobility, strength, or sensation in any limb or body part due to acid burns or chemical attack.
Damage to internal organs or bodily functions caused by administered acid, including harm to the digestive tract or respiratory system.
Partial hearing or sensory loss caused by acid exposure to the ear or surrounding areas.
what_it_excludes: Superficial or temporary injuries such as minor skin irritation or redness that heal completely without any lasting impairment or scarring.
Psychological or mental harm alone, without any accompanying physical damage or deformity to any body part.
Hurt or pain caused by non-corrosive, non-burning substances that does not result in any form of physical damage, deformity, or disability.
Injuries that amount only to simple hurt under Section 115, where no part of the body is damaged, deformed, disfigured, maimed, or disabled.
Damage caused purely by accident without any intention or knowledge of likely harm, as the section requires intent or knowledge on the part of the accused.

definitions.definition: A condition caused by throwing acid or administering acid or using any other means, wherein a person suffers a state of permanent vegetative state; for the purposes of Section 124, such permanent vegetative state shall not be required to be irreversible.
definitions.plain_english: A permanent vegetative state is a severe medical condition where a person is alive but has no awareness of themselves or their surroundings, resulting from an acid attack or similar assault. The person may have basic bodily functions like breathing, but cannot think, respond meaningfully, or interact with the world. Importantly, under this law, this condition does not need to be completely irreversible to qualify — even a prolonged or lasting state is sufficient.
real_world_examples: A woman in Delhi is doused with acid by a jilted suitor, resulting in severe brain damage from systemic acid poisoning; she remains alive but unresponsive and unaware of her surroundings for months — this constitutes a permanent vegetative state under Section 124.

A factory worker in Mumbai has concentrated acid forcibly administered to them, causing massive neurological damage; the victim shows no signs of consciousness or purposeful movement and requires full-time hospital care in Pune — triggering the enhanced punishment under Section 124.

A young student in Lucknow is attacked with acid, leading to a coma-like condition where she breathes independently but cannot communicate, recognise family, or follow commands — courts in Uttar Pradesh treat this as a permanent vegetative state for sentencing purposes under BNS 2023.

An acid attack survivor in Hyderabad who was admitted to a government hospital remains in a wakeful but completely unaware state for over a year post-attack, needing tube feeding and full medical care — the attacker is charged under Section 124 for causing a permanent vegetative state.

A domestic violence victim in Kolkata has acid poured on her by her husband, resulting in severe neurological impairment where she opens her eyes but shows no cognitive response — the husband faces a minimum ten-year imprisonment under Section 124 for inducing this state.
what_it_covers: A victim of an acid attack who is alive but completely unaware of self and environment, requiring full medical or nursing support for all bodily functions.

A condition where the victim may have sleep-wake cycles or open their eyes but exhibits no cognitive awareness, purposeful movement, or meaningful response to stimuli, caused by acid or similar means.

A prolonged or lasting state of unconscious wakefulness that, while not medically certified as permanent or irreversible, still qualifies under Section 124 as a permanent vegetative state for criminal liability purposes.
Any neurological state of total unawareness resulting from acid administration, acid throwing, or any other means used with intent or knowledge of causing such harm.
what_it_excludes: A victim who is in a temporary coma but has a clear prognosis of full neurological recovery, with no lasting unawareness — such a case would not qualify as permanent vegetative state.

A victim who suffers physical burns, disfigurement, or disability from an acid attack but retains full cognitive awareness and consciousness — these fall under the other limbs of Section 124 (damage, deformity, grievous hurt) rather than permanent vegetative state.
Natural medical conditions such as a vegetative state arising from a stroke, accident, or disease unconnected to any deliberate act of acid throwing or administration by another person.
A victim who is unconscious only briefly during the attack but regains full awareness and cognitive function within a short period without lasting neurological impairment.

The statutory clarification that such a state need not be irreversible significantly broadens the scope of this provision, ensuring perpetrators cannot escape enhanced liability by arguing the victim's condition may theoretically improve.

definitions.definition: Persistent vegetative state refers to a severe and permanent condition of unconsciousness in which a person suffers a complete and enduring loss of all cognitive functions and awareness, resulting from an injury inflicted upon them, yet retains certain basic autonomic functions such as breathing and heartbeat. As used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, it denotes a condition caused by an injury wherein the victim remains alive but in a state of total and irreversible neurological incapacitation, equated in gravity with permanent disability or death for the purpose of enhanced punishment.
definitions.plain_english: A persistent vegetative state is when a person is severely brain-damaged and permanently unconscious — they are alive in a biological sense, with their heart beating and lungs breathing, but they have no awareness of themselves or the world around them and cannot respond or communicate. This condition is caused by a serious physical injury and is considered irreversible. Under Indian criminal law, causing someone to end up in this condition is treated almost as seriously as causing their death.
real_world_examples: A woman in Delhi is gang-raped and during the assault suffers severe head trauma that leaves her completely unresponsive and dependent on life support in a hospital, with doctors confirming she will never regain consciousness — she is in a persistent vegetative state, attracting the enhanced punishment under Section 66 of the BNS.

A man in Mumbai is attacked by a group during a communal dispute; he is beaten so severely that he suffers irreversible brain damage and is admitted to a hospital in a vegetative state, never regaining awareness — the attackers face rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years under Section 117(3) of the BNS.

A factory worker in Chennai is assaulted by his employer with an iron rod over a wage dispute; the blow to his head causes catastrophic brain injury leaving him permanently unconscious on a ventilator — the employer is charged under Section 117 with the aggravated penalty applicable for causing persistent vegetative state.

A young woman in Hyderabad is attacked by an acid-like corrosive substance during a robbery gone violent; the resulting brain hypoxia leaves her in a permanent vegetative state — prosecutors invoke Section 66 or Section 117 depending on the nature of the primary offence, seeking the maximum punishment available under the respective provision.

A survivor of a brutal physical assault in Kolkata, after suffering repeated blows to the head during a robbery, is found by medical professionals to be in a persistent vegetative state with no reasonable chance of recovery, triggering the enhanced sentencing provisions under Section 117(3) against the perpetrators.

definitions.definition: A 'person interested' refers to any person who has a personal, emotional, familial, or material stake in the wellbeing, safety, reputation, or property of another person, such that injury, threat, or coercion directed at the primary sufferer or victim would also affect or be felt by that person. The term is used contextually across provisions dealing with extortion, wrongful confinement, and threatening to give false evidence to extend the scope of harm or coercion to those connected to the primary victim.
definitions.plain_english: A 'person interested' is someone who cares about or has a stake in the wellbeing of the main victim — such as a family member, close friend, or business partner. When a criminal threatens or harms a victim, they often do it knowing that someone close to the victim will also be affected or pressured. The law recognises this by extending its protection to cover not just the direct victim but also those connected to them.
real_world_examples: A kidnapper in Delhi abducts a businessman and threatens to harm him unless his wife (a person interested) pays a ransom, making her the target of coercive pressure under the extortion provisions.
A police officer in Mumbai tortures a suspect to extract a confession, knowing that the suspect's elderly father (a person interested) is watching and will pressure the suspect to comply.
A local goon in Chennai threatens a shopkeeper that he will attack the shopkeeper's son (a person interested) unless the shopkeeper gives false testimony in a court case under Section 232 BNS.
A landlord in Kolkata wrongfully confines a tenant and tells the tenant's wife (a person interested) that her husband will be released only if she signs over valuable property documents.
A criminal gang in Hyderabad threatens a witness that his sister's reputation will be destroyed (as a person interested in him) if he does not retract his statement before the court.
what_it_covers: A family member (parent, spouse, sibling, child) of the primary victim who is affected by threats or harm directed at the victim.
A business partner or creditor who has a financial or material interest in the wellbeing and actions of the person being threatened or harmed.
A close friend or guardian who has a personal relationship and stake in the safety or reputation of the person being coerced or confined.
Any person in whose favour the victim holds a fiduciary or protective duty, such that coercion of the victim is effectively coercion of that interested person.
A person whose property, valuable security, or legal rights may be transferred or compromised as a result of threats or harm inflicted on the primary victim.
what_it_excludes: A stranger with no personal, familial, financial, or emotional connection to the victim, even if they witness the harm.
The general public or community at large, who may be indirectly affected by the offence but do not have a specific stake in the individual victim's wellbeing.
A public servant acting in official capacity in relation to the victim, unless they also have a personal or direct interest beyond their official role.
A legal representative or advocate engaged purely in a professional capacity with no personal stake in the victim's wellbeing beyond their professional duty.
A person who is merely a co-accused or co-offender in the same matter, without any personal interest in the victim.
definitions.why_it_matters: The inclusion of 'person interested' expands the legal scope of offences such as extortion (Sections 119, 120 BNS), wrongful confinement (Section 127 BNS), and threatening to give false evidence (Section 232 BNS) to cover situations where the accused coerces or harms a third party connected to the primary victim in order to achieve an unlawful objective. Without this concept, offenders who avoid directly threatening the victim but instead target their loved ones or associates could escape liability under these provisions.

definitions.definition: A person of unsound mind is one who, at the time of doing an act, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law. Such a person lacks the mental capacity to form criminal intention and is therefore generally exempt from criminal liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: A 'person of unsound mind' is someone suffering from a mental condition so severe that they cannot understand what they are doing or that their action is wrong or illegal at the time they do it. This is not simply someone who is upset or confused — it means a genuine and serious mental disorder that removes the ability to reason. Because such a person cannot form criminal intent, the law generally does not punish them for acts that would otherwise be crimes.
real_world_examples: A person diagnosed with severe schizophrenia in a psychiatric hospital in Mumbai attacks a nurse during a psychotic episode, genuinely believing the nurse is a supernatural demon — having no awareness that the act is wrong or unlawful, the person qualifies as being of unsound mind under Section 22.

A man suffering from advanced dementia in a care home in Chennai wanders into a neighbour's house and breaks furniture, being entirely unaware of his surroundings or that his actions constitute criminal trespass or mischief — he may be considered a person of unsound mind.

A woman in Kolkata with a severe dissociative disorder during an acute episode sets fire to her own kitchen while in a trance-like state, unaware of the nature or consequence of her act — if it is established she could not comprehend her actions, she may be protected under Section 22 as a person of unsound mind.

A young man in Delhi with a documented history of severe bipolar disorder during a manic psychotic break attempts to stab a relative, genuinely believing he is carrying out a divine command and has no understanding that the act is wrong — courts may find him to be a person of unsound mind, exempting him from criminal liability.

A guardian in Bengaluru consents to a surgical procedure on behalf of an adult sibling with severe intellectual disability who cannot comprehend the nature of the medical intervention — the sibling's legal status as a person of unsound mind under Section 27 enables the guardian's consent to be valid in law.

A person with advanced paranoid psychosis attempts to assault a passerby in Hyderabad during a delusion that he is being attacked — even though the victim has the right of private defence under Section 36, the attacker's status as a person of unsound mind means he commits no offence.
semantic_tags: right of private defence against mentally ill
cognitive incapacity at time of act
involuntary harmful act due to mental disorder
what_it_covers: A person suffering from severe psychosis, schizophrenia, or a similar mental disorder who at the time of the act cannot understand the nature of what they are doing.
A person with profound intellectual disability or advanced dementia who is incapable of knowing that their action is wrong or contrary to law at the time of commission.
An adult under the lawful charge of a guardian who lacks the mental capacity to consent to or understand actions taken on their behalf, enabling guardian consent to substitute their own.
A person used by an abettor to commit an act while in a state of unsound mind, where the person themselves bears no criminal liability but the abettor is fully liable.
A person against whom others may exercise the right of private defence, even though the person of unsound mind commits no offence in law.
what_it_excludes: A person who is merely intoxicated by alcohol or drugs voluntarily consumed — intoxication is treated separately under the BNS and does not by itself constitute unsoundness of mind.
A person with a mild mental illness, anxiety disorder, or personality disorder who retains the capacity to understand the nature of their act and that it is wrong or unlawful.
A person who pleads ignorance of the law without any genuine mental incapacity — lack of legal knowledge alone does not make someone a person of unsound mind.
A person of low intelligence or poor education who nonetheless understands at a basic level that their act is wrong — mere dullness of intellect is insufficient.
A person who was of sound mind at the time of the act but becomes mentally ill after the commission of the offence — the unsoundness must exist at the precise time of the act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as being of unsound mind at the time of an act is decisive for criminal liability — it completely exempts them from punishment under Section 22, determines the validity of guardian consent for beneficial acts under Section 27, preserves the victim's right of private defence under Section 36, and fixes criminal liability squarely on an abettor who uses such a person as an instrument to commit an offence under Section 46.

definitions.definition: Personation means the act of falsely assuming the identity of another person — whether living, dead, or fictitious — for the purpose of voting at an election, making admissions or statements, confessing judgment, causing process to be issued, becoming bail or security, or doing any other act in a suit or criminal prosecution; it also includes intentionally causing oneself to be returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor when not legally entitled to be so.
definitions.plain_english: Personation means pretending to be someone else — a real person (alive or dead) or a made-up person — to gain a legal advantage or carry out an official act. For example, voting in another person's name, pretending to be someone else in a court case, or getting yourself selected as a juror-like assessor by fraud. The law treats this as a serious offence because it undermines the integrity of elections, courts, and legal proceedings.
real_world_examples: A person arrives at a polling booth in a Lok Sabha election in Mumbai and casts a vote by giving the name of a deceased voter registered on the electoral roll, thereby committing personation at an election under Section 172.

An accused in a civil property dispute in Delhi falsely claims to be the original plaintiff and makes admissions before the court about ownership of land, intending to bind the real plaintiff — this constitutes personation under Section 242.

A person bribes a court official to have himself empanelled as an assessor in a Sessions Court murder trial in Chennai, knowing he is legally disqualified from serving, thereby committing personation of an assessor under Section 268.

A man in a Hyderabad magistrate court, impersonating the defendant in a cheque dishonour case, provides a bail surety under the defendant's name, exposing the real defendant to legal consequences — an offence under Section 242.

During Vidhan Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, a booth-level agent organises a group of individuals to vote multiple times under different registered voter names on the electoral roll, amounting to organised personation under Section 172 read with Section 174.

A fraudster in a civil suit in Kolkata assumes the identity of a deceased creditor and causes the court to issue a process for recovery of debt against the debtor, committing personation under Section 242.
what_it_covers: Applying for a voting paper in the name of another person (living or dead) or a fictitious person at an election.
A person who has already voted once attempting to vote again in the same election in their own name.
Falsely assuming the identity of another person to make admissions, confess judgment, cause process to be issued, or become bail or security in a suit or criminal prosecution.
Intentionally causing oneself to be returned, empanelled, or sworn as an assessor in a case where one knows one is not legally entitled to serve.
Knowingly serving as an assessor after having been unlawfully empanelled or sworn contrary to law.
Abetting, procuring, or attempting to procure voting by any person through personation at an election.
what_it_excludes: A person authorised by law to vote as a proxy for an elector — voting as a duly authorised proxy is explicitly excluded from election personation under the proviso to Section 172.
Legitimate authorised representation in legal proceedings, such as a duly appointed power-of-attorney holder acting openly in the name of the principal with full disclosure to the court.
An actor or performer assuming a character or identity in a film, theatre, or entertainment context, as there is no intent to gain a legal advantage or deceive a legal authority.
A legal guardian or parent acting on behalf of a minor in court proceedings in their lawfully recognised capacity, which is authorised by law and not a false assumption of identity.
An advocate or legal representative making statements on behalf of a client in their professional capacity with proper authorisation and disclosure.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes personation determines whether the offender is liable for punishment under Sections 174 (up to one year imprisonment for election personation), 242 (up to three years for personation in suits or prosecutions), or 268 (up to two years for personation of an assessor); establishing personation is essential to triggering these criminal liabilities, while its absence means no such penal consequence arises and the act may be treated as a mere civil or procedural irregularity.

definitions.definition: A 'place of sepulchre' refers to any location designated or used for the burial or interment of human remains, including graveyards, cemeteries, tombs, mausoleums, and similar sites sanctified or set apart by religious custom or community practice for the final deposition of the dead. It encompasses any place of sepulchre, or any place set apart for the performance of funeral rites or as a depository for the remains of the dead, as used in Section 301 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: A 'place of sepulchre' is any location specifically dedicated to burying or keeping the remains of dead people — such as a graveyard, cemetery, tomb, or mausoleum. These are places that communities, religious groups, or families set aside as sacred or solemn spaces for laying the dead to rest. The law protects these places from trespass or any act intended to insult the religion or wound the feelings of the living.
real_world_examples: A person enters a Muslim qabrastan (graveyard) in Lucknow and deliberately defaces or vandalises graves with the intent to insult the religious sentiments of the Muslim community — this amounts to trespass on a place of sepulchre under Section 301.

An individual trespasses into a Christian cemetery in Goa, damages crosses on graves and scatters floral offerings, with the knowledge that such acts are likely to wound the feelings of the bereaved Christian family — this constitutes an offence under Section 301.

A group enters a Parsi Tower of Silence (Dakhma) in Mumbai — a designated place for the exposure and disposal of Parsi dead — without authorisation and with intent to insult Zoroastrian religious practices, thereby trespassing on a place of sepulchre.

Someone intrudes into a Hindu shamshan ghat (cremation ground) in Varanasi during off-hours and disturbs interred ashes or remains kept in urns within a memorial structure, intending to offend the religious sensibilities of the Hindu community.

A person unlawfully enters a Sikh samadhi (tomb of a Sikh saint or dignitary) in Punjab and commits acts of desecration with knowledge that such conduct will wound the feelings of the Sikh community, attracting liability under Section 301.

An individual trespasses into a Jewish cemetery in Kolkata and overturns headstones with the intention of insulting the Jewish religion, making the site a protected 'place of sepulchre' under the BNS.
what_it_covers: Graveyards and cemeteries maintained by any religious community, including Muslim qabrastans, Christian cemeteries, and Jewish burial grounds.
Tombs, mausoleums, and dargahs that serve as permanent repositories for the remains or relics of the deceased.
Hindu cremation grounds (shamshan ghats) and memorial structures housing ashes or remains set apart for that purpose.
Parsi Towers of Silence (Dakhmas) where the deceased are placed according to Zoroastrian rites.

Any plot, enclosure, or structure formally set apart by a community or religious body as a depository for the remains of the dead, regardless of whether it is enclosed or marked by formal legal title.
Sikh samadhis or Jain memorial structures specifically designated for housing remains of the deceased.
what_it_excludes: Private residences or homes where a body is temporarily kept before the funeral — these are not set apart as places of sepulchre.
Hospitals, mortuaries, or forensic facilities that store bodies temporarily for medical or legal purposes, as they are not designated for permanent interment or deposition of remains.
General open land or public parks where no formal or customary designation as a burial or resting place for the dead exists.

Places of worship such as temples, mosques, churches, or gurudwaras — these are separately protected as 'place of worship' and do not fall within the specific category of place of sepulchre unless they also contain a designated burial or interment area.
Archaeological or historical sites that may contain ancient human remains but are not currently used or set apart by any community for the purpose of burial or deposition of the dead.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a location qualifies as a 'place of sepulchre' determines whether an act of trespass committed there — accompanied by the requisite intention to wound religious feelings or insult religion — attracts criminal liability under Section 301 of the BNS, punishable with imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both. Without this classification, the same act of trespass would be treated under ordinary trespass provisions without the aggravated religious-offence dimension.

definitions.definition: A place of worship is any site, structure, or location dedicated to or used for the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies by any class of persons, including temples, mosques, churches, gurudwaras, synagogues, and any other religious premises held sacred by a religious community. Though not formally defined in a dedicated definitions section, the Act uses it consistently to refer to any consecrated or customarily recognized premises where religious observances are conducted. It is distinct from a place of sepulchre or a place set apart for funeral rites.
definitions.plain_english: A place of worship is any building, structure, or ground where people go to pray or perform religious rituals — like a temple, mosque, church, gurudwara, or synagogue. It is a location that a religious community considers sacred and uses for their spiritual practices. It does not need to be a grand structure; even a small local shrine or prayer hall can qualify if it is regularly used for religious worship by a recognizable group of people.
real_world_examples: A historic Hindu temple in Varanasi, such as the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, where devotees gather daily for puja and aarti — deliberately defiling such a site by smearing it with prohibited substances would attract liability under Section 298 of the BNS.

A local mosque in a Mumbai neighbourhood where Friday namaz is regularly offered — causing a deliberate disturbance during the prayer congregation would attract liability under Section 300 of the BNS, given its character as a place of worship.

A Sikh gurudwara in Amritsar or Delhi where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed and langar and kirtan are conducted — any act of criminal trespass committed with intent to insult the religion would trigger Section 301 of the BNS.

A small roadside Dargah (Sufi shrine) in Rajasthan that a Muslim community regularly visits for prayers and ceremonies — though not a grand mosque, it qualifies as a place of worship, making any act of vandalism or desecration punishable under Section 298.

A Catholic church in Goa where Sunday Mass is held — delivering a communally incendiary speech inside the church during a service would attract enhanced punishment under Section 196 subsection (2) of the BNS since the offence is committed in a place of worship.

A Buddhist monastery (vihara) in Bodh Gaya used by monks and pilgrims for meditation and religious rites — destroying or damaging any sacred object within its premises with intent to insult Buddhism would invoke Section 298 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Temples, mosques, churches, gurudwaras, synagogues, and fire temples (Agiari) that are formally consecrated and open to a religious community for worship.
Local or informal prayer halls, dargahs, or small shrines that are customarily and regularly used by a class of persons for religious worship even without formal legal registration.

Any structure or enclosed premises specifically dedicated to the performance of religious ceremonies, including private chapels or prayer rooms attached to institutions, where the primary use is religious observance.
Outdoor sacred sites such as a riverbank ghat used exclusively and customarily for religious bathing and ritual worship by a recognized religious community.
A temporary structure or pandal erected for a defined religious occasion (e.g., Durga Puja, Ganesh Utsav) that serves as the site of religious worship for the duration of the festival.
what_it_excludes: A place of sepulchre, cremation ground, burial ground, or any site set apart solely for funeral rites or as a depository for the remains of the dead — these are separately covered under Section 301 of the BNS and do not fall within 'place of worship'.

Secular educational institutions, community halls, or public auditoriums that are occasionally used for religious gatherings but are not primarily dedicated to or customarily recognized as places of religious worship.

A private residential dwelling where a family performs daily prayers or puja — the domestic and private nature excludes it from the public or communally recognized character required of a 'place of worship' under these provisions.

Government or municipal offices, courts, or public buildings where an oath or religious affirmation may be administered — the incidental religious act does not convert such premises into a place of worship.
A museum, archaeological site, or monument that displays religious artefacts or images but is not actively used by any class of persons for the performance of religious worship or ceremonies.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a location qualifies as a 'place of worship' directly determines the severity of punishment: offences such as promoting enmity (Section 196), disturbing assemblies (Section 300), or trespassing with intent to insult religion (Section 301) attract enhanced or distinct penalties when committed at a place of worship, compared to the same act committed elsewhere. Establishing this character is therefore a threshold factual question that can escalate the penal consequence for the accused and is central to framing charges under Sections 298, 300, 301, and 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

definitions.definition: The term 'poison' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 123, it refers to any substance which, when introduced into the human body by any means, is capable of causing death, grievous hurt, or serious injury to health by its chemical or toxic action. This includes naturally occurring, synthetic, or adulterated substances administered orally, topically, by injection, or by any other mode.
definitions.plain_english: A poison is any substance that can harm or kill a person when it enters their body, whether swallowed, inhaled, injected, or absorbed through the skin. This includes things like arsenic, cyanide, toxic plant extracts, or any chemical that damages the body through its toxic properties. The key feature is that the substance causes harm through its chemical or biological action on the body, not through physical injury like a blade or bullet.
real_world_examples: A person mixes arsenic trioxide into a family member's food in rural Rajasthan with the intent to cause death — the arsenic qualifies as poison under the provision.
A factory worker in Maharashtra is given a drink laced with organophosphate pesticide (such as monocrotophos) by a colleague intending to incapacitate or kill them — the pesticide constitutes poison.
A hired killer in Delhi injects potassium cyanide into a victim's beverage at a restaurant, causing death — cyanide is a classic poison triggering liability under Section 123.
A domestic worker in Chennai adds oleander extract (kaner plant toxin) into a child's milk with intent to harm — the plant-derived toxin is treated as poison under the BNS.

In a property dispute in Uttar Pradesh, a relative gradually administers small doses of rat poison (zinc phosphide) into an elderly person's meals, leading to slow deterioration — this constitutes administration of poison with intent to cause harm.

A person adulterates a competitor's water supply at a factory in Pune with a corrosive chemical capable of causing internal injury when consumed — such a substance falls within the meaning of poison in the context of Section 123.
what_it_covers: Metallic poisons such as arsenic, mercury, and lead compounds administered with intent to harm.
Organophosphate pesticides and agricultural chemicals capable of causing death or grievous injury when ingested or absorbed.
Plant-derived toxins such as aconite (aconitine), oleander extract, or nux vomica administered covertly.
Synthetic chemical compounds including cyanide salts, strychnine, and industrial solvents that cause toxic injury to the human body.
Adulterated food or drink substances into which a toxic agent has been mixed deliberately to cause harm.
what_it_excludes: Substances that cause physical injury through mechanical means alone (e.g., sharp objects, blunt force), which are not poisons as they do not act through chemical toxicity.
Medicinal preparations lawfully administered by a registered medical practitioner in therapeutic doses, which do not qualify as poison in the criminal sense.

Corrosive substances such as strong acids or alkalis used externally to cause burns, which are separately classified as 'acid' or 'corrosive substance' under the BNS and governed by distinct provisions.
Alcohol or intoxicants administered without intent to cause death or grievous hurt, which may fall under separate provisions related to intoxication rather than poisoning.
Substances that are merely noxious or unpleasant but incapable of causing death or grievous hurt through their chemical action.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as 'poison' under Section 123 determines if an accused is liable for the serious offence of administering poison or any stupefying, intoxicating, or unwholesome drug or substance with intent to cause hurt, wrongful confinement, or commission of an offence, which attracts imprisonment of up to ten years and fine. The classification directly triggers or bars culpability for attempted murder or grievous hurt offences where the means of harm is a toxic substance rather than physical force.

definitions.definition: A poisonous substance is any substance which, by its inherent chemical or toxic properties, is capable of endangering human life, causing hurt, or causing injury to a person when handled rashly or negligently or when adequate precautions for its safe custody are not taken. The term is used in Section 286 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, to cover any such toxic or noxious material in a person's possession or under their control.
definitions.plain_english: A poisonous substance is any material that is toxic or harmful enough to endanger a person's life or health if not handled carefully. This includes things like strong chemicals, pesticides, rat poisons, or industrial toxins. The law is concerned with such substances because careless handling of them can seriously hurt or even kill people nearby.
real_world_examples: A pesticide dealer in a rural Maharashtra village stores large quantities of organophosphate pesticide in open, unlabelled containers in a shared godown, without any safety warnings, resulting in a child being poisoned after accidental contact.

A factory worker in an industrial estate in Gujarat negligently leaves a drum of cyanide solution unsecured and unlabelled near a common walkway, endangering the lives of co-workers who pass by without knowledge of the hazard.
A rat-poison seller in a Delhi market carelessly packs rat killer (containing aluminium phosphide) alongside food items, creating a serious risk of accidental ingestion by customers.
A hospital pharmacist in Chennai negligently fails to properly secure a stock of concentrated morphine solution, leaving it accessible to unauthorised persons, thereby endangering human life.

A small-scale electroplating unit owner in Ludhiana dumps untreated hexavalent chromium waste water into an open drain running through a residential area, exposing residents to a highly toxic and carcinogenic poisonous substance.
what_it_covers: Pesticides and insecticides such as organophosphates, endosulfan, or aluminium phosphide commonly used in Indian agriculture that are toxic to humans.
Industrial chemicals with high toxicity such as cyanide compounds, concentrated acids used as poisons (distinct from corrosive use), arsenic, mercury compounds, or chlorine gas cylinders.
Rodenticides, rat poisons, and other toxic substances sold commercially or kept domestically that can endanger human life if mishandled or left unsecured.

Pharmaceutical substances and narcotics in concentrated toxic doses, such as morphine, strychnine, or other scheduled poisons under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, when possessed and handled negligently.
Naturally occurring toxic plant or animal-derived substances (e.g., aconite, nux vomica extracts) that are inherently lethal in uncontrolled quantities.
what_it_excludes: Fire or combustible matter, which is separately governed under Section 287 of the BNS, 2023, and is not classified as a poisonous substance.

Corrosive substances used primarily for their corrosive rather than toxic properties (e.g., concentrated sulphuric acid used to burn rather than poison), which may fall under the separate definition of 'corrosive substance' in the BNS.
Adulterated food or drink that may cause harm through impurity but is not itself a substance whose primary characteristic is acute toxicity endangering human life as contemplated under Section 286.

Medicines and drugs administered within prescribed therapeutic doses by a registered medical practitioner in the lawful course of treatment, as these do not constitute dangerous or negligent use of a poisonous substance.

Noxious substances that merely cause discomfort, annoyance, or minor irritation without posing a probable danger to human life or likelihood of causing hurt or injury at the level contemplated by Section 286.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as a 'poisonous substance' under Section 286 determines if a person who handles, stores, or omits to secure it negligently is criminally liable and can be punished with up to six months' imprisonment, a fine of up to five thousand rupees, or both. The definition is the threshold trigger for the offence of negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substances, without which no prosecution under Section 286 can be sustained.

definitions.definition: A police officer is a member of a police force duly constituted and empowered under law to maintain public order, prevent and investigate offences, and apprehend persons suspected of committing crimes. Though not exhaustively defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the term is used throughout the Sanhita to refer to a person holding a recognised position in a State or Central police organisation and bound by law to enforce it.
definitions.plain_english: A police officer is a government-appointed law enforcement official who belongs to an organised police force. Their job includes preventing crimes, arresting suspects, maintaining public peace, and assisting courts in criminal matters. In everyday terms, this includes constables, sub-inspectors, inspectors, and higher-ranked officers in any Indian police department. Because they are 'bound by law' to act, certain things they do in their official duty — like arresting someone without a warrant — are not treated as crimes.
real_world_examples: A Sub-Inspector of Delhi Police arrests a person accused of committing rape under Section 64 BNS without a warrant because the offence is cognizable — this is a lawful act protected under the 'bound by law' exception.

A constable of the Maharashtra Police apprehends a murder suspect caught in the act on a public street; though the person is confined, the constable is not guilty of wrongful confinement because he acted in his capacity as a police officer bound by law.

A police officer from the Tamil Nadu Police abets a robbery by deliberately ignoring it while on duty; under Section 56 BNS, he is liable to up to half the maximum imprisonment prescribed for robbery because of his public duty to prevent it.

A woman constable posted at a police station in Uttar Pradesh records the statement of a rape survivor under Section 64 BNS — her status as a police officer defines her official obligations and procedural duties in handling such sensitive cases.

An Inspector of the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) deployed at an airport detains a person found with counterfeit currency — he acts as a police officer exercising lawful apprehension powers under the applicable law.

A Station House Officer (SHO) in Bengaluru, upon receiving a complaint of sexual harassment, is duty-bound to register an FIR — failure to do so while holding the position of a police officer can attract legal consequences under the Sanhita.
what_it_covers: Constables, Head Constables, Sub-Inspectors, Inspectors, and all gazetted officers in any State Police force constituted under the Police Act
Officers of central police organisations such as CRPF, CISF, BSF, and CBI when exercising police powers under law
A Station House Officer (SHO) exercising powers of arrest, investigation, and charge-sheet filing under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita
A woman police officer designated under law to record statements of sexual offence survivors
A police officer acting temporarily in an official capacity or on a particular duty assignment such as election duty or VIP protection
what_it_excludes: Private security guards or bouncers employed by private agencies, who have no statutory law enforcement powers
Revenue officers, forest officers, or municipal inspectors who may have some enforcement powers but do not belong to a recognised police force
Members of the armed forces (Army, Navy, Air Force) acting in military capacity, who are governed by separate military law and not treated as police officers under the Sanhita
Civilians or vigilante groups who informally assist police but hold no official appointment or legal authority
Judicial officers and magistrates, even those who may issue warrants or remand orders, as they perform judicial rather than police functions
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'police officer' directly determines their legal obligations and protections under the Sanhita — for instance, under Section 64, special procedural requirements apply when rape is committed by a police officer, attracting enhanced punishment; and under Section 56, a police officer who abets an offence they are duty-bound to prevent faces up to half the maximum sentence, not merely a quarter, making the classification critical to both liability and sentencing.

definitions.definition: The term 'pornography' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Sections 75 and 95, it refers to any material — visual, audio, written, or electronic — that depicts sexual acts, explicit sexual conduct, or sexual exploitation, particularly when shown to a woman against her will (constituting sexual harassment) or when involving the use of a child for its production, distribution, or exhibition.
definitions.plain_english: Pornography, in the context of this law, means any content — such as videos, images, or written material — that shows sexual acts or explicit sexual behaviour. Showing such content to a woman without her consent is treated as sexual harassment. Using a child in any way to create, perform in, or distribute such content is treated as a serious criminal offence.
real_world_examples: A male colleague at an office in Mumbai opens explicit sexual videos on his work laptop and deliberately turns the screen toward a female coworker, forcing her to view the content — this constitutes showing pornography against the will of a woman under Section 75.

A man in Delhi sends unsolicited explicit images or video clips to a woman's mobile phone via WhatsApp without her consent, amounting to showing pornography against her will and attracting liability under Section 75.

A person in Chennai hires a minor child to appear in the filming of sexually explicit videos for online distribution — this falls squarely within Section 95 as hiring a child for pornography and sexual exploitation.

A supervisor in a Bengaluru workplace repeatedly shows pornographic clips on a shared office computer to female employees during meetings without their permission, constituting sexual harassment punishable under Section 75(2).

A trafficker in Kolkata uses minors to produce obscene photographic material for sale on the dark web — engaging a child in pornography under Section 95, with punishment for both the underlying offence and the act of engagement.
what_it_covers: Sexually explicit videos, images, or written material shown to a woman without her consent, triggering liability under Section 75 for sexual harassment.

what_it_excludes: Consensually shared sexual content between adults, where both parties have willingly agreed to view or exchange such material, does not attract Section 75 liability.

definitions.definition: A 'position of authority' refers to any role or status that confers power, control, or dominance over another person, enabling one to influence, direct, or exercise charge over that person, particularly in the context of Section 68 where such authority is abused to induce or seduce a woman under one's custody, charge, or present on one's premises to engage in sexual intercourse.
definitions.plain_english: A 'position of authority' means any role where a person has power or control over others — such as a boss, supervisor, jailor, or hospital manager — which gives them influence over the people under their care or charge. When someone in such a position uses that power to pressure or persuade a woman into sexual intercourse, it becomes a criminal offence. The key idea is that the authority creates an unequal power relationship that can be exploited.
real_world_examples: A senior doctor at a government hospital in Mumbai uses his authority over a junior female nurse under his supervision to coerce her into sexual intercourse by threatening negative performance reviews — this constitutes abuse of position of authority under Section 68.

The warden of a women's remand home in Delhi, who controls the daily life, privileges, and release recommendations of inmates, induces a female detainee to have sexual intercourse by promising early release — this is a classic abuse of position of authority.

A prison superintendent in a Rajasthan correctional facility uses his power over a female undertrial prisoner — controlling her food, medical care, and family visit permissions — to seduce her into sexual intercourse, invoking Section 68.

A male manager of a government-run children's institution in Chennai, who oversees the welfare and placement of female residents, abuses his administrative authority to induce a woman staff member present on the premises to engage in sexual intercourse with him.

A senior officer in a custodial facility who, by virtue of his rank and control over inmates' daily conditions, uses his authoritative position to sexually exploit a woman under his charge, even where the act does not amount to rape under Section 63.
what_it_covers: A jail superintendent or prison officer who exercises control over female inmates in a place of custody established under any law.
A hospital manager or staff member who holds administrative or medical authority over women present within the hospital premises.
A manager or superintendent of a women's institution or children's institution who has charge over the residents or staff therein.
Any person in a hierarchical role — such as a government official or institutional head — whose position gives them the power to influence, reward, or penalise the woman they are in contact with.
A person holding any office in a remand home or place of custody by virtue of which they can exercise authority or control over its inmates, as clarified in the Explanation to Section 68.
what_it_excludes: Equals or peers in a workplace or institution who share no supervisory or custodial power over the woman — a co-worker with no authority over the woman does not fall within this definition.
Private individuals in purely personal or social relationships with no institutional, official, or custodial power over the woman, such as friends, neighbours, or acquaintances.

Persons whose conduct amounts to rape under Section 63 — Section 68 explicitly applies only where the sexual intercourse does not amount to the offence of rape, making perpetrators of rape governed by a different provision.

Persons acting in a fiduciary relationship without any formal position of institutional or official authority — fiduciary relationship is listed as a separate category alongside position of authority in Section 68.
Former authority figures whose official relationship with the woman has completely and formally ended prior to the act, with no continuing power or influence over her circumstances.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person holds a 'position of authority' is determinative of liability under Section 68 of the BNS, 2023 — if established, it triggers a minimum five-year rigorous imprisonment sentence for inducing or seducing a woman under one's charge or custody into sexual intercourse, even where the act falls short of rape. The definition thus expands criminal accountability beyond rape to cover coercive or manipulative sexual conduct enabled by institutional power imbalances.

definitions.definition: The term 'possession' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used throughout the Sanhita, 'possession' denotes the actual or constructive control and custody of a person over any movable or immovable property, object, or thing, with the knowledge of its existence and the ability to exercise dominion over it, whether held personally or through another acting on one's behalf.
definitions.plain_english: Possession means having something under your control or in your keeping, either physically or through someone else acting for you. It includes situations where you know about the item and can access or use it, even if it is not directly in your hands. For example, drugs locked in your cupboard are in your possession even if you are not holding them at that moment.
real_world_examples: A person found by Delhi Police with a bag containing stolen gold jewellery under their seat in a bus is in actual possession of stolen property under Section 317 read with Section 303 of the BNS.

A landlord in Mumbai whose tenant secretly stores counterfeit currency notes in a rented room without the landlord's knowledge is NOT in possession of those notes, as there is no knowledge or control on the landlord's part.
A Bengaluru shopkeeper who keeps adulterated food items on their shop shelves for sale is in possession of adulterated food, making them liable under Section 274 of the BNS.

A person in Chennai who keeps house-breaking tools such as a jemmy and skeleton keys inside their locked almirah at home is in possession of those tools and may attract liability under Section 329 of the BNS.

A drug peddler in Kolkata who hands over a packet of contraband narcotics to an associate for safekeeping retains constructive possession of the drugs because the associate holds them on the peddler's behalf and under their direction.
A factory owner in Pune who stores explosive substances in a warehouse under their control without proper licensing is in possession of explosive substances for purposes of Section 291 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: Actual possession: physically holding or carrying an item on one's person, such as a weapon concealed in one's clothing.
Constructive possession: items stored in a place under the accused's control (e.g., a locker, home, or vehicle) where the person has knowledge and access.
Joint possession: two or more persons sharing control over a property, such as co-conspirators jointly holding proceeds of dacoity.
Possession through an agent: where a person directs another (servant, associate) to keep an item on their behalf, the principal retains possession.
Possession of intangible or recorded material: digital files or electronic records stored on a device under a person's control and with their knowledge.
what_it_excludes: Mere proximity without knowledge: a passenger on a train near a bag belonging to another person, without knowing its contents, is not in possession of those contents.
Involuntary possession: an item placed in someone's bag or vehicle without their knowledge or consent does not constitute possession by that person.
Bare ownership without any control or access: a property owner who has been completely dispossessed and has no ability to exercise dominion over the property.
Possession by a public servant acting in official capacity where custody is purely incidental to their duty and not personal, such as a policeman holding seized property in a malkhana.
Transient handling without intent to control: briefly touching or examining an object at another's request without assuming any dominion over it.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence or absence of possession directly determines criminal liability under multiple BNS offences including possession of stolen property (Section 303), possession of house-breaking tools (Section 329), and possession of counterfeit currency or explosive substances (Sections 291, 306, 315); a finding of possession can establish the actus reus of the offence and shift the presumption of guilt onto the accused, while absence of possession can negate the charge entirely.

definitions.definition: A power of attorney, as used in Section 337 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a written instrument by which one person (the principal) authorises another person (the agent or attorney) to act on their behalf in legal, financial, or other specified matters. Forging such a document is an offence punishable with imprisonment extending to seven years and liability to fine.
definitions.plain_english: A power of attorney is a legal document where one person gives another person the authority to act on their behalf — for example, to sign contracts, manage property, or represent them in court. In everyday terms, it is like giving someone a written permission slip to handle important matters in your name. The law treats forging such a document as a serious crime because it can be used to fraudulently transfer property, enter into contracts, or conduct legal proceedings without the real owner's consent.
real_world_examples: A person forges a power of attorney in the name of an elderly NRI property owner to fraudulently sell their flat in Mumbai to a third party without the owner's knowledge or consent.
A fraudster creates a fake power of attorney purportedly signed by a deceased person and uses it to withdraw funds from the deceased's bank account in Delhi.
An unscrupulous agent fabricates a power of attorney in a client's name to execute a sale deed for agricultural land in Punjab, pocketing the sale proceeds.

A litigant forges a power of attorney to appoint himself as the authorised representative of a company in a civil suit pending before a District Court in Chennai, allowing him to confess judgment against the company.
A builder forges a power of attorney from multiple flat buyers in Hyderabad to mortgage the entire housing project to a financial institution without the buyers' knowledge.
A family member forges a power of attorney in the name of another co-heir to register a partition deed and transfer ancestral property in Rajasthan solely into their own name.
what_it_covers: A written document granting one person authority to act on behalf of another in property transactions, such as sale or mortgage of immovable property.
An instrument authorising a person to institute, defend, or take proceedings in a court of law on behalf of the principal.
A document empowering an agent to execute contracts, sign agreements, or manage financial affairs including banking operations on behalf of the principal.
A general or special power of attorney registered or unregistered that purports to vest legal authority in an attorney-holder to confess judgment or settle legal disputes.
A power of attorney used in the context of a suit or legal proceeding to authorise appearance, filing of pleadings, or any procedural act before a court.
what_it_excludes: A genuine, duly executed, and validly registered power of attorney signed by the actual principal with free consent — forgery requires the document to be false or fabricated.
Oral authorisation or informal delegation of authority that does not take the form of a written instrument purporting to be a power of attorney.
Internal corporate resolutions or board authorisations that delegate authority within an organisation but do not constitute a formal power of attorney document.
A letter of authority or simple consent letter that does not purport to grant broad legal agency powers characteristic of a power of attorney.
A proxy form issued for voting at a company shareholders' meeting, which is governed separately and does not confer general legal agency authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Forging a power of attorney under Section 337 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 attracts imprisonment of either description for up to seven years along with a fine, making it one of the aggravated categories of forgery due to the potential for large-scale fraud in property, financial, and judicial matters. Whether a document qualifies as a power of attorney determines if the higher seven-year punishment under Section 337 applies, as opposed to the general forgery provisions, and also establishes the basis for related offences such as cheating, criminal breach of trust, or fraudulent property transfer.

definitions.definition: Preparation, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to a deliberate act or series of acts undertaken by a person with the intent to commit an offence, which goes beyond mere intention or planning but falls short of an actual attempt; it includes making ready the means or measures necessary to commit the offence, such as arranging tools, materials, or circumstances required for its commission. In the context of Section 130, preparation encompasses any physical act or readying of means that causes another person to apprehend imminent criminal force.
definitions.plain_english: Preparation means getting ready to commit a crime — it is the stage where a person has moved beyond just thinking about committing an offence and has started arranging the tools, resources, or conditions needed to carry it out, but has not yet taken the direct step of attempting the crime. For example, buying poison to use against someone or gathering weapons before an attack would count as preparation. It is an intermediate stage between intention (thinking about a crime) and attempt (actually trying to commit it).
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai purchases a large quantity of explosives and stores them in a warehouse with the intent to blow up a public building — this act of acquiring and stockpiling explosives constitutes preparation to commit an offence.

A group of individuals in Delhi gather weapons, scout a target's location, and assign roles among themselves before carrying out a dacoity — the scouting, weapon-gathering, and role assignment collectively constitute preparation for the offence of dacoity under Section 310.

A trader in Chennai begins to loosen the muzzle of a ferocious dog intending to frighten a rival, thereby causing the rival to apprehend imminent criminal force — this physical act of readying the dog is preparation constituting assault under Section 130.

A militant group in Jammu & Kashmir stockpiles arms, trains recruits, and maps government installations in advance of a planned attack on the state — these acts constitute preparation to wage war against the Government of India and attract criminal liability under the BNS.

A fraudster in Kolkata forges corporate letterheads, creates fake bank documents, and prepares a false identity card before approaching a bank for a large loan — the creation of these materials constitutes preparation for the offence of cheating by personation.

A person in Bengaluru researches the movements of a rival and acquires a corrosive acid substance, storing it near the rival's residence — this act of procurement and positioning constitutes preparation to cause grievous hurt by acid attack under the BNS.
semantic_tags: intermediate stage between intention and attempt
what_it_covers: Acquiring, procuring, or stockpiling weapons, tools, poison, explosive substances, or other instruments intended for use in committing an offence.
Physical acts or gestures made ready with the intent or knowledge that they will cause another person present to apprehend imminent criminal force, as under the assault provision in Section 130.
Making logistical arrangements such as scouting locations, assembling co-conspirators, or positioning oneself or materials at a site in readiness to commit an offence such as dacoity or depredation.
Preparing documents, records, or forged instruments prior to executing a fraud, forgery, or cheating offence.
Procuring or storing corrosive substances, poisons, or flammable materials with the intention of using them to cause hurt, grievous hurt, or mischief.
what_it_excludes: Mere intention or mental resolve to commit an offence, without any external physical act taken towards its commission — pure thought does not constitute preparation.
An attempt to commit the offence, which is a more advanced stage where the person has directly moved towards the commission of the crime and the preparation phase has been surpassed.

Innocent or lawful procurement of materials that have a legitimate purpose and are not accompanied by any criminal intent — e.g., a farmer purchasing fertilizer for agricultural use is not engaged in preparation for an offence.
Words alone, as explicitly stated in Section 130, which by themselves do not amount to preparation constituting assault unless accompanied by a gesture or physical act.
Completed commission of the offence itself, where preparation has merged into the act of perpetration.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as preparation determines criminal liability at a pre-attempt stage — under sections such as 310 (dacoity) and 154 (depredation against a foreign State), preparation itself is independently punishable even if the substantive offence was never completed, thereby enabling law enforcement to intervene and prosecute before harm occurs. Additionally, under Section 130, a preparatory act that causes apprehension of imminent criminal force constitutes assault, making the classification of an act as preparation directly determinative of whether an assault offence has been committed.

Examples: A person in Mumbai purchases a large quantity of explosives and stores them in a warehouse with the intent to blow up a public building — this act of acquiring and stockpiling explosives constitutes preparation to commit an offence. | A group of individuals in Delhi gather weapons, scout a target's location, and assign roles among themselves before carrying out a dacoity — the scouting, weapon-gathering, and role assignment collectively constitute preparation for the offence of dacoity under Section 310. | A trader in Chennai begins to loosen the muzzle of a ferocious dog intending to frighten a rival, thereby causing the rival to apprehend imminent criminal force — this physical act of readying the dog is preparation constituting assault under Section 130. | A militant group in Jammu & Kashmir stockpiles arms, trains recruits, and maps government installations in advance of a planned attack on the state — these acts constitute preparation to wage war against the Government of India and attract criminal liability under the BNS. | A fraudster in Kolkata forges corporate letterheads, creates fake bank documents, and prepares a false identity card before approaching a bank for a large loan — the creation of these materials constitutes preparation for the offence of cheating by personation. | A person in Bengaluru researches the movements of a rival and acquires a corrosive acid substance, storing it near the rival's residence — this act of procurement and positioning constitutes preparation to cause grievous hurt by acid attack under the BNS.

Covers: Acquiring, procuring, or stockpiling weapons, tools, poison, explosive substances, or other instruments intended for use in committing an offence.; Physical acts or gestures made ready with the intent or knowledge that they will cause another person present to apprehend imminent criminal force, as under the assault provision in Section 130.; Making logistical arrangements such as scouting locations, assembling co-conspirators, or positioning oneself or materials at a site in readiness to commit an offence such as dacoity or depredation.; Preparing documents, records, or forged instruments prior to executing a fraud, forgery, or cheating offence.; Procuring or storing corrosive substances, poisons, or flammable materials with the intention of using them to cause hurt, grievous hurt, or mischief.

Excludes: Mere intention or mental resolve to commit an offence, without any external physical act taken towards its commission — pure thought does not constitute preparation.; An attempt to commit the offence, which is a more advanced stage where the person has directly moved towards the commission of the crime and the preparation phase has been surpassed.; Innocent or lawful procurement of materials that have a legitimate purpose and are not accompanied by any criminal intent — e.g., a farmer purchasing fertilizer for agricultural use is not engaged in preparation for an offence.; Words alone, as explicitly stated in Section 130, which by themselves do not amount to preparation constituting assault unless accompanied by a gesture or physical act.; Completed commission of the offence itself, where preparation has merged into the act of perpetration.

Why it matters: Whether an act qualifies as preparation determines criminal liability at a pre-attempt stage — under sections such as 310 (dacoity) and 154 (depredation against a foreign State), preparation itself is independently punishable even if the substantive offence was never completed, thereby enabling law enforcement to intervene and prosecute before harm occurs. Additionally, under Section 130, a preparatory act that causes apprehension of imminent criminal force constitutes assault, making the classification of an act as preparation directly determinative of whether an assault offence has been committed.

definitions.definition: A 'prisoner of war' is a person held in lawful custody by the State as a consequence of armed conflict or war, who is confined in a designated place of confinement, and includes such a prisoner permitted to be at large on parole within certain limits in India, who is deemed to escape from lawful custody if he goes beyond those limits.
definitions.plain_english: A prisoner of war is someone captured and held by the Indian State as a result of a war or armed conflict between nations. They are kept under official custody, usually in a designated facility. Even if allowed limited movement on parole within a defined area in India, they are still considered to be in legal custody, and leaving that area counts as an escape.
real_world_examples: A Pakistani military officer captured by Indian armed forces during an armed conflict and detained in a designated facility in India under government orders qualifies as a prisoner of war under this provision.

A foreign combatant from a hostile nation captured during a border skirmish in Ladakh and transferred to a secure Indian military detention centre is a prisoner of war whose escape would attract liability under Section 156.

During the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, thousands of Pakistani soldiers were captured and held in Indian camps; a public servant guarding such a camp who deliberately allows one to escape would be guilty under Section 156.

A prisoner of war granted parole by the Government of India and permitted to reside within the limits of a specified district in Rajasthan, who then travels to Delhi without permission, is deemed to have escaped from lawful custody under Section 158.

A civilian working at a detention facility who knowingly helps a captured enemy combatant flee by providing false identity documents or a vehicle would be liable under Section 158 for aiding the escape of a prisoner of war.
what_it_covers: Foreign military personnel captured by Indian armed forces during a declared or undeclared armed conflict and held in a place of confinement designated by the State.
A prisoner of war who has been granted parole and permitted to remain at large within specified territorial limits in India, who remains subject to lawful custody within those limits.
Any enemy combatant or belligerent held by India pursuant to the laws of war, whose detention is authorised and supervised by a public servant or State authority.
A captured foreign fighter or soldier who attempts to escape, is rescued by a third party, or is harboured after escaping from an Indian detention facility.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary criminal prisoners or undertrials held in Indian jails for civilian offences, who are governed by separate provisions and do not qualify as prisoners of war.

State prisoners detained for political or security reasons under domestic law who are not captured combatants from a foreign armed conflict — they are a distinct category explicitly named separately as 'State prisoner' in the same sections.
Individuals detained under preventive detention laws such as the National Security Act or UAPA who have not been captured as part of an international armed conflict.
Civilian nationals of a foreign country arrested for espionage or immigration offences but not captured as combatants in the course of active hostilities between States.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a detainee qualifies as a 'prisoner of war' determines whether Sections 156, 157, and 158 are attracted — triggering severe criminal liability (up to life imprisonment) for public servants who allow such prisoners to escape voluntarily or negligently, and for any person who aids, rescues, harbours, or resists the recapture of such a prisoner. The classification also determines the scope of parole-based custody, as movement beyond permitted limits constitutes a deemed escape under the law.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 77, 'private act' includes an act of watching carried out in a place which, in the circumstances, would reasonably be expected to provide privacy and where the victim's genitals, posterior or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear; or the victim is using a lavatory; or the victim is doing a sexual act that is not of a kind ordinarily done in public.
definitions.plain_english: A 'private act' refers to something a person does in a location where they would reasonably expect not to be watched by others, such as changing clothes, using the toilet, bathing, or engaging in sexual activity. The key idea is that the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy in that moment. It covers situations where the body is exposed or where intimate or sexual behaviour is taking place away from public view.
real_world_examples: A woman changing clothes inside a trial room at a clothing store in a Mumbai mall is filmed through a hidden camera installed by the shop owner — this constitutes a private act as she reasonably expected privacy in that enclosed space.

A man installs a hidden camera in the bathroom of a paying-guest accommodation in Bengaluru and records female tenants bathing or using the toilet — use of a lavatory or bathing area qualifies explicitly as a private act.

A couple engaged in consensual sexual intercourse in a hotel room in Delhi is secretly recorded by a staff member through a peephole — this is a private act as the sexual activity is not of a kind ordinarily done in public.

A woman staying in a hostel in Chennai is filmed through a gap in the curtain while she changes into her nightwear, exposing her undergarments — the act of changing in her own room constitutes a private act protected under this section.

A person installs a spy camera in a women's changing room adjacent to a swimming pool in Pune to capture images of women in various states of undress — capturing such images in a space reasonably expected to provide privacy constitutes capturing a private act.

A domestic worker in a Kolkata household places a recording device in the employer's bedroom and captures the employer's spouse undressing — the bedroom, being a place reasonably expected to provide privacy, and the act of undressing qualifies as a private act.
what_it_covers: A woman using a toilet, urinal, or lavatory in any location, including public restrooms, private bathrooms, or outdoor facilities where privacy is expected.
Any person whose genitals, posterior, or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear in a location reasonably expected to provide privacy, such as a changing room, bedroom, or bathroom.
A sexual act between individuals carried out in a private setting such as a hotel room, bedroom, or any enclosed space where such acts are not ordinarily performed publicly.
An act of bathing, undressing, or dressing in a space — such as a trial room, hostel room, or home — where the person reasonably expects not to be observed.
what_it_excludes: Acts performed in genuinely public spaces where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy, such as a person walking on a street or sitting in an open park, even if filmed without consent.
Sexual or intimate acts voluntarily performed in public view or live-streamed with the knowledge and consent of the person, where no expectation of privacy exists.

Medical examinations or clinical procedures where a patient's body is exposed in a hospital setting before authorised medical personnel acting in official capacity, as no reasonable privacy expectation is violated in that context.
Surveillance footage captured by security cameras in common areas such as corridors or lobbies, which do not involve exposure of intimate body parts or use of lavatory facilities.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'private act' is the threshold factual determination for the offence of voyeurism under Section 77 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — if the act is a private act, watching or capturing its image without consent attracts imprisonment of one to three years (first conviction) or three to seven years (subsequent conviction) along with a fine. If the act does not meet this definition, the core element of the voyeurism offence fails and no conviction under Section 77 can be sustained.
