definitions.definition: Private defence is the right recognised under sections 34 to 40 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, by which every person is entitled to defend their own body or the body of any other person against any offence affecting the human body, and to defend movable or immovable property of themselves or any other person against theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass or attempts thereof, subject to the restrictions that no more harm than is necessary may be inflicted and that the right does not arise where recourse to public authorities is available in time.
definitions.plain_english: Private defence is your legal right to protect yourself or someone else from physical attack, or to protect your own or another person's property from crimes like theft or trespass, without being treated as a criminal for doing so. You can use reasonable force to stop the threat, but you cannot go overboard — the force used must match the danger faced. This right also applies even when the attacker is a child, a mentally ill person, or someone acting under a misunderstanding.
real_world_examples: A woman in Delhi is attacked by a man attempting to rape her late at night; she picks up a stone and strikes him to escape. She is protected under private defence and commits no offence.

A farmer in rural Maharashtra catches a thief breaking into his granary and physically restrains him, injuring the thief in the scuffle. Since the act was to defend his property against theft, the farmer is not guilty of causing hurt.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai finds an intruder armed with a knife threatening him inside his shop; he pushes the intruder, causing injury. Because the apprehension of grievous hurt was reasonable, the shopkeeper's act is covered by private defence.

A person of unsound mind in Chennai picks up an iron rod and attacks a passerby. The passerby pushes him away forcefully to avoid being hit. Even though the attacker is not legally guilty of an offence due to mental illness, the passerby's act of self-defence is lawful under section 36.

A neighbour in Kolkata, mistakenly believing another resident is a burglar at night, attacks him. The resident who is wrongly attacked has the full right of private defence against that neighbour despite the neighbour acting under a misconception.

A security guard in Bengaluru prevents an armed robbery attempt at a jewellery store by overpowering one of the robbers, fracturing his arm in the process. The guard's act falls within the right of private defence of property against robbery.
what_it_covers: Defending one's own body or another person's body against any offence affecting the human body, including assault, robbery, or attempted murder.
Defending movable or immovable property of oneself or another person against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts to commit such offences.
Exercising defensive force against acts by a person of unsound mind, a minor, an intoxicated person, or someone acting under a misconception, to the same extent as if the act were a full offence.

Using necessary and proportionate force against a public servant whose act causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, especially when the person does not know or have reason to believe the person is a public servant.
Defence exercised on behalf of a third party who is being attacked, not just for oneself.
what_it_excludes: Inflicting more harm than is necessary to repel the threat — the right does not extend to excessive or retaliatory force beyond what the situation demands.
Situations where there is sufficient time to seek protection from public authorities, such as police, as recourse to law enforcement removes the justification for private defence.
Acts against a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office whose act does not reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt, even if those acts are not strictly legal.

Acts done by the direction of a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office, where the person knows or has reason to believe the authority behind the act, and the act does not cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
Using private defence as a pretext for aggression or initiating attack rather than responding to an imminent or ongoing threat.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether private defence applies determines whether an act that would otherwise constitute an offence such as hurt, grievous hurt, or even culpable homicide is treated as no offence at all under section 34, completely exempting the person from criminal liability. It is therefore a complete defence that blocks conviction for offences against the body or property when all its conditions are met.

definitions.definition: The right of private defence of property is the legally recognised entitlement of a person to defend their own or another's property against an unlawful act, commencing when a reasonable apprehension of danger to the property commences and continuing according to the nature of the offence being committed, as governed by the restrictions specified in section 37 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Under section 41, this right extends to voluntarily causing death or any other harm to the wrong-doer where the offence occasioning the exercise of the right is robbery, house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, mischief by fire or explosive substance on a human dwelling or place for custody of property, or theft, mischief, or house-trespass under circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
definitions.plain_english: The right of private defence of property allows a person to protect their own or someone else's property from an unlawful act by using necessary force, including in extreme cases causing death. This right kicks in the moment there is a genuine and reasonable fear of danger to the property and lasts only as long as that threat continues. For example, if someone tries to rob you, break into your home at night, or set fire to your house, you are legally allowed to use force to stop them.
real_world_examples: A shopkeeper in Mumbai catches a thief attempting to forcibly snatch cash from his register at gunpoint (robbery), and in the struggle physically harms the robber to prevent the theft — the shopkeeper can invoke the right of private defence of property.

A homeowner in Delhi wakes up at midnight to find an intruder breaking into his house after sunset (house-breaking), and uses force to apprehend or harm the intruder — this falls squarely within the extended right under section 41.

A farmer in Punjab discovers arsonists attempting to set fire to his grain storage hut (used as a place for custody of property) using kerosene, and in repelling them causes grievous hurt to one arsonist — the farmer is protected by this right.

A woman in Chennai finds thieves attempting to steal her vehicle from her garage at night under circumstances where they are armed and she reasonably fears being seriously hurt if she intervenes — she may exercise the right of private defence of property extending to causing harm.

A security guard at a warehouse in Kolkata confronts dacoits who are looting the premises and, while the robbery is ongoing, uses force causing injury to one of the dacoits to protect the stored goods — the guard is legally justified under the right of private defence of property.

A resident in Hyderabad discovers a criminal trespasser on his property who is threatening him with a weapon (raising apprehension of grievous hurt), and retaliates with force to drive away the intruder — the right of private defence of property applies.
semantic_tags: defence of property from unlawful acts
what_it_covers: Defence against robbery, including situations where the offender uses force or threat to commit theft, entitling the defender to use force as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint.
Defence against house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, where the right continues as long as the house-trespass begun by such house-breaking continues.
Defence against mischief committed by fire or any explosive substance on a building, tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property.
Defence against theft, mischief, or house-trespass under circumstances that reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence if the right is not exercised.
Defence of another person's property, not just the defender's own property, when the same conditions are met.
what_it_excludes: Defence of property against simple theft or criminal trespass where there is no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt — in such cases, causing death to the offender is not justified.

Situations where the defender had sufficient time to seek assistance from public authorities and chose not to — the right does not extend to pre-emptive or retributive violence once the danger has passed.

Acts of private defence exercised after the offender has effected his retreat with the property and no further threat exists — the right against theft terminates once the offender has escaped with the stolen goods and the property has not been recovered.
Defence motivated by personal vengeance or disproportionate retaliation unrelated to the immediate threat to property — the right is strictly bounded by the restrictions in section 37.
Causing more harm than is necessary to repel the offence — the right does not justify unrestricted violence beyond what is reasonably required to protect the property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether this right applies determines whether an act of causing hurt or death to another person constitutes a criminal offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or is a legally justified act, thereby completely exempting the defender from criminal liability. If the right is validly exercised, no offence of culpable homicide, murder, grievous hurt, or assault is constituted; if it is exceeded or wrongly invoked, the defender may themselves face criminal prosecution.

Under section 41, this right extends to voluntarily causing death or any other harm to the wrong-doer where the offence occasioning the exercise of the right is robbery, house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, mischief by fire or explosive substance on a human dwelling or place for custody of property, or theft, mischief, or house-trespass under circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

Examples: A shopkeeper in Mumbai catches a thief attempting to forcibly snatch cash from his register at gunpoint (robbery), and in the struggle physically harms the robber to prevent the theft — the shopkeeper can invoke the right of private defence of property. | A homeowner in Delhi wakes up at midnight to find an intruder breaking into his house after sunset (house-breaking), and uses force to apprehend or harm the intruder — this falls squarely within the extended right under section 41. | A farmer in Punjab discovers arsonists attempting to set fire to his grain storage hut (used as a place for custody of property) using kerosene, and in repelling them causes grievous hurt to one arsonist — the farmer is protected by this right. | A woman in Chennai finds thieves attempting to steal her vehicle from her garage at night under circumstances where they are armed and she reasonably fears being seriously hurt if she intervenes — she may exercise the right of private defence of property extending to causing harm. | A security guard at a warehouse in Kolkata confronts dacoits who are looting the premises and, while the robbery is ongoing, uses force causing injury to one of the dacoits to protect the stored goods — the guard is legally justified under the right of private defence of property. | A resident in Hyderabad discovers a criminal trespasser on his property who is threatening him with a weapon (raising apprehension of grievous hurt), and retaliates with force to drive away the intruder — the right of private defence of property applies.

Tags: defence of property from unlawful acts, proportionate force against offender, causing death to protect property, commencement on reasonable apprehension, continuance during ongoing offence, robbery and house-breaking defence, private individual self-help remedy, justified harm without criminal liability, night-time house-breaking exception, arson and explosive threat defence, restriction against excessive force, property protection legal right

Covers: Defence against robbery, including situations where the offender uses force or threat to commit theft, entitling the defender to use force as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint.; Defence against house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, where the right continues as long as the house-trespass begun by such house-breaking continues.; Defence against mischief committed by fire or any explosive substance on a building, tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property.; Defence against theft, mischief, or house-trespass under circumstances that reasonably cause apprehension that death or grievous hurt will be the consequence if the right is not exercised.; Defence of another person's property, not just the defender's own property, when the same conditions are met.

Excludes: Defence of property against simple theft or criminal trespass where there is no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt — in such cases, causing death to the offender is not justified.; Situations where the defender had sufficient time to seek assistance from public authorities and chose not to — the right does not extend to pre-emptive or retributive violence once the danger has passed.; Acts of private defence exercised after the offender has effected his retreat with the property and no further threat exists — the right against theft terminates once the offender has escaped with the stolen goods and the property has not been recovered.; Defence motivated by personal vengeance or disproportionate retaliation unrelated to the immediate threat to property — the right is strictly bounded by the restrictions in section 37.; Causing more harm than is necessary to repel the offence — the right does not justify unrestricted violence beyond what is reasonably required to protect the property.

Why it matters: Whether this right applies determines whether an act of causing hurt or death to another person constitutes a criminal offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita or is a legally justified act, thereby completely exempting the defender from criminal liability. If the right is validly exercised, no offence of culpable homicide, murder, grievous hurt, or assault is constituted; if it is exceeded or wrongly invoked, the defender may themselves face criminal prosecution.

definitions.definition: A 'probable consequence' is an act or outcome that is the natural and foreseeable result of an abetment, committed under the influence of the instigation, or with the aid or in pursuance of the conspiracy which constituted the abetment. It refers to that which a person of ordinary prudence would anticipate as a likely result flowing from the abetted act under the given circumstances.
definitions.plain_english: A 'probable consequence' is something that a reasonable person would expect to happen as a result of encouraging or helping someone to do something. If you push someone to commit a crime, and a related harmful act occurs that any sensible person could have foreseen, you are legally responsible for that too. However, you are not responsible for completely unrelated or unexpected acts that happen alongside the crime you encouraged.
real_world_examples: A gang leader in Mumbai instructs members to forcibly evict a family from their home at night using violence. During the eviction, one member assaults and seriously injures a resident. Since violent resistance and injury was a foreseeable outcome of ordering a forcible nighttime eviction, the gang leader is liable for the assault as a probable consequence of his abetment.

A person in Delhi instigates a teenager to steal a car, providing tools for the job. While fleeing after the theft, the teenager accidentally injures a pedestrian. Since reckless driving during escape is a probable consequence of abetting car theft, the instigator may be held liable for the injury caused during the escape.

A landlord in Chennai instigates his employees to set fire to a rival's warehouse at night when it is likely to be unoccupied. An employee present inside the warehouse during the arson dies. Since death from arson of an occupied or potentially occupied building at night is a probable consequence, the landlord is liable for the death.

A person in Kolkata instigates two men to break into a house for robbery by providing them weapons and a plan. During the robbery, the men encounter and murder the homeowner while resisting apprehension. Since murder during an armed robbery of an inhabited house at night is a probable consequence, the instigator is liable for murder.

A person instigates a child in Hyderabad to mix a harmful substance into a neighbour's water tank but the child accidentally mixes it into a different family's tank next door. Since the misdirection of the act under the influence of instigation was a probable consequence, the instigator remains liable for the harm caused to the different family.
semantic_tags: causal link between abetment and act
what_it_covers: Acts that flow naturally and foreseeably from the abetted crime, such as violence during an instigated robbery of an inhabited house.
Misdirected acts performed under the influence of instigation, such as poison administered to the wrong person due to a mistake made while acting on the abettor's instructions.
Acts committed during the execution of an abetted plan where the resulting harm (e.g., death during arson) was an objectively foreseeable risk given the nature and circumstances of the abetment.
Any act done in pursuance of a conspiracy or with the aid of the abettor that a person of ordinary prudence would have anticipated as a likely result of the scheme.
what_it_excludes: Separate and distinct criminal acts committed independently by the principal offender that bear no foreseeable connection to the abetted act, such as theft committed simultaneously with an abetted arson.
Highly remote, unusual, or extraordinary consequences that no reasonable person could have anticipated from the abetment in the given circumstances.
Acts committed by the principal offender out of a personal motive entirely unrelated to and disconnected from the instigation, conspiracy, or aid that constituted the abetment.
Acts done after the abetted act is fully completed and the influence of the instigation has ceased, where no continuing causal connection exists.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'probable consequence' of the abetment determines whether the abettor bears the same criminal liability as if they had directly abetted the act actually done; if it does not qualify, the abettor escapes liability for that distinct act entirely. This standard is the pivotal threshold that either extends or limits the punishment available against an abettor under Section 51 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, including for serious offences such as murder.

definitions.definition: The term 'proceeding' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Section 73, it denotes any action, step, or process undertaken before a court, tribunal, or authority in the exercise of its legal or judicial functions, including both civil and criminal proceedings, and encompasses every stage from initiation to final disposal of a matter.
definitions.plain_english: A 'proceeding' refers to any official legal action or process that takes place before a court, judge, or authorised legal body. This includes everything that happens during a court case — from filing a complaint to hearings, trials, and final judgments. It covers both criminal cases (like a murder trial) and civil cases (like a property dispute).
real_world_examples: A criminal trial before a Sessions Court in Mumbai against an accused charged with robbery under the BNS, 2023 — all stages from framing of charges to pronouncement of sentence constitute a 'proceeding'.
A contempt inquiry initiated by a High Court in Delhi against a party who disobeyed a court order — the inquiry and hearing conducted by the court amounts to a 'proceeding'.
An inquiry conducted by a Magistrate in Chennai into a complaint of wrongful confinement filed by a victim — the entire inquiry process is a 'proceeding' before that Magistrate.

A hearing before a Special Court in Hyderabad for offences relating to organised crime under the BNS, 2023, including examination of witnesses and arguments — constitutes a 'proceeding' under the Act.
A summary trial conducted by a Judicial Magistrate in Kolkata for a minor offence such as public nuisance — from issuance of summons to final order, the entire process is a 'proceeding'.
what_it_covers: A criminal trial before a Sessions Court or Magistrate's Court at any stage from filing of charge-sheet to final judgment.
An inquiry or investigation conducted by a court or Magistrate into a complaint or offence under the BNS, 2023.
Any hearing, examination of witnesses, or arguments conducted before a legally empowered judicial body in exercise of its judicial functions.
Summary proceedings, contempt proceedings, and bail proceedings conducted before a court under the BNS, 2023.
Appeals, revisions, or review proceedings before a superior court arising out of an original criminal case.
what_it_excludes: Administrative or departmental inquiries conducted by executive authorities or government departments that do not exercise judicial functions.
Police investigations conducted under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 prior to filing of a charge-sheet, as these are investigative and not judicial proceedings.
Negotiations, settlements, or alternative dispute resolution processes conducted outside the formal court system, such as Lok Adalat mediations where no judicial order is passed.
Legislative proceedings or proceedings before Parliamentary or State Assembly committees, which are not judicial in nature.
Internal disciplinary proceedings of private bodies or organisations not empowered by law to act judicially.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of the term 'proceeding' under Section 73 determines whether certain acts — such as threats, intimidation, or harm directed at a person to deter participation — constitute offences like criminal intimidation or obstruction of justice under the BNS, 2023. Whether an act occurs 'in' or 'in relation to' a proceeding directly triggers liability for offences designed to protect the integrity of the judicial process.

definitions.definition: Proceeds of crime, as used in Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to any property, whether movable or immovable, that has been derived, obtained, or acquired through the commission of an organised crime or any continuing unlawful activity undertaken by a member of, or on behalf of, an organised crime syndicate, including the direct or indirect material or financial benefits flowing from such criminal activity.
definitions.plain_english: Proceeds of crime means any money, property, or assets that a person gains as a result of committing organised crime — such as money earned from drug trafficking, extortion, or kidnapping. It covers both directly obtained benefits (like ransom money) and indirectly derived gains (like property bought using crime money). Essentially, it is the profit or benefit that comes out of criminal activity carried out by organised criminal groups.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based organised crime syndicate extorts protection money from shopkeepers in a locality; the cash collected and any land or vehicles purchased using that money would constitute proceeds of crime under Section 111.

A gang involved in inter-state drug trafficking in Punjab sells narcotics and deposits the earnings into multiple bank accounts under fictitious names; the funds in those accounts are proceeds of crime.

An organised group in Delhi engaged in vehicle theft sells stolen cars through a network of fake dealers and uses the sale proceeds to buy real estate; those properties acquired from vehicle theft earnings are proceeds of crime.

A human trafficking syndicate operating across Odisha and West Bengal collects fees from exploiting trafficked persons for prostitution; the money received from such exploitation constitutes proceeds of crime.

A cyber-crime gang based in Jharkhand defrauds thousands of citizens through mass-marketing fraud schemes and transfers the fraudulently obtained funds abroad via hawala transactions; those transferred funds and any assets purchased from them are proceeds of crime.
A contract killing syndicate operating in Uttar Pradesh receives payment for carrying out assassinations; the payment received for such killings amounts to proceeds of crime.
what_it_covers: Cash, bank deposits, or liquid funds received directly as payment for or profit from an organised crime activity such as extortion, kidnapping for ransom, or drug trafficking.
Movable or immovable property — such as land, vehicles, jewellery, or equipment — purchased, acquired, or held using money or benefits derived from the commission of an organised crime.
Indirect financial benefits flowing from organised crime, including investments, shares, or business assets funded by proceeds generated through continuing unlawful activities of a syndicate.

Property in the possession of any person acting on behalf of a member of an organised crime syndicate that cannot be satisfactorily accounted for, thereby presumed to be linked to organised criminal proceeds.
Proceeds generated from economic offences carried out as part of organised crime, such as gains from counterfeiting currency, hawala transactions, or defrauding banks and financial institutions.
what_it_excludes: Legitimately earned income, savings, or property acquired through lawful means by a person who is separately associated with a convicted syndicate member, where no causal link to organised crime activity is established.

Property or financial benefits arising from isolated criminal acts that do not meet the threshold of 'continuing unlawful activity' — i.e., where more than one charge-sheet has not been filed before a competent court within the preceding ten years.

Proceeds or assets generated by activities that, although unlawful, are not cognizable offences punishable with imprisonment of three years or more, as they fall outside the definition of continuing unlawful activity.
Harboured or concealed assets belonging to an offender that are held by the offender's spouse, given the specific statutory exception carved out for spouses in Section 111.

Amounts or properties that are part of a bona fide legal settlement, court-decreed compensation, or insurance claim that merely happen to involve a party accused of organised crime, where the funds themselves have a lawful origin.
definitions.why_it_matters: Possession of proceeds of crime under Section 111 is itself a distinct punishable offence attracting imprisonment of not less than three years extending to life imprisonment and a fine of not less than two lakh rupees, making the classification of property as 'proceeds of crime' critical to establishing guilt independently of the primary organised crime offence. The determination of whether assets constitute proceeds of crime also triggers liability for unexplained possession, enabling prosecution of syndicate associates who hold such property without satisfactory accounting.

definitions.definition: The term 'process' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Section 242, it refers to any official legal process issued by a Court or public authority, including summons, warrants, orders, or notices, requiring a person to appear, produce documents, or take a legally mandated action, and extends to any document purporting to be such a process.
definitions.plain_english: A 'process' in this context means any official legal document or command issued by a court or government authority — such as a summons or warrant — that directs someone to do something, like appear before a court. It is the formal mechanism by which courts exercise their authority over individuals. Importantly, the law treats a forged or fabricated version of such a document as seriously as tampering with a real one.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai receives a fabricated court summons purportedly issued by the Sessions Court directing him to appear in a civil suit — the fabricated document itself constitutes a false 'process' under Section 242.

A Delhi-based clerk at a magistrate's court creates a counterfeit warrant of arrest using the court's seal and forged signature of the magistrate, and uses it to extort money from a local businessman — this is an offence involving a false process.

A litigant in Chennai, wanting to harass a rival, prints and serves a fabricated High Court notice in the name of a real judge ordering the rival to produce financial records — the fabricated notice is a false legal process.
An accused person in Kolkata, to avoid appearing before a tribunal, produces a forged stay order purportedly issued by the Calcutta High Court — this constitutes use of a false process.

A fraudster in Hyderabad circulates counterfeit eviction orders bearing a fictitious court seal to tenants, compelling them to vacate properties — each such order is a false process within the meaning of Section 242.
what_it_covers: A genuine summons issued by a Magistrate or Sessions Court directing a person to appear for examination or trial.
A court-issued warrant of arrest or search warrant bearing the seal and signature of a competent judicial authority.
A fabricated or forged document that purports to be a summons, warrant, order, or notice from a court or public authority, used to deceive or compel action.
Any official notice or direction issued by a tribunal, commission, or statutory authority acting under a law empowering it to compel appearance or production of evidence.
A counterfeit stay order or injunction purportedly issued by a High Court used to obstruct legal proceedings.
what_it_excludes: A private legal notice sent by a lawyer to another party on behalf of a client, which carries no judicial or statutory compulsion.
An informal communication or letter from a government department that does not carry the force of a judicial or statutory direction to appear or act.
Internal administrative orders or office memoranda issued within a government ministry that do not constitute a judicial command requiring compliance under penalty of law.
A demand notice under a contractual or civil arrangement that has not been issued by or in the name of any court or statutory authority.
A police intimation or call for voluntary statement that has not been backed by a formal court order or statutory summons.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'process' under Section 242 determines whether its forgery, fabrication, or fraudulent use attracts criminal liability for offences such as using a false document as genuine or fabricating false evidence; persons found creating or using forged processes face punishment for offences that undermine the authority and integrity of the judicial system.

definitions.definition: The term 'process of law' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 8, it refers to the legally authorised mechanisms by which a court or competent authority compels the payment or recovery of a fine imposed on a convicted offender, including attachment and sale of property, distress warrants, or other enforcement procedures sanctioned by law.
definitions.plain_english: Process of law means the official legal steps a court can take to forcibly collect a fine from someone who has been convicted and has not voluntarily paid it. This includes actions like seizing and selling the offender's property to recover the money owed. Essentially, it is the court's formal machinery to ensure that fines are actually collected rather than simply ignored.
real_world_examples: A Delhi Sessions Court sentences a convicted fraudster to pay a fine of ₹50,000. When he refuses to pay, the court issues a distress warrant directing bailiffs to attach and auction his bank account balance to recover the fine through process of law.

A Mumbai Magistrate's Court convicts a shopkeeper for selling adulterated food and imposes a fine of ₹10,000. The shopkeeper ignores the order, so the court uses process of law to attach his shop's till and recover the amount, terminating the default imprisonment the moment full recovery is made.

In a Kolkata court, an offender is sentenced to a fine of ₹1,00,000. After partial payment of ₹75,000, the remaining ₹25,000 is levied by process of law through attachment of his movable property within the six-year statutory window, discharging him from further imprisonment.

A Chennai court convicts a person for rash driving causing grievous hurt and imposes a fine. The convicted person absconds without paying. Within four years of sentencing, the court initiates process of law by attaching his two-wheeler and selling it to recover the outstanding fine amount.

An offender convicted in a Hyderabad court dies after paying only half the imposed fine. The court, acting through process of law, proceeds to levy the remaining fine amount from the estate left behind by the deceased, as the liability survives death under Section 8.
what_it_covers: Attachment and sale of the offender's movable or immovable property by court order to recover an unpaid fine.
Issuance of distress warrants or recovery certificates directed at recovering fines within the six-year limitation period specified in Section 8.
Recovery of unpaid fine amounts from the legal estate of a deceased offender whose property remains liable for his debts after death.
Partial levy of a fine through enforcement proceedings, resulting in proportional reduction of default imprisonment already being served.
Any coercive legal measure authorised by the Code of Criminal Procedure or its successor law to compel payment of court-imposed fines.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary payment of the fine directly by the offender or on his behalf, which is a separate mode of discharge distinct from compulsory process.
Informal or extrajudicial collection of fines by private parties without a court-issued order or authorised legal instrument.

Recovery attempts initiated after the expiry of six years from the date of sentencing (or after the maximum imprisonment period where that exceeds six years), which fall outside the legally permitted window.
Community service ordered in lieu of a fine, which is treated as a separate alternative under Section 8 and is not a 'levy' through process of law.
Administrative penalties or dues collected by government departments through revenue recovery mechanisms outside the criminal court's jurisdiction.
definitions.why_it_matters: The moment a fine is 'levied by process of law,' the default imprisonment that the offender is serving must legally terminate, directly affecting the offender's liberty and the court's sentencing outcome under Section 8. It also determines whether the State can pursue fine recovery from the offender's estate after death, and establishes the six-year outer limit within which enforcement action must be initiated.

definitions.definition: A proclaimed offender is a person against whom a declaration has been made under sub-section (4) of section 84 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, pronouncing him as such, after he has failed to appear at the specified place and specified time as required by a proclamation published under sub-section (1) of that section.
definitions.plain_english: A proclaimed offender is someone who has been officially declared by a court as an absconder — a person who was formally summoned by public notice to appear before the court but deliberately failed to do so. The court, after following due legal procedure, issues a formal declaration naming that person a proclaimed offender. This status carries a heavier criminal punishment than simply failing to appear in response to a court summons.
real_world_examples: A person accused of a serious fraud in Mumbai is issued a proclamation by the sessions court requiring him to appear on a set date. He flees to another state and does not appear. The court, after due inquiry, declares him a proclaimed offender under BNSS section 84(4), making him liable for up to seven years imprisonment under BNS section 209.

A rape accused from Uttar Pradesh, against whom a proclamation was published in newspapers and at his last known address, deliberately remains in hiding and fails to appear before the designated magistrate. The court formally declares him a proclaimed offender, triggering enhanced punishment.

An accused in a kidnapping case from Delhi, who has been evading arrest and ignoring court-issued proclamations, is declared a proclaimed offender after the court is satisfied that he is deliberately absconding, making him subject to both imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

A person accused of organised dacoity in Rajasthan, after a proclamation is published under BNSS section 84(1) requiring him to appear at a specified location on a specified date, travels abroad and refuses to return. The trial court records his deliberate non-appearance and issues a formal declaration pronouncing him a proclaimed offender.

A businessman in Chennai, charged with cheating multiple investors, is served with a court proclamation but continues to evade appearance. After the statutory period lapses and the court records his wilful absence, he is declared a proclaimed offender, exposing him to enhanced penal consequences under BNS section 209.
what_it_covers: A person who has been served with or is deemed to have notice of a proclamation under BNSS section 84(1) and deliberately fails to appear at the specified place and time.
An accused against whom a formal court declaration has been made under BNSS section 84(4) pronouncing him a proclaimed offender after a finding of wilful non-appearance.

A fugitive accused in any cognisable or serious criminal matter who absconds after a proclamation is issued and thereby attracts enhanced punishment of up to seven years imprisonment plus fine under BNS section 209.
Persons hiding within India or having fled abroad who refuse to comply with judicial proclamations requiring their appearance before a designated court or officer.
what_it_excludes: A person who fails to appear in response to a proclamation but against whom no formal declaration under BNSS section 84(4) has yet been made — such a person may be liable for simple non-appearance (up to three years or fine) but is not yet a proclaimed offender attracting the enhanced seven-year punishment.

An accused who appears before the court on or before the specified date as required by the proclamation, even if they initially delayed compliance, as no declaration of proclaimed offender status can be made against them.

A witness or a civil party summoned by proclamation for purposes other than those governed by BNSS section 84(1) in relation to a criminal accused, as the provision is specific to accused persons required to appear in criminal proceedings.

A person who is unable to appear due to genuine medical incapacity, natural calamity, or other sufficient cause beyond their control, as the declaration under BNSS section 84(4) presupposes deliberate or wilful non-appearance.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of a person as a proclaimed offender under BNS section 209 directly escalates the maximum punishment from three years to seven years of imprisonment with mandatory fine liability, fundamentally altering the sentencing framework applicable to the accused. It also enables authorities to attach the absconder's property under BNSS provisions and signals persistent, wilful defiance of court authority, which courts treat as an aggravating factor in subsequent proceedings.

definitions.definition: A proclamation is an official public announcement or directive issued under the authority of a public servant legally competent to direct such proclamation to be made, requiring a person to attend at a specified place and time or otherwise comply with a lawful direction, and includes proclamations issued under the authority of a court or other competent public authority.
definitions.plain_english: A proclamation is an official public notice or order issued by a government authority or court, directing a person to appear at a certain place and time or to do something required by law. It is a formal public announcement that carries legal force, meaning a person who receives or is subject to it is legally bound to comply. Ignoring or obstructing a proclamation can lead to criminal punishment.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Court in Mumbai issues a proclamation directing an accused who has absconded to appear before it on a specified date; the accused's neighbour intentionally tears down the posted notice to prevent the proclamation from being made public, attracting liability under Section 207.

A District Magistrate in Lucknow issues a proclamation under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita directing a witness to appear at a specific police station; the witness, being legally bound to appear, deliberately fails to attend at the required time, committing an offence under Section 208.

A public servant in Chennai directs a proclamation to be affixed on the outer wall of an accused person's house, but the accused's family member intentionally removes the proclamation from the wall before it can be read by others, thereby preventing its lawful publication under Section 207.

A court in Delhi issues a proclamation to a person required to produce documentary evidence at a hearing; the person, fully aware of the proclamation, leaves the court premises before the legally permitted time of departure, committing the offence under Section 208.

A tehsildar in Rajasthan issues an official proclamation requiring a landowner to appear before him to answer a revenue proceeding; the landowner bribes a peon to ensure the proclamation is never actually read out or affixed in the village, thereby intentionally preventing the lawful making of the proclamation under Section 207.
what_it_covers: A formal public announcement issued by a court directing an accused or witness to appear at a specified place and time.
An official notice directed to be made by a public servant competent to issue it, requiring compliance with a lawful direction such as attendance or production of documents.

A proclamation published under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, requiring a person to appear at a specified place and time, including those leading to a declaration of proclaimed offender status.
Any official public directive affixed at a location or read out under the authority of a legally competent public servant requiring a person to attend in person or through an agent.
A proclamation issued in the context of a court proceeding requiring the production of a document or electronic record.
what_it_excludes: Informal notices or private communications issued by individuals who are not public servants or do not possess legal competence to issue such directions.
General government advertisements, public service announcements, or policy notifications that do not legally bind a specific person to attend or comply.
Summons or orders that have not yet been formally directed to be made or issued by a competent public servant and therefore do not carry the authority of a proclamation.
Voluntary public statements or press releases by government bodies that do not constitute a legally enforceable directive to a specific person.
Religious or ceremonial proclamations made by private or religious bodies that carry no legal authority under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as a 'proclamation' determines whether a person is legally bound to comply with it under Sections 207 and 208 of the BNS, 2023, and whether interference with it or non-compliance with it constitutes a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment and/or fine. It also triggers the proclaimed offender regime under Section 209 read with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, carrying up to seven years' imprisonment.

definitions.definition: An order promulgated by a public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order, directing a person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with certain property in their possession or under their management. Such an order is duly promulgated when issued by a public servant acting within the scope of their lawful authority to issue such directions.
definitions.plain_english: A 'promulgated order' is an official direction or instruction formally issued by a government official who has the legal power to make such announcements to the public or to specific persons. It typically tells people either to stop doing something or to handle certain property in a specified way. For example, a District Magistrate announcing restrictions on public gatherings or movement of goods during a curfew or epidemic is issuing a promulgated order. Knowingly disobeying such an order is a criminal offence under this law.
real_world_examples: A District Magistrate in Uttar Pradesh issues a prohibitory order under Section 144 CrPC (now equivalent under BNSS) banning assembly of more than five persons in a sensitive area during communal tension; a person knowingly violates this order and participates in a group gathering, thereby committing an offence under Section 223 BNS.

A Municipal Health Officer in Mumbai promulgates an order during a dengue outbreak directing residents to drain stagnant water from all containers on their premises; a building owner knowingly ignores the direction, risking spread of disease, and is liable for punishment under Section 223 BNS.

A police commissioner in Bengaluru issues a promulgated order banning the carrying of firecrackers on a particular public road during a festival procession; a vendor knowingly disobeys the order by carrying firecrackers on that route, thereby causing risk of injury to persons lawfully employed in crowd management.

A revenue officer in Punjab promulgates an order directing a farmer not to remove or sell seized crops that are under attachment proceedings; the farmer knowingly sells the crop in violation of the order, thereby committing disobedience under Section 223 BNS.

A quarantine officer at Chennai airport issues a promulgated order directing that certain imported goods suspected of contamination be kept sealed and not moved; the importer knowingly shifts the goods, causing risk to public health, and is liable under Section 223 BNS.

A sub-divisional magistrate in Rajasthan issues an order during a riot-prone situation directing that a religious procession shall not pass through a particular street; the organiser knowingly proceeds on the prohibited route, causing danger of a riot, thus attracting the higher punishment under Section 223 BNS.
what_it_covers: An order issued by a District Magistrate or Executive Magistrate banning public assemblies or processions in a specified area during communal tension or law-and-order emergencies.
A health or quarantine officer's direction instructing property owners or traders to deal with goods, livestock, or premises in a specified manner to prevent spread of infectious disease.
An order by a revenue or court-empowered officer directing a person not to alienate, move, or interfere with property under attachment, seizure, or official management.
A police commissioner's promulgated notice restricting the use of certain routes, materials, or activities during public events to prevent obstruction or injury to persons on public duty.
Any formal, publicly announced or personally served direction by a public servant acting within their statutorily conferred power to regulate conduct or property for public safety or order.
what_it_excludes: Informal verbal instructions or requests given by a government employee who does not have the lawful power to promulgate binding orders; such instructions do not constitute a 'promulgated order' under Section 223.

Orders issued by a public servant who exceeds their jurisdiction or competence, i.e., where the servant is not 'lawfully empowered' to promulgate such an order — disobedience of such ultra vires directions does not attract Section 223.
Legislative enactments, judicial orders from courts, or executive notifications issued through the legislative process, which are governed by separate legal provisions and not by this section.

Private contractual directions or instructions given by an employer or private entity, even if that entity has quasi-public functions, unless the direction is issued under express statutory authority.

Orders where the person subject to them had no knowledge of the promulgation, since Section 223 expressly requires that the offender knew of the order — ignorance of a promulgated order negates the offence.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a direction qualifies as a 'promulgated order' under Section 223 determines whether knowing disobedience constitutes a criminal offence attracting imprisonment up to six months (for obstruction/annoyance) or up to one year with fine (where danger to life, health, safety, riot or affray results). Without the direction meeting the threshold of a duly promulgated order by a lawfully empowered public servant, no criminal liability under Section 223 can be established.

definitions.definition: The term 'property' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; however, as used throughout the Sanhita, 'property' encompasses both movable and immovable property of any description, including tangible and intangible assets, belonging to or in the possession of any person. 'Movable property' is expressly defined in Section 2 to include property of every description, except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the earth.
definitions.plain_english: Property refers to anything that a person owns, possesses, or has an interest in — including physical objects like money, jewellery, vehicles, and goods, as well as rights over things. It covers both things that can be moved (like a mobile phone or cattle) and things fixed to the ground (like a building or land). In most theft or criminal damage offences, 'property' is the thing that has been taken, damaged, or dishonestly dealt with.
real_world_examples: A pickpocket steals a wallet containing cash and a debit card from a commuter on the Delhi Metro — the wallet and its contents are 'property' for the purpose of theft under Section 303 of the BNS.

definitions.definition: A mark used for denoting that movable property belongs to a particular person is called a property mark. A false property mark is one used in a manner reasonably calculated to cause it to be believed that the property or goods so marked, or any property or goods contained in any receptacle so marked, belong to a person to whom they do not belong.
definitions.plain_english: A property mark is any symbol, sign, label, stamp, or marking placed on movable goods to identify who owns them. It is essentially an ownership identifier on physical items. If someone uses such a mark falsely to make people believe that goods belong to someone they actually do not belong to, that is called a false property mark and is a punishable offence.
real_world_examples: A dairy cooperative in Gujarat stamps its milk cans with its unique brand symbol to show ownership; a rival dairy fraudulently applies the same stamp to its own cans to pass them off as the cooperative's product — this constitutes use of a false property mark.

A textile mill in Surat marks its bales of fabric with a distinctive stencil indicating the mill's name; a trader replaces that mark with his own to claim the goods belong to him and sell them as his own stock — amounting to a false property mark offence.

A government railway workshop in Pune marks its tools and equipment with a departmental emblem to denote government ownership; a contractor removes and replaces those marks with his own insignia to misappropriate the tools — this triggers offences under Sections 345 and 346.

A tea garden in Assam uses a registered ownership mark on its chests of tea before dispatch; a dishonest intermediary counterfeits this mark on inferior tea chests to deceive buyers into believing the tea originates from that reputed garden — constituting counterfeiting of a property mark under Section 347.

A cold storage facility in Mumbai assigns numbered ownership tags to client produce stored therein; an employee swaps tags between different clients' consignments to cause wrongful gain to one party — amounting to tampering with a property mark under Section 346.
what_it_covers: Any symbol, stamp, stencil, label, or sign physically applied to movable goods or their packaging to identify the owner.
Marks placed on cases, packages, boxes, bags, or other receptacles containing movable property to denote ownership of the contents.
Marks used by public servants or government departments to denote that property has been manufactured at a particular place or time, is of a particular quality, or is entitled to any exemption.
Any mark counterfeited or falsely applied to make goods appear to belong to a person or entity other than the true owner.
Instruments such as dies, plates, or stamps made or possessed for the purpose of counterfeiting a property mark.
what_it_excludes: Marks affixed to immovable property such as land, buildings, or structures, since the definition is confined strictly to movable property.
Trade marks or brand marks used purely for indicating commercial origin or quality rather than denoting ownership of a specific item or batch of movable property.
Verbal or digital declarations of ownership that are not physically marked on the movable property or its receptacle.
Currency notes, coins, or government stamps that have their own distinct definitional and penal framework under separate provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
Electronic records or digital tags not physically inscribed or affixed to tangible movable property or its packaging.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a mark qualifies as a 'property mark' determines whether offences of using a false property mark (punishable up to one year imprisonment), tampering (up to one year), counterfeiting (up to two or three years), or making instruments for counterfeiting (up to three years) under Sections 345–348 are attracted. The definition also governs who bears the burden of proving absence of fraudulent intent, as the accused must disprove intent to defraud once use of a false property mark is established.

definitions.definition: The term 'prostitution' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used consistently to mean the employment or use of a person, particularly a child, for the purpose of sexual intercourse or sexual services in exchange for money or other consideration, whether such employment is compelled or induced. It encompasses the use of a person for illicit intercourse or any unlawful and immoral sexual purpose, as contextualised in Sections 98 and 99.
definitions.plain_english: Prostitution refers to the act of using a person, especially a child, for sexual services or intercourse, typically in exchange for money or other benefit. Under this law, the focus is on the exploitation of children for such purposes — whether by selling, buying, or otherwise trafficking them into such situations. It includes any unlawful or immoral sexual use of a person, not just formal sex work.
real_world_examples: A trafficker in Mumbai sells a 15-year-old girl from a rural village to a brothel operator in exchange for money, intending that the girl be used for sexual services — this constitutes selling a child for the purpose of prostitution under Section 98.

A person in Delhi purchases a 14-year-old boy from his impoverished family under the pretext of employment, but actually places him in a setting where he is sexually exploited by clients — this amounts to buying a child for purposes of prostitution under Section 99.

A brothel owner in Kolkata hires a 16-year-old girl from an intermediary, claiming she is an adult domestic worker, but uses her for sexual services within the establishment — the presumption under Section 99 applies since she is under 18.

A network operating across state lines in Rajasthan and Gujarat recruits minor girls from tribal communities and places them in establishments where they are made to engage in sexual acts with paying clients — this constitutes both prostitution of children and organised crime under Section 111.

A person in Chennai disposes of his 17-year-old niece to a known brothel keeper for a sum of money — under Section 98, the law presumes this was done with intent that she be used for prostitution, placing the burden on the accused to prove otherwise.
semantic_tags: sale of child for immoral purpose
what_it_covers: Employment or use of a child at any age for sexual intercourse or sexual services in exchange for money or other consideration.
Disposing of, selling, buying, or hiring a child with the intent or knowledge that the child will be used for sexual exploitation or immoral purposes.
Sexual exploitation of a female under 18 years of age by a brothel keeper or a prostitute who acquires possession of her, which raises a statutory presumption of intent for prostitution.
Human trafficking for prostitution as part of an organised crime syndicate's continuing unlawful activity under Section 111.
Any unlawful or immoral sexual use of a person that goes beyond or outside the bounds of recognised marital or quasi-marital unions.
what_it_excludes: Consensual sexual intercourse between adults within a lawful marriage or a union recognised as quasi-marital by the personal law or custom of the community.
Sexual intercourse between adults that is not transactional or exploitative in nature and does not involve any element of trafficking, sale, or commercial exchange.
Employment of adults in other forms of labour or domestic service that do not involve sexual exploitation, even if carried out under exploitative conditions.
Acts of sexual harassment or stalking that do not involve transactional sexual use or trafficking, which are governed by separate provisions of the Act.

Consensual adult relationships, including live-in relationships recognised under personal law or custom as quasi-marital, which are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'illicit intercourse' under Section 98.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct falls within the meaning of prostitution under Sections 98 and 99 directly determines whether the offences of selling or buying a child for immoral purposes are attracted, carrying punishments of up to ten and fourteen years imprisonment respectively, along with mandatory fines. It also triggers statutory presumptions of criminal intent against persons who dispose of or acquire possession of females under eighteen to or from brothel keepers, shifting the burden of proof to the accused.

definitions.definition: A proxy, in the context of Section 172, refers to a person who has been duly authorised under any law for the time being in force to vote on behalf of an elector at an election. Such a person is expressly exempted from the offence of personation at an election when voting strictly within the scope of that authorisation.
definitions.plain_english: A proxy is someone who is legally allowed to cast a vote on behalf of another registered voter (the elector) at an election. This permission must come from a recognised law. When this person votes in place of the elector, they are not committing any crime, because the law specifically permits them to do so. Without this authorisation, voting in someone else's name would be treated as election fraud.
real_world_examples: Under the rules governing elections to certain cooperative societies or local bodies in India, a member who is unable to attend may formally authorise another member to vote as their proxy; that authorised person is a 'proxy' under Section 172.

In elections to some professional bodies and trade associations registered under Indian law, an absent member submits a proxy form to the returning officer, and the designated person casts the vote lawfully on the member's behalf.

A shareholder of a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, who cannot attend the Annual General Meeting, appoints another person as proxy to vote on resolutions; while that is a corporate context, the concept mirrors the electoral proxy exemption in Section 172.

In certain Panchayat or municipal ward elections in states that permit proxy voting for specific categories of electors (such as persons with severe disabilities), a carer duly authorised by the State Election Commission votes on the elector's behalf and is shielded from liability under the proviso to Section 172.

A serviceman posted to a remote area who is registered as an elector in his home constituency may, under applicable service election rules, authorise a family member to vote as proxy, and that family member exercises the vote without committing personation.
what_it_covers: A person formally authorised under a statute or statutory rules to cast a vote on behalf of a named elector who cannot vote in person.
The act of voting at an election by such an authorised person strictly in place of and on behalf of the elector who granted the authorisation.
Any individual holding a valid proxy instrument issued under a law in force that expressly permits proxy voting in a particular class of elections.
The scope of the proxy's voting act — limited to the specific election and elector for whom the authorisation was granted.
what_it_excludes: A person who votes in another person's name without any legal authorisation — such a person commits personation under Section 172 and cannot claim the proxy exemption.
A person who has already voted once at the same election in their own name and then attempts to vote again, even purportedly on another's behalf, as the proviso does not protect double-voting.
Informal or private arrangements between individuals (e.g., a friend verbally agreeing to 'represent' another) that are not backed by a statutory provision permitting proxy voting.
A proxy who exceeds their authorisation, such as voting for an elector different from the one named in the proxy instrument, or voting at a different election than specified.
Persons who abet, procure, or attempt to procure unauthorised voting by others — the proviso protects only the authorised proxy acting within the terms of the authorisation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an authorised proxy determines whether their act of voting in another's name is a lawful exercise of a delegated electoral right or the cognisable offence of personation at an election under Section 172, which carries criminal liability. The definition creates a specific statutory shield that, if applicable, completely negates the offence; if it does not apply, the person faces prosecution for electoral fraud.

definitions.definition: An appeal to 'prurient interest' refers to a shameful or morbid interest in nudity, sex, or excretion that goes beyond a customary limit of candour, as used in Section 294 to characterise obscene material — being material that is lascivious or that appeals to such a degrading or unwholesome interest in sexual matters, tending to deprave and corrupt likely viewers, readers, or listeners.
definitions.plain_english: Prurient interest means an unhealthy, excessive, or degrading fascination with sexual content, nudity, or explicit bodily matters that most reasonable people would find offensive or morally corrupting. It goes beyond normal curiosity or artistic interest. If a book, image, video, or any other material is designed to arouse or appeal to this kind of shameful desire, it is considered obscene under the law.
real_world_examples: A Delhi-based online seller distributes e-books containing graphic sexual stories with no literary or artistic merit, designed purely to arouse degrading sexual curiosity in readers — such content appeals to prurient interest and qualifies as obscene under Section 294.

A Mumbai shop owner stocks and sells imported foreign magazines featuring explicit pornographic photographs with no educational or medical context, catering to customers' morbid sexual curiosity — this material appeals to prurient interest and attracts criminal liability.

A WhatsApp group administrator in Chennai circulates explicit videos of sexual acts among adult members solely for sexual gratification purposes, without any artistic, scientific, or educational justification — the content's appeal to prurient interest makes its distribution an offence.

A Kolkata print house produces pamphlets containing lurid, detailed descriptions of sexual acts targeting adolescents, with content calibrated to stimulate unhealthy sexual interest rather than serve any legitimate purpose — the pamphlets appeal to prurient interest and are prosecutable as obscene objects.

A Bengaluru mobile app developer creates and markets an application hosting user-generated explicit sexual content with no age-verification or legitimate purpose, where the sole draw is satisfying users' morbid or degrading interest in sexual material — this constitutes an appeal to prurient interest under Section 294.
what_it_covers: Sexually explicit books, pamphlets, or writings that are crafted solely to stimulate degrading or unhealthy sexual desire in readers, with no redeeming artistic, literary, or scientific value.
Digital or electronic content — including videos, images, or written material displayed or circulated online — that is designed to arouse a shameful or morbid interest in sexual acts or nudity.

Graphic representations, drawings, or figures (physical or electronic) depicting sexual acts in a manner that targets the degraded sexual curiosity of the audience rather than serving any legitimate purpose.
Advertisements or communications that knowingly promote access to material appealing to prurient interest, thereby facilitating the distribution of obscene content.
what_it_excludes: Bona fide artistic, literary, or scientific works that may contain sexual content but are intended and recognised to serve genuine aesthetic, educational, or research purposes — the overall effect must be assessed rather than isolated passages.

Medical or sex-education material produced and distributed by qualified professionals or recognised institutions for legitimate health, therapeutic, or educational purposes, where the intent is instructional rather than to arouse degrading interest.

Content protected under religious or cultural tradition that depicts sexuality in a symbolic or devotional context, such as classical temple sculpture reproductions or recognised ancient texts, where the dominant purpose is spiritual or cultural rather than prurient.

News reporting, journalism, or documentary content that references or depicts sexual matters in a factual, informational context for public awareness, without the purpose or effect of appealing to shameful sexual curiosity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether material appeals to 'prurient interest' is a decisive element in establishing that it is 'obscene' under Section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; if this threshold is met (alongside the tendency to deprave and corrupt), criminal liability is triggered for sale, distribution, exhibition, import, export, possession, or advertisement of the material, with imprisonment up to two years on first conviction and up to five years on subsequent conviction, plus fines. Conversely, if the material does not appeal to prurient interest and lacks the tendency to deprave and corrupt, it falls outside the definition of obscenity and no offence is made out.

Legal text: An appeal to 'prurient interest' refers to a shameful or morbid interest in nudity, sex, or excretion that goes beyond a customary limit of candour, as used in Section 294 to characterise obscene material — being material that is lascivious or that appeals to such a degrading or unwholesome interest in sexual matters, tending to deprave and corrupt likely viewers, readers, or listeners.

Examples: A Delhi-based online seller distributes e-books containing graphic sexual stories with no literary or artistic merit, designed purely to arouse degrading sexual curiosity in readers — such content appeals to prurient interest and qualifies as obscene under Section 294. | A Mumbai shop owner stocks and sells imported foreign magazines featuring explicit pornographic photographs with no educational or medical context, catering to customers' morbid sexual curiosity — this material appeals to prurient interest and attracts criminal liability. | A WhatsApp group administrator in Chennai circulates explicit videos of sexual acts among adult members solely for sexual gratification purposes, without any artistic, scientific, or educational justification — the content's appeal to prurient interest makes its distribution an offence. | A Kolkata print house produces pamphlets containing lurid, detailed descriptions of sexual acts targeting adolescents, with content calibrated to stimulate unhealthy sexual interest rather than serve any legitimate purpose — the pamphlets appeal to prurient interest and are prosecutable as obscene objects. | A Bengaluru mobile app developer creates and markets an application hosting user-generated explicit sexual content with no age-verification or legitimate purpose, where the sole draw is satisfying users' morbid or degrading interest in sexual material — this constitutes an appeal to prurient interest under Section 294.

definitions.definition: Though not explicitly defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'public duty' refers to a duty imposed on a person by law or by the nature of their office or position, the performance of which is of public interest and benefit, particularly as discharged by a public servant or person entrusted with functions of a public nature. It encompasses any obligation arising from a statutory mandate, official appointment, or lawful authority that requires the holder to act in the interest of the general public or the State.
definitions.plain_english: A 'public duty' is any official responsibility or obligation that a person must carry out because of their government job, legal authority, or public office. It is a duty owed not just to one individual but to society or the State as a whole. For example, a police officer's duty to register an FIR or a government doctor's duty to treat emergency patients are public duties. If someone interferes with or harms a person performing such a duty, the law treats it more seriously.
real_world_examples: A sub-divisional magistrate in Rajasthan is conducting a public hearing for land acquisition proceedings under statutory authority — his role in conducting that hearing constitutes a public duty, and any obstruction or violence against him while doing so attracts enhanced liability under Section 222 BNS.

A government doctor posted at a Primary Health Centre in Bihar who is legally required to provide emergency medical treatment to patients is performing a public duty; assaulting or threatening her while she attends to patients would be an offence under the framework of Section 222 BNS.

A municipal sanitation inspector in Chennai conducting an inspection of a factory's waste disposal system under environmental regulations is discharging a public duty; bribing or coercing him to overlook violations constitutes an offence premised on interference with public duty.

An election officer appointed by the Election Commission of India to oversee polling in a constituency in Uttar Pradesh is performing a public duty; any attempt to intimidate, harm, or obstruct him during election duties is a serious criminal offence under BNS.

A food safety officer in Maharashtra carrying out a statutory inspection of a restaurant under the Food Safety and Standards Act is discharging a public duty; physically obstructing or threatening her during the inspection engages liability under Section 222 BNS.

A tehsildar in Madhya Pradesh issuing caste or domicile certificates as part of their mandated administrative function is performing a public duty, and accepting bribes to alter official records amounts to a breach of that duty punishable under BNS.
what_it_covers: Duties mandatorily imposed on public servants by statute, such as a police officer's obligation to register a cognizable offence or an election officer's obligation to conduct free and fair polling.

Obligations arising from official appointments by the Government or a competent authority, such as a tax inspector's duty to conduct assessments or a health officer's duty to enforce quarantine regulations.

Functions of a quasi-judicial or administrative nature performed by persons empowered by law, such as a magistrate conducting an inquiry or a licensing authority processing applications under a statutory scheme.
Duties performed by persons temporarily vested with public authority, such as jurors, assessors, or court-appointed receivers acting in their official capacity.
Obligations of government doctors, engineers, or technical officers who are legally bound to perform specific acts in the public interest as part of their service conditions.
what_it_excludes: Private contractual obligations between individuals, even if one party is a government employee acting outside their official capacity — for example, a government officer entering into a personal business contract.
Voluntary acts of public service or charity performed without any legal mandate or official appointment, such as a private citizen helping at an accident scene.
Duties owed solely to a private employer by an employee of a private company or organisation, even if the company performs services that incidentally benefit the public.
Acts performed by a public servant that fall entirely outside the scope of their official role or are done in a purely personal capacity unrelated to their office.
Internal administrative procedures or ministerial acts with no direct bearing on the rights or welfare of the general public, where no legal obligation to the public arises.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person is discharging a 'public duty' at the time of an offence is critical under Section 222 BNS, as it determines whether enhanced punishment provisions apply to offences such as assault, obstruction, or harm directed at persons performing such duties. It also governs the scope of criminal liability for those who interfere with, corrupt, or coerce persons exercising public functions, thereby triggering offences that would otherwise attract lesser penalties if committed against a private individual.
