definitions.definition: An act done 'rashly' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to conduct carried out with a conscious disregard of an obvious and serious risk to human life or the personal safety of others, where the person is aware of the risk but proceeds regardless. It connotes a degree of recklessness beyond mere negligence, involving deliberate indifference to foreseeable danger arising from one's own actions.
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'rashly' means doing something in a reckless, headstrong manner where you are aware that your action could seriously hurt or endanger other people, but you go ahead with it anyway without caring about the consequences. It is more serious than being simply careless — it involves knowingly taking an unjustifiable risk. For example, speeding dangerously through a crowded market knowing people could get hurt would be acting rashly.
real_world_examples: A truck driver in Mumbai overtakes multiple vehicles on a narrow hill road at high speed during heavy rain, fully aware of the danger, causing a collision that injures pedestrians — this constitutes a rash act under Section 125.

A construction worker in Delhi fires a nail gun in the direction of co-workers as a 'joke', knowing it could cause serious injury, resulting in a colleague being wounded — the conscious disregard of risk makes this a rash act.

A factory worker in Surat carelessly stores explosive substances near an open flame without precaution, being aware of the risk of ignition, leading to an explosion that injures nearby workers — actionable as a rash act under Section 288.

A street vendor in Kolkata recklessly handles a leaking gas cylinder near a crowded market, knowing the substance is hazardous, thereby endangering lives — this qualifies as rashly endangering human safety under Section 125.

A motorcyclist in Bengaluru performs wheelies and zigzag manoeuvres through a busy intersection at peak hours, consciously aware of the grave risk to pedestrians and other motorists, constituting rash conduct endangering personal safety.
what_it_covers: Acts where the person is subjectively aware of the serious risk to life or safety but proceeds regardless, such as driving at extreme speed through a crowded bazaar.
Handling of dangerous substances — including explosive, poisonous, or combustible materials — in a manner that consciously disregards evident hazard to bystanders.

Any deliberate action that goes beyond ordinary carelessness and demonstrates an indifference to the obvious probability of injury or death to others, as seen in reckless use of firearms or heavy machinery near populated areas.
what_it_excludes: Purely negligent conduct where the person had no subjective awareness of the risk and merely failed to exercise due care — negligence is a distinct and lesser standard addressed separately in the same sections.
Intentional or deliberate acts committed with the specific purpose of causing harm, which fall under provisions relating to voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt rather than rash endangerment.

Accidents arising from an unforeseen and unforeseeable set of circumstances where even a reasonable person could not have anticipated the danger, as these lack the conscious risk-awareness element essential to rashness.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'rash' determines criminal liability under Sections 125, 286, 287, and 288 of the BNS, 2023, affecting the punishment ranging from three months to three years imprisonment depending on the outcome. The distinction between rashness and mere negligence is critical because rashness implies a higher degree of moral culpability and may attract stricter sentencing, while also differentiating these offences from those requiring specific criminal intention.

definitions.definition: A reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises when, from an attempt or threat to commit an offence, a person of ordinary prudence would genuinely believe that bodily harm is imminent or likely; such apprehension need not follow the actual commission of the offence but must be grounded in objective circumstances rather than mere imagination or unfounded fear.
definitions.plain_english: A 'reasonable apprehension' means a genuine, sensible fear that a person would feel when facing a real and credible threat of harm — not just nervousness or imagination. It is the kind of fear that any ordinary, reasonable person would experience given the same situation. The fear must be based on actual circumstances, like someone raising a weapon or making a threatening move, not on a vague or baseless worry.
real_world_examples: A woman walking alone at night in Delhi is approached by a man who brandishes a knife and moves toward her — she has a reasonable apprehension of danger to her body, activating her right of private defence under Section 40 of the BNS.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai sees a group of armed individuals entering his shop and one raises a rod toward him — the imminent threat gives rise to a reasonable apprehension, entitling him to defend himself even before any blow is struck.

A farmer in rural Uttar Pradesh is cornered by an individual who verbally threatens to kill him while holding an axe in a raised position — even though no physical attack has yet occurred, this creates a reasonable apprehension justifying defensive action.

A woman in Chennai is grabbed by the wrist by an assailant who states an intent to assault her — the attempt combined with the threat constitutes a reasonable apprehension of danger, triggering the right of private defence of the body.

During a communal altercation in Ahmedabad, a person is surrounded by an armed mob making explicit threats — the circumstances objectively generate a reasonable apprehension of bodily danger, permitting defensive response under BNS Section 40.
semantic_tags: danger arising from attempt or threat
what_it_covers: Fear arising from a direct attempt to commit an offence against the body, such as a person lunging with a weapon before contact is made.
Fear arising from an explicit verbal or gestural threat to commit bodily harm where a reasonable person would believe the threat is real and imminent.
Situations where an offence has not yet been committed but circumstances — such as an assailant blocking escape routes while armed — make danger to the body objectively believable.
Continuing apprehension of danger during an ongoing confrontation, so long as the threat persists and has not been neutralised.
Fear experienced by a kidnapping victim who is threatened with death or hurt by captors, giving rise to reasonable apprehension under the ransom provisions of Section 140.
what_it_excludes: Vague, unsubstantiated, or purely imaginary fears not supported by any overt act, gesture, or credible threat from another person.
Fear arising after the threat or danger has clearly passed — once the assailant has retreated and the danger is over, the apprehension ceases and the right of private defence does not continue.
Apprehension based solely on a person's past criminal record or reputation, without any present act or threat constituting actual danger.
Fear that a reasonable person would not share under the same objective circumstances, i.e., a purely subjective over-reaction disproportionate to the actual situation.
Apprehension of harm that is remote, conditional, or dependent on uncertain future events rather than immediate or impending danger.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of a 'reasonable apprehension' is the precise threshold that commences the right of private defence of the body under Section 40 of the BNS — without it, any act of self-defence may constitute an offence such as hurt, grievous hurt, or even culpable homicide. Conversely, once this apprehension is established and other conditions are met, it serves as a complete legal justification that shields the defender from criminal liability.

Why it matters: The existence of a 'reasonable apprehension' is the precise threshold that commences the right of private defence of the body under Section 40 of the BNS — without it, any act of self-defence may constitute an offence such as hurt, grievous hurt, or even culpable homicide. Conversely, once this apprehension is established and other conditions are met, it serves as a complete legal justification that shields the defender from criminal liability.

definitions.definition: A receptacle, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, refers to any closed container, case, package, or enclosure capable of holding or storing property or goods, including but not limited to boxes, trunks, safes, bags, and similar vessels used to keep movable property. It encompasses any such container that is closed or fastened and which contains or is believed to contain property.
definitions.plain_english: A receptacle is any kind of container or enclosure used to hold or store belongings or goods — like a box, trunk, safe, bag, or package. It must be something that is closed or sealed in some way. The law treats it as a receptacle whether it actually contains property or whether someone merely believes it does.
real_world_examples: A locked metal trunk (patara) kept in a household in rural Maharashtra containing jewellery and cash, which a thief attempts to break open dishonestly.
A sealed wooden crate at a warehouse in Mumbai marked with a false property mark to deceive customs officials about its contents.
A locked steel almirah or safe in a Delhi office building that a trusted employee entrusted with its custody breaks open to steal documents or valuables.
A sealed cardboard package at a courier depot in Chennai bearing a counterfeit property mark, sold by a trader who knows the mark is fake.
A locked cash box at a shop in Kolkata that a disgruntled employee forces open with the intent to misappropriate the day's earnings.
A sealed gunny bag containing agricultural produce at an APMC mandi in Pune, upon which a trader affixes a false mark misrepresenting the quality of goods inside.
what_it_covers: A locked metal safe, almirah, or strongbox used to store cash, jewellery, or documents.
Any sealed or closed case, package, box, trunk, or bag containing or believed to contain movable property or goods.
A shipping crate, gunny bag, or commercial package bearing a property mark and used to transport goods.
A locked drawer or sealed container entrusted to a person who does not have authority to open it.
Any enclosure upon which a false or counterfeit property mark has been affixed to misrepresent the nature or ownership of its contents.
what_it_excludes: Open or unsealed containers that are not closed or fastened in any manner, as the Act specifically addresses closed receptacles.
Immovable structures such as rooms, warehouses, or buildings, which are governed by separate provisions relating to house-trespass or house-breaking.
Abstract or intangible storage mediums such as electronic databases, computer files, or digital storage devices, which fall under electronic record provisions.
Containers that have never been associated with any property and are not believed to contain any property by the person interacting with them.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an object qualifies as a receptacle determines if the offence under Section 334 (dishonestly breaking open a receptacle) or Sections 345, 349, and 350 (false property marks on receptacles) is attracted, directly affecting criminal liability and the applicable punishment of up to two or three years of imprisonment. The definition also determines whether aggravated punishment applies when the accused was entrusted with the receptacle, making the breach of trust element operative.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 72(2)(iii), 'recognised welfare institution or organisation' means a social welfare institution or organisation recognised in this behalf by the Central Government or the State Government.
definitions.plain_english: A 'recognised welfare institution or organisation' is a social welfare body — such as an NGO or charitable society — that has been officially approved or recognised by either the Central Government or a State Government specifically for the purpose of receiving authorisation to publish the identity of a victim of sexual offences. Only the chairperson or secretary of such a body can receive written authorisation from the victim's next of kin to disclose the victim's identity. This recognition ensures that only accountable, government-vetted organisations can be trusted with sensitive victim information.
real_world_examples: An NGO working with rape survivors in Maharashtra, formally recognised by the Maharashtra State Government under its social welfare scheme, receives written authorisation from the next of kin of a deceased rape victim to publish her identity for advocacy purposes in compliance with Section 72.

A Central Government-recognised child welfare organisation in Delhi is authorised in writing by the guardian of a minor victim of an offence under Section 68 to disclose the child's identity in a report aimed at law reform — permissible under Section 72(2)(iii) because the organisation holds formal government recognition.

A charitable trust operating rape crisis centres across Tamil Nadu, recognised by the Tamil Nadu State Government, receives a written authorisation from the mother (next of kin) of a victim of unsound mind to publish details about the victim for the purpose of seeking specialised medical care — lawfully permitted under Section 72.

An unrecognised community support group in Uttar Pradesh attempts to receive authorisation from the next of kin of a trafficking victim to disclose her identity in a press statement; the authorisation is invalid because the group lacks formal Central or State Government recognition, making any subsequent publication an offence under Section 72(1).

A National Commission for Women-recognised women's rights institution in Kolkata, whose secretary receives a written authorisation from the husband of an acid attack victim (offence under Section 67) to reveal her identity in a public awareness campaign, lawfully publishes the information relying on its recognised status under Section 72(2)(iii).
what_it_covers: An NGO or charitable society formally recognised by the Central Government specifically for social welfare purposes related to victims of sexual offences.

A State Government-recognised social welfare institution — such as a state-approved women's shelter or child welfare organisation — whose chairperson or secretary is eligible to receive written authorisation from the next of kin of a victim.

A registered social welfare trust or society that has obtained specific recognition from the appropriate government (Central or State) to act in matters concerning the identity of victims under Section 72.
Multi-state social welfare organisations that hold recognition from the Central Government and therefore qualify in any state to receive such authorisation from a victim's next of kin.
what_it_excludes: Unregistered community groups or informal support networks that have not obtained formal recognition from either the Central Government or any State Government, regardless of the quality of their welfare work.

Privately run hospitals, media organisations, legal firms, or advocacy bodies that may work with victims but have not been specifically recognised as social welfare institutions by the Central or State Government for this purpose.
An individual activist or social worker acting in a personal capacity, even if affiliated with a welfare cause, who does not represent a formally recognised institution or organisation.

Organisations recognised by local bodies (municipalities or panchayats) only, as the provision requires recognition specifically by the Central Government or the State Government — not sub-state authorities.
Foreign or international welfare organisations operating in India that lack formal recognition from the Indian Central Government or a State Government under this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an institution qualifies as a 'recognised welfare institution or organisation' determines whether the next of kin of a deceased, child, or mentally unsound victim can validly authorise that body's chairman or secretary to publish the victim's identity — an authorisation given to any other person or unrecognised body is legally void, and any consequent publication constitutes an offence punishable with up to two years' imprisonment and fine under Section 72(1). This definition thus acts as a critical gatekeeper that restricts the Section 72(2)(iii) exception to government-vetted organisations, safeguarding victim privacy.

definitions.definition: The term 'record' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 256, it denotes any official or judicial document, register, or written entry maintained by a public authority or court that records facts, proceedings, transactions, or official acts, and includes electronic records maintained in digital form.
definitions.plain_english: A 'record' refers to any official written or electronic document kept by a government authority, court, or public body that captures facts, events, decisions, or transactions. This could be a court file, a government register, or any official entry made by a public servant. In simple terms, it is a formal written account of something that happened, stored for official purposes.
real_world_examples: A land revenue record (khatauni or Record of Rights) maintained by a patwari in a district in Uttar Pradesh showing ownership and possession of agricultural land — tampering with this record would invoke Section 256.

A court's official case register maintained by the Reader of a Sessions Court in Mumbai, recording the dates of hearings, orders passed, and disposals — any falsification of this register constitutes an offence relating to 'record'.

A birth and death register maintained by a Municipal Corporation in Delhi under statutory authority — forging or destroying an entry in such a register amounts to tampering with a 'record' under Section 256.

An official service record (service book) of a government employee maintained by the accounts department of a State Government, documenting promotions, leave, and pay — fabricating entries in this constitutes an offence against 'record'.

A police station's First Information Report (FIR) register or general diary maintained by the Station House Officer — unauthorised alteration or destruction of entries in this official log falls within the scope of tampering with a 'record'.
what_it_covers: Official registers and files maintained by courts, including case files, order sheets, and judgement books kept by judicial authorities.
Revenue and land records maintained by government authorities such as district collectors, patwaris, or municipal bodies.
Electronic records maintained by government departments or public offices in digital form, including digitised land records and court records.
Service records, log books, and official entries made by public servants in the course of their official duties.
Registers of births, deaths, and marriages maintained under statutory authority by municipal or panchayat bodies.
what_it_excludes: Private diaries, personal notebooks, or informal notes made by individuals in a personal capacity not connected to any official duty or public authority.
Purely commercial or business records maintained by private parties that are not submitted to or maintained by any public authority or court.
Oral statements or unrecorded verbal communications, even if made before a public servant, that have not been reduced to a formal written or electronic record.
Draft or unofficial working papers that have not been finalised or officially entered into the formal record-keeping system of a public authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: The applicability of the term 'record' under Section 256 determines whether an act of falsification, destruction, or tampering attracts criminal liability under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita; if the document in question qualifies as a 'record', the offender faces punishment for offences against public justice, including forgery of official records. It also governs evidentiary weight in legal proceedings, as tampering with a 'record' may additionally trigger provisions relating to fabricating false evidence.

definitions.definition: A 'register' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to an official or statutory record maintained by a public authority, institution, or body in which entries of persons, transactions, or facts are formally recorded and preserved for legal purposes, including registers such as the National Medical Register or State Medical Register maintained under applicable law.
definitions.plain_english: A register is an official book or database kept by a government body or authorised institution where important information — like names of licensed professionals, property records, or official entries — is formally recorded. These records are maintained according to law and carry legal weight. Think of it like an authorised government record that certifies something is official and can be checked or verified.
real_world_examples: The National Medical Register maintained under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, in which the names of qualified doctors are recorded — only those on this register qualify as 'registered medical practitioners' for the purposes of Section 106 of the BNS.

A State Medical Register kept by a State Medical Council in Maharashtra that lists all licensed MBBS doctors practising in the state, used to verify whether a doctor who caused a patient's death was legally registered.
A municipal birth and death register maintained by a local body in Tamil Nadu, entries in which constitute official proof of vital events and may be relevant in criminal proceedings under the BNS.

A land records register (Khatauni) maintained by the revenue department in Uttar Pradesh, which could be relevant in cases involving forgery of official documents or fraudulent property transfers prosecuted under the BNS.
A register of voters maintained by the Election Commission of India, entries in or falsification of which may be relevant to offences relating to elections under the BNS.

A prison register maintained by jail authorities recording names, sentences, and details of persons in custody, which may be referred to in proceedings concerning unlawful confinement or escape offences under the BNS.
what_it_covers: The National Medical Register or State Medical Register maintained under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, recognising qualified medical practitioners.
Any statutory register maintained by a government authority or body under an applicable law for recording official entries of persons, transactions, or facts.
Registers maintained by local authorities, professional councils, or public institutions where entries carry legal recognition and evidentiary value.
Electoral rolls, prison registers, and land records registers maintained by public bodies that may be relevant in criminal proceedings under the BNS.
Digital or electronic registers maintained by authorised government bodies that are recognised under applicable law as official records.
what_it_excludes: Informal or private records kept by individuals or non-statutory organisations that have no legal backing or official recognition under any applicable law.
Internal administrative logs or attendance sheets maintained by private companies or institutions that are not prescribed or recognised by any statute.
Unofficial membership lists or directories maintained by trade associations, professional clubs, or NGOs that carry no statutory authority or legal recognition.
Forged or fabricated documents designed to resemble official registers but not actually maintained under the authority of any law.
Preliminary or draft records that have not been formally authenticated or accepted into an official register by the competent authority.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person's name appears in a relevant register — such as the National Medical Register — directly determines their legal status as a 'registered medical practitioner' under Section 106 of the BNS, which in turn affects the quantum of punishment applicable when a death is caused by negligence during a medical procedure. Falsification of or fraudulent entries in an official register may attract offences related to forgery of public records or fabrication of false evidence under the BNS.

definitions.definition: A medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act.
definitions.plain_english: A registered medical practitioner is a doctor or other medical professional who holds a medical degree or qualification officially recognised by the National Medical Commission and is formally listed on either the central (National) or a state-level official register of medical professionals. In simple terms, it means a legally authorised and enrolled doctor in India. Only those who meet both conditions — recognised qualification and registration — qualify under this definition.
real_world_examples: A general physician in Mumbai who holds an MBBS degree recognised by the National Medical Commission and whose name appears on the Maharashtra State Medical Register performs a routine surgical procedure that leads to a patient's unexpected death due to negligence — this doctor qualifies as a registered medical practitioner and would face a reduced maximum sentence of two years under Section 106.

A specialist surgeon listed on the National Medical Register in Delhi administers anaesthesia incorrectly during a procedure, causing the patient's death — because she is a registered medical practitioner performing a medical procedure, the special sentencing provision of Section 106 applies to her case.

A homeopathy practitioner holding a degree recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and duly enrolled in the State Medical Register of Kerala, commits a rash act during a consultation leading to a patient's death — the definition would be examined to determine whether homeopathy qualifications fall within NMC-recognised categories.

An unregistered individual claiming to be a doctor in rural Rajasthan administers an injection that causes a patient's death — because this person's name does not appear in any NMC-recognised register, they cannot invoke the protection of the two-year cap under Section 106 and would face the standard five-year maximum sentence.

A dentist holding an MDS qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act and registered on the National Medical Register performs a tooth extraction procedure that results in a patient's death due to a negligent act — this dentist would be treated as a registered medical practitioner for the purposes of Section 106.
what_it_covers: An MBBS-qualified allopathic doctor whose name is entered in the National Medical Register maintained under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019.
A specialist medical professional (such as a cardiologist, surgeon, or gynaecologist) holding an NMC-recognised postgraduate qualification and enrolled in a State Medical Register.

Any medical practitioner — whether practicing modern medicine, Ayurveda, or another system — whose qualification is specifically recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and who is duly registered in the National or a State Medical Register.
A government-employed doctor performing medical procedures in a public hospital, provided their qualification is NMC-recognised and they appear on the relevant medical register.
what_it_excludes: An unregistered medical practitioner or quack whose name does not appear in either the National Medical Register or any State Medical Register, regardless of informal training or experience.
A foreign-qualified doctor practicing in India without an NMC-recognised qualification or without enrolment in an Indian medical register.

A pharmacist, nurse, paramedic, or other allied health worker who, despite having formal qualifications, does not hold a qualification specifically recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 or is not registered under that Act.
A medical student or intern who has not yet obtained a recognised qualification and has not been entered in the National or State Medical Register, even if supervised by qualified doctors.
An individual who once held registration but has been removed from the National Medical Register or State Medical Register due to disciplinary action or cancellation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'registered medical practitioner' under Section 106 directly determines the applicable maximum punishment for causing death by a negligent act during a medical procedure — a registered medical practitioner faces up to two years' imprisonment, whereas any other person causing death by negligence faces up to five years. This definition thus acts as both a sentencing shield for qualified doctors and a boundary that prevents unregistered practitioners from claiming the same reduced liability.

Examples: A general physician in Mumbai who holds an MBBS degree recognised by the National Medical Commission and whose name appears on the Maharashtra State Medical Register performs a routine surgical procedure that leads to a patient's unexpected death due to negligence — this doctor qualifies as a registered medical practitioner and would face a reduced maximum sentence of two years under Section 106. | A specialist surgeon listed on the National Medical Register in Delhi administers anaesthesia incorrectly during a procedure, causing the patient's death — because she is a registered medical practitioner performing a medical procedure, the special sentencing provision of Section 106 applies to her case. | A homeopathy practitioner holding a degree recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and duly enrolled in the State Medical Register of Kerala, commits a rash act during a consultation leading to a patient's death — the definition would be examined to determine whether homeopathy qualifications fall within NMC-recognised categories. | An unregistered individual claiming to be a doctor in rural Rajasthan administers an injection that causes a patient's death — because this person's name does not appear in any NMC-recognised register, they cannot invoke the protection of the two-year cap under Section 106 and would face the standard five-year maximum sentence. | A dentist holding an MDS qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act and registered on the National Medical Register performs a tooth extraction procedure that results in a patient's death due to a negligent act — this dentist would be treated as a registered medical practitioner for the purposes of Section 106.

definitions.definition: The term 'relative' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 85, it refers to any person related by blood, marriage, or adoption to the husband of a woman, who by virtue of that relationship may be in a position to subject such woman to cruelty. It encompasses individuals within the husband's family structure who exercise influence or authority over the woman in a domestic or matrimonial setting.
definitions.plain_english: A 'relative' in this context means a family member of the husband — such as his parents, siblings, uncles, aunts, or other kin — who is connected to him by blood, marriage, or adoption. These are the people within the husband's family who interact with the wife in a domestic setting. The law uses this term to ensure that not just the husband, but his entire family circle can be held responsible if they mistreat the wife.
real_world_examples: A mother-in-law in Rajasthan repeatedly taunts and physically harms her daughter-in-law for not bringing sufficient dowry — she qualifies as a 'relative' of the husband under Section 85 and can be prosecuted for cruelty.

A husband's brother in Maharashtra threatens and emotionally abuses his sister-in-law to coerce her into making demands on her parents for money — he is a 'relative' of the husband and liable under Section 85.

A husband's sister in Tamil Nadu spreads false rumours within the household and isolates the wife, causing her mental distress — as a relative of the husband, she may be charged under Section 85 for cruelty.

A father-in-law in Uttar Pradesh physically assaults his daughter-in-law after she refuses to hand over her jewellery — being a relative of the husband, he is covered under Section 85 and can face imprisonment up to three years.

A husband's uncle who lives in the same household in Punjab harasses the wife on behalf of the husband's family regarding dowry demands — he may be treated as a relative for purposes of Section 85 if his connection to the husband and his conduct are established.
what_it_covers: The husband's parents (mother-in-law and father-in-law) who subject the wife to emotional, physical, or economic cruelty.
The husband's siblings — brothers and sisters — who participate in harassing or mistreating the wife in a domestic setting.
The husband's extended kin such as uncles, aunts, or cousins who live in or are closely connected with the marital household and subject the wife to cruelty.
Persons related to the husband by adoption or marriage who exercise domestic authority over the wife.
what_it_excludes: The wife's own relatives, such as her parents or siblings, who are not connected to the husband's family and do not fall within the scope of Section 85.
Strangers or neighbours who may harass the woman but have no familial connection to the husband.
The husband himself, who is separately and specifically named in Section 85 alongside the relative, making him a distinct category of offender rather than a 'relative'.
Persons who are merely acquaintances or friends of the husband with no recognised blood, marital, or adoptive relationship to him.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'relative' of the husband determines whether they can be prosecuted under Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 for subjecting a woman to cruelty, which carries imprisonment of up to three years and a fine. It also has direct relevance to Section 80 (dowry death), where liability for causing dowry death extends to any 'relative of the husband', making the scope of this term critical to establishing criminal responsibility in matrimonial violence cases.

definitions.definition: Religious beliefs, as used in Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the doctrines, tenets, convictions, practices, rituals, and faith-based principles held sacred or integral by any class of citizens of India as part of their religion, the insult or attempted insult of which, with deliberate and malicious intention, constitutes a punishable offence. The term encompasses the spiritual, theological, and devotional convictions that define a class's religious identity and which, if outraged, trigger criminal liability.
definitions.plain_english: Religious beliefs means the core ideas, faith, teachings, rituals, and spiritual convictions that a group of people follow as part of their religion. This includes things like belief in particular gods, sacred texts, religious customs, and practices considered holy by that community. Under Indian law, deliberately insulting these beliefs with the intention of hurting the feelings of that religious group is a criminal act. It does not matter whether the insult is spoken, written, shown as a symbol, or posted online — if it targets the religious beliefs of a class of people maliciously, it is punishable.
real_world_examples: A social media user in Maharashtra posts a video deliberately mocking the core theological doctrines of Islam, such as the belief in the prophethood of Muhammad, with the intention of outraging Muslim citizens — this constitutes an insult to religious beliefs under Section 299.

A pamphlet distributed in Tamil Nadu caricatures the sacred beliefs of the Hindu community regarding the divinity of a particular deity, published with malicious intent to provoke communal tension — this falls within the ambit of insulting religious beliefs.

A public speaker in Delhi makes deliberate statements denying the spiritual authority of the Guru Granth Sahib in front of a Sikh gathering with the express intention of hurting their religious sentiments — this amounts to insulting the religious beliefs of that class.

A YouTube channel run from Hyderabad systematically ridicules the foundational tenets of Christianity, such as the belief in resurrection, with demonstrable malicious intent, reaching millions of viewers — this is an electronic insult to religious beliefs punishable under Section 299.

A novelist in Kolkata publishes a book that, in deliberate and malicious terms, portrays the Jain doctrine of non-violence and the concept of Tirthankaras as fraudulent and absurd, with intent to outrage the Jain community — this constitutes an insult to religious beliefs under the section.

A WhatsApp message chain forwarded across Uttar Pradesh containing images defiling symbols central to Buddhist belief, shared with deliberate intent to provoke hatred against Buddhist communities, amounts to an insult to their religious beliefs under Section 299.
what_it_covers: Core theological doctrines and tenets held sacred by any identifiable class of citizens, such as belief in a deity, prophet, scripture, or spiritual authority.
Religious rituals, practices, and customs that form an integral part of a community's faith identity and whose deliberate ridicule is intended to outrage that class.
Spiritual convictions including beliefs about afterlife, karma, resurrection, salvation, or any foundational principle central to a recognised religion practised in India.
Beliefs expressed through religious symbols, sacred texts, or iconography that a class of persons venerates, where insult to those symbols constitutes insult to the beliefs themselves.
The faith-based worldview of minority religious communities such as Parsis, Bahais, or tribal religious groups, whose beliefs are equally protected even if fewer in number.
what_it_excludes: Genuine academic, scholarly, or theological critique of religious doctrines made in good faith without deliberate or malicious intent to outrage any class of citizens.
Artistic or literary expression that engages with religious themes critically but lacks the specific ingredient of deliberate and malicious intention to insult religious beliefs.
Personal non-belief, atheism, or agnosticism expressed without targeting any particular class's religious beliefs with the intent to outrage or insult.
Neutral journalistic reporting on religious practices or interfaith debates that do not amount to an insult directed at the religious beliefs of any class.
Religious disagreements or theological disputes between members of the same faith community that are part of internal doctrinal discourse and not intended to outrage an external class.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act or expression targets 'religious beliefs' determines the applicability of Section 299 of the BNS, which prescribes imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both; without the element of insulting religious beliefs with deliberate and malicious intention, the offence under Section 299 is not made out, and criminal liability does not attach. This definition is the threshold that separates protected free expression from criminally punishable speech or conduct directed at a class's faith.

definitions.definition: Religious feelings, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, refers to the sentiments, sensibilities, and emotional convictions held by any class of citizens of India or any person with respect to their religion or religious beliefs, the outrage or wounding of which, when caused deliberately and maliciously through words, signs, visible representations, electronic means, sounds, gestures, or objects, constitutes a punishable offence. These feelings are inherently connected to the doctrines, practices, and beliefs of a religion as professed by a class or individual.
definitions.plain_english: Religious feelings refer to the deep emotional and spiritual sentiments that people hold regarding their religion, its beliefs, practices, symbols, and sacred figures. When someone deliberately and intentionally hurts or offends these sentiments — whether by speaking, writing, posting online, making gestures, or placing objects — it is treated as a serious wrong under the law. The law protects both groups of people (a class of citizens) and individuals from having their religious emotions wounded intentionally.
real_world_examples: A social media user in Mumbai posts a digitally altered image of a Hindu deity in a degrading or sexually explicit manner with the deliberate intent to provoke and offend members of the Hindu community, thereby outraging their religious feelings under Section 299.

A speaker at a public gathering in Hyderabad makes a deliberate and malicious speech mocking the Prophet Muhammad and the core tenets of Islam before a Muslim audience, with the clear intention of insulting their religious beliefs and outraging their religious feelings.

A person in a village in Punjab enters a Gurudwara and intentionally places beef near the Guru Granth Sahib to insult Sikh religious sentiments, thereby wounding the religious feelings of the Sikh congregation under Sections 298 and 299.

An individual in Chennai deliberately utters abusive slurs referencing Christian religious figures and the Bible loudly and repeatedly in the hearing of a known Christian colleague, intending to wound that person's religious feelings under Section 302.

A WhatsApp group administrator in Kolkata circulates a video through electronic means that deliberately ridicules Jain religious practices and sacred figures, with the malicious intent of outraging the religious feelings of the Jain community.

A street performer in Delhi makes obscene gestures mimicking Islamic prayer postures in full sight of worshippers leaving a mosque, with the deliberate intention of wounding their religious feelings under Section 302.
what_it_covers: The collective emotional and spiritual sentiments of an identifiable class of citizens of India connected to their religion, religious doctrines, sacred figures, texts, or practices, when outraged deliberately and maliciously through any mode of communication including electronic means.

The personal religious sensibilities of an individual that are wounded intentionally when another person utters words, makes sounds, gestures, or places objects in that individual's hearing or sight with the deliberate intent to cause such injury.

Sentiments associated with all recognised religions and religious communities in India, including Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, and others, without restricting protection to any one faith.

Feelings provoked by insult or attempted insult to religious beliefs conveyed through spoken or written words, signs, visible representations, electronic communications, or other means directed at a class or person.
what_it_excludes: Good faith academic, scholarly, or literary criticism and analysis of religious texts, doctrines, or practices that lacks deliberate malicious intent to outrage or wound religious feelings.

Accidental, inadvertent, or negligent acts or statements that may incidentally cause offence to religious sensibilities but are not accompanied by a deliberate and malicious intention to insult or wound.

Legitimate artistic, journalistic, or satirical expression that, though potentially controversial on religious subjects, is not made with the specific criminal intention of outraging or wounding religious feelings.

General philosophical, ethical, or political discourse that touches upon religious themes without targeting a specific religion's adherents with malicious or deliberate intent to insult their religious feelings.
Religious debates or inter-faith dialogues conducted in good faith even if they involve critique of another religion's beliefs, provided the intention is not to outrage or wound religious sentiments.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is found to have outraged or wounded 'religious feelings' is the central element determining criminal liability under Sections 299 and 302 of the BNS 2023; if established alongside deliberate and malicious intent, it exposes the accused to imprisonment of up to three years (Section 299) or one year (Section 302), fine, or both, while its absence negates the offence entirely. The presence or absence of this element also governs whether the act constitutes a cognisable offence triggering police power to investigate without a magistrate's warrant.

definitions.definition: A 'religious group' refers to any class of persons identified by reason of their being members of a common religion or religious faith, as contemplated under Section 197 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in the context of imputations, assertions, or communications that may cause disharmony, enmity, hatred, or ill-will between such members and other persons in India.
definitions.plain_english: A religious group means any identifiable group of people who share a common religion or religious belief, such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, or Parsis. The term is used to describe people who can be targeted by harmful speech or propaganda on the basis of their shared faith. In the context of this law, it refers specifically to such a group when false or prejudicial statements are made about their loyalty to India or their rights as citizens.
real_world_examples: A person publishes a pamphlet claiming that Muslims in India cannot be loyal to the Indian Constitution due to their religious beliefs, thereby targeting Muslims as a religious group under Section 197.

A social media post asserts that Christians in a particular state should be denied voting rights because of their religious affiliation, making that religious group the subject of a rights-denial assertion punishable under Section 197.
A speaker at a public rally propagates that Sikhs, as a religious group, are obligated to support a separatist movement, causing feelings of enmity between Sikhs and other communities in India.

An online video falsely claims that a particular Hindu sect is conspiring against the sovereignty of India, targeting that sect as a religious group and jeopardising national integration under Section 197.

A WhatsApp message spread in a sensitive region alleges that Jains, by virtue of their religion, cannot uphold the integrity of India, thereby making targeted imputations against them as a religious group.
what_it_covers: Any recognised religious community in India such as Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, or Parsis when targeted by prejudicial imputations about their constitutional loyalty.
Minority religious denominations or sects within a larger religion when they are collectively targeted by assertions denying their rights as Indian citizens.
Any assembly or class of persons identifiable by a shared religious faith who are the subject of communication likely to cause enmity, ill-will, or disharmony with other groups in India.
Religious groups targeted through electronic communication, written material, spoken words, or visible representations that question their allegiance to the sovereignty and integrity of India.
what_it_excludes: Racial or ethnic groups who are not defined by religion but by descent or ethnicity, as these are separately classified as 'racial groups' under Section 197.
Language or regional groups who share a common tongue or geographic identity but not necessarily a religious identity, which are separately enumerated in Section 197.
Caste groups or communities that may overlap with religion but are independently classified as 'caste' or 'community' under Section 197 and do not automatically constitute a religious group.
Individual persons holding personal religious beliefs who cannot be said to form a 'class of persons' or identifiable group for the purposes of Section 197.
Political organisations or ideological movements that may adopt religious symbolism but are not constituted on the basis of religious membership or faith.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a targeted group qualifies as a 'religious group' under Section 197 directly determines whether an imputation, assertion, or publication triggers criminal liability under the provision, carrying punishment of up to three years imprisonment or fine, or up to five years imprisonment if committed in a place of worship. Establishing that the targeted class is a religious group is a foundational element of the offence, as it anchors the prejudicial communication to a protected identity category for the purposes of national integration.

definitions.definition: Remission, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the conditional reduction or cancellation of a lawfully imposed punishment granted to a convict, subject to specified conditions. A convict who has accepted such conditional remission and knowingly violates any condition on which it was granted becomes liable to serve the original sentence or the unexpired portion thereof, as prescribed under Section 266.
definitions.plain_english: Remission means the government or a competent authority reduces or cancels a convicted person's punishment, but only on the condition that the person follows certain rules or conditions. If the person breaks any of those conditions knowingly, they must go back and serve the original punishment — either all of it or whatever is left. Think of it like being let out of jail early on a promise, and breaking that promise sends you back to serve the remaining time.
real_world_examples: A convict sentenced to 10 years imprisonment in Maharashtra is granted remission after 5 years on the condition that he does not leave the state and reports to the local police station every month. He knowingly travels to another state without permission — he is liable to serve the remaining 5 years of his original sentence.

A prisoner in Tihar Jail is granted remission of the remaining 2 years of his sentence on the condition that he maintains good conduct and abstains from alcohol. He is found drunk and in violation of the condition — he can be made to serve those 2 remaining years in prison.

A convict in Tamil Nadu who has served no part of his sentence is granted a conditional remission requiring him to perform community service and not associate with known criminals. He knowingly resumes association with a gang — under Section 266, he must serve the entire original punishment.

An undertrial prisoner in Uttar Pradesh convicted of a lesser offence is granted conditional remission requiring him to surrender his passport and not travel abroad. He knowingly attempts to flee the country — the full or remaining sentence is restored and enforced against him.

A convict released under remission in Rajasthan on the condition of periodic medical reporting (for a communicable disease) fails to report as required — the remission is treated as violated and the unexpired portion of his sentence is reimposed.
what_it_covers: A conditional reduction of an imposed criminal sentence granted by a competent authority to a convict who has accepted its terms.
Situations where a convict has served part of the sentence and then violates remission conditions — liability covers only the unserved portion of the original sentence.
Situations where a convict has served no part of the sentence but accepted conditional remission and then violates the conditions — liability covers the entire original sentence.
Any condition attached to the remission, the knowing violation of which triggers the penal consequence under Section 266, regardless of the nature of the condition imposed.
what_it_excludes: Unconditional remission or pardon — where no conditions are attached, there is no basis for violation under Section 266.
Commutation of sentence — which changes the nature or quantum of punishment and is governed separately; it is not the same as a conditional remission.
Situations where the convict unknowingly or accidentally violates a condition — Section 266 requires knowing violation, so innocent breach is excluded from its penal scope.
Remission granted by a court as part of a judicial order, as remission under Section 266 contemplates executive/governmental grant of conditional remission, not court-ordered sentence reduction.
Cases where the original sentence has been fully served before remission is granted — there is no remaining punishment to restore.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether this definition applies determines whether a convict who has been released or had punishment reduced can be legally required to serve the original or remaining sentence upon breach of conditions — triggering penal liability under Section 266. It directly affects the enforceability of conditions attached to governmental clemency and the quantum of punishment a convicted person must undergo.

definitions.definition: The term 'reputation' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used as a recognised component of 'injury,' which means any harm whatever illegally caused to any person in body, mind, reputation, or property. In the context of Section 351 (defamation), reputation refers to the esteem, regard, and social standing in which a person is held by others in the community, which may be harmed by the making or publishing of imputations concerning that person.
definitions.plain_english: Reputation means the general opinion or standing that other people hold about a person in society — whether they consider that person to be honest, respectable, competent, or trustworthy. It is the image or character that a person has built up in their community, workplace, or public life. When someone spreads false or harmful information about another person, it can damage that reputation, which the law treats as a serious harm.
real_world_examples: A prominent Mumbai businessman's competitor spreads false rumours on social media that the businessman has committed fraud, causing clients to withdraw business and damaging his standing in the trading community.

A teacher in a Delhi school is falsely accused by a colleague of misconduct with students; the accusation is circulated among parents through WhatsApp groups, destroying the teacher's professional reputation and social standing.

A political leader in Tamil Nadu is the subject of a pamphlet falsely claiming involvement in corruption; the pamphlet is distributed widely before elections, harming the leader's reputation among voters.

A Bollywood actress is targeted by a tabloid that publishes fabricated stories about her personal life, leading to public ridicule and loss of endorsement contracts, thereby causing reputational harm.
A doctor in Kolkata is falsely accused through an anonymous online post of negligence causing patient deaths, resulting in loss of patients and damage to her standing in the medical community.
semantic_tags: esteem in the eyes of others
what_it_covers: The standing, character, and esteem in which a person is held by their community, colleagues, or the general public.
Professional reputation of individuals such as doctors, lawyers, businesspersons, and public officials that may be harmed by false imputations.
Harm caused to a person's social or moral image through publication or communication of false statements to third parties.
The collective opinion formed about a person based on their conduct, integrity, and character as perceived by others in society.
Reputational harm suffered by a company, association, or body of persons in their commercial or public dealings.
what_it_excludes: Physical harm to the body, which falls under 'hurt' or 'grievous hurt' rather than reputational injury.
Mere private feelings of embarrassment or personal insult where no third party forms a diminished opinion of the person.
Truthful statements made in good faith about a person's conduct, which are protected exceptions to defamation under Section 351.
Loss of property or financial loss not connected to damage to one's standing or character in the eyes of others.
Psychological or mental distress that does not result from damage to one's public image or social standing.
definitions.why_it_matters: Reputation is a critical element in constituting 'injury' under the BNS and is the primary interest protected by Section 351 (defamation); whether an imputation lowers a person's reputation determines if the act amounts to defamation, attracting criminal liability including imprisonment up to two years, fine, or both. Without reputational harm being established, the offence of defamation cannot be made out, and the accused cannot be prosecuted under Section 351.

definitions.definition: Restraint, in the context of Section 307 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the act of wrongfully obstructing or preventing a person from proceeding in a direction in which that person has a right to proceed, as elaborated in Section 126, and includes any preparation made to cause such restraint or fear thereof in order to commit theft, effect escape after theft, or retain stolen property.
definitions.plain_english: Restraint means physically stopping or blocking someone from moving in a direction they are legally allowed to go. In the context of theft-related offences, it refers to preparing to physically hold, block, or pin down a person — or making them fear being held back — so that a thief can steal, escape, or keep stolen goods. It does not require that the restraint actually occur; even the preparation to cause it is sufficient to attract the more serious offence under Section 307.
real_world_examples: A pickpocket in a Mumbai local train stations accomplices near his target so that if the victim notices the theft and tries to chase him, the accomplices will physically block the victim's path — this constitutes preparation for restraint under Section 307.

A group of thieves in Delhi plan to snatch a gold chain from a woman; one member is assigned to grab her arms so she cannot run or resist while another snatches the chain, amounting to preparation for causing restraint.

A burglar breaking into a shop in Chennai carries rope with the intention of tying up the shopkeeper if he is discovered, so he can escape with the stolen goods — this preparation for causing restraint attracts the aggravated theft offence.

In a Kolkata market, a gang of shoplifters posts a lookout at the exit door with instructions to physically block the shopkeeper from leaving or raising an alarm while goods are taken — the posting of such a person constitutes preparation for causing restraint.

A thief at a Bengaluru ATM is accompanied by a person whose role is to stand in front of the victim and prevent them from pressing the alarm or moving towards security personnel, satisfying the element of preparation to cause restraint under Section 307.
semantic_tags: preparation to prevent escape or pursuit
fear of restraint as offence element
what_it_covers: Physically blocking a person's path so they cannot pursue a thief or raise an alarm.
Posting accomplices to hold back or obstruct the victim or bystanders during the commission of theft.
Preparation — such as carrying ropes, handcuffs, or stationing persons — intended to immobilise a person to facilitate theft, escape, or retention of stolen property.
Creating a credible fear in a person that they will be physically restrained if they resist or pursue the offender.
Any act of wrongfully obstructing a person from proceeding in a direction they have a legal right to proceed, in connection with theft.
what_it_excludes: Lawful detention or restraint carried out by a police officer, public servant, or private person under legal authority (e.g., lawful arrest).
Obstruction of a private way over land or water where the person genuinely and in good faith believes they have a lawful right to obstruct (as expressly excluded under Section 126).
Mere moral or social pressure, verbal warnings, or persuasion that does not physically obstruct movement.
Restraint incidental to a lawful act such as medical restraint in a hospital or restraint of a person of unsound mind by a lawful guardian.
Fear of restraint arising from a person's own imagination without any act or preparation by the accused directed towards causing such restraint.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether preparation to cause 'restraint' is established directly determines if an accused is convicted of simple theft (attracting lesser punishment) or the aggravated offence under Section 307, which carries rigorous imprisonment up to ten years plus fine. It also governs the duration of the right of private defence of property against robbery under Section 43, which continues only as long as the offender causes or attempts to cause wrongful restraint.

definitions.definition: The right of private defence is the legally recognised entitlement of every person to defend their own body or the body of any other person against any offence affecting the human body, and to defend movable or immovable property of themselves or any other person against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts thereof, subject to the restrictions in section 37, including that no more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence may be inflicted.
definitions.plain_english: The right of private defence is every person's legal right to protect themselves or others from being harmed, and to protect their own or someone else's property from theft, robbery, damage, or trespass. This right allows a person to use force against an attacker or wrongdoer, but only to the extent actually needed to stop the threat. The law excuses actions taken in genuine self-defence, meaning a person cannot be convicted of a crime for what they do while lawfully defending themselves or others.
real_world_examples: A woman walking alone in Delhi is attacked by a man trying to snatch her bag; she hits him with her umbrella to escape — her act is protected under the right of private defence of both body and property.

A farmer in rural Maharashtra finds an intruder attempting to steal grain from his locked storehouse at night; he physically restrains the intruder using reasonable force, which is covered under private defence of property.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai is confronted by an armed robber who threatens him with a knife; he strikes the robber with a nearby rod to prevent being stabbed — this constitutes lawful exercise of private defence of body.

A neighbour in Chennai witnesses a man attacking an elderly woman on the street and intervenes physically to stop the assault — the right of private defence extends to defending the body of any other person, not just oneself.

A resident of a housing colony in Hyderabad catches a person in the act of setting fire to his car; he tackles and overpowers the arsonist to prevent further damage, which qualifies as private defence of property against mischief.

A person of unsound mind attempts to attack a bystander in Kolkata; although the attacker commits no offence due to mental incapacity, the bystander still retains the full right of private defence against that act.
what_it_covers: Defence of one's own body against any offence affecting the human body, including assault, robbery, or attempted murder.
Defence of another person's body against offences affecting the human body, even if the defender has no familial or legal relationship with that person.
Defence of one's own or another person's movable or immovable property against theft, robbery, mischief, criminal trespass, or attempts to commit these offences.
Exercise of private defence against a person of unsound mind, a minor, or an intoxicated person whose act would otherwise constitute an offence, even though such person bears no criminal liability.
Defence exercised in situations where there is no time to seek protection from public authorities and immediate action is necessary.
what_it_excludes: Acts against a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office where the act does not reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt, unless the defender does not know or have reason to believe the person is a public servant.
Inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence — the right does not extend to excessive or retaliatory force beyond what is needed to stop the threat.
Situations where there is sufficient time to seek protection from public authorities, as recourse to law enforcement must be taken instead of exercising private force.
Acts carried out after the threat has ceased — the right of private defence does not justify continued violence once the danger has passed.
Pre-emptive or aggressive attacks launched without a reasonable apprehension of imminent harm to body or property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether this right applies determines whether an act that would otherwise constitute an offence such as hurt, grievous hurt, or culpable homicide is treated as no offence at all under section 34 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, thereby completely blocking criminal liability. Conversely, if the right is exceeded — for instance, by inflicting disproportionate harm — the excess may still attract criminal prosecution for the harm caused beyond what was necessary.

definitions.definition: Rigorous imprisonment is a form of imprisonment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, wherein the convicted person is required to perform hard labour as part of the sentence. It is a more severe form of imprisonment than simple imprisonment and may be accompanied by solitary confinement for prescribed portions of the term as provided under Section 11 of this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: Rigorous imprisonment means jail time where the prisoner must do hard physical work, such as grinding grain, digging, or other manual labour, as ordered by the court. It is stricter and harsher than simple imprisonment, where the prisoner is merely confined without being compelled to work. Courts impose this for more serious crimes to reflect a higher level of punishment.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of rape under Section 64 of the BNS is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a minimum of ten years, meaning they must perform hard labour in prison such as grinding grain, weaving, or other prescribed work throughout their sentence.

A gang of five persons convicted of dacoity in rural Maharashtra is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for seven years, requiring them to undertake hard physical labour within the prison facility as mandated by the court.

Two individuals convicted of criminal conspiracy to commit murder under Section 61 of the BNS, where the target offence carries rigorous imprisonment for two years or more, are subjected to hard labour in prison as part of their punishment.

A public servant convicted of aggravated rape on a woman in their custody under Section 64(2) is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life, meaning they must perform compulsory hard labour for the remainder of their natural life in prison.

A person found guilty of causing grievous hurt with a deadly weapon in a communal violence incident in Uttar Pradesh is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for five years, during which the court additionally orders one month of solitary confinement under Section 11 of the BNS.

A convicted offender in a case of rape of a woman under twelve years of age under Section 65 is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for twenty years with compulsory hard labour, as opposed to being simply confined without work obligations.
what_it_covers: Imprisonment sentences for rape and aggravated rape under Sections 64 and 65, which mandatorily prescribe rigorous imprisonment as the minimum punishment.
Sentences where a court may additionally impose solitary confinement under Section 11, such confinement being permitted only when the underlying sentence is rigorous imprisonment.
Criminal conspiracy cases under Section 61 where the target offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for two years or more, making the conspirator liable for equivalent punishment.

Any offence under the BNS for which the legislature has specifically prescribed rigorous imprisonment as the mode of sentence, requiring the convicted prisoner to perform hard physical labour throughout the sentence period.

Situations where the court exercises discretion to impose rigorous imprisonment for a specified term as part of a graded sentencing scheme, such as for offences involving grievous hurt or organised crime.
what_it_excludes: Simple imprisonment, which involves mere confinement in prison without any obligation to perform hard labour, and which is a distinct and lesser form of custodial punishment under the BNS.
Community service as a form of punishment, which involves unpaid work in the community outside prison and is not equivalent to or a substitute for rigorous imprisonment.

definitions.definition: A riot occurs whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly. Every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting when such force or violence is so used.
definitions.plain_english: A riot happens when a group of people who have gathered for an unlawful purpose actually starts using physical force or violence to achieve their goal. It does not matter whether every member personally commits an act of violence — if any one member does so in furtherance of the group's shared purpose, all members of that group are considered guilty of rioting. The law treats the collective action of the unlawful group as the defining feature, not just individual acts.
real_world_examples: A mob assembled during a communal dispute in a town in Uttar Pradesh begins throwing stones at shops and attacking passersby to drive out a particular community — every member of the mob is guilty of rioting under BNS Section 191.

A group of agitators blocking a highway in Punjab turns violent and begins physically assaulting police officers trying to clear the road — all participants in the unlawful assembly are guilty of rioting once force is used.

During an election campaign in Bihar, a politically motivated crowd storms a rival party's office, breaking windows and assaulting workers — each person present as part of that assembly is liable for rioting regardless of who personally struck the blows.

A gang of villagers in Rajasthan gathers to forcibly stop construction on disputed land and physically assaults the construction workers and their supervisors — their use of violence in furtherance of the common object constitutes rioting.

In Mumbai, a group of individuals assembled to protest a housing demolition drive resorts to overturning municipal vehicles and injuring officials — the moment force is used by any member, all assembly members become liable for rioting.

A crowd gathered outside a police station in Tamil Nadu demanding the release of a suspect begins physically attacking the police personnel on duty — the use of criminal force by members of the unlawful assembly in pursuit of their common object constitutes rioting.
what_it_covers: Use of physical force or violence by any member of an unlawful assembly in furtherance of the assembly's common object, making all members guilty.
Rioting committed while any member is armed with a deadly weapon or anything likely to cause death, attracting enhanced punishment of up to five years.
Liability of owners or occupiers of land where rioting takes place if they knew or had reason to believe the offence was being committed and failed to act (Section 193).
Acts of provocation — whether malignant or wanton — that intentionally cause rioting to occur, under Section 192.
Any member of the unlawful assembly, whether or not they personally used force, once force is used by the group in prosecution of the common object.
what_it_excludes: Peaceful assemblies or protests that do not involve force or violence — even if they obstruct public movement, they do not constitute rioting without actual use of force.
Spontaneous individual acts of violence by a lone person not forming part of an unlawful assembly — these may constitute assault or hurt but not rioting.
Assemblies of fewer than five persons, since an unlawful assembly requires a minimum of five members, meaning force used by a smaller group cannot constitute rioting.
Force used in lawful private defence, even within a group, does not qualify as rioting since it is legally justified and not in prosecution of an unlawful common object.
Persons who had already withdrawn from the unlawful assembly before force was used, and whose withdrawal was communicated clearly, are not automatically liable for rioting.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an incident qualifies as a riot determines collective criminal liability — all members of the unlawful assembly face punishment of up to two years (or up to five years if armed), even without personally using force. It also triggers ancillary liability for landowners under Section 193 and enables prosecution for wanton provocation under Section 192, directly affecting who can be arrested, charged, and punished in public order situations.

definitions.plain_english: Rioting happens when a group of people who have gathered for an unlawful purpose actually use force or violence to carry out that purpose. Every single person who is part of that group is considered guilty of rioting, even if only one or some of them actually used violence. The law holds all members equally responsible because they shared the same unlawful goal.
real_world_examples: A mob gathered in a Delhi market during a communal dispute begins attacking shopkeepers and destroying property — every member of the mob is guilty of rioting, including those who only cheered on without personally throwing stones.

During a land dispute in rural Uttar Pradesh, a group of villagers storms a rival farmer's field, beats farm labourers, and destroys crops — all participants in the group are liable for rioting regardless of their individual role.

A violent protest in Mumbai turns into a riot when agitators begin overturning and burning buses; all members of the unlawful assembly who remained and participated in the common object are guilty of rioting.

In Kolkata, a group armed with lathis gathers to forcibly evict tenants from a building and uses violence to do so — every member of the group is guilty of rioting, and those armed with deadly weapons face enhanced punishment of up to five years.

During an election-related clash in Tamil Nadu, supporters of rival political groups use force against each other in a public square; all members of the unlawful assembly on each side who used or supported the use of violence in furtherance of their common object are guilty of rioting.
what_it_covers: Every member of an unlawful assembly when any member uses force or violence in pursuit of the assembly's common object, regardless of individual participation in the actual violence.
A member of an unlawful assembly who is armed with a deadly weapon or any object likely to cause death when used as a weapon, attracting enhanced punishment of up to five years.
Situations where violence or force is used collectively or by even one member acting within the scope of the common unlawful objective of the entire assembly.
Cases where a person who gave provocation under Section 192 caused the rioting to be committed, making that instigator also liable alongside the rioters.
what_it_excludes: A peaceful gathering or lawful assembly that does not use force or violence in furtherance of any common object, even if it later disperses disorderly.

An individual who commits a separate personal act of violence unconnected to the common object of the assembly — such an act is not rioting but may constitute a different offence like assault or hurt.
A bystander or spectator who happens to be present near the unlawful assembly but is not a member of it and shares no common object with the group.
An assembly of fewer than five persons, since the predicate offence of being an 'unlawful assembly' requires a minimum of five persons sharing a common object.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of rioting is critical because it imposes collective criminal liability on every member of an unlawful assembly the moment any member uses force, triggering imprisonment of up to two years (or up to five years if armed with a deadly weapon), with fine or both. It also activates liability under Section 192 for any person who wantonly or malignantly provoked the riot, creating a chain of accountability from instigator to participant.
