definitions.definition: Robbery is theft or extortion in which, in order to commit theft or extortion, or in committing theft or extortion, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by theft or extortion, the offender voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or causes fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint. Every robbery is either theft or extortion, distinguished by the presence of force, threat of force, or fear applied immediately before, during, or immediately after the act.
definitions.plain_english: Robbery is a serious crime where a person uses violence or threatens violence to steal from someone or to force them to hand over property or valuables. The key difference from ordinary theft or extortion is that the criminal either uses physical force, causes injury, or puts the victim in immediate fear of being hurt or restrained. This can happen at the moment of stealing, while escaping with stolen goods, or while demanding property through fear.
real_world_examples: A snatcher in Mumbai grabs a woman's gold chain from her neck while riding a motorcycle, and when she resists, he pushes her to the ground causing injuries — this constitutes robbery as hurt is caused in the course of committing theft.

Armed men enter a jewellery shop in Delhi, point country-made pistols at the owner and staff, and demand they hand over the gold stock — this is robbery by extortion as fear of instant death is used to coerce delivery of property.

A pickpocket in a Kolkata market is caught in the act of stealing a wallet; he punches the victim in the face and runs away with the wallet — the use of hurt to carry away stolen property converts the theft into robbery.

A gang in Chennai surrounds an auto-rickshaw driver at night, threatens to kill him unless he surrenders his day's earnings, and he hands over the money out of fear of instant death — this amounts to robbery through extortion.

A person snatches a mobile phone from a passenger on a Bengaluru local bus and, while fleeing, wrongfully restrains another passenger who tries to stop him — the wrongful restraint during the escape converts the act into robbery.

Two individuals in Hyderabad threaten a shopkeeper with iron rods, demand that he open the cash register, and take cash — the threat of instant hurt used to obtain delivery of property constitutes robbery.
semantic_tags: force used to retain stolen property
what_it_covers: Theft accompanied by voluntary causing of hurt, death, or wrongful restraint to the victim at any stage — before, during, or after the taking of property.
Extortion committed by putting a person in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint to induce them to deliver property on the spot.
An attempt to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint during theft or extortion, even if no actual injury results, provided the attempt is made voluntarily.
Situations where the offender restrains or threatens the victim while carrying away or attempting to carry away property already obtained by theft.
Cases where multiple persons act together to intimidate a victim through threat of immediate violence in order to take or extort movable property.
what_it_excludes: Simple theft where no force, threat, or fear of immediate harm is involved — such as ordinary pickpocketing where the victim is entirely unaware and no restraint or hurt is caused.
Extortion by future threats, such as threatening to cause harm on a later date unless money is paid, which does not meet the 'instant' requirement for robbery.
Receiving stolen property or handling goods obtained through robbery without personally committing any act of force or threat.
Criminal intimidation or threats made at a distance or through intermediaries without the victim being present and in immediate fear.
Acts of cheating or fraud where property is obtained through deception alone, with no element of force, hurt, or fear of immediate harm.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as robbery determines whether the offender is charged under sections 309–313 of the BNS, which carry significantly heavier punishments — up to rigorous imprisonment for ten years and fine, and in aggravated forms (dacoity or robbery resulting in death or grievous hurt) up to imprisonment for life or death — compared to plain theft or extortion. The classification as robbery also triggers enhanced provisions for habitual offenders, gang-related offences, and dacoity under sections 310–313.

definitions.definition: A 'sailor' refers to a member of the Navy of the Government of India who is subject to naval discipline and service obligations. Though not expressly defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the term is used consistently alongside 'officer', 'soldier', and 'airman' to denote a person enrolled in the naval armed forces of the Government of India, distinct from officers of superior rank.
definitions.plain_english: A sailor is a person who serves in the Indian Navy as an enlisted member of the naval armed forces. This is someone who has taken an oath of allegiance and duty to serve the Government of India through naval service. The term refers to the rank-and-file naval personnel, similar to how a soldier serves in the Army or an airman in the Air Force.
real_world_examples: An Indian Navy seaman posted aboard INS Vikramaditya who is convinced by a foreign agent to leak classified information about naval operations could be the subject of an abetment to mutiny offence under Section 159 of BNS, 2023.

A civilian political activist in Mumbai who distributes pamphlets urging sailors at Naval Dockyard to disobey orders from their commanding officers could be prosecuted for attempting to seduce a sailor from his duty under Section 159.

A person who incites sailors stationed at INS Valsura in Gujarat to collectively refuse orders during a training exercise, resulting in an actual act of mutiny, could face prosecution under Section 160 for abetment of mutiny that is subsequently committed.

A civilian contractor working at a naval base who encourages a sailor to physically assault his superior officer during the execution of official duties would attract liability under Section 161 of the BNS, 2023.

A sailor enrolled in the Indian Navy serving on a warship who is persuaded by a third party to abandon his post during active operations at sea would trigger the provisions of Sections 159 and 164 relating to seduction from duty.

A person who, through social media, systematically targets sailors of the Eastern Naval Command with propaganda designed to undermine their loyalty to the Government of India could be charged with abetment of mutiny under Section 159.
what_it_covers: Enlisted personnel serving in the Navy of the Government of India, such as seamen, petty officers, and non-commissioned naval ranks who are bound by naval discipline and duty.
A naval serviceperson who is subject to the Naval Act and whose allegiance and duty to the Government of India can potentially be the subject of abetment, seduction, or incitement by a third party.
Any person in active naval service aboard a ship or at a naval establishment registered under the Government of India who is bound by an oath of service and subject to orders from superior officers.
Naval reservists or persons currently embodied into active naval service who are subject to naval command and discipline at the relevant time of the alleged offence.
what_it_excludes: Officers of the Indian Navy, who are separately categorised as 'officers' in the BNS provisions, though they may fall under the broader armed forces framework.
Merchant mariners or civilian sailors employed on commercial vessels, who are not members of the Government of India's naval forces and are not subject to military discipline under these provisions.
Soldiers of the Indian Army and airmen of the Indian Air Force, who are distinct categories expressly listed separately alongside 'sailor' in Sections 159–161.
Civilian employees working in naval dockyards, naval bases, or naval supply chains who are not enlisted in the Navy and do not owe naval allegiance.
Coast Guard personnel, who operate under a separate statutory framework and are not part of the Navy of the Government of India for the purpose of these sections.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'sailor' determines whether Sections 159, 160, and 161 of the BNS are triggered against any person who abets mutiny, attempts to seduce them from duty, or incites an assault on their superior officer — offences carrying punishment ranging from three years' imprisonment to life imprisonment or even death. The definition also determines whether the immunity carve-out in Section 1 of the BNS applies, preserving the operation of special military laws governing mutiny and desertion of naval personnel.

definitions.definition: A 'seal' refers to an impression, stamp, or device affixed to or used upon a document or blank paper as a means of authentication, execution, or authorisation, which renders such document capable of being converted into or treated as a valuable security. It functions as a formal authenticating mark equivalent to a signature in the execution of legally binding instruments.
definitions.plain_english: A seal is a stamp or impression that a person or organisation places on a document to show it is genuine and authorised, similar to a signature. In the context of Indian law, affixing one's seal on a document is treated as formally approving or authenticating it. A sealed blank paper is considered dangerous because anyone who gets it can write anything above the seal and use it as a legal document.
real_world_examples: A moneylender in Rajasthan threatens a farmer and forces him to affix his rubber stamp seal on a blank promissory note, which the moneylender later fills in to show a large debt — this constitutes extortion under BNS Section 308.

A company director in Mumbai is deceived into affixing the company's official seal on a blank transfer deed, which is subsequently filled in by a fraudster to transfer immovable property — amounting to cheating under BNS Section 318.
A village panchayat member in Bihar is coerced under threat of violence to affix his personal seal on a blank land document, enabling the extortionist to manufacture a fraudulent sale agreement.

A registered society in Delhi is tricked into placing its official seal on an incomplete bond document; the fraudster fills in terms obligating the society to pay large sums, treating it as a valid enforceable instrument.

A trader in Chennai affixes his traditional wax seal on a blank paper under duress from a local criminal gang, who then convert it into a fictitious agreement acknowledging receipt of goods never actually delivered.
what_it_covers: A rubber stamp impression affixed by an individual or entity on a document as a mark of authorisation or authentication.
A wax or embossed seal placed on a blank paper that can be subsequently filled in to create a binding legal or financial obligation.
An official company or organisational seal affixed to an instrument, rendering it capable of being treated as a valuable security.
A personal seal affixed under coercion or deception that enables the document to be converted into a promissory note, bond, or deed.
what_it_excludes: A mere decorative stamp or embossment that carries no legal authenticating authority and cannot be used to create enforceable obligations.
A government or court seal acting in its official statutory capacity, as opposed to the seal of a private individual used for personal authentication.
A digital or electronic signature or cryptographic seal, which is governed separately under the definition of 'electronic signature' and related provisions.
An unsigned and unsealed blank paper that has not yet had any authenticating mark applied and therefore cannot yet be converted into a valuable security.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document bears a 'seal' is legally significant because a sealed instrument — even if otherwise blank — is treated as capable of being converted into a valuable security, thereby triggering the aggravated offences of extortion under Section 308 and cheating under Section 318 of the BNS, 2023, which carry enhanced punishments of up to seven to ten years imprisonment. The presence of a seal elevates the gravity of the offence from mere wrongful inducement to the more serious category of dishonestly obtaining a potentially enforceable legal instrument.

definitions.definition: Secession, as used in Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the act or attempt of exciting or encouraging the separation or breaking away of any part of India's territory from the Union of India, thereby endangering the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India. It encompasses any action — by words spoken or written, signs, visible representation, electronic communication, or financial means — that purposely or knowingly promotes or attempts to promote such territorial or political separation.
definitions.plain_english: Secession means the attempt to split off or break away a part of India from the rest of the country, to form a separate nation or independent political entity. It involves actively promoting, encouraging, or attempting to cause a region or group within India to separate from the Indian Union. This is treated as a very serious threat to the country's unity and is a punishable offence under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A political leader in a border state publicly gives speeches demanding that the state declare independence from India and form a separate sovereign country, explicitly calling for separation from the Indian Union.
An individual in Punjab distributes pamphlets and posts social media content urging residents to support a movement to establish an independent Khalistan state by breaking away from India.

A group in Jammu & Kashmir uses encrypted messaging apps to coordinate and fund campaigns that advocate for the region's secession from India and merger with a foreign state or declaration of independence.

A YouTuber based in Tamil Nadu regularly broadcasts videos inciting viewers to support a separate Tamil Eelam nation carved out of South India, using emotionally charged rhetoric to mobilise separatist sentiment.

An organisation operating from abroad wires money to local activists in Manipur to sponsor rallies, print materials, and run campaigns demanding that Manipur secede from India and establish an independent nation-state.
what_it_covers: Publicly inciting or encouraging people, through spoken or written words, to support the separation of a state or region from the Indian Union.
Using electronic communication platforms such as social media, messaging apps, or websites to propagate or fund secessionist movements aimed at breaking up India's territorial integrity.
Financing, organising, or participating in activities — including rallies, publications, or campaigns — that purposely promote the idea of any part of India seceding from the nation.
Coordinating with foreign entities or domestic groups to plan or execute efforts that would result in the political or territorial separation of any part of India.
Producing or distributing propaganda materials — pamphlets, videos, audio recordings — that knowingly attempt to excite secessionist sentiments among the public.
what_it_excludes: Peaceful, lawful criticism of government policies, administrative decisions, or legislation, expressed with the aim of changing those policies through legal and democratic means, without inciting secession.

Academic, journalistic, or scholarly analysis and commentary on secessionist movements, historical separatist events, or geopolitical issues, presented in an objective or educational context without intent to excite secession.
Expressions of cultural, linguistic, or regional identity or pride that do not call for or attempt to excite the political or territorial separation of any region from India.
Lawful political advocacy for greater autonomy, federalism, or constitutional reforms within the framework of the Indian Union, without promoting a complete break from India.

Statements made in courts, academic institutions, or legislative bodies for the purpose of legal argument, policy debate, or research that do not purposely or knowingly attempt to excite secessionist activities.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'secession' under Section 152 determines whether a person is liable for the gravest offence against the State, attracting punishment of imprisonment for life or up to seven years along with a fine. The applicability of this definition directly distinguishes criminal secessionist conduct from constitutionally protected free speech and lawful political dissent, making it the threshold that separates permissible criticism from a capital-level threat to national sovereignty.

definitions.definition: The term 'sentence' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but is used to denote the formal pronouncement of punishment by a Court upon a person convicted of an offence, including the nature, quantum, and conditions of punishment such as imprisonment, fine, community service, or death, as prescribed under the relevant provisions of this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: A sentence is the official punishment that a judge or court announces after finding someone guilty of a crime. It tells the convicted person exactly what punishment they must undergo — such as going to jail for a set number of years, paying a fine, or performing community service. The sentence is the final legal consequence that a court imposes following a conviction.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Court in Mumbai convicts an accused of culpable homicide not amounting to murder and sentences him to rigorous imprisonment for ten years along with a fine of one lakh rupees under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
A Magistrate in Delhi convicts a person for causing hurt under the BNS and sentences them to simple imprisonment for one month or a fine of five thousand rupees, whichever is paid first.
A Special Court in Chennai convicts a gang leader under organised crime provisions and sentences him to life imprisonment with forfeiture of property acquired through criminal proceeds.

A Fast Track Court in Bengaluru convicts an offender of sexual harassment and sentences the accused to community service in addition to a fine, as the court exercises its discretion under the applicable sentencing provisions of the BNS.

A High Court in Kolkata, hearing an appeal against acquittal, convicts the respondent and sentences him to death for a murder committed with extreme brutality, after following the procedure under the applicable law.
what_it_covers: A formal order of imprisonment (simple or rigorous) pronounced by a competent Court upon conviction of an accused for a punishable offence under the BNS.
An order imposing a fine, with or without imprisonment, passed by a Magistrate or Judge after a finding of guilt in a criminal trial.
A sentence of death passed by a Sessions Court for capital offences such as murder under the BNS, subject to confirmation by the High Court.
An order of community service imposed as a punishment in lieu of or in addition to imprisonment, as permitted under the BNS.
A sentence of life imprisonment awarded by a court for offences where the BNS prescribes imprisonment for life as the maximum punishment.
what_it_excludes: A mere charge or framing of charge against an accused, which precedes any finding of guilt and does not constitute a sentence.
An order of acquittal or discharge passed by a court, as these do not involve any imposition of punishment upon the accused.
Administrative or departmental penalties imposed by government authorities or tribunals outside the framework of criminal adjudication by a Court.
A remand order or order of bail passed during the course of a criminal proceeding, which relates to custody rather than punishment after conviction.
Civil decrees or orders passed by civil courts awarding damages or compensation, which do not constitute criminal sentences under the BNS.
definitions.why_it_matters: The nature and quantum of a sentence directly determines the legal rights and obligations that arise post-conviction, including rights of appeal, eligibility for remission or commutation, computation of period of solitary confinement, and consequences under sections 8 and 263 of the BNS, which specifically regulate the aggregation and limits of sentences where multiple offences or trials are involved. Whether an act attracts a particular sentence also governs whether an offence is classified as cognizable, bailable, or a capital offence, affecting the entire course of criminal proceedings.

definitions.definition: A 'sentence of a Court' refers to the formal judicial pronouncement by a competent court imposing a legally prescribed punishment upon a person convicted of an offence, including sentences of death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a specified term, and encompasses such a sentence even where it has been subject to commutation by the appropriate authority.
definitions.plain_english: A 'sentence of a Court' is the official punishment decided and declared by a judge or magistrate after a person has been found guilty of a crime. It includes any type of court-ordered punishment such as the death penalty, life imprisonment, or a fixed jail term. Even if that original punishment is later reduced (commuted) to a lesser one, the reduced punishment is still treated as being 'under sentence of a Court' for legal purposes.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Court in Mumbai convicts an accused of murder and pronounces a sentence of death — the convict is thereafter 'under sentence of a Court' and any public servant who intentionally allows him to escape from judicial custody would be liable under Section 260 of the BNS.

A High Court in Delhi sentences a convict to life imprisonment for a heinous robbery offence; even if the Governor later commutes this to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment, the person remains subject to a 'sentence of a Court' and rules under Section 260 continue to apply to any public servant guarding him.

A Magistrate's Court in Chennai sentences a person convicted of causing grievous hurt to three years of simple imprisonment; a jailer who intentionally helps this convict escape from Puzhal Central Prison is punishable under Section 260 because the person is 'under sentence of a Court' for a term not exceeding ten years.

An accused is convicted by a Special Court in Hyderabad under anti-terror laws and sentenced to imprisonment for fifteen years; a police officer escorting him to prison who deliberately allows him to flee is punishable under Section 260 because the convict is subject to 'a sentence of a Court' for ten years or more.

A Fast Track Court in Kolkata pronounces a sentence of imprisonment for life on a convict for rape; a prison superintendent who knowingly aids the convict in absconding from Presidency Correctional Home becomes liable under Section 260 because the convict is under a 'sentence of a Court' to imprisonment for life.
what_it_covers: A sentence of death formally pronounced by a competent criminal court upon conviction for a capital offence.
A sentence of imprisonment for life awarded by a Sessions Court or High Court for serious offences such as murder or rape.
A determinate sentence of imprisonment (whether simple or rigorous) for a specified number of years or months awarded upon conviction.

A sentence that has been commuted by an authority such as the President or Governor to a lesser punishment, where the commuted punishment is treated as equivalent to the original court sentence for the purposes of Section 260.
A sentence imposing imprisonment for a term of ten years or more, which attracts the higher tier of punishment for derelict public servants under Section 260.
what_it_excludes: Lawful committal to custody that has not resulted from a conviction and sentencing by a court, such as remand of an under-trial prisoner or preventive detention under a statutory order — such persons are separately described as 'lawfully committed to custody' in Section 260.
An administrative or executive order of detention (such as under the National Security Act or Preventive Detention laws) that is not a sentence pronounced by a court upon conviction for an offence.
A mere bail condition, bond, or judicial direction to appear before a court, which does not constitute a punitive sentence imposed after conviction.
Acquittal orders or orders of discharge passed by a court, which do not impose any punishment and therefore cannot constitute a 'sentence of a Court'.

Sentences or punishments imposed by quasi-judicial or disciplinary authorities (such as departmental tribunals or military court-martial) unless specifically recognised as a 'sentence of a Court' under the relevant law.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person is 'under sentence of a Court' is the critical factual trigger that determines the specific tier of punishment applicable to a derelict public servant under Section 260 — the graver the sentence (death, life imprisonment, or ten years and above), the more severe the punishment for the errant official. It also distinguishes sentenced convicts from under-trial or lawfully committed persons, determining which limb of the offence under Section 260 is attracted.

definitions.definition: Separation, as used in Section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the state of a wife living apart from her husband, whether pursuant to a formal decree of separation passed by a competent court or by any other arrangement or circumstance, formal or informal, under which the spouses are not cohabiting together.
definitions.plain_english: Separation means a situation where a husband and wife are living apart from each other. This can happen either because a court has officially ordered them to live separately (a formal legal decree) or simply because they have chosen or been compelled to live apart for any reason. The key fact is that they are not staying together as a married couple at the time of the act in question.
real_world_examples: A couple in Mumbai files for divorce and the Family Court passes a decree of judicial separation; the wife moves to her parents' home in Pune while proceedings are pending — this constitutes separation under Section 67.

A wife in Chennai leaves her matrimonial home due to domestic violence and is residing at a women's shelter without any court order; the husband visits and forces sexual intercourse upon her — the informal living-apart arrangement still qualifies as separation.

A couple in Delhi mutually agrees to live separately while their divorce petition is being processed; the husband travels to the wife's new residence and has non-consensual intercourse — the agreed-upon informal separation suffices.

A wife in Kolkata has moved to a different city for employment and the couple is living separately without any formal legal proceeding; the husband forces himself upon her during a visit — this factual separation without a decree is covered under Section 67.

After a court in Hyderabad passes a decree of separation under the Hindu Marriage Act, the husband visits the wife's new address and commits non-consensual intercourse — the decree-backed separation squarely attracts Section 67.

A Christian woman in Goa obtains a judicial separation order from the District Court; her husband subsequently forces sexual intercourse on her — the formal decree establishes the requisite separation under Section 67.
what_it_covers: A wife living apart from her husband under a formal decree of judicial separation passed by a competent court under personal laws such as the Hindu Marriage Act or the Special Marriage Act.
A wife who has voluntarily left the matrimonial home and is residing separately without any court order, provided the factual state of non-cohabitation is established.
A wife living apart due to circumstances such as domestic violence, mutual agreement, or estrangement, even where no legal proceedings have been initiated.
A wife residing in a different city, state, or premises from her husband for any reason, making it clear that the couple is not living together as a cohabiting married couple at the relevant time.
what_it_excludes: A wife who is temporarily away from the matrimonial home for short durations such as visiting relatives, travelling for work, or medical treatment, with the intention of returning and with no break in cohabitation.
A situation where both spouses are living under the same roof and sharing the matrimonial home, even if their personal relations are strained or they are in conflict.

definitions.definition: The term 'servant' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Based on its use in Sections 3 and 306, 'servant' refers to a person employed in the service of another, whether as a domestic worker, attendant, or hired hand, who acts under the direction, control, and authority of an employer or master in exchange for wages or other consideration.
definitions.plain_english: A servant is a person who works for someone else under their supervision and control, following their instructions in return for payment or some other benefit. This typically includes domestic helpers, household staff, and personal attendants employed by an individual household or person. The key feature is that the servant's work is directed and controlled by the employer, known as the master.
real_world_examples: A cook (bai) employed in a Mumbai household who prepares meals daily under the instructions of the household owner and receives a monthly salary.
A domestic worker hired in a Delhi home to clean, wash clothes, and look after children, working under the direction of the homeowner.
A personal attendant (peon) employed by an individual to run errands, carry messages, and perform odd jobs as directed by that person.
A gardener employed by a residential household in Bengaluru to tend to the garden under the supervision of the house owner.
A driver employed by a private individual in Chennai to chauffeur family members, taking orders exclusively from the employing family.
what_it_covers: A domestic helper employed in a private household to perform household chores under the direction of the homeowner.
A personal attendant hired by an individual to assist with daily personal tasks such as errands, cooking, or cleaning.
A gardener, driver, or watchman employed by a private individual and subject to that individual's direct supervision and control.
A farm labourer employed by a landowner to work on agricultural land under the landowner's direction.
A live-in household worker who resides on the employer's premises and is subject to the employer's instructions round the clock.
what_it_excludes: An independent contractor who undertakes work for a principal but is not subject to direct day-to-day control and supervision.
A government employee or public servant who derives authority from law and serves the State rather than a private individual master.
A person performing voluntary or gratuitous services without any agreement for wages or other consideration.
A business partner or co-owner who shares authority rather than being subordinate to another person's direction.

A professional such as a doctor, lawyer, or chartered accountant engaged for specific professional services on a fee basis without being subject to the client's control over how the work is performed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'servant' directly affects the application of offences under Section 306 (relating to theft or breach of trust by a servant or clerk) and Section 3 (criminal liability for acts done by or through servants), where enhanced culpability or distinct offences may arise from the master-servant relationship. The definition determines whether an accused person attracts the aggravated provisions designed to address betrayal of trust inherent in domestic or personal employment.

definitions.definition: Sexual exploitation, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, refers to the engagement of a trafficked person or child in any act of a sexual nature for the gratification, benefit, or profit of another, including but not limited to prostitution, pornography, or any other form of commercial or non-commercial sexual abuse. It forms a component of the broader concept of 'exploitation' under Section 143, which expressly includes 'any form of sexual exploitation.' The term applies to conduct undertaken knowingly or with reason to believe that the victim has been trafficked.
definitions.plain_english: Sexual exploitation means using another person — especially a child or someone who has been trafficked — for sexual purposes against their will or without their free and genuine consent, often for money or other benefits. This includes forcing or coercing someone into prostitution, making pornographic content featuring them, or using them in any other sexual way for someone else's gain. The law treats it as a serious crime, particularly when the victim is a child or has been brought to the situation through trafficking.
real_world_examples: A brothel owner in Mumbai knowingly purchases a girl trafficked from West Bengal and forces her to provide sexual services to clients daily — this constitutes sexual exploitation of a trafficked child under Section 144.

A film producer in Delhi recruits a woman through false promises of acting work, then coerces her into shooting pornographic videos after confiscating her identity documents — this is sexual exploitation of a trafficked person.

A man in Hyderabad pays a trafficking agent to supply young women from rural Telangana, then runs an escort service using these women who have no freedom to leave — engaging them for sexual exploitation while knowing they were trafficked attracts liability under Section 144.

A couple operating a spa in Chennai hires young girls trafficked from Jharkhand and forces them to provide sexual services to male customers under the guise of massage therapy — knowingly engaging trafficked children for sexual exploitation triggers the higher punishment under Section 144.

An NGO worker discovers that a factory owner in Rajasthan has been harbouring trafficked adolescent girls and 'lending' them to local men for sexual purposes in exchange for money — the factory owner is liable for sexual exploitation of trafficked children under Section 144.

A recruitment agent in Kolkata lures women from Bangladesh with promises of domestic work, transfers them to a red-light district in Pune, and receives a share of their earnings from a local pimp who knowingly engages them — both the pimp and the agent are implicated in sexual exploitation of trafficked persons.
what_it_covers: Engaging a trafficked child in prostitution, knowing or having reason to believe the child was trafficked, regardless of whether payment is made directly to the child.

Using a trafficked adult person for any form of sexual service — including escort services, forced sexual intercourse, or sexual performances — with knowledge or reasonable belief of their trafficked status.

Producing, distributing, or profiting from pornographic content featuring a trafficked person or child, which also intersects with Section 95's coverage of using children for sexual exploitation or pornography.
Harbouring a trafficked person on one's premises and permitting or directing others to engage in sexual acts with that person for money or benefit.
Any act of physical sexual abuse carried out upon a trafficked individual under circumstances where the perpetrator had reason to believe the victim was trafficked.
what_it_excludes: Consensual adult sexual activity between persons who have not been trafficked and where no exploitation or coercion is involved — this does not fall within the definition as used in Sections 143–144.

Sexual offences committed against a person where there is no trafficking nexus — such cases are governed by other provisions (e.g., rape under Section 63 or sexual harassment under Section 75) rather than Section 144.
Mere knowledge of trafficking without any active engagement or use of the trafficked person for sexual purposes — passive awareness alone does not constitute sexual exploitation under Section 144.
Recruitment or transport of a person for trafficking purposes that has not yet proceeded to the stage of actual sexual engagement — that conduct is addressed under Section 143 on trafficking itself.
Economic or labour exploitation of trafficked persons that does not involve any sexual dimension, such as forced beggary or bonded labour without a sexual component.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as sexual exploitation of a trafficked person determines whether the accused faces the elevated punishments under Section 144 — a minimum of five years' rigorous imprisonment (extendable to ten years) for child victims and a minimum of three years (extendable to seven years) for adult victims — in addition to any liability under Section 143 for trafficking itself. It also triggers the application of child protection frameworks where the victim is a minor, compounding the severity of the legal consequences.

definitions.definition: A man commits sexual harassment when he engages in any of the following acts against a woman: physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; a demand or request for sexual favours; showing pornography against the will of a woman; or making sexually coloured remarks.
definitions.plain_english: Sexual harassment means any unwanted sexual behaviour by a man towards a woman, including touching or making sexual advances she has not welcomed, demanding sexual favours, forcing her to view pornographic material, or passing sexual comments or remarks. The law treats these as criminal offences, not just workplace or civil wrongs. Physical acts and demands carry heavier punishment than verbal remarks.
real_world_examples: A male supervisor at an IT company in Bengaluru repeatedly touches a female colleague's shoulders and makes comments about her appearance while asking her to stay late alone, constituting unwelcome physical contact with explicit sexual overtures.
A landlord in Mumbai tells his female tenant that he will waive her rent if she has sex with him, which amounts to a demand or request for sexual favours under the provision.

A male co-worker in a Delhi government office shows explicit pornographic videos on his phone to a female colleague without her consent, which is the offence of showing pornography against the will of a woman.

A male professor at a Chennai college consistently passes lewd and sexually suggestive comments about a female student's body in front of the class, constituting sexually coloured remarks punishable under the lesser punishment clause.
A male customer at a Kolkata retail store grabs a saleswoman's hand and makes explicit sexual propositions to her, amounting to physical contact involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures.
what_it_covers: Physical touching or bodily contact by a man that is sexually motivated and unwelcome to the woman, such as groping, grabbing, or persistent physical advances.
Explicit or implicit demands or requests by a man for sexual favours from a woman, whether oral, written, or communicated through gestures.
Forcing or showing pornographic material to a woman without her consent and against her will.
Oral or written sexually coloured remarks, lewd comments, or innuendos directed at a woman by a man.
Acts committed in any setting — workplace, public place, educational institution, or private premises — as the section does not restrict the location.
what_it_excludes: Sexual harassment by a woman against a man or same-sex sexual harassment, as the section is specifically framed around a man committing the act against a woman.
Consensual sexual banter or mutually agreed-upon communication between adults, since the definition requires the conduct to be unwelcome or against the woman's will.
Acts that amount to rape or assault under other sections of the BNS, which are governed by separate, more serious provisions and carry distinct punishments.
Mere accidental or non-sexual physical contact, as the definition requires the contact to involve explicit sexual overtures.

Workplace-specific civil remedies and employer obligations, which are governed by the Prevention, Protection and Redressal of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, a separate legislation.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as sexual harassment under Section 75 determines whether a man faces criminal prosecution and imprisonment of up to three years (for physical contact, sexual favour demands, or non-consensual pornography) or up to one year (for sexually coloured remarks), along with possible fines; the classification of the specific act among the four enumerated clauses directly controls the quantum of punishment imposed by the court.

definitions.definition: For the purposes of sections 67, 68, and 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, 'sexual intercourse' shall mean any of the acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of section 63, namely: penetration of the penis into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman; insertion of any object or body part (not being the penis) into the vagina, urethra or anus of a woman; manipulation of any part of the body of a woman so as to cause penetration into the vagina, urethra, anus or any part of her body; or application of the mouth to the vagina, anus or urethra of a woman.
definitions.plain_english: In this law, 'sexual intercourse' is not limited to just one type of physical act. It covers a wide range of sexual acts including penetration by the penis, insertion of objects or body parts, manipulation causing penetration, and oral contact with a woman's genitals or anus. This broad definition is used specifically in offences involving a husband acting against a separated wife, a person in authority abusing their position, or someone using deception to obtain sex.
real_world_examples: A husband who is legally separated from his wife forces himself upon her physically — the act of penile penetration qualifies as 'sexual intercourse' under Section 67 and attracts punishment of two to seven years' imprisonment.

A jail superintendent at a women's remand home in Delhi uses his authority to pressure an inmate into oral sex — this act of applying his mouth to her genitals constitutes 'sexual intercourse' under Section 68 and is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of five to ten years.

A manager at a hospital in Mumbai promises a female attendant a promotion and, under that false inducement, inserts a body part other than the penis into her body — this qualifies as 'sexual intercourse' under Section 69 even though it does not amount to rape.

A man in a position of fiduciary authority over a young woman in a children's institution in Chennai manipulates her body in a manner causing penetration — this act falls within the definition of 'sexual intercourse' under Section 68.

A man in Kolkata falsely promises marriage to a woman and has penile-vaginal intercourse with her without intending to marry her — this is 'sexual intercourse' within the meaning of Section 69, making him liable for up to ten years' imprisonment.

A public servant in Hyderabad, exploiting a woman in his official custody, induces her to engage in oral sex on him — this act of making her apply her mouth to his genitals falls within the definition of 'sexual intercourse' under Section 68.
what_it_covers: Penile penetration into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus of a woman by a man.
Insertion of any object or non-penile body part into the vagina, urethra, or anus of a woman.
Manipulation of any part of a woman's body so as to cause penetration into her vagina, urethra, anus, or any other body part.
Application of the man's mouth to the vagina, anus, or urethra of a woman (oral sex performed on a woman).
All such acts committed by a husband on a separated wife without her consent under Section 67.
Such acts committed through abuse of authority, fiduciary position, or public servant status under Section 68.
Such acts obtained through deceitful means or false promise of marriage under Section 69.
what_it_excludes: Acts that amount to rape as defined under Section 63 — Sections 68 and 69 expressly apply only where the act does not constitute rape.
Consensual sexual intercourse between a husband and wife not living under separation, which is expressly excluded from rape under Section 63.
Medical procedures or clinical interventions, which are explicitly stated not to constitute rape and by extension are not captured within this definition.
Sexual acts committed by a woman upon a man or between two women, as the definition applies specifically to acts by a man upon a woman.
Non-penetrative sexual acts or touching that does not fall within clauses (a) to (d) of Section 63, such as outward touching of the body without penetration.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'sexual intercourse' under this definition determines whether offences under Sections 67, 68, and 69 are triggered, attracting imprisonment ranging from two years (Section 67) to ten years (Sections 68 and 69), along with fines; acts falling outside this definition would not attract these specific offences, and acts rising to the level of rape under Section 63 are separately prosecuted under that provision rather than the lesser offences in Sections 67–69.

definitions.definition: Sexually coloured remarks are verbal or written statements of a sexual nature directed at a woman without her consent, constituting one of the enumerated acts of sexual harassment under Section 75 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Such remarks are those that carry an explicit or implicit sexual connotation, innuendo, or commentary targeting a woman and are unwelcome in nature.
definitions.plain_english: Sexually coloured remarks are comments, jokes, or statements that have a sexual tone or meaning, made to or about a woman in a way she finds offensive or unwelcome. This includes lewd comments about a woman's body, sexual jokes directed at her, or any verbal expression with sexual undertones made without her consent. Making such remarks to a woman is a criminal offence under Indian law.
real_world_examples: A male supervisor in a Mumbai office repeatedly makes comments about a female colleague's physical appearance, saying things like 'You have a great figure, I can't concentrate when you're around,' making her uncomfortable at work.
A male student in a Delhi college persistently passes sexual jokes and makes lewd remarks about a female classmate's body in front of others in the classroom or college canteen.
A male customer at a shop in Chennai makes unsolicited and explicitly sexual comments about a female sales executive's looks while she is assisting him, causing her distress.
A male neighbour in a residential colony in Kolkata shouts sexually suggestive comments at a woman as she leaves for work each morning, creating a hostile and threatening environment for her.
A male employee sends a female colleague a text message on a professional group containing a sexual innuendo directed specifically at her, humiliating her in front of coworkers.
A male auto-rickshaw driver in Hyderabad makes explicit verbal sexual remarks to a female passenger during a ride, making her feel unsafe and degraded.
what_it_covers: Verbal comments about a woman's body or sexual attributes made in a workplace, public place, or any other setting without her consent.
Lewd or sexually suggestive jokes, innuendos, or taunts directed at a specific woman or made in her presence in a manner targeting her.
Written or electronic messages, texts, or notes containing sexually charged language or commentary directed at a woman.
Repeated oral remarks of a sexual nature made to a woman that she has not invited or consented to, regardless of the setting.
Comments that sexualise a woman's appearance, behaviour, or character in an explicit or implicit manner, causing offence or distress.
what_it_excludes: Physical contact or unwelcome physical advances of a sexual nature, which are separately covered under clause (i) of Section 75(1) as a distinct and more seriously punished form of sexual harassment.
Demands or requests for sexual favours, which constitute a separate enumerated act under clause (ii) of Section 75(1) and are not classified under sexually coloured remarks.
Showing pornography against a woman's will, which is independently addressed under clause (iii) of Section 75(1) and carries a higher punishment than making sexually coloured remarks.
Neutral or non-sexual compliments or statements that do not carry any sexual connotation or innuendo, even if they make a woman uncomfortable.
Consensual adult conversations of a sexual nature where the woman has willingly participated and has not indicated the remarks are unwelcome.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a remark qualifies as a 'sexually coloured remark' determines whether the accused is guilty of sexual harassment under Section 75(1)(iv) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which triggers criminal liability punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term extending up to one year, or fine, or both. This classification as a distinct clause also separates it from more severely punished forms of sexual harassment under clauses (i), (ii), and (iii), directly affecting the sentencing outcome.

definitions.definition: Simple imprisonment is a form of custodial sentence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in which the convicted offender is confined in prison without being required to perform any hard labour or rigorous physical work. As provided under Section 7, a court may direct that any imprisonment which may be of either description shall be wholly simple, wholly rigorous, or partly each, depending on the circumstances of the offence.
definitions.plain_english: Simple imprisonment means sending a person to jail as punishment, but without forcing them to do any hard physical labour while inside. It is a lighter form of jail sentence compared to rigorous imprisonment. The person is confined but lives under ordinary prison conditions, not under harsh labour conditions.
real_world_examples: A man in Delhi who whistles and makes suggestive gestures at a woman on the street, intending to insult her modesty, may be sentenced to simple imprisonment of up to three years under Section 79 of the BNS, 2023, without being put to hard labour in prison.

A shopkeeper in Mumbai who physically blocks a public footpath to prevent a rival from passing, thereby wrongfully restraining that person, may be sentenced to simple imprisonment of up to one month under Section 126 of the BNS.

A prison guard in Chennai who negligently allows a prisoner of war to escape from custody may be punished with simple imprisonment for up to three years under Section 157 of the BNS, without being subjected to rigorous prison labour.

A person in Kolkata who slaps another during a heated argument triggered by sudden and grave provocation may be punished with simple imprisonment of up to one month under Section 136, meaning he serves time in jail under ordinary conditions without hard labour.

A Sessions Court in Hyderabad sentencing a first-time offender for a minor public order offence may, exercising discretion under Section 7, direct that part of the imprisonment be simple and part be rigorous, reflecting the mixed nature of the offence.
what_it_covers: Confinement of a convicted offender in a prison or jail under ordinary conditions without compulsory hard labour or rigorous physical work.
Sentences imposed by a court for offences under BNS where the punishment prescribed is imprisonment of either description, allowing the court to choose simple imprisonment in appropriate cases.
Partial sentences where a court directs under Section 7 that only a portion of the total imprisonment term shall be simple, with the remainder being rigorous.

Punishment for offences such as wrongful restraint (Section 126), insult to modesty of a woman (Section 79), assault on grave provocation (Section 136), and negligent escape of a state prisoner (Section 157), where the legislature has prescribed simple imprisonment specifically.
Cases involving first-time or less culpable offenders where the court, in its discretion, finds that rigorous imprisonment is disproportionate to the offence committed.
what_it_excludes: Rigorous imprisonment, which requires the convicted person to perform hard physical labour such as grinding grain, weaving, or other prison labour as prescribed by prison rules.
Imprisonment for life, which is a distinct and separate category of punishment not classified as either simple or rigorous imprisonment in the same sense as Section 7 contemplates.
Solitary confinement, which is an additional or separate punitive measure involving isolation of the prisoner and is not synonymous with simple imprisonment.
Detention or custody prior to conviction, such as remand or undertrial custody, which is not a sentence and does not constitute simple or rigorous imprisonment under the BNS.
Community service, which is a distinct non-custodial punishment recognised under the BNS and does not involve confinement in a prison at all.
definitions.why_it_matters: The classification of imprisonment as 'simple' rather than 'rigorous' directly determines the conditions a convict endures during their sentence — simple imprisonment means no forced labour, making it a significantly less onerous punishment. This distinction is legally consequential because courts must specify whether imprisonment is simple or rigorous when the offence carries imprisonment of either description, and an incorrect or absent specification can affect the validity of the sentence and the rights of the offender in prison administration.

definitions.definition: A 'slave' under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to a person who is held, treated, bought, sold, imported, exported, removed, or otherwise dealt in as property, subject to the ownership or control of another person, deprived of personal freedom and autonomy. The term is used in the context of Section 145, which penalises habitual dealing in slaves, and in Section 140, which criminalises kidnapping or abduction for the purpose of subjecting a person to slavery.
definitions.plain_english: A 'slave' is a person who is treated as if they are property — someone who can be bought, sold, transported, or traded by another person without their free consent. This person has no freedom to leave or make their own choices because they are controlled, owned, or exploited by another. In India, holding or trading in slaves is a serious crime under this law.
real_world_examples: A trafficking network operating across Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh abducts rural women and repeatedly sells them to different households as domestic workers, stripping them of any freedom or wages — these women are treated as slaves under Section 145.

A bonded labour racket in a brick kiln in Telangana where workers from tribal communities are purchased from their families by the kiln owner and cannot leave the premises or refuse work — these workers are effectively held as slaves.

A criminal gang in Mumbai imports undocumented migrants from Bangladesh and Nepal, keeps them confined, and sells them repeatedly to different employers for forced domestic or sexual labour, constituting habitual dealing in slaves.

A zamindar in rural Bihar kidnaps young men from impoverished families, sells them to other landowners in exchange for money, and habitually participates in this trade over several years — this constitutes the offence of habitual dealing in slaves under Section 145.

An organised crime syndicate that exports Indian children to Gulf countries by falsifying documents and selling them for domestic servitude — each child sold constitutes a transaction in slaves, and the habitual nature of the operation attracts Section 145.
what_it_covers: A person who is bought, sold, or transferred between individuals as if they were property, with no freedom of movement or consent.
A person kidnapped or abducted and placed in a condition of forced servitude, unable to leave or refuse work, for the benefit of another person.
Victims of organised trafficking networks who are habitually imported, exported, or traded across state or national borders as commodities.
Persons held in debt bondage where the condition of repayment effectively strips them of all personal freedom, autonomy, and legal rights.
Children or adults removed from their families and sold to employers, households, or criminal operations where they are treated as possessions.
what_it_excludes: A person who voluntarily enters into a lawful employment contract, even one with restrictive terms, as they retain legal rights and freedom of exit.
Prisoners or persons in lawful state custody who are detained by due process of law and not traded or sold as property.
Persons engaged in consensual domestic service or apprenticeship arrangements where they are free to leave and receive lawful remuneration.
Persons subject to lawful guardianship, such as minors under parental or court-appointed guardian care, as this does not constitute ownership or trade in persons.
Victims of isolated or one-time labour exploitation who are not part of a systematic buying, selling, or dealing arrangement that characterises slavery.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'slave' under the BNS is determinative for invoking Section 145 (habitual dealing in slaves), which carries punishment up to imprisonment for life, and for aggravating liability under Section 140 where kidnapping or abduction is committed for the purpose of subjecting the victim to slavery. It also directly connects to the exploitation framework under Section 143 (trafficking), where slavery is expressly listed as a form of exploitation.

definitions.definition: Slavery, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the condition of a person who is held in complete ownership or dominion by another, being treated as property and subjected to compelled service or labour without freedom or consent. It encompasses practices by which a person is reduced to a state of servitude akin to ownership, including being bought, sold, detained, or disposed of as chattel. Though not formally defined in a standalone provision, it is used in Section 140 to describe a grave condition of exploitation to which a kidnapped or abducted person may be subjected.
definitions.plain_english: Slavery means treating a person as if they are property — owning, controlling, or using them completely against their will, with no freedom to leave or refuse. It is one of the most severe forms of exploitation a person can be subjected to. In the context of this law, it refers to the situation where someone is kidnapped or abducted and then held in a slave-like condition, forced to work or serve another person without any rights or liberty.
real_world_examples: A trafficker kidnaps a young woman from a rural village in Jharkhand and sells her to a household in a city where she is kept locked up, forced to work without pay, and prevented from leaving — a condition amounting to domestic slavery.

A bonded labour racket in a brick kiln in Rajasthan kidnaps migrant workers from Odisha, confiscates their identity documents, and forces them to work indefinitely under threat of violence, effectively holding them in slavery.

A child is abducted from a slum in Mumbai and transported to another state where they are made to work in a carpet-weaving factory, denied education, freedom of movement, or wages — constituting slavery as contemplated under Section 140.

An organised crime group abducts men from Bihar, transports them to a remote agricultural estate in another state, and forces them to cultivate land under armed guard without pay or the ability to leave, meeting the threshold of slavery under the Act.

A young person is lured by a false job offer, then kidnapped and sold to a brothel operator who treats the victim as a purchased commodity with no autonomy, combining trafficking with practices of slavery.
what_it_covers: A person kidnapped or abducted and thereafter bought, sold, or held as a possession by another individual or group with full control over their movements and labour.
Any condition in which a human being is treated as chattel — denied wages, freedom of movement, and personal autonomy — as a result of being forcibly removed from their place of origin.
Holding an abducted person in a permanent state of compelled servitude under threat of violence, debt bondage, or physical restraint, without any legal basis for such detention.
Practices similar to slavery as described under Section 143, including servitude and forced labour arising from trafficking, where the victim is exploited as though owned by the perpetrator.
what_it_excludes: Voluntary employment relationships, even those involving harsh or exploitative working conditions that do not amount to complete loss of personal liberty and ownership over the person.
Imprisonment or lawful detention of convicted persons by the State, which involves restriction of liberty under due process of law and does not constitute slavery.
Contractual domestic service or bonded labour arrangements that, while potentially unlawful under other statutes, do not arise from kidnapping or abduction as required by the context of Section 140.
Situations of wrongful confinement under Section 126 where the motive is not subjection to slavery but rather temporary illegal detention without the element of treating the person as property.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a kidnapping or abduction is committed with intent to subject the victim to slavery determines the severity of punishment under Section 140, elevating the offence to one attracting imprisonment of either description for up to ten years along with fine. Establishing that the accused intended or knew the victim would be subjected to slavery is a key element that distinguishes this aggravated form of abduction from lesser offences of wrongful confinement or ordinary kidnapping.

definitions.definition: Theft is snatching if, in order to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes or secures or grabs or takes away from any person or from his possession any movable property.
definitions.plain_english: Snatching is a type of theft where someone suddenly, quickly, or forcibly grabs or takes away a belonging from another person or from their immediate possession. The key element is the abrupt or forceful manner of taking the property directly from the victim or from their control. It is treated as a distinct and more serious form of theft because of the direct interaction with the victim.
real_world_examples: A chain-snatcher on a motorcycle rides past a woman walking on a street in Mumbai and rips her gold necklace off her neck without stopping.
A thief at a busy railway station in Delhi suddenly grabs a passenger's mobile phone from their hand while they are looking at it and runs away.
An individual snatches a purse from an elderly woman's hand at a market in Bengaluru by yanking it forcibly while she is shopping.
A person on foot grabs a tourist's camera bag hanging from their shoulder in Jaipur and sprints away before the victim can react.
A snatcher at a bus stop in Hyderabad quickly seizes a commuter's wallet from their front pocket as the bus doors open and flees into the crowd.
what_it_covers: Suddenly grabbing a mobile phone, wallet, or jewellery directly from a person's hand or body.
Forcibly pulling away a bag or purse that a victim is actively holding or carrying.
Quickly seizing any movable property that is in the immediate physical possession or control of a person, whether on their body or held by them.
A snatch committed by a person on a vehicle (e.g., motorcycle) who grabs property from a pedestrian while passing.
Acts where the property is taken from the victim's possession even without physical assault, as long as the taking is sudden or quick.
what_it_excludes: Theft committed without any direct or immediate interaction with the victim, such as picking property from an unattended bag or an empty room (ordinary theft, not snatching).
Robbery, where the offender uses or threatens to use force beyond the act of snatching itself, causing or attempting to cause harm to ensure submission.
Extortion, where the offender compels the victim to deliver property through threats or coercion communicated in advance rather than sudden physical seizure.
Cheating or fraud-based taking of property, where the victim voluntarily hands over property due to deception rather than having it suddenly grabbed.

definitions.definition: The term 'soldier' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used throughout the Act, it refers to a person enrolled in the Army of the Government of India, subject to military law, who owes allegiance and duty to the State and may be bound by lawful orders of superior officers. A soldier is distinct from a sailor or airman, being specifically a member of the land-based armed forces.
definitions.plain_english: A 'soldier' is a person who is officially enlisted and serving in the Indian Army. This person is required to follow lawful orders from their commanding officers and owes loyalty and service to the Government of India. The term distinguishes Army personnel from those serving in the Navy (sailors) or Air Force (airmen).
real_world_examples: A jawaan of the Indian Army deployed during a riot in a sensitive district fires upon a mob on the direct order of his commanding officer acting within lawful authority — such a soldier commits no offence under Section 14 of the BNS, 2023.

A civilian attempts to bribe a soldier posted at a sensitive border installation to abandon his post or share classified movement information — the civilian can be prosecuted under Section 164 for seducing a soldier from his duty.

A political activist distributes pamphlets inside an Army cantonment area urging soldiers to disobey orders and stage a protest against government policy — this could constitute an attempt to seduce a soldier from his allegiance under Section 159.

A soldier serving in the Indian Army stationed in Jammu & Kashmir deserts his unit during an active counter-insurgency operation — while primarily governed by the Army Act, 1950, references to his status as a 'soldier' are also relevant to provisions of the BNS, 2023 concerning mutiny and desertion.

An individual knowingly spreads false propaganda online targeting soldiers of a particular regiment, urging them to mutiny against their officers — such a person may be liable under Section 159 for abetting mutiny of a soldier.

A soldier who, acting under a genuine mistake of fact and in good faith, believes he is bound by a lawful command and carries out an act that causes harm, is protected from criminal liability under Section 14 of the BNS, 2023.
what_it_covers: A commissioned or non-commissioned officer or enrollee serving in the Indian Army under the Government of India.
A soldier acting under lawful orders of a superior officer in situations such as riot control or crowd dispersal.
A soldier who may be the target of abetment of mutiny, seduction from duty, or attempts to undermine allegiance under Sections 159, 160, 164, 167, and 168 of the BNS, 2023.
A soldier who, by reason of a mistake of fact and in good faith, believes himself bound by law to carry out a particular act.
A person enrolled under the Army Act, 1950, serving in any capacity within the land forces of the Government of India.
what_it_excludes: Sailors, who are members of the Indian Navy and are separately categorised under the same provisions of the BNS, 2023.
Airmen, who serve in the Indian Air Force and are also separately identified as a distinct category from soldiers.
Officers of para-military or Central Armed Police Forces (such as CRPF, BSF, CISF) who are not part of the regular Indian Army.
Civilian defence employees or contractors working for the Ministry of Defence who do not hold a military enrolment or commission.
Retired or discharged Army personnel who are no longer in active service and thus no longer bound by military duty and allegiance in the operational sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'soldier' determines the applicability of special protections under Section 14 (act done under lawful command) and also defines who can be the victim of offences under Sections 159, 160, 164, 167, and 168 — such as abetment of mutiny or seduction from duty — which carry severe penalties including imprisonment for life or death. It also determines whether the saving clause in Section 1 regarding special military laws applies, potentially excluding the BNS, 2023 and invoking the Army Act, 1950 instead.

definitions.definition: Solitary confinement is a form of imprisonment ordered by a Court upon conviction of an offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment, whereby the offender is kept in isolation for a portion of the sentenced term, not exceeding three months in total, scaled to the length of imprisonment, and subject to the restriction that no single period of such confinement shall exceed fourteen days at a time, with intervening intervals of freedom from such confinement of not less duration than the confinement period itself.
definitions.plain_english: Solitary confinement means keeping a convicted prisoner completely alone and isolated from other prisoners for a limited portion of their jail sentence. A court can only order this when the punishment includes rigorous (hard labour) imprisonment, and it comes with strict time limits — no more than three months in total, and never more than fourteen days in a single stretch. After each period of isolation, the prisoner must be given a break of at least the same length before being put in solitary confinement again.
real_world_examples: A person convicted of armed robbery in Delhi and sentenced to two years of rigorous imprisonment may be ordered by the Sessions Court to undergo up to three months of solitary confinement in Tihar Jail, broken into periods of no more than fourteen days at a time.

A convict in Mumbai sentenced to eight months of rigorous imprisonment for a violent assault can be placed in solitary confinement for a maximum of two months in total, in isolated stretches not exceeding fourteen days each, with equally long free intervals in between.

A person convicted of dacoity and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year in a Kolkata court may be ordered to serve up to two months of solitary confinement in Alipore Central Jail, ensuring that no single stretch exceeds fourteen days and proper intervals are maintained.

A prisoner in Chennai's Puzhal Central Prison serving three years of rigorous imprisonment for a serious offence under the BNS can be subjected to solitary confinement for up to three months total, but each stint is capped at fourteen days and must be followed by a gap of at least fourteen days before the next begins.

A convict sentenced to five months of rigorous imprisonment for rioting in Pune may be ordered to undergo up to one month of solitary confinement, as the total imprisonment term does not exceed six months, with no single period of isolation lasting more than fourteen days.
what_it_covers: Any portion of a rigorous imprisonment sentence during which a convicted offender is kept in isolation from other prisoners, as expressly ordered by the sentencing court.
Periods of isolation not exceeding fourteen days at a time, provided the mandatory free intervals of equal or greater duration are observed between successive solitary confinement periods.

Graduated maximum durations of solitary confinement scaled to sentence length: up to one month for sentences of six months or less, up to two months for sentences between six months and one year, and up to three months for sentences exceeding one year.

Confinement ordered only in conjunction with a sentence of rigorous imprisonment, making the isolation a supplementary punitive measure imposed at the court's discretion within the convicted sentence.

Situations where, for sentences exceeding three months of rigorous imprisonment, the solitary confinement within any single calendar month of the total imprisonment term does not exceed seven days, with equal intervening intervals.
what_it_excludes: Prisoners sentenced to simple imprisonment, as solitary confinement under the BNS can only be ordered where the court has the power to impose rigorous imprisonment for the offence.
Any period of isolation exceeding fourteen consecutive days within a single stretch, which is absolutely prohibited regardless of the total sentence length or court order.
Solitary confinement extending beyond three months in aggregate over the entire sentence, even where the sentence is for a very long term of rigorous imprisonment.
Persons held in preventive detention, remand, or undertrial custody, as solitary confinement under Sections 11 and 12 applies only upon conviction and sentencing by a competent court.
Administrative disciplinary segregation imposed by prison authorities under prison regulations, which is distinct from judicially ordered solitary confinement under this Sanhita.
Confinement ordered without a corresponding interval of freedom of at least equal duration, as such intervals are a mandatory safeguard and their absence would render the confinement unlawful.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a sentence qualifies as solitary confinement under Sections 11 and 12 determines the legality of the mode and duration of a convict's isolation in prison — courts can only impose it alongside rigorous imprisonment, and any breach of the prescribed time limits or interval requirements renders the confinement illegal, potentially exposing prison authorities to liability and entitling the prisoner to legal relief. It directly governs the severity and manner of execution of a criminal sentence, acting as a constitutional and statutory safeguard against excessive punitive isolation.
