definitions.definition: Sovereignty, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, refers to the supreme and independent authority of India as a nation-state, encompassing its right to self-governance, freedom from external domination, and the inviolable power of the Indian State to govern its territory and people without interference. It is not expressly defined in a standalone provision but is consistently employed in Sections 113, 152, and 197 to denote the foundational constitutional attribute of India's independent statehood that must be preserved and upheld.
definitions.plain_english: Sovereignty means India's status as a fully independent country that has the ultimate power to govern itself without being controlled or dictated to by any foreign power or internal group seeking to break that authority. It is the idea that India alone decides its own laws, governance, and future. When someone tries to undermine this — through terrorism, rebellion, or spreading ideas that weaken India's independent authority — they are threatening sovereignty. Protecting sovereignty is one of the most fundamental duties recognised by Indian law.
real_world_examples: A group of individuals based in a foreign country funds and coordinates armed militants operating in Jammu & Kashmir to destabilise the Indian government's control over the region, directly threatening India's sovereignty — an act that could attract prosecution under Section 113 (terrorist act) and Section 152 of the BNS.

A social media influencer in India repeatedly publishes videos asserting that a particular northeastern state should secede and align itself with a neighbouring country, encouraging separatist sentiment — this endangers sovereignty and integrity of India and is punishable under Section 152.

A political speaker at a public rally makes speeches claiming that members of a particular religious community can never be truly loyal to India or uphold its sovereignty, thereby making imputations prejudicial to national integration — this falls under Section 197 of the BNS.

A terrorist cell plants explosives at a critical defence installation and transmits encrypted communications to a foreign state intelligence agency, aiming to overawe the Government of India — this constitutes a terrorist act threatening the sovereignty and security of India under Section 113.

A foreign-funded NGO circulates pamphlets demanding the creation of a separate nation carved out of Indian territory on the basis of linguistic identity, with the intent to excite subversive activities against the Union — this constitutes an act endangering sovereignty under Section 152.

An individual knowingly distributes large quantities of counterfeit Indian currency notes received from across the border to destabilise India's monetary system and weaken its economic sovereignty, attracting liability under Section 113 of the BNS.
what_it_covers: India's supreme authority to govern its entire territory free from foreign control or internal armed rebellion, as protected under Section 152.

The independent statehood of India that terrorist acts under Section 113 aim to threaten, including acts targeting defence infrastructure, essential supplies, or public functionaries with intent to overawe the Government.
The constitutional attribute of India's self-governance that citizens are expected to uphold, any imputation denying a class of persons' allegiance to which is penalised under Section 197.
Acts that use financial means, electronic communication, spoken or written words, or visible representation to excite secession or subversive activities that endanger India's sovereign status.
India's economic sovereignty, explicitly referenced in Section 113 through the inclusion of damage to monetary stability via counterfeit currency as a terrorist act.
what_it_excludes: Lawful criticism of government policies or administrative actions expressed through peaceful and democratic means, which is expressly saved by the proviso to Section 152 and does not constitute an attack on sovereignty.
Academic, journalistic, or literary discussions analysing India's sovereign status, federalism, or historical events that do not incite secession or armed rebellion.

Disputes between individuals or private parties relating to property, contracts, or personal rights, which do not implicate the State's supreme authority and thus fall outside the sovereignty framework of the BNS.
Electoral dissent, political opposition, or voting against the ruling government, which is a constitutionally protected democratic exercise and not a threat to sovereignty.
International treaties or agreements entered into by the Government of India that may limit certain exercises of power, as these are consensual acts of sovereign will, not threats to sovereignty.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is found to threaten India's sovereignty determines the applicability of the most severe offences under the BNS — including the terrorist act under Section 113 (punishable with death or imprisonment for life) and the offence under Section 152 (punishable with imprisonment for life or up to seven years) — making sovereignty a definitional threshold that directly governs whether the gravest criminal liabilities are triggered. Additionally, under Section 197, imputations denying a class of persons' duty to uphold sovereignty attract criminal punishment, making the concept central to offences against national integration.

definitions.definition: When property is in the possession of a person's spouse, on account of that person, it is in that person's possession within the meaning of this Sanhita. In the context of Section 249, 'spouse' refers to a legally married husband or wife, being the person to whom one is lawfully wedded under any personal law, customary law, or statutory law applicable in India.
definitions.plain_english: A 'spouse' is the person you are legally married to — your husband or wife. In Indian law under the BNS, this term is used to recognise the close legal bond between married partners, particularly in matters of property possession and matrimonial offences. For example, property held by your spouse on your behalf is treated as being in your own possession.
real_world_examples: A husband leaves his gold ornaments and cash with his wife for safekeeping while he travels abroad for work; under BNS Section 3, those valuables are legally considered to be in his possession, not hers, since she holds them on his account as his spouse.

A woman married under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is subjected to repeated cruelty by her husband demanding more dowry; she qualifies as a 'spouse' under BNS Section 249 which penalises cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards his wife.

A man married under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 is accused of causing mental harassment and wilful conduct to his wife that drives her to contemplate suicide; the wife is his 'spouse' for the purpose of invoking Section 249 of the BNS.

A Muslim woman lawfully married under personal law whose husband subjects her to repeated physical abuse is recognised as a 'spouse' under BNS Section 249, entitling her to protection under the cruelty provision regardless of the personal law governing her marriage.

A couple married under a tribal customary law recognised by the State claims the protection of BNS matrimonial provisions; the wife, as a lawfully wedded spouse, can invoke Section 249 if subjected to cruelty by her husband or in-laws.
what_it_covers: A wife lawfully married under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, who is subject to cruelty by her husband or his relatives under BNS Section 249.
A husband or wife married under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, or any other applicable statutory or personal law in India.
Property held by a spouse on behalf of the other spouse, which is deemed to be in the possession of that other spouse under Section 3 of the BNS.
A wife married under Muslim personal law or Christian marriage law whose husband subjects her to wilful conduct causing harm or danger.
A spouse in a customary marriage recognised by the applicable State law or tribal law, for the purpose of matrimonial offence provisions.
what_it_excludes: Live-in partners or couples in a relationship-in-the-nature-of-marriage who are not formally and lawfully wedded, as they do not acquire the status of 'spouse' under this provision.
A former spouse whose marriage has been dissolved by a valid decree of divorce, as the marital legal bond no longer subsists at the time of the alleged offence.
A party to a void marriage that has been declared null and void by a competent court, since no legal marital status exists between the parties.
Fiancés, betrothed persons, or individuals in engagement relationships who have not yet solemnised a lawful marriage.
Cohabitants or domestic partners who share a household but have not entered into a legally recognised marriage under any applicable personal, customary, or statutory law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'spouse' is critical because Section 249 of the BNS exclusively penalises cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards his wife, meaning the existence of a lawful spousal relationship is a prerequisite to attract the offence — without it, the provision cannot be invoked. Additionally, under Section 3, the spousal relationship determines constructive possession of property, which can affect liability in offences involving theft, misappropriation, or breach of trust.

Examples: A husband leaves his gold ornaments and cash with his wife for safekeeping while he travels abroad for work; under BNS Section 3, those valuables are legally considered to be in his possession, not hers, since she holds them on his account as his spouse. | A woman married under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is subjected to repeated cruelty by her husband demanding more dowry; she qualifies as a 'spouse' under BNS Section 249 which penalises cruelty by a husband or his relatives towards his wife. | A man married under the Special Marriage Act, 1954 is accused of causing mental harassment and wilful conduct to his wife that drives her to contemplate suicide; the wife is his 'spouse' for the purpose of invoking Section 249 of the BNS. | A Muslim woman lawfully married under personal law whose husband subjects her to repeated physical abuse is recognised as a 'spouse' under BNS Section 249, entitling her to protection under the cruelty provision regardless of the personal law governing her marriage. | A couple married under a tribal customary law recognised by the State claims the protection of BNS matrimonial provisions; the wife, as a lawfully wedded spouse, can invoke Section 249 if subjected to cruelty by her husband or in-laws.

definitions.definition: Stalking means any conduct by a man who follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact such woman to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest by such woman; or monitors the use by a woman of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication. Such conduct does not amount to stalking if the man proves it was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime, or was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law, or the conduct was reasonable and justified under the particular circumstances.
definitions.plain_english: Stalking is when a man keeps following or trying to contact a woman even after she has made it clear she is not interested, or when he secretly tracks or monitors her online activity, emails, or other digital communications. It is treated as a criminal offence under Indian law. However, if the person can prove the conduct was done for legitimate law enforcement, legal compliance, or was genuinely reasonable under the circumstances, it may not be considered stalking.
real_world_examples: A man in Mumbai repeatedly waits outside a woman's office and calls her multiple times a day despite her blocking his number and explicitly telling him to stop contacting her.
A rejected suitor in Delhi creates fake social media profiles to monitor a woman's Instagram, WhatsApp, and email activity and tracks her location through her posts without her knowledge.
A man in Bengaluru follows a woman on her daily commute route, appears at her gym, her marketplace, and her neighbourhood park after she has communicated she does not wish to interact with him.
An ex-boyfriend in Chennai uses spyware installed on his former partner's phone to intercept her WhatsApp messages, read her emails, and track her conversations with others.
A man in Kolkata sends repeated friend requests, messages through multiple platforms, and shows up at a woman's college campus after university authorities have already warned him to stay away.
what_it_covers: Physically following a woman to her workplace, home, or public spaces repeatedly after she has shown clear disinterest.
Monitoring a woman's internet usage, email accounts, or electronic communications such as WhatsApp, social media, or other digital platforms without her consent.
Repeatedly attempting to contact a woman through calls, messages, or social media to force personal interaction despite her explicit rejection.
Using third parties or intermediaries to gather information about a woman's whereabouts or digital activity as part of a pattern of surveillance.
Showing up uninvited at locations a woman frequents in a persistent pattern that signals intent to foster unwanted personal interaction.
what_it_excludes: Conduct pursued by a person for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime, provided the man can prove this justification.
Conduct carried out under a legal obligation, condition, or requirement imposed by a competent authority or law, such as a court-ordered supervision.
Incidental or single-instance contact that does not form part of a repeated pattern and is not accompanied by a clear indication of disinterest from the woman.
Conduct by a woman against another person, as Section 78 explicitly applies only to conduct by a man against a woman.
Reasonable and proportionate conduct that can be justified under the specific circumstances of the case, as recognised by the proviso to Section 78.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as stalking under Section 78 determines criminal liability, triggering imprisonment of up to three years on first conviction and up to five years on subsequent convictions, along with fines. The definition also activates the burden-shifting proviso, placing the obligation on the accused man to prove any claimed exemption, making it a critical threshold for prosecution and sentencing.

definitions.term: stamp issued by Government for purpose of revenue
definitions.definition: A stamp issued by the Government of India or any State Government for the purpose of collecting revenue, including court fee stamps, adhesive stamps used under the Stamp Act, and other fiscal stamps affixed to documents or instruments to evidence payment of duty or tax to the Government.
definitions.plain_english: A 'stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue' refers to any official stamp that the government uses to collect taxes or duties — for example, the stamps you paste on legal documents, court papers, or property agreements to show you have paid the required government fee. These are different from postage stamps used for mailing letters. Making, copying, or dealing in fake versions of such stamps is a serious crime.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai is found with a machine capable of printing counterfeit court fee stamps (used under the Court Fees Act, 1870) that are indistinguishable from genuine ones, intending to sell them to litigants to avoid paying legitimate court fees.

A stamp vendor in Delhi is caught with forged non-judicial stamp papers (commonly used for agreements and affidavits under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899) and a die used to emboss the fake Government seal on blank paper.
A syndicate in Hyderabad manufactures and distributes counterfeit revenue stamps used by the state government on property sale deeds, depriving the State exchequer of stamp duty revenue.

A shopkeeper in Kolkata is discovered in possession of chemicals and printing materials specifically used to replicate the distinctive design of Central Government adhesive revenue stamps used for share transfer documents.

A government contractor in Chennai is found with machinery capable of producing fake e-stamps (issued by the Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd. on behalf of the state government) used for registration of immovable properties.
what_it_covers: Court fee stamps issued under the Court Fees Act, 1870, affixed to plaints, petitions, and other judicial documents to evidence payment of court fees.
Non-judicial stamp papers issued by State Governments under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, used for agreements, affidavits, sale deeds, and other instruments attracting stamp duty.
Adhesive revenue stamps issued by the Central or State Government used on share transfer forms, receipts, insurance policies, and other dutiable instruments.
E-stamps or electronically generated revenue stamps issued by authorised government agencies for property registration and other revenue purposes.
Special adhesive stamps issued by State Governments for specific fiscal purposes such as those used under the Bombay Stamp Act or similar state legislation.
what_it_excludes: Postage stamps issued by the Department of Posts for the purpose of prepaying postal charges, which are not issued for revenue collection purposes.
Bank-notes and currency-notes, which are separately enumerated in Section 181 as distinct categories and are not considered stamps issued for revenue.
Commemorative or philatelic stamps issued by the Government for collection purposes that carry no revenue or fiscal function.
Private or corporate stamps, seals, or tokens that may resemble official stamps but are not issued by any Government authority for tax or duty collection.
Fictitious stamps, which are separately defined under the BNS and fall under a distinct legal category governing forgery of documents.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an item qualifies as a 'stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue' is critical because Section 181 of the BNS imposes the extreme penalty of imprisonment for life (or up to ten years with fine) on anyone who makes, mends, buys, sells, or possesses machinery or materials for forging or counterfeiting such stamps; the definition thus determines whether this severe penal provision is attracted or whether a lesser offence under forgery or fraud applies.

definitions.definition: A 'State lottery' means a lottery conducted or organised by the State Government itself, or a lottery expressly authorised by the State Government, which is thereby distinguished from a private or unauthorised lottery. The term is used in Section 297 to carve out a lawful exception to the offence of keeping a lottery office.
definitions.plain_english: A State lottery is a lottery that is either run directly by a state government or officially permitted by it. Because the government has sanctioned it, running an office for such a lottery is legal and not a punishable offence. This is different from private or unlicensed lotteries, which are illegal under the law.
real_world_examples: The Kerala State Lotteries Department conducts weekly draws such as 'Win-Win' and 'Akshaya' — these are classic State lotteries, and a licensed ticket-selling shop operating for them is fully protected under Section 297.

The Punjab State Lotteries organised by the Directorate of Punjab State Lotteries is a State lottery; any office established to conduct its draws is explicitly exempted from prosecution under Section 297.

Nagaland's Directorate of Nagaland State Lotteries operates 'Dear' branded lotteries across India — a distributor's office handling these draws qualifies as operating for a State lottery and is not an offence.

A Maharashtra State-authorised lottery scheme run under a government gazette notification would be a State lottery, meaning an agent selling tickets from a registered premise would not be liable under Section 297.

If a private company obtains a formal authorisation from the State Government of Sikkim under applicable lottery regulations to operate a lottery on behalf of the state, that lottery is 'authorised by the State Government' and thus qualifies as a State lottery for the purposes of Section 297.

A private entity operating a lottery without any state sanction — even if it calls itself a 'state fund raiser' — does not qualify as a State lottery and its operators remain liable under Section 297.
what_it_covers: Lotteries directly conducted and managed by a State Government through its own department or directorate, such as Kerala State Lotteries or Nagaland State Lotteries.
Lotteries operated by a private entity that has received formal, documented authorisation from a State Government through a gazette notification or statutory order.
Offices or premises established specifically to draw tickets, manage results, or sell tickets for a lottery falling under either of the above two categories.
Bumper or special lottery draws conducted under the banner of an existing State lottery scheme, as they derive their authority from the same state sanction.
what_it_excludes: Privately organised lotteries with no state sanction or authorisation, even if they are philanthropic or charitable in nature.
Online or digital lottery schemes operated by private companies without explicit State Government authorisation, regardless of their commercial popularity.
Lotteries authorised by a foreign government or a Union Territory administration that lacks the specific status of a 'State Government' under Indian law.
Informal chit-fund style draws or raffles conducted within housing societies or clubs, which are not backed by any State Government authority.
Lotteries that may have previously been authorised but whose authorisation has expired, been revoked, or was not renewed by the State Government.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a lottery qualifies as a 'State lottery' is the decisive factor under Section 297 — operating an office for a State lottery or a State-authorised lottery is entirely lawful, whereas running an equivalent office for any other lottery attracts imprisonment up to six months or a fine or both. The classification thus either completely immunises the operator from criminal liability or exposes them to prosecution.

definitions.definition: A 'State prisoner' is a person confined by order of the Government on grounds of State security, political reasons, or reasons of State policy, as distinguished from a person confined under the ordinary criminal law. Such a prisoner is held in lawful custody and their escape, whether facilitated voluntarily or negligently by a public servant, or aided by any person, constitutes a distinct category of offence under this Sanhita.
definitions.plain_english: A State prisoner is someone who is locked up by the government not because they committed an ordinary crime, but for political or national security reasons — for example, someone considered a threat to the stability or safety of the country. They are held under special government orders rather than through the regular criminal court process. Because of the sensitive nature of their detention, the law treats any escape or assistance in escaping very seriously.
real_world_examples: A person detained by the Central Government under a preventive detention law such as the National Security Act, 1980, on grounds of acting in a manner prejudicial to national security, and held in a designated jail, qualifies as a State prisoner.

A foreign national captured during an armed border conflict with a neighbouring country and held in an Indian detention facility under government orders pending diplomatic resolution would be treated as a State prisoner.

A political leader detained by the State Government under a special executive order during a period of internal disturbance, without being charged under ordinary criminal law, would fall within the category of a State prisoner.

A separatist leader from a sensitive region detained by the Union Government under executive authority due to concerns about the integrity of India, and held in a high-security prison, would be classified as a State prisoner.

An individual detained pursuant to a detention order issued under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA) on grounds affecting the economic security of the State, when held under direct government authority, may be classified as a State prisoner.
what_it_covers: Persons detained by the Central or State Government under executive authority for reasons of State policy, public safety, or national security, without being tried under ordinary criminal law.
Individuals held under preventive detention statutes such as the National Security Act, where the government believes their release would be prejudicial to national security or public order.
A State prisoner who is permitted to move on parole within defined limits in India but goes beyond those limits, as such a person is expressly deemed to have escaped from lawful custody.
Foreign nationals or enemy agents detained during wartime or periods of armed conflict under government orders pending the resolution of hostilities or diplomatic proceedings.
Persons detained under special executive orders during internal disturbances or emergencies, where ordinary criminal proceedings have not been initiated.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary criminal undertrial prisoners or convicts detained pursuant to a court order under the regular criminal justice process, who are governed by separate provisions.
Prisoners of war, who are separately categorised and recognised as a distinct class alongside State prisoners in Sections 156, 157, and 158 of the Sanhita.

Persons held in police custody or judicial remand during the ordinary investigation or trial of a cognizable offence, as their detention flows from a judicial or magistrial order rather than executive State authority.
Civil prisoners detained for failure to comply with civil court decrees or orders, such as for non-payment of a debt, as their confinement is neither on grounds of State policy nor national security.
Persons detained in hospitals, mental institutions, or rehabilitation centres under welfare or health legislation, as such confinement is not for State security or political reasons.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a confined person qualifies as a 'State prisoner' directly determines which penal provisions apply to those who facilitate or enable their escape: a public servant who voluntarily allows a State prisoner to escape faces imprisonment for life or up to ten years under Section 156, while negligent sufferance of escape attracts up to three years under Section 157, and any person aiding, rescuing, or harbouring such a prisoner faces life imprisonment or up to ten years under Section 158. The classification thus triggers a significantly more severe penal regime than applies to the escape of ordinary criminal prisoners.

definitions.definition: A State prisoner is a person confined by order of the Government or under authority of the State on grounds of State security, political reasons, or public safety, rather than pursuant to an ordinary criminal conviction. A State prisoner permitted to be at large on parole within certain limits in India is deemed to escape from lawful custody if he goes beyond the limits within which he is allowed to be at large.
definitions.plain_english: A 'state prisoner' is someone who has been imprisoned by the government for reasons related to the security or safety of the country or state — for example, someone considered a political threat — rather than for an ordinary crime. Even if such a person is allowed to move around freely within certain permitted boundaries (parole), if they cross those boundaries, they are treated as having escaped from lawful custody. This is different from a regular criminal prisoner who is jailed after a court conviction.
real_world_examples: A person detained under a preventive detention law such as the National Security Act, 1980, by order of a State Government due to suspected threat to public order, who is kept in a designated facility — such a person qualifies as a state prisoner.

A political detainee held during a period of civil unrest in a sensitive region of India, confined by executive order without a criminal trial, who is kept in a designated jail or camp under government custody.

A foreign national or agent believed to be engaged in espionage against India, detained by executive order of the Central Government pending diplomatic or security proceedings, held in a secure facility.

A state prisoner granted conditional parole allowing movement only within the district of Pune; if he travels to Mumbai without permission, he is deemed to have escaped from lawful custody under Section 158 of the BNS, 2023.

A leader of a separatist movement detained by the Government of a State under executive powers on grounds of threat to the integrity of India, held in a specified prison — assisting such a person to flee would attract liability under Section 158.
what_it_covers: Persons detained by executive order of the Central or State Government on grounds of national security or public safety without a criminal trial.
Individuals held under preventive detention laws (e.g., National Security Act, COFEPOSA) who are confined in a designated place by government authority.
A state prisoner released on parole but restricted to specific geographic limits in India, who is still considered in lawful custody while within those limits.
Foreign nationals detained by order of the Government of India as a threat to sovereignty or public order, confined pending State action.

definitions.definition: A 'statement of fact' means any assertion or representation purporting to convey factual information, as distinguished from opinion or commentary, made in relation to the personal character or conduct of a candidate in connection with an election. Under Section 175, such a statement becomes legally significant when it is false and is made or published with intent to affect the result of an election, and the maker either knows or believes it to be false or does not believe it to be true.
definitions.plain_english: A 'statement of fact' is a claim that presents itself as a true, verifiable piece of information about a real person or event — not merely someone's opinion or prediction. In the context of elections, it refers specifically to a factual claim made about a candidate's personal character or behaviour. The law treats this type of statement seriously because voters may rely on such claims when deciding how to vote.
real_world_examples: A political pamphlet distributed in a Lok Sabha constituency falsely states that the opposing candidate was convicted of fraud in 2019 — this is a statement of fact about personal conduct that the distributor knows to be untrue.
A social media post circulated during Maharashtra state elections falsely claims that a candidate accepted bribes from a builder, presented as a factual report rather than an allegation or opinion.

A press release issued by a rival party during Panchayat elections in Uttar Pradesh falsely asserts that a candidate abandoned his wife and children, intending to damage his reputation and electoral prospects.

A WhatsApp forward circulated widely in a Chennai constituency during Tamil Nadu elections falsely claims that a candidate holds foreign citizenship, a verifiable factual claim that the sender knows is false.

A campaign poster in Rajasthan falsely states that a female candidate was involved in a criminal case that was actually registered against a different person, presenting it as established fact to mislead voters.
what_it_covers: A written or oral claim about a candidate's past criminal record that is presented as factual but is known to be false by the person making it.

A published report asserting verifiable facts about a candidate's personal conduct — such as alleged corruption, marital misconduct, or financial fraud — that the publisher does not believe to be true.
Any digitally shared content (posts, videos, audio clips) that presents false biographical or behavioural information about a candidate as established fact during an election period.
Printed campaign material circulated by a rival party that falsely attributes specific disgraceful acts to a candidate, framed as factual reporting rather than political criticism.
what_it_excludes: Statements of opinion, political commentary, or value judgments about a candidate's policies or ideology, which do not purport to assert verifiable facts.
True statements about a candidate's personal character or conduct, even if damaging to their electoral prospects, since the provision requires the statement to be false.
Statements made without any intent to affect the result of an election, such as academic or journalistic analysis published outside the electoral context.
Satirical or clearly hyperbolic content that no reasonable person would interpret as a genuine factual claim about a candidate's personal conduct.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as a 'statement of fact' under Section 175 determines whether the speaker can be held criminally liable and punished with fine for electoral falsehoods; if the communication is classified as mere opinion or satire, no offence under this section is made out. The distinction directly triggers or blocks prosecution for knowingly publishing false factual claims to manipulate election outcomes.

definitions.definition: Property the possession whereof has been transferred by theft, or by extortion, or by robbery, and property which has been criminally misappropriated or in respect of which criminal breach of trust has been committed, is designated as 'stolen property'; whether the transfer has been made, or the misappropriation or breach of trust has been committed, within or without India. But, if such property subsequently comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to the possession thereof, it then ceases to be stolen property.
definitions.plain_english: Stolen property refers to any property that has been wrongfully taken or misused through theft, extortion, robbery, criminal misappropriation, or criminal breach of trust — regardless of whether this happened inside or outside India. The property retains its 'stolen' status as long as it remains out of the hands of its rightful owner. Once the rightful owner or someone legally entitled to it regains possession, the property is no longer considered stolen property.
real_world_examples: A pickpocket steals a mobile phone from a passenger on the Delhi Metro; the phone is stolen property in the hands of the pickpocket or any subsequent buyer who receives it knowing it was stolen.

A warehouse manager entrusted with storing gold bullion for a jeweller in Mumbai dishonestly sells it to a third party; the gold constitutes stolen property as it was obtained through criminal breach of trust.
A gang in Bengaluru forcibly snatches a car at gunpoint (robbery) and sells it to a second-hand dealer who is aware of its origin; the car remains stolen property in the dealer's possession.

A contractor in Chennai collects advance payment through extortion from a business owner and uses the money to purchase equipment; that money is stolen property because its possession was transferred by extortion.

A domestic worker in Kolkata secretly takes jewellery from her employer's locker without consent; if the police recover the jewellery from a pawnshop where it was pledged, it remains stolen property until returned to the rightful owner.

Goods smuggled from across the border through criminal misappropriation of a government consignment remain stolen property even though the offence occurred outside India, as the Act expressly covers such cross-border cases.
what_it_covers: Movable property whose possession was transferred by theft under Section 303, including goods snatched or taken without consent.
Property obtained through extortion, where the victim was compelled by threat or force to part with it.
Property taken in the course of a robbery or dacoity where force or threat was used against the possessor.
Property that has been criminally misappropriated, i.e., dishonestly converted to one's own use by a person who came into possession of it lawfully.
Property in respect of which criminal breach of trust has been committed, such as funds or goods dishonestly dealt with by a trustee, agent, or employee.
Property falling under any of the above categories even if the original offence was committed outside India, provided the property is found within India.
what_it_excludes: Property that has been returned to and re-possessed by its lawful owner or a person legally entitled to possess it, as it ceases to be stolen property upon such restoration.
Property taken under a genuine and honest claim of right, where there is no dishonest intention, since such taking does not constitute theft or criminal misappropriation.
Immovable property such as land or buildings, as stolen property under the Act is confined to movable property capable of being transferred through theft, robbery, extortion, or misappropriation.
Property obtained through fraud or cheating alone (without a theft, robbery, extortion, misappropriation, or breach of trust), as the definition does not expressly include such offences.
Property in the possession of a bona fide purchaser who has acquired a legally valid title, once a court determines that lawful entitlement has been established and restored.
Lost property found and retained in good faith without knowledge of any prior criminal taking, where no criminal intent existed at the time of taking possession.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether property qualifies as 'stolen property' directly determines liability under Section 317 BNS, which punishes knowingly receiving or retaining such property, or assisting in its concealment or disposal; without this designation, no offence of receiving or handling stolen goods can be established. It also governs the scope of Section 252 (taking a gift to help recover stolen property) and the illustrations under Section 120 relating to coercive extraction of information about stolen property.

definitions.definition: The term 'substance' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; however, as used in Section 128, it denotes any physical material, matter, or medium — whether solid, liquid, gaseous, or otherwise — upon which marks, letters, figures, or expressions can be inscribed, impressed, or otherwise recorded, or which can be administered to or applied upon a person or thing to cause a particular effect.
definitions.plain_english: A 'substance' in this law simply refers to any physical material or matter. This could be anything from paper, metal, or wood that something is written on, to a chemical, liquid, or other material that is given to or applied on a person. The law uses this word broadly to cover any kind of material that plays a role in committing or describing an offence.
real_world_examples: A fraudster in Mumbai inscribes a fake government seal onto a piece of paper (a substance) to forge an official document, making the paper the substance upon which the deception is carried out under Section 128.
A person in Delhi slips a sedative powder (a substance) into someone's drink to render them unconscious before committing a crime, invoking the use of a harmful substance administered to the victim.
An accused in Chennai uses an acid or corrosive liquid (a substance) to destroy incriminating writing on a document, relying on the material to obliterate evidence relevant to an offence.
A counterfeiter in Kolkata uses metallic alloy (a substance) to mint fake coins resembling Indian currency, with the metal being the substance on which the counterfeit impression is made.
A factory owner in Surat adulterates food items by mixing a chemical substance into edible goods, where the adulterant material qualifies as a substance that causes harm when consumed.
what_it_covers: Paper, parchment, metal, wood, or any solid material on which letters, figures, or marks are inscribed to constitute a document or instrument of fraud.
Chemical compounds, liquids, powders, or gases administered to or applied upon a person or object to cause harm, unconsciousness, or destruction of evidence.
Metallic alloys or other materials used as the base for counterfeit coins, tokens, or seals bearing false impressions.
Edible or drinkable materials into which a noxious or harmful agent is mixed, resulting in adulterated food or drink.
Any corrosive, flammable, or explosive material used to damage property or injure persons in furtherance of an offence.
what_it_excludes: Intangible or purely digital data that exists only in electronic form without any physical medium, as these would fall under 'electronic record' rather than 'substance' in the physical sense.
Abstract concepts, ideas, or oral communications that have no material or physical form capable of being touched, inscribed upon, or administered.
Land or things permanently attached to the earth, which are separately categorised under 'movable property' definitions and are not treated as a 'substance' in the context of Section 128.
Living human beings or animals, who are distinct legal entities and are not classified as a 'substance' even when they are the target of a harmful material.
Legally recognised currency notes or bank notes in their proper form, which are specifically defined and governed under separate provisions of the Sanhita.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a material qualifies as a 'substance' under Section 128 directly determines whether an act of administering, applying, or inscribing upon it constitutes a cognisable offence, affecting charges related to poisoning, adulteration, forgery, or causing hurt by dangerous means. Misidentification of the material as falling outside the scope of 'substance' could block prosecution for serious offences involving physical harm or document fraud.

definitions.definition: Subversive activities, as used in Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, means any act, conduct, or activity — whether by words spoken or written, signs, visible representation, electronic communication, financial means, or otherwise — that purposely or knowingly seeks to undermine, destabilise, or overthrow the established constitutional order, sovereignty, unity, or integrity of India, particularly through exciting or attempting to excite secession or armed rebellion, or encouraging separatist sentiments.
definitions.plain_english: Subversive activities refer to actions that secretly or openly try to weaken or destroy the government, national unity, or the constitutional structure of India. This includes spreading propaganda, funding groups, or using any means of communication to encourage people to break away from India or take up arms against the State. The term covers a wide range of conduct — from speeches and pamphlets to online posts and financial support — that is aimed at destabilising the country from within.
real_world_examples: A person in Jammu & Kashmir systematically distributes pamphlets and operates encrypted social media channels calling for armed uprising against the Indian government and urging citizens to join secessionist militant groups.

An individual based in Punjab uses online fundraising platforms to channel money to organisations that openly advocate for the creation of a separate Khalistan state, knowing the funds will be used to incite rebellion.

A public speaker in a northeastern state delivers speeches at rallies explicitly encouraging local tribes to take up arms and secede from India, while simultaneously circulating videos of the speeches via messaging applications.

A group of persons, acting in concert, operates a network of websites and YouTube channels that disseminate content glorifying anti-India armed militant movements and actively recruiting youth to join separatist organisations operating along India's borders.

A journalist-turned-activist knowingly publishes fabricated reports accusing the Indian Army of genocide, designed not to seek lawful redress but specifically to incite communal violence and armed rebellion in a sensitive border district.

A financier covertly transfers funds through hawala networks to a banned organisation classified as a terrorist group, with full knowledge that the money will be used to sponsor subversive activities including bomb-making and sabotage of government installations.
what_it_covers: Spreading spoken, written, or digitally transmitted propaganda that actively encourages people to wage armed rebellion against the Indian State or its constitutional institutions.
Providing financial support or using monetary means to fund organisations or individuals engaged in secessionist movements or activities aimed at breaking up India's territorial integrity.

Organising, participating in, or inciting public gatherings, rallies, or online campaigns that explicitly promote separatism or encourage violent resistance against the sovereignty and unity of India.

Using electronic communications — including social media, encrypted messaging apps, or websites — to recruit individuals into armed separatist or anti-national organisations operating within or outside India.
Creating and distributing visible representations such as posters, banners, videos, or graphics that glorify secessionist movements or call for armed insurrection against the Indian government.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate criticism or disapprobation of government measures, policies, or administrative actions expressed through lawful means and aimed at obtaining reform through legal channels, as explicitly protected by the proviso to Section 152.

Peaceful political advocacy, democratic protests, or petitions calling for constitutional amendments, greater autonomy, or policy changes, provided they do not excite or attempt to excite secession, armed rebellion, or separatist feelings.

Academic, journalistic, or scholarly analysis of secessionist movements, historical rebellions, or separatist ideologies undertaken for bona fide research or education purposes without intent to incite such activities.
Artistic or literary works — films, novels, plays — that depict or critically examine themes of separatism or armed conflict without the purpose of exciting or encouraging actual subversive conduct.

Statements made by elected representatives or public functionaries within legislative forums, protected by parliamentary privilege, that critique government policy on sensitive matters such as federalism or regional autonomy.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as a 'subversive activity' under Section 152 determines whether the accused is liable to punishment of imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to seven years along with fine; establishing this element is essential to constitute the offence of endangering the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India under that section. The distinction between subversive activities and lawful disapprobation is also critical, as the latter is expressly excluded from criminal liability, making this definition central to balancing free speech with national security.

definitions.definition: The term 'sufficient cause' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 269, it denotes a legally adequate and reasonable justification or ground that excuses a person from the consequences of an act or omission that would otherwise constitute an offence, being a cause of such weight and cogency that a reasonable, prudent person would consider it a valid excuse in the circumstances.
definitions.plain_english: Sufficient cause means a good enough reason that justifies or excuses a person's behaviour under the law. It is a reason strong enough that a reasonable person would accept it as a valid excuse for not doing something or for doing something that might otherwise be wrong. Courts decide whether the reason given in a particular case is good enough to qualify as 'sufficient cause'.
real_world_examples: A person suffering from a sudden and severe infectious illness who unknowingly enters a public market and spreads disease may argue sufficient cause if they had no reasonable means to know they were carrying a communicable disease at that time.

A patient who is not informed by their treating doctor that they carry a contagious disease and therefore does not take precautions may claim sufficient cause for any resultant spread of that disease under Section 269.

A food vendor who sells items contaminated by a supplier without any visible or detectable signs of adulteration, having exercised all due care, may argue sufficient cause in defence against a charge of negligently spreading infection.

A migrant worker who travels between states before symptoms of a quarantinable disease appear, genuinely believing themselves to be healthy, may invoke sufficient cause to contest liability under Section 269 of the BNS.

A person who resides in a chawl in Mumbai and shares common facilities, contracting and unknowingly spreading a communicable disease due to no fault of their own, may raise sufficient cause if they had no prior indication of their infection.
what_it_covers: Lack of knowledge of a material fact that would have altered conduct, where such ignorance is genuine and reasonable in the circumstances.
Circumstances beyond the accused's control that made compliance with a legal duty impossible, such as sudden incapacitation or unavailability of medical care.
Reasonable reliance on a medical professional's advice or clearance that led the person to believe their conduct was safe and legally permissible.
Situations where a person took all practicable precautions but harm still occurred due to unforeseeable external factors.
what_it_excludes: Wilful negligence or deliberate disregard of a known risk of spreading a disease or infection, which cannot qualify as sufficient cause.
Self-induced intoxication or impairment that leads to failure to recognise or act upon a known health hazard.
Ignorance of the law itself, as mere legal ignorance is never accepted as sufficient cause in Indian criminal jurisprudence.
Conduct motivated by economic convenience, such as continuing to work despite knowledge of carrying a dangerous communicable disease, purely to avoid loss of income.
definitions.why_it_matters: Under Section 269 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a person is liable for negligently spreading a disease dangerous to life only if they lacked sufficient cause for their act or omission; if sufficient cause is established, criminal liability under that section is negated and no punishment is attracted. The presence or absence of sufficient cause thus directly determines whether the accused is convicted or acquitted of the offence of negligently doing any act known to be likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life.

definitions.definition: Suicide, as used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, refers to the act of voluntarily causing one's own death. Under Section 108, any person who abets the commission of suicide by another person is liable to punishment, with enhanced liability where the person who dies is a child, a person of unsound mind, a delirious person, or an intoxicated person incapable of understanding the nature of the act.
definitions.plain_english: Suicide means when a person intentionally ends their own life. While attempting or committing suicide is not itself a punishable offence under this law, the Act punishes those who encourage, incite, or assist another person in taking their own life. The law is especially strict when the deceased was a vulnerable person such as a child or someone mentally unwell.
real_world_examples: A husband repeatedly harasses his wife over dowry demands, driving her to end her life by consuming poison — the husband may be prosecuted for abetment of suicide under Section 108 read with Section 85-86 for cruelty.
A factory supervisor continuously humiliates and threatens a young apprentice worker, who subsequently hangs himself — the supervisor can be charged with abetment of suicide under Section 108.

A group of college students relentlessly bully a classmate on social media, posting defamatory content that leads the classmate to jump from a building — the perpetrators may face abetment of suicide charges.

A moneylender repeatedly threatens a farmer with public humiliation and physical harm over unpaid loans, causing the farmer to consume pesticide and die — the moneylender can be prosecuted for abetting the farmer's suicide.

A person sets up a fake romantic relationship online with a vulnerable teenager, then emotionally manipulates and threatens the teenager until the teenager takes their own life — the perpetrator faces enhanced punishment under Section 108 due to the victim being a child.
what_it_covers: The act of a person voluntarily ending their own life as a result of instigation, encouragement, or abetment by another person.
Cases where a woman is driven to commit suicide due to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives, attracting liability under Section 108 and related provisions.
Situations where a child or person of unsound mind is abetted into suicide, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 108.
Suicide resulting from persistent coercion, threats, or unlawful demands made by another person, establishing a causal link sufficient for abetment liability.
Any act, conspiracy, or intentional aid by a third party that facilitates or encourages the deceased to take their own life.
what_it_excludes: Accidental death that resembles suicide but lacks voluntary intent on the part of the deceased — such as unintentional overdose without suicidal intent.
Death caused directly by another person's physical act, which constitutes culpable homicide or murder rather than suicide abetment.

Cases where the deceased was under such extreme intoxication or unsoundness of mind that they had no capacity to form any intent — the criminal liability shifts entirely to the abettor but the act itself may not qualify as a willed suicide.
Euthanasia or assisted dying pursuant to a lawful court order or medical directive, which is governed separately and does not fall under this provision.
Mere expression of frustration or distress by a third party, without any direct instigation or intentional encouragement that a reasonable person would understand as abetment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as abetment of suicide under Section 108 determines criminal liability and sentencing — if established, the abettor faces imprisonment of up to ten years and fine, or up to twenty years where the deceased is a minor or person of unsound mind. This definition also intersects with cruelty offences under Section 85-86, where conduct driving a woman to suicide independently constitutes a punishable offence.

definitions.definition: The term 'suit' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 242, it refers to a civil proceeding instituted in a court of law by one party against another for the purpose of enforcing a right or obtaining a remedy, as distinct from a criminal prosecution. It encompasses any formal civil action before a competent court involving parties seeking adjudication of their legal rights, claims, or disputes.
definitions.plain_english: A 'suit' is a civil court case where one person takes another person or party to court to resolve a dispute, claim money, enforce a contract, or protect their rights. It is different from a criminal case, which is brought by the state. Examples include property disputes, divorce cases, debt recovery cases, or breach of contract claims filed in civil courts.
real_world_examples: A property owner files a civil suit in a District Court in Mumbai against a tenant for eviction and recovery of unpaid rent; someone impersonates the tenant during court proceedings and makes admissions on their behalf, attracting liability under Section 242.

A business partner in Delhi files a civil suit against another partner for dissolution of partnership and recovery of dues; a third party falsely personates the defendant and confesses judgment, causing wrongful financial loss.
In a land dispute suit in a Patna civil court, an impersonator poses as the plaintiff and withdraws the suit, thereby defrauding the genuine plaintiff of their legal remedy under Section 242.

A creditor in Chennai files a civil recovery suit against a debtor; an impersonator poses as the debtor, appears before the court, and causes a process to be issued against false addresses, obstructing justice.

In a matrimonial civil suit filed in a family court in Kolkata, a person falsely personates the respondent spouse and makes admissions regarding matrimonial property, leading to an unjust decree being passed.
what_it_covers: Civil suits for recovery of money or debt filed before a civil court in India.
Property dispute suits, including eviction suits, partition suits, and title declaration suits filed before competent civil courts.
Matrimonial suits such as divorce, maintenance, or restitution of conjugal rights filed before family courts.
Suits for specific performance of contracts or injunctions filed in civil courts.
Insolvency and dissolution suits filed by creditors or partners before appropriate civil forums.
what_it_excludes: Criminal prosecutions or criminal cases initiated by the State, which are separately referenced in Section 242 alongside suits.
Administrative or quasi-judicial proceedings before tribunals, regulatory bodies, or government authorities that are not courts of civil jurisdiction.
Writ petitions filed before High Courts or the Supreme Court under constitutional provisions, which are distinct from ordinary civil suits.
Arbitration proceedings conducted outside the court system, even if they resolve civil disputes between parties.
Revenue or tax proceedings before revenue authorities or income tax appellate forums, which are not civil suits in the traditional sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act of false personation occurs 'in a suit' is a qualifying condition under Section 242 of the BNS, 2023 — if the impersonation takes place within the context of a civil suit or criminal prosecution, the offender is liable for imprisonment up to three years, fine, or both. Without the suit or criminal prosecution nexus, the act of impersonation may not attract this specific penal provision, and the definition therefore directly determines the applicability and scope of criminal liability under Section 242.

definitions.definition: A summons is a formal legal direction or order issued by a public servant legally competent to do so, requiring a person to attend in person or by agent at a specified place and time, or to produce a document or electronic record before a court or authority. Though not expressly defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, it is used consistently across Sections 206, 207, and 208 as a compulsory process emanating from a competent public servant, non-compliance with which attracts criminal liability.
definitions.plain_english: A summons is an official written order from a government authority or court telling a person to appear at a particular place and time, or to bring documents. If you receive a summons, you are legally required to follow its instructions. Ignoring, hiding from, or trying to block a summons is a criminal offence under this law.
real_world_examples: A District Court in Lucknow issues a summons to a witness asking them to appear before the judge on a specific date in a criminal trial; the witness deliberately avoids receiving it by staying away from home — this amounts to absconding under Section 206.

A tax officer issues a summons to a businessman in Mumbai directing him to produce GST-related financial records before the authority; the businessman's employee physically blocks the process server from delivering the summons, attracting liability under Section 207.

A Magistrate in Chennai issues a summons to an accused person to appear before the court on a hearing date; the accused appears initially but leaves the courtroom before the proceedings conclude without permission, constituting an offence under Section 208.

A Labour Commissioner in Pune issues a notice-cum-summons to a factory owner to attend an inquiry in person regarding wage disputes; the factory owner intentionally tears down the summons affixed to the factory gate, violating Section 207.

A High Court in Delhi issues a subpoena (a form of summons) to a witness in a high-profile corruption case; the witness, without any lawful excuse, simply fails to appear on the required date, committing the offence described under Section 208.
what_it_covers: A written order from a Magistrate or court directing an accused, witness, or party to appear in person on a specified date.
A direction issued by a competent public servant requiring a person to produce a document or electronic record before a court or authority.
A notice issued by a government officer such as a tax commissioner, labour officer, or police officer requiring personal attendance at an inquiry or proceeding.
A subpoena issued by a High Court or subordinate court compelling a witness to appear and give evidence.
Any formal summons affixed to a premises by a process server in accordance with law when personal service is not possible.
what_it_excludes: Informal verbal requests or calls by a public servant that carry no formal legal compulsion — these do not constitute a summons.
Notices or communications issued by persons who are not legally competent public servants, such as private parties or unauthorised officials.
Voluntary invitations to attend a meeting or inquiry that impose no legal obligation on the recipient and carry no penal consequence for non-attendance.
Internal administrative orders directed at government employees under service rules, which do not arise from judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings.
Requests made under private contracts or arbitration clauses that require appearance before a private tribunal, as these do not proceed from a competent public servant.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a communication qualifies as a summons under Sections 206, 207, and 208 determines whether a person who absconds, obstructs service, or fails to attend is criminally liable for simple imprisonment up to six months and/or a fine up to ten thousand rupees; if the communication is not a valid summons from a competent public servant, no criminal offence under these sections is made out.

definitions.definition: 'Superintendent', in relation to a jail, remand home or other place of custody or a women's or children's institution, includes a person holding any other office in such jail, remand home, place or institution by virtue of which such person can exercise any authority or control over its inmates.
definitions.plain_english: A 'superintendent' is not just the person officially designated as superintendent of a jail, remand home, or similar institution — it includes any staff member or officer at such a place who has the practical power to control or exercise authority over the people held there. This broad definition ensures that anyone who misuses positional power over inmates is covered, regardless of their formal job title. It prevents offenders from escaping liability by claiming they held a different official designation.
real_world_examples: The head warden of a district jail in Uttar Pradesh, though officially designated 'Chief Warden' rather than 'Superintendent', exercises full disciplinary control over all prisoners and thus qualifies as a 'superintendent' under Section 68.

A deputy manager of a government-run women's shelter home in Maharashtra who oversees daily operations, assigns tasks to inmates, and controls their movements falls within the definition of 'superintendent' even though his formal title is 'Deputy Manager'.

An officer-in-charge of a remand home for juveniles in Delhi who has authority to grant or deny privileges to children held there is covered under this definition, enabling prosecution under Section 68 if he abuses that position.

A senior matron at a state-run women's correctional facility in Tamil Nadu who controls the inmates' daily schedule, enforces discipline, and can recommend punitive measures is considered a 'superintendent' for the purposes of this section.

A guard supervisor at a Central Jail in Rajasthan who holds supervisory authority over male and female inmates under a specific institutional order, though formally titled 'Supervising Jailor', qualifies as a superintendent under the inclusive definition in Section 68.
what_it_covers: The officially designated Superintendent of a jail, remand home, or place of custody established under any law in force.
Any officer or staff member at such an institution who, by virtue of their office, has authority or control over inmates — regardless of their formal designation or title.
Persons holding managerial or supervisory roles in a women's or children's institution who exercise practical authority over residents or inmates held there.
A deputy or acting superintendent who temporarily exercises authority and control over the inmates of a custodial institution.
Any institutional functionary whose office grants them the power to make decisions affecting the liberty, discipline, or welfare of the inmates.
what_it_excludes: Administrative or clerical staff at such institutions who perform purely back-office functions and have no authority or control over inmates (e.g., accountants, data entry operators).
External contractors or service providers (e.g., repair workers, caterers) visiting the institution who have no institutional authority over inmates.

Medical staff or visitors attached to the institution whose role does not confer any disciplinary or custodial authority over inmates — such persons are separately governed by the 'hospital' provisions in Section 68.

Persons who hold a title containing 'superintendent' in entirely different contexts (e.g., Superintendent of Police, Superintendent Engineer) who are not connected to a jail, remand home, or women's or children's institution.
Family members or legal guardians of inmates who visit the institution but hold no official position conferring authority over any inmate.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'superintendent' under Section 68 determines whether sexual intercourse induced by that person with a woman in custody constitutes the aggravated offence under Section 68, attracting mandatory rigorous imprisonment of not less than five years and up to ten years; if the definition does not apply, the conduct may not attract this specific provision, potentially resulting in a lesser charge or no charge under this section.

superintendent: A 'superintendent' is not just the person officially designated as superintendent of a jail, remand home, or similar institution — it includes any staff member or officer at such a place who has the practical power to control or exercise authority over the people held there. This broad definition ensures that anyone who misuses positional power over inmates is covered, regardless of their formal job title. It prevents offenders from escaping liability by claiming they held a different official designation.

Legal text: 'Superintendent', in relation to a jail, remand home or other place of custody or a women's or children's institution, includes a person holding any other office in such jail, remand home, place or institution by virtue of which such person can exercise any authority or control over its inmates.

Examples: The head warden of a district jail in Uttar Pradesh, though officially designated 'Chief Warden' rather than 'Superintendent', exercises full disciplinary control over all prisoners and thus qualifies as a 'superintendent' under Section 68. | A deputy manager of a government-run women's shelter home in Maharashtra who oversees daily operations, assigns tasks to inmates, and controls their movements falls within the definition of 'superintendent' even though his formal title is 'Deputy Manager'. | An officer-in-charge of a remand home for juveniles in Delhi who has authority to grant or deny privileges to children held there is covered under this definition, enabling prosecution under Section 68 if he abuses that position. | A senior matron at a state-run women's correctional facility in Tamil Nadu who controls the inmates' daily schedule, enforces discipline, and can recommend punitive measures is considered a 'superintendent' for the purposes of this section. | A guard supervisor at a Central Jail in Rajasthan who holds supervisory authority over male and female inmates under a specific institutional order, though formally titled 'Supervising Jailor', qualifies as a superintendent under the inclusive definition in Section 68.

Tags: positional authority over inmates, custodial institution officer, inclusive statutory definition, jail or remand home staff, abuse of custodial power, women's institution oversight, formal title irrelevant, control over confined persons, sexual offence by authority, institutional accountability

Covers: The officially designated Superintendent of a jail, remand home, or place of custody established under any law in force.; Any officer or staff member at such an institution who, by virtue of their office, has authority or control over inmates — regardless of their formal designation or title.; Persons holding managerial or supervisory roles in a women's or children's institution who exercise practical authority over residents or inmates held there.; A deputy or acting superintendent who temporarily exercises authority and control over the inmates of a custodial institution.; Any institutional functionary whose office grants them the power to make decisions affecting the liberty, discipline, or welfare of the inmates.

Excludes: Administrative or clerical staff at such institutions who perform purely back-office functions and have no authority or control over inmates (e.g., accountants, data entry operators).; External contractors or service providers (e.g., repair workers, caterers) visiting the institution who have no institutional authority over inmates.; Medical staff or visitors attached to the institution whose role does not confer any disciplinary or custodial authority over inmates — such persons are separately governed by the 'hospital' provisions in Section 68.; Persons who hold a title containing 'superintendent' in entirely different contexts (e.g., Superintendent of Police, Superintendent Engineer) who are not connected to a jail, remand home, or women's or children's institution.; Family members or legal guardians of inmates who visit the institution but hold no official position conferring authority over any inmate.

definitions.definition: A 'superior officer' refers to any officer in the Army, Navy, or Air Force of the Government of India who holds a higher rank or command over another officer, soldier, sailor, or airman, such that the latter is subject to the former's authority and orders in a military hierarchy. The term is used in the context of Sections 161 and 162 in relation to the execution of official military duties.
definitions.plain_english: A 'superior officer' is a higher-ranking military person in the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force who has authority over lower-ranked personnel. This could be an officer whose rank and position place them above another soldier, sailor, or airman in the chain of command. The term is relevant when the superior officer is carrying out their official duties at the time of an incident.
real_world_examples: A Brigadier in the Indian Army is a superior officer relative to a Captain serving under his command in the same unit; if someone abets the Captain to assault the Brigadier while the Brigadier is conducting a routine inspection, Sections 161 and 162 are attracted.

A Wing Commander in the Indian Air Force is the superior officer of a Flight Lieutenant under his squadron; abetting the Flight Lieutenant to physically attack the Wing Commander during a parade would constitute an offence under Section 161.

A Commander in the Indian Navy holds superior rank over a Sub-Lieutenant; if a civilian or fellow sailor incites the Sub-Lieutenant to assault the Commander while the Commander is issuing operational orders, the abettor is liable under Section 162 if the assault is actually carried out.

A Colonel directing troop deployment during a military exercise is in execution of his office; any person who instigates a Lance Naik under that Colonel's command to assault the Colonel during the exercise can be prosecuted under Sections 161 or 162.

During a court martial proceeding, a Major acting as a presiding officer is in execution of his office; abetting a soldier to assault him at that time would invoke the provisions relating to 'superior officer' under these sections.
what_it_covers: Any commissioned or non-commissioned officer in the Indian Army who holds a rank higher than the person alleged to have committed the assault, while in execution of his office.
A senior officer in the Indian Navy (such as a Captain or Commander) who is discharging official naval duties at the time of the alleged or abetted assault.
An officer in the Indian Air Force of superior rank who is actively performing official duties, such as conducting drills, issuing operational orders, or presiding over military proceedings.
what_it_excludes: Civilian government officials or bureaucrats who supervise defence ministry personnel but do not hold military rank within the Army, Navy, or Air Force.
A military officer who is not 'in execution of his office' at the time of the assault — for example, an officer acting in a purely personal capacity outside the scope of his military duties.
Officers of paramilitary or police forces such as CRPF, BSF, or state police, as the provision specifically refers to the Army, Navy, and Air Force of the Government of India.
An officer of equal rank, since the definition implies a hierarchical relationship where one person holds authority over the other by virtue of higher rank or command.
definitions.why_it_matters: The legal status of the person assaulted as a 'superior officer in execution of his office' is the defining criterion that triggers the enhanced criminal liability under Sections 161 and 162 of the BNS; without this status, the offence would be treated as ordinary assault or abetment thereof, attracting lesser punishment rather than imprisonment up to three or seven years respectively. It also serves as a safeguard for military discipline and command integrity within the Indian Armed Forces.
