definitions.definition: For the purposes of Section 72, 'victim' means any person against whom an offence under section 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, or 71 is alleged or found to have been committed, whose identity is protected from unauthorised disclosure. The term is also used across the Act to refer to the person who suffers the harm constituting the offence in question, including for the purposes of fine payment and rehabilitation.
definitions.plain_english: A 'victim' in this context is the person who has been subjected to a sexual offence such as rape or related crimes under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The law protects this person's identity from being made public without authorisation. When fines are imposed on convicts for such offences, those fines are to be paid directly to the victim to help cover medical and rehabilitation costs.
real_world_examples: A woman in Mumbai who has been raped and whose case is registered under Section 64 of BNS is a 'victim' — a newspaper cannot print her name or photograph without committing an offence under Section 72.

A twelve-year-old girl in rural Uttar Pradesh who is sexually assaulted under Section 65 is a 'victim', and the fine imposed on the convict must be paid to her (or her guardian) for medical expenses and rehabilitation.

A survivor of gang rape in Delhi whose case is filed under Section 70 is a 'victim'; she may authorise in writing the publication of her own identity, but no other person can disclose it without facing imprisonment of up to two years.

A woman in a persistent vegetative state following rape in Chennai whose case is prosecuted under Section 66 is a 'victim'; her next of kin may authorise disclosure of her identity only to the chairman or secretary of a recognised welfare institution.

A survivor of acid attack or sexual assault under Section 69 in Kolkata is a 'victim'; a police officer investigating the case may disclose her identity in writing in good faith for investigative purposes only, without committing an offence under Section 72.
what_it_covers: A woman against whom rape under Section 64 or 65 is alleged or found to have been committed.
A woman who has been subjected to gang rape under Section 70, whether or not the perpetrators have been convicted.
A woman who is in a persistent vegetative state or has died as a result of an offence under Section 66, whose identity continues to be protected.
A child (person under eighteen years) who is the survivor of any of the specified sexual offences under Sections 64–71.
A person of unsound mind who is a survivor of any specified sexual offence and whose next of kin may act on their behalf for identity disclosure authorisation.
what_it_excludes: Persons who have suffered offences not listed under Sections 64–71 (e.g., victims of theft, fraud, or assault under other sections) are not covered by the identity-protection provisions of Section 72.
The accused or offender in a sexual offence case, even if they claim counter-harm, does not fall within the definition of 'victim' under these sections.
Witnesses or bystanders who are incidentally harmed but are not the direct target of the scheduled sexual offences under Sections 64–71.

Legal entities such as companies or organisations cannot be 'victims' under this definition, which is restricted to natural persons — specifically women — against whom the enumerated offences are committed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'victim' under Section 72 directly determines whether the identity-protection prohibition applies, making unauthorised disclosure punishable with imprisonment up to two years and fine. It also determines entitlement to receive court-imposed fines for medical expenses and rehabilitation under Sections 65, 70, and related provisions.

definitions.definition: A void marriage, as used in Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is a marriage that is legally invalid and of no effect from its very inception by reason of its having taken place during the lifetime of a living husband or wife of one of the contracting parties. Such a marriage confers no legal status upon the parties and is treated as though it never occurred.
definitions.plain_english: A void marriage is one that is completely invalid under the law — it is treated as if it never happened at all. This situation arises when a person who is already legally married to someone else goes through a marriage ceremony with a different person while the first spouse is still alive. Because bigamy is prohibited, the second marriage has no legal standing whatsoever.
real_world_examples: Ramesh, a resident of Lucknow, is legally married to Sunita under Hindu law. Without obtaining a divorce, he travels to another city and marries Priya in a temple ceremony. Since Sunita is still alive and no divorce has been granted, the second marriage to Priya is a void marriage under Section 82 of the BNS.

Fatima, a Muslim woman legally married to her first husband in Hyderabad, converts to Hinduism and enters into a second marriage with Suresh in Pune without dissolving her first marriage. The second marriage is void because it took place during the lifetime of her first husband.

A Christian woman in Kerala, already married in a church ceremony and whose husband is alive, undergoes a civil marriage ceremony with another man at a registrar's office while concealing her marital status. The second marriage is void and she is liable for enhanced punishment under Section 82 for concealment.

A retired government officer in Delhi, estranged from his wife for years but never legally divorced, registers a second marriage with a younger woman. Despite the long separation, since the first wife is alive and no legal divorce was obtained, the second marriage is void and constitutes bigamy under BNS Section 82.

An NRI living abroad who was married in India returns and enters into a fresh marriage ceremony in Mumbai without presenting any divorce decree from a competent court. The second marriage is void by reason of the subsisting first marriage during the lifetime of the first spouse.
semantic_tags: spousal existence at time of marriage
nullity of marriage by operation of law
what_it_covers: A marriage solemnised by a person whose lawfully wedded spouse is alive and no valid divorce or annulment has been obtained from a competent court prior to the second marriage.
A second marriage ceremony conducted under any personal law, custom, or civil procedure where the first spouse is living, irrespective of religious or regional differences between the two marriages.
A marriage entered into after a merely informal or customary separation from the first spouse, without a legally recognised dissolution of the first marriage, while the first spouse remains alive.
A marriage where the first spouse has been fraudulently declared dead or missing without a court order, and the second marriage is subsequently entered into on that false basis.
what_it_excludes: A second marriage entered into after a legally valid divorce decree has been granted by a competent court and has become final and absolute, as the first marriage is no longer subsisting.

A marriage contracted after the death of the first spouse, since the condition of the first husband or wife 'living' is no longer satisfied, removing the basis for the marriage being void under Section 82.

A marriage that is invalid for reasons entirely unrelated to a subsisting prior marriage, such as prohibited degrees of relationship or lack of consent, as Section 82 specifically addresses voidness arising from a living prior spouse.
Cases where the prior marriage itself was legally void or annulled by a competent court before the second marriage was contracted, as there would be no living husband or wife in the legal sense.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a marriage qualifies as a 'void marriage' under Section 82 is the central determinant of criminal liability for bigamy: if the second marriage is void by reason of a living prior spouse, the offender is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine, escalating to ten years if the prior marriage was concealed from the second partner. The definition also directly affects the legal rights of the second spouse and any children of the second union, who may be denied legal recognition arising from a marriage that has no standing in law.

definitions.definition: A person is said to cause an effect 'voluntarily' when he causes it by means whereby he intended to cause it, or by means which, at the time of employing those means, he knew or had reason to believe to be likely to cause it.
definitions.plain_english: Something is done 'voluntarily' when a person either intended to bring about a particular result, or knew (or had good reason to know) that their actions were likely to produce that result. It does not require that the person wanted the exact harm that occurred — it is enough that they used means they knew could cause it. This standard covers both deliberate acts and recklessly knowing ones.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai picks up a heavy iron rod and strikes another person on the head during a dispute. Even if he claims he only meant to scare, he voluntarily caused grievous hurt because he knew hitting the head with a rod was likely to cause serious injury.

A driver in Delhi, fully aware that his brakes are faulty, continues to drive at high speed through a crowded market and injures pedestrians. The act of driving under those circumstances is voluntary because he knew the likely consequence of his actions.

A factory worker in Surat deliberately pours acid into a colleague's water bottle intending to poison him. This is a voluntary act because the means used (adding acid) were intended to cause harm and he knew the likely result.

During a communal dispute in Hyderabad, a person fires a gun into a crowd without aiming at any specific individual. Since he knew that firing into a crowd was likely to hurt someone, any resulting injury is voluntarily caused even if he had no specific target.

A person in Chennai administers a substance to another knowing it to be a poison, though claiming he thought it was medicine. If it is established he had reason to believe it was poisonous, the administration is treated as voluntary under law.

A landlord in Kolkata deliberately cuts off electricity to a tenant's room during extreme summer, knowing this is likely to cause harm to the tenant's health. The act is voluntary as he had reason to believe harm would result.
what_it_covers: Acts where the person specifically intended to cause the particular harm that resulted.
Acts where the person used means knowing, at the time of acting, that such means were likely to produce the harmful result, even without specific intent to harm.
Acts where the person had 'reason to believe' the means employed were likely to cause the result, making wilful ignorance or recklessness sufficient.
Causing hurt or grievous hurt through an instrument or method whose dangerous nature was known to the actor at the time of use.
Indirect causation where the accused set in motion a chain of events using means they knew were likely to cause harm.
what_it_excludes: Purely accidental acts where the person neither intended the harm nor had any reason to believe the means used could cause such harm.
Acts committed under complete absence of knowledge or foresight, such as an unforeseeable medical emergency causing a driver to lose control.
Acts done under genuine mistake of fact, where the person had no reason to know the means would produce the harmful result.
Harm caused by an intervening external force entirely outside the actor's knowledge or control that breaks the chain of causation.
Acts committed under total coercion or compulsion where the person had no voluntary choice in employing the means.
definitions.why_it_matters: The characterisation of an act as 'voluntary' is a foundational requirement for offences under Sections 115, 117, 118, 122, 126, 221, and 279 of the BNS, including voluntarily causing hurt and grievous hurt; if an act is not voluntary, criminal liability for these offences cannot be established, reducing or eliminating punishment. It directly determines whether a person is guilty of a more serious intentional offence or a lesser negligence-based offence.

definitions.definition: A person is said to 'voluntarily cause grievous hurt' when he both causes grievous hurt and intends or knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt. He is also said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt if, intending or knowing himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt of one kind, he actually causes grievous hurt of another kind.
definitions.plain_english: This term describes a situation where someone deliberately injures another person in a serious way, knowing that the injury they are about to cause is likely to be severe. The person must both intend to cause serious harm and actually succeed in causing it. Even if the exact type of serious injury that results is different from what was intended, the act still counts as voluntarily causing grievous hurt.
real_world_examples: During a land dispute in rural Uttar Pradesh, a man strikes his neighbour with a sharp sickle intending to permanently disfigure him; the blow instead fractures the neighbour's skull causing loss of hearing — this still constitutes voluntarily causing grievous hurt as the intention to cause serious harm was present.

A gang member in Mumbai deliberately pours acid on a rival's arm intending to cause permanent disfigurement; the resulting injuries cause permanent disability of the arm, satisfying both the intent and result requirements under the definition.

In a communal riot in Delhi, a group of six persons acting together beat a person from another community with iron rods, causing multiple bone fractures — each member of the group is liable for voluntarily causing grievous hurt.

A factory supervisor in Chennai knowingly uses a heated metal rod to burn a worker's leg as punishment for an alleged theft, causing severe burns that result in permanent scarring, constituting voluntarily causing grievous hurt given the deliberate and knowing nature of the act.

A man in Kolkata attacks his estranged wife with a cricket bat aiming to break her arm; she ends up in a persistent vegetative state due to a severe head injury — the accused is liable for the aggravated form of voluntarily causing grievous hurt punishable with rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years.
what_it_covers: An act where the accused intends to cause grievous hurt of one kind but actually causes grievous hurt of a different kind — the transferred intention still satisfies the definition.

Group violence where five or more persons acting in concert cause grievous hurt to a victim on grounds of race, caste, sex, language, place of birth, or personal belief — each member is individually liable.
Cases where the accused causes grievous hurt resulting in permanent disability or persistent vegetative state, attracting enhanced punishment of rigorous imprisonment for not less than ten years.

Acts committed using dangerous weapons or means (such as acid, fire, explosive substances, poisonous substances, or cutting instruments) that cause grievous hurt, covered under related provisions triggered by this definition.
Grievous hurt inflicted for the purpose of extortion, constraining the victim to commit an illegal act, or obtaining property or valuable security.
what_it_excludes: Mere causing of simple hurt, even if intentional — the injury caused must meet the threshold of 'grievous hurt' as defined in the Act; otherwise, the provision for voluntarily causing hurt applies instead.

Acts where the accused neither intended nor knew themselves to be likely to cause grievous hurt — accidental or reckless infliction of serious injury without the requisite mental state falls outside this definition.
Acts covered by lawful exceptions under Section 122, such as hurt caused during lawful medical treatment or surgical procedures carried out with consent and in good faith.
Grievous hurt caused purely by negligence or rash conduct without intention or knowledge of likely grievous harm, which is governed by separate negligence-related provisions of the Act.
Situations involving consent of the victim where the act is justified by law, such as medical operations performed in good faith for the patient's benefit.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'voluntarily causing grievous hurt' determines the severity of punishment — ranging from up to seven years of imprisonment for ordinary grievous hurt to life imprisonment for grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or for extortion, and mandatory rigorous imprisonment of at least ten years where permanent disability or persistent vegetative state results. It also triggers distinct offence liability for abettors who knew the grievous hurt was likely to be caused.

definitions.definition: Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said 'voluntarily to cause hurt'. (Section 115, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)
definitions.plain_english: A person 'voluntarily causes hurt' when they deliberately do something meaning to injure someone, or knowing that their action will likely injure someone, and that injury actually results. The key requirement is a mental element — either intention or knowledge — combined with the actual physical result of hurt. It is not enough to accidentally hurt someone; the person must have meant to cause harm or known it was likely to happen.
real_world_examples: During a street brawl in Delhi, one person punches another in the face, intending to injure them, resulting in a broken nose — this constitutes voluntarily causing hurt.

A factory supervisor in Mumbai throws a heavy tool at a worker during an argument, knowing it is likely to injure the worker, and it strikes the worker's arm causing bruising and swelling — this amounts to voluntarily causing hurt.

During a village dispute in Rajasthan, a person beats another with a stick multiple times across the back, each blow causing bodily pain — the entire beating, as well as each individual blow, falls within voluntarily causing hurt, though punishment is given for the whole act.

A person in Chennai deliberately pushes a rival down a flight of stairs intending to injure them, and the rival sustains cuts and bruises — the act qualifies as voluntarily causing hurt under the Sanhita.

A rowdy crowd member at a protest in Kolkata deliberately strikes a bystander with their hand knowing it will cause pain — even without a weapon, the intentional act resulting in hurt satisfies the definition.
what_it_covers: An act done with the intention of causing hurt to a specific person that results in actual hurt, such as punching or slapping someone during a quarrel.
An act done with knowledge that it is likely to cause hurt to any person, even if hurt to a specific individual was not the primary intention, provided hurt is actually caused.
A series of acts forming a single beating episode, where the cumulative conduct results in hurt, as illustrated in the example of fifty blows given with a stick.
Situations where the offender intends hurt of one kind but actually causes hurt of a different kind, provided the resulting harm still qualifies as 'hurt' rather than grievous hurt.
Acts using the bare body (fists, feet) or ordinary objects not qualifying as dangerous weapons, where intention or knowledge of likely hurt is present and hurt results.
what_it_excludes: Purely accidental acts where neither intention to cause hurt nor knowledge that hurt was likely to result is present — for example, a person who unintentionally bumps into another causing a minor injury.

Acts that cause grievous hurt as defined under Section 117, where the intended or likely harm is of a grievous nature — such cases fall under voluntarily causing grievous hurt, not merely voluntarily causing hurt.

Acts of hurt covered by the specific exception in Section 122(1), which provides for a separate regime for certain categories of hurt and is expressly excluded from the punishment provision under Section 115.
Hurt caused purely by omission without any underlying act, unless such omission itself constitutes an act within the meaning of the Sanhita.

Acts of a separate person against a third party during the same incident — for example, where A beats Z and Y separately intervenes, the blow to Y is a distinct act and not part of A voluntarily causing hurt to Z.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'voluntarily causes hurt' determines whether the accused is liable for punishment under Section 115 (up to one year imprisonment and/or fine up to ten thousand rupees) or for more aggravated offences under Sections 117 or 118 involving grievous hurt or dangerous weapons. It is also a foundational element for establishing culpability in Section 121 and related provisions, and the presence or absence of the required mental element (intention or knowledge) is decisive in determining guilt.

definitions.definition: A 'voter' means any person who has an electoral right to vote in an election, and includes any candidate or person whose free exercise of such electoral right may be interfered with or threatened under the provisions relating to undue influence at elections.
definitions.plain_english: A voter is any person who is entitled to cast a vote in an election. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the term is used specifically in the context of protecting a person's free right to vote without being threatened, coerced, or misled. If someone tries to interfere with how a voter exercises that right, it becomes a criminal offence.
real_world_examples: A registered voter in a Lok Sabha constituency in Bihar is threatened by a local strongman who warns him not to vote for a particular candidate or face physical harm — this voter is the protected party under Section 171.

A village woman in Rajasthan who is registered on the electoral roll is told by a religious leader that she will face divine punishment if she votes for a certain political party — she is a voter whose electoral right is being interfered with.

A slum resident in Mumbai who holds a valid Voter Identity Card is induced by a local party worker with liquor and cash to vote for a specific candidate — he is a voter being subjected to treating and undue influence.
A factory worker in Tamil Nadu whose employer threatens to dismiss him if he does not vote for the management-preferred candidate is a voter facing undue influence at an election.

A first-time voter in Uttar Pradesh who is prevented from going to the polling booth through intimidation by a group of persons is a voter whose free exercise of electoral right is being obstructed under Section 171.
what_it_covers: Any person registered on the electoral roll who is entitled to vote in a Parliamentary, State Legislature, or local body election.
A person who is threatened with injury, spiritual censure, or divine displeasure to coerce or influence their voting choice.
A person in whom a candidate or voter is interested, where threats or inducements are directed at such associated persons to indirectly influence the voter.
A voter whose Voter Identity Card has been forged or whose electoral participation is otherwise obstructed through fraudulent means.
what_it_excludes: A person who is not registered on the electoral roll and thus has no electoral right to exercise in a given election.
A candidate standing for election, who is separately categorised and protected under the term 'candidate' even though they may also hold voting rights.
A public servant or election official administering the election process, who does not fall within the category of voter in the context of being protected from undue influence.
A person who voluntarily abstains from voting and has not been subjected to any interference with their electoral right.
definitions.why_it_matters: The determination of who qualifies as a 'voter' is central to establishing whether the offence of undue influence under Section 171 has been committed, as the offence is specifically defined in terms of interference with the electoral right of a voter or candidate. Criminal liability for threats, inducements, and spiritual coercion attaches only where the target of such conduct is a voter or a person connected to one.

definitions.definition: A voting paper is the official ballot document issued to an elector at an election, upon application in the elector's own name, which enables that elector to record a vote; it is the instrument through which electoral participation is formally exercised and whose fraudulent application forms the basis of the offence of personation under Section 172.
definitions.plain_english: A voting paper is the official ballot slip or card given to a voter at a polling station so they can cast their vote in an election. It is the physical or official document that represents one person's right to vote. Only the registered voter whose name appears on the electoral roll is entitled to receive and use this document.
real_world_examples: During a Lok Sabha election in Bihar, a person walks into a polling booth and asks for a voting paper using the name of a deceased registered voter from the electoral roll — this constitutes fraudulent use of a voting paper under Section 172.

In a Municipal Corporation election in Mumbai, a voter who has already cast their ballot returns to the same booth and requests another voting paper in their own name in an attempt to vote twice — this is the offence of double voting involving a voting paper.

During a Vidhan Sabha election in Uttar Pradesh, a political worker applies for a voting paper using a completely fictitious name that does not appear on the electoral roll, in an effort to stuff extra votes — this misuse of a voting paper amounts to personation.

In a Panchayat election in Rajasthan, a person obtains a voting paper in the name of a migrant neighbour who is registered but has not come to vote, and proceeds to cast that vote — this constitutes personation through fraudulent appropriation of another's voting paper.

During an assembly by-election in Tamil Nadu, an organised group systematically applies for voting papers in the names of electors who have not yet voted, intending to cast bogus votes — each voting paper wrongfully obtained forms part of the criminal act of personation.
what_it_covers: The official ballot paper or slip issued by polling officials to a registered elector upon verification of identity at a polling station during a lawful election.
Any official document or instrument issued at an election that formally authorises and records an elector's entitlement to cast a single vote in that particular election.
A voting paper applied for in a deceased person's name, a living elector's name, or a fictitious name — all of which constitute the wrongful procurement of a voting paper under Section 172.
A second voting paper applied for by the same voter in their own name after having already voted once in the same election, making it an instrument of double voting.
what_it_excludes: A proxy vote cast by an authorised proxy on behalf of an elector under any law in force — such authorised proxy voting does not constitute wrongful use of a voting paper under the proviso to Section 172.
Electronic voting machine (EVM) ballot units or digital voting interfaces that do not involve a physical paper document being issued or applied for at a polling station.
Voter identity cards (EPIC) or electoral roll entries, which are identification documents and registration records respectively, not the voting paper itself issued at the time of voting.

Postal ballots sent to eligible electors such as service voters or senior citizens, which operate under a separate legal framework and are not applied for at a physical polling station in the manner contemplated by Section 172.
definitions.why_it_matters: The voting paper is the central instrument of the offence of personation at elections under Section 172 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — wrongfully applying for or obtaining a voting paper in another's name, a fictitious name, or a second time in one's own name directly constitutes a cognisable criminal offence. Whether a document qualifies as a voting paper determines whether the acts of applying, abetting, or procuring its fraudulent use attract criminal liability for personation, which undermines the integrity of democratic elections.

definitions.definition: Waging war refers to the act of levying armed hostilities or engaging in organised armed conflict against the Government of India or, by extension under Section 153, against the Government of any foreign State at peace with the Government of India; it encompasses not only the actual commission of such armed conflict but also attempts and abetment thereof, as well as preparatory acts such as collecting men, arms, or ammunition with the intention of waging such war.
definitions.plain_english: Waging war means taking up arms or leading an organised armed uprising against the Indian government or against the government of a friendly foreign country. It is not just the actual fighting — even trying to start such a conflict, helping others do it, or gathering weapons and people with that intention counts as waging war. This is one of the most serious offences in Indian criminal law.
real_world_examples: A militant group in a northeastern state organises armed cadres, acquires weapons and explosives, and launches coordinated attacks on Indian Army posts and government installations with the aim of seceding from India — this constitutes waging war against the Government of India.

A group of Indian nationals secretly recruits fighters, raises funds, and crosses into a neighbouring country (such as Nepal or Sri Lanka, which is at peace with India) to conduct armed attacks against that country's government — this falls under waging war against a foreign State at peace with India under Section 153.

A terrorist organisation based in India stockpiles arms, trains combatants, and plans a simultaneous assault on Parliament and key government ministries in New Delhi to overthrow the constitutional government — the planning and preparation phase itself constitutes collecting arms with intent to wage war under Section 149.

During a separatist insurgency in Kashmir, an individual provides financial support, logistical assistance, and safe houses to an armed group that is actively fighting Indian security forces with the declared aim of overthrowing Indian sovereignty — this constitutes abetment of waging war.

A faction within a region holds armed rallies, blocks highways with armed force, and issues ultimatums demanding independence by force, while stockpiling weapons to back their demand — even before any direct clash with government forces, these acts constitute preparation to wage war.
what_it_covers: Actual armed combat or coordinated military-style attacks launched against the Government of India or its forces with the aim of undermining or overthrowing its authority.
Attempts to wage war, including mobilisation of armed groups and initiation of hostilities even if the full-scale conflict does not succeed.
Abetment of waging war, such as financing, recruiting, training, or providing material support to groups engaged in armed conflict against the government.
Preparatory acts under Section 149 — collecting men, arms, or ammunition with the intent of waging war, even before actual hostilities commence.
Waging war against the government of any foreign State at peace with India, or attempting or abetting such acts, as covered under Section 153.
what_it_excludes: Peaceful protests, civil disobedience, or non-violent agitation against government policies, even if disruptive or large-scale, which do not involve armed force.

definitions.definition: The term 'war' is not formally defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in Section 153, it refers to an armed conflict or hostile military engagement waged against the Government of India or any foreign State, including any organised and concerted use of force, violence, or armed operations intended to overthrow, coerce, or resist the authority of the State or its allies. It encompasses both conventional armed conflict and any organised armed hostility aimed at subverting national sovereignty or integrity.
definitions.plain_english: War, in this law, means any serious armed conflict or organised military hostility directed against India's government or a foreign country. It is not just a formal declaration of war between nations — it includes any large-scale, coordinated violent effort to challenge or overthrow state authority using weapons or armed force. Think of it as any situation where a group or person takes up arms in an organised way to fight against the government or a nation.
real_world_examples: A group of armed insurgents in a northeastern Indian state launches coordinated attacks on Indian Army posts with the stated aim of forcing secession from India — this constitutes waging war against the Government of India.

A foreign-backed militant organisation based in Pakistan infiltrates Indian territory and carries out simultaneous bomb blasts and armed assaults on government installations in Jammu & Kashmir to destabilise the Indian State — this amounts to war-like hostility against India.

Indian nationals recruited by a foreign terrorist organisation take up arms alongside enemy combatants during a border conflict between India and a neighbouring country to assist that country's military — their actions could be characterised as waging war against India.

A large armed faction within India, inspired by separatist ideology, occupies government buildings in a state capital and engages security forces in sustained armed combat to declare an independent territory — this organised violent resistance constitutes war against the Indian State.

Indian mercenaries join an armed conflict between two foreign nations and participate in hostilities against one of those nations with which India has friendly relations, potentially triggering provisions related to war against a foreign State allied with India.
what_it_covers: Coordinated armed attacks by insurgent groups or foreign-backed militants against Indian government forces or installations with the intent to overthrow or coerce state authority.
Participation by Indian nationals in organised armed hostilities alongside enemy combatants or foreign forces fighting against India or an allied foreign State.
Large-scale armed rebellion or insurrection within Indian territory involving sustained military-style combat against the armed forces or government of India.
Any organised use of lethal force, weapons, or armed operations aimed at subverting the sovereignty or integrity of India, even without a formal declaration of war.
what_it_excludes: Peaceful protests, demonstrations, or civil disobedience movements, even if they are large-scale and aimed at opposing government policies, since they do not involve armed force.
Individual or isolated acts of violence such as a single assault on a police officer or a random act of terrorism not connected to a broader organised armed campaign against the State.
Lawful military operations conducted by the Indian armed forces or state-sanctioned paramilitary forces acting under orders within Indian territory or abroad.
Diplomatic disputes, economic sanctions, or political conflicts between India and a foreign State that do not involve actual armed hostilities or organised military engagement.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'war' under the BNS determines the applicability of offences such as waging or abetting war against the Government of India under Section 147 and related provisions, which attract the most severe punishments including death or imprisonment for life. The classification also determines whether related offences under Sections 147–153 — covering conspiracy, design, collection of arms, and concealment — are triggered against accused persons.

definitions.definition: An instrument which, when used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The term encompasses any object — not necessarily designed as a weapon — that is wielded in a manner that renders it capable of causing death, as contextually determined by its use rather than its intrinsic nature.
definitions.plain_english: A 'weapon of offence' is any object used to attack or threaten someone in a way that could cause death, even if that object was not originally made to be a weapon. The key test is not what the object is, but how it is being used — if it can kill when wielded as a weapon, it qualifies. For example, a heavy iron rod, a sharp agricultural tool, or a glass bottle, when used to strike someone, can all be treated as weapons of offence.
real_world_examples: A farmer in rural Punjab uses his iron sickle (a farming tool) to strike a neighbour during a land dispute, wielding it in a manner likely to cause death — the sickle qualifies as a weapon of offence under Section 118.

During a communal clash in Uttar Pradesh, members of an unlawful assembly carry sharpened bamboo lathis capable of causing lethal injury — these lathis are treated as weapons of offence under Section 189, attracting enhanced punishment of up to two years imprisonment.

A group of rioters in Mumbai use heavy iron chains to assault police officers during a protest that turns violent — the chains, used as weapons of offence likely to cause death, invoke the aggravated rioting provision under Section 191, carrying punishment up to five years.

In a road-rage incident in Delhi, an aggressor smashes a thick glass bottle over a victim's head — the bottle, though ordinarily a household item, is considered a weapon of offence because it was used in a manner likely to cause death.

A construction worker in Chennai uses a heavy masonry hammer to assault a co-worker during a dispute at a building site — the hammer, wielded as a weapon capable of causing death, constitutes a weapon of offence under the BNS.
what_it_covers: Any instrument — whether purpose-made or improvised — that is wielded in a manner likely to cause death, such as an iron rod, a sharpened agricultural tool, a heavy chain, or a glass bottle used to strike.
Objects not conventionally classified as weapons but used offensively in a lethal manner, including household items like bricks, hammers, or iron pipes when applied with deadly intent.

Instruments used by members of an unlawful assembly or rioters that elevate the severity of the offence under Sections 189 and 191, such as lathis sharpened to a point or machetes carried during group violence.
what_it_excludes: Instruments specifically listed separately in Section 118 as distinct categories — such as firearms (instruments for shooting), knives (instruments for stabbing or cutting), fire, poison, corrosive substances, explosive substances, or animals — which attract liability on their own terms without the 'likely to cause death' test.

An object held or carried passively with no offensive use or intent — mere possession of a potentially dangerous item does not make it a weapon of offence unless it is actually used or readied for use in a manner likely to cause death.

Objects causing hurt that clearly cannot cause death regardless of how they are used, such as a thin plastic ruler or a soft cushion, which fall outside the scope of this definition even if used to strike someone.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an object qualifies as a 'weapon of offence' directly determines the severity of punishment: under Section 118, it distinguishes simple hurt (up to one year) from aggravated hurt (up to three years); under Section 189, being armed with such a weapon escalates an unlawful assembly member's punishment to two years; and under Section 191, rioting with such a weapon increases the penalty from two years to five years imprisonment.

definitions.definition: Wilful conduct means any deliberate and intentional conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman, as used in the context of cruelty under section 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: Wilful conduct refers to behaviour that a person deliberately chooses to do — not by accident or mistake — that is so harmful or oppressive toward a woman that it could push her toward suicide or cause serious physical or mental harm. The key idea is that the person knew what they were doing and did it on purpose. It forms one part of what the law calls 'cruelty' when done by a husband or his relatives toward a wife.
real_world_examples: A husband in Delhi repeatedly threatens his wife that he will throw her out of the house and take away their child unless she brings more dowry from her parents, causing her severe depression and suicidal thoughts — this deliberate pattern of threats constitutes wilful conduct.

A mother-in-law in Chennai systematically withholds food from her daughter-in-law, forces her to do excessive physical labour, and verbally humiliates her daily, leading to deterioration of the woman's mental and physical health — such a deliberate course of action amounts to wilful conduct.

A husband in Mumbai secretly records intimate moments with his wife and threatens to release them unless she signs over her property, causing her extreme psychological distress and danger to her mental health — the intentional use of such coercive threats is wilful conduct.

A husband in Kolkata, aware that his wife has a cardiac condition, deliberately creates situations of extreme emotional stress by falsely accusing her of infidelity in front of family and neighbours on repeated occasions, worsening her health condition — this constitutes wilful conduct.

A husband in Hyderabad forces his wife to consume alcohol or drugs against her will to weaken her resistance, or physically assaults her whenever she refuses to comply with his financial demands — such deliberate physical abuse is a clear example of wilful conduct.
what_it_covers: Deliberate and repeated physical violence by a husband against his wife that endangers her life or limb.
Intentional psychological torture, such as persistent verbal abuse, threats, isolation, or humiliation, that is likely to drive the woman to contemplate or attempt suicide.
Consciously planned acts of deprivation — such as withholding medical care, food, or basic necessities — that endanger the woman's health.
Deliberate false accusations of infidelity or moral character made repeatedly with full knowledge of the mental harm they cause to the woman.
Intentional acts of intimate partner violence, including non-consensual physical harm, done with awareness of the likely consequences to the woman's life or health.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or negligent conduct that causes harm without any deliberate intention, such as an unintentional injury during a household accident.

Harassment specifically linked to coercing the woman or her relatives to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security, which is separately covered under the second limb of section 86 and is not classified under wilful conduct.
Acts done under genuine mistake of fact or without knowledge of their likely consequences on the woman's life or health.
Conduct that, while unpleasant or unkind, does not rise to the threshold of being 'likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health'.
Mutual marital disputes or ordinary domestic disagreements that do not involve deliberate intent to cause serious harm or danger to the woman.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether conduct qualifies as 'wilful conduct' under section 86 directly determines whether a husband or his relatives can be prosecuted for the offence of cruelty under section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which is punishable with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine. The presence of wilfulness distinguishes criminal cruelty from mere marital discord, thereby triggering or blocking criminal liability and protecting a married woman's right to life and health.

definitions.definition: A person is said to commit wilful misrepresentation when, by deliberately and intentionally making a false or misleading statement of fact (as opposed to an accidental or innocent misstatement), he voluntarily causes or procures, or attempts to cause or procure, a thing to be done, thereby instigating the doing of that thing within the meaning of abetment under Section 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
definitions.plain_english: Wilful misrepresentation means deliberately telling someone something false or misleading — knowing it is untrue — in order to make them do something they otherwise would not do. It is not an honest mistake; the person intentionally deceives to achieve a particular outcome. Under Indian law, doing this makes you responsible for instigating whatever action results from your false statement.
real_world_examples: A person knowingly tells a police officer that a specific innocent individual is the wanted accused named in an arrest warrant, causing the officer to arrest the wrong person — as illustrated by the example in Section 45 itself where B tells A that C is Z.

A fraudulent contractor deliberately misrepresents to a government official that all quality tests have been passed for construction materials, causing the official to approve substandard work on a public infrastructure project.
A person deliberately informs a bank employee that a forged power of attorney is genuine, causing the bank to release funds from another person's account to an unauthorised individual.

A real estate broker wilfully tells a prospective buyer that a disputed property has clear title and no pending court cases, inducing the buyer to register the property — resulting in the buyer committing a legally invalid transaction.
A recruiter knowingly misrepresents to rural youth that a factory job abroad is legitimate and well-paying, causing them to travel and hand over their documents, facilitating their trafficking.
what_it_covers: A deliberate and knowing false statement of fact made to another person with the intent to cause that person to do a specific act they would not otherwise do.
Situations where the accused is fully aware that the representation is false or misleading and still makes it in order to procure a particular outcome or action.

Positive acts of deception — including oral, written, or electronically communicated false statements — that directly cause or attempt to cause another person to act, thereby constituting instigation for the purpose of abetment.

Cases where a person uses partial truths or misleading framing that they know will be understood falsely, so long as the intent is deliberate and the misrepresentation is material to the resulting action.
what_it_excludes: Innocent or honest mistakes where the person genuinely believed the statement to be true at the time of making it — absence of wilful intent takes the act outside this definition.

Wilful concealment of a material fact, which is treated as a separate but parallel ground for instigation under Section 45 and is governed by the concept of 'wilful concealment' rather than wilful misrepresentation.
Mere negligent or careless misstatements made without deliberate intent to deceive, even if they result in another person taking a harmful action.
Expressions of opinion, belief, or prediction about future events that turn out to be wrong, where no present false fact was asserted with intent to deceive.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as wilful misrepresentation determines whether a person can be held liable as an abettor by instigation under Section 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and thereby be punished with the same punishment as the principal offender for the instigated offence. It is the critical element distinguishing criminal abetment through deception from innocent conduct, triggering full abettor liability.

definitions.definition: A person acts 'wilfully' when they act with full knowledge and deliberate intent, consciously choosing to do or omit something they know to be wrong or contrary to their legal duty, without any accident, mistake, or compulsion. As used in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, wilful conduct involves an intentional, purposeful act or omission carried out with awareness of its nature and consequences, particularly in contexts such as wilful misrepresentation (Section 45), wilful concealment of material fact, and wilful sufferance of another to commit a breach of trust (Section 316).
definitions.plain_english: Acting 'wilfully' means doing something on purpose, fully knowing what you are doing and intending to do it — not by accident, carelessness, or mistake. It means the person made a deliberate choice to act or not act in a way they knew was wrong or against their duty. For example, if someone intentionally gives false information to a police officer while knowing it is false, that is a wilful act.
real_world_examples: A warehouse keeper in Mumbai, entrusted with a client's goods, knowingly allows his associate to misappropriate a consignment of electronics, actively choosing not to intervene — this constitutes wilful sufferance under Section 316 (criminal breach of trust).

A village watchman in rural Rajasthan, aware that a gang is heading to commit dacoity at a merchant's house, deliberately tells the police they are heading in a different direction to mislead them — this is wilful misinformation under Section 212.

A landlord in Delhi, knowing that a murder was committed on his property, deliberately informs the local Magistrate that the death was accidental — this is a wilful misstatement of facts to a public servant.

A company director in Bengaluru, legally bound to disclose a material financial fact to a regulatory authority, intentionally conceals it to prevent investigation — this constitutes wilful concealment of a material fact as described under Section 45.

A public officer's assistant, knowing that the person being apprehended is not the named accused, deliberately represents to the officer that he is, causing wrongful apprehension — this is wilful misrepresentation under the illustration to Section 45.

An employer in Chennai deducts provident fund contributions from employees' salaries and, knowing his legal obligation, deliberately fails to deposit them into the PF account — constituting wilful breach of trust under Section 316.
what_it_covers: Deliberately providing false information to a Magistrate or police officer while knowing it is false, as in the illustrations to Sections 212 and 45.
Intentionally concealing a material fact that one is legally bound to disclose, in order to cause another person to do something they otherwise would not do.
Consciously allowing or permitting another person to misappropriate or misuse property entrusted to oneself, knowing that doing so constitutes a breach of trust under Section 316.
Deliberately misrepresenting the identity of a person to a public officer, fully aware of the falsity of the representation, as illustrated in Section 45.
An employer who knowingly and purposefully fails to deposit deducted provident fund contributions into the legally mandated fund.
what_it_excludes: Accidental or inadvertent misrepresentation made without knowledge of its falsity — such as genuinely mistaking one person for another without fraudulent intent.
Acts or omissions arising from honest mistake of fact, where the person had reasonable grounds to believe their action or statement was correct.

Negligent conduct that results in harm or false information but lacks the deliberate, conscious intent to mislead or breach a duty — negligence without knowledge of wrongdoing does not qualify as wilful.
Conduct carried out under coercion, duress, or force majeure, where the person had no real choice or opportunity to act otherwise.
Omissions resulting from ignorance of the law or of a relevant fact, where the person genuinely did not know they were legally bound to act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is 'wilful' is a critical threshold for criminal liability under the BNS, 2023: offences such as criminal breach of trust (Section 316), furnishing false information (Section 212), and abetment by instigation through misrepresentation (Section 45) require proof of wilfulness to establish guilt, and without it, conduct may only attract civil liability or lesser charges. Establishing wilfulness elevates the mental element from mere negligence to deliberate wrongdoing, directly determining the severity of punishment and whether an offence is made out at all.

definitions.definition: The term 'will' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. As used in Sections 338 and 343, 'will' refers to a testamentary document by which a person declares their intention regarding the disposition of their property or other legal rights to take effect after their death, and which is capable of being used as evidence of that intention.
definitions.plain_english: A 'will' is a written document made by a person during their lifetime that says how they want their belongings, money, or property to be distributed after they die. It is a legal declaration of a person's final wishes. In the context of the BNS, a will is treated as a type of valuable document that can be subject to forgery or fraud.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai businessman executes a registered will bequeathing his flat in Andheri to his son and his savings to a charitable trust; a fraudster later forges a second will to redirect the flat to himself, committing an offence under Section 338.

An elderly woman in Kolkata dictates her will to a lawyer, leaving her gold jewellery to her daughter; her nephew, knowing the will is being prepared, fabricates a document purporting to be her will leaving everything to him under Section 343.

A farmer in rural Punjab writes a handwritten will dividing his agricultural land among his three children; after his death, one child alters the document to claim an additional share, attracting liability under the BNS for forgery of a will.

A retired government employee in Chennai creates a will nominating his wife as the sole beneficiary of his provident fund and property; a distant relative creates a counterfeit will claiming to be the rightful heir, triggering criminal prosecution under Section 338.

A Delhi resident executing a will through a registered lawyer is impersonated by a fraudster who executes a second will under the same name, fraudulently diverting property to a third party in violation of Section 343.
what_it_covers: A registered will executed before a Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act, 1908, declaring distribution of immovable property after death.
An unregistered but duly signed and witnessed handwritten will (holograph will) expressing testamentary intention regarding movable property.
A will executed by a person of sound mind disposing of both tangible assets such as land and jewellery and intangible rights such as bank deposits and insurance proceeds.
A codicil — a document that amends or supplements an existing will — as it constitutes a testamentary instrument within the same category.
A forged or fabricated document that purports to be a will, in the context of offences under Sections 338 and 343 of the BNS.
what_it_excludes: A gift deed executed during the lifetime of the donor, even if intended to take effect immediately, as it is not a testamentary instrument.
A nomination form filed with a bank, insurance company, or provident fund authority, as it does not constitute a testamentary declaration of the same legal character as a will.
An oral statement or deathbed declaration of intent regarding property distribution, as it lacks the written documentary form required of a will.
A trust deed creating an inter-vivos trust operative during the settlor's lifetime, which is distinct from a testamentary disposition.
A power of attorney, which operates during the grantor's lifetime and is not a disposition of property upon death.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'will' is critical under Sections 338 and 343 of the BNS because forgery, fabrication, or fraudulent use of a will attracts enhanced criminal punishment, given that wills are instruments affecting property rights, succession, and the legal interests of heirs and beneficiaries. The classification of a document as a will determines whether the more serious offences of forgery of a valuable security or will apply, as opposed to ordinary document forgery.

definitions.definition: "Woman" means female human being of any age. This definition is implied by the structure of Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which defines "man" as a male human being of any age, thereby establishing "woman" as the corresponding female counterpart across all ages.
definitions.plain_english: A 'woman' under this law means any female human being, regardless of her age — from a newborn girl to an elderly female. This definition is broad and inclusive, covering all stages of a female person's life. It is used throughout the law to identify the specific victims or subjects of certain offences that are designed to protect females.
real_world_examples: A 25-year-old woman in Mumbai who is sexually assaulted by her employer falls within this definition, making the offence of rape under Section 63 applicable.

A 14-year-old girl in rural Bihar who is subjected to sexual intercourse by an adult male is covered under this definition, attracting the aggravated provisions of Section 65 which prescribes enhanced punishment for rape of a woman under eighteen years of age.

A 35-year-old married woman in Delhi whose husband subjects her to cruelty and harassment for dowry is protected under this definition, making Section 85 and related provisions applicable to her case.

A 60-year-old widow in Chennai who is forced into sexual intercourse by a person in a position of authority is protected as a 'woman' under this definition, enabling prosecution under relevant sections of the Sanhita.
A newborn female infant who is subjected to harm or whose birth is concealed falls within this definition, enabling application of relevant protective offences under the Sanhita.

A transgender individual who is legally and officially recognised as female under applicable personal law or court order may also be considered within the scope of this definition given the gender-neutral pronoun provision under Section 2.
what_it_covers: A female infant or girl child of any age, including newborns, who is a victim of an offence under the Sanhita.
An adult female of any age, whether married, unmarried, widowed, or separated, who is subjected to rape, sexual harassment, or cruelty under the relevant sections.
A female who is pregnant or 'with child', as she continues to fall within the definition of 'woman' and may attract additional protections under the Act.
A minor girl below the age of eighteen years who is a victim of rape, attracting the enhanced punishment provisions under Section 65.
A female victim of voyeurism, stalking, or trafficking offences under the Sanhita.
what_it_excludes: A male human being of any age, who is separately defined as 'man' under Section 2 and is not covered by offences specifically directed at protection of 'women'.
A company, association, or body of persons, which is covered under the definition of 'person' but does not qualify as a 'woman'.
An animal or non-human living creature, which is separately defined under Section 2 and cannot be a 'woman' for purposes of gender-specific offences.
A fictional or legal entity such as a corporation or trust, which has no biological sex and cannot fall within this definition.
A male individual who has not obtained legal recognition as female, irrespective of gender identity, unless accorded such status by law.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'woman' is critical because several offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — including rape (Section 63), aggravated rape (Section 65), outraging modesty (Section 76), and word or gesture intended to insult the modesty of a woman (Section 79) — are specifically constituted with 'woman' as the protected subject or victim, meaning criminal liability and punishment are triggered only when the victim satisfies this definition. Misidentification of the victim's status as a 'woman' can determine whether a prosecution succeeds or fails under these gender-specific provisions.

definitions.definition: A 'woman with child' refers to a woman who is pregnant, i.e., who is carrying a child in her womb at any stage of gestation. The term encompasses pregnancy from conception onward, and is used in the context of offences relating to causing miscarriage or acts done with intent to cause miscarriage, including situations where such acts result in the death of the pregnant woman.
definitions.plain_english: A 'woman with child' simply means a woman who is pregnant — someone who is carrying a baby in her womb. This term is used in the law to identify the victim in crimes involving attempts to end a pregnancy illegally or acts that accidentally or intentionally cause the death of a pregnant woman. It covers any stage of pregnancy, from very early on to just before birth.
real_world_examples: A woman in her second trimester of pregnancy in Mumbai is administered a substance by her partner without her knowledge in an attempt to terminate the pregnancy — she qualifies as a 'woman with child' under Section 90.

A woman in rural Rajasthan who is eight months pregnant is physically assaulted by her in-laws with the intent to cause miscarriage and dies as a result — she is a 'woman with child' and the offence under Section 90 is attracted.

A doctor in Chennai performs an illegal procedure on a six-week pregnant woman without her consent, intending to end the pregnancy, and the woman dies — the woman was 'with child' at the time, triggering enhanced punishment under Section 90.

A woman in Kolkata, newly confirmed pregnant by a home test, is given harmful pills by a person who knew of her pregnancy and intended to cause miscarriage — even at this very early stage, she is a 'woman with child' for the purposes of the Act.

A factory worker in Pune who is three months pregnant is subjected to hazardous conditions deliberately by her employer with intent to cause miscarriage and suffers fatal consequences — she is a 'woman with child' under the relevant provisions.
what_it_covers: A woman at any stage of pregnancy, including very early gestation, where conception has occurred and the pregnancy is subsisting.
A woman who is visibly pregnant and known to be carrying a child at the time the offending act is committed against her.
A woman who is in the early weeks of pregnancy, even before the foetus is 'quick with child' (i.e., before perceptible foetal movement), as the term 'with child' covers all stages of pregnancy.
A woman who is pregnant as a result of any circumstances, including consensual or non-consensual conception, for the purposes of attracting offences under Sections 88 and 90.
A woman who causes herself to miscarry, as she is explicitly brought within the ambit of Section 88 and thus is also a 'woman with child' for the purposes of the Act.
what_it_excludes: A woman who is not pregnant at the time of the act — absence of pregnancy means the term and its associated offences do not apply.
A woman who has already delivered her child or whose pregnancy has otherwise ended (by miscarriage, stillbirth, or delivery) prior to the commission of the act, as she is no longer 'with child'.
A woman who merely suspects she might be pregnant but is not in fact pregnant — the term requires an actual existing pregnancy.
Acts committed against a woman where there is no knowledge or intent concerning her pregnancy, which may affect culpability but does not change who falls under this definition.
A deceased foetus or child already expelled from the womb — the term attaches to the living pregnant woman, not the child independently after separation from the mother.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a woman qualifies as a 'woman with child' is a threshold condition for attracting offences under Sections 88 and 90 of the BNS, 2023 — without this status, the specific offences of causing miscarriage and causing death with intent to miscarry cannot be established, and the enhanced punishments (up to 10 years, or life imprisonment where consent is absent) cannot be applied. The term also determines whether the aggravated offence of causing death of a pregnant woman with intent to miscarry is made out, distinguishing it from ordinary culpable homicide or hurt.

definitions.definition: "Women's or children's institution" means an institution, whether called an orphanage or a home for neglected women or children or a widow's home or an institution called by any other name, which is established and maintained for the reception and care of women or children.
definitions.plain_english: A women's or children's institution is any place—regardless of what it is officially called—that is set up and run specifically to shelter, house, or take care of women or children. This includes orphanages, widow homes, and homes for neglected women or children. The name or label given to such a place does not matter; what matters is that its purpose is the reception and care of women or children.
real_world_examples: A government-run orphanage in Lucknow housing minor children without parental care, where a staff member in a supervisory role commits rape on an inmate — the orphanage qualifies as a women's or children's institution, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 64(2).

A widow rehabilitation home operated by a registered NGO in Mumbai, providing shelter and vocational training to destitute widows — a superintendent of such a home who sexually abuses a resident can be prosecuted under Section 68 for sexual intercourse by a person in authority.

A State-run 'Nari Niketan' (home for neglected women) in Delhi run by the Department of Women and Child Development — any management or staff member of such an institution who commits rape on an inmate attracts the aggravated sentencing provision under Section 64(2)(vi).

A privately managed children's home in Chennai registered under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, providing residential care to abandoned children — if a warden assaults a child resident, the institution's classification as a women's or children's institution triggers the harsher penal provisions of the BNS.

A 'Balika Griha' (girls' home) run by a State government in Patna for homeless adolescent girls — a manager or staff member who coerces a resident into sexual intercourse (not amounting to rape) can be prosecuted under Section 68, given the institution's status as a women's or children's institution.
what_it_covers: A government-run orphanage established for the care and shelter of abandoned or parentless children.
A widow's home or 'Vidhwa Ashram' maintained by a State government or NGO for the reception and care of widowed women.
A home for neglected women, including shelters for destitute, abused, or homeless women, irrespective of the specific name used for the institution.
Any privately or publicly managed residential institution—regardless of its official title—whose primary purpose is the reception and care of women or children.
A 'Balika Griha' or girls' home established under welfare schemes for housing vulnerable adolescent girls.
what_it_excludes: Hospitals or medical institutions whose primary purpose is medical treatment or convalescence, even if they house women or children as patients (covered separately under the definition of 'hospital').
Schools, colleges, or educational hostels that primarily provide education and incidentally house female students, as their core purpose is education rather than reception and care.
Jails, remand homes, or other places of custody established under law for detention purposes, which are treated as a distinct category under Sections 64 and 68.
Day-care or crèche facilities that do not provide residential reception and care but only temporary daytime supervision of children.
Private households or family homes, even where a woman or child may be under the care of a guardian, as these are not institutionally established for the reception and care of women or children.

definitions.definition: A 'writ' in the context of Section 127 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 refers to a formal written order or command issued by a court or competent authority, including a summons, warrant, order, notice, or other mandatory legal process requiring a person to do or refrain from doing a specified act, or compelling attendance or compliance before a court or authority.
definitions.plain_english: A writ is an official written command issued by a court or government authority that legally requires someone to do something, stop doing something, or appear before a court. It is a binding legal document that carries the force of law. Examples include court orders to appear, arrest warrants, and official notices compelling compliance.
real_world_examples: A Sessions Court in Mumbai issues a writ summoning a witness to appear before it on a specified date in a murder trial under BNS, 2023.
The High Court of Delhi issues a writ in the nature of habeas corpus directing the jail superintendent to produce an undertrial prisoner before it to examine the legality of his detention.
A Magistrate in Chennai issues a writ ordering a person to execute a bond for keeping the peace, and the person knowingly disobeys it, attracting liability under Section 127 of BNS.

A court in Kolkata issues a written order commanding a public servant to refrain from interfering with the conduct of a lawful election, and any disobedience of this writ triggers criminal consequences under Section 127.
A Judicial Magistrate in Hyderabad issues a writ in the form of a warrant of arrest commanding a police officer to apprehend an accused person absconding from justice.
what_it_covers: A summons issued by a Magistrate requiring a person to appear before the court on a specified date and time.
A warrant of arrest issued by a competent court directing law enforcement to apprehend an accused or witness.
A court order or notice issued under judicial authority compelling a person to execute a bond, desist from an act, or fulfil a legal obligation.
Any formal written command issued by a court that is disobeyed, thereby attracting criminal liability under Section 127 of BNS, 2023.
High Court writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, and quo warranto when issued in the exercise of judicial authority.
what_it_excludes: Informal verbal directions or oral instructions given by a court official that are not reduced to a formal written order.
Administrative circulars or executive orders issued by government departments that are not issued in the exercise of judicial authority by a court.
Legislative enactments or statutory rules made by Parliament or State Legislatures, which are not writs in the judicial sense.
Private contractual notices or demand letters between parties that do not carry the force of a court-issued mandate.
Internal departmental orders or service communications issued by superior officers to subordinates outside the context of judicial proceedings.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a document qualifies as a 'writ' determines whether its disobedience or obstruction attracts criminal liability under Section 127 of the BNS, 2023, which punishes non-compliance with court orders and judicial process; classifying something as a writ also determines whether fabricating, altering, or knowingly using a false version of it constitutes an offence relating to false documents or contempt.

definitions.definition: The term 'writing' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, but as used in the Act (including Section 183), it means any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures, or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to communicate or record information, including electronic and digital records where the context so permits.
definitions.plain_english: Writing refers to any form of communication or recording done using letters, numbers, symbols, or marks on a surface or medium — this includes handwritten notes, typed documents, printed text, and even digital or electronic text. It is essentially any visible representation of words or information meant to be read or used as a record. In legal proceedings, something qualifies as 'writing' if it expresses meaning through marks that can be read and interpreted.
real_world_examples: A tenant in Mumbai writing a handwritten notice to their landlord about vacating the premises — this constitutes 'writing' for the purposes of a formal communication under the Act.
A shopkeeper in Delhi maintaining a written ledger or account book recording credit transactions with customers — such a ledger qualifies as 'writing' that may be used as evidence.
An accused person in a criminal case in Chennai who sends a typed or printed threatening letter to a witness — the letter constitutes 'writing' relevant to offences of criminal intimidation.

A contractor in Kolkata submitting a signed written bid or tender document to a government department — this written document forms the basis of any contractual or fraudulent dealing scrutinised under the Act.
An FIR complaint submitted by a victim in Bengaluru in typed form to the police station — this constitutes 'writing' recording facts relevant to investigation and prosecution.

A WhatsApp message or email sent in electronic text form in Hyderabad threatening a person — electronic text may constitute 'writing' in its digital form where the Act's provisions extend to electronic records.
what_it_covers: Handwritten letters, notes, or communications made on paper using ink or pencil.
Typed or printed documents including agreements, notices, and complaints prepared on a computer and printed.
Electronic text such as emails, text messages, or digital documents that express information through letters and figures on a screen or stored digitally.
Official written declarations, affidavits, or sworn statements submitted before a court or public authority.
Written entries in registers, account books, or ledgers recording transactions or facts.
Inscriptions or markings on any physical substance — including stone, metal, or cloth — that communicate meaning through recognisable letters or figures.
what_it_excludes: Purely oral or verbal statements made without any written record, as these are not expressed through letters, figures, or marks.
Gestures, sign language, or non-verbal communication that does not result in any visible marks or recorded text on a medium.
Audio recordings or voice messages that record only sound without any textual or written component.
Purely pictorial or graphic images that carry no letters, figures, or marks expressing a readable meaning.
Mental or cognitive intentions not yet expressed or recorded in any written or electronic form.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether something qualifies as 'writing' determines whether it can serve as formal notice, a declaration, or evidence in proceedings under Section 183 of the BNS, 2023, which deals with false statements made in writing to public servants — establishing the 'writing' element is essential to constitute the offence. The presence or absence of 'writing' affects whether an act of communication meets the statutory requirement for triggering liability, evidentiary admissibility, or procedural compliance.
