definitions.definition: Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful confinement occurs when someone illegally restricts another person's movement so completely that the person cannot move beyond a defined boundary or enclosed space in any direction. Unlike mere wrongful restraint, which blocks movement in a particular direction, wrongful confinement surrounds the person and prevents them from leaving a bounded area entirely. It is essentially trapping someone without legal justification.
real_world_examples: A factory owner in Surat locks migrant workers inside the factory premises overnight to prevent them from leaving the job, thereby confining them within the factory walls without legal authority.
A landlord in Delhi padlocks the door of a tenant's room from outside while the tenant is inside, preventing the tenant from exiting the premises as a means of pressuring them to vacate.
A group of men in a village in Rajasthan surrounds a woman and forcibly takes her into a room, stationing guards at all exits so she cannot leave, as part of an illegal detention.

A private security guard at a shopping mall in Mumbai detains a customer in a back office on mere suspicion of shoplifting, without any lawful authority or warrant, preventing the customer from leaving.
A political rival's henchmen in Uttar Pradesh hold a voter inside a vehicle during election hours, driving around to prevent the person from reaching the polling booth and casting their vote.
what_it_covers: Locking a person inside a room, building, vehicle, or walled space so they cannot exit in any direction.
Surrounding a person with armed or threatening individuals at all exits of a premises so that escape is not possible in any direction.
Detaining a person inside a police station, private office, or enclosure without lawful authority or warrant.
Preventing a person from leaving a moving or stationary vehicle against their will by controlling all doors and exits.
Confining a worker, domestic servant, or debtor within a workplace or residence to coerce payment or compliance.
what_it_excludes: Lawful apprehension or arrest by a police officer acting under legal authority, as expressly illustrated under Section 3(b) of the BNS.
Wrongful restraint that only blocks movement in a particular direction without completely enclosing or surrounding the person, which falls under Section 126 instead.
Confinement carried out under a valid court order, judicial warrant, or other lawful direction of a competent authority.
Consensual restriction of movement where the person voluntarily agrees to remain within certain limits.
Quarantine or lawful detention ordered by public health authorities under statutory powers.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether wrongful confinement is established determines liability under Sections 127 through 140 of the BNS, with graded punishments depending on the duration of confinement and any associated harm (e.g., confinement to extort a confession, to compel restoration of property, or causing danger to life). It also serves as a predicate element in more serious compound offences such as kidnapping and abduction.

definitions.definition: 'Wrongful gain' means gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled. A person is said to gain wrongfully when such person retains wrongfully, as well as when such person acquires wrongfully.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful gain means obtaining someone else's property through illegal or unauthorized means, when you had no legal right to that property in the first place. It also includes illegally holding on to property that you are not entitled to keep. Essentially, it is any enrichment of yourself at another's expense through unlawful action.
real_world_examples: A bank employee in Mumbai transfers funds from a customer's account to his own personal account without authorization — he has made wrongful gain by acquiring property he had no legal right to.
A property dealer in Delhi fraudulently registers a plot of land in his own name using forged documents, thereby wrongfully gaining ownership of property legally belonging to another person.
A shopkeeper in Chennai short-changes customers systematically by manipulating the weighing scale, gaining extra money he is not legally entitled to receive.
A government contractor in Bengaluru submits inflated bills for work never performed and receives excess payment from the state treasury, amounting to wrongful gain from public funds.
A tenant in Kolkata refuses to vacate or pay rent while continuing to use the landlord's premises after the tenancy agreement has expired, wrongfully retaining the benefit of the property.
An insurance agent in Hyderabad collects premium payments from clients but never deposits them with the insurance company, wrongfully retaining money that belonged to the insurer.
what_it_covers: Acquiring money or property through fraud, cheating, or deception when the accused had no legal entitlement to it.
Retaining possession of another person's property after one's legal right to hold it has expired or was never valid.
Obtaining a financial benefit through forgery, misrepresentation, or criminal breach of trust.
Receiving overpayments through manipulation of accounts, false billing, or fraudulent claims.
Taking physical possession of movable or immovable property by force, theft, or extortion.
what_it_excludes: Lawfully acquiring property to which one is legally entitled under a valid contract, will, or court order — even if the other party suffers a loss.
Receiving property through a bona fide mistake of fact by the accused, where there was genuine belief of legal entitlement.
Gains made through legitimate commercial transactions, market competition, or enforcement of legal rights, even if the other party considers it unfair.
Profits earned through lawful means such as salary, dividends, or contractual payments duly owed to the person.
Retaining property pursuant to a valid lien, security interest, or court-sanctioned attachment.
definitions.why_it_matters: The definition of 'wrongful gain' is a foundational element of the term 'dishonestly' under the BNS 2023, which in turn is an essential ingredient of major offences including theft (Section 303), cheating (Section 318), criminal breach of trust (Section 316), and offences under Section 324 involving dishonest or fraudulent removal of property; proof of wrongful gain (or wrongful loss) is therefore indispensable to establishing the mens rea required for conviction under these provisions.

definitions.definition: 'Wrongful loss' is the loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is legally entitled. A person is said to lose wrongfully when such person is wrongfully kept out of any property, as well as when such person is wrongfully deprived of property.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful loss means illegally taking away or withholding something from a person who has a legal right to it. It covers two situations: when someone is unlawfully deprived of their property outright, and when someone is unlawfully prevented from accessing or using property they are entitled to. The loss must be caused by an unlawful act, not a lawful one.
real_world_examples: A shopkeeper in Mumbai refuses to return a customer's gold jewellery left for repair, despite full payment, thereby wrongfully keeping the owner out of their property.
A landlord in Delhi illegally withholds a tenant's security deposit without any valid legal ground after the tenant vacates the premises.
A bank employee in Chennai fraudulently transfers funds from a customer's savings account to another account, causing wrongful loss to the account holder.
A business partner in Kolkata misappropriates inventory belonging to the firm, depriving the other partners of property to which they are legally entitled.
A government contractor in Hyderabad submits inflated bills and receives excess payment, causing wrongful loss to the government exchequer.
An employer in Bengaluru illegally deducts wages already earned by a worker, keeping the worker out of money they were legally entitled to receive.
what_it_covers: Unlawful deprivation of movable or immovable property from a person who has a legal right to it.
Situations where a person is wrongfully kept out of property they are legally entitled to possess or enjoy, even if not permanently deprived.
Fraudulent transfer or misappropriation of funds or assets belonging to another, resulting in that person being unable to access what is theirs by law.
Illegal retention of goods, securities, or money owed to another person under a lawful contract or entitlement.
Causing financial loss to a government body or institution through unlawful acts such as fraudulent billing or misuse of public funds.
what_it_excludes: Loss arising from a lawful act, such as a court-ordered attachment or execution of a legitimate legal judgment against a person's property.
Voluntary relinquishment of property by the owner, where no unlawful means are employed by the other party.
Loss resulting from a genuine contractual dispute or civil wrong not involving an unlawful or criminal act as defined in the Sanhita.
Mere financial disadvantage or opportunity cost that does not involve deprivation of property to which the person has an existing legal entitlement.
Loss suffered due to natural causes, accidents, or events not attributable to any illegal act or omission by another person.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of 'wrongful loss' is a key ingredient in establishing offences such as cheating (Section 318), criminal breach of trust (Section 324), and extortion-related provisions (Section 256), as these offences require proof that the accused intended to cause or did cause wrongful loss to another. Without wrongful loss (or wrongful gain), the mental element of 'dishonestly' cannot be satisfied, which can defeat the prosecution of major property and fraud offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

Covers: Unlawful deprivation of movable or immovable property from a person who has a legal right to it.; Situations where a person is wrongfully kept out of property they are legally entitled to possess or enjoy, even if not permanently deprived.; Fraudulent transfer or misappropriation of funds or assets belonging to another, resulting in that person being unable to access what is theirs by law.; Illegal retention of goods, securities, or money owed to another person under a lawful contract or entitlement.; Causing financial loss to a government body or institution through unlawful acts such as fraudulent billing or misuse of public funds.

Excludes: Loss arising from a lawful act, such as a court-ordered attachment or execution of a legitimate legal judgment against a person's property.; Voluntary relinquishment of property by the owner, where no unlawful means are employed by the other party.; Loss resulting from a genuine contractual dispute or civil wrong not involving an unlawful or criminal act as defined in the Sanhita.; Mere financial disadvantage or opportunity cost that does not involve deprivation of property to which the person has an existing legal entitlement.; Loss suffered due to natural causes, accidents, or events not attributable to any illegal act or omission by another person.

Why it matters: The presence of 'wrongful loss' is a key ingredient in establishing offences such as cheating (Section 318), criminal breach of trust (Section 324), and extortion-related provisions (Section 256), as these offences require proof that the accused intended to cause or did cause wrongful loss to another. Without wrongful loss (or wrongful gain), the mental element of 'dishonestly' cannot be satisfied, which can defeat the prosecution of major property and fraud offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

(Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)

definitions.definition: Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person. The obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes himself to have a lawful right to obstruct is not an offence within the meaning of this section.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful restraint means deliberately blocking or stopping someone from moving in a direction they are legally allowed to go. It does not require physical touching — simply standing in someone's path or barricading a road can count. The key element is that the obstruction is intentional and without any lawful justification. It is a lesser form of restricting freedom compared to wrongful confinement, which completely locks a person within boundaries.
real_world_examples: A landlord in Delhi stands at the gate of a housing society and physically blocks a tenant from entering the premises, preventing the tenant from accessing their own rented flat.
A group of protestors in Mumbai form a human chain across a public road and refuse to let a commuter pass through a lane where the commuter has every right to walk.
A factory supervisor in Pune stands in the doorway of a factory exit and prevents a worker from leaving the premises after the shift ends, though no locked room is involved.

A shopkeeper in Chennai places his vehicle across a narrow lane — the only access to a neighbour's house — intentionally preventing the neighbour from driving through, despite knowing the neighbour has a right to use that lane.

A goon hired by a rival business in Kolkata stations himself outside a competitor's shop and intimidates and physically blocks customers from entering, thereby restraining their free movement into the shop.
what_it_covers: Physically standing in a person's path to prevent them from walking in a direction they have a lawful right to proceed.
Blocking a public or private road, path, or passage using objects, vehicles, or persons to stop someone from moving forward.
Causing fear of harm to induce a person to stop moving, as an element within robbery under Section 309.
A group of persons surrounding an individual and preventing them from leaving an open area in any direction.
Placing armed persons at exits of a building to deter a person from attempting to pass through, even without physical walls enclosing them.
what_it_excludes: Obstruction of a private way over land or water where the person blocking it in good faith believes they have a lawful right to do so — this is explicitly not an offence under Section 126.
Wrongful confinement, which requires restricting a person within circumscribing limits preventing movement in all directions — a more severe form of restraint governed by Section 127.
Lawful detention or arrest by a police officer or public servant acting within the scope of their legal authority and lawful power.
Incidental or accidental blocking of a person's path without any voluntary or intentional act to obstruct their movement.
Situations where the person being 'restrained' has no legal right to proceed in that direction, such as trespassers being stopped from entering private property lawfully.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes wrongful restraint determines criminal liability under Section 126 (punishable with simple imprisonment up to one month or fine up to five thousand rupees or both), and it also operates as a key ingredient elevating theft into robbery under Section 309, which carries rigorous imprisonment up to ten years. It additionally determines when the right of private defence of property against robbery arises and continues under Section 43.

definitions.definition: Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person. This encompasses both physical enclosure and coercive means (such as threat of force) that restrict a person's freedom of movement within defined boundaries.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongfully confining someone means unlawfully trapping or restricting a person so that they cannot move freely beyond a certain area or boundary. This can happen through physical means like locking someone in a room, or through threats that prevent the person from leaving a place. The key point is that the person is deliberately stopped from going where they have the right to go, without any legal justification.
real_world_examples: A landlord in Mumbai locks a tenant inside their rented flat to force payment of dues, preventing the tenant from stepping outside until the rent is paid — this constitutes wrongful confinement.

A factory owner in Surat keeps migrant workers inside a locked compound with armed guards at the gates and refuses to let them leave until they complete unpaid overtime — this is wrongful confinement.

A husband in a domestic dispute in Delhi physically blocks all exits of the home and threatens his wife that she will be harmed if she attempts to leave the house — this amounts to wrongful confinement.

A group of villagers in rural Bihar surrounds a person accused of theft and forcibly keeps them in a room, preventing them from leaving until the police arrive, without any lawful authority to detain — this constitutes wrongful confinement.

A hospital in Chennai refuses to discharge a patient and physically prevents them from leaving the premises until a disputed medical bill is fully paid, restricting their movement to the hospital ward — this can amount to wrongful confinement.
what_it_covers: Physically locking a person inside a room, building, or enclosed space preventing them from exiting in any direction.
Stationing armed persons or guards at exits and threatening to use force if the confined person attempts to leave.
Using coercive threats, intimidation, or psychological pressure to prevent a person from crossing a defined boundary or leaving a location.
Keeping a kidnapped or abducted person in confinement after the act of kidnapping or abduction, as referenced in Section 142.
Confining a person within any circumscribed area — whether a room, building, compound, or any defined space — regardless of the size of that space.
what_it_excludes: Lawful detention or custody carried out by a police officer or public authority under due process of law, such as arrest following a cognizable offence.
Voluntary restriction of movement where a person willingly chooses to remain within a space without any coercion or unlawful act by another.

Wrongful restraint that merely restricts movement along a particular route or direction without enclosing the person within circumscribing limits (which is covered under wrongful restraint, not wrongful confinement).
Temporary and incidental delays caused without any intent to confine, such as a crowd accidentally blocking a person's path.
Confinement carried out under a valid court order, writ, or other legally justified process.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'wrongfully confines' under Section 127 determines the applicability and severity of punishment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — ranging from imprisonment up to one year for basic confinement to up to five years for confinement of ten days or more, with enhanced penalties for secret confinement or confinement for extortion. Under Section 142, establishing wrongful confinement of a kidnapped or abducted person triggers punishment equivalent to that of the kidnapping or abduction itself, making this definition pivotal to prosecuting persons who harbour or detain such victims.
